{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:36:04.992984+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_00399677f4c7470547891a24483b71811bb43e6fa6a8ecbfa2bef1b9f745d190","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 1 (Young integral for H\"older continuous functions) of arXiv:2604.01336, 'Euler scheme for stochastic functional differential equations driven by fractional Brownia'] Let $\alpha, \  \beta \in (0, 1]$ such that $\alpha+\beta> 1$,
		$h\in C^\alpha([0, T]; \mathbb{R}) $ and $g\in C^\beta([0, T]; \mathbb{R})$. Then, for $(s,t)\in{\mathcal S}_{2}([0,T])$, the Young integral 
		$\int_{s}^{t} h(r) \, dg(r)$
		is defined as the limit of Riemann sums. That is,
		$$\int_{s}^{t} h(r) \, dg(r)=\lim_{|\pi_{s,t}|\to0}\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}h(r_i)\delta g(r_i,r_{i+1}),$$
		where $\pi_{s,t}=\{s=t_0<t_1,\ldots<,t_m=t\}$ is a partition of $[s,t]$.
		Furthermore, there exists a constant $c_{\alpha,\beta}>0$ such that
		\begin{equation*}
			\left| \int_{s}^{t} h(r) \, dg(r)  \right|
			\le

\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{(\PP \circ \PP) \circ \PP} && {\PP \circ (\PP \circ \PP)} \\
	{\PP \circ \PP} && {\PP \circ \PP} \\
	& \PP
	\arrow["{{{a_{\PP,\PP,\PP}}}}", from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["{{\mu \circ \id_{\PP}}}"', from=1-1, to=2-1]

	\arrow["\mu", from=2-3, to=3-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{\mathcal{J} \circ \PP} && {\PP \circ \PP} && {\PP \circ \mathcal{J}} && {\PP \circ \PP} \\
	& \PP &&&& \PP
	\arrow["{{\eta \circ \id_{\PP}}}", from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["{{l_{\PP}}}"', from=1-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow["\mu", from=1-3, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{{\id_{\PP} \circ \eta}}", from=1-5, to=1-7]

Consider two fixed locations $\lambda_1,\lambda_2\in[-(2-\kappa)\sqrt{n},(2-\kappa)\sqrt{n}]$ such that $|\lambda_1-\lambda_2|\geq \Delta n^{\sigma-1/2}$.

Then there exist two constants $c>0,C>0$ depending on $\zeta$ and on $\kappa,\Delta,\sigma$ such that for any $\delta_1,\delta_2\geq 0$, we have the joint estimate
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb{P}\left(\sigma_{min}(A_n-\lambda_i I_n)\leq\delta_i n^{-1/2},\quad\text{ for each }i=1,2\right)\leq C\delta_1\delta_2+2e^{-cn^{\sigma/2}}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

    \item We say that $u$ has \emph{finite speed of propagation} (FSOP), if for any $x_0 \in \mathbb{T}^d\setminus \mathrm{supp}(u_0)$  and $r\in (0,R_0(x_0))$, we have 
    \[
    \PP\left( \tau_r(x_0) >0  \right) = 1.
    \]
    \item  For $x_0 \in \mathbb{T}^d\setminus \mathrm{supp}(u_0)$, we say  that $u$ exhibits a \emph{waiting time phenomenon}  (WTP) associated with the ball $B_{R_0}(x_0)$, if $\mathbb{P}(\tau_{R_0} >0) = 1$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Independent coordinates, arbitrary measurable state spaces; measurable real f and E Z^2 finite","Each resampling copy independent of original coordinates","Coordinate-infimum application requires a real X_{-i}-measurable infimum; additive equality means equality almost surely"],"created_at":"2026-10-13T09:56:14+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_00a8a829ba7b0cabcfb6107b8a3fcda1a7239d151268d11bb0e4036b513850d6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1,...,X_n be independent random variables on arbitrary measurable coordinate spaces, let f be measurable and real valued, and let Z=f(X_1,...,X_n) belong to L^2. For each i let X_i_prime be an independent copy of X_i, independent of all original coordinates, and let Z^{(i)} replace X_i by X_i_prime in f. Write X_{-i} for the other coordinates and m_i=E[Z|X_{-i}]. Then Var(Z)<=v:=sum_i E[(Z-m_i)^2]=(1/2)sum_i E[(Z-Z^{(i)})^2]=sum_i E[((Z-Z^{(i)})_+)^2]. For arbitrary real X_{-i}-measurable Z_i, Var(Z)<=sum_i E[(Z-Z_i)^2], interpreted in the extended nonnegative sense; if the right side is finite, each Z_i is square integrable. In particular v is the minimum over such square-integrable Z_i, attained at Z_i=m_i. A coordinate infimum inf_x f(X_1,...,X_{i-1},x,X_{i+1},...,X_n) may be used as Z_i only when it defines a real X_{-i}-measurable random variable; those properties are additional conditions, not automatic consequences of measurability of f on arbitrary spaces. Equality Var(Z)=v holds exactly when Z=c+sum_i g_i(X_i) almost surely for some square-integrable one-coordinate functions g_i and constant c. Equality in the arbitrary-Z_i bound holds exactly when this almost-sure additive condition holds and Z_i=m_i almost surely for every i. The Efron-Stein bound is Boucheron-Lugosi-Massart, Concentration Inequalities (2013), Theorem3.1, printedpages54-55; the iff equality characterization here is independently derived using the finite orthogonal Hoeffding decomposition, rather than attributed to the theorem text.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["W, X, Y, Z are normed spaces","for the closedness statement (b), Y is a Banach space","A and B are bounded linear operators"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.571693+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, compact operators","id":"claim_00c34ebc01ffe7cd76ec19aee5ec59eab2fdded5e599d839cb4200170e49dd3d","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let W, X, Y, Z be normed spaces. (a) K(X,Y) is a linear subspace of B(X,Y). (b) If Y is a Banach space, K(X,Y) is closed in B(X,Y) for the operator norm; in particular every operator-norm limit of bounded finite-rank operators X -> Y is compact. (c) If T is in K(X,Y), A in B(W,X) and B in B(Y,Z), then BTA is in K(W,Z). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:25:35.781092+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_00e0947885a67f78ae9453942e53d374f56a51e10788ae2770d0fcdf5687e5ad","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def.lesspeaked of arXiv:2603.11043, 'An asymptotically optimal bound for the concentration function of a sum of independent int'] Let $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ be finite measures on integers.

Let $\epsilon \ge 0$.
We write
\[
\mu_1 \preccurlyeq_\epsilon \mu_2
\]
    and say \emph{the concentration function
    of $\mu_1$ is $\epsilon$-dominated by the concentration function of $\mu_2$}
if for each positive integer $j$
\[
    \mathcal{Q}_j(\mu_1) = \mu_1^+(I_j) \le (1+\epsilon) \mathcal{Q}_j(\mu_2) = (1+\epsilon)\mu_2^+(I_j).
\]
When the measures are probability measures, we extend the notation $\preccurlyeq_\epsilon$
to random variables distributed according to them.
For exact domination (i.e., the case $\epsilon = 0$) we use notation $\preccurlyeq$ 

to mean
$\preccurlyeq_{0}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:43:55.657388+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_01168ae2a4ec1ed0721be5bc9ce9164a2baf8b552207e5b8b791f7a61872881c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:q-adic-linear-pvar of arXiv:2604.05941, 'Banach spaces of continuous paths with finite $p$-th variation'] Fix $p>1$, an integer $q \ge 2$, and $a\in\mathbb R^{q-1}\setminus\{0\}$.     \[

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:56:21.583397+00:00","domain":"mathematical logic","id":"claim_0143593c9533c892a728d6d489a657fa87d876ed1b66d476c0807d570b7c0586","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For first-order logic, Godel's completeness theorem states that a formula is provable from a set of axioms by a standard formal proof system if and only if it is semantically entailed by those axioms, that is, true in every model satisfying them. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:56:21.583151+00:00","domain":"linear algebra","id":"claim_014678b4f3cb617ba9549a52110422cfba00bf13a4e692be47c4d2dce870cf79","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be an n by n complex matrix with entries a_ij. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:15:36.156023+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_01589e834dbb7cc49db6008cf2e824f2649ad1978708a8334edcbfd427735bfe","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 6 of arXiv:2609.01574, 'A linear bound for Fujita's freeness conjecture'] A \emph{pair} $(X,\Delta)$ consists of a normal variety $X$ and an effective $\mathbb Q$-divisor $\Delta$ such that $K_X+\Delta$ is $\mathbb Q$-Cartier. If the boundary is not assumed effective, we call $(X,\Delta)$ a $\mathbb Q$-sub-pair, or simply a \emph{sub-pair}. A germ $x\in(X,\Delta)$ consists of a pair and a closed point $x\in X$. For a divisor $D$ on a normal variety and a prime divisor $F$, we write $\mult_FD$ for the coefficient of $F$ in $D$. If $F$ is a prime divisor on a birational model $\pi\colon X'\to X$, write
\[
 K_{X'}+\Delta_{X'}=\pi^*(K_X+\Delta),
 \qquad
 A_{X,\Delta}(F):=1-\mult_F\Delta_{X'}.
\]
The sub-pair is \emph{sub-lc} if $A_{X,\Delta}(F)\geq0$ for every prime divisor $F$ over $X$. A pair is \emph{log canonical} (respectively, \emph{klt}) if $A_{X,\Delta}(F)\geq0$ (respectively, $>0$) for every prime divisor $F$ over $X$. A prime divisor $F$ with $A_{X,\Delta}(F)=0$ is an \emph{lc place}, and its center $c_X(F)$ on $X$ is an \emph{lc center}. 

For an effective $\mathbb Q$-divisor $\Delta$ on a smooth variety $X$, we denote by $\mathcal J(X,\Delta)$ its multiplier ideal \cite[\S9.2]{Laz04}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T01:41:54.341505+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_01857436ec8579ea71e837361a18437e35878cc5f88248a8f87c0395135c7e3e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Stochastically continuous Feller semigroup of arXiv:2412.01381, 'Ergodicity and mixing for locally monotone stochastic evolution equations'] We say that $(P_t)_{t\ge 0}$ is a stochastically continuous Feller semigroup if for every $x\in H$ and every $r>0$ it follows that
\[\lim_{t\to 0} P_t^\ast\delta_x (B(x,r))=1
\quad \textrm{ and }\quad
P_t(C_b(H))\subset C_b(H),
\]
where $B(x,r):=\{y\in H:\|y\|_H<r\}$,
$\delta_x$ denotes the Dirac delta measure at $x$
and 
 $C_b(H):=\{F:H\to \mathbb{R}:\,F\textrm{ is continuous and bounded}\}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["product measure","all the events increasing (the proof uses FKG on the decreasing complements)"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542929+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_01ce16ef6218f32c1f9919a8d7c88e3c9ce4ae7ffd8d9803708ef6d53c50695b","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let P be a product measure on {0,1}^E and let A_1, ..., A_k be INCREASING events with the same probability. Then max_i P(A_i) = P(A_1) >= 1 - ( 1 - P( union_i A_i ) )^{1/k}. More generally, without assuming equal probabilities, max_i P(A_i) >= 1 - (1 - P(union_i A_i))^{1/k}. The name comes from the case k = 2, where the bound reads P(A_1) >= 1 - sqrt(1 - P(A_1 or A_2)): if the union is very likely then at least one of two increasing events is likely, quantitatively. This is the standard device for turning a statement like 'some crossing of a box occurs' into 'a crossing in a specific direction occurs with probability bounded below', and it is the engine of Zhang's argument that theta(1/2) = 0 for bond percolation on Z^2. The events must be INCREASING, since the proof is Harris-FKG applied to their complements; for arbitrary events the inequality is false. [standard; e.g. Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., proof of Theorem 11.11, and Bollobas-Riordan, Percolation]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:31:49.911380+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_02226d0305699fc8df867aac2b245862e2b7c846577df6c0bc5516ad46dfb522","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:main of arXiv:2608.27828, 'Scaling limit of the 3D abelian Yang--Mills Langevin dynamics'] Let $d=3$ and $\bar\beta=1$. Let $\xi=(\xi_1,\xi_2,\xi_3)$ have independent space-time white-noise components on $\R\times\mathbf{T}^3$, defined on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$, and let $\xi^\eps$ be the lattice approximation (equation eq:Disc_white_noise of the paper).

Let $I$ and $\{h_\lambda\}_{\lambda\in I}$ satisfy Assumption~(assmp:YMAction of the paper).
For every sufficiently small $\eps$, let $\lambda_\eps\in I$ and write $h_\eps = h_{\lambda_\eps}$. Let $\theta^\eps$ solve the DeTurck-gauge-fixed lattice Langevin equation (equation eq:NParaDisc of the paper), with $h=h_\eps$ and (possibly random) initial condition $\theta^\eps(0)$, up to the stopping time $\tau_\eps$.

Let $\theta=(\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3)$ solve the continuum stochastic heat
equation
\[  \partial_t\theta_i
    =
    \Delta\theta_i+\xi_i
\]
 with (possibly random) initial condition 
 $ \theta_i(0)$ 
 for  $i=1,2,3$.
Fix $\kappa>0$ sufficiently small and let
\[
-\frac23+\frac53\kappa<\eta<0,
\qquad
\gamma=\bigl(\eta+\tfrac12\bigr)\wedge 0.
\]

Suppose that there is a deterministic constant $M<\infty$ such that, almost surely,
\[
\sup_{0<\varepsilon\le1}\|\theta^\varepsilon(0)\|_{\mathcal C_\varepsilon^\eta}
+\|\theta(0)\|_{\mathcal C^\eta}
\le M.
\]
If
$\|\theta^\varepsilon(0);\theta(0)\|_{\mathcal C_\varepsilon^\eta}\to0$
in probability, then for every $T>0$ and $\delta>0$,
\begin{equ}
\lim_{\eps\to0}
\mathbb P\left(
\tau_\eps>T,
\ \|\theta^\eps;\theta\|_{\CC_{\gamma,\eps}^{-1/2-\kappa,T}}
\leq \delta
\right)=1.
\end{equ} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:54:12.250027+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_024d4e58d5540875d80cc3e02217a5b2b0aca72c63809dc5e0b5493afba2ff04","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma OU flow property of arXiv:2603.14163, '\LARGE \bf Tail Bounds for Queues with Abandonment: Constant, Moderate, Large Deviations, '] Let $p>1$ and let $X\in \mathbb{R}^d$ a random vector with law $\mathcal{L}(X)\in\mathcal{P}_p(\mathbb{R}^d)$. Let $T:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ be a Borel measurable map such that $Y:=T(X)$ is a real random variable with $\mathbb{E}|Y|^p<\infty$. Let $Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ be independent of $X$. For $t>0$ define
\[
F_t := e^{-t}Y + \sqrt{1-e^{-2t}}\,Z,
\]
and let $f_t$ denote the density of $F_t$ (w.r.t.\ Lebesgue measure). Then the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item (OU representation) \textnormal{[fang2022wasserstein]} The family $(F_t)_{t>0}$ is the Ornstein--Uhlenbeck semigroup acting on $Y$; equivalently, $(F_t)$ is a version of the solution to the SDE
        \[
            dF_t = -F_t\,dt + \sqrt{2}\,dB_t,\qquad F_0=Y,
        \]
        where $(B_t)$ is a standard Brownian motion independent of $Y$.

    \item (Smooth positive density) \textnormal{[johnson2001entropy]} For every $t>0$ the law of $F_t$ admits a strictly positive, smooth density $f_t$.
    \item (Commutation of OU semigroup and differentiation) \textnormal{[bakry2013analysis] [bonis2020steins]} For every $t>0 , k\in\mathbb{N}$, and $g \in C^{\infty}_c(\mathbb{R})$,
        \[
            \frac{d^k}{dx^k} P_t g(x) = e^{-kt} P_t\!\Bigl(\frac{d^k}{dx^k} g\Bigr)(x),\qquad x\in\mathbb{R},
        \]
        where $P_t g(x):=\mathbb{E}[g(F_t)\mid F_0=x]$ is the OU semigroup acting on $g$. Moreover,
        \[
         P_t \frac{d^k}{dx^k}g(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1- e^{-2t}}^k} \mathbb{E}[h_k(Z) g(e^{-t}x + \sqrt{1-e^{-2t}}Z)], \qquad x\in\mathbb{R},
        \]
        where $h_k(x) = (-1)^k e^{x^2/2} \frac{d^k}{dx^k}e^{-x^2/2}$ is the $k$-th Hermite Polynomial.

    \item (Continuity equation) For every $t>0$ the density $f_t$ satisfies the continuity equation
        \[
            \partial_t f_t(x) + \frac{d}{dx}\bigl(f_t(x)\,\rho_t(x)\bigr)=0,\qquad x\in\mathbb{R},
        \]
        where $\rho_t(x):=-\partial_x\log f_t(x)-x$ is the score function of $f_t$.

    \item (Score representation) \textnormal{[bonis2020steins]} For each $t>0$ the score admits the conditional expectation representation
        \[
            \rho_t(F_t)\;\overset{d.}{=}\; \mathbb{E}\!\Bigl[e^{-t}Y-\frac{e^{-2t}}{\sqrt{1-e^{-2t}}}\,Z\;\Big|\;F_t\Bigr],
        \]
        and, consequently,
        \[
            t\mapsto \|\rho_t(F_t)\|_{L^p(\mathcal{L}(F_t))}\in L^1((0,\infty)).
        \]

    \item (Moment bound and weak continuity) The curve $t\mapsto\mathcal{L}(F_t)$ is weakly continuous on $(0,\infty)$, and
        \[
            \sup_{t>0}\|F_t\|_{L^p}<\infty,
        \]
        (equivalently $\sup_{t>0}\|x\|_{L^p(\mathcal{L}(F_t))}<\infty$).
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:33.594471+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0270c8d5466fa07589c2cf4196e187c61ca535420ed250d63406839e0c371909","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Abstract of arXiv:2609.02491, 'Generalised Random Parking for Trapeziums on a Strip'] In this article, we study a generalisation of R\\'{e}nyi’s car-parking problem in which isosceles trapeziums are sequentially deposited on a strip. We derive an explicit formula for the parking constant in terms of the lengths of the two bases, recovering the classical rectangular and triangular models as special cases. We further obtain quantitative finite-size asymptotics for both the expected number and the variance of deposited trapeziums, with convergence rates that depend explicitly on the geometry of the deposited particle. In particular, although the recursive construction involves two different substrate geometries, their variances have the same leading asymptotic density. Finally, we show that the parking constant depends non-monotonically on the ratio of the two base lengths and possesses a unique minimiser, so that the least efficient shape is a genuine trapezium rather than a triangle.","status":"unverified"}

    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
        \item If there are two simple saddle points on $\mathcal{C}_2$, then $(x,y)$ is in the \textit{frozen region}. 
        \item If there are two simple saddles points not in the real part of $\mathcal{R}$, then $(x,y)$ is in the \textit{rough region}.

    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:33:11.986739+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_029bfac2e165c41f710bfc623b194bdbf2c0160f43385e09470b8055ce423701","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:3.2 of arXiv:2608.27474, 'Nonlocality of Cover-Time Changes Under Edge Addition'] Let \(H\) be a finite connected graph with distinguished vertex \(c\),
and assume \(W=V(H)\setminus\{c\}\ne\varnothing\). Form \(G\) by
adjoining three new vertices \(s,u,v\) and the three edges \(cs,cu,cv\),
with no other edges incident to \(s,u,v\). Let

\[
G'=G+uv,
\qquad
m=|E(G)|,
\]

and start at \(s\).

Work on a product probability space. At \(c\), give every directed
departure edge \((c,z)\) an independent rate-one Poisson process. At
each ring, attach an independent mark having the law of a complete
discrete simple-random-walk excursion that starts with \(c\to z\) and
ends on its first return to \(c\). Marks belonging to distinct rings are
independent. The superposed ring order is therefore an i.i.d. uniform
sequence of departure edges, exactly matching successive departures from
\(c\) in the discrete walk.

Let:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(T\) be the artificial time at which the remote vertices \(W\) have
  all been visited by remote excursion marks;
\item
  \(A\) be the artificial completion time of the old local pair
  \(\{u,v\}\);
\item
  \(B\) be the artificial completion time of the new local triangle
  \(cuv\);
\item
  \(R_T^{\mathrm{rem}}\) be the physical length of the unused suffix of
  the terminal remote excursion, from the instant at which the last
  unvisited vertex of \(W\) is first visited until return to \(c\);
\item
  \(\mathscr G_T\) be the sigma-field generated by the remote artificial
  ring times, departure labels, and excursion paths only through that
  first completion instant; and
\item
  \(J=\mathbb E[R_T^{\mathrm{rem}}\mid\mathscr G_T]\), the conditional
  expected unused remote suffix.
\end{itemize}

Use independent local marked processes to define \(A\) and \(B\), each
independent of the common remote process defining \(T,J\). Put

\begin{equation}
a=\mathbb E e^{-T},
\qquad
b=\mathbb E e^{-3T/2}.

\end{equation}

Then \(T,A,B,J\) are integrable, \(a,b\) are finite, and

\begin{equation}
\boxed{
\delta_s(G;uv)
=2\mathbb ET
-2(2m-1)\left(a-\frac23b\right)
-2\mathbb E\!\left[J\left(e^{-T}-e^{-3T/2}\right)\right].
}

\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:16:53.610608+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_02b18d7cbe52e44a33ef343af6a5cc6c212e4e91bcea58359c4f3d82242a8dbe","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:lift of arXiv:2412.05491, 'Near-critical and finite-size scaling for \\ high-dimensional lattice trees and animals'] Let $\mathbb{T}_r^d = (\mathbb{Z}/r\mathbb{Z})^d$ be the $d$-dimensional discrete torus of period $r$,
with the spread-out edge set inherited from projecting the $\mathbb Z^d$ edge set
$\mathbb{E}=\{\{x,y\}: 0< \|y-x\|_\infty \le L\}$ to the torus.
Assume that $r \ge 2L+1$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{(Lift of a walk.)}
Let $\omega=(\omega_0,\omega_1,\dots,\omega_n)$ be a torus walk
starting from $\omega_0 = 0$ and taking steps from $\mathbb{E}$.
The \emph{lift} of $\omega$ is
the $\mathbb{Z}^d$ walk $\bar \omega$ defined by $\bar\omega(0)=0$ and
\begin{equation}

\bar \omega(k) - \bar \omega(k-1) = \omega(k) -  \omega(k-1)
	\qquad (1\leq k \leq n),
\end{equation}
using the identification of $\mathbb{T}^d_r$ with $\Lambda_r = [ - \frac r 2, \frac r 2 )^d \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$.
The restriction $r \ge 2L+1$ ensures that the lift is a bijection
from torus walks starting from the origin
to $\mathbb Z^d$ walks starting from the origin.

\item \emph{(Lift of a lattice tree.)}
Let $T$ be a torus lattice tree containing $0$,
so that for any $x\in T$,
there is a unique self-avoiding walk in the tree from
$0$ to $x$.  The \emph{lift} of $T$ is defined to be the union over $x \in T$
of the lifts of those torus walks to $\mathbb Z^d$.
This defines an injection from
torus lattice trees containing the origin
to $\mathbb Z^d$ lattice trees containing the origin.
It is not a surjection because lifted trees cannot contain
any pair of $\mathbb Z^d$ vertices that project to the same torus vertex.

\item \emph{(Lift of a lattice animal.)}
We use the lexicographic order on $[-L,L]^d \cap \mathbb Z^d \setminus \{ 0 \}$
and on $\Lambda_r$, and we use the order on $\Lambda_r$ to induce an order on
the torus vertices.
Let $A$ be a torus animal containing $0$.
We first grow a spanning tree in $A$ recursively as follows,
starting from $\{0\}$.
Given the current tree,
we choose its first
vertex which is incident to an edge in $A$ that would not create a cycle when added to the tree,
and we add the first such edge to the tree.
The process terminates
in a spanning tree $T$ for $A$ when no further edges can be added.
We lift $T$ to a $\mathbb Z^d$ tree $\hat T$.
For the remaining excess edges in $A \setminus T$,
we write them in the form $\{u,v\}$
with $u$ less than $v$ in the torus vertex order,
and we lift the edge
 to $\{ \hat u, \hat u + (v-u) \}$
where $\hat u\in \hat T$ projects to $u$.
The lifting is injective because we can recover the torus animal by projection.
See Figure~(figure:LTlift of the paper) for an example.

\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:53:11.424897+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_02f1285232c393083a60732072cf0020cc0d775181db6bcb6640da4dc39c882f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 14 of arXiv:2606.09691, '\textsc{Degenerate Diffusions on Continuum Percolation and Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman Equatio'] Let $\mathcal C(\omega):=\bigcup_{y\in\omega} B_{1/2}(y)$ 
and as before assume $\mathcal C(\omega)$ has a unique unbounded connected component $\mathcal C_\infty(\omega)$. Let
$$
U=\mathcal C_\infty(\omega),
\qquad
\rho(x,\omega):=\rho_{\mathcal C_\infty(\omega)}(x).
$$
with $\rho$ being the function constructed in Lemma \ref{lemma}. 
Let $\theta\in C^\infty([0,\infty))$ satisfy
$\theta(0)=0$, $\theta(r)=r \quad \text{for }0\le r\le \frac12$, 
$\theta(r)=1 \quad \text{for }r\ge 1$, 
$0\le \theta(r)\le 1$, 
$\theta(r)>0 \text{ for } r>0$ and 
$|\theta'(r)|+|\theta''(r)|\le C$.
Define
$$
a(x,\omega):=
\begin{cases}
\theta(\rho(x,\omega)) I_{d\times d},
& x\in \mathcal C_\infty(\omega),\\
0,
& x\notin \mathcal C_\infty(\omega).
\end{cases}
$$
Then the following properties hold:
\begin{itemize}

\item The function $\xi(x,\omega):=\theta(\rho(x,\omega))$  satisfies the following:  
for $x\in \mathcal C_\infty(\omega)$, $\xi(x,\omega)\in(0,1]$ and for any $x\in \R^d$ and $\omega\in \Omega$, $\langle a(x,\omega)v,v\rangle
=\xi(x,\omega)|v|^2$ and $\xi(x,\omega)=\xi(0,\tau_x\omega)$. 
\item $\R^d\ni x \mapsto a(x,\omega)$ is globally Lipschitz, 
\item The map 
$$
\mathcal C_\infty(\omega)\ni x \mapsto \sigma(x,\omega):=\sqrt{\theta(\rho(x,\omega))}\, I_{d\times d}
$$ 
is locally Lipschitz on every set $\{x\in \mathcal C_\infty(\omega): d(x,\partial \mathcal C_\infty(\omega))\ge \varepsilon\}$, 
\item The map $x \mapsto \operatorname{div}a(x,\omega)=\nabla\rho(x,\omega)$ 
is bounded and locally Lipschitz away from the boundary, because 
\[
|D^2\rho(x,\omega)|\le C\, d(x,\partial \mathcal C_\infty(\omega))^{-1}.
\]

\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.191093+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_02f8ef901ce9a0e22850103c9eb2a8251cfa175ba32d3aa3ab18e07a105da31b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 110 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $f:\R\to[0,\infty)$ be a smooth function which integrates to one and has compact support. Then the derivative of $f^{1/2}$ is uniformly bounded, that is,
	\[ \|(f^{1/2})'\|_\infty
	= \frac12 \bigg\|\frac{f'}{f^{1/2}}\bigg\|_\infty
	\le O(1)\,,\]
where $O(1)$ indicates a constant depending on $f$.

\begin{proof}
Since $f$ is smooth, we have $\|f''\|_\infty \le C$ where $C$ is a constant depending only on $f$. Assume without loss that $C$ is large. Now suppose $f(y)>0$ is small while $|f'|$ is large, say
$f'(y) \ge 2 C f(y)^{1/2}$. The bound on $f''$ implies $f'(x) \ge C f(y)^{1/2}$ for all $|x-y| \le f(y)^{1/2}$. It follows that
	\[
	f\Big(y-f(y)^{1/2}\Big)
	\le f(y) - Cf(y)^{1/2} \cdot f(y)^{1/2}
	< 0\,,
	\]
contradicting the assumption that $f\ge0$. The case $f'(y) \le - 2 C f(y)^{1/2}$ leads to a similar contradiction, so we conclude 
	\[\bigg\|\frac{f'}{f^{1/2}}\bigg\|_\infty
	\le 2C\,,
	\]
which proves the claim.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

 We set  $|\patchi| := n-1$ and call it the \textup{length of $\patchi$}. 
 For each $e \in E(U)$, we set $m_{e}(\patchi) := |\{ i \in [n-1] \colon e_i=e\}|$ the \textup{multiplicity} of $e$ in $\patchi$, i.e.\ the number of times the path $\patchi$

{"assumptions":["X has independent coordinates and P is a product measure","for the corollary: f convex and 1-Lipschitz for the Euclidean norm, coordinates valued in [0,1]","the corollary centres at a MEDIAN, not the mean"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628352+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0376bec83a9d7056e168a9ba341af418dbb0c42d6ec3f78d13a9c52d6fe37ac1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X = (X_1, ..., X_n) have INDEPENDENT coordinates taking values in arbitrary measurable spaces, and let P be the product law on the product space. For a subset A and a point x define the convex distance d_T(x, A) = sup { inf_{y in A} sum_{i=1}^n alpha_i 1{x_i != y_i} : alpha in R^n, alpha_i >= 0, |alpha|_2 <= 1 }. Then for every measurable A, E[ exp( d_T(X, A)^2 / 4 ) ] <= 1 / P(A), and consequently P(A) P( d_T(X, A) >= t ) <= exp( - t^2 / 4 ) for every t > 0. COROLLARY for convex Lipschitz functions: if f : [0,1]^n -> R is CONVEX and 1-Lipschitz with respect to the Euclidean norm and the coordinates of X are independent with values in [0,1], then for every t > 0, P( |f(X) - M| >= t ) <= 4 exp( - t^2 / 4 ) where M is a median of f(X). The hypotheses are exactly: independence, a product structure, and for the corollary convexity together with a bounded range. Convexity cannot be dropped - the conclusion is false for general Lipschitz functions of bounded independent variables at this strength, which is why the bounded-differences (McDiarmid) inequality with its sum-of-squared-ranges denominator is the general-purpose tool and Talagrand's is the sharp one for convex functionals. The centring is at a MEDIAN; converting to the mean costs an absolute constant. [Talagrand (1995), Publ. IHES 81; see Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Theorem 7.11 and Section 7.4]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-10T02:20:17.000000+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_038aeec00adcff1f433d16d10823ab9aa59fecfe5d9edd7e388f1e17d09b9549","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, the axiom of choice, abbreviated AC or AoC, is an axiom of set theory. Informally put, the axiom of choice says that given any collection of non-empty sets, one can identify another set containing one element chosen from each set, even if the collection is infinite. Formally, the axiom establishes existence rather than a construction; it states that for every set I and every I-indexed family (S_i)_{i in I} of nonempty sets, there exists an I-indexed set (x_i)_{i in I} of elements of the union of the S_i such that x_i in S_i for every i in I. The axiom of choice was formulated in 1904 by Ernst Zermelo in order to formalize his proof of the well-ordering theorem.","status":"verified_replacement"}

$$
   \lambda_t := b_t^{(\nu)} - 2 \inf_{0 \leq s \leq t} b_s^{(\nu)} \ ,

is a Markov process, whose natural filtration is strictly contained in that of $b$, i.e. for all $t > 0$, ${\mathcal F}_t^\lambda \varsubsetneq {\mathcal F}_t^b$.

\item[$\rm(3)$] For the version of $\partial_\mu V$ mentioned above and for any $(t,x,\mu)\in[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)$, the mapping $\mathbb{R}^d\ni v\mapsto\partial_\mu V(t,x,\mu)(v)\in\mathbb{R}^d$ is continuously differentiable and its derivative, denoted by $\mathbb{R}^d\ni v\mapsto\partial_v\partial_\mu V(t,x,\mu)(v)\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$, is locally bounded and is jointly continuous in $(t,x,\mu,v)$ at any point $(t,x,\mu,v)$ such that $v\in\textnormal{supp}(\mu)$.

Assume further that, for every compact subset $\mathcal{K}\subset\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)$,

&+\int_{0}^{t}\tilde{\mathbb{E}}\big[\partial_\mu V(r,\xi(r),\mathcal{L}_{X(r)})(\tilde{X}(r))\cdot\tilde{b}(r)\big]dr\\

{"assumptions":["A closed (so that the resolvent is bounded by the closed graph theorem) and the resolvent set nonempty.","The lower bound on the distance to the spectrum is an equality only for normal operators on Hilbert space;","for a non-normal operator the resolvent norm can be enormous far from the spectrum, which is the pseudospectrum phenomenon and the reason spectral information alone does not control transient behaviour."],"created_at":"2026-09-12T14:06:45.871209+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator theory","id":"claim_03d939c2a79f6b612a799b18298a7e6a00ccdd46f92d2f060d60503cc6b9e0b0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be a closed operator on a Banach space with resolvent set rho(A) and resolvent R(z) = (z I - A)^{-1}. Then: (i) the FIRST RESOLVENT IDENTITY R(z) - R(w) = (w - z) R(z) R(w) holds for z, w in rho(A), so resolvents at different points commute; (ii) rho(A) is OPEN and R is analytic on it, with the Neumann expansion R(z) = sum over k >= 0 of (w - z)^k R(w)^{k+1} valid whenever |z - w| is strictly less than 1 / ||R(w)||; (iii) consequently the distance from w to the spectrum is at least 1 / ||R(w)||, so the resolvent norm blows up at least like the reciprocal of the distance to the spectrum as z approaches it. For a BOUNDED A the series R(z) = sum over k >= 0 of A^k / z^{k+1} converges for |z| > the spectral radius.","status":"unverified"}

The coefficients $\ab,\asig,\aw$ obey the budget constraints \eqref{eq:is-budget-constraint}, that is,
	\[
	\bE \bigg[(\ab_t)^2 + \frac{(tp)'(t)}{p(t)}(\asig_t-1)^2\bigg]
        \le \frac{(\bE \aw_t)^2 }{ \alpha}\,,\]
for all $t\in [q_0,1]$;

\item 
$|Z^{\Ising}(1)|=1$ almost surely;

\item 
$Z(q_0)=0$ almost surely, and $\bE[Z^{\Ising}(q_0)^2]=q_0$;

\item 
$\zeta^\Ising\in\cP([-1,1])$,
the space of Borel probability measures on $[-1,1]$.\footnote{We note that since $Z^\Ising$ is a martingale with $|Z^{\Ising}(1)|=1$ almost surely, the initial distribution cannot have support outside of $[-1,1]$.}
\end{enumerate}
Given any
$q_*,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising$
(same $p$ as above),
let $X,X^\Ising$ be given by \eqref{e:sde.x} and \eqref{e:sde.x.ising} on the time interval $[q_*,1]$, with $X(q_*)\sim\zeta$ and $X^\Ising(q_*)\sim\zeta^\Ising$.
Then for any $\epsilon>0$ there exist parameters $q_*,b,\sigma,w,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising$ such that the following hold: 
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item 
$b_t= b(t,X_t)$, $\sigma_t=\sigma(t,X_t)$, and $w_t= w(t,X_t)$,
for $C$-Lipschitz functions
$b:[q_*,1]\times\R\to[-C,C]$
and $\sigma,w:[q_*,1]\times\R\to[0,C]$, for a constant $C=C(L,\epsilon)$.
 
\item 
 $|\bE[(w_t)^2] -1| \le\epsilon$
 for all $t\in[q_*,1]$. 
 
\item 
 $X$ and $X^{\Ising}$ approximately obey the budget constraints at each time $t$, that is,
	\[\bE \bigg[(b_t)^2 + \frac{(tp)'(t)}{p(t)}(\sigma_t-1)^2\bigg]
        \le \frac{(\bE w_t)^2 }{ \alpha}
        +\epsilon\]
for all $t\in[q_*,1]$.

\item  The initial distributions of $(X,X^\Ising)$ and $(Z,Z^\Ising)$ are close:
\[\begin{aligned}
\bbW_2(\zeta,\acute{\zeta}) &= 
\bbW_2(\Law(X(q_*)),\Law(Z(q_0)))
\leq \epsilon\,,\\
\bbW_2(\zeta^\Ising,\acute{\zeta}^\Ising)
&= \bbW_2(\Law(X^{\Ising}(q_*)),
        	\Law(Z^{\Ising}(q_0)))
\leq \epsilon\,.
\end{aligned}\]

\item  
The initial time $q_*$ lies in $[q_0,q_0+\epsilon]$.
\end{enumerate}
Lastly, we have
	\beq
    \begin{aligned}
	\bbW_2(\Law(X(1)),\Law(Z(1)))
	&\leq \epsilon\,,\\
	\bbW_2(\Law(X^{\Ising}(1)),
        	\Law(Z^{\Ising}(1)))
	&\leq \epsilon
    \end{aligned}
	\eeq
Thus the more general diffusions $(Z,Z^\Ising)$ are well approximated by the Markovian SDE solutions

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:27:14.893988+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0485a9c24356541ddadb4ac080c4142fd8a79ad23b7c1ec9d8a1fe495553d046","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 10 (Stochastic Kessler Syndrome) of arXiv:2608.23491, 'Stochastic Dynamics of Low Earth Orbit Near Full Capacity'] The Feller diffusion has the explicit extinction probability
\[
\pr\big(z_F(\tau) = 0\big) = \exp\!\left( -\frac{\theta\, z_{F,0}}{\kappa_5\,\big(1 - e^{-\theta \tau}\big)} \right),
\]
which at exact criticality ($\theta = 0$) reduces to $\exp\!\big(-z_{F,0}/(\kappa_5 \tau)\big)$. Hence:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \emph{Exactly critical ($\theta = 0$):} the debris population goes extinct almost surely, but the time to extinction is heavy-tailed, $\pr(z_F(\tau) > 0) \sim z_{F,0}/(\kappa_5 \tau)$, and excursions scale like $\sqrt{\tau}$.
    \item \emph{Subcritical ($\theta < 0$):} extinction almost surely, at an exponential rate.
    \item \emph{Supercritical ($\theta > 0$):} survival with positive probability $1 - e^{-\theta z_{F,0}/\kappa_5}$, on which event $\E[z_F(\tau)] = z_{F,0}e^{\theta \tau}$ grows exponentially --- a stochastic Kessler runaway.
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:34:09.907336+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_049702db7fea9954186a15de5b4a1461e0ef53abd3b24c1cc7db7000a15cbec5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 1 of arXiv:2603.26228, 'A local limit theorem for nonlattice multidimensional random walks in cones'] \cite[Lemmas 3.6]{DW2019} {\rm Harmonic function for random walks killed at the boundary of $\cC$.} 
Assume hypotheses {\bf C},  {\bf M} and {\bf N}. Then,  the function $V : \mathcal C \rightarrow \bR^+$ defined by
\[
V({\bf x}) := \lim_{n \to \infty} {\bE}(u({\bf x} +S(n)); \tau({\bf x})>n)
\]
is well-defined,  finite and harmonic for $({\bf x} +S(n))_{n \geq 0}$ killed at leaving $\mathcal C$; in other words, 
\[
V({\bf x})= \bE(V({\bf x} +S(n)); \tau({\bf x})>n),  \quad {\bf x} \in \cC,  n \geq 1.
\]
Furthermore,  the function $V$ satisfies the following properties:
 	\begin{itemize}
	 		\item[(i)] (Positivity) The function 	$V$ is positive    on the set  $\mathcal C$.
			
		\item[(ii)] (``monotony" inside the cone)   If ${\bf x} \in \cC$ then $V({\bf x})\leq V({\bf x} +{\bf a})$ for  all  ${\bf a}\in \mathcal C$ such that ${\bf a} +\cC\subset \cC$.
		
		\item [(iii)]There exists $C_V>0$ such that $0\leq V({\bf x}) \leq C_V(1+\vert {\bf x}\vert^p)$ for any ${\bf x} \in \cC$.
				
		\item[(iv)] (Asymptotic behavior)  For any ${\bf x} \in   \Sigma, $
		\[V(t{\bf x})\sim t^p m_1({\bf x})\quad {\rm  as } \quad t \to \infty, \]
		the convergence being  uniform on compact set of $ \Sigma$.
		\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:53:10.208971+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_04a00cc1d82f05f3b9492717c0af5d5f92c3417bb0a7c80a2988cebfb139d0dc","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defi Def:Product-DW of arXiv:2608.29013, 'Weighted Homology and Cohomology of Weighted Polyhedra'] \ \vskip 0.1cm
  Let $(X,\lambda)$ be a descending type weighted polyhedron and $R$ be a commutative ring with unit.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:32:20.020410+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_04a663ce158dadf8b85d15688fa5ca40274c7e63c7246ed1ce116c6afad90366","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 25 (The density of the absolutely continuous part) of arXiv:2608.03353, '\bfseries A Direct Route to Markov Chain Convergence\\[2mm] \Large via Asymptotic Equivale'] Let $\alpha : \XXA \to [0,\infty)$ be a finite measure and let
$\alpha = \alpha_{\acp{\pi}} + \alpha_{\sgp{\pi}}$ be its Lebesgue decomposition with

$\nu := \alpha$, with $\alpha_{\sgp{\pi}}$ carried by a set $S \in \XXA$ with
$\pi(S) = 0$; both summands are finite, and
$\sing(\alpha\mid\pi) = \alpha_{\sgp{\pi}}(\XX)$ by \eqref{eq:singsg}. By the
Radon--Nikodym theorem we may fix a map
\[
  g_{\alpha} : \XX \longrightarrow [0,\infty),
  \qquad
  \alpha_{\acp{\pi}}(A) = \int_{A} g_{\alpha} \dd\pi \quad (A \in \XXA),
\]
finite at every point, and call it \emph{the density of the absolutely continuous part
of $\alpha$}; by \ref{conv:representative} it is a genuine map, and every statement
below about it is invariant under changing it on a $\pi$-null set.

\eqref{eq:singdens} of Proposition \ref{prop:singforms} expresses the \emph{reversed}
singular mass through this same density:
\begin{equation}
  \sing(\pi\mid\alpha) \;=\; \pi\bigl( \{ g_{\alpha} = 0 \} \bigr) ,
  
\end{equation}
so that $\pi \ll \alpha$ if and only if $g_{\alpha} > 0$ $\aewhere$, by the last

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:52:08.666279+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_04dc9bb9f19fe88b29d641576bdef3842dd1498561b284e4d50c063f7c26580b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 7 (Fixed-threshold almost-flat/torus-bundle alternative) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let \(M\) be \(\TT^3\), a compact \(\Nil\) torus bundle with nontrivial
unipotent monodromy, or a compact \(\Sol\) torus bundle with hyperbolic
monodromy, and let \(g(t)\) be an immortal Ricci flow on \(M\).  Let \(K\) be
a Type-III constant supplied by Proposition~\ref{input:bamler-typeIII}.
Fix any \(c_0\in(0,1)\) such that
\begin{equation}
        Kc_0^2<\eps_{\mathrm{af}}.
\end{equation}
The parameter \(c_0\) is used only as the diameter threshold separating the two
geometric alternatives below; it is not an analytic smallness parameter and will not
be decreased later to meet compactness or stability tolerances.

There exist a finite time \(T_B(c_0)<\infty\) and a nonincreasing function
\[
        \eps_B^{c_0}:[T_B(c_0),\infty)\longrightarrow(0,\tfrac12],
        \qquad \eps_B^{c_0}(t)\longrightarrow0,
\]
with
\begin{equation}
        \eps_B^{c_0}(t)<c_0,
        \qquad t\geq T_B(c_0),
\end{equation}
such that every \(t\geq T_B(c_0)\) belongs to exactly one of the following
diameter-defined alternatives.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
If
\begin{equation}
        \diam(M,g(t))<c_0\sqrt t,
\end{equation}
then
\begin{equation}
 \bigl(\sup_M|\sec_{g(t)}|\bigr)\diam(M,g(t))^2
 <Kc_0^2<\eps_{\mathrm{af}}.
\end{equation}
Thus the slice is quantitatively almost flat.

\item
If
\begin{equation}
        \diam(M,g(t))\geq c_0\sqrt t,
\end{equation}
then there exist a torus fibration \(\pi_t^B:M\to S_t^1\) and an invariant metric \(g_t^B\), in the sense described in
Subsection~\ref{subsec:torus-bundle-conventions}, such that
\begin{equation}
        (1+\eps_B^{c_0}(t))^{-1}g_t^B\leq g(t)
        \leq(1+\eps_B^{c_0}(t))g_t^B.
\end{equation}
Moreover, for every integer \(m\) with
\(0\leq m<\bigl(\eps_B^{c_0}(t)\bigr)^{-1}\), the metric
\(t^{-1}g_t^B\) is \(\eps_B^{c_0}(t)\)-close to \(t^{-1}g(t)\) in
\(C^m\), relative to \(t^{-1}g(t)\), and every fiber has
\(g(t)\)-diameter at most \(\eps_B^{c_0}(t)\sqrt t\).
\end{enumerate}
Labels~(\ref{item:bamler-small-slice}) and~(\ref{item:bamler-large-slice})
refer only to the diameter inequalities.  A torus comparison
may also exist in the first alternative, but it is not used there.  In the
second alternative the fibration, quotient circle, and comparison metric may
depend on \(t\), with no asserted compatibility or uniqueness. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:51:11.463438+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_04e0112b21c82f29c54eeda6054b42e970c45c40f236c034283cc22e814e1009","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 22 ({\cite[Theorem~2.22) of arXiv:2609.02561, 'NON-NEF LOCI IN MIXED CHARACTERISTIC'] {INS}}]
Let $A$ be a normal excellent local domain of residue characteristic $p>0$.
Then $A$ is the underlying ring of a local log-regular ring
if and only if
there exist a fine, sharp, and saturated monoid $\mathcal{Q}$, a morphism of monoids $\alpha:\mathcal{Q}\rightarrow A$, and $r\in\Z_{\geq 0}$ satisfying one of the following:
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
$A$ is of characteristic $p>0$ and
there exists a commutative diagram
\[
  \xymatrix{
    \mathcal{Q} \ar[r] \ar[d]_{\alpha} & k[[\mathcal{Q}\oplus\N^{r}]] \ar[d]^{\phi} \\
    A \ar[r] & \widehat{A},
  }
\]
where $\phi$ is an isomorphism.
\item
$A$ is of mixed characteristic and
there exists a commutative diagram
\[
  \xymatrix{
    \mathcal{Q} \ar[r] \ar[d]_{\alpha} & {C}_{k}[[\mathcal{Q}\oplus\N^{r}]] \ar[d]^{\phi} \\
    A \ar[r] & \widehat{A},
  }
\]
where $\ker\phi =(\theta)$ for some $\theta\in {C}_{k}[[\mathcal{Q}\oplus\N^{r}]]$ whose constant term is $p$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:49:15.410781+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_04f49ccf0f00f4dfbdfa59b1cb8b29dd1807e54eec319a50f273a8057591b016","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary Main Corollary of arXiv:2608.27248, 'Optimal Transport and the ABP Method in Higher Codimension'] Let $n\geq2$ and $1\leq m\leq4$.  Let
$X:\Sigma\to\mathbb{R}^{n+m}$ be a smooth immersion of a compact $n$-dimensional
manifold with smooth boundary, where the boundary may be empty, and let
$\mathcal E$ be a centered ellipsoid.  Then every positive
$f\in C^\infty(\Sigma)$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \int_\Sigma h_{\mathcal E}(\nabla^\Sigma f+fH)\,\mathrm d\mu
 +\int_{\partial\Sigma}f h_{\mathcal E}(\eta)\,\mathrm d\sigma
 \geq nV_*(\mathcal E)^{\frac1n}
 \left(\int_\Sigma f^{\frac n{n-1}}\,\mathrm d\mu\right)^{\frac{n-1}{n}}.
\end{equation}
Equality holds if and only if $\Sigma$ is connected, $f$ is constant, and,
for some $n$-plane $P$ realizing $V_*(\mathcal E)$, $X$ is an embedding onto
$x_0+r\,\overline{\operatorname{proj}_P\mathcal E}$ for some
$x_0\in\mathbb{R}^{n+m}$ and $r>0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

 \int_{\mathcal{C}}\varphi(\Phi(x,y))\frac{\det Q_x(y)}{\vartheta(x)}
 \,\mathrm d\mu(x)\,\mathrm dy
 =\int_{\mathcal K}\varphi(\xi)\,\mathrm d\xi.
\end{equation}
Both sides are understood as extended nonnegative integrals.

\item Let $\rho$ be a nonnegative Borel function satisfying
$\int_{\mathcal K}\rho\,\mathrm d\xi=1$, and set
\[
 I_\rho(x)=\int_{\mathcal{C}_x}\rho(\Phi(x,y))\det Q_x(y)\,\mathrm dy,
 \qquad
 \mathrm d\lambda_{u,\rho}(x)=\frac{I_\rho(x)}{\vartheta(x)}\,\mathrm d\mu(x).
\]
By part \textup{(i)}, $I_\rho(x)<\infty$ for $\mu$-almost every $x$.
For $0<I_\rho(x)<\infty$, define
\begin{equation}
 \mathrm d\nu_{x,\rho}(y)
 =\frac{\rho(\Phi(x,y))\det Q_x(y)}{I_\rho(x)}
 \mathbf1_{\mathcal{C}_x}(y)\,\mathrm dy.
\end{equation}
On $\{I_\rho=0\}\cup\{I_\rho=\infty\}$ set
$\nu_{x,\rho}=\delta_0$.  Then $x\mapsto\nu_{x,\rho}$ is a Borel
probability kernel, $\lambda_{u,\rho}$ is a probability measure, and the plan
$\pi_{u,\rho}$ defined by
\begin{equation}
 \int \zeta\,\mathrm d\pi_{u,\rho}
 =\int_\Sigma\int_{N_x\Sigma}
 \zeta(x,v(x)+y)\,\mathrm d\nu_{x,\rho}(y)\,\mathrm d\lambda_{u,\rho}(x)
\end{equation}
for bounded Borel $\zeta$ has marginals $\lambda_{u,\rho}$ and
$\rho\,\mathrm d\xi$, and is optimal for
$c(x,\xi)=\frac12|X(x)-\xi|^2$.

\item Let
\begin{equation}
 \Psi(\xi)=\max_{z\in\Sigma}
 \{\langle X(z),\xi\rangle-u(z)\}.
\end{equation}
As a supremum of affine functions, $\Psi$ is convex and hence differentiable
almost everywhere.  Then $T=\nabla\Psi$ is the Brenier map from
$\rho\,\mathrm d\xi$ to $X_\#\lambda_{u,\rho}$ and
\begin{equation}
 T_\#(\rho\,\mathrm d\xi)=X_\#\lambda_{u,\rho}.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["G has independent N(0,1) entries, m >= n","expectations are over the Gaussian matrix; the concentration statements use the 1-Lipschitz property of singular values in the Frobenius norm","the square case m = n is NOT covered by the lower bound (it gives 0); see the smallest-singular-value theorem for square matrices"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T15:17:03.040820+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_052a3d5f610725674865636ab27b13687c810c26f61037934682b44a583a40cc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let G be an m x n matrix (m >= n) with independent standard Gaussian entries, and let s_max(G) >= s_min(G) denote its largest and smallest singular values (the extreme values of |G x| over unit vectors x in R^n). Then sqrt(m) - sqrt(n) <= E s_min(G) <= E s_max(G) <= sqrt(m) + sqrt(n). Both maps G |-> s_max(G) and G |-> s_min(G) are 1-Lipschitz in the Frobenius (Euclidean) norm, so Gaussian concentration gives, for every t >= 0, P( s_max(G) >= sqrt(m) + sqrt(n) + t ) <= exp(-t^2/2) and P( s_min(G) <= sqrt(m) - sqrt(n) - t ) <= exp(-t^2/2). In words: an m x n Gaussian matrix with m substantially larger than n is a well-conditioned near-isometry, with condition number about (sqrt(m) + sqrt(n)) / (sqrt(m) - sqrt(n)); for square matrices (m = n) the lower bound degenerates to 0 and the smallest singular value is of order n^{-1/2} (a separate theorem). The constants are sharp in the sense that both bounds match the Marchenko-Pastur edges (1 +- sqrt(n/m)) sqrt(m) to first order.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T08:42:36.709135+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_05325b965e8d415a9ca55cf42540127a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In statistics, the Neyman–Pearson lemma describes the existence and uniqueness of the likelihood ratio as a uniformly most powerful test in certain contexts. It was introduced by Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson in a paper in 1933. The Neyman–Pearson lemma is part of the Neyman–Pearson theory of statistical testing, which introduced concepts such as errors of the second kind, power function, and inductive behavior. The previous Fisherian theory of significance testing postulated only one hypothesis. By introducing a competing hypothesis, the Neyman–Pearsonian flavor of statistical testing allows investigating the two types of errors. The trivial cases where one always rejects or fails to reject the null hypothesis are of little interest but it does prove that one must not relinquish control over one type of error while calibrating the other. Neyman and Pearson accordingly proceeded to restrict their attention to the class of all $\\alpha$ level tests while subsequently minimizing type II error, traditionally denoted by $\\beta$. Their seminal 1933 paper, which includes the Neyman–Pearson lemma showed not only the existence of tests with the most power that retain a prespecified level of type I error ( $\\alpha$), but also provided a way to construct such tests. The Karlin-Rubin theorem extended the Neyman–Pearson lemma to settings involving composite hypotheses with monotone likelihood ratios.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:36:31.233054+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_056b1d82d89798fd61215d786f24f7e068d4bc4e15478fab9d7f57f5f028616d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorema 3 of arXiv:2609.00567, 'Hodge--Tate splitting and Akizuki--Nakano vanishing in positive characteristic'] Let \(k\) be a perfect field of characteristic \(p>0\).
\begin{enumerate}
\item
Let \(X\) be a smooth quasi-\(F\)-split \(k\)-variety, and let \(D\)
be a simple normal crossings divisor on \(X\).  Then \((X,D)\) is
log HT-split (\Cref{qFs-to-HT}).

\item
Let \(X\) be a smooth \(k\)-variety, and let \(D\)
be a simple normal crossings divisor on \(X\).
Let \((X,D)\) be a log HT-split pair, and let
\[
\pi\colon Y \defeq \operatorname{Bl}_Z(X) \to  X
\]
be the blow-up along a stratum \(Z\) of \(D\) and $D_Y \defeq (\pi^{-1}D)_{\red}$. 
Then \((Y,D_Y)\) is log HT-split.  In particular, \(Y\) is HT-split (\Cref{HT-ascent-stratum-blowup}).

\item
Let \(T\) be a toric variety with Cox ring \(S_T\).  
Suppose that a smooth
closed subvariety \(Z\subseteq T\) is defined by a homogeneous regular sequence.
Then \(Z\) is HT-split (\Cref{complete-intersection}).

\item Let $\pi \colon X \to Y$ be a morphism of smooth $k$-varieties.
If $\cO_Y \to R\pi_*\cO_X$ splits and $X$ is HT-split, then $Y$ is HT-split (\Cref{finite-cover}).
In particular, if $\pi$ is a linearly reductive good quotient and $X$ is HT-split, then $Y$ is HT-split.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:25:44.582447+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_057c78eb2ba5c0dfba7d38f21408ed5476701ac24a5fa45a3572cf4c37f07ba5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm intro2 of arXiv:2509.08659, 'Gap metrics for stationary point processes and quantitative convexity of the free energy'] Consider $\varphi(x)=|x|^{-s}$ for $s>1$ and the metric space $( X^{a}_{p},\mathscr W_{gap,p})$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:37:08.318896+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_058555514aa3f7ac9f57d90efea8b076cd019b72d8052b4c6baaff168f6609e2","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Singular graph of arXiv:2608.30973, 'Pseudo-Anosov flow and dynamics on guts'] Let \(F_{\tau}(z)\) be a transverse facet relatively carried by \(\tau\) and \(T\) be a ladderpole tube.
We define the \emph{singular graph} \(G_{T}(F_{\tau}(z))\) associated to \(T\) and \(F_{\tau}(z)\) as follows.
The vertices of \(G_{T}(F_{\tau}(z))\) is the set of ladderpole curves \(\mathrm{ld}_{T}\) in \(T\). Two vertices are connected by an edge if they are boundaries of an annular component of \(F_{\tau}(z)\cap T\).

{"assumptions":["X is a real or complex Banach space","A is linear on a subspace D(A)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.769837+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator semigroups","id":"claim_05b342a8dbfbe497827c01268d9e092d3b7a5c5940a131f4d29aa0e10be41ee7","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a Banach space with dual X*. The duality set of x ∈ X is J(x) = {x* ∈ X* : ⟨x, x*⟩ = ‖x‖² = ‖x*‖²}, which is nonempty by the Hahn-Banach theorem. A linear operator A: D(A) ⊂ X → X is dissipative if for every x ∈ D(A) there exists some j ∈ J(x) with Re⟨Ax, j⟩ ≤ 0. Equivalently (Lumer-Phillips lemma), ‖(λ − A)x‖ ≥ λ‖x‖ for all λ > 0 and all x ∈ D(A). In a Hilbert space (J(x) = {x}) this reads Re⟨Ax, x⟩ ≤ 0 for all x ∈ D(A). A is m-dissipative (maximal dissipative) if it is dissipative and Ran(λ − A) = X for some λ > 0 (then for every λ > 0). A is accretive (m-accretive) if −A is dissipative (m-dissipative). For a dissipative A, λ − A is injective for λ > 0 and its inverse on Ran(λ − A) has norm at most 1/λ.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:57:51.743017+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_05fc6acce41a9e99821a268e7adb0b6bba2e1cdefc17177014719dfc18a5d7fe","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 2 of arXiv:2608.30138, 'High-frequency wave propagation for the viscoelastic wave equation with singular memory'] There exists $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that, for every $0\le \varepsilon\le \varepsilon_0$,
the eikonal equation \r{eik2} 
admits a solution $\psi\in C^\infty(B(0,R_T))$, which also depends smoothly on $\varepsilon \in [0,\varepsilon_0]$ and on $\omega$. Consequently, $\psi$ admits a Taylor expansion in $\varepsilon$,
\[
\psi(x,\eps)
\sim \sum_{j\ge0}\varepsilon^j\psi_j(x)
\qquad \text{in } C^\infty(B(0,R_T)),
\]
with
\[
\psi_0(x)=x\cdot\omega,
\qquad
\psi_j(x)=\frac1{j!}\,\partial_\varepsilon^j\psi(x,\eps)\big|_{\varepsilon=0},
\]
and the coefficients satisfy
\begin{equation}
2\,\omega\cdot\nabla \psi_j
=
(-1)^j\sigma_{\mathfrak{m}}^j
-
\sum_{\ell=1}^{j-1}\nabla\psi_\ell\cdot\nabla\psi_{j-\ell},
\qquad j\ge1,
\end{equation}
together with
\[

\qquad \text{for } x\in B(0,R_T),\quad x\cdot\omega<-R.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:00:22.669309+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0618213138cca97e6ebfcdfa0464383b989fcc43731f9dcb6ccedc0b6da5458c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem T:general V of arXiv:2411.01364, 'Global Dynamics of Granular Media Equations via Stochastic Order'] Suppose Assumption (asp:potential of the paper) holds, and $V'$  has finite zeros and they are all simple. Then there exist $\theta_0>0, \ \sigma_0>0$  such that for all $\theta\geq \theta_0$ and $\overline{\sigma}\leq \sigma_0$,
    \begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)}]
\item \textnormal{(Total Orderedness)} there are exactly $(2n-1)$ invariant measures $\{\nu_k\}_{k=1}^{2n-1}$ with $\nu_1<_{\mathrm{st}}\nu_2<_{\mathrm{st}}\cdots<_{\mathrm{st}}\nu_{2n-1}$ for some integer $n\geq 1$;
\item \textnormal{(Connecting Orbits)} for all $k=1,2,\dots,n-1$, there are a decreasing connecting orbit $\{\nu^{k,\downarrow}_t\}_{t\in \mathbb R}$ from $\nu_{2k}$ to $\nu_{2k-1}$ and an increasing connecting orbit $\{\nu^{k,\uparrow}_t\}_{t\in \mathbb R}$ from $\nu_{2k}$ to $\nu_{2k+1}$;
\item \textnormal{(Locally Attracting)} there exist $r>0$ and $a_1<\cdots<a_k$ such that for all $1\leq k\leq n$, $\nu_{2k-1}\in B(\delta_{a_k},r)$  and
\[
\mathcal W_2(P_t^*B(\delta_{a_k},r),\nu_{2k-1})=\sup_{\mu\in B(\delta_{a_k},r)}\mathcal W_2(P_t^*\mu,\nu_{2k-1})\to0\text{ as }t\to\8;
\]
\item \textnormal{(Attracting Unbounded Open Neighbourhoods)}
if $\mu\leq_{\mathrm{st}}\nu$ for some $\nu\in B(\delta_{a_1},r)$, then
\[
\mathcal W_2(P_t^*\mu,\nu_1)\to0\text{ as }t\to\8.

If $\mu\geq_{\mathrm{st}}\nu$ for some $\nu\in B(\delta_{a_n},r)$, then
\[
\mathcal W_2(P_t^*\mu,\nu_{2n-1})\to0\text{ as }t\to\8.

\mathcal W_2(P_t^*\mu,\nu_{2n-1})\to0\text{ as }t\to\8\ \text{ for all $\mu\in\bigcup_{a\geq0}B(\delta_{a_n+a},r)$}.

\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Even fixed K>=2, N=Kn, n>=1, P>=1; independent Gaussian blocks and patterns","Hidden weights have norm sqrt(n), both readout signs occur K/2 times, threshold zero, ReLU hidden activation","Labels fixed or random independently of inputs; no balance or inter-label independence required for asymptotic exclusion","Every unit is inactive whenever its readout sign differs from the pattern label; arbitrary input-dependent assignments and same-sign overlaps are allowed"],"created_at":"2026-10-22T02:50:47.905518+00:00","domain":"statistical learning theory; Gaussian random constraint satisfaction","id":"claim_0624ebd58741ec6f217055c471d6888848d7dc2f311e49d732afec5f13380dfb","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Proof (unaudited), elementary route obstruction; no novelty claimed. Let K>=2 be even, N=Kn, and let a ReLU tree committee have independent standard Gaussian input blocks, spherical hidden weights of norm sqrt(n), fixed balanced readout signs and zero threshold. Labels are fixed independently of inputs. Restrict to classifiers in which every unit is inactive on every opposite-label pattern, but allow assignments to depend arbitrarily on all inputs and allow same-sign overlaps. Conditional on positive and negative label counts M_+,M_-, strict storage probability is at most q(M_-,n)^(K/2) q(M_+,n)^(K/2), where q(0,n)=1 and q(m,n)=2^(1-m) sum_{r=0}^{min(n-1,m-1)} binom(m-1,r) for m>=1. Thus positive sequential wide-limit load requires allowing wrong-sign active votes in this model; this is not an upper bound on unrestricted ReLU capacity.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.501490+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_062b22585439db726a0b6f470b0037a36b8af3520acc59696c5e337e8b8a8398","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma Strict finite-support profile of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[lemma]{lem:strict-profile}
Let \(K\) be a compact neighborhood in \(\mathbb S^{N-1}(1)\), let \(x_0\) lie in its relative interior, and suppose a continuous function \(P\) satisfies
\[
 P(x_0)=\max_KP,

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:12:46.874389+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_065ff3d17e006b24f4d31dfe2e0076ac6a6f5b33b738e19e4cc9d2d6dfcf0bd0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:kac-moment of arXiv:2608.08375, 'Algebraic formulas for first-passage times of Markov processes in the linear framework: ge'] Let $G$ be a strongly connected graph and choose $u \in \mathcal{V}(G)$. \end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Independent rate-one Poisson offspring displacement processes.","The layer-tail recursion is the one stated in the source paper."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.363857+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_066f8d6d147ffdc831735ab62b26710560d8571ba00afcc1c575fa46962eb6bf","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; tested by direct Monte Carlo simulation of the Poisson-weighted infinite tree (4000 replicates, k=2,5,10,12), agreeing with the recursion within about 1.5 standard errors] This is the campaign's branching-walk identification behind Conjecture 1 of H. Stepanyants, P. L. Krapivsky, H. Hartle and D. Krioukov, The rank and layer distributions in random recursive trees, arXiv:2608.04303. Let the Poisson-weighted infinite tree have root position zero, with children of each vertex at the points of an independent rate-one Poisson process on (0,infinity), translated by their parent's position. Let M_k be the minimum position of generation k, and set M_0=0. Define s_0(y)=1 for y>=0 and s_k(y)=1-exp(-integral_0^y s_{k-1}(z)dz) for k>=1. Put bar_ell_k=integral_0^infinity s_k(y)exp(-y)dy and ell_k=bar_ell_k-bar_ell_{k+1}. In the source, ell_k is the limiting fraction of vertices in layer k of a random recursive tree, formed by joining each new vertex j uniformly to one of vertices 1,...,j-1. Layer zero consists of the initial leaves, and subsequent layers are obtained by successive leaf removals. For every k>=0 and y>=0, s_k(y)=P(M_k<=y). Consequently bar_ell_k=E[exp(-M_k)] and ell_k=E[exp(-M_k)-exp(-M_{k+1})]. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:09:23.951975+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_06870559133682874b5682f9820fb3efbceef0bf8aff357d6d5a5e44e2766e08","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 1 of arXiv:2607.21759, 'Marchenko--Pastur law for tensor powers of exchangeable unconditional vectors'] Let $\binom{[n]}{d}$ be the collection of subsets of $[n]$ with size $d$, and let $[n]^{d}=\{1,\dotsc,n\}^d$. These index sets have sizes $\binom{n}{d}$ and $n^d$, respectively. Further, let $\nu$ be a probability measure on $\R^n$ and let $\mathbf X = (X_1,\dotsc, X_n) \sim \nu$. We define the following random tensor models.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
    \item Set $p = \binom{n}{d}$ and index the coordinates of  $\R^p$ by $\binom{[n]}{d}$. We define a random vector $\mathbf x \in \R^p$ by
    \[
         \mathbf x = \biggl(\prod_{\alpha \in i} X_\alpha\biggr)_{i \in \binom{[n]}{d}}.
    \] In this case, we say $\mathbf x$ is a \df{principal tensor generated from the base distribution $\nu$}, and denote its law by $\PrincipalT(n,d,\nu)$.
   \item Set $q = n^d$, and index the coordinates of $\R^q$ by $[n]^d$. We define another random vector $\mathbf x \in \R^q$ by \[
       \mathbf x = \biggl(\prod_{j=1}^d X_{i_j}\biggr)_{i \in [n]^d},
    \]
    where $i=(i_1,\dots,i_d)\in[n]^d.$ In this case, we say $\mathbf x$ is a (full) \df{tensor power generated from the base distribution $\nu$}, and denote its law by  $\PowerT(n,d,\nu)$.
        \end{enumerate}
    With a slight abuse of notation, we will usually write $\mathbf X$ in place of $\nu$, or omit them completely when the context is clear. When we are discussing both models simultaneously, we will just call them the tensor power models.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.177505+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_06bcc8c744c35f9e53258930c2a42e4230c2963bfb9ddbaddd3c27b6b7d32b10","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 77 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\gamma:[q_0,1]\to[q_0,1]$ be a monotone and absolutely continuous function, and define its generalized inverse
	\[
	\lambda:[q_0,\gamma(1)]\to[q_0,1]\,,\quad
	\lambda(s)
	\equiv\inf\Big\{
	t : \gamma(t)>s
	\Big\}\,.
	\]
Then the set $\{s : \gamma'(\lambda(s))=0 \}$ has zero Lebesgue measure.

\begin{proof}
It is straightforward to verify that $\lambda$ is a right-continuous function with $\gamma(\lambda(s))=s$ for all $s$. For any measurable set $A\subseteq\R$, consider the preimage $\lambda^{-1}(A)$: we have $s\in \lambda^{-1}(A)$ if and only if $\lambda(s)\in A$, which implies $s=\gamma(\lambda(s)) \in \gamma(A)$. This proves that 
	\[\lambda^{-1}(A)
	\subseteq \gamma(A)\]
(the converse need not hold). Let $A=\{t\in[q_0,1] : \gamma'(t)=0\}$: by absolute continuity of $\gamma$, we have
	\[|\gamma(A)|
	= \int_{q_0}^1 \gamma'(t)
	\ind\{t\in A\}
	\,dt = 0\,.\]
Since $\lambda^{-1}(A)\subseteq \gamma(A)$, it follows that
	\[
	|\lambda^{-1}(A)|
	=\bigg| \Big\{s : \gamma'(\lambda(s))=0
	\Big\}\bigg|=0\,,
	\]
as claimed.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:38:58.683023+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_06d33a069c6151dab2253c61a92e30547b9d5481c5bbc8307bf1a1d01726dc1a","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma of arXiv:2510.18792, 'The frog model with death revisited'] \thlabel{lem:biased-walk-bounds}
Let $(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a nearest-neighbor random walk on $\mathbb Z$ with $X_0=n> 0$ that moves left with probability $0<p<1/2$ and right with probability $1-p$ at each step. Let $\rho = p/(1-p)$. We let $\Geo(r)$ denote the geometric distribution supported on the nonnnegative integers. 
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item
For $\tau_{n-1}=\inf\{t\ge1: X_t=n-1\}$, it holds that
$$\frac{\tau_n-1}{2} \preceq \Geo\left(r\right) \quad 
\text{ with } \quad r = \exp\left(-\frac{3(1 - 2p)^2}{2(1 + 4p)} \right).$$

\item Let $T_n = \max \{t \colon X_t =n\}$ be the time of the last visit to $n$. It holds that 
    $$\frac{T_n}{2}\ \preceq \Geo(s) \quad \text{ with } \quad s=(1-2p)r.$$
\item
Suppose the walk is conditioned to never go left of $n$ i.e.\ conditioned on the event $A=\{X_t \geq n \text{ for all $t \geq 0$}\}$. 
Let $T_n'$ denote the time of its last return to $n$. Then $T_n' \preceq T_n$. 

\end{enumerate}
It follows that the length of each excursion between steps taken by the recursive frog model on $\mathbb T_d$ is stochastically dominated by the $2\Geo((1-p)(1-\rho)r) +1$ distribution. Moreover, these excursion lengths are independent between non-backtracking steps by the strong Markov property of random walk.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:25:49.848163+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_06e3e3886aae71981bf48a96b99d8f66a0769f097737e8b80f342ad532f7e826","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 19 of arXiv:2609.01996, 'Baumslag--Solitar Subgroups Obstruct Model Companions for Fields with Group Actions'] For every integer \(\nu\geq1\), put
  \[
    H_\nu:=\langle\sigma,\tau^\nu\rangle\leq\BS(m,n).
  \]
  Then
  \[
    \tau^\nu\sigma^{m^\nu}=\sigma^{n^\nu}\tau^\nu,
  \]
  and hence there is a surjective homomorphism
  \[
    \varphi_\nu:\BS(m^\nu,n^\nu)\twoheadrightarrow H_\nu.
  \]
  If \(\sigma_\nu,\tau_\nu\) denote the standard generators of the source, then
  \[
    \varphi_\nu(\sigma_\nu)=\sigma,\quad \varphi_\nu(\tau_\nu)=\tau^\nu.
  \]
  Let \(\beta_\nu\) be the intrinsic 1-cocycle and \(\ell_\nu\) the \(\tau_\nu\)-exponent-sum homomorphism of \(\BS(m^\nu,n^\nu)\).
  Identifying
  \[
    \Z\left[\frac1{m^\nu n^\nu}\right]=\Z\left[\frac1{mn}\right],
  \]
  one has
  \[
    \beta\circ\varphi_\nu=\beta_\nu,\quad \ell\circ\varphi_\nu=\nu\ell_\nu.
  \]
  Consequently,
  \[
    \ker\varphi_\nu\subseteq\ker\beta_\nu\cap\ker\ell_\nu.
  \]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:51:11.952064+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_06e59369e21e8b9751742db14876319e58b2670cbda83547a825586651b3823e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 4 (Bessel Kernel) of arXiv:2608.07365, 'A pathwise Ito formula \\for weakly differentiable functions'] The Bessel kernel $g_{\alpha}\colon \Rr^d\to \Rr,\, \alpha>0$ is defined by its Fourier transform
\[
\hat g_{\alpha}(\xi):= \frac 1 { (1+4\pi ^{2}\vert \xi \vert ^{2})^{\alpha/2}}.
\]
where the Fourier transform is defined as
\[
\hat {f}(\xi )={\mathcal {F}}(f)(\xi)=\int _{\mathbb {R} ^{d}}f(x )e^{-2\pi i\, x\cdot \xi }\,\d x.
\]
Equivalently, one has
\[
 (I-\Delta )^{-\alpha/2}f=g_{\alpha}\ast f,
\]
where $\Delta:= \sum_{i=1}^{n}{\frac {\partial ^{2}}{\partial x_{i}^{2}}}$ is the Laplace operator.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:53:39.146807+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_06f7432d524b71ac0dfa225933e83fc4430d92fc3a47111f3069874190036fdc","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 11 of arXiv:2608.26953, '2608.26953'] A differential graded algebra \(\Omega^\bullet\) is \emph{graded commutative} if \(\alpha\wedge \beta =\ (-1)^{\lvert \alpha\lvert \lvert \beta\lvert }\beta\wedge \alpha, \text{ for all homogeneous } \alpha, \beta \in \Omega^\bullet\). It is \emph{exterior} if \(\Omega^1\) satisfies the surjectivity condition, and the iterated wedge 
\[\wedge\colon (\Omega^1)^{\otimes_An}
\rightarrow \Omega^n \] is surjective for each \(n\ge1\). 
For \((\Omega^\bullet, \wedge,d)\) a DGA, a \emph{differential graded ideal} \(I^\bullet \subseteq\Omega^\bullet\) is a graded two-sided ideal such that \[
\Omega^p \wedge I^q \subseteq I^{p+q},\quad
I^p \wedge \Omega^q \subseteq I^{p+q},\quad
d(I^q)\subseteq I^{q+1}\quad\text{for all }p,q\ge 0.
\]
A \emph{differential graded left $\Omega^\bullet$-module} (DG-module) is a graded left $\Omega^\bullet$-module \((M^\bullet, \cdot, d_M )\), where \(d_M: M^\bullet \rightarrow M^{\bullet+1}\) is a degree one \(\Bbbk\)-linear map satisfying \(d_M^2=0\), as well as \(d_M(\alpha\cdot m)= d(\alpha)\cdot m + (-1)^{\lvert \alpha\lvert } \alpha\cdot d_M(m), \ \text{for all homogeneous } \alpha\in \Omega^\bullet,\ m \in M^\bullet.\)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the counterexample is a 2-dimensional real l^p computation (the ratio at (1, 1/2) is 1.7268 and the maximum over x = (1,t) is attained near t = 0.62 at about 1.7320)","complexification bound: ||T_C f||_q <= ||T u||_q + ||T v||_q for f = u + i v"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.553381+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis, interpolation of operators","id":"claim_0730394901107dee5537f5da05c6f3480958fb025978d553df02c49ce8dba25d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Two hypotheses of the Riesz-Thorin theorem are load-bearing and are routinely dropped in write-ups. (1) COMPLEX SCALARS. The proof interpolates through an analytic family f_z, so the conclusion ||T||_{p_theta -> q_theta} <= M_0^{1-theta} M_1^{theta} is a theorem about complex L^p spaces. Counterexample for real scalars: on R^2 with the l^p norms let T(x_1, x_2) = (x_1 - x_2, x_1 + x_2). Over the REALS, ||T||_{l^infinity -> l^1} = 2 (the maximum of |x_1-x_2| + |x_1+x_2| = 2 max(|x_1|,|x_2|) over the unit cube) and ||T||_{l^2 -> l^2} = sqrt(2) (T is sqrt(2) times a rotation). Interpolating the endpoints (p_0,q_0) = (infinity,1) and (p_1,q_1) = (2,2) at theta = 1/2 gives (p,q) = (4, 4/3) and the putative bound 2^{1/2} (sqrt 2)^{1/2} = 2^{3/4} = 1.6818...; but the real operator norm from l^4 to l^{4/3} is about 1.7320 (already the vector (1, 1/2) gives the ratio 1.7268 > 1.6818). No contradiction with the complex theorem: over C the norm ||T||_{l^infinity -> l^1} is 2 sqrt 2 (take (1, i)), and the complex bound becomes (2 sqrt 2)^{1/2} (sqrt 2)^{1/2} = 2, which is consistent. Remedy: for a real-linear T, complexification costs at most a factor 2, so the real conclusion holds with constant 2 M_0^{1-theta} M_1^{theta}. (2) LINEARITY. Riesz-Thorin is false as stated for merely sublinear operators, and it also requires STRONG endpoint bounds; an operator with only weak endpoint bounds, or one that is sublinear (such as a maximal operator), must be interpolated with the Marcinkiewicz theorem instead, whose constant is not M_0^{1-theta} M_1^{theta} and blows up at the endpoints.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.357926+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_074da0e685fb432dc28bacba60057e21af057b6ad4f19b226aa9d9ae921892d7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 245 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Assume that $L\ge1$ and that condition \eqref{e:deriv.p.bound} holds. Let $\vX\equiv \vX^N$ be the process defined by \eqref{e:X.decomp} and \eqref{e:Delta.X.Ising}. Then the process $X^\RomI$ satisfies the estimate
	\[ \max_{a\in[M]}
	\E\bigg[ \max_{0\le d\le\dmax}
	 \Big(X^\RomI(q_d,a)
	 -\E X^\RomI(q_d,a)\Big)
	 ^8\bigg] \le L^{O(1)}\,,\]
with the estimate holding uniformly in $N$.
\begin{proof} Similarly as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.II.III.Ising}, let us abbreviate
	\[
	\frac{\Delta X^{\RomI}(q_d,a)}{\delta_d p'(q_d)^{1/2}}
	\equiv \mathfrak{y}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
	\equiv \frac{(\bmeta^a(q_{d+1}),\by(q_{d+1}))}{N^{1/2}}\,.
	\]
Define truncated $\tilde{\bmeta}$ and $\tilde{\by}$ similarly as
in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.II.III.Ising}, and define
	\[
	\frac{\Delta \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)}{\delta_d p'(q_d)^{1/2}}
	\equiv \tilde{\mathfrak{y}}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
	\equiv \frac{(\tilde{\bmeta}^a(q_{d+1}),
		\tilde{\by}(q_{d+1}))}{N^{1/2}}\,.
	\]
By the same argument as for \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4.step2} or for \eqref{e:RomII.tilde.discrepancy.second.mmt.bound}, we have
	\beq
	\bigg|\E\bigg[
	\Big(
	\mathfrak{y}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
	- \tilde{\mathfrak{y}}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
	\Big)^8
	\bigg]\bigg|
	\le e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq
Let $\tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)$ be the process started from zero with increments
$\Delta \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)$. (As before, we regard this as a process indexed by time $q_d$, for fixed $a\in[M]$.) Applying \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4.step2.RomI} gives
	\beq
	\E\bigg[ \max_{0\le d \le \dmax}\Big(
	X^{\RomI}(q_d,a)- \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)\Big)^8\bigg]
	\le o_N(1)\,.
	\eeq
Then consider the centered increments
	\begin{align*}
	\frac{\Delta \bar{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)}{\delta_d p'(q_d)^{1/2}}
	&\equiv
	\frac{\Delta \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)}{\delta_d p'(q_d)^{1/2}}
	-\E\bigg[
	\frac{\Delta \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)}{\delta_d p'(q_d)^{1/2}}
		\,\bigg|\, \cG(q_d)
		\bigg]\\
	&= \tilde{\mathfrak{y}}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
	- \E\Big[\tilde{\mathfrak{y}}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
		\,\Big|\,\cG(q_d)\Big]\,.
	\end{align*}
Each increment above is a Lipschitz function of the gaussian noise, with Lipschitz constant $L^{O(1)}\delta_d$, and has mean zero conditional on $\cG(q_d)$.
Let $\bar{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)$ be the process started from zero with increments
$\Delta \bar{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)$. (Again, we regard this as a process indexed by time $q_d$, for fixed $a\in[M]$.)
Then $\bar{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)$ is a \emph{martingale}, whose increments are subgaussian with variance proxy $L^{O(1)} (\delta_d)^2$. Similar arguments as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.II.III.Ising} give (cf.\ \eqref{e:bar.X.II.martingale.exponential.concentration})
	\[
	\E \Big[\exp\{ \theta \bar{X}^{\RomI}(1,a)\}\Big]
	\le \exp( \theta^2 L^{O(1)} \delta)\,,\]
and combining with Doob's $L^p$ martingale inequality gives (cf.\ \eqref{e:martingale.bar.X.II.application.of.Doob})
	\beq
	\E\Big[ \max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	\bar{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)^8\Big] 
	\le L^{O(1)} \delta^4\,.
	\eeq
It remains to address the discrepancy between $X^{\RomI}$ and $\bar{X}^{\RomI}$. Since $\tilde{X}^{\RomI}$ has subgaussian increments, we have
	\[
	\E\bigg[
	\Big( \Delta \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a) - \E \Delta \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
	\Big)^8\bigg] \le  L^{O(1)}\delta^8\,,
	\]
and summing over increments gives
	\beq
	\E\bigg[ \max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	\Big(
	 \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a) - \E \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)\Big)^8\bigg]
	 \le L^{O(1)}\,.
	\eeq
It also follows from  
\eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4.step2.RomI}
or \eqref{e:martingale.X.I.to.tilde.X.I.error}
that
 \beq
 \max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
 \bigg|\E \Big[ \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
 - X^{\RomI}(q_d,a) \Big] \bigg| \le o_N(1)
 \eeq
 where we recall $\E X^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
 = \E X(q_d,a)$.  Combining \eqref{e:martingale.X.I.to.tilde.X.I.error}, \eqref{e:martingale.tilde.X.I.close.to.mean}, and \eqref{e:martingale.tilde.X.I.close.to.X.I} gives the conclusion.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:25:06.155347+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_075a5e3f04857c8f4c22a0960c24f5ab191f362d08ec1cf05178e000522956ca","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 15 (Entropic rates of convergence on compact groups) of arXiv:2608.22534, 'Entropy power inequalities in compact groups'] Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent random variables in a connected, 
compact and metrizable abelian group $G$. Let $S_n = \sum_{i=1}^nX_i$
and write $j^*$ for the index that achieves
$$h(X_{j^*})=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}h(X_i),$$
with any ties broken arbitrarily. Then
$$
D(S_n\|U_G)
\leq
\Big[
\prod_{1\leq i\leq n, i\neq j^*}r(h(X_i))\Big]
D(X_{j^*}\|U_G)
\leq
r\Bigl(\min_{1\leq i\leq n} h(X_i)\Bigr)^{n-1}
\min_{1\leq i\leq n}D(X_i\|U_G),
$$
where
$$
r(x)
=
1-\min\left\{
\frac14,
\frac{\bigl(1-\operatorname{sinc}(e^{6x-2})^2\bigr)^2}
{8+16\frac{\operatorname{sinc}(e^{6x-2})^2}{e^{6x-2}}}
\right\},
\qquad x\in(-\infty,0],
$$
and as usual $\mathrm{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin(\pi x)}{\pi x}, x \in \mathbb{R}.$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:41:29.029454+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_075b8c327ecdb925771ebd173cc97003a86c237509b4c666b5c4f89a68d655cb","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 2 of arXiv:2608.26565, 'A Horizon-Free Extrinsic Penrose Inequality'] A compact smooth two-sided properly embedded surface

 \qquad \mathcal E_+\cap\Omega(\Sigma)=\varnothing.
\]
Both $\Sigma$ and $\Omega(\Sigma)$ may be disconnected. The
collection of admissible separators is denoted by $\mathcal A_S$, and

 A_S=\inf_{\Sigma\in\mathcal A_S}|\Sigma|.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:57:59.865459+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_079b3568943c34ff7886a38189a3165973231e85bcd46d14037b710f4593649c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:rooted-matching-tree of arXiv:2607.05384, 'Well-invertible column subsets of sparse matrices are rare'] Let $G=(I,J,M)$ be a weighted bipartite graph. Fix a right vertex $j_\star\in J$, 
and set
\[
I_\star:=N_G(j_\star).
\]
We say that $G$ contains an $m$-matching rooted tree at $j_\star$ if, for each $i\in I_\star$, there is a set
\[
\mathcal K_i\subseteq N_G(i)\setminus\{j_\star\},
\qquad
|\mathcal K_i|=m,
\]
such that
\[
N_G(j)\cap I_\star=\{i\}
\qquad
\forall i\in I_\star,\ \forall j\in\mathcal K_i,
\]
the sets $\mathcal K_i$, $i\in I_\star$, are pairwise disjoint, and the outer left neighborhoods
\[
N_G(j)\setminus I_\star,
\qquad
j\in\bigcup_{i\in I_\star}\mathcal K_i,
\]
are pairwise disjoint. Indeed, these vertices form a three-layer rooted tree in the support graph, including all neighbors of the right vertices in the tree:
\begin{itemize}
  \item $j_\star$ is the root,
  \item $I_\star$ is the first left layer, 
  \item the vertices in $\bigcup_i\mathcal K_i$ are the second right layer, and 
  \item the sets $N_G(j)\setminus I_\star$ for $j \in \bigcup_{i\in I_\star}\mathcal K_i$ form the third left layer.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}
