{"assumptions":["transversal Volterra quadratic stochastic operator with a finite fixed-point set","the object asked for is a periodic ITINERARY, a symbol sequence, not a periodic orbit","m = 3 for the affirmative half; the m = 4 case is open"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T15:09:50+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_0d1240b9b017496fe1d07198e8276e9848accae193a3447d35c49891e4cf5c60","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign status: unreviewed - author-checked against the source's exact wording; verification unreviewed] For a transversal Volterra quadratic stochastic operator the ITINERARY of a trajectory is the sequence of fixed-point neighbourhoods it visits; Rozikov (2009, p. 4) asks whether some trajectory has a periodic itinerary. CLAIM, in two halves. (i) YES at m = 3, by an example already in the literature: for the cyclic Volterra operator with a = b = c = 1, matrix A = [[0,1,-1],[-1,0,1],[1,-1,0]], whose leading 2x2 minor is 1 so the operator is transversal and whose fixed-point set - the three vertices and the centre - is finite, the itinerary of every non-fixed interior point is periodic, 1 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> ..., with sojourns 12, 51, 1073, ... growing geometrically by the heteroclinic-cycle mechanism of Ganikhodzhaev and Zanin (2004). (ii) OPEN at m = 4: in the proof of Theorem 5 of Ganikhodjaev and Zanin (arXiv:1205.3841) the trajectory passes between the epsilon-neighbourhoods of the vertices along the routes 1-4-3-2-1, 1-4-2-1 or 1-4-3-1, and a simulated cyclic-type m = 4 map produced the mixed finite prefix 1,4,3,2,1,4,2,1. A finite prefix cannot show that an itinerary is not periodic (every finite word extends to a periodic one), and one trajectory cannot answer an existence question in the negative, so the m = 4 case is not settled here. THE SHARP OPEN QUESTION, which is what the source presumably meant: is every itinerary eventually periodic, or which matrices A force it? The 2012 route analysis is the starting point. A periodic ITINERARY is a symbol sequence, not a periodic ORBIT: periodic orbits are typically absent while periodic itineraries need not be.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:09.850320+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0d13ae038fd9406c6117e2c0470b7b3883dd66014b46ac803d003bab28e95a0c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 1 (Log-concavity, PF$_2$, and TP$_2$) of arXiv:2605.18751, '\mytitle'] A positive function \(a:J\to(0,\infty)\) on an interval \(J\subseteq E\) is \emph{log-concave} if \(\log a\) is concave on \(J\). In the discrete case this is equivalent to \(\Delta^2\log a(k)\le0\) for every admissible \(k\in J\) and in the continuous case it is equivalent to \((\log a)''(x)\le0\) wherever the second derivative exists.

For a sequence \(b=(b_k)_{k\in\Z}\), we say that \(b\) is a \emph{P\'olya frequency sequence of order 2} (PF$_2$) if \(b_k\ge0\) for all \(k\), the support \(\{k:b_k>0\}\) is an interval in \(\Z\), and \(b\) is log-concave on its support.  A probability distribution \(F\) on \(\N_0\) is PF$_2$ if its mass sequence, extended by zero outside its support, is PF$_2$.

A nonnegative kernel \(M:I\times J\to[0,\infty)\) on two totally ordered sets is \emph{totally positive of order 2} (TP$_2$) if
\[
M(i,j)M(i',j')\ge M(i,j')M(i',j)
\]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.744633+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0d9a176282a96c93b294a74a824ca937dc5efa7fe2e71bf4175a378aace79fca","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] The ordinary generating function of $H$ is
  \[
    \phi_H(z) = (1-p)^m \binom{m/z - 1}{m}^{-1}.
  \]
  \begin{proof}
    We use the Laplace--Borel transform with $m$ applications of integration
    by parts:
    \begin{align*}
      \frac{\phi_H(x)}{(1-p)^m} &= \int_0^\infty
        \left( e^{xt/m} - 1 \right)^m
        e^{-t} \, dt\\
      &= \underbrace{\left. \left( e^{xt/m} - 1 \right)^m \left(-e^{-t}\right)
          \right|^{t=\infty}_{t=0}}_0\\
      &\quad + \int_0^\infty m\left( e^{xt/m} - 1 \right)^{m-1} \left(\frac{x}{m} \, e^{xt/m}\right)
      e^{-t} \, dt\\
      &= \frac{m\left(x/m\right)}{1} \int_0^\infty \left(e^{xt/m}-1\right)^{m-1}
            e^{-(1-x/m)t} \, dt\\
      &= \frac{m \left(m-1\right) (x/m)^2}{1-x/m} \int_0^\infty \left( e^{xt/m}-1\right)^{m-2}
            e^{-(1-2x/m)t} \, dt\\
      &\ \,\vdots\\
      &= \frac{m!\left(x/m\right)}{\left(m/x - 1\right)^{\underline{m-1}}} 
            \int_0^\infty e^{-(1-x)t} \, dt\\
      &= \frac{m!}{\left(m/x-1\right)^{\underline{m}}} = \binom{m/x - 1}{m}^{-1},
      \quad 0 < x < 1.
    \end{align*}
    The right-hand side is a rational function of $x$, say
    $f(x) / g(x)$ where $f(z)$ and $g(z)$ are real polynomials in $z$.
    Then $f(z) \, g(z)^{-1}$ is a well-defined object in the ring 
    of formal power series $\mathbb{R}[[z]]$ and we can
    restate our result for $\phi_H(z)$;
    see Section~\ref{language}.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:10.199295+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0db07c367058b56a2de60fe0ef4a7c4f660ee4bfbde586f8bdfe004fb915704f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 7 (Varying environment: interval bounds) of arXiv:2605.04048, 'Catastrophe--dispersion models in random and varying environments across generations'] Consider the Poissonian growth with binomial survival of Example~\ref{ex:poisson-binomial}. Let $(\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a deterministic environment sequence whose components satisfy, for all sufficiently large $n$,
\[
\theta_n\in[\theta_-,\theta_+],\quad
\lambda_n\in[\lambda_-,\lambda_+],\quad
p_n\in[p_-,p_+],\quad
d_n\in[d_-,d_+],
\]
with $0<\lambda_-\le\lambda_+<\theta_-\le\theta_+<+\infty$, $0<p_-\le p_+\le1$, and integers $1\le d_-\le d_+$. Then, for every dispersion mechanism $\Delta^{(j)}$, $j=1,2,3,4$:

\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T01:54:57.568626+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0db0898f2916195f042f88ecc11d3171ae1c4b8f02152a2dfd052c928461981f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:hypLP of arXiv:2412.03366, 'Regularity of Weighted Tensorized Fractional Brownian Fields and associated function space'] \begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] For any $\bar{j} = (j_1,j_2) \in \mathbb{N}^2$ and any
$\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1,\xi_2) \in \mathbb{R}^2$ set
$$
\theta_{\bar{j}}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) := \theta_{j_1}(\xi_1) \theta_{j_2}(\xi_2) \;.
$$
The function $\theta_{\bar{j}}$ belongs to $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^2)$ for all $\bar{j} \in \mathbb{N}_0^2$ and is compactly supported
on a dyadic rectangle. Further $\sum_{\bar{j} \in \mathbb{N}^2}  \theta_{\bar{j}} = 1$ and
$(\theta_{\bar{j}})_{\bar{j} \in \mathbb{N}^2}$ is called a hyperbolic resolution of unity.
\item[(ii)] For $f \in \mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^2)$ and $\bar{j} \in \mathbb{N}^2$ set
$$
\Delta_{\bar{j}}f :=  {\mathcal{F}}^{-1} (\theta_{\bar{j}} {\mathcal{F}}f )\;.
$$
The sequence $(\Delta_{\bar{j}}f)_{\bar{j}\in \mathbb{N}^2}$ is called a hyperbolic Littlewood-Paley analysis of $f$.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:01:01.729621+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0dbee470dbae3c5ee350e9632d53649296341276414ebb284c4e619c48c5fbcd","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lemma-shape-potential-neck of arXiv:2609.00108, 'The double sphere solution in the liquid drop model'] Let \(\Sigma=\partial\Omega\), and let
		\[
		\Sigma_h
		=
		\{
		\hat x= x+h(x)\nu(x):

		\}
		\]
		be a sufficiently small normal graph enclosing $\Omega_h$. Then for $x \in \Sigma$
		\begin{equation}
			N_{\Omega_h} (\hat x)-N_\Omega (x)
			=
			m\varepsilon^3 \left(
			\int_\Sigma
			\frac{h(\sigma)}{|x-\sigma|}
			\,d\sigma
			+\nabla_x N_\Omega (x) \cdot \nu (x) \, h (x) \right) +
			\tilde  N_\varepsilon[h](x),

		where
		\(

		=

		\)

		\begin{equation}

				|\tilde  N_\varepsilon[h](x)|
				\lesssim{}&

				\sup_{|t|\le |h(\sigma)|}

				{|x-\sigma-t\nu(\sigma)|}

				\lesssim

				\bigl(

{"assumptions":["H and K are complex Banach spaces","A and B are BOUNDED linear operators on H and K respectively","sigma(A) and sigma(B) are disjoint compact subsets of C","C is a bounded operator from K to H","Gamma is a cycle in the resolvent set of B winding once around sigma(A) and not at all around sigma(B)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.091249+00:00","domain":"operator theory, Sylvester equations, Riesz functional calculus","id":"claim_0ddcfb960219b5d37190ff5731d811c9cbc7554da88e7737e484070a46e2973a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"CAUTION ON THE NAME: this is the other result commonly called 'Rosenblum's argument' - the contour-integral solution of the Sylvester equation; the scattering-theory Hilbert-Schmidt estimate is a different theorem of the same author, so a citation naming Rosenblum must be matched to its context. STATEMENT: let H and K be complex Banach spaces, A a bounded operator on H, B a bounded operator on K, and suppose their spectra are disjoint: sigma(A) intersect sigma(B) is empty. Then for every bounded operator C from K to H the equation A X - X B = C has a UNIQUE bounded solution X from K to H, and it is given by X = (1 / (2 pi i)) times the contour integral over Gamma of (A - z)^(-1) C (B - z)^(-1) dz, where Gamma is a finite union of positively oriented rectifiable Jordan curves lying in the resolvent set of B, encircling sigma(A) once and sigma(B) not at all. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) disjointness of the spectra is what gives both existence and uniqueness. With A = B and C = 0 the equation A X - X A = 0 is solved by every operator commuting with A, so uniqueness fails badly; and with A = B = 0 on a one-dimensional space the equation is unsolvable for nonzero C. (ii) It is the SPECTRA, not the norms, that matter: no smallness of C is assumed, the solution depends linearly on C, and the bound on X is controlled by the length of Gamma and by the size of the two resolvents on Gamma - a bound that blows up as the spectra approach each other, which is the quantitative content usually needed in perturbation arguments. (iii) The theorem as stated is for BOUNDED A and B; for unbounded operators the analogous statement requires separate hypotheses (sectoriality, semigroup generation), and the contour formula must be justified anew. (iv) Finite-dimensional corollary: for matrices, A X - X B = C is uniquely solvable precisely when A and B have no common eigenvalue.","status":"unverified"}

# Target 1: two-cycle exclusion and necessary overshoot for periodic GD

Version 1, proof unaudited. This excludes possible third fates; it does not
classify all factored-GD trajectories or prove convergence.

Consider the factored model of claim 010 with any eta>0. More generally the
argument applies to any real update
 v_+=v+eta F(v,kq),
 k_+=k+delta q, q_+=q+delta k,
 delta=eta v G(v,kq),
where G is strictly positive at every finite point and F(0,s) has a unique
zero p_bar. The softmax logistic model satisfies these conditions.

1. Every orbit of period dividing two with k^2-q^2!=0 is a fixed point.
   It lies on v=0,kq=p_bar. This holds at every fixed step size.
2. Every nonstationary finite periodic orbit with k^2-q^2!=0 at one (hence
   every) iterate must contain an iterate with delta^2>=2. Equivalently,
   any periodic orbit on which |eta vG|<sqrt(2) throughout is stationary.

Neither statement excludes balanced-plane cycles, long cycles with large
overshoot, unbounded nonconvergent orbits, or nonperiodic bounded invariant
sets. This is a special obstruction result, not a scored global classification.

## Proof of two-cycle exclusion

Let U=k+q and D=k-q. Their exact simultaneous updates are
 U_+=(1+delta)U, D_+=(1-delta)D.
The nonzero imbalance is C=UD, so U,D are both nonzero initially.
For a returning two-step orbit, with a=delta_0,b=delta_1,
 (1+a)(1+b)=1, (1-a)(1-b)=1.
Expansion and addition yield 2ab=0; subtraction yields 2(a+b)=0.
Over the reals this forces a=b=0. Since eta>0 and G>0, v_0=v_1=0.
The factors therefore do not move. The head update then forces
F(0,kq)=0, hence kq=p_bar. This is a fixed point, as claimed.

## Proof of the overshoot requirement

The exact imbalance update is C_+=(1-delta^2)C. If an r-step orbit returns
with C_0!=0, no intermediate C can vanish, and
 product_{t=0}^{r-1}(1-delta_t^2)=1.
If every delta_t^2<2, every absolute factor is <=1, strictly less than 1
whenever delta_t!=0. The product can have absolute value 1 only if every
delta_t=0. Then every v_t=0, the factors stay fixed, and F(0,kq)=0.
Thus any nonstationary periodic orbit requires at least one delta_t^2>=2.

## Relation to the remaining gap

The flow's invariant imbalance is unavailable in GD, but its multiplicative
replacement still excludes every nonbalanced two-cycle, including at steps
beyond the normal-stability threshold of claim 013. A loss of an attracting
normal multiplier therefore does not by itself provide a two-cycle witness.
The unresolved step is controlling general, possibly large factor updates
well enough to show eventual entry into one of claim 010's escaping regions,
or finding a third fate that persists off the balanced planes.


# Target 1: exact balanced two-cycle and its transverse multiplier

Version 1, proof unaudited. Boundary check for claim 014, not a positive-volume
counterexample to an almost-everywhere theorem.

Fix any n>=2 and any distinct positive kappa_i. Put
 b_i=2 cosh(kappa_i)^2/kappa_i,
 a_i=b_i tanh(kappa_i).
These satisfy 0<a_i<b_i. In the usual coupled factored model
h_i(s)=a_i+b_i tanh(kappa_i s), all links have
 h_i(-1)=0, h_i'(-1)=2.

For EVERY fixed eta>0, simultaneous Euclidean GD on the average logistic
loss has an exact two-cycle
 (v,k,q)=(2/eta,1,-1) <-> (2/eta,-1,1).
At both points the loss is log 2, the product is -1, and k^2-q^2=0.
The two-step Jacobian has a transverse multiplier 9 normal to k=-q.
Thus the nonzero-imbalance assumption in 014 is necessary. This cycle
does not establish a positive-measure basin or rule out almost-everywhere
endpoint convergence.

## Proof

At either displayed state every h_i(kq)=0, so g_i=1/2, F=0 and
G=mean_i g_i h_i'=1. The head therefore stays fixed and
delta=eta vG=2. The factor update sends
 (k,q)->(k+2q,q+2k).
It exchanges (1,-1) and (-1,1). The cycle is nonstationary and has exact
period two; the loss remains log(1+exp(0))=log 2. The construction uses
different nonlinear scales, rather than requiring repeated identical examples.

The full factor-sum identity is U_+=(1+delta)U, U=k+q. At U=0 its
linearization gives dU_+=(1+delta)dU=3dU; the term U d(delta) vanishes.
After two steps dU_{++}=9dU, an exact normal multiplier even when v and
the product vary in the perturbation. No stability assertion at a unit
multiplier is involved.

The same constructed family has finite stationary points at v=0,kq=-1,
whereas the displayed periodic points have v=2/eta>0. Hence a classification
of every finite initialization by stationary points and escaping selections
alone would be false at any positive constant step. The exceptional balanced
plane must be allowed, as it is in claim 012's flow statement (which is a
different dynamical system).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["rows independent and identically distributed (the pairs bootstrap resamples rows, not residuals, so heteroscedasticity is allowed)","finite fourth moments and a converging empirical second-moment matrix (Freedman 1981); the predictor is a fixed measurable map of the sample, applied identically to every resample"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T12:03:52.456149+00:00","domain":"regression / resampling","id":"claim_0e4e01deefe6a25c51c622bfa99085bafd98403f8cc1a516a140a42803b61b73","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a least-squares predictor yhat(x) = x' beta_hat fitted on n rows, the textbook variance at a new point x is sigma^2 x'(X'SX)^(-1) x (sigma^2 times the leverage), and the hat matrix H = X(X'SX)^(-1)X'S has trace equal to the number of parameters. Both statements require X'SX to be invertible. On a design that is rank-deficient - here, an ensemble whose members include exact duplicates, so the member-prediction Gram of every output is singular by the number of duplicates - the leverage is undefined: the trace of the hat matrix drops to the rank (21 instead of 24 on the s104 Y1 cell of the EMIT pool), and inverting through a tiny ridge assigns any new point that leaves the duplicates' span an arbitrarily large leverage (a load 11.8 times the whole prediction error on that cell), which is a property of the ridge, not of the predictor actually used. The pairs bootstrap sidesteps this: resample the n rows with replacement B times, refit the predictor exactly as it is fitted in production (with its own ridge or pseudo-inverse and its own constraints), and take the empirical variance of the B predictions at x. Under Freedman's (1981) conditions for the pairs (correlation-model) bootstrap - independent rows, finite fourth moments of the regressors and errors, and a design whose empirical second-moment matrix converges - the bootstrap variance of a linear predictor is consistent for its sampling variance, and it remains well defined on a singular design because every resample is fitted by the same regularised map as the original. It is the right variance estimator when the estimator's regularisation, rather than an invertible Gram, determines its behaviour; it also applies unchanged to a constrained estimator (a long-only stack) for which no closed form exists. Cost: B refits per cell; B = 8 was enough to rank rows and cells in the RMT ensemble program (the ranking, not the level, was used).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:56:21.583220+00:00","domain":"number theory","id":"claim_0e4e7deb917b3150b7dab2783409723279992df00cdf342119ce3a93e92881b5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let pi(x) denote the number of primes less than or equal to x. The prime number theorem states pi(x) is asymptotic to x / log(x) as x tends to infinity, meaning the ratio pi(x) / (x / log x) tends to 1; equivalently pi(x) is asymptotic to the logarithmic integral Li(x), a sharper approximation. Assuming the Riemann hypothesis, the error term satisfies pi(x) = Li(x) + O(sqrt(x) log x). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.454072+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0e8b7c6ee0d52d7623ece31112df7ff29419743b0b431fb70e169c0294a62f03","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:VarY_exceeds_VarX of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] Let $X \sim \Bern(p,a,b)$ for some $p \ne \frac{1}{2}$. 
Then, any independent symmetrizer $Y$ of $X$ satisfies $\Var(Y) \ge \Var(X)$, with equality if and only if $f_Y = f_{-X}$. 

\begin{proof}
By (lem:affine_invariance of the paper) we may take $X \sim \Bern(p,-1,1)$. 

Let $f \in \Sym$, 
define $R_f$ as in (thm:Bernoulli_calY_representation of the paper), 
and define 
for each $r \in R_f$ constants $c_r \coloneqq \sum_{z \in S^r}f(z)$ and PMFs $g_r(\cdot) \coloneqq \frac{1}{c_r}f(\cdot)\mathds{1}_{S^r}(\cdot) \in \Sym^r$ as in (lem:Sr_restriction_of_symmetrizers_produces_symmetrizers of the paper). 

Then $f = \sum_{r \in R_f} c_r g_r$ and, by the concavity of the variance,
\begin{align}
\Var(f) 
\ge \sum_{r \in R_f} c_r \Var(g_r) \nonumber
&= \sum_{r \in R_f} c_r (M_2(g_r) - M_1(g_r)^2) \nonumber \\
 &\ge \sum_{r \in R_f} c_r (1 - (p-q)^2) \\

&= 1 - (p-q)^2 
= \Var(f_{-X}) \nonumber
\end{align}
where we have used (lem:calYr_min_M2s of the paper) in ((eq:varsymmres2 of the paper)). 

Note that by (lem:calYr_min_M2s of the paper), equality is attained 

in ((eq:varsymmres2 of the paper)) if and only if for all $r \in R_f$, $M_2(g_r) = 1$. 

In this case $R_f = \{1\}$ and $f = g_1 = \hat{f}_0^1$. 

\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

  \[
    e_K(x) = \indic{x \in K}\ \P(\mathcal{T}_-^x \cap K = \emptyset),\quad x \in \mathbb{Z}^d.
  \]
  The \textbf{branching capacity} of $K$ is defined by
  \[
    \mathrm{BCap}(K) = \sum_{x \in K} e_K(x).
  \]
  We can normalize the equilibrium measure and define a probability measure $\widetilde{e}_K(x)$ by

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:47.651197+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0ecba4327d83e6bcf5f0e9ab526d9f8854fb6f5e939a15167f6eb56dad9c0344","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 1 of arXiv:2605.07050, 'Universality of the fluctuations of the free energy in generalized Sherrington--Kirkpatric'] Suppose that $\sqrt{N} W_{ij}$ $(1 \leq i<j \leq N)$ are i.i.d., symmetric, and strictly sub-Gaussian random variables with variance $1$. Suppose that $\sqrt{N} x_k$ $(1 \leq k \leq N)$ are i.i.d., symmetric, and strictly sub-Gaussian random variables with variance $1$, independent of $\sqrt{N} W_{ij}$. Let
\beq 
	Z_N \equiv Z_N(\beta) = \E_{\caX} \left[ \exp \left( \beta N \sum_{i<j} W_{ij} \frac{x_i x_j}{\| \bsx \|^2} \right) \right], \qquad F_N \equiv F_N(\beta) = \frac{1}{N} \log Z_N.
\eeq
(When $\| \bsx \| = 0$, we define $x_i x_j / \| \bsx \|^2 = 0$ for all $i, j$.) Then, for any $\beta \in (0, 1)$,
\[
	F_N(\beta) \to F(\beta) := \beta^2 /4
\]
and
\[
	N(F_N(\beta) - F(\beta) ) \Rightarrow \caN(m_F, V_F),
\]
as $N \to \infty$, i.e., $N(F_N(\beta) - F(\beta) )$ converges in distribution to the Gaussian with mean $m_F$ and the variance $V_F$ as $N \to \infty$. Here,
\[
	m_F = \frac{1}{4} \log (1- \beta^2) + \frac{\beta^2 (1-m_4)}{4} + \frac{\beta^4 (w_4-3)(m_4^2 -3)}{48}
\]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:04:39.773972+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0f22a9cbc5f0fcf5d3cf93befa811dcda34f6b05effd61604d8a9aa3348900b9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition eqn:SplittingMap of arXiv:2609.01464, 'Removability of non-isolated singularities for Einstein metrics and RCD spaces'] Let $n\geqslant 2$ be an integer. Let $(X,\mathrm{d},\mathcal{H}^n)$ be an $\mathrm{RCD}(-1,n)$ metric measure space, and let $1\leqslant k\leqslant n$. Let $\delta>0$, $r>0$. We say that $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_k):B_r(x)\to \mathbb R^k$ is a {\rm $\delta$-splitting map} if there is a constant $C=C(n)$ such that the following hold:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $u_i$ is harmonic on $B_r(x)$ for every $i=1,\ldots,k$.
        \item $|\nabla u_i|\leqslant C$ for every $i=1,\ldots,k$.
        \item We have, for every $i,j=1,\ldots,k$,
        \[
        \fint_{B_r(x)} |\nabla u_i\cdot \nabla u_j-\delta_{ij}|\ensuremath{\mathrm d}\mathcal{H}^n \leqslant \delta.
        \]
        \item We have, for every $i=1,\ldots,k$ 
        \[
        r^2\fint_{B_r(x)} |\operatorname{Hess} u_i|^2\ensuremath{\mathrm d}\mathcal{H}^n \leqslant \delta
        \]
    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:45:05.500139+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0f27b71947b91775276c94f322ca7c67b70c48eadb9c76f927b70dd6d2fb9e7f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 9 of arXiv:2608.05185, '\large\bf ON THE HEAT FLOW CONJECTURE FOR RANDOM MATRICES'] Fix \(s>0\), \(u\in\C\) with \(\left|u\right|=1\), and
\(c_0\in\C\) with \(\left|c_0\right|\leq s\).  Put \(c_1=su^2\).
Let \(\mathbf{A}_N=\mathbf{A}_N^*\) be deterministic and satisfy
\[
 \sup_N\left\|\mathbf{A}_N\right\|<\infty,
 \qquad
 L_{\mathbf{A}_N}\overset{\mathrm{w}}{\longrightarrow}\mu_0,
\]
and let \((b_N)\) be a deterministic scalar sequence with
\(b_N\to b\in\C\).  Let
all the matrices \(\mathbf{Z}_N(s,c_j)\), \(N\geq1\), \(j=0,1\), be
defined on a common probability space.  Assume that, for each \(N\) and
\(j\), the entries of \(\mathbf{Z}_N(s,c_j)\) are centred and jointly
real-Gaussian, and satisfy
\[
 \E[(\mathbf{Z}_N(s,c_j))_{ab}
       \overline{(\mathbf{Z}_N(s,c_j))_{kl}}]
 =\frac{s}{N}\delta_{ak}\delta_{bl},
 \qquad
 \E[(\mathbf{Z}_N(s,c_j))_{ab}
       (\mathbf{Z}_N(s,c_j))_{kl}]
 =\frac{c_j}{N}\delta_{al}\delta_{bk}.
\]
The matrices may be coupled arbitrarily with each other and across \(N\).
Define
\[
 p_N(z)=\det\!\left(z\mathbf{I}-b_N\mathbf{I}
              -u\mathbf{A}_N-\mathbf{Z}_N(s,c_0)\right),
 \qquad
 q_N=\exp\!\left(-\frac{c_1-c_0}{2N}\partial_z^2\right)p_N.
\]
Then, almost surely,
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 \nu_{q_N}
 &\overset{\mathrm{w}}{\longrightarrow}
 (x\mapsto b+ux)_*(\mu_0\boxplus\mathfrak{sc}_s),\\
 L_{\,b_N\mathbf{I}+u\mathbf{A}_N+\mathbf{Z}_N(s,c_1)}
 &\overset{\mathrm{w}}{\longrightarrow}
 (x\mapsto b+ux)_*(\mu_0\boxplus\mathfrak{sc}_s).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:58:38.106090+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0f374c70c306674d7630b16f11a3e75ccdbfc7408376b614f7778b5608c8fd95","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2606.21556, 'Mean field limit of non-exchangeable interacting diffusions on co-evolutionary networks'] Given a constant \(W \geq 0\), we define the set of graphons with uniformly bounded weights in \([-W,W]\) as 
	\[
		\mathcal{G}_W := \left\{w \in L^{\infty}([0,1]^2) : \|w\|_{L^{\infty}} \leq W\right\}.
	\]
	For any two graphons \(w,\bar{w} \in \mathcal{G}_W\), the labeled cut distance is defined as 
	\[
		d_{\square}(w,\bar{w}) := \sup_{S,T\subset [0,1]} \left\vert \iint_{S\times T} (w(\xi,\xi')-\bar{w}(\xi,\xi')) d\xi d\xi' \right\vert,
	\]
	where the supremum is taken over all measurable sets \(S,T\subset [0,1]\). The unlabeled cut distance is defined as 
	\[
		\delta_{\square}(w,\bar{w}) := \inf_{\varphi \in S_{[0,1]}} d_{\square}(w,\bar{w}^{\varphi}),
	\]
	where \(\bar{w}^{\varphi}\) represents the rearrangement of \(\bar{w}\) by \(\varphi\), that is,
	\(\bar{w}^{\varphi}(\xi,\xi') = \bar{w}(\varphi(\xi),\varphi(\xi'))\).","status":"unverified"}

Let $\vec{x}, \vec{y} \in W_k^{\circ}$, $a,b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and $f: [a,b] \rightarrow (-\infty, \infty]$ and $g: [-\infty, \infty)$ be two continuous functions. We also assume that $f(t) > g(t)$ for all $t \in [a,b]$, $f(a) > x_1$, $f(b) > y_1$, $g(a) < x_k$ and $g(b) < y_k$. 

With the above data we define the $(f,g)$-avoiding Brownian line ensemble on the interval $[a,b]$ with entrance data $\vec{x}$ and exit data $\vec{y}$ to be the $\llbracket 1 , k \rrbracket$-indexed line ensemble $\mathcal{Q}$ on $\Lambda = [a,b]$ whose law is the same as that of $\{B_i\}_{i = 1}^k$ (with law $\mathbb{P}_{\operatorname{free}}^{a,b, \vec{x}, \vec{y}}$), conditioned on the event
$$E = \{f(r) > B_1(r) > B_2(r) > \cdots > B_k(r) > g(r) \mbox{ for all $r \in [a,b]$} \}.$$
We denote the law of $\mathcal{Q}$ by $\mathbb{P}_{\operatorname{avoid}}^{a,b,\vec{x},\vec{y},f,g}$, and expectations with respect to this measure by $\mathbb{E}_{\operatorname{avoid}}^{a,b,\vec{x},\vec{y},f,g}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["each F_n nondecreasing, right-continuous, with values in [0,1]","no tightness is assumed, and without it the limit can be defective"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752559+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0fba1416669badf1de8ab735445eeb6c5d50526da69885c6f0c2f43871a867fd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (F_n) be a sequence of distribution functions on R, that is nondecreasing right-continuous functions with values in [0,1]. Then there exist a subsequence (F_{n_k}) and a nondecreasing right-continuous F : R -> [0,1] such that F_{n_k}(x) -> F(x) at every continuity point x of F. The limit F need NOT be a distribution function: mass can escape to plus or minus infinity, and with F_n the distribution function of the point mass at n one gets F identically 0. This is exactly the gap that tightness closes: the family is tight, meaning sup_n (1 - F_n(M) + F_n(-M)) -> 0 as M -> infinity, if and only if every such subsequential limit is a proper distribution function, which is Prokhorov's theorem on R. Nothing is assumed about the F_n beyond monotonicity, right-continuity and the range [0,1] - no continuity, no tightness, no common support. [standard; e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 3.2.6]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:37:08.317921+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0fc55d5b28778e0892aa88d5f66ff073b6be1c19e6923912958dee43a0a349ce","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Homology guts of arXiv:2608.30973, 'Pseudo-Anosov flow and dynamics on guts'] Let \(z\) be a primitive element in \(H_{2}(M,\partial M;\mathbb{Z})\).
A \emph{facet surface} \(F(z)\) for \(z\) is the union of a maximal collection of disjoint, non-parallel, properly norm-minimizing surfaces \(S_{1},\ldots ,S_{k}\) in \(M\) such that
\[ [S_{i}]=z \text{ in } H_{2}(M,\partial M;\mathbb{Z}),\quad \forall i=1,\ldots,k. \]

We define the \emph{homology guts} \(\mathrm{Guts}(M,z)\) of \(M\) associated to \(z\) as the sutured guts of \(M - F(z)\) where \(F(z)\) is an arbitrary facet surface for \(z\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.375658+00:00","domain":"general topology","id":"claim_0fc6ca3efccfbfb81740d50ff4b42e6d92b545e1d6116f465b8a720d7d0ba797","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A topological space X is compact if every open cover of X has a finite subcover: whenever X is the union of a family of open sets {U_i : i in I}, there are finitely many indices i_1, ..., i_n such that X is the union of U_(i_1), ..., U_(i_n). A subset K of a space is compact if it is compact in the subspace topology; equivalently, every cover of K by sets open in the ambient space admits a finite subfamily covering K. For metric spaces, compactness is equivalent to sequential compactness (every sequence has a convergent subsequence) and to being complete and totally bounded; for subsets of R^n it is equivalent to being closed and bounded (Heine-Borel theorem).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:41:28.175431+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0fe92c2c3a66065cf6b5bdef344e3592858a429adda497c795705a803f8618aa","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition $(r-2)_*$-BP of arXiv:2510.26724, 'Sharp Fuss-Catalan thresholds in graph bootstrap percolation'] Let $T$ be a $K_r$-tree
and $S\subset V(T)$ a set of {\it seeds}, 
which we consider to be initially {\it infected}. 
Then, in each step of the process, either 
\begin{itemize}
\item {\it (usual step)} some vertex $v$ with at least $r-2$ 
infected neighbors becomes infected; or else
\item {\it (special step)} if no such $v$ exists, but 
for some internal edge $e$, there are two cliques $H_i\neq H_j$ 
containing $e$ such that $H_i$ has $r-4$ infected vertices 
and $H_j$ has $1$ infected vertex,  
and all $r-3$ of these vertices are not in $e$, 
then  we infect an arbitrarily chosen vertex $u\in e$; and 
otherwise, 
\item {\it (terminal step)} if neither type of step is possible, 
then the process terminates. 
\end{itemize}
We call this process {\it $(r-2)_*$-BP} 
on $T$, 
and let $\langle S;T\rangle_*$ denote the set of 
eventually infected vertices in $T$ started with 
the seed set $S$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["1 <= p < infinity","for p = 1: mu sigma-finite (or localizable)","no hypothesis on mu for 1 < p < infinity"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752289+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_100fb934fa9d5d9538b1e3ae23bbcd65c2cf4181580ee3941350c3dff3f9394b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (Omega, F, mu) be a measure space and 1 <= p < infinity with conjugate exponent q = p/(p-1) (q = infinity when p = 1). For 1 < p < infinity the map g -> (f -> integral f g dmu) is an isometric isomorphism from L^q(mu) onto the dual space L^p(mu)^*, for ANY measure space. For p = 1 the same map from L^infinity(mu) onto L^1(mu)^* is an isometric isomorphism provided mu is sigma-finite (or, more generally, localizable); without such a hypothesis it can fail to be surjective. The dual of L^infinity is strictly larger than L^1 whenever L^infinity is infinite-dimensional: on ([0,1], Lebesgue) a Banach limit or a Hahn-Banach extension of the functional f -> lim_{x -> 0} f(x) from C[0,1] gives an element of (L^infinity)^* not represented by any L^1 function. So the duality chain (L^1)^* = L^infinity does NOT continue to (L^infinity)^* = L^1, and L^1 is not reflexive; L^p is reflexive exactly for 1 < p < infinity. [standard; e.g. Folland, Real Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 6.15]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:55:37.368878+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_101ffb92aa1710fdc766771588065123d2203bfc1e6dd9e5742efc214a6d5c9a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 8 (Generalized Gaussian product factorization) of arXiv:2606.18458, 'Stable size-biasing and the positive scale-mixture order of generalized Gaussian laws'] Let $p,q>0$, and let $X_p\sim N_p(0,1)$ and $X_q\sim N_q(0,1)$. Then
\[
X_p\scle X_q\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p\le q.
\]
Equivalently, there exists a strictly positive random variable $V$, independent of $X_q$, such that
\[
X_p\stackrel{d}{=}VX_q
\]
if and only if $p\le q$. When such $V$ exists, its law is unique.

More precisely:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $p=q$, one may take $V=1$.
\item If $p<q$, put $a=1/p$, $b=1/q$, $\alpha=b/a=p/q$, let $S_\alpha$ be positive $\alpha$-stable, put $W_0=S_\alpha^{-b}$, let $W$ be the $W_0$-size-biased version of $W_0$, chosen independent of $X_q$, and define
\[
V=2^{a-b}W.
\]
Then $V>0$ almost surely, $V\perp X_q$, and $VX_q\stackrel{d}{=}X_p$.
\item If $p>q$, no such strictly positive independent factor exists.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:37:33.910787+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_102666e82e9e76f7e09da78626d9abe77aa7299d69a63249634afccb3ce8a949","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"The spiked covariance model (Johnstone, 2001) is the family of $p \\times p$ population covariance matrices $\\Sigma = \\sigma^2 (I_p + \\sum_{k=1}^{r} \\theta_k u_k u_k^T)$ with orthonormal vectors $u_1, \\dots, u_r$, spike sizes $\\theta_1 \\ge \\dots \\ge \\theta_r > 0$, and a fixed rank $r$ that does not grow with $p$. The data are $n$ independent rows $x_i \\in \\mathbb{R}^p$ with covariance $\\Sigma$ (Gaussian in the sharpest results; finite fourth moments suffice for the eigenvalue statements), and the object studied is the sample covariance $S = \\frac{1}{n} \\sum_i x_i x_i^T$ in the proportional regime $p, n \\to \\infty$ with $p/n \\to \\gamma \\in (0, \\infty)$. All but $r$ population eigenvalues equal the noise level $\\sigma^2$ (the bulk); the model asks which spikes are visible in $S$ and how far the sample eigenvalues and eigenvectors are from the population ones. With $\\theta_k = 0$ for all $k$ the sample spectrum follows the Marchenko-Pastur law with ratio $\\gamma$ and variance $\\sigma^2$, whose support is $[\\sigma^2 (1 - \\sqrt{\\gamma})^2, \\sigma^2 (1 + \\sqrt{\\gamma})^2]$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["U and V are open subsets of R^n of the same dimension n","phi : U -> V is a bijection, continuously differentiable, with continuously differentiable inverse (equivalently injective C^1 with nonvanishing Jacobian determinant and image V)","Lebesgue measure and Lebesgue measurable functions are used on both sides","f is measurable and either nonnegative or integrable"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090563+00:00","domain":"real analysis, measure theory, integration in R^n","id":"claim_1047e7e34c38c2168c64f635d6e025f096e2d64b3ad9dc9fbd5d8a3856bb2cb5","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let U and V be open subsets of R^n and let phi : U -> V be a C^1 DIFFEOMORPHISM: phi is a bijection of U onto V, phi is continuously differentiable, and its inverse is continuously differentiable. (By the inverse function theorem it is equivalent to assume phi is injective, C^1, onto V, with det Dphi(x) nonzero for every x in U.) Let Dphi(x) denote the Jacobian matrix. Then for every Lebesgue measurable f : V -> [0, +infinity], the integral of f(y) dy over V equals the integral of f(phi(x)) |det Dphi(x)| dx over U, both sides being simultaneously finite or infinite; the same identity holds for complex-valued f, with f integrable over V if and only if (f composed with phi) times |det Dphi| is integrable over U. Taking f an indicator gives the measure statement: the Lebesgue measure of phi(E) equals the integral of |det Dphi| over E, for every measurable E contained in U. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) the ABSOLUTE VALUE of the determinant is required. The density is |det Dphi|; the sign records orientation and belongs to the theory of differential forms, not to Lebesgue integration. (ii) Injectivity cannot be dropped without paying for multiplicity: for a general C^1 map the correct statement is the area formula, the integral of f(phi(x)) |det Dphi(x)| dx over U equals the integral over V of f(y) N(y) dy, where N(y) is the number of preimages of y in U; N identically 1 is exactly injectivity. (iii) Smoothness cannot be relaxed to 'differentiable almost everywhere'. One needs the Luzin (N) property, that null sets map to null sets, which C^1 and Lipschitz maps have: in dimension one the Cantor function is continuous and nondecreasing with derivative 0 almost everywhere, yet it maps a null set onto a set of measure 1, and the naive substitution formula is false for it. (iv) The hypothesis is a diffeomorphism between OPEN sets; for maps defined on closed or lower-dimensional sets the statement must be routed through the area or coarea formula.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:41:28.165285+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_10481ef2ca34f8c3e5d918c755a8fb020f38f279aafadc53589ce33814706e5b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Order of TWGs of arXiv:2510.26724, 'Sharp Fuss-Catalan thresholds in graph bootstrap percolation'] The {\it order} $\vartheta(T)$ of a TWG

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.199654+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1071a2338358110494cec48ce2da366826450939e1b46a3f99b8559e9fb42441","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 133 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $t\notin \oJ$ (recall Lemma~\ref{l:bad.J}) and parameters as in \eqref{eq:order-of-limits}:

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:06:06.299765+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1078611bccc031a28b58a0008adc81dceb3a33555eeca0c8a88acf99100cfb16","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:Buse_basic_properties of arXiv:2605.26048, 'Classification of the eternal solutions and multiple coalescing shocks in the KPZ fixed po'] [Busa-Sepp-Sore-22a] 
On the space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb P)$, there exists a process
\[
\Bigl(W^{\xi}(x,s;y,t): \xi \in \mathfrak{X}, (x,s;y,t) \in \mathbb{R}^4\Bigr)
\]
such that for each fixed $t \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\xi \in \mathfrak{X}$, $\xi \in \Xi^c$, and $x \mapsto W^\xi(0,t;x,t)$ is a Brownian motion with diffusion coefficient $\sqrt 2$ and drift $2\mathcal P(\xi)$. Furthermore, the process satisfies the following properties on a single event of probability one:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), font=\normalfont]
\item{\rm(Continuity)}  The $\mathbb{R}^4 \times \mathfrak{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ function  $(x,s;y,t;\xi) \mapsto W^{\xi}(x,s;y,t)$ is  continuous. Furthermore, if $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^4$ is a compact set, then for all $\xi \in \mathfrak{X}$ and sequences $\xi_n \to \xi$, there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ so that for all $n \ge N$, we have 
\[
W^{\xi_n}(x,s;y,t) = W^{\xi}(x,s;y,t),\quad \text{for all }(x,s;y,t) \in K.
\]
 \item {\rm(Additivity)}  For all $\xi \in \mathfrak{X}$ and $p,q,r \in \mathbb{R}^2$, 
    $W^{\xi}(p;q) + W^{\xi}(q;r) = W^{\xi}(p;r)$.   In particular, \\ $W^{\xi}(p;q) = -W^{\xi}(q;p)$ and $W^{\xi}(p;p) = 0$.
    \item {\rm(Monotonicity along a horizontal line)}
     Whenever $\xi_1< \xi_2$ in $\mathfrak{X}$, $x < y$, and $t \in \mathbb{R}$,
    \[
  W^{\xi_1}(x,t;y,t) \le W^{\xi_2}(x,t;y,t).
    \]
    \item \rm{(Divergence to $\pm \infty$)} 
    For all $\xi_1 < \xi_2$ and $t \in \mathbb{R}$,
    \[
\lim_{x \to \pm \infty} W^{\xi_2} (0,0;x,t) -W^{\xi_1}(0,0;x,t) = \pm \infty.
\]
    \item {\rm(Eternal solution)} For 
    all $\xi \in \mathfrak{X}$, $x,y \in \mathbb{R}$, and $s < t$,
    \begin{equation}
    W^{\xi}(x,s;y,t) = \sup_{z \in \mathbb{R}}\{W^{\xi}(x,s;z,s) +
 \mathcal{L}(z,s;y,t)\}.
    \end{equation}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:11:09.319730+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_10ae89aad78e0fc69097f30e9fe9c191ff493e03ff3e432047db1bff53018b87","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:subdivided-graph of arXiv:2411.06195, 'Restrictions of some reinforced processes to subgraphs'] For $r\in{\mathbb N}_0$, the \emph{$2^r$-subdivision}
$G_r=(\Lambda_r,E_r)$ of $G$ is obtained by replacing every edge by a series
of $2^r$ edges as follows.
\begin{itemize}
\item $\Lambda_r$ is obtained from $\Lambda$ by adding $2^r-1$ new vertices $v_{e,2^{-r}j}$,
  $j=1,\ldots,2^r-1$ for
  any edge $e\in E$. We say that these new vertices are located on the edge $e$. 
  In particular, $\Lambda\subseteq \Lambda_r$. 
\item Every edge $e\in E$ is replaced by a series of $2^r$ edges $e_{1,r},\ldots,e_{2^r,r}$ as follows.
  For bookkeeping purposes only, we endow $e$ with a direction, and 
  call $v_{e,0}$ and $v_{e,1}$ the two vertices it consists of. Then, $e$ is
  replaced by the new edges $e_{j,r}=\{v_{e,2^{-r}(j-1)},v_{e,2^{-r}j}\}$, $1\le j\le 2^r$,
  which we view as being located on the edge $e$. Thus, 
  $E_r=\{e_{j,r}:e\in E, 1\le j\le 2^r\}$.
\end{itemize}
Note that $\Lambda_0=\Lambda$ and $\Lambda_r\subseteq\Lambda_{r+1}$. 
For technical convenience, we introduce also the set of
direct self-loops $\Delta_r:=\{\{i,i\}:i\in\Lambda_r\}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:52:45.032175+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_10cd640abdf3b79fdcaf6e5d0de0f082fe7edacd7ce4e77992384ac463dfce3f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 14 (Maximal Solution) of arXiv:2606.07290, 'Boundary behaviour of the Volterra square-root process'] The mapping $u \longmapsto V_u(t)$ is nondecreasing for each $t > 0$. Define the maximal solution
    \[
        V_{\infty}(t) := \sup_{ u \geq 0} V_u(t).
    \]
    Then the following assertions hold:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(a)] If $K$ is regularly varying of the form \eqref{eq: regularly varying} where $\alpha \in (1/2,1)$ and $\ell$ is slowly varying at zero, then for each $\eta \in (0,1)$ there exists $t_0 > 0$ such that
        \[
            V_{\infty}(t) \leq (1+\eta)\frac{2C_{\alpha}}{\sigma^2}\frac{t^{-\alpha}}{\ell(t)}, \qquad t \in (0,t_0),
        \]
        where the constant is given by
        \[
        C_{\alpha} = \frac{4^{\alpha}\sqrt{\pi}}{|\Gamma\left(\frac{1}{2} - \alpha\right)|} = \frac{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}{|\Gamma(1-2\alpha)|}.
        \]
        Moreover, the function $V_{\infty}$ satisfies the fractional Riccati differential equation
        \begin{equation} 
            (D_LV_{\infty})(t) = \beta V_{\infty}(t) - \frac{\sigma^2}{2}V_{\infty}(t)^2, \qquad t > 0.
        \end{equation}
        \item[(b)] For the pure fractional kernel $K(t) = \frac{t^{\alpha-1}}{\Gamma(\alpha)}$, we obtain 
        \[
            V_{\infty}(t) \leq \frac{2C_{\alpha}}{\sigma^2} t^{-\alpha} + \mathbbm{1}_{\beta > 0} \frac{2\beta}{\sigma^2}, \qquad t > 0.
        \]
        with equality when $\beta = 0$.
    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:18:54.371986+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_10cefe5b37cf18d47df9a0a64154be5a5a4b64ac1cecfb2540514c8833698c22","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The orthonormal polynomials for $L^2[-1,1]$, subject to
$$\int_{-1}^1P_k(x)P_l(x)\,dx=\delta_{kl}$$
and called Legendre polynomials, satisfy the following differential equation,
$$(1-x^2)P_k''(x)-2xP_k'(x)+k(k+1)P_k(x)=0$$
which is the Legendre equation from physics. Moreover, we have the formula
$$(k+1)P_{k+1}(x)=(2k+1)xP_k(x)-kP_{k-1}(x)$$
called Bonnet recurrence formula, as well as the formula
$$P_k(x)=\frac{1}{2^kk!}\cdot\frac{d^k}{dx^k}\left(1-x^2\right)^k$$
called Rodrigues formula for the Legendre polynomials.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:54:18.239674+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_10f0dbad1eaf8af2c306fe342b19bc0c5c230c06db91a298f11f1c48bd16b0f6","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:upper-box-to-requests of arXiv:2608.29561, 'Ball codes: A coding characterization of Hausdorff and packing dimensions'] Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and bounded, and let \(q>0\) satisfy

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:10:05.675939+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_11000472bd74a779265b6835e9c550245fffe4f84bed98dcd2568da600171155","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 6 (Wendel's formula: Probabilistic version) of arXiv:2608.16752, 'Absorption Probabilities for Random Convex Hulls: Distribution-Freeness via the Wall-Cross'] Let $\xi_1, \dots, \xi_n$ be random vectors in $\R^d$ whose joint distribution is invariant under sign flips, that is,
$$

$$
Suppose additionally that the configuration $X := (\xi_1 \,|\, \dots \,|\, \xi_n)$ is regular almost surely, i.e.\ $\pr(X \in \mathcal D) = 0$. Then

    = \frac{1}{2^{\,n-1}} \sum_{j=0}^{d-1} \binom{n-1}{j}.
\end{align*}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:07:48.565696+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_110df421c266063940869b8aa4b9c64dca3cadb684c0d1281fad2c2c7713ce6b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 23 (The Weighted Functional Santal\'o inequality) of arXiv:2609.01460, 'On cost-induced Santal\'o-type inequalities \\ in Polish measure spaces'] Let $q \in (0, n)$, let $a\in L^\frac{n}{q}(\s)$ be non-negative and define $$C_{n,q}(a) = \frac{n-q}{n\|a\|_{L^1(\s,\sigma_{n-1})}} \left(\frac{n}{n-q}\|a\|_{L^\frac{n}{q}(\s,\sigma_{n-1})}\right)^{\frac{n}{2n-q}}.$$ Then, for every function $f \in \mathcal{F}_n$ and any non-negative measurable function $g$ on $\R^n$ that satisfy the pointwise bound

{"assumptions":["(X_n) a submartingale for a filtration (F_n)","sup_n E[X_n^+] < infinity (for a martingale: sup_n E|X_n| < infinity)","no uniform integrability is assumed, and without it convergence is only almost sure"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627158+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_111070f1050f003220fb4766d3ba4d411602ec9050d0c6e450a5eeb448ccb643","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X_n) be a submartingale with sup_n E[X_n^+] < infinity. Then X_n converges almost surely to a limit X_infinity with E|X_infinity| < infinity. For a MARTINGALE the hypothesis is equivalent to sup_n E|X_n| < infinity, since E[X_n] is constant and E|X_n| = 2E[X_n^+] - E[X_n]. Convergence is ONLY almost sure: it need not hold in L^1, and E[X_infinity] need not equal E[X_0]. Standard failure: let (X_n) be the product of independent nonnegative mean-one factors, for instance X_n = prod_{k <= n} (1 + eps_k) with eps_k = +1 or -1 with probability 1/2 each - equivalently X_n = 2^n on the event that all signs were +1 and 0 otherwise. Then X_n is a nonnegative martingale with E X_n = 1 for every n, so it is L^1-bounded and converges a.s., but the limit is 0 almost surely and E X_infinity = 0 != 1 = E X_0. Nonnegative supermartingales always converge a.s. because X_n^+ = X_n has bounded expectation; upgrading to L^1 convergence is exactly what uniform integrability supplies. [standard; e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 4.2.11]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:28:08.660922+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_111e04d7407e518dbc2b8eb97fe19053a3cddf9ce81b560743bede5f72906e9d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 4 (See, e.g., {\cite[Fact~3.5) of arXiv:2607.29495, 'Fast Mixing for Low-Temperature Potts Models via Poisson Trees'] {CLV21a}}]
Let $\nu$ be a Gibbs distribution over $[q]^{V}$ and $P$ denote the Glauber dynamics for $\nu$. Let $\nu_{\mathrm{min}}=\min_{\sigma: \nu(\sigma)>0} \nu(\sigma)$. Then the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item $T_{\mathrm{mix}}(\epsilon)\leq \frac{1}{\gamma}\log \frac{1}{\epsilon\nu_{\mathrm{min}}}$ where $\gamma$ is the spectral gap of $P$.
    \item $T_{\mathrm{mix}}(\epsilon)\leq \frac{1}{\alpha}\big(\log\log \frac{1}{\nu_{\mathrm{min}}}+\log \frac{1}{2\epsilon^2}\big)$ where $\alpha$ is the log-Sobolev constant of $P$
    \item $T_{\mathrm{mix}}(\epsilon)\leq \frac{1}{\hat\alpha}\big(\log\log \frac{1}{\nu_{\mathrm{min}}}+\log \frac{1}{2\epsilon^2}\big)$ where $\hat\alpha$ is the modified log-Sobolev constant of $P$.    
\end{enumerate}
It holds that $\alpha\leq \hat\alpha\leq 2\gamma$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-06T03:36:16.690087+00:00","domain":"harvested statement (arXiv 2512.18592, 2025): mathematics","id":"claim_115c89f8a67d4fce88f37c87ae749bc1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2.4 (Erdős–Rényi, SBMs and logistic RDPGs) in the first version of arXiv:2512.18592, 'Wavelet Latent Position Exponential Random Graphs'] Fix $c\\in\\mathbb{R}$ and a real symmetric Hilbert–Schmidt matrix $S=(s_{rs})_{r,s\\geq 0}$, and let $G_{n}\\sim\\mathrm{WL\\mbox{-}ERG}(c,S)$ be generated as in Definitions 2.1 – 2.3. 1. {"assumptions":["characteristic 0 (over Q or a field containing Q); the criterion needs the field to contain, or to be extended by, roots of unity","'general' means indeterminate coefficients; a particular polynomial of degree >= 5 may well be solvable (x^5 - 2 is)"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.626563+00:00","domain":"algebra","id":"claim_115d87a98ec962f9b30fe189acf038bc99ce62e12c2461843b01819a67bf4895","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For n >= 5 the general polynomial equation of degree n, x^n + a_1 x^{n-1} + ... + a_n = 0 with independent indeterminate coefficients over Q (the field Q(a_1, ..., a_n)), is not solvable by radicals: there is no formula for its roots built from the coefficients by field operations and extraction of k-th roots. Moreover specific polynomials over Q are not solvable by radicals, for instance x^5 - x - 1 and x^5 - 4x + 2, whose Galois groups over Q are S_5. For n <= 4 the general equation IS solvable by radicals (the quadratic formula; Cardano's formula for cubics, 1545; Ferrari's method for quartics). GALOIS'S CRITERION, which subsumes the theorem: a polynomial over a field of characteristic 0 is solvable by radicals if and only if its Galois group is a solvable group.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A a square complex matrix; eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity in the refinement","the discs are closed; a point of the union may fail to be an eigenvalue (the theorem localises, it does not characterise)"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479038+00:00","domain":"linear algebra","id":"claim_118eb1edbdd586661b78b6b8a406c50d9aa31e793c06b918802f39726a6468d2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A = (a_ij) be a complex n x n matrix and for each i let R_i = sum_{j != i} |a_ij| be the i-th deleted absolute row sum and D_i = { z in C : |z - a_ii| <= R_i } the i-th Gershgorin disc. Then every eigenvalue of A lies in the union of the discs D_1, ..., D_n. Applying the theorem to the transpose, every eigenvalue also lies in the union of the column discs (radii the deleted column sums), so the spectrum lies in the intersection of the two unions. Refinement: if a union of k of the discs is disjoint from the union of the other n - k, then exactly k eigenvalues (counted with algebraic multiplicity) lie in the union of those k discs. Consequences: a strictly diagonally dominant matrix (|a_ii| > R_i for all i) is invertible, since 0 lies in no disc; a Hermitian strictly diagonally dominant matrix with positive diagonal is positive definite; and the discs can be shrunk by a diagonal similarity D^{-1} A D, which changes the radii to sum_{j != i} |a_ij| d_j / d_i.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:10.016420+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_119d43813e76545de1e2529f61bcbe76b0041d46bdb7534e3ff8a898685af7f1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 52 (No universal bound below the first moment) of arXiv:2602.14618, 'Finitary coding and Gaussian concentration\\ for random fields'] Let $d\ge1$. Suppose there exist a constant $K>0$ and a nondecreasing functional
\[
\Psi:\ \{ \text{nonnegative integer-valued random variables} \}
\longrightarrow [0,\infty]
\]
with the following \emph{universality property}:

\smallskip

For every finitary coding $\varphi$, every i.i.d.\ input $X$, every local observable $f$, and every $n\in\mathbb N$,
\[
\E\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}\big(c_i^{(n)}(X)\big)^2
\ \le\ K\,\|\delta f\|_2^2\, \Psi\big(r_\varphi^{(n)}(X)\big),
\]
where $r_\varphi^{(n)}$ denotes the truncated coding radius at the origin.

\smallskip

Then, for all $n$,
\[
\E\,\big|B_\infty\!\big(0,r^{(n)}_\varphi(X)\big)\big|
\ \le\ K\, \Psi\big(r_\varphi^{(n)}(X)\big),
\]
and letting $n\to\infty$,
\[
\E\,\big|B_\infty\!\big(0,r_\varphi(X)\big)\big|
\ \le\ K\, \liminf_{n\to\infty}\Psi\big(r_\varphi^{(n)}(X)\big).
\]

In particular, any universal squared-influence bound depending only on the random variable $r_\varphi$
must control at least the first moment of the coding volume; no strictly smaller such functional
can replace it.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.476988+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_11b452e7f62e7bd5150fe2be71047976f821de421d83b02882c1e20f2cc19c08","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition eq:entropy limit property of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] For all odd $k \ge 3$ and any distinct $i,j \in [k]$, there exist asymmetric two-point distributions supported on $\{i,j\} \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_k$ which are not symmetrization resistant. 

\begin{proof}
By affine invariance ((lem:affine_invariance of the paper)), we may take $p > 1/2$, and we may take our two-point PMF $f = f_k$ on $\mathbb{Z}_k$ to be such that $f_k(-1) = 1-p$ and $f_k(1) = p$ and zero elsewhere. 
We will construct a PMF $g = g_k$ for each $k$ such that $f * g$ is symmetric and 
\begin{equation} \lim_{p \downarrow \frac{1}{2}} H(g_k) = 0 . \end{equation}

We begin by writing $k = 2l + 1$ and $\delta = \frac{2p-1}{kp-l} = \frac{2p-1}{2lp+p-l}$. 
Define $g(0) = 1-l\delta$; the values of $g$ at the $2l$ remaining elements of $\mathbb{Z}_k = \mathbb{Z}_{2l+1}$ will be $\delta$ ($l$ times) and $0$ ($l$ times), according to the following pattern:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item If $k \equiv_4 1$, 
 $g_k(1) \coloneqq g_k(2) \coloneqq 0$ 
and $g_k(3) \coloneqq g_k(4) \coloneqq \delta$. 
\item If $k \equiv_4 3$, 
 $g_k(1) \coloneqq \delta$,
 $g_k(2) \coloneqq 0$;
and when $k > 3$, 
 $g_k(3) \coloneqq 0$ and 
 $g_k(4) \coloneqq \delta$. 
\item For all $k \ge 11$, for all integers $r \in [5,l]$, $g_k(r) \coloneqq g_k(r-4)$. 

\item Finally, for all $r \in [l]$, $g(-r) \coloneqq 0$ iff $g(r)=\delta$ and $g(-r)\coloneqq \delta$ iff $g(r)=0$. 
\end{enumerate}
Intuitively, $g$ consists of one large mass at the origin, and alternating pairs of zeros and $\delta$s on the rest of $\mathbb{Z}_k$. 

Note that $\lim_{p \downarrow \frac{1}{2}} \delta = 0$, so that
$\lim_{p \downarrow \frac{1}{2}} g_k = \mathds{1}_{0}$ and therefore $g_k$ satisfies (equation eq:entropy limit property of the paper). 
It remains to show that $g_k$ is a symmetrizer of $f_k$, i.e., that $(g_k * f_k)(r) = (g_k * f_k)(-r)$ for all $r \in [l]$. 

For $r \ge 2$, noting that $g(\pm(r-1)), g(\pm(r+1)) \in \{0, \delta\}$ with $g(-(r-1)) = \delta$ iff $g(r-1) = 0$ iff $g(r+1) = \delta$ iff $g(-(r+1))=0$, 
we have $g(-(r-1)) = g(r+1)$ and $g(-(r+1)) = g(r-1)$, so that
\[
(f * g)(r) 
= pg(r-1) + (1-p)g(r+1)
= pg(-r-1) + (1-p)g(-r+1) 
= (f * g)(-r) .
\]
Finally, noting that the values of $g_k(2) = 0$ and $g_k(-2) = \delta$ for all $k$, we compute
\begin{align*}
(f* g)(1) 
&= pg(0) + (1-p)g(2) \\

&= \frac{p^2}{2lp + p -l} \\
&= \frac{p^2 - (1-p)p + (1-p)p}{2lp + p -l} \\
&= \frac{p(2p - 1)}{2lp + p -l} + (1-p)g(0) \\
&= p \delta + (1-p)g(0) \\

&= (f* g)(-1). \qedhere
\end{align*}
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

For every fixed $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the entropy number $\varepsilon_n(\mathcal{M})_X$ is the infimum of all $\varepsilon > 0$ for which $2^n$ balls with centers from $X$ and radius $\varepsilon$ cover $\mathcal{M}$. Formally, we write
    \[
        \varepsilon_n(\mathcal{M})_X
        =

    \]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:53:10.159922+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_11dba8d96b3ee019c555414aab40d141b426fbd14ec02e18a2e6efe002943189","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm MO-as-colim of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] The cocone $\sigma_{[0]}$ exhibits $\textbf{\textup{MO}}=\smash{\textbf{\textup{MOP}}^{[0]}}$ as the global colimit of $\smash{{\mathpalette\ulhelper{\mathfrak J}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{gl}|_{\ul\textup{VRep}_{[0]}}}$.
    \begin{proof}
        We will more generally prove this for any $d\in{\mathbb{Z}}$, and similarly to before it will suffice to show that $\tilde\sigma_{[d]}$ exhibits $\textbf{\textup{BOP}}^{[d]}\hookrightarrow\textbf{\textup{BOP}}$ as a colimit.

        As $\ul\textup{VRep}=\coprod_{d\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\smash{\ul\textup{VRep}_{[d]}}$, we get an equivalence
        \[
            \mathop{\textup{colim}}_{\ul\textup{VRep}}\bar y_{\textup{top}} \simeq \coprod_{d\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\,\mathop{\textup{colim}}_{\ul\textup{VRep}_{[d]}}\,\bar y_{\textup{top}}|_{\ul\textup{VRep}_{[d]}}

        in ${{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_\textup{gl}[\textbf{\textup{BOP}}]$. As the left-hand side is terminal by Proposition~(prop:MOP-as-colim of the paper), so is the coproduct on the right-hand side. Thus, the coproduct of the maps 
        \[
            \mathop{\textup{colim}}\bar y_{\textup{top}}|_{\ul\textup{VRep}_{[d]}}\to\big(\textbf{\textup{BOP}}^{[d]}\hookrightarrow\textbf{\textup{BOP}}\big)

As a coproduct of maps in ${{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_\textup{gl}[\textbf{\textup{BOP}}]\simeq({{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_{\textup{gl}})_{/\textbf{\textup{BOP}}}$ (or any other $\infty$-topos) is an equivalence only if each summand is so, this completes the proof of the theorem.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:03:59.343356+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_11f2164fdf0cb4847c636b8d0698ad9b63dfdf120cc4e2333fe53967dafefdfa","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Satz thm:HigherOrderLSq of arXiv:2507.08692, 'Some notes on higher order concentration of measure'] Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on ${\mathbb R}^n$ which satisfies an $\mathrm{LS}_q$-inequality with constant $\sigma^q > 0$, and let $f\colon {\mathbb R}^n \to {\mathbb R}$ be a $\mathcal{C}^d$-smooth function with ${\mathbb E} f = 0$.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item Assuming that $\lVert f^{(j)} \rVert_{\mathrm{op}(q),1} \le \sigma^{d-j}$ for all $j=1,\ldots,d-1$ and $\lVert f^{(d)} \rVert_{\mathrm{op}(q),\infty} \le 1$, it holds that
		\[
		\int \exp\Big\{\frac{c_{p,d}}{\sigma^p} |f|^{p/d} \Big\} d\mu \le 2,
		\]
		where a possible choice of the constant $c_{p,d}$ is given by
		\[
		c_{p,d} = \frac{2^{2p-3}(q^{1/p}-1)^p(p-1)^p}{eq \log^{p-1}(2)\max(q, p/d)}.
		\]
		\item For any $t\ge 0$, it holds that
		\[
		\mu(|f| \ge t)\le
		2 \exp\Big\{- \frac{C_p}{(d\sigma)^p} \min\Big(\min_{j=1, \ldots,d-1} \Big(\frac{t}{\lVert f^{(j)} \rVert_{\mathrm{op}(q),1}}\Big)^{p/j}, \Big(\frac{t}{\lVert f^{(d)} \rVert_{\mathrm{op}(q),\infty}}\Big)^{p/d}\Big)\Big\},
		\]
		where a possible choice of the constant $C_p$ is given by
		\[
		C_p = \frac{4^{p-1}(p-1)^p}{q\log^{p-2}(2) e^p}.
		\]
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:39:41.406858+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_11f35caf7ab02bd304bd797fa301c5ac92ab82d81e2acbcc1ea560fec3367eab","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 4 (Colored height function) of arXiv:2604.06532, 'Random permutations from $q$-Demazure products'] For a color threshold $c \in \{0, 1, \dots, n\}$, a row $S$, and a column $Y$, define
\[
  H(c;\, S,\, Y)
  \;:=\;
  \#\bigl\{\, Y' \ge Y : \text{the vertical arrow at column } Y',\, \text{row } S
  \text{ has color } \le c \,\bigr\}.
\]
At the top row $S = n$, this is related to the permutation height function by
$H(c;\, n,\, Y) = c - Y + 1 + n \cdot H_\sigma\!\bigl(\tfrac{Y-1}{n},\, \tfrac{c}{n}\bigr),$

{"assumptions":["Discrete Gaussian free field on a two-dimensional lattice domain with Dirichlet boundary conditions","Gibbs-Markov (domain Markov) property and lattice Green function asymptotics","Random-walk-below-a-barrier (ballot) estimates for the scale walk"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.987849+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_11fcc5b0b92d4300329a446dd3a28c80e7535335cb27eaecb364b7fce9c12206","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The concentric decomposition (Biskup-Louidor) describes the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field h in a box of side N as seen from a point x where the field is near its maximum. Around x one takes nested dyadic annuli; conditioning on the values of h on the boundaries of the concentric boxes, the Gibbs-Markov property splits h into (i) a random walk S_k along the scales, whose increments are the Gaussian binding fields' values at x, with variance of order g log 2 per scale, with the maximum constraint acting as a barrier the walk must stay below (entropic repulsion), (ii) independent zero-boundary fields in the annuli, and (iii) explicit bounded error terms from the non-exact scale invariance of the lattice Green function. The maximum-at-x event becomes a ballot-type event for the walk S_k, handled by random-walk-below-a-barrier estimates, which yield tightness of the centred maximum, the local limit law of the maximum, and the description of the cluster of near-maximal points around x (the cluster law nu). It is the tool behind the full extremal process of the DGFF (Biskup-Louidor 2016, 2018) and the intermediate level sets. It does not by itself give universality for other log-correlated fields: the binding-field structure uses the DGFF's exact Gibbs-Markov property. Typical failure: Treating the annulus fields phi_k as exactly independent rather than approximately so, and carrying a multiscale second-moment computation through without tracking the coupling error terms; because the GFF is only log-correlated rather than an exact branching random walk, the independence used in the concentric decomposition is an approximation that must be explicitly controlled, and skipping this step is a common source of unjustified exponent claims for GFF level-set percolation. Canonical reference: Biskup and Louidor, 2016, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Biskup and Louidor, 2018, Advances in Mathematics; Biskup, Extrema of the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field, PIMS-CRM lecture notes, 2020, Springer.","status":"unverified"}

Method: Asymptotic influence bounds for polynomial thresholds exact calculation or structural obstruction Result: The desired C*d*sqrt(n) bound holds when the polynomial is a product of d affine linear forms with no cube zeros. Indeed its sign is a product of d threshold functions. If that product changes on a coordinate flip, at least one factor changes, so its influence is at most the sum of the factor influences. For a threshold g, unateness gives Inf_i(g)=|ghat(i)| and hence I(g)<=sqrt(n)*sqrt(sum_i ghat(i)^2)<=sqrt(n). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.355487+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_120844a9e4d83f44ff30daf26d429f2a5182a56faf96997588561c50bbb77eb5","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 223 (relaxed domains) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\dist(\cdot,\cdot)$ denote the Euclidean distance in $\R^N$, and define
\beq
\begin{aligned}
    S_N(\iota)
    &\equiv\bigg\{\bx\in\R^N :
    \frac{\dist(\bx,S_N)}{N^{1/2}} \le \iota
    \bigg\}\,, &
    \Sigma_N(\iota)
    &\equiv\bigg\{\bx\in\R^N :
    \frac{\dist(\bx,\Sigma_N)}{N^{1/2}} \le \iota
    \bigg\}\,.
\end{aligned}\eeq
We call $S_N(\iota)$ the \textbf{$\iota$-relaxed spherical domain},
and $\Sigma_N(\iota)$  the \textbf{$\iota$-relaxed Ising domain}.\footnote{While these relaxed domains are needed in the Ising setting for the notion of a Lipschitz algorithm to make sense, any point in $S_N(\iota)$ or $\Sigma_N(\iota)$ can be rounded to a point in $S_N$ or $\Sigma_N$ with nearly the same performance; see Remark~\ref{r:relaxed-wlog}.}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["G finite, connected, undirected, without isolated vertices (weighted graphs work verbatim with weighted degrees and volumes)","the spectral gap is that of the NORMALISED Laplacian; for regular graphs it is (d - mu_2)/d, and the unnormalised version scales by d","conductance is measured against volume; the vertex-count edge expansion h(G) is the same quantity only for regular graphs"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:49:11.846189+00:00","domain":"spectral graph theory","id":"claim_123dda5b10ef9e8af280ba37a63254fd3b1973ad6a342a5785086a24af3d21fc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let G = (V, E) be a finite connected graph with vertex degrees d(v), volume vol(S) = sum_{v in S} d(v), and for a vertex set S with 0 < vol(S) <= vol(V)/2 let phi(S) = e(S, V - S) / vol(S) be its conductance, where e(S, V - S) counts the edges leaving S. The conductance (Cheeger constant) of G is phi(G) = min over such S of phi(S). Let 0 = lambda_1 < lambda_2 <= ... <= lambda_n <= 2 be the eigenvalues of the normalised Laplacian L = I - D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2}. CHEEGER'S INEQUALITY (Alon-Milman, Sinclair-Jerrum, Dodziuk; the graph form of Cheeger's 1970 Riemannian inequality): lambda_2 / 2 <= phi(G) <= sqrt(2 lambda_2). For a d-regular graph with adjacency eigenvalues d = mu_1 >= mu_2 >= ..., lambda_2 = (d - mu_2)/d and the edge expansion h(G) = min e(S, V-S)/|S| (over |S| <= n/2) satisfies (d - mu_2)/2 <= h(G) <= sqrt(2 d (d - mu_2)). Both sides are sharp up to constants: the cycle C_n has phi of order 1/n and lambda_2 of order 1/n^2 (so the square root is needed), while the hypercube and expanders have phi and lambda_2 of the same order. Consequences: a graph is an expander (phi bounded below) if and only if it has a spectral gap bounded below; the mixing time of the random walk is O(log(n) / lambda_2) and at least of order 1/phi; the sweep cut of the second eigenvector (the proof of the upper bound) is the spectral partitioning algorithm, with the guarantee phi(S) <= sqrt(2 lambda_2) for the set it returns; higher-order Cheeger inequalities (Lee-Oveis Gharan-Trevisan) relate lambda_k to k-way partitions, and the improved Cheeger inequality bounds phi by lambda_2 / sqrt(lambda_3).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:51:11.463204+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_124528d929f6d734b3af9da0d623a149f8e9b2fbbd826f9c30808973fd01d0e6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 20 ({\cite[Definition~6.2, 6.9, and Proposition~6.10) of arXiv:2609.02561, 'NON-NEF LOCI IN MIXED CHARACTERISTIC'] {MS}}]
With notation as above,
set $d:=\dim R$.
Let $(R,\Delta)$ be a log $\Q$-Gorenstein pair, and let $E_R(k)$ be the injective hull of $k$ as an $R$-module.
Fix a canonical divisor $K_R \geq 0$.
Write
$K_R +\Delta=\frac{1}{m}\divi(f)$ for some $0\neq f\in R$ and some $m\in\Z_{>0}$.
Take a representing element $f^{\frac{1}{m}}\in R^+$.
Let $B$ be a perfectoid big Cohen-Macaulay $R^{+}$-algebra and
let $\phi:H_{\m}^{d}(R(K_R)) \rightarrow H_{\m}^{d}(B)$ denote the morphism such that
the composition of the natural morphism $H_{\m}^{d}(R) \rightarrow H_{\m}^{d}(R(K_R))$ and $\phi$ is identical to the morphism induced by the multiplication by $f^{\frac{1}{m}}$.

The BCM-test ideal of $(R,\Delta)$ with respect to $B$ is defined as
\[ \tau_{B}(R,\Delta) 
:= {\Image( E_R(k) \cong H_{\m}^{d}(R(K_R)) \xrightarrow{\phi} H_{\m}^{d}(B))}^{\vee} \subset R, \]
where ${(-)}^{\vee}$ denotes Matlis duality.
The BCM-test ideal of $(R,\Delta)$ is defined as
\[ \taubcm(R,\Delta) := \bigcap_{B} \tau_B (R,\Delta) \subset R.\]
We say
that $(R,\Delta)$ is $\BCM_B$-regular if $\tau_B (R,\Delta)=R$
and
that $(R,\Delta)$ is BCM-regular if $\taubcm(R,\Delta)=R$.
These definitions are independent of the choices of $K_R$ and $f^\frac{1}{m}\in R^+$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["mu is a product measure on {0,1}^n, or satisfies the FKG lattice condition (log-supermodular)","A and B are both increasing (or both decreasing) events; f and g both monotone in the same direction","the reversed inequality needs one increasing and one decreasing event","no conclusion for events that are not monotone, and none for a non-FKG measure"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.048644+00:00","domain":"percolation and correlation inequalities (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_12642faa7ec3d8f83d07d4fc84666d17c25bf65b9cb7021607d2e1967b320070","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let mu be a product probability measure on {0,1}^n (Harris 1960), or more generally a measure on a finite distributive lattice satisfying the FKG lattice condition mu(x v y) mu(x ^ y) >= mu(x) mu(y) (Fortuin, Kasteleyn, Ginibre 1971). If A and B are both increasing events, then mu(A and B) >= mu(A) mu(B); equivalently, for increasing functions f and g, E[f g] >= E[f] E[g]. The same holds when both are decreasing. If one event is increasing and the other decreasing, the inequality reverses: mu(A and B) <= mu(A) mu(B). The inequality says nothing about a pair of events that are neither increasing nor decreasing, and it fails for a general (non-FKG) measure.","status":"unverified"}

Let $\mathbf{X}\in \Omega G_p([a,b],V)$ and $\mathbf{Y}\in \Omega G_q([c,d],W)$, and set $\kappa=\lfloor p\rfloor$ and $\lambda=\lfloor q\rfloor$. \[
g(Z) \in \mathcal{D}^{p,q}_{\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}}([a,b]\times[c,d], S).
\]
Moreover, $g(Z)$ is characterized by the identity
\[
g(Z)_{t,v}[\eta,\xi] = g\left(Z^{(0,0)}_{t,v}\right)[\eta,\xi],
\qquad
\text{for all } \eta \in V^{\otimes 0},\ \xi \in W^{\otimes 0}.

The higher level components of $g(Z)$ are given as follows. For

\[
g(Z_{t,v})[\xi_j,\eta_k] :=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
\displaystyle
\sum_{m=1}^{\kappa-1} \frac{1}{m!}
D^m g\left(Z^{(0,0)}_{t,v}\right) \circ Z_{t,v}^{\otimes m}
\circ \left(\tilde{\Delta}^m \boxtimes \mathrm{id}_{T^{<\lambda(W)}}\right)
[\xi_j,\eta_k],

\displaystyle
\sum_{n=1}^{\lambda-1} \frac{1}{n!}
D^n g\left(Z^{(0,0)}_{t,v}\right) \circ Z_{t,v}^{\otimes n}

[\xi_j,\eta_k],

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. observations with finite variance (Andrews states the result under moment conditions for the CLT)","the constraint is active at the true parameter (theta = 0); for theta > 0 the bootstrap is consistent"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T09:23:59.828365+00:00","domain":"resampling / constrained estimation","id":"claim_128317036fe4b38de221748567b9dd5e4b220bf4b14f749dabab4f8dd0bb0ff4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $X_1, \\dots, X_n$ be i.i.d. with mean $\\theta \\ge 0$ and variance $\\sigma^2$, and let the estimator respect the constraint: $\\hat\\theta_n = \\max(0, \\bar X_n)$. When the true parameter is interior ($\\theta > 0$) the nonparametric bootstrap is consistent: the conditional law of $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n^* - \\hat\\theta_n)$ converges to $N(0, \\sigma^2)$, the law of $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n - \\theta)$. When the true parameter is on the boundary ($\\theta = 0$) it is not: $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n - \\theta) \\Rightarrow \\max(0, Z)$ with $Z \\sim N(0, \\sigma^2)$, a law with an atom of mass $1/2$ at zero, whereas the bootstrap law of $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n^* - \\hat\\theta_n)$ converges, conditionally on the data, to the law of $\\max(0, Z + \\zeta) - \\max(0, \\zeta)$ with $\\zeta \\sim N(0, \\sigma^2)$ a random shift that does not vanish - so the bootstrap distribution is random in the limit and does not equal the sampling distribution (Andrews 2000, Theorem 1). The same failure holds for maximum-likelihood and least-squares estimators under inequality constraints whenever the true parameter has an active constraint, in particular for nonnegatively constrained regression and portfolio weights with coordinates at zero: the bootstrap replicates flip the constrained coordinates between zero and positive values, and the spread of the replicates is not the spread of the estimator. Consistent alternatives: the $m$-out-of-$n$ bootstrap with $m \\to \\infty$, $m/n \\to 0$, and subsampling, both of which recover the limit law at the boundary.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H is a finite bipartite graph with specified parts L and R","the network is layered s -> L -> R -> t, terminal capacities are 1, middle capacities are positive integers","the flow is integral"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T02:29:07.665547+00:00","domain":"finite bipartite graphs and their flow networks","id":"claim_129bed04f6bb1485d3e8c8182389b81f3a48db36763f86564b6ce5e5ab32147c","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H = (L, R, E) be a finite bipartite graph and take the network with a source s, a sink t, arcs s->u of capacity 1 for u in L, arcs u->v for each edge uv, and arcs v->t of capacity 1 for v in R, the middle arcs carrying positive integer capacities. In every feasible integral s-t flow, the middle arcs with positive flow carry exactly one unit each and form a matching whose size is the flow value; conversely, every matching gives an integral flow of the same value, one unit along each path s-u-v-t. The integrality is needed: in the network on K_{2,2}, flow 1/2 on each of the four middle arcs and 1 on each terminal arc is a maximum flow of value 2 whose support is not a matching. Integer capacities guarantee that some maximum flow is integral, not that every one is.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.740854+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_12b24723aa93f050871e7949f914605cbec33b4efdc7c35f81ec8af464b9628e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] Let $\{ C_n \}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be uniformly random elements of $[m]\coloneqq\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$, and let
$\{ U_n \}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be uniformly random elements of $(0, 1)$.
Assume the family $\{ U_n, C_n \}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is independent.
The random variable $C_n$ denotes the coupon type
obtained on day $n$.
Define the random variables
\[
  L(i, n) \coloneqq \sup\{ k \leqslant n \mid C_k = i \}, \quad i \in [m], \quad n > 0.
\]
Then $L(i, n)$ is the most recent day no later than $n$ that coupon
type $i$ was issued.
For clumsiness probability $p \in [0, 1)$, the 
clumsy coupon collection time can be defined by
