{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:55:18.060710+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1d14d0b7e9076743e4b8eb70c925c6f8a70259997b39f59d9cc901a99a3944d0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2606.17381, 'Large deviation principle for friendship-biases\\ in Galton--Watson trees'] {\bf [LDP for type fractions along a random path]}

Under the joint law of the Galton--Watson tree $\mathcal{T}_\infty$ and the random exploration path, the family of random variables $\{\Upsilon_j\}_{j\in\N_4}$ satisfies the LDP in the Polish space $(0,\infty) \times \mathcal{S}_2$ with rate $j$ and with good rate function $J$ given by
\[
J(x,s) = \inf_{\nu \in \Phi(x,s)} I(\nu), \qquad x \in (0,\infty),\, s \in \mathcal{S}_2.
\]
Here,
\begin{itemize}
\item 
$I\colon\,\mathcal{P}(E) \to [0,\infty]$ is the good rate function given by
\[
I(\nu) =
\begin{cases}
H\left(\nu\,\middle\|\, \pi_{1,2}\nu \otimes \zeta^{\otimes 2}\right), & \text{if } \pi_{1,2}\nu=\pi_{2,3}\nu,\\[1ex]
\infty, & \text{otherwise,}
\end{cases}
\]
where $H(\cdot\, \|\, \cdot)$ denotes relative entropy and $\pi_{1,2}$, $\pi_{2,3}$ denote the projection onto the first two, respectively, the last two of the three coordinates.
\item
The constraint on $\nu$ is to the subset of $\mathcal{P}(E)$ given by
\[
\Phi(x,s) = \big\{\nu \in \mathcal{P}(E)\colon\,\|G(\nu)\|_1 = x,\,G(\nu)/\|G(\nu)\|_1 = s\big\},
\qquad x \in (0,\infty),\,s \in \mathcal{S}_2,
\]
where $G = (G^\chi)_{\chi \in S}$ with $G^\chi\colon\,\mathcal{P}(E) \to [0,\infty]$ is given by
\[
G^\chi(\nu) = \int_{E} h^\chi\,\mathrm{d}\nu
\]
with $h^\chi\colon\,E \to \N_0$ given by
\[
\begin{aligned}
h^{-}\big((a,a^\prime),(b,b^\prime),(c,c^\prime)\big)
&= \mathbbm{1}_{\{c>0\}}
+ \mathbbm{1}_{\{b=0,\, c>0\}}
+ \mathbbm{1}_{\{b=0,\,c=0,\, c^\prime>0\}}, \\[6pt]
h^{0}\big((a,a^\prime),(b,b^\prime),(c,c^\prime)\big)
&= c-\mathbbm{1}_{\{c>0\}}-\mathbbm{1}_{\{c>1\}}
+ \mathbbm{1}_{\{b=0,\,c=0,\,c^\prime=0\}}, \\[6pt]
h^{+}\big((a,a^\prime),(b,b^\prime),(c,c^\prime)\big)
&= \mathbbm{1}_{\{c>0\}} + \mathbbm{1}_{\{c>1\}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

Y. Shmalo, Partition quadratic stochastic operators converge to the empty body (2026). An F-quadratic stochastic operator acts on the simplex over types {0, 1, ..., m}, where 0 is the empty body: parents of the same sex, or a pair containing 0, produce 0; Rozikov and Zhamilov proved that every such operator has the unique fixed point e_0 and that every trajectory converges to it exponentially fast. Problem 10 of Ganikhodzhaev, Mukhamedov and Rozikov, Quadratic stochastic operators and processes: results and open problems (arXiv:0902.4207), asks whether the same holds when the two sexes are replaced by the blocks E_1, ..., E_q of an arbitrary partition of {1, ..., m}, with same-block pairs producing the empty body. The answer is yes: with y = 1 - x_0, every such operator V satisfies y(V(x)) <= (1 - 1/q) y(x)^2, so e_0 is the unique fixed point and y(V^n(x)) <= c^{-1} (c y(x))^{2^n} with c = 1 - 1/q, and the inequality is an equality at every step along some trajectories for each q. Without the rule that pairs containing 0 produce 0 the statement fails: (x_0, x_1) -> (x_0^2 + x_1^2, 2 x_0 x_1) has a second, attracting fixed point (1/2, 1/2). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.167563+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1dc5a679e2211368b630985d58800be61bf289fc83995d52c07c31a39ab91041","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 57 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\star$ as in \eqref{e:star.options} and $\mu \in \sM^\star(\alpha,q_0)$, we have
        \[\|\mu\|_{L^2}^2 \le
    \frac{10}{\alpha}
    +6 + O(\epsilon)\,.\]
\begin{proof}
Let $X$ be given by \eqref{e:formal.sde.main}. Let us write
$X(1)= X(q_*)+\textup{(a)}+\textup{(b)}$ where (a) denotes the drift term and (b) denotes the martingale term.
We have $\bbE[X(q_*)^2] \le \epsilon$ under either of the initialization conditions \ref{it:6.1} or \ref{it:6.2}. Next, using the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, we have
    \begin{align*}
    \E[\textup{(a)}^2]
    &= \E\bigg[
    \bigg(\int_{q_*}^1
    p'(t)^{1/2} b_t\,dt\bigg)^2
    \bigg]
    \le \E\bigg[
    \bigg(\int_{q_*}^1 p'(t)\,dt\bigg)
    \bigg(\int_{q_*}^1 (b_t)^2 \,dt
        \bigg)\bigg]
    \le
    \int_{q_*}^1 \E[(b_t)^2] \,dt\\
    &\le \int_{q_*}^1 \Cost(t)\,dt
    \le \int_{q_*}^1 \budget(t;\alpha)\,dt + \epsilon
    \le \frac{1+\epsilon}{\alpha} + \epsilon\,,
    \end{align*}
where the last two inequalities hold under any of the budget conditions
\ref{it:4.1}, \ref{it:4.2}, or \ref{it:4.3}
combined with either condition
\ref{it:2.1} or \ref{it:2.2}. Lastly, we have from \eqref{e:loc.mg.L2.bounded} that 
    \[
    \E[\textup{(b)}^2]
    \le \int_{q_*}^1 s(t)^2
    \E[(\sigma_t)^2] \,dt
    \le 2\bigg\{ \frac{1+\epsilon}{\alpha}
        + \epsilon + 1\bigg\}\,.\]
Combining the above bounds gives altogether
    \[
    \E[X(1)^2]
    \le 3\bigg\{
    \E[X(q_*)^2]
    +\E[\textup{(a)}^2]
    +\E[\textup{(b)}^2]\bigg\}
    \le 3\bigg\{
    \frac{3(1+\epsilon)}{\alpha}
    +2 + 4\epsilon\bigg\}\,,
    \]
proving the claim.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.474645+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1e202035132140ea4bc4f7953ae24f53864051500bde104688dcc6d4af941e2f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] \label[theorem]{thm:hypercube_entropy}
Let $X = (X_1, \dots, X_d) \in_R \{\pm1\}^d$ with every $X_i$ asymmetric. 
Let $Y = (Y_1, \dots, Y_d) \in \Sym(X)$. 
Then, $H(Y) \ge \frac{1}{d} H(X)$, with equality if and only if the following conditions are all satisfied: 
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item There exists an index $i \in [d]$ such that both $f_{Y_i} = f_{-X_i}$ and $H(Y) = H(Y_i)$,
\item $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{p_1-\frac{1}{2}} = \dots = \@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{p_d-\frac{1}{2}}$, 
\item the random variables $X_i$ are mutually independent. 
\end{enumerate}
\begin{proof}
Let $j \in \arg\max_{i \in [d]} H(X_i) = \arg\min_{i \in [d]} \@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{p_i-\frac{1}{2}}$. 
Note that $Y_j$ is an independent symmetrizer of $X_j$ by (lem:Rd_projection_works of the paper). 
Thus we may apply (thm:HY_exceeds_HX of the paper) to $X_j$ and $Y_j$. 
Then, 
\begin{align}
H(Y) &\ge H(Y_j) \label[ineq]{ineq:hypercube_entropy_a}\\
&\ge H(X_j) \label[ineq]{ineq:hypercube_entropy_2}\\

&\ge \frac{1}{d} \sum_{i=1}^d H(X_i) \label[ineq]{ineq:hypercube_entropy_3}\\
&\ge \frac{1}{d} H(X) \label[ineq]{ineq:hypercube_entropy_4}
\end{align}
where we used the entropy chain rule in ((ineq:hypercube_entropy_a of the paper)), 
(thm:HY_exceeds_HX of the paper) in ((ineq:hypercube_entropy_2 of the paper)), 
and the entropy chain rule and the fact that conditioning reduces entropy in ((ineq:hypercube_entropy_4 of the paper)). 

Equality is attained in $H(Y) \ge \frac{1}{d} H(X)$ if and only if it is attained in each of ((ineq:hypercube_entropy_a of the paper)-

(ineq:hypercube_entropy_4 of the paper)). 
The equality condition of ((ineq:hypercube_entropy_4 of the paper)) is $H(X) = \sum_{i=1}^d H(X_i) $
which is in turn equivalent to mutual independence of the $X_i$ (see e.g. [PW25:book]). 
The equality condition of ((ineq:hypercube_entropy_3 of the paper)) is exactly (ii). 
Now consider the conditions

\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] $f_{Y_j} = f_{-X_j}$,
\item[(b)] $H(Y) = H(Y_j)$.
\end{itemize}
Equality is attained in (equation ineq:hypercube_entropy_2 of the paper) exactly when $H(X_j) = H(Y_j)$, which, in light of (thm:HY_exceeds_HX of the paper), is equivalent to (a). 
Equality is attained in (equation ineq:hypercube_entropy_a of the paper) exactly when (b) is true. 

We claim that (a-b,ii-iii) is equivalent to (i-iii). 
Clearly (a-b) implies (i); we need only show the converse. 
If (i-iii) is fulfilled, then
$$ H(X_j) = H(X_i) = H(Y_i) = H(Y) \ge H(Y_j) \ge H(X_j) $$
where we have used (in order), condition (ii), condition (i), condition (i) again, the entropy chain rule, and (thm:HY_exceeds_HX of the paper). 
Thus, the last two inequalities are equalities, which forces (b) and also forces $H(Y_j) = H(X_j)$. 
The equality condition of (thm:HY_exceeds_HX of the paper) (applied to $X_j$ and $Y_j$) then implies (a). 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Ω ⊂ R^n open","F continuous on Ω × R × R^n","u continuous on Ω"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.415708+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: Hamilton-Jacobi equations","id":"claim_1e25d63418d6f4a5169a94db2c01063496e715960b47674a81764905279ec8b8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Ω ⊂ R^n be open and F: Ω × R × R^n → R continuous. A function u ∈ C(Ω) is a viscosity subsolution of F(x,u,Du) = 0 in Ω if for every φ ∈ C^1(Ω) and every x0 ∈ Ω at which u - φ has a local maximum, F(x0, u(x0), Dφ(x0)) ≤ 0. It is a viscosity supersolution if for every φ ∈ C^1(Ω) and every x0 ∈ Ω at which u - φ has a local minimum, F(x0, u(x0), Dφ(x0)) ≥ 0. It is a viscosity solution if it is both. For the evolution equation u_t + H(x,Du) = 0 in R^n × (0,T) apply the definition in the variables (x,t), with test functions φ(x,t) of class C^1 and F((x,t), r, (p,s)) = s + H(x,p); so at a local maximum of u - φ one requires φ_t + H(x0, Dφ) ≤ 0, and at a local minimum φ_t + H(x0, Dφ) ≥ 0. Equivalent variants giving the same class: C^1 test functions may be replaced by C^2 or C^∞ ones, local extrema by strict local extrema, and one may normalize φ(x0) = u(x0). The definition is NOT invariant under F ↦ -F: in general the viscosity solutions of F = 0 and of -F = 0 differ. The correct symmetry is: u is a viscosity subsolution of F(x,u,Du) = 0 iff -u is a viscosity supersolution of G(x,r,p) = 0, where G(x,r,p) := -F(x,-r,-p).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["uniform measure"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T09:12:41.903248+00:00","domain":"analysis of Boolean functions","id":"claim_1e28a5a429b99a0db85ae0b3d2a9ddaa08e4fffcb279cf779cc8441cc57f3f52","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"On the uniform cube {-1, 1}^n let f be real, f^(S) = E[f chi_S] its Walsh coefficients and W_k = sum over |S| = k of f^(S)^2. For rho in [-1, 1], T_rho is the noise operator: T_rho f(x) = E[f(Y)] where the Y_i are independent with P(Y_i = x_i) = (1 + rho)/2, so T_rho chi_S = rho^|S| chi_S. of \eqref{EqGeneralMatrixCovariance}.  Write
\(d=|d|\mathrm{e}^{2\mathrm{i}\theta}\), taking \(\theta=0\) when
\(d=0\).  Let \((\mathscr{A},\varphi)\) be a tracial
\(*\)-probability space containing a free centred semicircular pair
\(\mathsf{s}_1,\mathsf{s}_2\) of variance one, and define

       \left(\alpha\mathsf{s}_1+\mathrm{i}\beta\mathsf{s}_2\right),

\[
 \tr_N R(\mathbf{Y}_N,\mathbf{Y}_N^*)

 \qquad\text{almost surely}.
\]

Let Gamma be a finite group and Q a Gamma-equivariant positive contraction on l^2(Gamma) with 0 < Q < I, and P_Q the determinantal measure with kernel Q. Let HM(Q) be the harmonic mean of the eigenvalues of Q. Then P_Q stochastically dominates the product Bernoulli measure of density HM(Q), and P_Q is dominated by the product measure of density 1 - HM(I - Q). Precise chain: the minimal conditional ODDS of presence is s_min = 1/(J^{-1})_ee = HM/(1 - HM) with J = Q(I-Q)^{-1}, and the minimal conditional PROBABILITY is s_min/(1 + s_min) = 1/(Q^{-1})_ee = HM(Q) (revision 2 states the odds and the probability separately, after a reviewer noted the two had been conflated in a side note). This is weaker than Lyons's Conjecture 5.7 (geometric mean / Fuglede-Kadison determinant), which numerical monotone-coupling linear programs on Z/nZ, n <= 6, satisfy exactly, with FK + 0.01 failing on a tested instance; those LP results are floating-point evidence, not certificates.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Discrete Gaussian free field on a two-dimensional lattice domain with Dirichlet boundary conditions","Gibbs-Markov (domain Markov) property and lattice Green function asymptotics","Random-walk-below-a-barrier (ballot) estimates for the scale walk"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1e595d1ddd4d31f5d20f20448b8cd74340f097f418011ebff2ea7ceb8a77b1af","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The concentric decomposition (Biskup-Louidor) describes the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field h in a box of side N as seen from a point x where the field is near its maximum. Around x one takes nested dyadic annuli; conditioning on the values of h on the boundaries of the concentric boxes, the Gibbs-Markov property splits h into (i) a random walk S_k along the scales, whose increments are the Gaussian binding fields' values at x, with variance of order g log 2 per scale, with the maximum constraint acting as a barrier the walk must stay below (entropic repulsion), (ii) independent zero-boundary fields in the annuli, and (iii) explicit bounded error terms from the non-exact scale invariance of the lattice Green function. The maximum-at-x event becomes a ballot-type event for the walk S_k, handled by random-walk-below-a-barrier estimates, which yield tightness of the centred maximum, the local limit law of the maximum, and the description of the cluster of near-maximal points around x (the cluster law nu). It is the tool behind the full extremal process of the DGFF (Biskup-Louidor 2016, 2018) and the intermediate level sets. It does not by itself give universality for other log-correlated fields: the binding-field structure uses the DGFF's exact Gibbs-Markov property. Typical failure: Treating the scale walk S_k as an exact random walk with identically distributed increments, as if the field were an exact branching random walk, and carrying a multiscale second-moment computation through without tracking the error terms; because the GFF is only log-correlated rather than an exact branching random walk, the comparison of S_k with a random walk (scale-dependent variances, the bounded error terms (iii)) must be explicitly controlled, while the Gibbs-Markov pieces themselves are exactly independent; skipping this control is a common source of unjustified exponent claims for GFF level-set percolation. Canonical reference: Biskup and Louidor, 2016, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Biskup and Louidor, 2018, Advances in Mathematics; Biskup, Extrema of the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field, PIMS-CRM lecture notes, 2020, Springer.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["each K_eps is Lebesgue integrable"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.262329+00:00","domain":"real and harmonic analysis","id":"claim_1e5d0188dd28e245626b909ca5c58042ec03419fa53232852fb9172b6eb55d7d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A family $(K_\\varepsilon)_{\\varepsilon>0}$ in $L^1(\\mathbb R^d)$ (or a sequence $K_N$ with $N\\to\\infty$; the same definition works on $\\mathbb T$) is an approximate identity if (i) $\\int K_\\varepsilon=1$ for every $\\varepsilon$; (ii) $\\sup_\\varepsilon\\|K_\\varepsilon\\|_1<\\infty$; (iii) for every $\\delta>0$, $\\int_{|x|\\ge\\delta}|K_\\varepsilon(x)|\\,dx\\to0$ as $\\varepsilon\\to0$. If $K\\in L^1(\\mathbb R^d)$ with $\\int K=1$, the dilates $K_\\varepsilon(x)=\\varepsilon^{-d}K(x/\\varepsilon)$ form an approximate identity. Standard examples: the Gauss-Weierstrass (heat) kernel $\\varepsilon^{-d}e^{-\\pi|x|^2/\\varepsilon^2}$, the Poisson kernel of the half-space, the Fejer kernel $F_N$ and the Poisson kernel $P_r(x)=\\sum_n r^{|n|}e^{2\\pi i n x}$ ($r\\uparrow1$) on $\\mathbb T$. Non-example: the Dirichlet kernel $D_N$ satisfies (i) but not (ii), since $\\|D_N\\|_1\\to\\infty$; this is the root of the divergence phenomena for Fourier series. Some texts add the stronger condition $\\sup_{|x|\\ge\\delta}|K_\\varepsilon(x)|\\to0$, which is the convenient hypothesis for convergence at a point of continuity of a merely integrable $f$ (the tail is then controlled by $\\|f\\|_1$). Almost-everywhere convergence at Lebesgue points needs more than either condition: the usual hypothesis is the dilation structure $K_\\varepsilon(x)=\\varepsilon^{-d}K(x/\\varepsilon)$ together with an integrable radially nonincreasing majorant of $|K|$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the entries a_i are real and nonnegative","in the weighted form the weights are nonnegative and sum to exactly 1","the geometric mean is the nonnegative real root of the product","the convention 0^0 = 1 is used for zero weights"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090495+00:00","domain":"real analysis, classical inequalities","id":"claim_1f1e654f8c410c52b8d725a17d45f62a04496de0ecc32675cb38e67a595827dd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For NONNEGATIVE real numbers a_1, ..., a_n, (a_1 + ... + a_n)/n >= (a_1 a_2 ... a_n)^(1/n), with equality if and only if a_1 = ... = a_n. WEIGHTED FORM: if w_1, ..., w_n >= 0 with w_1 + ... + w_n = 1 and a_1, ..., a_n >= 0, then w_1 a_1 + ... + w_n a_n >= a_1^(w_1) ... a_n^(w_n), with the convention 0^0 = 1, and with equality if and only if all a_i with w_i > 0 are equal. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) nonnegativity is essential. With n = 2 and a_1 = a_2 = -1 the arithmetic mean is -1 while the product is 1 and its positive square root is +1, so the inequality as usually read reverses; the theorem is about nonnegative entries, never about arbitrary reals. (ii) With at least one zero entry and n >= 2 the geometric mean is 0 and the inequality is strict unless every entry is 0. (iii) The weights must be nonnegative AND sum to 1; dropping the normalisation makes the statement false, and the correct inhomogeneous relative is Young's inequality ab <= a^p/p + b^q/q with 1/p + 1/q = 1. (iv) The inequality is homogeneous of degree one, so it can be rescaled but never used to compare means of different orders; that is the power mean inequality, of which AM-GM is the limiting case as the exponent tends to 0.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H is a complex Hilbert space","A is self-adjoint","B is symmetric with D(B) ⊃ D(A)","relative bound a < 1 in ‖Bx‖ ≤ a‖Ax‖ + b‖x‖ on D(A)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.770689+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, perturbation theory, Schrodinger operators","id":"claim_1f4ab59f173a44abadbf58bf5376c8c9b2832575e6d08115bf54538bf8f08703","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be a self-adjoint operator on a complex Hilbert space H and let B be symmetric with D(A) ⊂ D(B) and ‖Bx‖ ≤ a‖Ax‖ + b‖x‖ for all x ∈ D(A), where 0 ≤ a < 1 and b ≥ 0. Then A + B, defined on D(A + B) = D(A), is self-adjoint, and it is essentially self-adjoint on every core of A. If in addition A is bounded below by M, then A + B is bounded below by M − max{b/(1 − a), a|M| + b}. (Wüst's theorem covers the borderline a = 1: if B is symmetric with D(A) ⊂ D(B) and ‖Bx‖ ≤ ‖Ax‖ + b‖x‖, then A + B is essentially self-adjoint on D(A), though possibly not self-adjoint there.) Standard application (Kato): for n ≤ 3 and V ∈ L²(ℝⁿ) + L^∞(ℝⁿ) real valued, multiplication by V has −Δ-bound 0, so −Δ + V is self-adjoint on H²(ℝⁿ) and essentially self-adjoint on C_c^∞(ℝⁿ); this covers V(x) = −γ/|x| in ℝ³, the hydrogen Hamiltonian.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["E contains the empty set and admits countable covers of X, so every subset has at least one admissible cover","rho : E -> [0, +infinity] with rho(empty set) = 0; nonnegativity is essential for the rearrangement of the double sum","the family (A_n) is countable; the sets need not be measurable, disjoint or nested","the conclusion is an inequality only; additivity requires the Caratheodory criterion"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.402499+00:00","domain":"measure theory, outer measures","id":"claim_1f8c36eb2db254c54ff701dd08d6243e0a9c40ab1d83ef4c3b9be279b1744140","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let E be a family of subsets of a set X with the empty set in E and with X covered by countably many members of E, let rho : E -> [0, +infinity] satisfy rho(empty set) = 0, and define mu*(A) = inf { sum over k of rho(E_k) : E_k in E, A contained in the union of the E_k } for every subset A of X. Then mu* is an outer measure: mu*(empty set) = 0; A contained in B implies mu*(A) <= mu*(B); and for EVERY countable family (A_n) of subsets of X, measurable or not, mu*(union of the A_n) <= sum of mu*(A_n). In particular Lebesgue outer measure on R^n is countably subadditive on all subsets of R^n, and finite subadditivity follows by padding the family with empty sets. WHERE THE INEQUALITY CANNOT BE IMPROVED: (a) equality fails in general even for pairwise DISJOINT sets. Let V be a Vitali set in [0,1] (one representative of each coset of the rationals) and let V_q = V + q for q in a countable enumeration of the rationals in [-1,1]. The V_q are pairwise disjoint, their union contains [0,1] and is contained in [-1,2], and by translation invariance all of them have the same Lebesgue outer measure; countable additivity would force that common value to be simultaneously 0 (giving outer measure 0 for [0,1]) and positive (to fill [0,1]), so the outer measure of the disjoint union is strictly less than the sum. Additivity is recovered exactly on the Caratheodory measurable sets. (b) Countable is sharp: the inequality does not extend to uncountable families - [0,1] is the union of its singletons, each of Lebesgue outer measure 0, while the union has outer measure 1. (c) No structure on rho is needed - rho need not be monotone, additive or a premeasure; that is why the construction is so robust, and also why mu* generally does not extend rho (mu*(E) <= rho(E) always, and equality for E in E requires rho to be a premeasure and E to be well behaved).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:27:36.725532+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1f96d6cd70eada662d44338b599396678b2f0ab12197c3cde9e08652b29c65ca","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 40 of arXiv:2511.13559, 'Asymptotic analysis of rare events in high dimensions'] Suppose $\g\in C^{2L}(\us(R\e)), \z \in C^{2L+2}(\us(R\e))$, $R^4d^2/\la\leq\CR$, $R\geq1$, and
\bs
\sup_{x\in\us(R\e)}\|\nabla^\ell\z(x)\|_H&\leq C_{k,\z} d^{\lceil \ell/2\rceil-2}\qquad\forall \ell=3,\dots,2L+2,\\
\sup_{x\in\us(R\e)}\|\nabla^\ell\g(x)\|_H&\leq C_{\ell,\g} d^{\lceil \ell/2\rceil}\qquad\forall \ell=0,\dots,2L.
\es
Then
\bs
\frac{1}{\mathcal Z}\int_{\us(R\e)}\g(x)e^{-\la \z (x)}\dd x = \sum_{k=0}^{L-1}\nu_k(\g)\la^{-k} + \Rem_L,
\es where
\bs
\max_{k=0,\dots,L-1}d^{-2k}|\nu_k(\g)|&\leq C_{L,\z,\g},\\
|\Rem_L|&\leq C_{L,\z,\g,R}\left((d^2/\la)^L+e^{-(R-1)^2d/4}\right).
\es Here, $C_{L,\z,\g}$ depends on $L$, on $C_{\ell,\z}$, $\ell=3,\dots,2L+2$, and on $C_{\ell,\g}$, $\ell=0,\dots,2L$. The constant $C_{L,\z,\g,R}$ is analogous and also depends on $\CR$. We have $\nu_0(\g)=\g(0_d)$, and the formula for $\nu_k(\g)$, $k\geq1$ is given by $A_{2k}$ in~\cite[(2.20)]{A24}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:30:28.827360+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1fb655af0af51c6fd1c94e68562250b7d6520db202e17d88f0a7aea05e01d7a5","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 15 of arXiv:2609.02105, 'Contact fundamental forms and \\ adjoint varieties'] Let $M$ be a complex manifold  with a contact structure $H \subset TM$. 
\begin{itemize} \item[(i)]
For each $z \in M$, define $\fn_{z, 1} := H_z$ and $\fn_{z, 2} := T_z M/H_z$. Then $\fn_z = \fn_{z,1} + \fn_{z, 2}$ has a graded Heisenberg algebra structure given by Lie brackets of vector fields. We call it the {\em symbol algebra} of the contact structure $H \subset TM$ at $z \in M$.  Its universal enveloping algebra $U(\fn_z)$ has a grading coming from the grading $\fn_z = \fn_{z,1} + \fn_{z, 2}$ (this grading is not compatible with the natural filtration of the universal enveloping algebra), which we denote by $$U(\fn_z) \  = \ \oplus_{k \geq 0} U_k(\fn_z).$$  As $z$ varies, it defines a vector bundle $U(\fn)$ on $M$ with the fiber $U(\fn)_z = U(\fn_z)$  and a vector subbundle $U_k(\fn)$ for each $k \geq 0$ with the fiber  $U_k(\fn)_z = U_k(\fn_z)$.
\item[(ii)] For each $z \in M$,  define the {\em weighted order} ${\rm ord}_z(\varphi)$ of a local holomorphic function $\varphi \in \sO_{M, z}$ to be  zero.
The {\em weighted order} ${\rm ord}_z (\xi)$ of a nonzero local vector field $\xi$ is defined to be 1 if it is a local section  of $H$ and 2 otherwise.  A local monomial  differential operator  on $M$ of the form $\xi_1 \cdots \xi_r$ has weighted order $${\rm ord}_z (\xi_1 \cdots \xi_r) \ := \ {\rm ord}_z (\xi_1) + \cdots + {\rm ord}_z(\xi_r).$$ A local differential operator on $M$ is {\em of weighted order $\leq k$} at $z$ if each of its monomial terms has weighted order at most $k$. 
\item[(iii)]
A local holomorphic function $\varphi \in \sO_{M,z}$ has {\em weighted vanishing order $\geq k+1$} at $z \in M$, if $P\varphi$ vanishes at $z$ for any local differential operator $P$ of weighted order $\leq k$. Denote by $\bm^k_z \subset \sO_z$ the ideal of local holomorphic functions with weighted vanishing order $\geq k$ at $z$ and set $ J^k_z := \sO_z / \bm^{k+1}_z.$ The vector bundle $J^k$ on $M$ whose fiber at $z$ is $J^k_z$ is called the {\em bundle of contact $k$-jets}. 
A local holomorphic function $\varphi \in \sO_{M,z}$ naturally determines a local section $j^k(\varphi) \in \sO(J^k)_z$, called the {\em contact $k$-jet} of $\varphi$ at $z$. 
There is a natural surjective homomorphism of vector bundles $ \pi^{k}_{k-1}: J^{k} \to J^{k-1}$ yielding an exact sequence of  vector bundles 
$$0 \to U_{k}(\fn)^* \longrightarrow J^{k} \stackrel{\pi^{k}_{k-1}}{\longrightarrow} J^{k-1} \to 0,$$ where $U_k(\fn)^*$ denotes the dual of the vector bundle $U_k(\fn)$.  \end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.751928+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1fc20a5681643b475f0f39f7026b6a8536ea7fa315fd2f91358dbeb6b84e3c43","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 26 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] Fix $c > 0$ and let $Q_t$ be the birth-death process
  with
  \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item $Q_0 \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(c)$;
    \item $n \mapsto n +1$ transitions of rate $c$; and
    \item $n \mapsto n - 1$ transitions of rate $n$.
  \end{enumerate}
  Then the first hitting time of $0$,
  \[
    \tau_c \coloneqq \inf\{ t \geqslant 0 \mid Q_t = 0 \},
  \]
  has Laplace transform
  \[
    \E e^{-s\tau_c} = e^{-c}
    \left[1 - c\int_0^1 \left(1-x\right)^{s} e^{-cx} \, dx
    \right]^{-1},
    \quad s \geqslant 0.
  \]
  \begin{proof}
    Fix $s > 0$. By total expectation,
    \[
      \E e^{-s \tau_c}
      = \sum_{n = 0}^\infty
      \E\left(e^{-s\tau_c} \middle| Q_0 = n\right)
      \PP(Q_0 = n)\\
      = e^{-c} \sum_{n = 0}^\infty \frac{c^n}{n!}\, \phi_n(s)
    \]
    where $\phi_n(s) \coloneqq \mathbb{E}(e^{-s\tau_c} \mid 
    Q_0 = n)$. So if $\Phi_s$ is defined on $[0, c]$ by
    \begin{equation}
      
      \Phi_s(y) \coloneqq \sum_{n=0}^\infty
      \phi_n(s) \, \frac{y^n}{n!}
      \quad \text{then} \quad
      \E(e^{-s\tau_c}) = e^{-c} \, \Phi_s(c).
    \end{equation}
    Clearly $\phi_0(s) = 1$ and first-step analysis gives
    \[
      (c+n+s) \, \phi_n(s) = 
      n \, \phi_{n-1}(s) + c \, \phi_{n+1}(s),
      \quad n > 0.
    \]
    By taking a weighted sum of this recurrence,
    \[
      \sum_{n = 1}^\infty
      \frac{y^n}{n!} \left(c + n + s \right)
      \phi_n(s) = \sum_{n = 1}^\infty
      \frac{y^n}{n!}
      \left[ n \, \phi_{n-1}(s)
      + c \, \phi_{n+1}(s)\right].
    \]
    The left-hand side is
    \[
      (c+s) \sum_{n=1}^\infty
      \frac{y^n}{n!} \, \phi_n(s)
      + y \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{y^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} \, \phi_n(s)
      =
      (c+s)\left[\Phi_s(y) - 1\right]
      + y \, \Phi_s'(y)
    \]
    while the right-hand side is
    \[
      y \sum_{n=1}^\infty
      \frac{y^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} \, \phi_{n-1}(s)
      + c \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{y^n}{n!} \, \phi_{n+1}(s)
      = y \, \Phi_s(y) + c
      \left[ \Phi_s'(y) - \phi_1(s)\right].
    \]
    We are left with the differential equation
    \[
      (c+s) \left[\Phi_s(y) - 1\right]
      + y \, \Phi_s'(y)
      = y \, \Phi_s(y) + c
      \left[\Phi_s'(y) - \phi_1(s) \right]
    \]
    or equivalently,
    the initial value problem
    \begin{align}
      
      \left(c-y\right) \Phi_s'(y)
      + \left(- c + y - s\right) \Phi_s(y)
      &= \overbrace{c \, \phi_1(s) - c - s}^{-K}\\ \notag
      \Phi_s'(y) + \left(-1-\frac{s}{c-y}\right) \Phi_s(y)
      &= -\frac{K}{c-y}
    \end{align}
    with condition $\Phi_s(0) = 1$.
    Use the integrating factor $I_s(y) = e^{-y} \, (c-y)^s$ to write
    \begin{align*}
      \left[e^{-y} \left(c-y\right)^s \Phi_s(y)\right]'
      &= \frac{-K}{c-y} \, e^{-y} \left(c-y\right)^s\\
      e^{-y} \left(c-y\right)^s \Phi_s(y)
      - e^{-0} \left(c - 0\right)^s \Phi_s(0) 
      &= \int_0^y \frac{-K}{c-x} \, e^{-x} \left(c - x\right)^s \, dx
      \intertext{for any $y < c$. It's clear from \eqref{eq:Phi} that
      $\Phi_s$ is continuous, so take the $y \uparrow c$ limit:}
      \frac{c^s}{\int_0^c e^{-x} \left(c-x\right)^{s-1} dx}
      &= K.
    \end{align*}
    Finally, the $y \uparrow c$ limit of \eqref{eq:IVP}
    informs us $-s \, \Phi_s(c) = -K$, thus
    \begin{align*}
      \E e^{-s\tau_c}
      &= e^{-c} \, \Phi_s(c)
      = \frac{e^{-c}\, c^s}{\int_0^c e^{-x} \, s \left(c-x\right)^{s-1} dx}\\
      &= \frac{e^{-c} \, c^s}{c^s - \int_0^c e^{-x} \left(c-x\right)^s dx}
      = \frac{e^{-c} \, c^s}{c^s - \int_0^1 c \, e^{-cx} \left(c-c\,x\right)^s dx}\\
      &= e^{-c} \left[1 - c \int_0^1 \left(1-x\right)^s e^{-cx}\, dx \right]^{-1}.
      \qedhere
    \end{align*}
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["psi(lambda) = log E e^{lambda X} finite for some lambda > 0 (otherwise the bound is vacuous)","for the i.i.d. rate statement: independent and identically distributed summands"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627588+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1fe4f3b747b727689cb17f579418ee4b2fd98070d9ff3fa9527f2e43df172cf8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a random variable with cumulant generating function psi(lambda) = log E[exp(lambda X)], finite on an interval containing 0 in its interior on the right. Then for every t, P(X >= t) <= exp(-psi^*(t)) where psi^*(t) = sup_{lambda >= 0} (lambda t - psi(lambda)) is the (one-sided) Legendre transform of psi. If X = sum_{i=1}^n X_i with the X_i independent and identically distributed with cumulant generating function psi_1, then psi = n psi_1 and P(X >= n t) <= exp(-n psi_1^*(t)): the exponent is LINEAR in n with rate psi_1^*(t), the Cramer rate function. Cramer's theorem says this exponential rate is exactly right, that is (1/n) log P(X >= n t) -> -psi_1^*(t) for t > E[X_1] under a finiteness condition on psi_1 near 0, so the Chernoff bound loses nothing at the level of the exponential rate although it can lose polynomial factors. The method requires SOME finite exponential moment: without it psi^* is identically 0 for t above the mean and the bound is vacuous, which is the correct behaviour for heavy-tailed laws. [standard; e.g. Dembo and Zeitouni, Large Deviations Techniques and Applications, 2nd ed., Chapter 2]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Finite alphabet with distinguished bot, p(bot)=0, n>=1 and |Y|>n+1.","IID samples; uniform two-level generator; exact score-level calibration."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:47:07.141514+00:00","domain":"Probability and statistical learning","id":"claim_1fe7454ed03fbc5eeea1731233890e57bc9fbe461251031ca9ef44c62ace1df2","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Y be finite with a distinguished always-true empty fact bot, let n>=1 and |Y|>n+1, and let p be any probability law on Y with p(bot)=0. Let B(g) be the partition into nonempty equal-g-probability level sets, let p^B be uniform within each level set with its original p mass, and define Mis_infinity(g,p)=TV(p^B,g). Deterministically, g(H)<=GT and Mis_infinity(g,p)<=|p(U)-GT|. Hence, for every delta in(0,1], Pr(g(H)<=GT and Mis_infinity(g,p)<=3*sqrt(log(4/delta)/n))>=1-delta. This is a deliberately inefficient matching construction in the source calibration notion. If factoids have a surjective document representation, choosing one representative document per factoid realizes g as a document generator. The zero empty-fact mass and alphabet-size assumptions here make all singleton and denominator conventions explicit; no claim for arbitrary non-iid corpora is included. If the two assigned per-symbol scores are distinct, Mis_infinity(g,p)=|p(U)-GT| exactly. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:33:06.539656+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1fea0f5c0f54d9f9c823de33004b7daa6c88e4fde46eb8ae58981add9445da37","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 17 of arXiv:2608.25829, 'Topology of low-dimensional generalized Ricci solitons and string backgrounds'] Let $(M, g, J)$ be a compact BHE threefold such that the finite cover guaranteed by Theorem \\ref{t:splitting} has $k = 1$. Thus $Z^\\mathcal H = 0$.  Thus $Z \\in \\mathrm{span} \\{V, JV \\}$, and using that it generates a trivial $S^1$ action, it follows from the Hermitian-Einstein equation for $JV$ that $\\IP{Z, JV} = 0$. The family is uniformly integrable if and only if there exists a nondecreasing convex function G : [0, infinity) -> [0, infinity) with G(t)/t -> infinity as t -> infinity such that sup_{i in I} E[G(|X_i|)] < infinity. The sufficiency direction is the one used in practice: a uniform bound on any superlinear moment, for example sup_i E[|X_i|^p] < infinity for a single p > 1, or sup_i E[|X_i| log^+ |X_i|] < infinity, forces uniform integrability. A uniform bound on the FIRST moment does not: on ([0,1], Lebesgue) the family X_n = n 1_{(0,1/n)} has E|X_n| = 1 for all n and is not uniformly integrable. [standard; e.g. Dellacherie and Meyer, Probabilities and Potential, or Williams, Probability with Martingales, Section 13.3]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.686380+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_20379a5dab6d932dbb7f2d5de4b388201a8eeacc73402556dcd59bdc4ce9d0cc","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 15 (Resonant skew-Hermitian endpoint identity) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $\Lambda\subset 2\pi\Q$ be finite and symmetric, and choose $m\geq1$ such that

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:32:35.610180+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2047058969970faf847b7f2324be353be0b235fdd8f019ee565f68c8925fae8c","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma Monotonicity of arXiv:2606.13264, 'Interference Queueing Networks: A Replica Mean-Field Approach in the Symmetric Setting'] The Markov chain $Q$ is monotone with respect to the arrival rate, the initial condition, and the departure rate. More precisely:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Monotonicity in the arrival rate.} If $\lambda_1 < \lambda_2$, then the chains $Q^{(1)}$ and $Q^{(2)}$ defined by \emph{(2)} with arrival rates $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2$ and $Q^{(1)}(0)=Q^{(2)}(0)$ satisfy
    \[
    Q^{(1)} \leq_{\mathrm{st}} Q^{(2)}.
    \]

    \item \textbf{Monotonicity in the initial condition.} If $x \leq y$, then the chains $Q^x$ and $Q^y$ defined by \emph{(2)} with initial conditions $Q^x(0)=x$ and $Q^y(0)=y$ satisfy
    \[
    Q^x \leq_{\mathrm{st}} Q^y.
    \]

    \item \textbf{Monotonicity in the departure rate.} If for all $i \in [1;N]$, $f \leq \mu_i$ (resp. $f \geq \mu_i$), and $Q^f(0)=Q(0)$, then the chain $Q^f$ defined by \emph{(2)} with departure rate $\mu_i = f$ for every $i$ satisfies
    \[
    Q \leq_{\mathrm{st}} Q^f
    \qquad (\text{resp. } Q^f \leq_{\mathrm{st}} Q).
    \]
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["uniform measure","[n] = J u K a partition","Walsh coefficients of a restriction are taken on its own cube"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T09:29:33.705548+00:00","domain":"analysis of Boolean functions","id":"claim_207104880458c0a7ad3072764e2ab46f87bf491d4f949fb38e8f34f9097538d1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"On {-1, 1}^n (n >= 1) with the uniform probability measure mu, chi_S(x) = prod over i in S of x_i for S inside [n], and f^(S) = E[f chi_S] is the Walsh-Fourier coefficient of a real function f, so f = sum over S of f^(S) chi_S. If Z is uniform on {-1, 1}^K, then E_Z[f_{J|Z}^(S)] = f^(S), E_Z[f_{J|Z}^(S)^2] = sum over T inside K of f^(S u T)^2, and E_Z ||f_{J|Z}||_2^2 = ||f||_2^2, each norm under the uniform measure of its own cube. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:57:59.871767+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_207bdb765cc205e69712a966a37eaf6b75efb9ca522347af69adc7399d52a032","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop sparsestack-fails-osi of arXiv:2607.05384, 'Well-invertible column subsets of sparse matrices are rare'] There is a universal constant $c>0$ with the following property.
Let $\zeta_k\ge2$ be an integer sequence with $\zeta_k\mid k$, set

\[
\rho k\le r(k)\le k
\quad\text{for some fixed }\rho\in(0,1],
\qquad
\frac{n_k}{r(k)}\to\infty.
\]
Set
\[
s_k:=\min\left\{k,\frac{n_k}{k}\right\},
\]
and assume
\[
\zeta_k=O\big(\log s_k\big)^c.
\]
For each such $k$, let $S^{(k)}\in\mathbb R^{n_k\times k}$ be a SparseStack
matrix with row sparsity $\zeta_k$ and block size $b(k)$. Let
$T_k\subseteq[n_k]$ be any deterministic subset with $|T_k|=r(k)$.
Then
\[
s_{\min}\left(((S^{(k)})^\top)_{T_k}\right)=o(1)
\]
with probability $1-o(1)$. In particular, 
the SparseStack with the given parameters
is not $(r(k),1/2)$-OSI. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.348858+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_208f7c4d1a65f4167efac3277e11eddaa90b1e153739b4d3e12334ae49c18c70","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 165 ($\by$ is Lipschitz) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Take $\by\equiv \by(q_{d+1})$ as in \eqref{e:normalized.vectors.y}, so it is measurable with respect to $\cG(q_{d+1})$, as defined by \eqref{e:gaus.filt}. 
Conditional on $\cG(q_d)$,
the random vector $\by$ has mean zero, and is subgaussian with variance proxy $L^{O(1)}$.

\begin{proof} Let us abbreviate
	\[
	\bXi
	\equiv \bXi^{d+1}
	\equiv \frac{\bG(q_{d+1})
		-\bG(q_d)}{\sqrt{p_{d+1}-p_d}}\,,
	\]
so this is a gaussian independent of $\cG(q_d)$. Then we can express
	\begin{align*}
	\sqrt{\delta_d}\by
	&\stackrel{\eqref{e:normalized.vectors.y}}{=}
	\E\bigg[ \cA\Big(
		\bG(q_d)
		+(p_{d+1}-p_d)^{1/2}\bXi
		+ (1-p_{d+1})^{1/2} \bG'\Big)\,\bigg|\,\bG(q_d),\bXi
		\bigg]\\
	&\qquad-\E\bigg[ \cA\Big(
		\bG(q_d)
		+(p_{d+1}-p_d)^{1/2}\bXi
		+ (1-p_{d+1})^{1/2} \bG'\Big)\,\bigg|\,\bG(q_d)\bigg] \,.
	\end{align*}
Thus, conditional on $\cG(q_d)$,
the vector $\by$ has mean zero.
It follows by the assumption on $\cA$ together with assumption~\eqref{e:deriv.p.bound} that
 $\by$ is $L^{O(1)}$-Lipschitz in $\bXi$, so the subgaussian claim follows using Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:33.592384+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2092f4f49ea0d52063ec02bc8e3f7158aa9283d9f4c1bbf8e17c9a7aebe64b24","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Abstract of arXiv:2609.03466, 'Least-Favorable Location for Binomial Top-$t$ Selection'] Consider $k$ independent Bernoulli populations, each sampled $n$ times, and select the $t$ populations with the largest success counts, breaking ties uniformly. {"assumptions":["X is a topological space and T: X → X a map","for the orbit-closure characterization, T is continuous"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.111010+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics","id":"claim_20ab9dec4c9cbfd28df1fff4fca5251efcaf20965cb1e82ec6c01020cfd918be","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a topological space and T: X → X a map. A set A ⊂ X is (forward) invariant if T(A) ⊆ A. A minimal set is a nonempty closed invariant set M that contains no proper nonempty closed invariant subset. Some authors require T(M) = M (strict invariance); for a continuous T on a compact Hausdorff space a minimal set in the above sense automatically satisfies T(M) = M, since T(M) is then itself nonempty, closed (compact image) and invariant, hence equal to M. Characterization (T continuous): a nonempty closed invariant M is minimal if and only if for every x ∈ M the forward orbit {Tⁿx : n ≥ 0} is dense in M. Proof of the equivalence: for x ∈ M the orbit closure cl{Tⁿx : n ≥ 0} is nonempty, closed, contained in M, and invariant because continuity gives T(cl O) ⊆ cl T(O) ⊆ cl O; so minimality forces it to equal M; conversely, if every orbit in M is dense and N ⊂ M is nonempty closed invariant, any x ∈ N has its orbit inside N, so M = cl(orbit) ⊆ N. The system (X,T) itself is called minimal if X is a minimal set, i.e. every forward orbit is dense. Examples: a periodic orbit is a minimal set; an irrational rotation of the circle is minimal; the closure of a non-periodic orbit is in general NOT minimal (e.g. the orbit closure of a point of the doubling map whose orbit is dense contains the fixed point 0 as a smaller minimal set). Continuity is used in the orbit-closure characterization; the definition of a minimal set itself does not need it. For flows and group/semigroup actions the same definitions apply with 'orbit' read as the (semi)group orbit.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["INFINITE exchangeability; the theorem is false for finite exchangeable sequences","values in a Polish space, so that regular conditional distributions and a countable determining class exist"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.781914+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_20e7e94fd93a2e51ba5becdbc47068b21245cc7d9d4def4e9e32ec611d9265ad","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, X_2, ... be an INFINITE exchangeable sequence of random variables taking values in a Polish space S, meaning that for every n the law of (X_1, ..., X_n) is invariant under permutations of the n coordinates. Then there is a random probability measure Theta on S, measurable with respect to the exchangeable sigma-algebra, such that CONDITIONALLY on Theta the X_i are i.i.d. with common law Theta. Equivalently the law of the sequence is a MIXTURE of i.i.d. laws, and Theta is the almost sure limit of the empirical measures (1/n) sum_{i <= n} delta_{X_i}. The theorem is FALSE for finite exchangeable sequences. Counterexample with n = 2: let (X_1, X_2) be uniform on {(0,1), (1,0)}. This is exchangeable, but any mixture of i.i.d. Bernoulli sequences has Cov(X_1, X_2) = E[p^2] - (E p)^2 = Var(p) >= 0, whereas here E[X_1] = E[X_2] = 1/2 and E[X_1 X_2] = 0 give Cov = -1/4 < 0. Sampling without replacement is exactly the mechanism, and it produces the negative correlation that no mixture of i.i.d. can. What DOES survive in finite length is a quantitative approximation, due to Diaconis and Freedman: an exchangeable sequence of length n, restricted to k of its coordinates, is close in total variation to a mixture of i.i.d. sequences, with an error of order k/n. So infinite exchangeability is the hypothesis and it is not decorative; 'exchangeable' alone, applied to a finite sample, does not license treating the data as conditionally i.i.d. [de Finetti (1931); Hewitt and Savage (1955) for the general Polish case; Diaconis and Freedman (1980) for the finite version]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the chain is reversible with respect to pi (real eigenvalues); the bounds are stated for the absolute spectral gap","aperiodicity (e.g. laziness) so that gamma* > 0","the upper bound carries the factor log(1/pi_min); the lower bound holds for epsilon < 1/2"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.049135+00:00","domain":"Markov chains and mixing (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_2114caacee9ef704ca7243abee0f8be7a280413638cb34b387097351ec0f2be3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let P be the transition matrix of an irreducible, reversible Markov chain on a finite state space with stationary distribution pi, and let gamma* = 1 - max{|lambda| : lambda an eigenvalue of P other than 1} be the absolute spectral gap, with relaxation time t_rel = 1/gamma*. Then for every epsilon in (0, 1/2) the total-variation mixing time satisfies (t_rel - 1) log(1/(2 epsilon)) <= t_mix(epsilon) <= t_rel log(1/(epsilon pi_min)), where pi_min is the smallest stationary probability (Levin, Peres, Wilmer, Theorems 12.4 and 12.5). Mixing time is therefore the relaxation time up to a factor between log(1/(2 epsilon)) and log(1/(epsilon pi_min)); on a state space of size N the gap between the two sides can be as large as log N, and neither side can be dropped in general. For a lazy chain (holding probability at least 1/2) all eigenvalues are nonnegative, so the absolute gap equals the ordinary gap 1 - lambda_2; a periodic chain (a simple random walk on a bipartite graph) has an eigenvalue -1, gamma* = 0, and never mixes.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:54:18.238551+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2129a3e63d44cbe12a6958ceaaec34446380d2b5315c4e8987f6dc50d7a3a782","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:packing-dimension of arXiv:2608.29561, 'Ball codes: A coding characterization of Hausdorff and packing dimensions'] {Falconer2014}}]

Let \(E\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(s\ge0\), and let \(\delta>0\).
A \(\delta\)-packing of \(E\) is a finite or countable, possibly empty, family \((B_i)_i\) of pairwise
disjoint closed balls of positive radius such that each \(B_i\) has center in \(E\) and
radius at most \(\delta\).  Define
\[
\mathcal P^s_\delta(E)
=
\sup
\left\{
\sum_i (\diam B_i)^s:
(B_i)_i \text{ is a }\delta\text{-packing of }E
\right\}.
\]
Then put
\[
\mathcal P^s_0(E)
=
\lim_{\delta\to0}\mathcal P^s_\delta(E).
\]
The \(s\)-dimensional packing measure of \(E\) is
\[
\mathcal P^s(E)
=
\inf
\left\{
\sum_{j=1}^\infty \mathcal P^s_0(E_j):
E\subseteq\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j
\right\}.
\]
The packing dimension of \(E\) is
\[
\dim_P(E)
=
\inf\{s\ge0:\mathcal P^s(E)=0\}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:31:57.866085+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_215bdd42b029f2faca44ec2589e5bd0f812548361f87037ecf3ccc313ab831c8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition d:dirstructure of arXiv:2510.13659, 'On the energy image density conjecture of Bouleau and Hirsch'] A \emph{Dirichlet structure}  $(X,\mathcal{X},\mu,\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{F})$ 	is a probability space $(X,\mathcal{X},\mu)$ along with a quadratic form $(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F})$ on $L^2(X,\mu)$ that satisfies the following properties.
		\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
			\item (densely defined, non-negative definite, quadratic form) $\mathcal{E}: \mathcal{F} \times \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}$ is bilinear, where $\mathcal{F}$ is a dense subspace of $L^2(X,\mu)$ and $\mathcal{E}(f,f) \ge 0$ for all $f \in \mathcal{F}$.
			\item (closed form) $(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F})$ is a \emph{closed} form; that is, $\mathcal{F}$ is a Hilbert space equipped with the inner product
			\[
			\mathcal{E}_1(f,g):= \mathcal{E}(f,g)+ \langle f,g \rangle_{L^2(\mu)}, \quad \mbox{for all $f,g \in \mathcal{F}$}.
			\]
			\item (Markovian property) $f \in \mathcal{F}$ implies that $\widetilde{f}:=0 \vee (f \wedge 1) \in \mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{E}(\widetilde{f},\widetilde{f}) \le \mathcal{E}(f,f)$.
			\item $\mathds{1} \in \mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{E}(\mathds{1},\mathds{1})=0$, where $\mathds{1}$ is the constant function on $X$ that is identically one.
			\item (existence of carr\'e du champ operator) For all $f \in \mathcal{F} \cap L^\infty(m)$, there exists $\gamma(f,f) \in L^1(m)$ such that for all $h \in \mathcal{F} \cap L^\infty(m)$, we have 
			\[
			\mathcal{E}(fh,f)- \frac{1}{2}\mathcal{E}(h,f^2)= \int h \gamma(f,f) \,d\mu.
			\]
			\item (strong locality) For all $f,g \in \mathcal{F}$ and $a \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $(f+a)g =0$ implies $\mathcal{E}(f,g)=0$.
		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:04:39.233271+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_217e2b9eebc4a73fc416b05fff2af3851bb25c18fbd04d21c9a23748409d43b6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 32 (Finite measurements in the Gaussian-origin formal branch) of arXiv:2608.14475, '\vspace{-1.2cm}\textbf{Finite Gaussian Reconstruction of Polynomial Orbits:\\ From Correla'] Let \(m\geq3\), let \(P\in\mathcal P_{d,m}\) be real,
\(r\geq1\), and
\(\Sigma\in\operatorname{Sym}_r^{++}(\R)\).  Define
\(\widehat\Phi^{\mathrm G}_{P,r,\Sigma}\) by the Wick series
\eqref{eq:central-Gaussian-Wick-series}, which is meaningful for every
polynomial \(P\), and put
\[
 Z_\Sigma=(2\pi)^{-rd/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-d/2}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 M_{P,r}(\Sigma)
 =
 i^{-r}
 [\rho^{(m-2)r}\lambda_1\cdots\lambda_r]\,
 \widehat\Phi^{\mathrm G}_{P,r,\Sigma}
 (\rho,\boldsymbol\lambda).}
 
\end{equation}

Assume in addition \eqref{eq:principal-isolated}.  Then this Wick series is
the formal period of the marked local Gaussian branch constructed in
\cref{prop:marked-Gaussian-level}.  If the leading rescaled phase is Morse
and satisfies \eqref{eq:central-nonresonance}, this branch is the canonical
rank-one zero-action summand of the full formal period system.  On every
origin-preserving radial chamber for which the rescaled phase is tame, Morse,
and has pairwise distinct critical values, the same identity is
\begin{equation}
 M_{P,r}(\Sigma)
 =
 i^{-r}
 [\rho^{(m-2)r}\lambda_1\cdots\lambda_r]\,
 \operatorname{Reg}^{\mathrm G}_0
 \left\{
 Z_\Sigma
 C_{\mathrm{Betti}}^{(r)}
 \mathcal P_{\mathrm{th}}^{(r)}
 B_{\mathrm{Jac}}^{(r)}e_{[1]}
 \right\}.
 
\end{equation}
Here \(\operatorname{Reg}^{\mathrm G}_0\) means projection of the complete
scalar period over the continued Gaussian contour in the sense of
\cref{def:marked-central-regular-part}.  The three matrices inside the
braces are multiplied before this projection.
The coefficient is extracted only after the origin summand has been
identified with its canonical polynomial formal extension
\(\widehat\Phi^{\mathrm G}_{P,r,\Sigma}
\in\C[\boldsymbol\lambda][[\rho]]\); it is not a Taylor coefficient of the
three separate chamber matrices at \(\boldsymbol\lambda=0\).
Here \(e_{[1]}\) denotes the coordinate vector of the constant Jacobi class
\([1]\) with its unnormalised volume form.
In rescaled coordinates, the Gaussian volume vector is
\[
 Z_\Sigma\rho^{-rd}e_{[1]}.
\]

Equivalently, for
\[
 \phi_{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}(t)
 =\Phi_{P,r,\Sigma}(t\boldsymbol\varepsilon),
 \qquad
 \boldsymbol\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}^r,
\]
one has the finite radial polarisation formula
\begin{equation}
 M_{P,r}(\Sigma)
 =
 \frac{i^{-r}}{2^rr!}
 \sum_{\boldsymbol\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}^r}
 \left(\prod_{a=1}^r\varepsilon_a\right)
 \phi_{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}^{(r)}(0).
 
\end{equation}
Suppose that every signed radial direction below is represented by an
origin-preserving chamber for which the rescaled phase is tame, Morse, and
has pairwise distinct critical values, and set
\[
 \bigl(
 C_{\boldsymbol\varepsilon},
 \mathcal P_{\boldsymbol\varepsilon},
 B_{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}
 \bigr)(\rho)
 =
 \bigl(
 C_{\mathrm{Betti}}^{(r)},
 \mathcal P_{\mathrm{th}}^{(r)},
 B_{\mathrm{Jac}}^{(r)}
 \bigr)(\rho^{m-2}\boldsymbol\varepsilon).
\]
After \(t=\rho^{m-2}\), the polarisation formula then becomes
\begin{equation}
 M_{P,r}(\Sigma)
 =
 \frac{i^{-r}}{2^r}
 \sum_{\boldsymbol\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}^r}
 \left(\prod_{a=1}^r\varepsilon_a\right)
 [\rho^{(m-2)r}]
 \operatorname{Reg}^{\mathrm G}_0
 \left\{
  Z_\Sigma C_{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}
  \mathcal P_{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}
  B_{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}e_{[1]}
 \right\}.
 
\end{equation}

For \(1\leq r\leq r_*(d,m)\) and
\(\Sigma\in\mathcal S_r\), the finite collection of coefficients in
\eqref{eq:normal-symbol-Torelli} is exactly the measurement vector
\(\mathbf J_{d,m}(P)\) defined in \eqref{eq:intro-finite-probe-map}.  Hence,
for arbitrary real \(P,Q\in\mathcal P_{d,m}\), equality of these finite
coefficient vectors is equivalent to \(Q=P\circ U\) for some \(U\in O(d)\).
Under \eqref{eq:central-nonresonance}, they are coefficients of the
canonical rank-one Gaussian-origin formal factor; under the stronger chamber
hypotheses above, they are recovered from the projected factorised period.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:31:49.910289+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_21931244b4db91d736e19507a99eae5d45246650639f17658377c90a511ac411","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:shifted-contours of arXiv:2608.26745, 'Moderate Deviations for the Largest Eigenvalue of a Randomly Deformed Gaussian Unitary Ens'] There exist constants $c,C,\eta>0$ such that, uniformly for
$\bm\xi\in\mathcal G_N$, the following statements hold for all sufficiently large
$N$.

If $r=d+t(1\pm {\rm i})\in\Gamma^\pm$, then
\begin{align}
 \Re\Phi_N(r)
 &\le C-ct^3,
 &&0\le t\le T_N^*,                                    \\
 \Re\Phi_N(r)
 &\le-cN-cN^{2/3}(t-T_N^*),
 &&T_N^*\le t<\infty.                                          
\end{align}

If $s=-d-t\pm {\rm i}t\in\Sigma^\pm$, then
\begin{align}
 -\Re\Phi_N(s)
 &\le C-ct^3,
 &&0\le t\le T_N^*,                                    \\
 -\Re\Phi_N(s)
 &\le-cN-cN^{2/3}(t-T_N^*),
 &&T_N^*\le t<\infty.                                          
\end{align}

On the local pieces $0\le t\le N^\eta$,
\begin{align}
 \Big|e^{\Phi_N(r)}-e^{r^3/3}\Big|
 \le CN^{-c}(1+t^4)e^{-ct^3},                          \\
 \Big|e^{-\Phi_N(s)}-e^{-s^3/3}\Big|
 \le CN^{-c}(1+t^4)e^{-ct^3}.                          
\end{align}

Moreover, after decreasing $\eta$ if necessary, for every fixed integer
$m\ge0$ there is a constant $C_m>0$ such that, whenever
$L^3\le c\log N$, uniformly for $0\le q\le L$,
$\rho\ge0$, and either choice of sign,
\begin{align}
 &\int_{N^\eta}^{\infty}(1+t^m)
 \exp\!\left\{\Re\Phi_N(d+t(1\pm {\rm i}))+q(d+t)-\rho(d+t)\right\}\,\mathrm d t
 \le C_m e^{-cN^{3\eta}}e^{-d\rho},  \\
 &\int_{N^\eta}^{\infty}(1+t^m)
 \exp\!\left\{-\Re\Phi_N(-d-t\pm {\rm i}t)+q(d+t)-\rho(d+t)\right\}\,\mathrm d t
 \le C_m e^{-cN^{3\eta}}e^{-d\rho}. 
\end{align}

The same estimates hold with $\Phi_N(\zeta)$ replaced by $\zeta^3/3$.  For a
nonnegative spatial variable (denoted by $x$ on $\Sigma$ and by $y$ on
$\Gamma$), the corresponding estimates hold after extracting $e^{-dx}$ or
$e^{-dy}$, respectively, and omitting the positive term $q(d+t)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.530224+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_21d2a5018cf74284bf204467cf2d5730a77c94fcd7b28d93caf66cb23f5f62f9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition eq:cutoff-event of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[proposition]{prop:quenched-cutoff}
Fix \(0\le\varepsilon<1/2\) and a Borel set \(B\subset\mathbb R\), with no
independence, identical-distribution, density, or genericity condition.
Set
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_{N,\varepsilon}
 =\left\{\max_{I\in[N]^p}|J_I|
 \le N^{1/2-\varepsilon}\right\},\qquad
 \delta_{N,\varepsilon}
 =\mathbb P(\mathcal T_{N,\varepsilon}^c),
\end{equation}
and, whenever the conditioning event has positive probability, write
\(\mathbb P_{N,\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{cut}}
:=\mathbb P(\,\cdot\mid\mathcal T_{N,\varepsilon})\).  If merely
\(\delta_{N,\varepsilon}=o(1)\), then the event has positive probability
for all sufficiently large \(N\), and
\[
 \left\lVert\nu-\nu'\right\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}
 :=\sup_A\left\lvert\nu(A)-\nu'(A)\right\rvert
\]
satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \left\|
 \mathcal L_{\mathbb P}\bigl(Q_N^J(B)\bigr)
 -\mathcal L_{\mathbb P_{N,\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{cut}}}
 \bigl(Q_N^J(B)\bigr)
 \right\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \le\delta_{N,\varepsilon}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, for every deterministic sequence \(a_N\), every
\(\eta>0\), and every bounded measurable
\(\varphi:[0,\infty]\to\mathbb R\),
\begin{align}
 &\left|
 \mathbb P\bigl(\left\lvertQ_N^J(B)-a_N\right\rvert>\eta\bigr)
 -\mathbb P_{N,\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{cut}}
  \bigl(\left\lvertQ_N^J(B)-a_N\right\rvert>\eta\bigr)
 \right|
 \le\delta_{N,\varepsilon},\\
 &\left|\mathbb E\varphi(Q_N^J(B))
 -\mathbb E_{N,\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{cut}}\varphi(Q_N^J(B))\right|
 \le2\left\lVert\varphi\right\rVert_\infty\delta_{N,\varepsilon}=o(1).
 
\end{align}
In particular, convergence of \(Q_N^J(B)\) in probability to a
deterministic limit is equivalent under the original and conditioned
laws.

The hypothesis \(\delta_{N,\varepsilon}=o(1)\) follows, for example,
from the marginal bound
\[
 \sup_{I\in[N]^p}\mathbb E\exp(J_I^2/K^2)\le2,
\]
which requires no independence and gives
\begin{equation}
 \delta_{N,\varepsilon}
 \le2N^p\exp\{-K^{-2}N^{1-2\varepsilon}\}=o(1).
\end{equation}
Mean comparison needs only a separate integrability input.  In
particular, if \(0\le Q_N^J(B)\le M_N\) almost surely and
\(M_N\delta_{N,\varepsilon}\to0\), then
\begin{equation}
 \left|\mathbb E Q_N^J(B)
 -\mathbb E_{N,\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{cut}}Q_N^J(B)\right|
 \le M_N\delta_{N,\varepsilon}=o(1).
\end{equation}
The critical-count ceiling \({\rm(CC)}_p\) is sufficient, with
\[
 M_N=\frac1N\log(1+D_{N,p})=O(1).
\]
Algebraic genericity gives the explicit \(N\)-independent choice
\begin{equation}
 M_N=M_p:=
 \log(p-1)+\log\left(1+\frac2{p-2}\right).

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.455056+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_21e45b969afbe673d949cb53a8009ea9ca25d0fc8aa7dccc755ee6f74c7ef167","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] \label[lemma]{lem:calYzero_negative_coefficient_control}
Let $f \in \Sym^0$ and write
\( f = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \alpha_k^0 \hat{f}_k^0 \)
as in (lem:calYzero_representation of the paper).
Then $\alpha_1^0 \ge 0$, and for all integers $j \ge 2$ such that $\alpha_j^0 \le 0$, we have $\min\{\alpha_{j\pm1}^0\} \ge \frac{p}{q}\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{\alpha_j^0}$. 

\begin{proof} 
Clearly 
\[ 0 \le f(0) = \sum_{k \ge 1} \alpha_k^0 \hat{f}_k^0(0) = \alpha_1^0 \hat{f}_1^0(0) = \frac{\alpha_1^0}{2}, \]
thus $\alpha_1^0 \ge 0$. 
Now let $j$ be such that $\alpha_j^0 \le 0$. 
Then, 
\begin{align*}
0 \le f(-2j) 
&= \alpha_{j+1}^0 \hat{f}_{j+1}^0(-2j) + \alpha_{j}^0 \hat{f}_{j}^0(-2j) \\
&= \alpha_{j+1}^0 \left(\frac{q}{2}\right) + \alpha_{j}^0 \left( \frac{p}{2} \right) , 
\end{align*}
thus $\alpha_{j+1}^0 \ge -\frac{p}{q}\alpha_j^0 = \frac{p}{q}\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{\alpha_j^0}$. 

The same argument applied at $f(2j-2)$ yields
\[
0 \le f(2j-2) = \left(\frac{p}{2}\right)\alpha_j^0 + \left(\frac{q}{2}\right)\alpha_{j-1}^0 ,
\]
thus $\alpha_{j-1}^0 \ge -\frac{p}{q}\alpha_j^0 = \frac{p}{q}\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{\alpha_j^0}$ as well. 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:48:27.285724+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_21fa667e4f20a4dba84be8b1f1a34ab39cdaaa7cb51486ab9a34f61c7d673963","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 15 (Concept retrieval for variable sizes) of arXiv:2604.25470, 'A mathematical analysis of hierarchical Hopfield models'] Fix $\delta\in(0,1)$, $\rho\in\mathbb N_0$, and $a,b>0$. Let $1\le \ell\le u$  and

	\[
	\widehat\alpha_{\ell,u}(x)
	:=

	\mathrm{score}^{\mathrm{pen}}_\beta(x).
	\]
	Then for every concept $\alpha$,
	\[
	\mathbb P\bigl(\widehat\alpha_{\ell,u}(x)\neq\alpha\bigr)
	\le
	\mathbb P\bigl(\mathcal G_\alpha(\delta,\rho)^c\bigr)
	+
	\mathbb P\bigl(L_\alpha\notin[\ell,u]\bigr)

	\mathbb P\Bigl(
	\max_{\beta\in\mathcal A_{\ell,u}\setminus\{\alpha\}}
	|S_\alpha\cap S_\beta|
	\ge t_{\ell,u}+1
	\Bigr). 
	\]
    Consequently, by Lemma \ref{lem:overlap-random-sizes}, we have that
	\[\begin{split}
	\mathbb P\bigl(\widehat\alpha_{\ell,u}(x)\neq\alpha,\ \alpha\in\mathcal A_{\ell,u}\bigr)
	\le
	&~\mathbb P\bigl(\mathcal G_\alpha(\delta,\rho)^c,\ \alpha\in\mathcal A_{\ell,u}\bigr)
	+
	\mathbb P(L_\alpha\notin[\ell,u])
    \\
	&{}\quad+
	(P-1)\binom{u}{t_{\ell,u}+1}
	\Bigl(\frac{u}{M-t_{\ell,u}}\Bigr)^{t_{\ell,u}+1}.
	\end{split}
    \]","status":"unverified"}

\[

    \[

    \]
    The image of $I$ has order $\ell(\ell - 1)$ and can be represented as
    \[
        H_2=\left\{\begin{pmatrix} a & b\\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}: a\in \mathbb{F}_{\ell}^{\times},\ b\in \mathbb{F}_{\ell}\right\}.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.475849+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2241c2dcbe935c83a527a497c055a37d9e332d394c44443d2d28ea2978e92471","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:no_symmetrizers_in_interior of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] Let $G$ be a compact group with Haar measure $\mu$ and let $f$ be a probability density with respect to $\mu$. 
If $\inf_{x \in G} f(x) > 0$, 
then $f$ is \emph{not} symmetrization resistant in $G$. 

\begin{proof}
By (lem:f_- and u are symmetrizers of the paper), $f_-$ and the uniform $u$ are both in $\Sym(f)$. 
Without loss of generality we take $\mu(G)=1$. 

In the case $h(f) = h(u)$, we have $h(u) - h(f) = D_{KL}\infdivx{f}{u} \ge 0$, with equality if and only if $f = u$ $\mu$-a.e.. 
Thus $f * g = u * g = u$ for any probability density $g$ on $G$, so this $f$ is not symmetrization resistant. 
Thus we assume $h(f) < h(u)$. 

Define $\varepsilon \coloneqq \inf f_- = \inf f  \in (0,1)$ and $b = \frac{f_- - \varepsilon u}{1-\varepsilon}$. 
Since $b \ge 0$, $b$ is a probability measure, and since the symmetry equations are linear, $b \in \Sym(f)$. 
Thus $f_- = (1-\varepsilon)b + \varepsilon u$. 
Applying concavity of entropy, 
\begin{align*} h(f) 
= h(f_-) 
= h(\varepsilon u + (1-\varepsilon) b)
&\ge \varepsilon h(u) + (1-\varepsilon) h(b) \\
&> \varepsilon h(f) + (1-\varepsilon) h(b) 
\end{align*}
so that $h(f) > h(b)$. 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

	\[\Phi_L:=\left(\prod_{w\in W/W_{[L]}} wL\right)^{n(L)}\in \text{Sym}^*(\mathfrak{t}^*)^W,\]
	where $W_{[L]}$ is the stabilizer of $[L]:=\{\pm L\}\in \mathfrak{t}^*/\{\pm 1\}$, $n(L)=1$ or 2 depending on whether $\displaystyle\prod_{w\in W/W_{[L]}}wL$ is $W$-invariant or $W$-anti-invariant, i.e.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:07:35.020004+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_22579e0013e3790d51f813ba1becd014cb593a5097ee0a2b9087ed0d03bfb032","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 35 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Let \(Z\) be a connected normal complex space whose dense analytic

intrinsic length distance, and that \((Z,d)\) is a complete locally
compact length space equal to the metric completion of \((\cR,g)\).

positive current with bounded potential, and that every point has a
local closed holomorphic embedding
\(V\hookrightarrow\Omega_V\subset\C^L\) for which
\begin{equation}
                     \omega_g\ge c_V\omega_{\C^L}
                     \quad\text{on }V\cap\cR.
\end{equation}
Let $G:Z\to\C^r$ be continuous and holomorphic, and
assume on $\cR$ that
\begin{equation}
 \nabla dG^a=0,\qquad
 \left[\langle dG^a,d\overline{G^b}\rangle_{g^{-1}}\right]_{a,b=1}^r
 \text{ is positive definite}.
\end{equation}
Then, after composing \(G\) with an element of

biholomorphic isometry
\begin{equation}
                         Z\cong\C^r\times Z'
\end{equation}
under which $G$ is the projection.  The factor $Z'$ is connected, complete,
normal, and klt; write \(g'\) for its induced regular K\"ahler metric.
It inherits the bounded-local-potential K\"ahler current
and the local ambient metric lower bound of $Z$, and
\begin{equation}
                         \Sing Z=\C^r\times\Sing Z'.
\end{equation}

If, in addition, $f$ is locally Lipschitz on $Z$, smooth on $\cR$, and
satisfies \(\Rc+\nabla^2f=g/2\) on $\cR$, then
\[
                 f(z,y)=\frac{|z|^2}{4}+\ell(z)+f'(y),
\]
where $\ell$ is real affine-linear and $f'$ is locally Lipschitz; if $f$
is proper, then $f'$ is proper.  If also
\begin{equation}
                         \int_{\cR}e^{-f}\,dV_g<\infty,
\end{equation}
then \(\int_{\Reg Z'}e^{-f'}\,dV_{g'}<\infty\).  Finally, assume that
the flow of \(\nabla f\) is complete and preserves \(\cR\), and that its
canonical self-similar maps extend to the metric completions.  Then the

{"assumptions":["Bernoulli percolation on the discrete torus, d > 6","Mean-field cluster geometry (intrinsic diameter m^{1/2}, Euclidean diameter m^{1/4})"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T07:48:45.952251+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2279334a78f40f9f470203698541f2090e13571639d4fc686f5a52efb3646d33","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"PRIVATE MECHANISM NOTE, author-recorded. On the torus T_{n,d} with volume V, a critical cluster of size V^{2/3} has intrinsic geometry of a critical tree embedded four-dimensionally, so its Euclidean diameter is of order (V^{2/3})^{1/4} = V^{1/6}, while the torus side is V^{1/d}. Since V^{1/6} > V^{1/d} iff d > 6, above six dimensions the window clusters wrap around the torus many times and see the torus uniformly; this is why the exploration process should have the same global (mass-proportional) depletion as in G(n,p), which is what the multiplicative-coalescent scaling limit (Heydenreich-van der Hofstad Open Problems 13.3 and 13.5) needs. The torus plateau theorem (Hutchcroft-Michta-Slade) is the two-point version of this uniformity; the open step is the exploration-level (higher-point) version. Same reason makes eps >> V^{-1/3} lie above the correlation-length crossover eps >> V^{-2/d} for d > 6 (Open Problem 13.2).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Galton-Watson with P(D=2) = 3/5, P(D=3) = 2/5","consistent equivariant flow rule choosing uniformly among same-coloured children"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:11:19.450036+00:00","domain":"probability, trees, ergodic theory","id":"claim_22df461caf6d08479ba0f1da9d8fdedbb4603bca52d4395ae62573d0bad9bec1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Lyons and Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks (version 19 August 2026), Question 17.18 (p. 575) asks whether a consistent equivariant flow rule admitting a stationary measure EQUIVALENT to Galton-Watson measure must induce an ergodic Markov chain; their Proposition 17.17 proves it when all child weights are strictly positive, and Exercise 17.22 gives a non-ergodic example whose stationary measure is only absolutely continuous, so equivalence is the point of the question. Our result (id P0033, 2026-09-08): NO. Take Galton-Watson with P(D=2) = 3/5, P(D=3) = 2/5 (mean 12/5) and an isomorphism-invariant colour in {0,1} defined by AND at two-child vertices and OR at three-child vertices; both preserve unanimity, so every vertex has at least one child of its own colour, and the flow chooses uniformly among those. Galton-Watson measure is stationary, the root colour is invariant along the chain and takes each value with probability 1/2 - a non-constant invariant function, hence no ergodicity - and the stationary measure equals Galton-Watson measure, trivially equivalent to it. The colour exists because F(p) = (3/5) p^2 + (2/5)[1 - (1-p)^3] fixes 1/2, and r_n = E[q_n^2] satisfies r_{n+1} = 3/10 + (3/5) r^2 + (2/5) r^3 whose increment factors as (r - 1/2)[(2/5) r^2 + (4/5) r - 3/5], driving r_n from r_0 = 1/4 up to 1/2 and giving E[q(1-q)] = 0. Verification as the source words it: the step the proof leaves implicit, and which was checked, is that Galton-Watson really is stationary - it holds because, conditioned on the children's colours, the child subtrees are independent, each distributed as Galton-Watson conditioned on its own colour, so the chosen subtree is exactly GW given colour = c, the uniform choice adds no bias, and mixing over c returns GW. Prior art unchecked; the tree-automaton and factor-of-iid literature is where to look.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:37:15.060495+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_22e3220c4d656df74b5d8f73283dcfda6cb7f51a72f552e1865f5f268dc96bb6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 20 of arXiv:2607.11756, 'Full replica symmetry breaking in the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick model'] Let $\nu$ be a Borel probability measure on $[0,1]$, and write
\[
 \alpha_\nu(s)=\nu([0,s]),\qquad u=u_\nu.
\]
Let $X^\nu$ be the optimal diffusion
\[
 \dd X_s^\nu
 =\beta^2\alpha_\nu(s)u_x(s,X_s^\nu)\dd s+\beta\dd W_s,
 \qquad X_0^\nu=0.
\]
For every $s>0$, the law of $X_s^\nu$ has a strictly positive
$C^\infty$ density $p_\nu(s,\cdot)$. Define
\begin{equation}
 r_\nu(s,x)
 =\exp\{-\alpha_\nu(s)u(s,x)\}p_\nu(s,x),
 \qquad
 V_\nu(s,x)=-\log r_\nu(s,x).
\end{equation}
Then, for every $s>0$,
\begin{equation}
 r_\nu(s,x)
 =g_{\beta^2s}(x)
 \E_{\mathrm{br}}\exp\left\{
 -\int_{[0,s]}
 u\left(t,\frac tsx+\beta\mathfrak b_t^{\,s}\right)
 \nu(\dd t)
 \right\}.
\end{equation}
If $\alpha_\nu\equiv m$ on an open interval $(a,b)$, then
\begin{equation}
 (r_\nu)_s=\frac{\beta^2}{2}(r_\nu)_{xx}
 \qquad\text{on }(a,b)\times\R.
\end{equation}
If $q\in(0,1]$ is an atom of $\nu$ of size $c=\nu(\{q\})$, then
\begin{equation}
 r_\nu(q,x)=\e^{-cu(q,x)}r_\nu(q-,x),
\end{equation}
where
\[
 r_\nu(q-,x)
 =\e^{-\alpha_\nu(q-)u(q,x)}p_\nu(q,x).
\]
Finally, $r_\nu(s,\cdot)$ is even and log-concave, and
\begin{equation}
 (V_\nu)_x(s,x)\ge0,
 \qquad
 (V_\nu)_{xx}(s,x)\ge0,
 \qquad
 (V_\nu)_{xxx}(s,x)\le0,
 \qquad x>0.
\end{equation}
By parity,
\[
 (V_\nu)_x(s,0)=(V_\nu)_{xxx}(s,0)=0.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:02:17.961506+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_22f066ca6a6a6ee0da22eaed93c3cba977632e205ded78faf177c1b8cef9af89","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:trajectory of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix a positive integer~$j$. Fix a send sequence~$\overline{p}$ with $p_0=1$, a non-negative integer~$\tau$, and a $\lambda\in (0,1)$. 
Let $\mathcal{P}$ be a distribution with support $(\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0})^j$.
Let $Y$ be a $j$-jammed process with send sequence~$\overline{p}$, start time~$\tau$, birth rate~$\lambda$, and initial population size distribution~$\mathcal{P}$.
Let $t\geq\tau$ be an integer.

A \emph{ball trajectory} up to time~$t$ is a 
tuple \newsym{tr}{ball trajectory up to time $t$}{\overline{\mathrm{tr}}  := ({\mathrm{tr}}_\tau,\ldots,{\mathrm{tr}}_t)} of integers in $\{0, \ldots, j+1\}$ 
such that
$\mathrm{tr}_\tau \leq j$ and, for all $t' \in \{\tau+1,\ldots,t\}$,
$\mathrm{tr}_{t'} \in 
\{\mathrm{tr}_{t'-1}, \mathrm{tr}_{t'-1} + 1\}$.  
 

For any $t'\in \{\tau,\ldots,t\}$ such that ${\mathrm{tr}}_{t'} \in [j]$, a ball following trajectory~$\overline{\mathrm{tr}}$ is in  $\mathbf{b}_{{\mathrm{tr}}_{t'}}^Y(t')$.
If  ${\mathrm{tr}}_{t'} = 0$, then the ball is born after time~$t'$ -- that is, there is a $t''>t'$ such that the ball is in $\mathbf{n}^Y(t'')$.
If ${\mathrm{tr}}_{t'} = j+1$, then the ball sends from bin~$j$ (and leaves the system) by time~$t'$ -- that is, there is a $t'' \leq t'$ such that the ball is in $\mathbf{s}_j^Y(t'')$.

 
 
For every   integer~$t\geq \tau$ and every
$x\in \{0,\ldots,j+1\}$, let 
\newsym{T-x-t}{set of ball trajectories ending in bin $x$}{\mathcal{T}^Y(x,t)} be the set of all ball trajectories up to time~$t$ 
with ${\mathrm{tr}}_t = x$. 
Let 
\newsym{T-x}{set of ball trajectories}{\mathcal{T}^Y(t)} be the set of all ball trajectories up to time~$t$, that is $\mathcal{T}^Y(t) = \cup_{x\in \{0,\ldots,j+1\}} \mathcal{T}^Y(x,t)$.
For $\mathrm{tr} \in \mathcal{T}^Y(t)$, let 
\newsym{b-tr}{set of balls following a trajectory}{\mathbf{b}^Y_\mathrm{tr}} be the set of balls that follow trajectory~$\mathrm{tr}$ and let 
\newsym{b-tr-2}{$|\mathbf{b}^Y_\mathrm{tr}|$}{b^Y_\mathrm{tr}} be  $|\mathbf{b}^Y_\mathrm{tr}|$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:52:05.645560+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2324fec8f9d3b1041bafe226425b97d612553bf00e5d428e0437ee0d7723d8e0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn Local sets of arXiv:2602.06011, 'Excursion decomposition of the XOR-Ising model'] A coupling $(\phi,A,\phi_A)$ between a GFF $\phi$ in $D$, a random closed set $A \subset \bar{D}$ and a distribution $\phi_A$ is called a \emph{local set (coupling)} if

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:05:52.484116+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_232ad64da67b53b2162d8c096bfce0dbcf0c9f8dd1389336552f8794cebade9f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition eq:v-grad of arXiv:2505.02685, 'On the Spectral Expansion of Monotone Subsets of the Hypercube'] We say that $F : L^2(V) \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$ is \emph{Fréchet differentiable} at $f \in L^2(V)$ if there
    exists a bounded linear operator $A : L^2(V) \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$ such that
    \[
        \lim_{\|h\|_{2} \to 0} \frac{\abs*{F(f+h) - F(f) - Ah}}{\|h\|_{2}} = 0 \,.
    \]
    In this case, we call $DF(f) \vcentcolon= A$ the \emph{Fréchet derivative} of $F$ at $f$. Moreover,
    by the Riesz representation theorem there exists a unique vector $v \in L^2(V)$ satisfying
    \begin{equation}
        
        Ah = \inp{h}{v}
    \end{equation}
    for all $h \in L^2(V)$. We call $\nabla F(f) \vcentcolon= v$ the \emph{gradient} of $F$ at $f$.
    Finally, we say that $F$ is (Fréchet) $C^1$ if it is Fréchet differentiable at every $f \in
    L^2(V)$ and the map $f \mapsto DF(f)$ (from $L^2(V)$ to the space of bounded linear operators
    $L^2(V) \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$) is continuous.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X compact metric, T continuous and topologically exact","T is a local homeomorphism with finite fibres, so that L maps C(X) into C(X)","the weight w is continuous and strictly positive everywhere","there exist lambda > 0 and h in C(X) with h > 0 everywhere and L h = lambda h","there exists a Borel probability measure nu with L* nu = lambda nu (used only for algebraic simplicity)","the conclusion is about the eigenvalues of L acting on C(X); no Banach space of Holder or bounded-variation functions and no quasi-compactness is assumed"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090835+00:00","domain":"thermodynamic formalism, transfer operators, Perron-Frobenius theory","id":"claim_237e639d0e9ed9df151e70d43e37add45d9d02ba588674ca6999612a5fb36cf3","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"SETTING: X a compact metric space; T : X -> X a continuous, topologically exact map which is a local homeomorphism with finite fibres (so that the operator below sends continuous functions to continuous functions); w : X -> (0, infinity) a continuous weight. Define the transfer (Ruelle) operator on complex continuous functions by (L f)(x) = the sum of w(y) f(y) over the finitely many y with T(y) = x; L is a bounded positive operator on C(X). Assume the Perron data exist: a number lambda > 0 and a strictly positive h in C(X) with L h = lambda h, together with a Borel probability measure nu with L* nu = lambda nu, i.e. the integral of L f with respect to nu equals lambda times the integral of f with respect to nu for all f in C(X). CONCLUSION: (1) if f in C(X) is complex-valued and L f = z f with |z| = lambda, then z = lambda and f is a constant multiple of h - so lambda is the only eigenvalue of modulus lambda in C(X) and its eigenspace is one dimensional; (2) lambda is ALGEBRAICALLY simple: there is no f in C(X) with L f - lambda f = h, hence no Jordan block at lambda. WHERE THE HYPOTHESES BITE: (i) exactness cannot be weakened to minimality, unique ergodicity or transitivity. Take X the circle, T an irrational rotation and w identically 1, so that L f = f composed with T^{-1}: every character exp(2 pi i n x) is an eigenfunction with an eigenvalue of modulus 1, so the peripheral spectrum is infinite - and the system is minimal and uniquely ergodic but not exact (it is invertible, hence never exact). (ii) Strict positivity of the weight is essential. If w may vanish, the irreducibility can become periodic: in the finite-state model, where L is a nonnegative matrix, the statement above is the PRIMITIVE case of the Perron-Frobenius theorem, and an irreducible matrix of period p > 1 has exactly p eigenvalues of modulus equal to its spectral radius, so simplicity of the peripheral eigenvalue genuinely fails. (iii) The conclusion concerns the peripheral eigenvalue only and gives NO spectral gap: to place the rest of the spectrum in a strictly smaller disc one needs quasi-compactness (a Lasota-Yorke or Ionescu-Tulcea-Marinescu inequality on a Holder or bounded-variation space), a separate hypothesis on the regularity of w and the expansion of T. (iv) The existence of h and nu is assumed here, not proved; producing them is the other half of the Ruelle-Perron-Frobenius theorem and needs its own hypotheses.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A finite with at least two elements (for N = 1 the maximum has mean 0)","the signs are independent and symmetric; the bound is on the expectation over the signs only, the vectors are fixed"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:40:13.706093+00:00","domain":"probability and learning theory","id":"claim_238153b7dd2c94196c2f503107fe4086af1bd720d344b15f76689b1605667c76","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be a finite subset of R^n with N = |A| >= 2 elements, and let r = max_{a in A} ||a||_2. Let sigma_1, ..., sigma_n be independent Rademacher signs (uniform on {-1, +1}). Then E_sigma [ max_{a in A} sum_{i=1}^{n} sigma_i a_i ] <= r sqrt(2 log N), and consequently E_sigma [ max_{a in A} (1/n) sum_i sigma_i a_i ] <= r sqrt(2 log N) / n. Two consequences used constantly in learning theory: (1) for a finite class F of functions bounded by B on a sample x_1, ..., x_n, the empirical Rademacher complexity satisfies R_hat_S(F) = E_sigma sup_{f in F} (1/n) sum_i sigma_i f(x_i) <= B sqrt(2 log |F| / n), since each vector (f(x_1), ..., f(x_n)) has Euclidean norm at most B sqrt(n); (2) for a class C of sets of VC dimension d, restricting to the sample leaves at most s(C, n) <= (e n / d)^d distinct indicator vectors (Sauer-Shelah), each of norm at most sqrt(n), so R_hat_S(C) <= sqrt(2 d log(e n / d) / n) for n >= d. The logarithm cannot be removed at this generality: for A = {-1, +1}^n (N = 2^n, r = sqrt(n)) the maximum is exactly n while the bound reads n sqrt(2 log 2), so the lemma is sharp up to the constant sqrt(2 log 2) = 1.18; for VC classes Dudley's chaining removes the logarithm, R_hat_S(C) <= C sqrt(d / n).","status":"unverified"}
