{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.179244+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3e7c028e15ea54077751c874676a322fafb4f9ef09b31515f5992a62c85933b6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 91 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] We have $\sM^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0) \subseteq \sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha,0)$.
\begin{proof} Consider any $\mu \in \cM^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)$.
    Then, there exists
    \[
        (q_*,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising) \in \Adm^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)
    \]
    such that $\mu^{\sym}(q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta) = \mu$.
    Let $\tilde p$ denote the restriction of $p$ to $[q_*,1] \subseteq [q_0,1]$.
    Note that $(b,\sigma,w,\tilde p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising)$ satisfies the assumptions of
    Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-chaotic} with $q_*$ in place of $q_0$.
    Indeed, conditions~\ref{it:1.1}, \ref{it:2.1}, \ref{it:3.1}, \ref{it:4.2}, \ref{it:5.1}, and \ref{it:6.1} provide assumptions~(\ref{i:IAMP-main-coefs}), (\ref{i:IAMP-main-diffusivity}), (\ref{i:IAMP-main-p}), (\ref{i:IAMP-main-budget}), (\ref{i:IAMP-main-endpt}), and (\ref{i:IAMP-main-init}) of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}.

    By Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-chaotic}, there exists $\iota = \iota(\epsilon)$ with $\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0} \iota(\epsilon) = 0$ such that for all (sufficiently large) $N$, there exists a $C(L,\epsilon)$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$ with
    \[
        \WERR^\sym(\cA_N,\mu)=
        \max\bigg\{
            \bbW_2\Big(\sym(\mu(\cA_N)), \mu\Big),
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_N), \cP(\{\pm 1\})\Big)
        \bigg\}
        \le \iota\,,
    \]
    which furthermore satisfies $\chi_{\cA_N}(0) = 0$ and $\chi_{\cA_N}(1-\iota) \le \iota$.
    This implies
    \[
        \cM^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon) \subseteq \cM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha,0;C(L,\epsilon),\iota(\epsilon))\,.
    \]
    The rest of the proof is identical to that of Lemma~\ref{l:IAMP.in.Lip}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

Let d,q>=1 be finite, H a constant symmetric positive definite q by q
matrix, and 0<m<=lambda(H)<=M. Fix sigma,D>=0, 0<rho<2 and
0<eta<=rho/M. Let (F_k) be a filtration and (u_k,v_k) adapted, with

noise (xi_k^u,xi_k^v) in R^d x R^q be F_{k+1}-measurable, with

    E[xi_k^v (xi_k^v)^T|F_k] <= sigma^2 H,
    E[|xi_k^u|^2|F_k] <= sigma^2 D^2 |v_k|^2.           (1)

Then, for every T>=0,

      |E F(u_K,v_K)-F(u_0,0)| <= eta C(T),
    C(T)=c[F_vv/2+T sigma^2 D^2 F_2/2+F_uv sigma D/gamma]. (3)

{"assumptions":["X, Y Banach spaces"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:57.492197+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator theory","id":"claim_3ecf47d2e1941e3ed3b704c1615dceb455e30d7da6c0085069f13dc22e065c98","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X, Y be Banach spaces. A linear operator K : X → Y is compact if it maps the closed unit ball of X onto a relatively compact subset of Y; equivalently, for every bounded sequence (x_n) in X the sequence (Kx_n) has a norm-convergent subsequence. Compact operators are bounded. They form a norm-closed two-sided ideal in the bounded operators: norm limits of compact operators are compact, and BK and KB are compact whenever K is compact and B is bounded. Every bounded finite-rank operator is compact; in a Hilbert space (and in every Banach space with the approximation property) every compact operator is a norm limit of finite-rank operators. K is compact iff its adjoint K* is compact (Schauder). The identity of an infinite-dimensional space is not compact (Riesz), so on an infinite-dimensional space a compact operator never has a bounded inverse. A compact operator maps weakly convergent sequences to norm-convergent sequences; the converse (complete continuity implies compactness) holds when X is reflexive, e.g. a Hilbert space, but fails in ℓ^1 (Schur property).\n\nExamples: diag(λ_n) on ℓ^2 is compact iff λ_n → 0; integral operators with L^2 kernels (Hilbert–Schmidt operators) are compact; the embedding H^1_0(Ω) → L^2(Ω) for bounded open Ω is compact (Rellich), so the inverse of the Dirichlet Laplacian is a compact self-adjoint operator on L^2(Ω). Non-examples: the shift operators on ℓ^2; multiplication by a function f on L^2[0,1] is compact only when f = 0 a.e.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:26:02.422944+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3eefb59a1324152e1ef9432863caac5337b298a906111d3a3e91bcc737ca96ad","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem commutatortrick of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $N$ be an even positive integer. Let 
    $$\Homeo_{N\mathbb{Z}}^+(\mathbb{R}) \coloneqq \big\{f\in \Homeo_+(\mathbb{R}) \mid \forall x \in \mathbb{R}, \ f(x+N) = f(x) + N \big\}.$$
    Let $0 < \varepsilon < 1/100$, and suppose $f$, $g$, $\overline{f}$, and $\overline{g}$ are four elements of $\Homeo^+_{N\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{R})$ satisfying the following properties:

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:01:48.632723+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3f2a27cd682ee0d5c317e0d7af12a3f1c8654de548c0f8a755c4fc28db0c0893","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma l:prior.W.logconcave of arXiv:2607.02013, 'Resolution of the Detection Threshold Conjecture for Random Geometric Graphs in the $d>n$ '] For $d \ge (1+\epsilon)n$, the prior distribution $W\sim\mathbb{P}_{0}$ conditioned on ${\mathcal{H}}$ in \prettyref{eq:calH}
is $(c_0 d)$-strongly log-concave, where $c_0$ is a positive constant depending on $\epsilon$.

\begin{proof}
Under the prior distribution $\mathbb{P}_{0}$, 
the density of $W$ is given by (see e.g.\ [anderson2003introduction])
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}_0(W) 
&\propto e^{-V(W
)} \mathbf{1}\{ I+W \succ 0\}\,, \\
V(W) &= - \frac{d-n-1}{2}\log \det(I+W)\,.
\end{align*}
Abbreviate ${\widetilde{W}}=I+W$, and denote by 
$\nabla^2$  the Hessian with respect to the lower triangular elements of $W$. Let $H$ be an $n\times n$ symmetric matrix with zero diagonal. Then
    \begin{align*}
    \log\det({\widetilde{W}}+\epsilon H)
    &=\log\det({\widetilde{W}})
    +\log\det(I+\epsilon B)\,,\\
    B &= {\widetilde{W}}^{-1/2}H{\widetilde{W}}^{-1/2}\,.
    \end{align*}
$B$ is a symmetric matrix. Denoting its eigenvalues by $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$, we have
    \begin{align*}
    \log\det({\widetilde{W}}+\epsilon H)
    &= \log\det({\widetilde{W}})
    +\sum_{i=1}^n\log(1+\epsilon\lambda_i) 
    = \log\det({\widetilde{W}})
    +\epsilon \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i
    -\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}
    \sum_{i=1}^n (\lambda_i)^2\\
    &= \log\det({\widetilde{W}})
    +\epsilon \mathop{\rm tr}(B)
    -\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}
    \mathop{\rm tr}(B^2)\,.
    \end{align*}
It follows that
\begin{equation}
-H^\top\nabla^2 \big[\log\det \widetilde{W} \big] H =\mathop{\rm tr}(\widetilde{W}^{-1}H\widetilde{W}^{-1}H)=\|\widetilde{W}^{-1/2}H\widetilde{W}^{-1/2}\|_{\operatorname{F}}^2\ge \frac{\|H\|_{\operatorname{F}}^2}{\|\widetilde{W}\|_{\operatorname{op}}^2}\,,

\end{equation}
that is to say, the log-determinant function is strongly log-concave.\footnote{From  \prettyref{eq:hess-prior} we see that 
as long as $d\geq n+1$,
the prior distribution $\mathbb{P}_{0}$ is always strongly log-concave with constant $\Theta(\frac{d-n-1}{n^2}$); this is tight when all $x_i$'s are aligned. Lemma~(l:prior.W.logconcave of the paper) improves the curvature to $\Theta(d)$ by truncating on the typical behavior of $W$.} Next recall from \prettyref{eq:calH} that 
${\mathcal{H}}=\{\|\widetilde{W}\|_{\operatorname{op}} \leq 4\}$, which is a convex set in $W$. 
For each $W \in {\mathcal{H}}$, the right-hand side of \prettyref{eq:hess-prior} is further lower bounded by $\|H\|^2/16$, and hence
\[
\nabla^2 V(W)\succeq \frac{d-n-1}{16}I_{n(n-1)/2}\succeq c_0 d I_{n(n-1)/2}\,,
\]
for a constant $c_0>0$ depending on $\epsilon$. This proves the claim.
\end{proof}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:29:21.937766+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3fdace46589bad5debb6120ca9be17ea43249d6d1744c105bb93b475c04e2bf0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 24 (see \cite{FrGue}) of arXiv:2608.01516, 'Nondegeneracy and regularity of polynomial pushforwards'] Let $K$ be a compact convex set in $\mathbb R^n$, let
$p\in\mathbb N$, and let
\[
u_j\colon K\to\mathbb R,
\quad j=1,\ldots,p,
\]
be continuous functions. Let $P_{u_1,\ldots,u_p}(K)\ne\emptyset$ be the set of all
log-concave measures $\nu$ supported in $K$ such that
\[
\int_K u_j\,d\nu\ge0,
\quad j=1,\ldots,p.
\]
Let
\[
\Phi\colon P(K)\to\mathbb R
\]
be a convex continuous functional, where $P(K)$ is the space of all Borel
probability measures on $K$, equipped with the weak topology. Then
\[
\sup_{\nu\in P_{u_1,\ldots,u_p}(K)} \Phi(\nu)
\]
is attained at a log-concave measure $\nu\in P_{u_1,\ldots,u_p}(K)$ such that
the affine span $S(\nu)$ of $\operatorname{supp}(\nu)$ satisfies
\[
\dim S(\nu)\le p.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\sup_{\mu\in P_{u_1,\ldots,u_p}(K)} \Phi(\nu)
=
\sup_{\substack{\nu\in P_{u_1,\ldots,u_p}(K)\\ \dim S(\nu)\le p}}
\Phi(\nu).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:26:26.773775+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3fde682e505a7c0edd5ed0500488cd217436017f30313df22d097b5c3d4e2706","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:sc-dual-Darboux of arXiv:2608.02772, 'Non-Abelian Hirota-Miwa Equations for the KPZ Universality Class'] Let $K$ be dual dressing compatible with $(\Psi, \Phi)$, with
resolvent $R(u) = (I - zK(u))^{-1}$.  Define the dressed

\[
\widehat\Psi(u) \vcentcolon= R(u)\Psi(u), \qquad
\widehat\Phi(u) \vcentcolon= \Phi(u)R(T^{-1}u).
\]
Then $\mathcal{M}(u)$ is invertible for every
$u \in \mathcal{V}$.  The dressed waves
$\widehat\Psi, \widehat\Phi$ satisfy the dual
linear problem
(equation eq:sc-dual-linear-1 of the paper)--(equation eq:sc-dual-linear-j of the paper) and

and $\widehat K(u) \vcentcolon= K(u)R(u)$ is dual dressing compatible

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:04:55.801533+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3fe9562c4925f0ccf9ece0d325ec2bd77ccad2f9bd79ee37ef8bad2a698c9b49","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn d:noise of arXiv:2607.18194, 'Temperature chaos in directed polymers'] For $d\in\mathbb{N}$, a \emph{$d$-dimensional noise} consists of a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$, a collection of sub-$\sigma$-algebras $\{\mathcal{F}_R\}_{R\in\mathcal{R}}$ where $\mathcal{R}$ is the set of open $d$-dimensional rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and a measurable $\mathbb{R}^d$-action $\{\theta_h\}_{h\in\mathbb{R}^d}$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$,
    such that the following properties hold.
    \begin{enumerate}[label={\rm(N\arabic*)},ref={\rm N\arabic*}]
        \item
        \textup{(Exhaustive filtration).} $\mathcal{F} = \bigvee_{R\in\mathcal{R}} \mathcal{F}_R$.
        \item 
        \textup{(Translation covariance).}
        For all $h\in\mathbb{R}^d$, we have $\theta_h(\mathcal{F}_R) = \mathcal{F}_{R+h}$.
        \item 
        \textup{(Independence).}
        For all $R_1,R_2\in\mathcal{R}$ with $R_1\cap R_2=\varnothing$, the $\sigma$-algebras $\mathcal{F}_{R_1}$ and $\mathcal{F}_{R_2}$ are independent.
        \item
        \textup{(Join).}
        For all $R_1,R_2,R_3\in\mathcal{R}$ with $R_1\cap R_2=\varnothing$ and $\overline{R_1\cup R_2}=\overline{R_3}$, we have $\mathcal{F}_{R_1}\vee \mathcal{F}_{R_2} = \mathcal{F}_{R_3}$ up to null sets.
    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space and T is continuous","the metric enters only through the compact topology"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438163+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics, entropy","id":"claim_3fe95da80d1756dae2bb8c43b479ad29fb9efff8bf12406c39a668547d7335d9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $T: X \\to X$ be a continuous map of a compact metric space $(X, d)$. For $n \\ge 1$ define the dynamical metric $d_n(x, y) = \\max_{0 \\le k < n} d(T^k x, T^k y)$. A set $E \\subset X$ is $(n, \\varepsilon)$-separated if $d_n(x, y) > \\varepsilon$ for all distinct $x, y \\in E$; let $s(n, \\varepsilon)$ be the maximal cardinality of such a set (finite by compactness). A set $F$ is $(n, \\varepsilon)$-spanning if every $x \\in X$ has $d_n(x, y) \\le \\varepsilon$ for some $y \\in F$; let $r(n, \\varepsilon)$ be the minimal cardinality. The topological entropy is\n$$h_{top}(T) = \\lim_{\\varepsilon \\to 0} \\limsup_{n \\to \\infty} \\frac{1}{n} \\log s(n, \\varepsilon) = \\lim_{\\varepsilon \\to 0} \\limsup_{n \\to \\infty} \\frac{1}{n} \\log r(n, \\varepsilon) \\in [0, \\infty],$$\nusing $r(n,\\varepsilon) \\le s(n,\\varepsilon) \\le r(n, \\varepsilon/2)$; the limit in $\\varepsilon$ exists by monotonicity, and replacing the $\\limsup$ in $n$ by a $\\liminf$ gives the same value. The value is independent of the compatible metric (this uses compactness) and coincides with the open-cover definition $h_{top}(T) = \\sup_{\\mathcal{U}} \\lim_n \\frac1n \\log N(\\mathcal{U}^n_0)$ where $N$ counts the minimal subcover of the join $\\mathcal{U}^n_0 = \\bigvee_{k<n} T^{-k}\\mathcal{U}$. Basic properties: $h_{top}(T^m) = m\\, h_{top}(T)$ for $m \\ge 1$; $h_{top}(T^{-1}) = h_{top}(T)$ for homeomorphisms; $h_{top}$ is an invariant of topological conjugacy; a Lipschitz map of a compact metric space of finite box dimension has finite entropy, but a continuous map of a compact metric space can have $h_{top} = \\infty$. On a NON-compact space the separated-set quantity depends on the metric, not merely on the topology, and the equalities above can fail.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:52:08.674398+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3ff619da11f26838eeebd63e4e7ab7d17c07daa25e94177b4f2168ecd887ce56","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 42 (Difference equation for two Ricci--DeTurck solutions) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let \(s(t)\) be a Ricci-flow background and let \(v_0(t)\) and \(v_1(t)\)
be two positive definite solutions of the Ricci--DeTurck equation relative to
\(s(t)\) on the same time interval.  Put
\[
        U=v_1-v_0,
        \qquad v_\vartheta=v_0+\vartheta(v_1-v_0),
        \quad 0\leq\vartheta\leq1,
\]
and assume that every \(v_\vartheta\) is positive definite.  With \(\nabla\)
the connection of \(s(t)\), the difference satisfies a homogeneous linear
system
\begin{equation}
        \partial_tU-P^{pq}\nabla_p\nabla_qU
        =B^p\nabla_pU+CU,
\end{equation}
where the second-order part is diagonal in the tensor components: in a fixed
frame, every component \(U^A\) is acted on by the same operator
\(P^{pq}\nabla_p\nabla_q\), and no second derivative of a different component
occurs.  More precisely, for
\[
        \mathcal Q_s(v)=-2\Ric(v)+\Lie_{W(v,s)}v,
\]
one has the structural formula
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
        \mathcal Q_s(v)
        ={}&v^{pq}\nabla_p\nabla_qv
        +v^{-1}*v^{-1}*\nabla v*\nabla v \\
        &\quad+\mathcal R(\Rm(s),v,v^{-1}),
\end{split}
\end{equation}
and the mean-value identity
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
        \partial_tU
        &=\mathcal Q_s(v_1)-\mathcal Q_s(v_0)\\
        &=\int_0^1D\mathcal Q_s|_{v_\vartheta}[U] \,d\vartheta.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Differentiating \eqref{eq:rdt-structural-form} gives
\begin{equation}
        D\mathcal Q_s|_{v_\vartheta}[Z]
        =v_\vartheta^{pq}\nabla_p\nabla_qZ
          +\mathcal B_\vartheta^p\nabla_pZ+\mathcal C_\vartheta Z,
\end{equation}
with
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
        \mathcal B_\vartheta
        &=v_\vartheta^{-1}*v_\vartheta^{-1}*\nabla v_\vartheta,\\
        \mathcal C_\vartheta
        &=v_\vartheta^{-1}*v_\vartheta^{-1}*\nabla^2v_\vartheta
          +v_\vartheta^{-1}*v_\vartheta^{-1}*v_\vartheta^{-1}
             *\nabla v_\vartheta*\nabla v_\vartheta\\
        &\qquad+\mathcal R_1(\Rm(s),v_\vartheta,v_\vartheta^{-1}).
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Here \(*\) denotes universal tensor contractions, and \(\mathcal R\) and
\(\mathcal R_1\) are algebraic in the displayed arguments; in particular,
\(\mathcal R_1\) contains no derivatives of \(v_\vartheta\).  The
coefficients in \eqref{eq:rdt-difference-system} are
\[
 P^{pq}=\int_0^1v_\vartheta^{pq}\,d\vartheta,
 \qquad B^p=\int_0^1\mathcal B_\vartheta^p\,d\vartheta,
 \qquad C=\int_0^1\mathcal C_\vartheta\,d\vartheta.
\]
Consequently, uniform metric equivalence and finite-order bounds for
\(v_0,v_1\), and \(s\) give the corresponding ellipticity and H\"older bounds
for \(P,B,C\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:34:33.537240+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_402cc7a17e09582be87b6b33999c970f349a537eefdc570e9d42f1df8933d920","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 8 of arXiv:2603.28226, '2603.28226'] Let \(f\ge0\) belong to \(L^1(\mathcal F_\infty)\), let \(\lambda>0\), and let
\(\theta\ge0\). Retain the notation of Section~\ref{sec:proof} and
\eqref{eq:s-theta}; thus
\[
r:=\inf\{n\ge1:\ f_n>\lambda\},
\qquad
\varepsilon_n:=d f_n\,\mathbf1_{\{r=n\}},
\qquad
\gamma_n:=d f_n\,\mathbf1_{\{r>n\}},
\]
\[
\Lambda_0:=0,
\qquad
\Lambda_m:=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\mathbb E_k[\varepsilon_{k+1}],
\qquad
s_\theta:=\inf\{m\ge1:\ \Lambda_m>\theta\lambda\},
\qquad
t_\theta:=r\wedge s_\theta.
\]
Also set
\[
r^-:=r-1 \ \text{on }\{r<\infty\},
\qquad
r^-:=\infty \ \text{on }\{r=\infty\}.
\]

Define
\[
g_\theta:=f-f_{t_\theta},
\]
\[
h_{\theta,n}:=
\sum_{j=1}^{n}
\bigl(\varepsilon_j-\mathbb E_{j-1}[\varepsilon_j]\bigr)\mathbf1_{\{s_\theta\ge j\}},
\qquad n\ge1,
\]
\[
k_{\theta,n}^{\mathrm{st}}
:=
\sum_{j=1}^{n}\gamma_j\,\mathbf1_{\{s_\theta\ge j\}},
\qquad
k_{\theta,n}^{\mathrm{pr}}
:=
\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathbb E_{j-1}[\varepsilon_j]\mathbf1_{\{s_\theta\ge j\}},
\qquad n\ge1.
\]
Then \(h_{\theta,n}\) converges almost surely and in \(L^1\) to a limit
\(h_\theta\in L^1(\mathcal F_\infty)\), and the sequences
\[
k_{\theta,n}^{\mathrm{st}},
\qquad
k_{\theta,n}^{\mathrm{pr}}
\]
converge almost surely and in \(L^1\) to limits
\[
k_\theta^{\mathrm{st}},
\qquad
k_\theta^{\mathrm{pr}}
\in L^1(\mathcal F_\infty).
\]
Moreover,
\[
f=g_\theta+h_\theta+k_\theta^{\mathrm{st}}+k_\theta^{\mathrm{pr}}.
\]

\medskip
\noindent\textup{(a)}
\[
\mathbb P\Bigl(\sup_{n\ge1}|\mathbb E_n[g_\theta]|>0\Bigr)
\le \frac{\|f\|_1}{\lambda},
\qquad
\|g_\theta\|_1\le 2\|f\|_1.
\]

\noindent\textup{(b)}
\[
\Bigl\|\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
\bigl|\mathbb E_n[h_\theta]-\mathbb E_{n-1}[h_\theta]\bigr|
\Bigr\|_1
\le 2\|f\|_1.
\]
In particular,
\[
\|h_\theta\|_1\le 2\|f\|_1.
\]

\noindent\textup{(c)}
\[
k_\theta^{\mathrm{st}}=f_{s_\theta\wedge r^-},
\qquad
0\le k_\theta^{\mathrm{st}}\le \lambda
\quad\text{a.s.}
\]

\noindent\textup{(d)}
\[
k_\theta^{\mathrm{pr}}
=
\Lambda_{s_\theta-1}\,\mathbf1_{\{s_\theta<\infty\}}
+
\Bigl(\sup_{m\ge1}\Lambda_m\Bigr)\mathbf1_{\{s_\theta=\infty\}},
\qquad
0\le k_\theta^{\mathrm{pr}}\le \theta\lambda
\quad\text{a.s.}
\]

\noindent\textup{(e)}
\[
\mathbb E[h_\theta]=\mathbb E[\varepsilon_1],
\]
\[
\|k_\theta^{\mathrm{st}}\|_1+\|k_\theta^{\mathrm{pr}}\|_1
=
\|f\|_1-\mathbb E[\varepsilon_1]
\le \|f\|_1,
\]
\[
\|k_\theta^{\mathrm{st}}\|_2^2
\le \lambda\|k_\theta^{\mathrm{st}}\|_1,
\qquad
\|k_\theta^{\mathrm{pr}}\|_2^2
\le \theta\lambda\|k_\theta^{\mathrm{pr}}\|_1,
\]
and
\[
\|k_\theta^{\mathrm{st}}+k_\theta^{\mathrm{pr}}\|_2^2
\le (1+\theta)\lambda\|f\|_1.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726542+00:00","domain":"dispersive partial differential equations","id":"claim_4035e0f47d8f89385856e3a0fa89ee495b32f2ab6d982252999b8813bc8feedd","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: finite speed of propagation and the domain-of-dependence cone are properties of the wave equation (and of symmetric hyperbolic systems), proved by a local energy identity on the cone. The Schrödinger equation has no such identity and propagates instantaneously. Concrete counterexample: let f ∈ L¹(R^n) be nonzero and compactly supported and let t ≠ 0. By the kernel formula, e^{itΔ}f(x) = (4πit)^{−n/2} e^{i|x|²/(4t)} · G(x/(2t)) where G is the Fourier transform of the compactly supported integrable function y ↦ e^{i|y|²/(4t)}f(y). By the Paley–Wiener theorem G extends to an entire function on C^n, and it is not identically zero, so its zero set contains no nonempty open set. Hence e^{itΔ}f is nonzero almost everywhere on every open subset of R^n at every t ≠ 0: compactly supported data instantly become globally supported. The same phenomenon rules out any cone-shaped domain of dependence, and the heat equation behaves the same way. What survives for Schrödinger are local smoothing, dispersive decay and (pseudo)locality statements about wave packets moving at velocity ≈ 2ξ, not a finite propagation speed; the wave equation's finite-speed argument must never be transplanted to a dispersive or parabolic equation.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:06:07.078127+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_40499db85848ffefdfdcd5e77731522500404a4250fb26b00f2814cc03ed372c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 9 (Weak stability of positive \(L^2\) Stein kernels) of arXiv:2608.27657, '\bfseries Stein Kernels and Normal Approximation\\ for Log-Concave Bilinear Forms'] Let \(\mu_k\Rightarrow\mu\) weakly on \(\R^n\), where each \(\mu_k\)
is centered and has finite second moments.  Let \(Y_k\sim\mu_k\), and
suppose that \(\mu_k\) admits a symmetric positive-semidefinite Stein
kernel \(\tau_k\) such that
\begin{equation}
  L:=\sup_k\E\|\tau_k(Y_k)\|_{\HS}^2<\infty.
  \tag{4.2}
\end{equation}
Then \(\mu\) is centered, \(\mu_k\to\mu\) in \(W_2\), and \(\mu\)
admits a symmetric positive-semidefinite Stein kernel \(\tau\) satisfying
\begin{equation}
  \E\tau(Y)=\Cov(Y),
  \qquad
  \E\|\tau(Y)\|_{\HS}^2
  \leq
  \liminf_{k\to\infty}\E\|\tau_k(Y_k)\|_{\HS}^2,
  \tag{4.3}
\end{equation}
where \(Y\sim\mu\).  The same kernel may be chosen with the following
additional permanence properties.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item
If \(F:\mathsf S_n\to[0,\infty]\) is convex and lower semicontinuous and
\(\sup_k\E F(\tau_k(Y_k))\leq C_F\), then
\[
  \E F(\tau(Y))\leq C_F.
\]

\item
If, for every \(A\in\mathsf S_n\),
\[
  \Var\!\left(\Tr(A\tau_k(Y_k))\right)
  \leq C_{\rm tr}\Tr(A^2),
\]
then
\begin{equation}
  \Var\!\left(\Tr(A\tau(Y))\right)
  \leq C_{\rm tr}\Tr(A^2)
  \qquad(A\in\mathsf S_n).
  \tag{4.4}
\end{equation}

\item
If, for every \(A\in\mathsf S_n\),
\[
  \E\Tr(A\tau_k(Y_k)A\tau_k(Y_k))
  \leq C_{\rm en}\Tr(A^2),
\]
then
\begin{equation}
  \E\Tr(A\tau(Y)A\tau(Y))
  \leq C_{\rm en}\Tr(A^2)
  \qquad(A\in\mathsf S_n).
  \tag{4.5}
\end{equation}

\item
If a constant \(C_{\rm wp}\) satisfies
\[
  \Var_{\mu_k}g
  \leq
  C_{\rm wp}\,
  \E\langle
    \tau_k(Y_k)\nabla g(Y_k),\nabla g(Y_k)
  \rangle
\]
for every \(k\) and every \(g\in C_c^\infty(\R^n)\), then
\begin{equation}
  \Var_\mu g
  \leq
  C_{\rm wp}\,
  \E\langle
    \tau(Y)\nabla g(Y),\nabla g(Y)
  \rangle
  \qquad(g\in C_c^\infty(\R^n)).
  \tag{4.6}
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:56:00.644364+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_40658383d73c2daa11882684ab966c56e5f0169a89242bc5148e792df711f679","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def-adm of arXiv:2603.17861, 'Gaussian concentration, integral probability metrics, and coupling functionals\\ for infin'] A probability measure $\mu$ on $(\Omega,\mathfrak{F})$ is said to be asymptotically
decoupled if there exist $g:\mathds N\to\mathds N$ and $c:\mathds N\to [0,\infty)$ such that
$\lim_{n\to\infty}g(n)/n=0$, $\lim_{n\to\infty} c(n)/|\ensuremath{\Lambda}_n|=0$, and
\[
\forall j\in\mathds Z^d,\ \forall n\in\mathds N,\ \forall A\in\mathfrak{F}_{\ensuremath{\Lambda}_n+j},\

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:32:20.750211+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_40782c8ef2e8fe14ad800047fe81a9eb9c771f74956e308c38f73f3be9a45a45","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 8 (Error bound for the realised volatility classifier) of arXiv:2609.00402, '2609.00402'] Suppose Assumption~\ref{ass:volatility} holds. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:42.312267+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_40871787fc45aea8c87bcfc71952dd37f18724345a7ff0c0c4b0ecef144b6d99","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 20 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] For a function $g : X \to Y$, where $X = \T^d$ or $\R^d$ and $Y$ is a Banach space, we define for $s \geq 0$ the (semi)norm space $\mathcal{C}^s$ as follows. For $s=0$, we let
    \[\|g\|_{\mathcal{C}^0(X) Y} := \sup_{x \in X} \|g(x)\|_Y.\]
    For $s \in (0,\infty)$---letting $s = n + r$ where $r \in (0,1]$ and $n \in \N$---we define $\mathcal{C}^s(X)$ as a seminorm on a subspace of $C^n(X)$ by
    \[\|g\|_{\mathcal{C}^s(X) Y} := \sup_{x,x' \in X, x \ne x'} \frac{\|\nabla^n g(x) - \nabla^ng(x')\|_Y}{|x-x'|^r}.\]
    We note in particular that $\mathcal{C}^1$ is the Lipschitz seminorm and that $\mathcal{C}^0$ is the natural norm on the space of bounded functions---rather than $C^1$ and $C^0$ which have additional qualitative regularity hypotheses that we do not want to require, as we will frequently be working with Lipschitz functions that are not $C^1$.

    We also consider for $p \in [1,\infty), s\geq 0$ the fractional Sobolev (semi)norm spaces $W^{s,p}$. For $s \in \N$, we just let $\|g\|_{W^{s,p}(X)Y} := \|\nabla^s g\|_{L^p(X)Y}$, and for $s>0$ and $s \not \in \N$, we again write $s = n+r$ where $r \in (0,1)$ and $n \in \N$ and define
    \[\|g\|_{W^{s,p}(X) Y} := \Big(\int_X \int_X \frac{\|\nabla^n g(x) - \nabla^n g(x')\|^p_Y}{|x-x'|^{d + rp}}\,dx\,dx'\Big)^{1/p}.\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:02:08.110539+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_409a3e33c1df9381430d4b9d4fbbec10802401ba997b7427a3a1efa6df8ae8c2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2608.27398, 'Strict Stability and Strict Minimality of Regular Area-Minimizing Hypercones: A Quantitati'] For $\nu\geq0$, let $J_\nu$ be the Bessel function of the first kind of
order $\nu$, and let $j_{\nu,1}$ denote its first positive zero.  Then, for
every $R>0$,
\begin{equation}
    \lambda_\C^D(R)
    =\frac{\lambda_\C^D(1)}{R^2}
    =\frac{j_{b_1,1}^2}{R^2}
    \geq\frac{4}{R^2}>0.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, $\frac{j_{b_1,1}^2}{R^2}$ is the optimal coefficient in
the quadratic inequality
\[
    Q_\C(\varphi)
    \geq\frac{j_{b_1,1}^2}{R^2}
      \int_\C\varphi^2\,d\cH^n,
    \qquad
    \varphi\in C^1(\C),\quad
    \spt\varphi\Subset B_R.
\]
Moreover, the sharp $|x|^{-2}$-weighted Jacobi inequality is
\[
    Q_\C(\varphi)
    \geq b_1^2
      \int_\C\frac{\varphi^2}{|x|^2}\,d\cH^n,
    \qquad
    \varphi\in C_c^1(\C\setminus\{0\}).
\]
In particular, $\C$ is strictly stable in the sense of
\cite{caffarelli1984minimal} if and only if $b_1>0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:57:28.721388+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_40ca71dd6ef3c68ffc4d0f55c284dac5dd8311461393016f2d79d105c2651331","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 3 of arXiv:2609.01190, 'Rough differential equations on manifolds via natural bundles'] Let $m,n,\ell\in\Nsf$, let $U\subseteq\Rsf^m$ be an open convex set, and let $\phi:U\to\Rsf^\ell$ be a smooth function. Let $p\in [1,3)$, let $\omega$ be a control function on interval $[S,T]$, and let $X=(X^\tau)$ be an $n$-dimensional branched rough path on interval $[S,T]$ with regularity $p$ and control $\omega$. Let $Y: [S,T]\to U$ be a continuous curve in $U$ and let $f_\tau^i:U\to\Rsf$ (for $\tau\in\Fcal_n^2$ and $i\in\llbracket 1,m \rrbracket$) be smooth functions. Assume that there exists $C\in (0,\infty)$ such that the inequality 
	\begin{equation}
	
		\bigg| 
			Y^i(t) - Y^i(s) 
			- f_{\ta}^i(Y(s)) X^{\ta}(s,t) 
			- \frac{1}{2} f_{\tab}^i(Y(s)) X^{\tab}(s,t) 
			- f_{\tc}^i(Y(s)) X^{\tc}(s,t) 
		\bigg| 
		\leq C \omega(s,t)^\frac{3}{p}
	\end{equation}
holds for every $i\in\llbracket 1,m \rrbracket$ and $(s,t)\in\Delta[S,T]$. Then there is a constant $\widetilde{C}\in (0,\infty)$ such that 
	\[
		\bigg|
			\phi^i(Y(t)) - \phi^i(Y(s)) 
			- g^i_{\ta}(Y(s))X^{\ta}(s,t) 
			- \frac{1}{2} g^i_{\tab}(Y(s)) X^{\tab}(s,t) 
			- g^i_{\tc}(Y(s))X^{\tc}(s,t) 
		\bigg| 
		\leq \widetilde{C}\omega(s,t)^\frac{3}{p},
	\]
where 
	\[
		g^i_{\ta} := \frac{\partial\phi^i}{\partial y^j}f_{\ta}^j, 
			\quad 
		g_{\tab}^i := \frac{\partial\phi^i}{\partial y^j}f_{\tab}^j + \frac{\partial^2 \phi^i}{\partial y^j\partial y^k} f_{\ta}^jf_{\tb}^k, 
			\quad\mbox{and}\quad  
		g_{\tc}^i := \frac{\partial\phi^i}{\partial y^j}f_{\tc}^j,
	\]
holds for every $i\in \llbracket 1,\ell \rrbracket$ and $(s,t)\in\Delta[S,T]$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Fixed L>0 and eta>0; deterministic square X with operator norm at most L.","Independent standard Gaussian feature-weight vectors; coordinates of the resulting ReLU column need not be independent.","Each symmetric R_j excludes w_j from its measurability and has norm at most 1/eta.","Any auxiliary randomness is independent of all Gaussian feature weights.","Random-input extension requires independence from feature weights and a tight input norm; only convergence in probability is claimed there.","Owner-work proof (unaudited), w737 T385-C13 v1; no independent PASS or novelty claim."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T17:02:46.507882+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory; nonlinear random features; conditional concentration","id":"claim_40f4831c7471e288197440d464ad019ecdc928316db1ec18bf8e195faef67995","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own-work METHOD DRAFT; proof (unaudited), attributed to w737 T385-C13 v1; no independent PASS or novelty claim. Fix L>0 and eta>0. For each n let X be a deterministic real n by n matrix with operator norm at most L, and w_1,...,w_n independent N(0,I_n) vectors. Put h_j=ReLU(Xw_j), mu=E h_j, z_j=h_j-mu, Phi=E[h_j h_j^T], and Sigma=E[z_j z_j^T]. Let R_j be real symmetric, measurable in X and the columns w_k with k!=j (and optionally auxiliary randomness independent of all feature weights), with operator norm at most 1/eta almost surely. The recorded unaudited derivation gives, for each fixed epsilon>0, P(max_j |z_j^T R_j z_j/n-Tr(Sigma R_j)/n|>epsilon)<=C n exp[-c n min(epsilon^2,epsilon)], with C,c depending only on L,eta. The centering step uses the exact identity z^T R z-Tr(Sigma R)=h^T R h-Tr(Phi R)-2 mu^T R(h-mu) for deterministic symmetric R. Louart-Liao-Couillet quadratic-form concentration controls the raw term. Gaussian Lipschitz concentration controls the mean correction. Indeed mu_i=||x_i||/sqrt(2 pi), ||mu||^2<=n L^2/(2 pi), and w->mu^T R ReLU(Xw) is Lipschitz with constant at most sqrt(n/(2 pi))*L^2/eta. Condition on all columns except j before applying those bounds; integrate and take a union bound, without asserting independence between deviation events. Thus the method allows correlations among coordinates within each feature column, but R_j must exclude the tested column. For X=I and eta=1, taking the same-column R=zz^T/||z||^2 makes z^T R z/n tend to kappa=1/2-1/(2 pi)>0 while Tr(Sigma R)/n=kappa/n, illustrating failure if this independence hypothesis is removed. For random X independent of all w_j with tight operator norm, conditioning first on ||X||<=L and then letting L grow gives convergence in probability, rather than a uniform unconditional exponential rate. This is a fixed-positive-ridge concentration ingredient; it supplies neither an edge law nor a justification for a ridge tending to zero. {"assumptions":["A measurable, uniformly parabolic with constants lambda, Lambda (no continuity assumed)","divergence form (the analogous statement for nondivergence form with merely measurable coefficients is a different theory)","s < t; for equations with lower-order terms or on a finite time interval, constants also depend on T and those bounds"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.106308+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations / heat kernel estimates","id":"claim_410506486d1fb1210e085fe9677cd4acaa4ae438a0aa72b12c79fd1a43a41833","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $A(x,t)$ be real measurable on $\\mathbb R^n\\times\\mathbb R$ and uniformly parabolic with constants $0<\\lambda\\le\\Lambda<\\infty$, and consider $\\partial_tu=\\mathrm{div}(A(x,t)\\nabla u)$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:47:22.245900+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_414774552018474bc5ee76321ba5e7b66cb73ff5fb105f49125c1862c38a7ec9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 19 of arXiv:2605.26664, 'Mixing times for Glauber dynamics of lozenge tilings of the hexagon'] [Liquid and frozen region, arctic boundary]
  Given any open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, we call a function $F : \overline{\Omega} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ \emph{admissible} if $F$ is $1$-Lipschitz and satisfies $\nabla F (z) \in \overline{\mathcal{T}}$ for Lebesgue almost every $z \in \Omega$. Let $\Adm (\Omega)$ denote the set of admissible functions $F : \overline{\Omega} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and, for any function $f : \partial \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, let $\Adm (\Omega; f)$ denote the set of $F \in \Adm (\Omega)$ satisfying $F |_{\partial \Omega} = f$.  Define the \emph{liquid region} $\mathfrak{L}_F \subseteq \Omega$ associated with an admissible height function $F \in \Adm (\Omega)$ by 
         \begin{flalign*}
         	\mathfrak{L}_F = \big\{ z \in \Omega : \nabla F(z) \in \mathcal{T} \big\},
         \end{flalign*}
         where the condition $\nabla F(z) \in \mathcal{T}$ in particular implies that $\nabla F(z)$ exists.

         In particular, we define the liquid region of $\cH_{q;a,b,c}$ as
         \[\mL_{q;a,b,c}:=\mL_{\cH_{q;a,b,c}}.\] The  boundary
        $\mathfrak A_{q;a,b,c}:=\partial\mL_{q;a,b,c}$ is called the
        \emph{arctic boundary} and the interior of

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:32:23.740632+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_41918c410806fda3d6ce81068e83f01a2801742dd5d07ae6173c787e38cd6ca1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:rw_reset of arXiv:2603.24803, 'Critical Spectral Invariants in Random Walks with Geometric Resetting'] Let $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$ be a probability space. 
Fix $a \in \mathbb{N}$ and $z \in \{1,\dots,a-1\}$. 
Let $\{X_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ be a discrete-time stochastic process on 
$\{0,1,\dots,a\}$ with initial condition $X_0=z$.

Let $\{\xi_n\}_{n\ge1}$ be i.i.d.\ random variables, independent of 
everything else, with
\[
\mathbb{P}(\xi_n=+1)=p, 
\qquad 
\mathbb{P}(\xi_n=-1)=q=1-p.
\]

Let $\{\sigma_i\}_{i\ge1}$ be i.i.d.\ geometric random variables with 
parameter $\gamma\in(0,1)$, supported on $\{1,2,\dots\}$:
\[
\mathbb{P}(\sigma_i=k)=\gamma(1-\gamma)^{k-1}, 
\qquad k\ge1,
\]
independent of $\{\xi_n\}$. Define reset times recursively by
\[
\mathbf{t}_0:=0,
\qquad
\mathbf{t}_i := \sum_{j=1}^{i} \sigma_j,
\quad i\ge1.
\]

Then the process evolves according to
\[
X_n =
\begin{cases}
z, & \text{if } n \in \{\mathbf{t}_i\}_{i\ge1}, \\[6pt]
X_{n-1}+\xi_n, & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\qquad n\ge1,
\]
and is absorbed upon first hitting $0$ or $a$. Equivalently, at each 
step the walker resets to $z$ with probability $\gamma$ or performs a 
standard biased step with probability $1-\gamma$, independently of its 
current position.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:55.646077+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_41d57af92ecc43fc976e5213f2f26cbe3fa94008afca39b8e326dfe13a314480","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 23 (Uniform moment bounds for the shifted process) of arXiv:2605.24937, '2605.24937'] Let $p\ge 1$ and define the shifted process $\widetilde Y_n := (1-\eta_n)Y_n' + \eta_n \widehat X_n$ for $n\ge0$. Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:P-moment-drift} (with constants $q, C > 0$), and assuming $\widehat M_p := \sup_{n\ge 0} \E\|\widehat X_n\|^p < \infty$, we have
\[
  \E\|\widetilde Y_n\|^p \le e^{-q\lambda n}\E\|\widetilde Y_0\|^p + \frac{C\lambda+\widehat M_p}{1-e^{-q\lambda}},
\]
yielding the uniform bound $\sup_{n\ge 0} \E\|\widetilde Y_n\|^p \le \E\|\widetilde Y_0\|^p + \frac{C\lambda+\widehat M_p}{1-e^{-q\lambda}} < \infty$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:01:39.423732+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_41ec281780e228555015ad321135da7c10041d8812e04a31bc646c231f823757","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:max_lh of arXiv:2607.22291, 'Rare subtree patterns in size-conditioned Bienaymé trees: Poisson approximation and declum'] Assume that $\mu$ is critical and belongs to the domain of attraction of a stable law.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)]  Assume that $\mu_{1}>0$. There exists a constant $C_{\mu}>0$ such that the following holds. Set
$$k^*_{n} =  \frac{1}{\log(1/\mu_{1})}\log n +  \frac{1}{\log(1/\mu_{1})} \log\bigl((1-\mu_1)C_{\mu}\bigr).$$
Then for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$ we have
\[
\P\bigl(\lambda(\mathcal{T}^n) \leq \lfloor k^*_{n} + t\rfloor\bigr) - \exp\bigl(-\mu_1^{t+1 - \{k^*_{n} + t\}}\bigr) \to 0.
\]
\item[(ii)] Assume that $\mu_{1}=0$. Set $\kappa = \min\{i \geq 2 : \mu_i > 0\}$. There exists a constant $D_{\mu} \in (0,1)$ such that the following holds. Set
$$
k_{n}^{**} \coloneqq  \log_\kappa \log n - \log_\kappa \log(1/D_{\mu}).
$$
 Write $m_n=\lfloor k_n^{**}\rfloor$ and
$\theta_n=\{k_n^{**}\}$, and define
$$
  J_n=
  \begin{cases}
    \{m_n-1,m_n\},&\theta_n\le\tfrac12,\\
    \{m_n,m_n+1\},&\theta_n>\tfrac12.
  \end{cases}
$$
Then $\P(\lambda(\mathcal T^n)\in J_n)\longrightarrow1$. In addition, if $\liminf_n\min(\theta_n,1-\theta_n)>0$, then
$\P(\lambda(\mathcal T^n)=m_n)\to1$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:41:33.837802+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_41f0ac2dc87f9493b558ac938b189efc7b69d3228f3992da9385b68aa984406e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 8 of arXiv:2604.11489, '2604.11489'] \cite{C-S}
 Let $X_1, X_2, \cdots, X_n$ be independent and not necessarily identically distributed random variables with zero means and finite variances. Define $W=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$ and assume that $Var(W)=1$.  $$

 \frac{\ee |X_i|^3I_{\{|X_i|\le 1+|x|\}}}{(1+|x|)^3}\right).
 $$
 Furthermore, we have
 $$
 \sup_{x}|F(x)-\Phi(x)|\le C\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\ee X_i^2I_{\{|X_i|>1\}}+
 \ee |X_i|^3I_{\{|X_i|\le 1\}}\right).
 $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:27:08.837281+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_41f0e308989b80a243e75480709f0bf7e5e8fba6621915831fc762a3a8377a65","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 ({\cite[Definition~3.3) of arXiv:2511.09930, 'Martingale dimensions for a class of metric measure spaces'] {Hi10}}]
The \emph{AF-martingale dimension} $d_{\mathrm{m}}$ of $\bfM$ or of $(\cE,\cF)$ is the smallest number $d$ such that, there exist $d$ elements $M^{(1)},M^{(2)},\dots,M^{(d)}$ in $\maruM$ such that each $M\in\maruM$ is expressed as
\[
M=\sum_{i=1}^d (\ph^{(i)}\bullet M^{(i)})
\]
for some $\ph^{(i)}\in L^2(K,\mu_{\la M^{(i)}\ra})$, $i=1,2,\dots,d$.
If such a number does not exist, $d_{\mathrm{m}}$ is defined as $\infty$. Moreover, $d_{\mathrm{m}}$ is defined as $0$ if $\maruM=\{0\}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-12T07:22:43.761193+00:00","domain":"graph theory","id":"claim_41f1607fe0ca61747b32e0ca370c278bba715b149e9ab306a7f07d7712059878","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A graph G = (V, E) is a finite set V of vertices together with a set E of edges, each an unordered pair of vertices; G is simple if it has no loops or repeated edges. A subgraph uses a subset of the vertices and edges. The degree of a vertex is the number of incident edges, and the handshake lemma gives sum of degrees = 2|E|. A walk is a vertex-edge alternation; a path has distinct vertices, a cycle is a closed path, and G is connected if every two vertices are joined by a path. Standard families: the complete graph K_n (all pairs adjacent), a tree (connected and acyclic, with |V|-1 edges), and a bipartite graph (vertices two-colorable so every edge crosses, equivalently no odd cycle). The vertex connectivity kappa(G) and edge connectivity lambda(G) are the least numbers of vertices, respectively edges, whose deletion disconnects G (or reduces it to a single vertex), and kappa(G) <= lambda(G) <= min-degree.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X and Y are Banach spaces","T is linear on a linear subspace D(T) of X"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.769166+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, unbounded operators","id":"claim_41fdcf41b301c72abeac970dc8d13d7e8412473ffc482e2582494edf964e1f49","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X, Y be Banach spaces and T: D(T) ⊂ X → Y a linear operator defined on a linear subspace D(T). Its graph is G(T) = {(x, Tx) : x ∈ D(T)} ⊂ X × Y. T is closed if G(T) is closed in X × Y; equivalently, whenever x_n ∈ D(T), x_n → x in X and Tx_n → y in Y, then x ∈ D(T) and Tx = y. Equivalently, D(T) is complete under the graph norm ‖x‖_T = ‖x‖ + ‖Tx‖. S is an extension of T (written T ⊂ S) if D(T) ⊂ D(S) and Sx = Tx for x ∈ D(T). T is closable if it has a closed extension; equivalently, x_n ∈ D(T), x_n → 0 and Tx_n → y imply y = 0; equivalently, the closure of G(T) is the graph of an operator, called the closure T̄ (the smallest closed extension). If T is closed, a subspace D_0 ⊂ D(T) is a core for T if D_0 is dense in D(T) for the graph norm, i.e. the closure of T restricted to D_0 equals T. A closed operator need not be bounded, and being closed says nothing about D(T) being dense; by the closed graph theorem a closed operator with D(T) = X is bounded.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:04:39.234804+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_420a645d67dbdf8ce3464524c57609ebb234e7624abad9039ffdf8e7717b360c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 42 (Coxeter orbit of the monomial physical contour) of arXiv:2608.14475, '\vspace{-1.2cm}\textbf{Finite Gaussian Reconstruction of Polynomial Orbits:\\ From Correla'] In the adjacent basis of

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.349563+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4227cc72423df9e86220706666cf0c5942ecb93c47543ebc0343a142107821ab","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 171 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let indices $a(q_d),a^\frozen(q_d)$
be sampled as in Definition~\ref{d:rerand}, and let
indices $i(q_d),i^\frozen(q_d)$
be sampled as in Definition~\ref{d:rerand.Ising}. 
For $N$ large enough, we have
	\[\max_{\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII\}}
	\E\bigg[
	\max_{r\in[s,t]} 
	\bigg|
	\sum_{\ell=s}^{r-1}
	\Delta X^\sigma(q_\ell,a(q_{\ell+1}))
	\bigg|^8
	\bigg]
	\le L^{O(1)} (q_t-q_s)^4
	\]
for all $0\le s\le t\le \dmax$.
The same bound holds
	with $\Delta X^{\trunc,\sigma}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))$
	or $\Delta X^{\frozen,\sigma}(q_d,a^\frozen(q_{d+1}))$
	in place of $\Delta X^\sigma(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))$.
We also have
	\[
	\E \left[
	\max_{r\in[s,t]}
	\left|
	\sum_{\ell=s}^{r-1}
	\Delta X^{\Ising}(q_\ell,i(q_{\ell+1}))
	\right|^8
	\right]
	\le L^{O(1)}(q_t-q_s)^4\,,
	\]
and likewise with $\Delta X^{\trunc,\Ising}(q_\ell,i(q_{\ell+1}))$ or $\Delta X^{\Isplus}(q_\ell,i^\frozen(q_{\ell+1}))$ in place of $\Delta X^{\Ising}(q_\ell,i(q_{\ell+1}))$.

\begin{proof}
This follows by a very similar argument as for Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.II.III.Ising}. We will describe the proof for $X^\RomII$. A key difference is that in Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.II.III.Ising} we considered $X^\RomII(q_d,a)$ as a process indexed by time $q_d$ for a fixed index $a\in[M]$, with respect to the filtration $\cG(t)$. Here, we instead consider the process $X^\RomII(q_d,a(q_d))$, with respect to the filtration $\cFt(t)$ defined by \eqref{e:gaus.filt.plus}. With this change, repeating the argument of
Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.II.III.Ising} gives the conclusion for $X^\RomII$ (cf.\ \eqref{e:martingale.X.holder.estimate}). The conclusions for $X^\RomIII$ and $X^\Ising$ follow similarly. It is straightforward to verify that the same bounds hold for the modified processes 
$X^{\trunc,\sigma}$ and $X^{\frozen,\sigma}$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:44:27.959154+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4240a05f2ac937ca3b8e24871530fc01f1137b374f00302be45ec317c1ea3d45","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 9 (Poisson-type concentration of roots) of arXiv:2607.13210, 'Punctured Wilson--Evolving Sets and Root Identities for Massive Kirchhoff Forests'] For $U\subset V$, let $\mu_q(U):=\sum_{x\in U}\beta_q(x).$\\
For every family $(s_x)_{x\in U}$ of non-negative numbers, we have:
\begin{equation*}
  \Ee\left[
    \prod_{x\in U}\left(1+s_x\1_{\{x\in\Root\}}\right)
  \right]
  \leq
  \prod_{x\in U}(1+s_x\beta_q(x)).
\end{equation*}
Consequently, for every $\theta\geq0$, it results:
\begin{equation}
  \Ee[e^{\theta N_q(U)}]
  \leq
  \prod_{x\in U}\left(1+\beta_q(x)(e^\theta-1)\right)
  \leq
  \exp\left(\mu_q(U)(e^\theta-1)\right).
\end{equation}
For every $\delta>0$, one finds:
\begin{equation}
  \Pp\left(N_q(U)\geq(1+\delta)\mu_q(U)\right)
  \leq
  \exp\left[-\mu_q(U)
  \bigl((1+\delta)\log(1+\delta)-\delta\bigr)\right].
\end{equation}
Moreover, one gets:
\begin{equation*}
  \Ee[(N_q(U))_k]
  \leq
  k!\,e_k\bigl((\beta_q(x))_{x\in U}\bigr)
  \leq\mu_q(U)^k.
\end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X a normed space; no completeness of X is needed","for metrizability and sequential compactness of the ball: X separable","Tychonoff (hence a form of the axiom of choice) in the general case"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T15:38:23.784925+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_424daabf6bab4c23b100ce5671977a4d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a normed vector space over R or C. The closed unit ball B of the dual space X^* is COMPACT in the weak-* topology, that is the topology of pointwise convergence on X. Two refinements matter. (a) If X is SEPARABLE then the weak-* topology restricted to B is metrizable and B is weak-* SEQUENTIALLY compact, so bounded sequences of functionals have weak-* convergent subsequences; without separability compactness need not give sequential compactness. (b) The general theorem uses Tychonoff's theorem for a product of compact scalar discs and therefore, in ZF, is not provable without some choice; the separable case needs only a diagonal argument. The theorem does NOT say the ball is norm-compact: by Riesz's lemma the closed unit ball of a normed space is norm-compact if and only if the space is finite-dimensional. Nor does it say the ball of X itself is weakly compact - that characterises reflexivity (Kakutani). [standard; e.g. Rudin, Functional Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 3.15]\n\nFor every neighborhood U of 0 in X, its polar U^circ = {phi in X^*: |phi(u)| <= 1 for every u in U} is weak-* compact. Here X^* is the continuous dual and the weak-* topology is pointwise convergence on X; neither completeness nor separability of X is needed.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:43:04.762576+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_427f6d2898e71cd3f7a55e55f825c4a562dc98ad06bb2909f6325d84f0207f8f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 4 (Upper and lower Minkowski content) of arXiv:2605.18198, 'Large deviations of crowding in finite $\beta$-ensembles'] Let $A\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ and let $0\le d\le n$ be an integer. Denote
	\(
	A_r:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\operatorname{dist}(x,A)<r\}
	\), the $r$-neighbourhood of $A$.
	The $d$--dimensional upper Minkowski content of $A$ is defined as
	\[
	\mathcal M^{*d}(A)
	=
	\limsup_{r\downarrow 0}
	\frac{m(A_r)}{\alpha(n-d)\,r^{\,n-d}},
	\]
	and the $d$--dimensional lower Minkowski content is defined as
	\[
	\mathcal M_{*}^{d}(A)
	=
	\liminf_{r\downarrow 0}
	\frac{m(A_r)}{\alpha(n-d)\,r^{\,n-d}},
	\]
	where $\alpha(k)$ denotes the Lebesgue measure of the unit ball in
	$\mathbb{R}^k$. If $	\mathcal M^{*d}(A)=\mathcal M_{*}^{d}(A)$, then the common value is called
	the $d$--dimensional Minkowski content of $A$ and is denoted by
	$\mathcal M^{d}(A)$.","status":"unverified"}

    \[

    \]
    and generating acyclic cofibrations
    \[
        J=\{\textbf{\textup{O}}(V,-)\smashp_\varphi G_+\smashp(D^n\hookrightarrow D^n\times I)_+ : \text{$V\in\textbf{\textup{O}}$, $H\subset {\textup{O}}(V)$, $\varphi\colon H\to G$, $n\ge0$}\}.
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_n => X in distribution","Y_n -> c in probability with c a CONSTANT (not a random variable)","for the quotient: c != 0"],"created_at":"2026-10-07T01:09:09+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_42d5d8144efc7c7815ae88f7a13799ed","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_n converge in distribution to a real random variable X and let Y_n converge in probability to a real constant c. Then (X_n,Y_n) converges jointly in distribution to (X,c). Consequently X_n+Y_n converges in distribution to X+c, X_n Y_n converges in distribution to cX, and, if c!=0, X_n/Y_n converges in distribution to X/c. For the quotient, define its value arbitrarily on {Y_n=0} when necessary; that event has probability tending to zero. Convergence Y_n=>c in distribution is equivalent to convergence Y_n->c in probability, so either hypothesis gives the same conclusion for a constant target. With a nonconstant target, separate marginal convergence alone does not identify the joint limit: if X is a nondegenerate symmetric random variable, X_n=X and Y_n=-X, then both marginal laws converge to the law of X, but X_n+Y_n=0 does not converge to the law of 2X. A random second limit is allowed when joint convergence (X_n,Y_n)=>(X,Y) is supplied; the continuous mapping theorem then gives the corresponding sum and product limits, and the quotient limit if P(Y=0)=0. [Re-derived local source, M9; textbook cross-reference: van der Vaart, Asymptotic Statistics, Theorem 2.8.]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:55:18.952198+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_42d674ff5e4aefc9091a3202fb07bce94a88314a20a13a94b9d080df712106c3","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Discrete connection on a graph of arXiv:2602.08591, 'The Yang--Mills measure on compact surfaces as a \\ universal scaling limit of lattice gau'] A \emph{discrete connection} on $\mathbb{G}$ is a map
\[
g : \mathbb{E}_+ \cup \mathbb{E}_- \longrightarrow G
\]
such that for every $e \in \mathbb{E}_+$ we have
\[
g(e_+) = g(e_-)^{-1}.
\]
For an edge $e\in \mathbb{E}_+\cup \mathbb{E}_-$, we denote by $i(e)$ and $f(e)$ the vertices such that $e=(i(e),f(e))$. A path in $\mathbb{G}$ is a sequence of edges  $a_1,\dots,a_n$ such that $f(a_k)=i(a_{k+1})$ for all $k=1,\dots,n-1$. If $c = a_1 \cdots a_n$ is a path in $\mathbb{G}$, given as a concatenation of oriented edges $a_i \in \mathbb{E}_+ \cup \mathbb{E}_-$, we define the \emph{holonomy} of $g$ along $c$ by
\[
\mathrm{Hol}(g,c) \coloneqq g(a_1)\cdots g(a_n) \in G.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:23:37.815538+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_42d869bc98cb9f208052e0350c480289da6e27a0d7ddfbbe9fac30ca8037ffc7","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 5 of arXiv:2609.03634, 'Joint Laws of Maximum Drawdown and Maximum Drawup for Spectrally Negative L\'{e}vy Process'] Consider a spectrally negative L\'{e}vy process $X$ with $q$-scale functions $W^{(q)}$ and $Z^{(q)}$. Let $a<0$, $b>0$, $x\in[0,b]$, and $q\geq0$. Then, for $v>0$,
\[
\mathbb E_x\left[e^{-q\tau_a^-};\,M_{\tau_a^-}^{+}\leq v,\ S_{\tau_a^-}\leq b\right]
=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
e^{-\left((x-a)\frac{W_+^{(q)\prime}(v)}{W^{(q)}(v)}\right)},
& 0<v\leq b-x,\\[1.3em]
\displaystyle
e^{-\left((b-a-v)\frac{W_+^{(q)\prime}(v)}{W^{(q)}(v)}\right)}
\left[
Z^{(q)}(x-b+v)-Z^{(q)}(v)\frac{W^{(q)}(x-b+v)}{W^{(q)}(v)}
\right],
& b-x<v\leq b-a,\\[1.3em]
\displaystyle
Z^{(q)}(x-a)-Z^{(q)}(b-a)\frac{W^{(q)}(x-a)}{W^{(q)}(b-a)},
& b-a\leq v.
\end{cases}
\]
In particular,
\[
\mathbb E_x\left[e^{-q\tau_a^-};\,M_{\tau_a^-}^{+}\leq v\right]
=
\exp\!\left(-(x-a)\frac{W_+^{(q)\prime}(v)}{W^{(q)}(v)}\right).
\]","status":"unverified"}

Equipping the Cantor space with two standard metrics, we show that under both, a typical martingale diverges at a typical point. By a ``typical martingale'', we mean an element of a co-$\\sigma$-porous set when $p\\in[1,\\infty)$ and of a co-porous set when $p=\\infty$. Specifically, we show that while a typical martingale diverges on a co-$\\sigma$-porous set with respect to the first metric, no martingale diverges on a co-$\\sigma$-porous set with respect to the second metric. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:33:21.478361+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_43624cfb0d0aeb543c3ad7cc9de650d2b3c963cb430da22556eb9c96f8ca470d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:moment-problems of arXiv:2606.21391, 'Extreme points and faces in the moment problem'] Building on Definition~(def:moment-constraints of the paper), we assume that $\mathbf{p}\colon X\to\mathbb{R}^d$ 
and $f\colon X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ are measurable with respect to the $\sigma$-algebra 
$\mathcal{F}$. We define the linear optimization problems
\begin{align}

g_\mathrm{fin}(C) & \textstyle
:= \inf\{ \int f\mathrm{d}\mu : \mu\in G_\mathrm{fin}(C) \},\\

g_\mathrm{a.i.}(C) & \textstyle
:= \inf\{ \int f\mathrm{d}\mu : \mu\in G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C) \}
\end{align}
on the spaces $G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)\subset G_\mathrm{fin}(C)$ of finitely atomic measures. If $f$ is 
bounded below by a real constant, then we also define
\begin{align}

g(C) & \textstyle
:= \inf\{ \int f\mathrm{d}\mu : \mu\in G(C) \},\\

g_\mathrm{ext}(C) & \textstyle
:= \inf\{ \int f\mathrm{d}\mu : \mu\in \ext G(C) \}.
\end{align}
The optimization problem $g(\mathbf{q})$ in (equation eq:PM of the paper) at a specific point $\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ 
is an example of the problem of moments [shapiro01]. This problem is also known 
as the generalized moment problem if $\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{B}(X)$ is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on a Borel 
[lasserre10], closed [henrion-etal20], or compact [klerk-laurent19] set 
$X$ in $\mathbb{R}^k$. Loosely speaking, we refer to each of 
(equation eq:PM-atomic of the paper)--(equation eq:PM-ext of the paper) as a \emph{generalized moment problem}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:55.643087+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_43642bc6c97fa91517e6d43355abe203afdd42e9710168b5c4cb642c6ac2a30a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 20 of arXiv:2605.23659, '2605.23659'] Let \(g\) be the right-continuous inverse of the function

X^{(i)}_\lambda(t):=

where the family

consists of independent stable subordinators characterized by

and

for \(q,t\ge0\).
Then

on \(D([0,\infty),\bR^{I_0})\).","status":"unverified"}

Let $\\lambda_k, u_k$ be the sample eigenvalues and eigenvectors and let $g_E(z) = \\frac{1}{p}\\operatorname{tr}(z I - E)^{-1}$ be the Stieltjes transform of the sample spectrum, and $g(z) = \\int (z - x)^{-1} F(dx)$ that of its almost-sure limit $F$, the limiting sample spectral distribution, with $g(\\lambda - i0) := \\lim_{\\eta \\downarrow 0} g(\\lambda - i\\eta)$ inside the bulk (the finite-sample $g_E(\\lambda - i\\eta)$ has no useful limit as $\\eta \\downarrow 0$: it diverges at each sample eigenvalue and is real between them). THEOREM (Ledoit and Peche, 2011, Theorem 4; in the form of Bun, Bouchaud and Potters 2017). The oracle eigenvalues $\\xi_k^{\\mathrm{or}} = u_k^T C u_k$, as the weighted measure $\\frac{1}{p}\\sum_k \\xi_k^{\\mathrm{or}} \\delta_{\\lambda_k}$, converge almost surely to $\\xi(\\lambda) F(d\\lambda)$ on $(0, \\infty)$, where $$\\xi(\\lambda) = \\frac{\\lambda}{\\big|\\, 1 - q_0 + q_0\\, \\lambda\\, g(\\lambda - i0) \\,\\big|^2};$$ informally $\\xi_k^{\\mathrm{or}} \\approx \\xi(\\lambda_k)$ for sample eigenvalues inside the bulk (the theorem is about the weighted measure, not a limit for each $k$). This limit depends on the population covariance $C$ only through the observable sample spectrum, so it is a consistent, computable estimator (the rotationally invariant estimator, RIE, or nonlinear shrinkage): replace each sample eigenvalue by $\\xi(\\lambda_k)$, keep the sample eigenvectors. In practice $g_E$ is evaluated at $\\lambda_k - i\\eta$ with a small $\\eta$ of order $n^{-1/2}$ times the eigenvalue scale, and the result is floored at a small positive fraction of the bulk level. When $C = \\sigma^2 I$ the formula returns $\\sigma^2$ for every eigenvalue (the Marchenko-Pastur spread is entirely removed); for a spike above the bulk it returns approximately the debiased population spike. Applying the formula to a matrix whose largest eigenvalue is a signal one is trying to keep, and flooring relative to that top eigenvalue, destroys the small eigenvalues that the inverse depends on.","status":"unverified"}

 P(r\theta)=r^\lambda P(\theta),

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:23:25.637365+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_43ea18ffd576a59e2be8d183b05edef8cc7608a86b5036251964165957bbf5cf","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn def:formal_qMPL of arXiv:2609.01458, 'Confluence relations for $q$-analogues of multiple zeta values'] We denote by $\hat{\mathcal{F}}$ the set
of formal symbols
\[
\mathbb{L}_{k_{1},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{d}),
\]
where $d\geq0$, $k_{1},\dots,k_{d}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq1}$, and
\[
x_{i}\in\{z^{h}q^{m}\mid h\in\{0,\pm1\},m\in\mathbb{Z}\}\qquad(1\leq i\leq d),
\]
satisfying
\begin{equation}
x_{i}\cdots x_{d}\in zq^{\mathbb{Z}}\cup q^{\mathbb{Z}_{>0}}\qquad(1\leq i\leq d).
\end{equation}
We write the case $d=0$ as $\mathbb{L}(\emptyset)$. We call the
elements of $\hat{\mathcal{F}}$ formal $q$MPLs. We call $k_{1}+\cdots+k_{d}$
the weight. We also call $k_{i}$ the weight of the $i$-th position.
In this section, we introduce several subsets of $\hat{\mathcal{F}}$.
Although each subset is defined when it first appears, their definitions
and inclusion relations are collected in (app:notation-summary of the paper)
for the reader's convenience. For $\mathcal{X}\subset\hat{\mathcal{F}}$,
we denote by $\mathbb{Q}\mathcal{X}$ the $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space
with basis $\mathcal{X}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:57:07.301416+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_441a897f603a059b42aa79285dc9e441fe3aab7e983c6c57893a61446e90bc87","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 1 of arXiv:2606.23896, 'The one-point Schreier Poisson boundary of Thompson's group \(F\)'] Let \((X_n)\) be a Markov chain on a countable state space
\(E\), with transition kernel \(P\). Let \(A\subset E\) be nonempty. Assume
that, starting from every \(x\in E\), the chain hits \(A\) almost surely, and
that, starting from every \(a\in A\), it returns to \(A\) infinitely often
almost surely.

Define

\[
\tau_0=\inf\{n\ge 0:X_n\in A\},
\]

and, for \(k\ge 0\),

\[
\tau_{k+1}=\inf\{n>\tau_k:X_n\in A\}.
\]

The trace chain on \(A\) is

\[
Y_k=X_{\tau_k}
\]

with transition kernel

\[
P_A(a,b)=\mathbb P_a(X_{\tau_1}=b),
\qquad a,b\in A .
\]

Then restriction gives an isometric order-isomorphism

\[
H^\infty(E,P)\cong H^\infty(A,P_A).
\]

Consequently the Poisson boundaries of \((E,P)\) and \((A,P_A)\) are
isomorphic.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:37:33.911755+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning","id":"claim_44346e151009d85ee2b6ef52041da819cd6f25e04627d15b65a60bf4ba58a87a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"When one ensemble of $M$ members predicts $D$ output coordinates (spectral bands, pixels, reduced coefficients) and a separate affine stack is fitted per output, the $D$ least-squares weight vectors form a matrix $\\hat W \\in \\mathbb{R}^{D \\times (M+1)}$ with $\\hat W = W + Z$: row $d$ of the noise $Z$ has covariance $\\sigma_d^2 (X_d^T X_d)^{-1}$, $X_d$ the calibration design of output $d$ and $\\sigma_d^2$ its residual variance, while the true $W$ has low effective rank whenever the optimal weighting varies smoothly across outputs (neighbouring bands weight the same members similarly). The relevant random-matrix ratio is then $\\beta = (M+1)/D$ - not $M/n_{\\mathrm{cal}}$ - and the problem is low-rank matrix denoising: after scaling row $d$ by $1/\\sigma_d$ (and, when the designs $X_d$ are nearly common across outputs, right-whitening by $\\bar G^{1/2}\\sqrt{n}$ with $\\bar G$ the average of $X_d^T X_d / n$), the Gavish-Donoho optimal singular-value shrinkage selects the rank as the number of singular values above the Marchenko-Pastur edge $1 + \\sqrt\\beta$ and debiases each retained singular value, with no cross-validation. Shrinking every row toward one global weight vector by a cross-validated scalar - the best heuristic found on the EMIT/OCO-2 pools, beating per-output least squares on 69 of 70 cells by 3.1 percent - is the rank-one special case of this estimator with the direction fixed and the amount tuned by hand. For EMIT ($M = 23$, $D = 285$) $\\beta = 0.084$; for OCO-2 ($M = 18$, $D = 40$) $\\beta = 0.475$, a wide bulk in which only strong structure clears the edge.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.501240+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_447b097c91911dd606f656732b99fcd4ef5f1356ba2a290440b07e25757d8a35","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem eq:conditional-remainder-cost of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[theorem]{thm:one-spike}
Assume that \(J_{1\cdots1}\) has law \(\mu\).  Fix \(M<\infty\),

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:33:23.329614+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_447d384f508f4bec36dcdfebd7923a7a2f23961c83560f4311915feff646bb76","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 2 of arXiv:2506.21829, 'Some notes on Lamperti's recurrence of stochastic sequences'] (Lamperti \cite{L}.)
Assume that a nonegative stochastic sequence $X_n$ satisfies \eqref{1}, and assume that for $x\to\infty$, we almost surely have
\begin{eqnarray}
\mu(x)&=&\mathsf{E}\{X_{n+1}-X_n~|~X_n=x, X_{n-1},\ldots,X_0\}=\frac{\xi}{2x}+O\left(\frac{1}{x^{1+\epsilon}}\right), \\
v(x)&=&\mathsf{E}\{(X_{n+1}-X_n)^2~|~X_n=x,  X_{n-1},\ldots,X_0\}=r^2+O\left(\frac{1}{x^{\epsilon}}\right),\nonumber\\
&&\text{where}\ \xi \ \text{is a positive value}.\nonumber
\end{eqnarray}
Then the stochastic sequence is recurrent, if for almost all $x\to\infty$,
\[
\mu(x)\leq \frac{v(x)}{2x}+O\left(\frac{1}{x^{1+\epsilon}}\right).
\]
If instead for some $\theta>1$ and  almost all large $x$,
\[
\mu(x)\geq\frac{\theta v(x)}{2x},
\]
then the stochastic sequence is transient. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["alpha,rho,lambda are fixed strictly positive real numbers","M_N=floor(exp(alpha N)); the energies within each N are independent N(0,rho^2/N)","All arrays are on a common probability space; arbitrary dependence across different N is permitted","For the pattern interpretation, x_N has norm rho sqrt(N) and is independent of every competing Gaussian pattern"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:33:41.510256+00:00","domain":"random energy model; REM; Derrida; Gaussian noise; quenched free energy; condensation threshold; dense associative memory","id":"claim_4498555a06d1cc33d3838c2b27ffe673f5b4cd6f3617e875afcf85b094a712bb","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Fix alpha>0, rho>0 and lambda>0, all independent of the positive integer N. For each N let M_N=floor(exp(alpha N)), and let epsilon_(1,N),...,epsilon_(M_N,N) be independent centered Gaussian variables, each of variance rho^2/N. Define phi_N=(1/(lambda N)) log(sum_(mu=1)^(M_N) exp(lambda N epsilon_(mu,N))). On any common probability space for these arrays, phi_N converges almost surely to alpha/lambda+lambda rho^2/2 when lambda<=lambda_c=sqrt(2alpha)/rho, and to rho sqrt(2alpha) when lambda>=lambda_c. The two expressions agree at lambda_c. Independence is required within each N; no independence across different N is needed. Equivalently, for independent Gaussian patterns xi_mu~N(0,I_N) and a state x_N of norm rho sqrt(N), chosen independently of these patterns, one may take epsilon_(mu,N)=<x_N,xi_mu>/N. The result applies to that fixed state or independently chosen state sequence. It does not assert a uniform limit over pattern-dependent states or along an adaptive retrieval trajectory. This is the classical Gaussian random energy model condensation formula, used as a noise free-energy computation, not a retrieval or basin theorem. Source: Lucibello--Mezard, arXiv:2304.14964v4, equations (4)--(5), PDF p2; variational derivation Appendix A, PDF pp7--9. The exponentially large count may equally be exp(alpha N)-1 with the usual integer rounding, since its logarithmic rate is unchanged.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:39:11.672717+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_44a00bf9d70bf3e168ed85b93e37b42ce29ad13f969cd2ff4a2a0c77e60460fd","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 20 (The i.i.d.\ entry model) of arXiv:2608.04824, 'Strong Convergence for a General Class of Random Matrix Models'] Fix \(d\in\mathbb N\).  Given a probability space, let
\[
 \bigl(\xi^{(\kappa)}_{ij}\bigr)_{i,j\geq1},
 \qquad 1\leq\kappa\leq d,
\]
be mutually independent infinite arrays.  Within each color \(\kappa\), the
entries are i.i.d.\ copies of a complex random variable \(\xi^{(\kappa)}\)
satisfying
\[
 \E\xi^{(\kappa)}=0,
 \qquad
 \E|\xi^{(\kappa)}|^2=\sigma_\kappa^2,
 \qquad
 \E|\xi^{(\kappa)}|^4<\infty.
\]
For \(n\geq1\), set
\[
 X_{\kappa,n}
 =\frac1{\sqrt n}
   \bigl(\xi^{(\kappa)}_{ij}\bigr)_{1\leq i,j\leq n}.
\]
Thus, for each color, the unnormalized entry blocks are nested upper-left
corners of one infinite array; the matrix at size \(n\) is obtained by applying
the normalization \(n^{-1/2}\) to the corresponding corner.  This coupling
across \(n\) is used for every almost-sure statement below.  No restriction is
placed on
\(\E[(\xi^{(\kappa)})^2]\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:45:38.342700+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_44a033795770c3dc6be26e226dc8359ae17a479f2952668f857791b434b84225","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 27 of arXiv:2604.20514, 'Macroscopic loops in the random loop model on sparse random graphs'] Fix \(u\in[0,1]\) and \(\theta>0\). Define
\[
C_\theta:=
\begin{cases}
1, & \theta=1,\\[1ex]
\dfrac{\theta |\log \theta|}{|\theta-1|}, & \theta\neq 1.
\end{cases}
\]

Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite graph with \(|V|=n\), and assume that for some \(\eta,\varepsilon>0\),
\[
e_G(S)\le (1+\varepsilon)|S|
\qquad\text{for every }S\subset V\text{ with }|S|\le \eta n.
\]
Assume moreover that
\[
\frac{|E|}{n}\in [m_-,m_+]
\]
for some \(m_-,m_+>0\).
Then for every \(a\ge 0\) and every \(s>0\),
\[
\frac1s\int_a^{a+s}\Pbb^G_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\,\dd t
\ge
\frac{
m_- - c_{\theta,u}(1+\varepsilon)-C_\theta/s
}{
(1+\theta)m_+ - c_{\theta,u}(1+\varepsilon)
},
\]
provided the denominator is positive.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the perturbation K is compact","lambda is a nonzero scalar","the ambient space is a Banach space (Hilbert space for the adjoint form with conjugated lambda)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.573224+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Fredholm theory","id":"claim_44c2b247a9f29b24f5479cb03b211daeeab0cd1b96adb5f6a3837b72135ca330","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The alternative 'injective implies surjective' for operators of the form lambda I - K is carried entirely by two hypotheses: K is compact, and lambda is nonzero. (1) Compactness is load-bearing. On l^2 the unilateral shift S(x_1, x_2, ...) = (0, x_1, x_2, ...) is bounded and injective but not surjective, and S = I - K with K = I - S bounded but not compact; its index is -1, not 0. So for a general bounded perturbation of the identity the two alternatives can both fail to be the right dichotomy: the equation x - K x = y can be uniquely solvable for some y and unsolvable for others, with no finite-dimensional solvability condition of equal dimensions on the two sides. What actually powers the alternative is that the index is 0, which compactness guarantees; a Fredholm operator of nonzero index (like S) is a counterexample to the dichotomy but not to Fredholm theory. (2) lambda nonzero is load-bearing. Take K = diag(1, 1/2, 1/3, ...) on l^2, which is compact and injective, with dense but proper range (the sequence (1/n) is not in ran K, since it would need preimage (1, 1, 1, ...)). So for lambda = 0, 'injective' does not give 'surjective', the range is not closed, and 0 is in the spectrum of every compact operator on an infinite-dimensional space. (3) In the Hilbert-space version the solvability condition uses the conjugate: lambda x - K x = y is solvable exactly when y is orthogonal to ker(conjugate of lambda times I - K*), not to ker(lambda I - K*); forgetting the conjugation is a common slip for complex lambda. (4) The dimension identity dim ker(lambda - K) = dim ker(lambda - K') is an identity of the two kernels, not a claim that the kernels correspond naturally, and it fails for non-compact perturbations (for S, ker S = 0 while ker S' is one-dimensional).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["C a class of measurable sets (or of {0,1}-valued functions); the suprema are assumed measurable (a countable class, or the standard measurability conditions)","i.i.d. sampling from an arbitrary P on X","the constants 4, 8 and 8, 32 are the classical ones; several textbooks state slightly different constants from the same proof"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:40:13.706632+00:00","domain":"statistical learning theory","id":"claim_44ca0346ee27a0d7980b7facd63807b8439c3deb8db5ffcd25f0f1d03c270b4a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"DEFINITIONS. For a class C of subsets of X and points x_1, ..., x_n, the number of distinct traces |{ A intersect {x_1, ..., x_n} : A in C }| is at most 2^n; the growth (shatter) function is s(C, n) = max over all n-point sets of this number; the VC dimension d = VC(C) is the largest n with s(C, n) = 2^n (infinite if s(C, n) = 2^n for all n). Sauer-Shelah: if d < infinity then s(C, n) <= sum_{i <= d} binom(n, i) <= (e n / d)^d for n >= d. THEOREM (Vapnik and Chervonenkis, 1971). Let X_1, ..., X_n be i.i.d. from P and P_n the empirical measure. For every eps > 0 and n >= 2 / eps^2, P( sup_{A in C} |P_n(A) - P(A)| > eps ) <= 4 s(C, 2n) exp( -n eps^2 / 8 ); a form valid for all n is P( sup_{A in C} |P_n(A) - P(A)| > eps ) <= 8 s(C, n) exp( -n eps^2 / 32 ). COROLLARIES. If VC(C) = d < infinity, then sup_A |P_n(A) - P(A)| -> 0 almost surely for EVERY P (C is a uniform Glivenko-Cantelli class), with E sup_A |P_n(A) - P(A)| <= C_0 sqrt(d / n) for an absolute constant C_0 (Talagrand's sharpening of the log-free bound); the sample size n = O( (d log(1/eps) + log(1/delta)) / eps^2 ) makes the sup at most eps with probability 1 - delta; and the condition is also necessary: if VC(C) = infinity there is a distribution P for which the sup does not converge to 0 in probability (Vapnik-Chervonenkis; Assouad; Dudley). In learning: for a class of classifiers of VC dimension d, every classifier's true error is within eps of its training error simultaneously once n is of order d / eps^2 (up to logarithms), so empirical risk minimisation is consistent exactly for finite VC dimension (the fundamental theorem of statistical learning, PAC learnability iff finite VC dimension).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A measurable, uniformly parabolic with constants lambda, Lambda; divergence form","u >= 0 and a local weak solution on the whole cylinder B_{2r} x (t_0 - 4r^2, t_0)","the two cylinders are separated in time, with Q^- earlier than Q^+"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.106483+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations / Harnack inequalities","id":"claim_44dbfa0199ed26c36b75aa732eeca6cc025e4e1a57803299d2f6b3708baf81ca","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $A$ be measurable and uniformly parabolic with constants $\\lambda,\\Lambda$ and let $u\\ge0$ be a local weak solution of $\\partial_tu=\\mathrm{div}(A\\nabla u)$ in $B_{2r}(x_0)\\times(t_0-4r^2,t_0)$. Set $Q^-=B_r(x_0)\\times(t_0-3r^2,t_0-2r^2)$ and $Q^+=B_r(x_0)\\times(t_0-r^2,t_0)$. Then $\\sup_{Q^-}u\\ \\le\\ C\\,\\inf_{Q^+}u$ with $C=C(n,\\lambda,\\Lambda)$. The time lag is essential and so is the direction: the past cylinder's supremum is controlled by the future cylinder's infimum, never the reverse, and no inequality of this form holds on a single time slice. Nonnegativity on the whole cylinder $B_{2r}\\times(t_0-4r^2,t_0)$ is required. Consequences: interior Holder continuity of solutions, the near-diagonal lower bound for the fundamental solution, and (through chaining) Aronson's Gaussian lower bound; the inequality is equivalent to the conjunction of the volume doubling property and a Poincare inequality in the Grigor'yan-Saloff-Coste characterization on manifolds and graphs.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:21:28.836546+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_44e454c4a3fb98f8ef6fdda283afac1db278935752df13ef947d999bcb42659e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corr FRSB of arXiv:2605.05631, 'Wandering Exponents and the Free Energy of the High-Dimensional Elastic Polymer'] Consider the model $B(x)=(1+x)^{-\gamma}$ for $\gamma<1$ at some fixed $(\beta,t)$. The Larkin mass $\mu_{Lar}(\beta;t)$ exists and is given by the unique $\mu$ which solves the equation
		\[2\gamma(\gamma+1)\left(1+\frac{2}{\beta \sqrt{\mu t}}\right)^{-\gamma-2}=\sqrt{\mu^3t}.\] 
		For all $\mu\ge \mu_{Lar}(\beta;t)$ the model is RS, and for all $\mu<\mu_{Lar}(\beta;t)$ the model is FRSB.\\
		
		\noindent Moreover, in the FRSB case, the Parisi pair, $(q_c,\zeta_c)$, in Theorem (theorem:intro:1-d continuum T>0:FRSB of the paper) may be found explicitly. The value for the unique triple $(q_0,q_*,q_c)$ immediately follows from the equations
		\[q_c-q_0=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{c_0}{\mu^{\frac{3}{2(2+\gamma)}}}-1\right),\;\;\; q_0=c_1\mu^{\frac{3(\gamma+1)}{2(2+\gamma)}+3},\;\;\; q_c-q_*=\frac{1}{\beta\sqrt{\mu_{Lar}(\beta;t)t}}, \]
		with constants given by $c_0=(\frac{2\gamma(\gamma+1)}{\sqrt{t}})^{1/(\gamma+2)}$ and $c_1=\frac{\gamma t}{c_0^{1+\gamma}}$. The measure $\zeta$ can then be found from its CDF, which is given for $s\in [q_0,q_*)$ by 
		\[\zeta_c([0,s])=\frac{\gamma+2}{3\beta}\left(\frac{4}{t\gamma(\gamma+1)}\right)^{1/3}(1+2q_c-2s)^{\frac{\gamma-1}{3}}, \]
		and otherwise by $\zeta_c([0,s])=0$ if $s\in [0,q_0)$ and $\zeta_c([0,s])=1$ if $s\in [q_*,q_c]$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:23:05.300964+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_45335c4ddd389e0162937528dc826fd5f85d749df3a02030b02af149d2559f9f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 19 (Posterior Gaussian-mixture geometry) of arXiv:2608.21709, 'Posterior Information Dynamics of Diffusion Models for Linear Inverse Problems'] For \(c\in\{\pm1\}\),

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T07:57:26.273086+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_453cdc3caad94d439041d887f802b242","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In information theory, the entropy of a random variable quantifies the average level of uncertainty or information associated with the variable's potential states or possible outcomes. Given a discrete random variable $X$, which may be any member $x$ within the set ${\\mathcal {X}}$ and is distributed according to $p\\colon {\\mathcal {X}}\\to [0,1]$, the entropy is $\\mathrm {H} (X):=-\\sum _{x\\in {\\mathcal {X}}}p(x)\\log p(x),$ where $\\Sigma$ denotes the sum over the variable's possible values. The choice of base for $\\log$, the logarithm, varies for different applications. Base 2 gives the unit of bits (or \"shannons\"), while base e gives \"natural units\" nat, and base 10 gives units of \"dits\", \"bans\", or \"hartleys\". An equivalent definition of entropy is the expected value of the self-information of a variable.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:17:13.068309+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_454058caabfd204fb46afdb88783af5796c6dbc759e845c3e4bc7fa24234a1d6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:H of arXiv:2509.06273, 'Normalized Matching Property for Competing Urn Models'] Let \. $X\subseteq [m]$ \. be an  odd set, and set \. $k:=\tfrac{|X|-1}{2}$.
Define the bipartite graph \. $H_X:=(W_1,W_2,F):=(W_1(X), W_2(X), F(X))$ \.  by
\begin{align*}
	& W_{1} \ := \ \binom{X}{k}, \quad W_{2} \ := \  \binom{X}{k+1}, \\
	& F \ := \ \{ \. (S,T) \in W_{1} \times W_{2}  \. \mid \. S \subset T \. \}.
\end{align*}
Let 
$\nu$ be a probability measure on $[m]$ (corresponding to the random balls ending in the
$n$-th urn).
We define a weight function  \. $g_{\nu}:=g_{\nu,X}$ \. on the vertices of  $H_X$  by

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:20:07.913525+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_455a60571276a5980c784e8a027162555c51d4cdab57f4504c62040134d03228","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 2boxtimesfp of arXiv:2608.29914, 'Fixed points in abstract provability structures'] Let $S$ be an APS and let $\triangle v$ be a one-variable APS term of degree two. 
Then $\mathsf{E}_S(\triangle)$ holds. 
More precisely, the following statements hold.  
Let $k, m, n$ be natural numbers. 
 \begin{enumerate}
        \item If $m \geq n$, then $\boxtimes \Box^m \boxtimes \Box^n v$ has a fixed point $\boxtimes \top$.
        
        \item If $m < n$, then $\boxtimes \Box^m \boxtimes \Box^n v$ has a fixed point $\boxtimes \Box^m \boxtimes \top$.
        
        \item If $m \geq n + k$, then $\Box^k \boxtimes \Box^m \boxtimes \Box^n v$ has a fixed point $\Box^k \boxtimes \top$.
        
        \item If $m < n + k$, then $\Box^k \boxtimes \Box^m \boxtimes \Box^n v$ has a fixed point $ \Box^k \boxtimes\Box^m \boxtimes \top$.
