{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.160651+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_53144a8d46bb675c6426a29502ef6aad25df8a850910735bdde4294bf23b9834","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 6 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall the definition of $\Surplus(\YY;\lambda,\mu)$ from the statement of Proposition~\ref{p:convex.body.polytope.bound.new}. 
Recall $\cD_+$ from \eqref{e:cD-plus}.
Given any $\mu$, define 
    \[
        \cD_{+,\mu}(2) \equiv \Big\{
            \YY = (\BBb,\vvv,\UUu,\www) \in \cD_+ : (\mu, \www) \le 2
        \Big\}\,,
    \]
For $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$ and $\dot{\YY}, \ddot{\YY} \in \cD_{+,\mu}(2)$, we have
    \[\Big|\Surplus(\dot{\YY};\lambda,\mu) - \Surplus(\ddot{\YY};\lambda,\mu)\Big|
        \le
        \frac{4\|\Delta\YY\|_2
            +  6\|\Delta\YY\|_2^{1/2}}{\iota \min\{1,\alpha\}}\,,
    \]
where we abbreviate $\Delta\YY \equiv \dot{\YY} - \ddot{\YY}$. 
That is, $\YY \mapsto \Surplus(\YY;\lambda,\mu)$ is uniformly continuous in $\cD_{+,\mu}(2)$, uniformly in $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$.

\begin{proof}
We will bound separately the differences 
	\baln
	\Delta\Cost
	& \equiv\Cost(\dot{\YY};\lambda) - \Cost(\ddot{\YY};\lambda)\,,\\
	\Delta\Budget
	& \equiv\Budget(\dot{\YY};\mu) - \Budget(\ddot{\YY};\mu)\,.
	\ealn
Note that for any $\xxxx \in \bbR^r$, the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives
    \[
        \sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j |\xxxx_j|
        \le \bigg(\sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j |\xxxx_j|^2\bigg)^{1/2}
        \le \|\xxxx\|_2\,.
    \]
    Thus, abbreviating $\Delta\YY
    \equiv(\Delta\vBBb,\Delta\vvvv,\Delta\vUUu,\Delta\vwww)
    \equiv\dot{\YY}-\ddot{\YY}$, we have
    \baln
        |\Delta\Cost|
        &\le \sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j \bigg\{
            |\Delta\vBBb_j|
            + |\Delta\vUUu_j|
            + \Big|
            (\dot{\vvvv}_j-\dot{\vUUu}_j)_+ - (\ddot{\vvvv}_j-\ddot{\vUUu}_j)_+
            \Big| 
            + 2 \Big|(\dot{\vvvv}_j-\dot{\vUUu}_j)_+^{1/2} - (\ddot{\vvvv}_j-\ddot{\vUUu}_j)_+^{1/2} 
            \Big|
        \bigg\} \\
        &\le \|\Delta\vBBb\|_2
        + \|\Delta\vUUu\|_2
        + \Big\|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+ - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+
        	\Big\|_2 
        + 2\Big\|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+^{1/2} - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+^{1/2}
        \Big\|_2\,,
    \ealn
    where the operations $x\mapsto x_+$ and $x\mapsto (x_+)^{1/2}$ are applied entrywise.
    Since $x\mapsto x_+$ is a contraction,
    \[
        \|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+ - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+\|_2
        \le \|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu}) - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})\|_2
        \le \|\Delta\vvvv\|_2 + \|\Delta\vUUu\|_2\,.
    \]
Furthermore, since $|a^{1/2}-b^{1/2}| \le |a-b|^{1/2}$ for all $a,b\ge0$, for any vectors $\vec{a},\vec{b}\in[0,\infty)^r$ we can bound
	\[
	\Big(\|\vec{a}^{1/2}-\vec{b}^{1/2}\|_2\Big)^2
	=\sum_{j=1}^r \Big((a_j)^{1/2}-(b_j)^{1/2}\Big)^2
	\le \sum_{j=1}^r |a_j-b_j| = \|\vec{a}-\vec{b}\|_1\,.
	\]
Applying this estimate gives 
    \baln
        &\bigg(\Big\|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+^{1/2} - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+^{1/2}\Big\|_2\bigg)^2
        \le 
        \Big\|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+ - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+
        \Big\|_1 \\
        &\qquad \le 
            \|\Delta\vvvv\|_1
            + \|\Delta\vUUu\|_1 
            \le r^{1/2} \Big(
            \|\Delta\vvvv\|_2
            + \|\Delta\vUUu\|_2
        \Big)\,.
    \ealn
    Finally, crudely upper bounding 
$\|\Delta\vBBb\|_2,
        \|\Delta\vvvv\|_2,
        \|\Delta\vUUu\|_2$ by $\|\Delta\YY\|_2$,
    we obtain
    \[
        |\Delta\Cost|
        \le 4 \|\Delta\YY\|_2
        + 2
        \Big(2 r^{1/2} \|\Delta\YY\|_2 \Big)^{1/2} \,.
    \]
This gives a continuity estimate for the $\Cost$ function.

We next turn to the $\Budget$ function.
    For all $\YY  \in \cD_{+,\mu}(2)$, we have
    \[
        0\le \alpha \cdot \Budget(\YY;\mu) \le (\mu,\vwww) \le 2\,,
    \]
    where the intermediate step is by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality.
    Therefore,
    \baln
        \alpha |\Delta\Budget| 
        &= \alpha^{1/2} \Big|
        \Budget(\dot{\YY};\mu)^{1/2} + 
        \Budget(\ddot{\YY};\mu)^{1/2}\Big| 
        \cdot 
        \alpha^{1/2} \Big|
        \Budget(\dot{\YY};\mu)^{1/2}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:20:15.493454+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5315a14d5e97dd4ffe3a5565200336690752ef5dcc2f635db0d824803f6e9f6e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 12 of arXiv:2512.02538, 'On the spectral geometry of Liouville quantum gravity'] There a.s. exists a family $(\mathbf{p}_t (\cdot ,\cdot))_{t\ge 0}$ of (jointly in all three arguments) measurable functions such that for all $t \ge 0$, for all $x \in \Sigma$,
 $$\mathbf{P}_t f(x) = \int_\Sigma \mathbf{p}_t (x,y) f(y) \mu_{\ph} (\dd y).$$ This family of functions $\mathbf{p}_t (x,y)$ (a priori only defined for all $t\ge 0$, for all $x\in \Sigma$ and $\mu_\ph-$almost every $y \in \Sigma$ is called the \textbf{Liouville heat kernel} and satisfies the following properties:

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:35:04.198653+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_536bd7c1ff7c9dfdf0d52119fd89b617427aac6937b66c002d5a9671a818d0f0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 13 (Boundary states) of arXiv:2608.03497, 'Connective Constants on Nested Fractal Graphs'] A \emph{linear forest} is an acyclic graph whose vertices have degree at
most two.  A \emph{boundary forest} in \(F_m\) is a nonempty edge
subgraph \(\Gamma\subset F_m\) such that
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item \(\Gamma\) is a linear forest;
\item every vertex of degree one belongs to \(\partial F_m\);
\item every connected component contains at least one edge.
\end{enumerate}
Thus every component is a self-avoiding path with two distinct endpoints
in \(\partial F_m\).

An \emph{abstract boundary forest} is a nonempty linear forest whose
vertex set is contained in \(V_0\) and which has no isolated vertices;
equivalently, each connected component is a path containing at least one
edge.  Let \(\cS\) be the finite set of all such abstract boundary
forests.  Thus an element \(\sigma\in\cS\) may consist of one path or of
several vertex-disjoint paths; it records only a possible finite
combination of boundary connections, not an actual walk in \(F_m\).

To pass from the actual boundary forest \(\Gamma\subset F_m\) to its
abstract boundary pattern, consider each component of \(\Gamma\) in
\(F_m\).  List the boundary vertices in the order in which the path meets
them.  Keep only these listed vertices, replace each portion
between two consecutive listed vertices by one abstract edge, and relabel the
retained vertices by \(\iota_m^{-1}\).  This compression operation is
called taking the \emph{boundary trace}.  The resulting nonempty linear
forest on \(V_0\), hence an element of \(\cS\), is the \emph{boundary
state} of \(\Gamma\), denoted by \(\operatorname{tr}_m(\Gamma)\).  It
records which boundary vertices are visited and how consecutive visits
are connected along each path; it does not record the internal vertices
or the lengths of the individual portions.

For \(\sigma\in\cS\), put
\[
  \cC_m(\sigma)
  =
  \{\Gamma\subset F_m:
    \Gamma\text{ is a boundary forest and }
    \operatorname{tr}_m(\Gamma)=\sigma\},
\]
and, for \(\beta\ge0\), define
\begin{equation}
  Z_m^\sigma(\beta)
  =
  \sum_{\Gamma\in\cC_m(\sigma)}
  e^{-\beta\#E(\Gamma)},
  \qquad
  \bZ_m(\beta)
  =
  \bigl(Z_m^\sigma(\beta)\bigr)_{\sigma\in\cS}.
  
\end{equation}
We call \(\bZ_m(\beta)\) the \emph{boundary-state partition vector}.
We adjoin the \emph{empty state} \(\varnothing\) and set
\(Z_m^\varnothing(\beta)=1\).","status":"unverified"}

(0,\infty )$ is multivariate totally positive of order $2$ ($MTP_{2}$) if 
\begin{equation}
l(x\wedge y)\,l(x\vee y)\ \geq \ l(x)\,l(y),\qquad x,y\in \lbrack 0,1]^{d},

\end{equation}
where $\wedge ,\vee $ denote coordinatewise minimum and maximum. It is 
\textit{multivariate reverse regular of order }$2$ ($MRR_{2}$) if the
reverse inequality holds: 
\begin{equation}
l(x\wedge y)\,l(x\vee y)\ \leq \ l(x)\,l(y),\qquad x,y\in \lbrack 0,1]^{d}.

\end{equation}
We say that $l$ is strictly $MRR_{2}$ ($SMRR_{2}$) if for every compact set $
K\subset (0,1)^{d}$ there exists a set of full \textit{Lebesgue measure} in $
K\times K$ on which ((2000b of the paper)) holds with strict inequality whenever $x$
and $y$ are incomparable (i.e.\ neither $x\leq y$ nor $y\leq x$
coordinatewise). Equivalently (and more concretely), on each $K\subset
(0,1)^{d}$ on which $l$ is bounded away from $0$, ((2000b of the paper)) is strict
for all incomparable $x,y\in K$.","status":"unverified"}

$(X_i,Y_i)$ are generated successively in the form
\[
 (X_i,Y_i)=F_i(Y_{<i},\xi_i),
\]
where, for every admissible value of $Y_{<i}$, the first marginal of the

\[
 Z_i=\abs{X_i-Y_i},\qquad
 g_i=\E(Z_i\mid X_i,Y_{<i}),\qquad
 \widetilde g_i=\E(Z_i\mid Y_{\le i}).
\]

\begin{align}
 \E(Z_i\mid X)&=\E(g_i\mid X),
 \\

\end{align}

\begin{align}
 \E\big[\E(Z_i\mid X)^2\big]&\le\E g_i^2,
 \\
 \E\big[\E(Z_i\mid Y)^2\big]&=\E\widetilde g_i^2.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:48:47.287549+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_53a63231a14d32986d7b01d953bf29a23589cb9731216344d145a1b7856dcfd9","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma gradient TAP of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Recall $\mathrm{TAP}$ from (equation def:TAPmu of the paper) and $k_\zeta$ from~(equation def:kqm of the paper).
		Fix $\mathbf{m}\in(-1,1)^N$ and set $q=\frac{1}{N}\Vert \mathbf{m}\Vert^2$.
		Let $\zeta$ be a probability measure on $[q,1]$. Then for every $i\in[N]$:
		\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
			\item (\emph{Exact gradient at the minimizer}) If $\zeta_\mathbf{m}$ is the minimizer in Definition~(def:zetam of the paper), then
			\begin{equation}
				\partial_i \mathrm{TAP}(\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})})=-\frac{1}{N}k_{\zeta_\mathbf{m}}(q,m_i).
			\end{equation}
			
			\item (\emph{Exact defect formula and explicit boundary stability}) One has
			\begin{equation}
				-N\partial_i \mathrm{TAP}(\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})},\zeta)
				=
				k_\zeta(q,m_i)-m_i\,\xi''(q)\,\Delta_\zeta^{\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})}},
			\end{equation}
			where $\Delta_\zeta^{\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})}}$ is defined in (equation eq:def-Delta of the paper).
			Consequently, if
			\[
			\max_{j\in[N]}|m_j|\le 1-\delta
			\qquad\text{for some }\delta\in(0,1),
			\]
			and
			\[
			\zeta(\{q\})\ge u_0>0,
			\]
			then there exists $C=C(\xi,u_0)<\infty$ such that
			\begin{equation}
				\Bigl|\partial_i \mathrm{TAP}(\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})},\zeta)+\frac{1}{N}k_{\zeta}(q,m_i)\Bigr|
				\le \frac{C}{N\delta}\,\mathrm{dist}(\zeta_\mathbf{m},\zeta).
			\end{equation}
		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:45:01.813237+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_53af0126f520cd915056952b6859ace03d2e4ec86b1fc26e40678c2a6c3dac2a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:technical extended version of arXiv:2512.18435, 'Indistinguishability for recurrent clusters'] Let $\mathscr A$ be a component property and let $(G,\eta,o)$ be a random rooted network.
        Let $(v_n)$ be a stationary sequence started at $v_0=o$ on $(G,\eta,o)$, meaning that $(G,\eta,v_n)$ has the same distribution as $(G,\eta,o)$, and such that $v_n\in\mathcal P_{G,\eta}(o)$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$. It can depend on $(G,\eta,o)$ and additional randomness.
    Furthermore, let $S_{G,\eta,o}$ be a $(G,\eta,o)$-measurable subset of $G$ and $\psi$ a random increasing function $\mathbb N\longrightarrow \mathbb N$ such that, almost surely:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\limsup_{n\rightarrow \infty}\frac n{\psi(n)} >0$,

 \cJ_r(H)

 {1-e^{-rt}}.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.376271+00:00","domain":"general topology","id":"claim_53b62a4d4b0ea879e3c5457fa6f8ecdb78aba2e92827a95ead2ce3351cd5f4ff","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A sequence (x_n) in a metric space (X, d) is Cauchy if for every epsilon > 0 there is an index N such that d(x_m, x_n) < epsilon for all m, n >= N. Every convergent sequence is Cauchy, but not conversely in general: the rationals with the usual distance are not complete, while the real line R and Euclidean space R^n are complete. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T01:29:08.755493+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_53cd53a3c64890c99d77c5c7c432486b23a4395d3088ccd473c393e003538cca","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm smasympexGOEGSE of arXiv:2412.00593, 'A new approach to strong convergence II.\\The classical ensembles'] There exist universal constants $C,c>0$, and a compactly supported

{"assumptions":["F is continuous","u is continuous on Ω","the equation is written in the form F = 0 with a fixed sign convention"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.110816+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations, Hamilton–Jacobi equations","id":"claim_53dfc94ed0a9e05577bb2bf64ec2af288dc9f26b2353c233536514d102e5795c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Ω ⊂ ℝⁿ be open and F: Ω × ℝ × ℝⁿ → ℝ continuous; consider the equation F(x, u(x), Du(x)) = 0 in Ω. A function u ∈ C(Ω) is a viscosity SUBsolution if for every φ ∈ C¹(Ω) and every point x₀ ∈ Ω at which u − φ has a local maximum, F(x₀, u(x₀), Dφ(x₀)) ≤ 0. It is a viscosity SUPERsolution if for every φ ∈ C¹(Ω) and every local minimum point x₀ of u − φ, F(x₀, u(x₀), Dφ(x₀)) ≥ 0. It is a viscosity solution if it is both. (Equivalent reformulations: replace 'local' by 'strict local' or 'global' max/min, or use C^∞ test functions, or use super-/subdifferentials D⁺u(x₀) and D⁻u(x₀): the conditions read F(x₀, u, p) ≤ 0 for all p ∈ D⁺u(x₀) and ≥ 0 for all p ∈ D⁻u(x₀).) Every classical C¹ solution is a viscosity solution, and a viscosity solution that is differentiable at x₀ satisfies the equation pointwise there. For time-dependent equations u_t + H(x, Du) = 0 on Ω × (0,T) apply the same definition with the gradient variable (u_t, Du) and test functions of (x,t). SHARP EDGE — the sign of F matters: writing the same equation as −F = 0 interchanges the roles of sub- and supersolutions, so the two forms have DIFFERENT viscosity solutions. Example: on (−1,1) with boundary values u(±1) = 0, the function 1 − |x| is a viscosity solution of |u'| − 1 = 0 but NOT of 1 − |u'| = 0, while |x| − 1 is a viscosity solution of 1 − |u'| = 0 but not of |u'| − 1 = 0 (at the kink x = 0, a concave kink admits only test functions touching from above, and a convex kink only test functions touching from below). Viscosity solutions are in general only continuous, are stable under uniform limits, and for convex H coincide with Lipschitz solutions that are semiconcave; the notion is designed so that comparison/uniqueness theorems hold where classical and a.e. solutions are non-unique.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.348469+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5416a777be1cc30c7c8f9a9bebbe4d2ca70960a8272285b96d45fe6a1e694b32","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 162 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $I$ be a finite, nonempty index set. Let 
  \[
    \lt(\Theta, 
    \vec{\hat{Z}}\equiv
    (\hat Z_i)_{i\in I},
    \vec{\tilde{Z}}
    \equiv(\tilde Z_i)_{i\in I}\rt)
  \]
  be a random variable where
  $(\vec{\hat{Z}},\vec{\tilde{Z}})$
  are centered, jointly gaussian, and independent of $\Theta$. 
  Assume that $\vec{\hat{Z}}$ and $\vec{\tilde{Z}}$ are equidistributed,
 and that, for distinct $i,k\in I$,
  \[
    \bbE[\hat Z_i\hat Z_k]
    =\bbE[\tilde Z_i\tilde Z_k]
    =\bbE[\hat Z_i\tilde Z_k]=0.
  \]
Let $F$ and $G$ be measurable functions
such that $F(\Theta,\hat Z)$ and 
$G(\Theta,\hat Z)$ have finite variance, and such that
	\beq
    \bbE\Big[F(\Theta,\hat Z) 
    	\,\Big|\, \Theta\Big] = 0 = 
    \bbE\Big[G(\Theta,\tilde Z) 
    	\,\Big|\, \Theta\Big]\,,
    \eeq
  $\Theta$-almost surely.
Then the covariance between $F(\Theta,\hat{Z})$ and $G(\Theta,\tilde{Z})$ is bounded by
  \beq
    \lt| \bbE[F(\Theta,\hat Z) G(\Theta,\tilde Z)] \rt|
    \le
    \rho_{\max} \cdot
    \bbE[F(\Theta,\hat Z)^2]^{1/2}
    \bbE[G(\Theta,\tilde Z)^2]^{1/2}\,, 
    
  \eeq
where $\rho_i\in[-1,+1]$ denotes the correlation between $\hat{Z}_i$ and $\tilde{Z}_i$, and 
$\rho_{\max} 
   \equiv\max\{|\rho_i|: i\in i\}$.
 
\begin{proof}
Let $\sigma_i$ denote the standard deviation of $\hat{Z}_i$, and denote
  \[
    \hat W_i \equiv 
    \frac{\hat Z_i}{\sigma_i}\,, \quad
    \tilde W_i 
    \equiv \frac{\tilde Z_i}{\sigma_i}\,,
  \]
which are marginally standard gaussians. It follows from the assumptions that
$(\hat W_i,\tilde W_i)$ are independent over $i\in I$, and $\bbE[\hat W_i\tilde W_i]=\rho_i$.
Let $(h_m)_{m\geq 0}$ denote the orthonormal Hermite polynomials for the
one-dimensional standard gaussian measure. We note that if $W$ and $\tilde{W}$ are marginally standard gaussians, and $(W,\tilde{W})$ is jointly gaussian and $\rho$-correlated, then it is straightforward to verify that
	\beq
	\E[ h_n(W) h_m(\tilde{W})]
	= \ind\{n=m\} \rho^n\,.\eeq
 For a multi-index $\vec n=(n_i)_{i\in I}\in\bbZ_{\ge 0}^I$, define the multivariate Hermite polynomial
  \[
    H_{\vec n}(w)
    \equiv\prod_{i\in I}h_{n_i}(w_i).
  \]
  We expand $F,G$ in the Hermite bases of $\hat W$ and $\tilde W$ respectively, conditional on $\Theta$, to obtain Hermite coefficients $a_{\vec n}(\Theta)$ and $b_{\vec n}(\Theta)$ such that
  \begin{align*}
    F(\Theta,\hat Z)
    &= \sum_{\vec n}a_{\vec n}(\Theta)
        H_{\vec n}(\hat W)\,, \\
    G(\Theta,\tilde Z)
    &= \sum_{\vec n}b_{\vec n}(\Theta)
        H_{\vec n}(\tilde W)\,.
  \end{align*}
  The assumption \eqref{e:conditional-centering} ensures $a_{\vec 0}(\Theta)=b_{\vec 0}(\Theta)=0$, $\Theta$-almost surely.
  Consequently, expanding in the Hermite bases and applying \eqref{e:hermite.corr.ip} gives
  \begin{align*}
    &\bigg|
      \bbE\Big[
        F(\Theta,\hat Z)G(\Theta,\tilde Z) \,\Big|\, \Theta
      \Big]
    \bigg|
    \le
      \sum_{\vec n\neq\vec 0}
         |a_{\vec n}(\Theta)b_{\vec n}(\Theta)|
         \prod_{i\in I}|\rho_i|^{n_i}\\
    &\qquad\le
      \rho_{\max}
      \bigg(\sum_{\vec n\neq\vec 0}
        a_{\vec n}(\Theta)^2
        \bigg)^{1/2}
      \bigg(\sum_{\vec n\neq\vec 0}
        b_{\vec n}(\Theta)^2
        \bigg)^{1/2}
    =\rho_{\max}
      \bbE\Big[F(\Theta,\hat Z)^2 
      	\,\Big|\, \Theta\Big]^{1/2}
      \bbE\Big[G(\Theta,\tilde Z)^2 
      	\,\Big|\, \Theta\Big]^{1/2}\,.
  \end{align*}
  Taking expectation over $\Theta$ and again applying the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality proves the conclusion.
\end{proof}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:22:46.423015+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_544b0ab65a69238eb286093a8a9952f69bb63ad7dd593d0e1c9470af795aa98a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 (Causality and extendibility of curves) of arXiv:2609.03101, 'The emergence of the Cauchy horizon from the crease for $3D$ compressible Euler flow'] Let $\mathcal{M} \subset \R^{1+3}$ be an open subset of spacetime on which the fluid variables

{"assumptions":["Real g in L^2 of the standard Gaussian measure; orthonormal probabilists Hermite convention.","For the finite-energy first-order expansion, also g in H^1(gamma)."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:46:50.165893+00:00","domain":"Gaussian analysis and neural-network capacity","id":"claim_546ec58f320bb143f8e7e8d299063a32dddcbcf5a1b864e0c2639fe6302e7d43","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let gamma be the standard normal probability measure on R and g be a real function in L^2(gamma). Use the orthonormal probabilists Hermite basis H_k=He_k/sqrt(k!) and coefficients a_k=E[g(Z)*H_k(Z)], Z~gamma. For jointly standard normal X,Y with correlation q in (-1,1), define C_g(q)=Cov(g(X),g(Y)) and V=Var_gamma(g). Then C_g(q)=sum_(k>=1) a_k^2*q^k and V=sum_(k>=1) a_k^2. In particular, lim_(q up to 1) [V-C_g(q)]/(1-q)=sum_(k>=1) k*a_k^2, allowing the value +infinity. This sum is finite exactly when g has a weak derivative g_prime in L^2(gamma), that is, g belongs to H^1(gamma); weak derivative means the usual distributional derivative with respect to Lebesgue measure. In that case ||g_prime||_(L^2(gamma))^2=sum_(k>=1) k*a_k^2 and V-C_g(q)=||g_prime||_(L^2(gamma))^2*(1-q)+o(1-q). These are Gaussian analytic identities used in the authors' activation-smoothness calculation. They do not require the replica ansatz and do not assert a rigorous storage-capacity threshold.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the operator is densely defined but not assumed symmetric or closed","a closure or a core argument is being invoked"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.772684+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, unbounded operators","id":"claim_54940f80014d70dd9eb95c49c095eba47a53c4de71e730a15c0f74ec018b6e59","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: 'take the closure of T' presupposes that T is closable, i.e. that x_n ∈ D(T), x_n → 0 and Tx_n → y force y = 0; equivalently (in a Hilbert space) that D(T*) is dense. What fails: without closability the closure of the graph is not a graph, and 'the smallest closed extension' does not exist. Counterexample: H = ℓ², D(T) = finitely supported sequences, T x = (Σ_n x_n) e_1. T is densely defined and linear. Take x^{(k)} = (1/k, ..., 1/k, 0, 0, ...) with k entries: ‖x^{(k)}‖ = 1/√k → 0 while T x^{(k)} = e_1 for every k, so the graph closure contains both (0,0) and (0, e_1) and T is not closable. Consistently, ⟨Tx, y⟩ = (Σ x_n) conj(y_1) is ℓ²-bounded in x only if y_1 = 0, so D(T*) = {y : y_1 = 0} is not dense - exactly the criterion. The same phenomenon occurs for pointwise evaluation f ↦ f(0)g on L²(ℝ) restricted to continuous L² functions. Related traps: (i) an operator can be closable while its closure has strictly larger domain on which a defining formula no longer holds pointwise, so identities proved on D(T) must be re-derived by continuity in the graph norm; (ii) symmetry rescues closability (a symmetric operator is always closable, since T ⊂ T* and T* is closed), which is why this pitfall bites mainly for non-symmetric operators such as first order operators with unbalanced boundary conditions or multiplication-composition operators; (iii) a core argument ('it suffices to verify on a dense subspace') is valid only if the subspace is dense in the graph norm of the closed operator, not merely dense in the ambient space.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:05:37.773038+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_54a170f683c2fe03b70c7a88e764fe8ab8dc2fc7b3e02b8c7b87103064904edb","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem prop2 of arXiv:2608.00295, 'Quadratic Perturbations of Markov Systems'] Let ${\bf A}=(A_i)_{1\leq i\leq n}$ such that   $A_i=(a_{i}^{(s,t)})_{1\leq s,t\leq d}\in M_d(\mathbb{R})$ is a stochastic $d\times d$ matrix for each $1\leq i\leq n$, and ${\bf b}=(b_{i,j})_{1\leq i, j\leq n}$ such that each $b_{i,j}=(\alpha_{i,j}^{(s)})_{1\leq s\leq d}\in \mathbb{R}^d$ is a null-sum vector for each $1\leq i, j\leq n$ (with the convention  that $b_{i,i}=0$ for all $1 \leq i\leq n$).  We define the nonlinear operator 
$$T({\bf A};{\bf b}):\overbrace{\mathbb{R}^d \times  \mathbb{R}^d \times \dots \times \mathbb{R}^d}^{n \text{ times}}\to \overbrace{\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d \times \dots \times \mathbb{R}^d}^{n \text{ times}},$$ 
determined by 
$$T({\bf A};{\bf b})\begin{bmatrix}
v_1\\
v_2\\
\vdots\\
v_n
\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}
{\displaystyle A_1v_1+\sum_{j=1}^n\langle v_1,v_j\rangle b_{1,j}}\\
{\displaystyle A_2v_2+\sum_{j=1}^n \langle v_2,v_j\rangle b_{2,j}}\\
\vdots\\
{\displaystyle A_nv_n+\sum_{j=1}^n \langle v_n,v_j\rangle b_{n,j}}
\end{bmatrix}.$$
The following are equivalent. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item For all the possible combinations of $\pm$ sign of the null-sum vectors $b_{i,j}$ we have that $T({\bf A};{\bf \pm b})$ induces a well defined operator from $\Delta_{d-1}^n$ to  $\Delta_{d-1}^n$. 
\item For each $1\leq i\leq n$ and $1\leq s\leq d$ we have $${\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^n|\alpha_{i,j}^{(s)}|\leq \min_{1\leq t\leq d} \{a_{i}^{(s,t)}\}}.$$  
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:10.025497+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_54ae114798ca9a256a2c70700fa791a86f298aba79d645fb75c2a110914ca5b2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 16 (Kac's walk applied to the Johnson--Lindenstrauss transform) of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] There is a universal constant $C_{\mathrm{JL}}<\infty$ such that the following holds. Let $n\geq 2$, let $x\in\So{n}$, and let $M\sim\kacdist_{n,T,x}$ be the endpoint of $T$ steps of Kac's walk started from $x$. Let $\mathcal X\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ have $N\geq2$ points, and let $0<\varepsilon,\delta<1/2$. Set
\be 
r=\left\lceil \log\frac{N}{\delta}\right\rceil,
\ee
and assume $4r<n$. Let $\ell$ be an integer satisfying
\be 
C_{\mathrm{JL}}\varepsilon^{-2}r\leq \ell<n.
\ee

If
\be 
T\geq
C_{\mathrm{JL}}\,n(4r+\log n)\left(r\log\frac{n}{\varepsilon}+\log\frac{N}{\delta}\right),
\ee
then, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over $M\sim\kacdist_{n,T,x}$,
\be 
(1-\varepsilon)\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2
\leq
\|A_M(x_i-x_j)\|_2^2
\leq
(1+\varepsilon)\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2
\ee
for every pair $1\leq i<j\leq N$.

In particular, for fixed $\varepsilon$ and $N/\delta\leq n^A$, with $A<\infty$ fixed, the usual Johnson--Lindenstrauss target dimension $\ell=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(N/\delta))=O_A(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)$ \vnote{Isn't the JL target dimension $\epsilon^{-2}\log N$? EDIT: Ah, I see what's going on, $N$ is set to polynomial in $n$. But see below.} is achieved by taking $T\geq C_A n\log^3 n$. \vnote{I am worried that this is not the best illustration of our bound. In particular, when $N$ is polynomial in $n$, the JL embedding dimension $\ell$ is already $O(\log n)$ and so applying the matrix already only costs $O(n\log n)$. Shouldn't we be thinking about very large point sets of size, say $2^{n^{\epsilon'}}$ for some constant $0 < \epsilon' < 1$.} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:07:15.756214+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_54bc151f1da4abc0a9d417c2b9341ca78c23cb6add0cda5142a647ec2cb1b350","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:abstract-square-transversality of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] Let $\nu_{\rm ref}$ be a sigma-finite positive Radon measure on $S$, and let

\begin{equation}
 A_\mu\phi_i=\Lambda_i\phi_i,
 \qquad
 \Lambda_i>0,
 \qquad
 \Lambda_i\ne\Lambda_j\ (i\ne j),

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751292+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_54d64fad1e4608f5ad2108eaf3e69d53ceffd8a53470cf0276a225deb916e63a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Tonelli's theorem needs BOTH measures sigma-finite and the integrand nonnegative and product-measurable; it then asserts that the double integral and both iterated integrals agree in [0, infinity], with no integrability assumption. Fubini's theorem needs both measures sigma-finite and f in L^1(mu tensor nu); it then asserts the same equality with all three quantities finite. Two failure modes are standard and are NOT the same failure. (1) Integrability dropped, sigma-finiteness kept: on (0,1)^2 with Lebesgue measure take f(x,y) = (x^2 - y^2)/(x^2 + y^2)^2. Since d/dy [ y/(x^2+y^2) ] = (x^2 - y^2)/(x^2+y^2)^2, the inner integral over y in (0,1) is 1/(1+x^2), so integrating in x afterwards gives pi/4; f is antisymmetric under swapping x and y, so the other order gives -pi/4. Both iterated integrals exist and are finite and they differ, so f cannot be in L^1 of the product. (2) sigma-finiteness dropped, nonnegativity kept: let mu be Lebesgue measure on [0,1], nu counting measure on [0,1], and f the indicator of the diagonal. Then integral over x of (integral over y of f dnu) dmu = integral 1 dmu = 1, while integral over y of (integral over x of f dmu) dnu = integral 0 dnu = 0. Tonelli's conclusion fails although f >= 0, because nu is not sigma-finite. A third, quieter caveat: for COMPLETE measure spaces the correct statement is that ALMOST every section is measurable, not every section, since a null set in the product can have non-measurable sections; the theorem for the completed product measure is stated that way. In practice the usable recipe is: apply Tonelli to |f| first to decide integrability, then apply Fubini to f. [standard; e.g. Folland, Real Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorems 2.37 and 2.39]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:35:19.876191+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_550f9f8a3b419eb6f07e3074b654c0e830eb5b9c8987ff82123178743b7fdb0e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn of arXiv:2608.27939, 'Entropy and domination for quasi-Hitchin representations'] Let $X$ be a marked hyperbolic structure on $S$, let
$\rho_0:\pi_1(S)\to\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb R)$ be its holonomy, and identify
$\widetilde X$ with $\mathbb{H}^2$. Given a representation
$\rho:\pi_1(S)\to\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{C})$, a \emph{$\rho$-equivariant pleated plane}
is a continuous map  $\Psi:\widetilde X\longrightarrow \mathbb{H}^3$
such that
\[
        \Psi\bigl(\gamma \cdot x\bigr)
        =\rho(\gamma)\Psi(x)
        \qquad
        \text{for every $\gamma\in\pi_1(S)$ and $x\in\widetilde X$,}
\]
and with the following properties:

(i) There is a geodesic lamination $\lambda$ on $X$ such that $\Psi$ is a totally-geodesic embedding on the closure of every complementary component of its lift $\tilde{\lambda} \subset \tilde{X}$. Such a component $P$ is called a \textit{plaque} and its $\Psi$-image lies on a totally-geodesic copy of the hyperbolic plane $H_P \subset \mathbb{H}^3$, called the \emph{support plane} of $P$.

(ii) $\Psi$ is path-isometric: for every rectifiable arc
$a\subset\widetilde X$, $\ell_{\mathbb{H}^3}(\Psi(a))
        =\ell_{X}(a)$, 
where the length on the left is the length of the parametrized
image. The smallest geodesic lamination for which these properties
hold is the \emph{pleating locus}.

(iii) The pleating locus is equipped with a transverse measure recording
the bending angles. More precisely, if a leaf $\ell\subset \widetilde\lambda$, of weight
$\theta\in(0,\pi]$ separates two plaques $P_-$ and $P_+$, the support plane $H_{P_+}$ is obtained from
$H_{P_-}$ by an elliptic rotation about the geodesic
$\Psi(\ell)$ through angle $\theta$; the direction of rotation is
determined by the chosen orientations.

More generally, let $a$ be an oriented arc transverse to
$\widetilde\lambda$, with endpoints in plaques $P$ and $Q$.
Approximating the measured lamination in a neighborhood of $a$ by
finitely many weighted leaves, one may compose, in their order along
$a$, the rotations through the corresponding bending angles about
the successive images of their leaves. The convergence theorem for
quakebend cocycles (see
[EpsteinMarden], and also
[BonShear]) implies that these ordered products converge in
$\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{C})$ to an isometry  $B_{\widetilde\lambda}(P,Q)\in\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{C})$. 
The limit is independent of the finite approximation and satisfies
\begin{equation*} 
    B_{\widetilde\lambda}(P,R)
        =
                B_{\widetilde\lambda}(P,Q) 
        B_{\widetilde\lambda}(Q,R)
\end{equation*} 
where the composition is from left to right. This $B_{\widetilde\lambda}$ is the
\emph{bending cocycle} (see also [Dumas]). 
The rotation-angle component of the bending defines a transverse measure  on $\widetilde\lambda$; from the equivariance it descends to a measured
geodesic lamination $\lambda$ on $X$ that we call the \textit{bending lamination}. Moreover, 

the \emph{straightening} of $\Psi$ is obtained by replacing the bending cocycle by the trivial cocycle; its intrinsic hyperbolic structure is $X$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(L1) subadditivity","(L2) stationarity of the sequence of blocks of each fixed length","(L3) the row law does not depend on the starting index","(L4) E[X_{0,1}^+] finite and a linear lower bound on E[X_{0,n}]","ergodicity of the block sequences is needed only for a constant limit"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542341+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory","id":"claim_5512c8e378a10d1dd7b71a2d5741379e9a70c5f5d022ab969d1836e21965a057","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let {X_{m,n} : 0 <= m < n} satisfy: (L1) X_{0,n} <= X_{0,m} + X_{m,n} for every 0 < m < n; (L2) for each m >= 1 the sequence {X_{nm, (n+1)m} : n >= 1} is STATIONARY; (L3) the distribution of the row {X_{m, m+k} : k >= 1} does not depend on m; (L4) E[X_{0,1}^+] < infinity and E[X_{0,n}] >= -c_0 n for every n, for some finite c_0. Then: (a) gamma = lim_n E[X_{0,n}]/n = inf_n E[X_{0,n}]/n exists in [-c_0, infinity); (b) X = lim_n X_{0,n}/n exists almost surely and in L^1, with E[X] = gamma; (c) if in addition all the stationary sequences in (L2) are ERGODIC then X = gamma almost surely. The difference from Kingman is that (L2) and (L3) together are strictly WEAKER than joint stationarity of the whole array: they demand stationarity only along each fixed block length and equality of the row laws, not invariance of the full joint distribution. That weakening is what lets the theorem apply to models where the array is not generated by a single measure-preserving transformation. Note also that (L4) asks only for the POSITIVE part of X_{0,1} to be integrable, weaker than Kingman's E|X_{0,1}| < infinity. Quoting Kingman's hypotheses when using Liggett's conclusion, or the reverse, is the standard misquotation here. [Liggett (1985), 'An improved subadditive ergodic theorem', Ann. Probab. 13, 1279-1285; textbook form in Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 6.6.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["targets at every design point are mean plus noise with the noise independent of the calibration sample (so Cov(e, f(x)) = 0)","the weights on each point set sum to one; the family f_t is any family of fitted predictors (linearity in t is not needed for the identity, only for the cheap computation of the blend's cross-validated and bootstrap predictions)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T12:56:40.878952+00:00","domain":"regression / model assessment / transductive selection","id":"claim_553662417244b971618b1a8e4cc64e9cead1479c7050963b070adb0204ea329f","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f be a predictor fitted on a calibration sample, evaluated at design points x with targets y = mu(x) + e, where e has mean zero and variance sigma^2(x) and is independent of the sample. For a weighted average over a set of evaluation points E and the same average over the calibration points C (weights w_x summing to one on each set), write R_E = sum_E w_x E(y - f(x))^2 for the expected weighted risk on E, R_C the same on C, V_S = sum_S w_x Var f(x) for the average estimation variance on a set S, B_S = sum_S w_x (mu(x) - E f(x))^2 for the average squared bias, and N_S = sum_S w_x sigma^2(x) for the average noise. Then R_E = R_C + (V_E - V_C) + (B_E - B_C) + (N_E - N_C). Consequently, for a family of predictors f_t indexed by t (for instance a blend that is linear in t between two fitted bases), the minimiser over t of R_E(t) is the minimiser of R_C(t) + [V_E(t) - V_C(t)] + [B_E(t) - B_C(t)], the noise difference being free of t. A label-free criterion that replaces R_C(t) by the cross-validated risk on the calibration rows and V_E(t), V_C(t) by pairs-bootstrap estimates - the transductive covariance penalty used to choose the amount of simplex constraint at the scored rows - is this identity with the bias-shift term dropped; its single assumption is that the squared bias of the family shifts between the two point sets by an amount that does not depend on t, or does so less than the variance shift. What it cannot see is exactly the bias shift, which needs the targets at the new points; that is why such a criterion recovers only part of the hindsight-best t and errs toward the endpoint the calibration rows favour.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_i independent with E[X_i] = 0","one-sided bound X_i <= b almost surely (no lower bound needed for the upper tail)","v = sum_i E[X_i^2] finite"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627726+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5539ab1dd12776494ca55d16665e0670d5e85f01452dc2694daade30bd0d0cca","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent random variables with E[X_i] = 0 and X_i <= b almost surely for every i - a ONE-SIDED bound suffices for the upper tail - and let v = sum_{i=1}^n E[X_i^2]. Then for every t > 0, P( sum_i X_i >= t ) <= exp( - (v/b^2) h(bt/v) ) where h(u) = (1+u) log(1+u) - u. Bennett's inequality implies Bernstein's inequality through h(u) >= u^2/(2(1 + u/3)), which gives the familiar P(sum X_i >= t) <= exp(-t^2/(2(v + bt/3))), and it is strictly sharper in the large-deviation regime bt/v large, where Bennett decays like exp(-(t/b) log(bt/v)) - a Poisson tail - while Bernstein decays only like exp(-3t/(2b)). This is the right inequality when the summands are bounded but their variance is much smaller than the square of the bound, the regime where Hoeffding's inequality is badly lossy. [Bennett (1962); see Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Theorem 2.9]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-06T03:36:16.697768+00:00","domain":"harvested statement (arXiv 2512.18592, 2025): mathematics","id":"claim_553e933b88264eee9732d2a61a730e1b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 3.3 (Adaptive wavelet estimation) in the first version of arXiv:2512.18592, 'Wavelet Latent Position Exponential Random Graphs'] Assume that conditional on observed latent positions $U_{1},\\dots,U_{n}\\in[0,1]$, the edges $\\{A_{ij}:1\\leq i<j\\leq n\\}$ are independent with $A_{ij}\\mid(U_{k})_{k=1}^{n}\\sim\\mathrm{Bernoulli}\\bigl(W(U_{i},U_{j})\\bigr),$ for a symmetric graphon $W:[0,1]^{2}\\to[0,1]$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:35:19.873914+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5547254edcb16a77cf208749f2a9dea83f0c9955664164ca7d90e3604a1b049e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn lengths of arXiv:2608.27939, 'Entropy and domination for quasi-Hitchin representations'] Given a representation $\rho:\pi_1(S)\to \mathrm{PSL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ and $\gamma\in\pi_1(S)$, let $A\in \mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ be a determinant-one  lift of $\rho(\gamma)$ and let $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ be the eigenvalues of $A$ ordered so that $|\lambda_1|\le\cdots\le |\lambda_n|$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The \emph{Hilbert length} of $\gamma$ with respect to $\rho$ is
\[
\ell^H_{\rho}(\gamma):=\log\Bigg|\frac{\lambda_n}{\lambda_1}\Bigg|.
\]
\item The \emph{translation length} of $\gamma$ with respect to $\rho$ is the translation length of $\rho(\gamma)$ in the symmetric space $\mathbb{X}_n=\mathrm{PSL}_n(\mathbb{C})/\mathrm{PSU}(n)$, namely
\[
\ell_{\rho}(\gamma):=\ell_{\mathbb{X}_n}(\rho(\gamma))
=\sqrt{2\big((\log|\lambda_1|)^2+\cdots+(\log|\lambda_n|)^2\big)}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
(These expressions are well-defined, i.e.\ independent of the choice of the determinant-one lift $A$; two such lifts differ by multiplication by an $n$-th root of unity.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.190459+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_556f2b6181c59184ef7ab9c6102e0e7432deb1fea508d31399e6848f0fcaf303","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 106 (SDE coefficients with spatial smoothing
	and coordinate sum projection) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\sphicirc:\R\to[0,\infty)$ be a smooth nonnegative function that integrates to one and has support $[-1,1]$. We also assume that we have
$\sphicirc(\vx)\ge \Omega(1)$ for all $\vx\in[-1/2,1/2]$. With an abuse of notation, for $\vx\in\R^d$ for any $d\ge1$ we will denote
	\beq
	
	\sphicirc(\vx)
	= \prod_{i=1}^d
	\sphicirc(x^i)\,,\quad
	\sphi(\vx)\equiv 
	\frac{1}{\sep^d}
	\sphicirc\bigg(
	\frac{\vx}{\sep}\bigg)\,,
	\eeq
so that $\sphi$ also integrates to one and has support $[-\sep,\sep]^d$.
Recall from above that we use the abbreviation 
$\rho_t\equiv \rho_{\vY,N,t}$. It will also be convenient to factorize $\rho_t=\varrho_t\otimes\varsigma_t$ where $\varrho_t$ refers to the first three spatial coordinates while $\varsigma_t$ refers to the fourth spatial coordinate (cf.\ \eqref{e:a.i.factorization}). We then have $\rho_{D,t} = \varrho_{D,t}\otimes\varsigma_t$, etc., as well as $\rho_{\www,t}= \varrho_t\otimes\varsigma_{\www,t}$.
 Recall from Definition~\ref{d:projected.coeffs} the notation $\rho\mapsto\bar{\rho}$ for the coordinate sum projection.
Then, analogously to
\eqref{e:discrete.ratio.occ.B}--\eqref{e:discrete.ratio.occ.U}, we let
	\begin{align*}
	\sB^N(t,y)
	&\equiv
	\frac{\overline{\varrho_{D,N,t}*\sphi}(y)}
		{\overline{\varrho_{\vY,N,t}*\sphi}(y)}
	\equiv
	(p^N)'(t)^{1/2} \cdot \sbbb^N(t,y)\,,\\
	\sV^N(t,y)
	&\equiv
	\frac{\overline{\varrho_{V,N,t}*\sphi} (y)}
		{\overline{\varrho_{\vY,N,t}*\sphi} (y)}

	&\equiv
	\frac{\overline{\varrho_{U,N,t}*\sphi} (y)}
		{\overline{\varrho_{\vY,N,t}*\sphi} (y)}

Likewise, analogously to \eqref{e:discrete.ratio.occ.r.w}, we let
	\[

{"assumptions":["(X, B, mu, T) is an invertible measure-preserving system on a standard (Lebesgue) probability space","T is ergodic with respect to mu","G is a compact metrizable group with normalized Haar measure m","phi : X -> G is measurable and the extension is T_phi(x,g) = (Tx, phi(x) g) on mu x m","solutions F of the transfer equation are required only to be measurable (matrix-valued), not continuous"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.732127+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, skew products, cocycles and group extensions","id":"claim_55b03d25b04f083e6d2634636c495b808dc293ac41f7f84754595cf15210a9be","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, B, mu, T) be an invertible measure-preserving system on a standard probability space with T ERGODIC. Let G be a compact metrizable group with normalized Haar measure m, let phi : X -> G be measurable, and let T_phi(x, g) = (T x, phi(x) g) be the associated group extension of (X x G, mu x m). Then:

  T_phi is ergodic  <=>  for EVERY nontrivial irreducible unitary representation pi : G -> U(d_pi), the functional (transfer) equation
        F(T x) = pi(phi(x)) F(x)      for mu-a.e. x
  has no nonzero MEASURABLE solution F : X -> M_{d_pi}(C).

Equivalently, ergodicity fails exactly when some nontrivial pi admits such a nonzero F. A nonzero solution can always be normalized so that its Hilbert-Schmidt norm is constant, because ||F(x)||_HS is then a T-invariant function and T is ergodic.

Abelian case (the form most often used). If G is abelian, the irreducible representations are the characters chi in the dual group, and the criterion reads: T_phi is ergodic if and only if for every nontrivial character chi there is NO measurable h : X -> S^1 with h(T x) = chi(phi(x)) h(x); i.e. no nontrivial character of phi is a measurable multiplicative coboundary. For G = S^1 and phi written additively this is: for every nonzero integer n, the equation u(T x) - u(x) = n * phi(x) (mod 1) has no measurable solution u.

SHARP EDGES. (1) Ergodicity of the BASE T is a hypothesis, not a conclusion: if T is not ergodic then T_phi is not ergodic either (invariant sets of the base lift), and the displayed equivalence is false as stated without it. (2) Compactness of G is essential -- the proof uses the Haar PROBABILITY measure and the Peter-Weyl decomposition of L^2(G); for noncompact G (e.g. G = R, cylinder flows) the natural invariant measure is infinite and ergodicity is a genuinely different problem. (3) 'Measurable' cannot be weakened to 'continuous': a cocycle can be a measurable coboundary without being a continuous one, so verifying that the equation has no CONTINUOUS solution does not certify ergodicity. (4) Every nontrivial irreducible pi must be tested, not one convenient one. Example: G = S^1 and phi taking values in {+1, -1} with the induced two-point extension ergodic. Then for the character chi_1(z) = z the equation has no solution (that is exactly ergodicity of the two-point extension), yet chi_2(z) = z^2 satisfies chi_2(phi(x)) = 1, so h identically 1 solves the equation for chi_2 -- and indeed T_phi is not ergodic, since phi lives in the proper closed subgroup {+1,-1}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.474985+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_55bbd733eba566dc827de7bee3c9b6c283ae23c66d4fb31cd4128e4a7b7915e3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] \label[lemma]{lem:psd_diagonal_dominance}
Let $A = [a_{ij}] \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ be positive semidefinite. 
Then, for all $i, j \in [d]$, 
\begin{equation} \@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{a_{ij}} \le  \frac{1}{2}(a_{ii} + a_{jj}) =  \frac{1}{2}(\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{a_{ii}} + \@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{a_{jj}}). \label[ineq]{ineq:psd_diagonal_dominance} \end{equation}
Moreover, for $i \ne j$, the following conditions are equivalent: 
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item Equality is attained in ((ineq:psd_diagonal_dominance of the paper)). 
\item  The $2 \times 2$ principal submatrix $A[\{i,j\}]$ is not positive definite. 
\item The $2 \times 2$ principal submatrix $A[\{i,j\}]$ is not full rank. 
\item $a_{ii} = a_{jj} = \@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{a_{ij}}$. 
\end{enumerate}

\begin{proof}
We first note that for all $i \in [d]$, $e_i^T A e_i = a_{ii} \ge 0$ 
(with any equality implying $A$ is not positive definite), 
so $a_{ii} = \@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{a_{ii}}$. 
We compute 
\[
0 \le (e_i - e_j)^T A (e_i - e_j) 

= a_{ii} + a_{jj} - 2a_{ij} 
\]
and similarly
\[
0 \le (e_i + e_j)^T A (e_i + e_j) 
= a_{ii} + a_{jj} + 2a_{ij} 
\]
so that $2\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{a_{ij}} \le a_{ii} + a_{jj}$. 

Finally, when $i \ne j$, equality in (equation ineq:psd_diagonal_dominance of the paper) implies $(e_i - e_j)^T A (e_i - e_j) = 0$ or $(e_i + e_j)^T A (e_i + e_j) = 0$, hence $A[\{i,j\}]$ is not positive-definite and therefore not full rank. 

Then, $\det(A[\{i,j\}])=0$, so that $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{a_{ij}} = \sqrt{a_{ii}a_{jj}}$. 
In turn this forces $2\sqrt{a_{ii}a_{jj}} = a_{ii} + a_{jj}$, which is to say the vector $(a_{ii},a_{jj})$ attains equality in the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality.
Therefore $a_{ii}=a_{jj}$, and in turn $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{a_{ij}} = \sqrt{a_{ii}^2} = a_{ii}$ as well. 

That (iv) implies (i) is obvious. 

\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["1 <= p < infinity","all three conditions (boundedness, uniform translation-continuity, uniform tightness); on a bounded domain tightness is automatic"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752488+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_55f7009e84a2c8aa0d6a0ebd9fd1b1397cfed669b44ad4e89536ea54eab897b5","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let 1 <= p < infinity. A subset F of L^p(R^d) is relatively compact in the norm topology if and only if all three of the following hold: (i) F is BOUNDED, sup_{f in F} ||f||_p < infinity; (ii) F is uniformly continuous under translation, sup_{f in F} ||f(. + h) - f||_p -> 0 as h -> 0; (iii) F is uniformly TIGHT, sup_{f in F} integral_{|x| > R} |f|^p dx -> 0 as R -> infinity. Conditions (ii) and (iii) are each independent of the rest and cannot be dropped: the family {n^{d/p} 1_{B(0,1/n)}} is bounded in L^p and tight but not uniformly translation-continuous, since for |h| >= 2/n the translate is disjoint from the original; and the family {1_{[n, n+1]}} is bounded and uniformly translation-continuous but not tight, and has no L^p-convergent subsequence. Boundedness is listed as a separate condition here for safety - some treatments observe that it can be derived from the other two - and stating it explicitly costs nothing. On a bounded domain condition (iii) is automatic and the criterion reduces to (i) and (ii). The criterion is FALSE for p = infinity, where the analogue is Arzela-Ascoli on compacts plus a suitable equicontinuity. This is the L^p analogue of Arzela-Ascoli, with translation-continuity playing the role of equicontinuity. [Kolmogorov (1931), M. Riesz (1933), Frechet (1937); see Hanche-Olsen and Holden, 'The Kolmogorov-Riesz compactness theorem', Expo. Math. 28 (2010)]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:41:11.649647+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5616c88e86c184a5906752e46579ef1877c0cc14aab314dc20269c1a16f40246","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop generator_continuous_process of arXiv:2411.13964, 'Long-time analysis of a pair of on-lattice and continuous run-and-tumble particles with ja'] Let $\mathcal L$ be
  the generator of the continuous process. Its domain $D(\mathcal L)$
  is the set of bounded measurable functions
  $f : E_D \rightarrow \mathbb R$ such that
\begin{itemize}
\item for $\sigma \in \Sigma_+ \setminus \Sigma_-$ the function
  $f( \cdot, \sigma)$ is absolutely continuous on $[0, \ell)$ and
  $\lim_{x \rightarrow \ell} f(x, \sigma) =
  f\left(\ell,*_\sigma^\ell\right)$,
\item for $\sigma \in \Sigma_+ \setminus \Sigma_-$ the function
  $f(\cdot, \sigma)$ is absolutely continuous on $(0, \ell]$ and
  $\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} f(x, \sigma) = f\left(0, *_\sigma^0\right)$.
\end{itemize}

For $f \in D(\mathcal L)$ one has that
\begin{itemize}

&\quad + \underbrace{\lambda(x,\nu) \int_{E_D} \left(f(\tilde x, \tilde \nu) - f(x, (\sigma^1, \sigma^2))\right) dQ\left((x, (\sigma^1, \sigma^2)); (\tilde x, \tilde \nu)\right)}_{\text{\normalfont jump term}},
\end{align*}
\item whereas for boundary states
  $(x, \nu) \in \cup_{\nu \in \partial K} E_\nu$ the generator is
  given only by the jump term
$$
\mathcal L f(x, \nu) = \lambda(x, \nu) \int_{E_D} \left(f(\tilde x, \tilde
  \nu) - f(x, \nu)\right) dQ((x, \nu); (\tilde x, \tilde \nu))

{"assumptions":["Same fixed-basis model and empirical half squared loss; D>=1 and eta>0.","Equal scalar factors at initialization with product strictly between zero and S; continuous gradient flow."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:24:35.629353+00:00","domain":"Multitask sparse parity and skill emergence","id":"claim_561e08a721ae1832fff05ab9cc23e7b3fe34ab76e533bc828d513d4f75c0f76e","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Nam-Fonseca-Lee-Mingard-Louis Lemma1: exact balanced gradient-flow skill dynamics. Use the finite fixed-basis noiseless model in the companion definition, with f(i,x)=sum_{k=1}^N a_k*b_k*g_k(i,x), target amplitude S>0 and 1<=N<=n_s. Fix D>=1 training examples and let d_k be the number whose task is k, so sum_{k=1}^{n_s} d_k=D. The source samples them iid from its task/bit distribution; the identity below holds conditional on any realized sample. Run continuous-time gradient flow with eta>0 on empirical half squared loss L_D=(1/(2D))*(sum_{k<=N} d_k*(S-a_k*b_k)^2+sum_{k>N} d_k*S^2). For each represented k assume a_k(0)=b_k(0) and 0<R_k(0)=a_k(0)*b_k(0)<S. Then for every T>=0, a_k(T)=b_k(T), R_k(T)=a_k(T)*b_k(T)=S/[1+(S/R_k(0)-1)*exp(-2*eta*S*(d_k/D)*T)], and L_k(T)=(S-R_k(T))^2/2. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:56:17.351045+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5622d06ddf11e35fc65ff475211735aedbc6efa583be327f3d6c775499ca8cce","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem T:Markov-process of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] For $\rho \in \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty\}$, take any half-space pre-landscape $\mathcal{M}^\rho$, continuously extended to $\mathbb{H}^2_\uparrow$.
 Consider a function $f \in \operatorname{UC}_{0,+}$.
For each $t > 0$, define the process
$\mathfrak{h}^\rho_t f = f \diamond \mathcal{M}^\rho_{0, t}$, and set $\mathfrak{h}^\rho_0 f = f$.
Then $(\mathfrak{h}^\rho_t, t \ge 0)$ is a time-homogeneous Markov process on $\operatorname{UC}_{0,+}$, whose law does not depend on the choice of pre-landscape. Moreover, for almost surely $\mathcal{M}^\rho$, $(t,f)\mapsto \mathfrak{h}^\rho_tf$ is continuous on $\operatorname{UC}_{0,+}$, and $\mathfrak{h}^\rho_t f$ is a continuous function for each $t > 0, f \in \operatorname{UC}_{0,+}$. Lastly, for any finite set $Y \subset \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}, t > 0$ and any function $f \in \operatorname{UC}_{0,+}$  satisfying
\begin{equation}
    
    \limsup_{x \to \infty}\frac{f(x)}{x} < \infty,
\end{equation}
the marginal
$
(\mathfrak{h}^\rho_t f(y) : y \in Y)
$
is given by Theorem (T:half-space-fixed-point of the paper). 
The Markov process $(\mathfrak{h}^\rho_t, t \ge 0)$ is the \textbf{KPZ fixed point in half-space} with parameter $\rho$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the joint law of the points is invariant under reflection of any subset through the origin","the points are almost surely in general position (every d or fewer are linearly independent)","independence of the points is not required"],"created_at":"2026-08-20T03:43:30.215579+00:00","domain":"geometric probability","id":"claim_5624e3058d31a9a0d57cd8be58c608b9944691397689c7cd52a7d35a6247e504","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $x_1,\\dots,x_N$ be random points in $\\mathbb{R}^d$ whose joint law is invariant under reflection of any subset of them through the origin, and which are almost surely in general position. Note that symmetry alone does not suffice: general position is needed, since for instance two points i.i.d. uniform on $\\{\\pm e_1\\} \\subset \\mathbb{R}^2$ are symmetric yet give probability $0$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:52:08.674656+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_563635ce248309438812ffeb056905e9e435f832b097a31d3275e454fae19268","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 44 (Uniform lifted linear Schauder estimate) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Fix \(m\geq2\) and \(\sigma\in(0,1)\).  Let \(s(t)\), \(a\leq t\leq b\),
be a Ricci flow satisfying \(\PBG_m(s;\Lambda;[a,b])\) for some \(\Lambda\geq1\).
Let \(E\) be a fixed finite-rank tensor bundle and consider,
on the universal cover and in the charts of
Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform-parabolic-atlas}, a system
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal P U
 =\partial_tU-a^{ij}\nabla_i\nabla_jU-B^i\nabla_iU-CU=F.
\end{equation}
Assume that the second-order part is diagonal in the bundle components and
uses the same coefficient matrix \(a^{ij}\) on every component.  For fixed
constants \(0<\lambda_-\leq\lambda_+<\infty\), suppose that
\[
 \lambda_- s^{ij}\xi_i\xi_j\leq a^{ij}\xi_i\xi_j
 \leq\lambda_+ s^{ij}\xi_i\xi_j,
\]
and that the local
\(C^{m-2+\sigma,(m-2+\sigma)/2}\)-norms of \(a,B,C\) are bounded by
\(A_0\).

Every smooth bounded solution on the universal cover satisfies, for
\(\theta>0\) with \(a+\theta\leq b\),
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 \|U\|_{C^{m+\sigma,(m+\sigma)/2}_{\mathrm{uloc}}
          (\widetilde M\times[a+\theta,b],s)}
 \leq C_\theta\bigl(&
       \|U\|_{C^0(\widetilde M\times[a,b],s)}\\
       &+\|F\|_{C^{m-2+\sigma,(m-2+\sigma)/2}_{\mathrm{uloc}}}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
For the global estimate, assume in addition that \(\mathcal P\) is
deck-invariant, equivalently that the coefficient fields \(a,B,C\) descend to
\(M\).  If \(U\) and \(F\) are deck-invariant and descend to tensors \(u\)
and \(f\) on \(M\), with \(u(a)\in C^{m,\sigma}\) and
\(f\in Y_s^m[a,b]\), then
\begin{equation}
 \|u\|_{X_s^m[a,b]}
 \leq C\left(
      \|u(a)\|_{C^{m,\sigma}(M,s(a))}
      +\|f\|_{Y_s^m[a,b]}\right).
\end{equation}
The constants depend only on
\(m,\sigma,\Lambda,\lambda_-,\lambda_+,A_0\), on \(\theta\) in the interior
estimate, and on an upper bound for \(b-a\).  The interior and initial-face
estimates are based, respectively, on Lieberman's interior Schauder theorem
\cite[Theorem~4.9, p.~59]{Lieberman} and his Cauchy--Dirichlet Schauder theorem
\cite[Theorem~4.28, p.~77]{Lieberman}.  All atlas-radius, overlap, and cutoff
constants, fixed-coordinate ellipticity constants, localized initial-face
boundary-chart constants, and coefficient H\"older constants are uniform over
the admissible family specified by \(\PBG_m\) and the displayed bounds.  In
particular, the constants are independent of collapse of the compact quotient.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X, Sigma, mu) is a measure space","f is Sigma-measurable","0 < p < infinity for the quasi-norm formula"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.551797+00:00","domain":"real analysis, Lp spaces","id":"claim_56428cce7b939634b8046806c62ca819a8a8f81caa9b6e1f7436a073f0e11f58","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a measurable f on a measure space (X, Sigma, mu), the distribution function is d_f(t) = mu({x : |f(x)| > t}) for t > 0; it is nonincreasing and right-continuous. For 0 < p < infinity the weak L^p quasi-norm is ||f||_{L^{p,infinity}} = sup_{t>0} t * d_f(t)^{1/p}, and weak L^p = L^{p,infinity}(mu) is the set of (a.e.-classes of) measurable f with this quantity finite; by convention L^{infinity,infinity} = L^infinity. It is a quasi-norm: ||f+g||_{L^{p,infinity}} <= max(2, 2^{1/p}) (||f||_{L^{p,infinity}} + ||g||_{L^{p,infinity}}), from d_{f+g}(t) <= d_f(t/2) + d_g(t/2). Chebyshev's inequality gives L^p contained in L^{p,infinity} with ||f||_{L^{p,infinity}} <= ||f||_p, and the inclusion is strict in general: on R^n, |x|^{-n/p} lies in L^{p,infinity} but not in L^p. For 1 < p < infinity, L^{p,infinity} admits an equivalent norm; L^{1,infinity}(R^n) admits none.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space","for the homeomorphism notion f is invertible; for positive expansiveness f is only assumed continuous"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.437766+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics","id":"claim_5676c1f151b4a57362148ab72f2407ae791df1e012af3b7099cc8435b4d96949","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, d)$ be a compact metric space. A homeomorphism $f: X \\to X$ is expansive with expansivity constant $\\varepsilon > 0$ if whenever $x \\ne y$ there is some $n \\in \\mathbb{Z}$ (positive OR negative) with $d(f^n x, f^n y) > \\varepsilon$; equivalently, $d(f^n x, f^n y) \\le \\varepsilon$ for all $n \\in \\mathbb{Z}$ forces $x = y$. A continuous map $f: X \\to X$ (not necessarily invertible) is positively expansive (forward expansive) with constant $\\varepsilon$ if $d(f^n x, f^n y) \\le \\varepsilon$ for all $n \\ge 0$ forces $x = y$. Positive expansiveness is much stronger than expansiveness: a positively expansive HOMEOMORPHISM of a compact metric space exists only when $X$ is finite (Schwartzman; Keynes-Robertson), so for an infinite compact space the notion is meaningful only for genuinely non-invertible maps such as expanding maps and one-sided shifts. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:43:16.153542+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_567ba93f45b03b7d30f47078a59d3f8f0824d3160f0e9c119aea409c50560064","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 6 of arXiv:2604.13819, 'Convolution, cumulants and infinitesimal generators in the formal power series ring'] The $t$-deformed cumulants $\{\kappa_{i}^{t}(A)\}_{i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge1}}$ are unique maps satisfying the following conditions:

$$
\kappa_{i}^t(A) = \frac{t^{i-1}}{(t)_{\underline{i}}}p_{i}(A) + F_{i}(p_{1}(A), \dots, p_{i-1}(A)).
$$ 
\item Homogeneity: $\kappa_{i}^{t}(D_{r}[A]) = r^{i}\kappa_{i}^{t}(A)$ for any $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and $i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge1}$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:42:16.237987+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_56839dea1b7ce06cbf4cd396dc396cdbb45d34317fe48d97924c6d838019fa9c","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem mobius-primitive of arXiv:2607.00311, 'Thermal Concentration and Poisson--Dirichlet Edge Statistics for Random-Lattice Gibbs Ense'] Let $\mu:\mathbb N\to\{-1,0,1\}$ be the M\"obius function. 
Thus $\mu(1)=1$, $\mu(d)=0$ if $d$ is divisible by the square of a prime, and
$\mu(d)=(-1)^r$ if
$$
d=p_1p_2\cdots p_r
$$
with distinct primes $p_1,\ldots,p_r$.

The elementary M\"obius inversion identity is
$$
\sum_{d|N}\mu(d)=
\begin{cases}
1, & N=1,\\
0, & N\ge2.
\end{cases}
$$
Consequently, for every nonzero vector $\bm q\in\mathbb Z^n$,
$$
\chi_{\mathbb Z^n_{\operatorname{prim}}}(\bm q)=\sum_{d|\bm q}\mu(d),
$$
where $d|\bm q$ means that $d$ divides every coordinate of $\bm q$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["E finite (or the event depends on finitely many coordinates of an infinite product space)","the measure is a product of Bernoulli(p_e) coordinates; the single-parameter form takes p_e = p for all e","the pivotal (influence) form of the right-hand side needs A increasing; the general form P_p(A^e) - P_p(A_e) holds for every event","the sharp-threshold consequences are cited, not proved"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T15:38:02.592676+00:00","domain":"percolation and Boolean functions","id":"claim_569ccbdb68319948c30d7d0358dc8c699ed1907ce85a36c356879bd884bd847d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Omega = {0,1}^E for a finite set E (the coordinates e in E are 'edges' or 'bits'), and let P_p denote the product measure under which the coordinates omega_e are independent Bernoulli(p_e) variables, p = (p_e) in [0,1]^E; write P_p also for the case p_e = p for all e. For an event A (a subset of Omega) and a coordinate e write A^e = { omega : omega^e in A } and A_e = { omega : omega_e in A }, where omega^e and omega_e are omega with the coordinate e set to 1 and to 0 respectively; A^e and A_e do not depend on the coordinate e. The coordinate e is PIVOTAL for A at omega if exactly one of omega^e, omega_e lies in A; Piv_A(omega) is the set of pivotal coordinates and its size |Piv_A| is the number of pivotal coordinates. THEOREM (Margulis 1974, Russo 1981). For every event A, p |-> P_p(A) is a polynomial in the p_e and, for every coordinate e, d/dp_e P_p(A) = P_p(A^e) - P_p(A_e). With a single parameter p, d/dp P_p(A) = sum over e in E of ( P_p(A^e) - P_p(A_e) ). If A is INCREASING (closed under raising coordinates) then A_e is contained in A^e, A^e minus A_e is exactly the event that e is pivotal for A, and the formula reads d/dp P_p(A) = sum over e of P_p( e is pivotal for A ) = E_p |Piv_A| = sum over e of I_e^p(A), where I_e^p(A) = P_p(e pivotal for A) is the influence of e on A under P_p. In particular an increasing event's probability is nondecreasing in p (and in every p_e), and its derivative is the expected number of pivotal coordinates. The formula holds verbatim for an event on an infinite product space that depends on finitely many coordinates; for a general increasing event depending on infinitely many coordinates the right-hand side is only known to bound the derivative from below in the appropriate one-sided sense, and the finite-dimensional form is the one used in practice (finite boxes, then limits).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:15:16.654450+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_569e1c3b7bb06729e7b9ebdfec318cd8373b8cfa46f373d7ba9b1dc7b2665c96","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 22 of arXiv:2608.30752, '2608.30752'] Let \(\mathscr H_{\mathrm{id}}\) denote the marking-preserving homotopy class
of Lipschitz maps \(v:X_0\to Y\). In a \(q\)-natural coordinate
\(z=x+iy\), define
\[
  H_q(v)
  :=
  \frac12
  \int_{X_0\setminus Z(q)}
  |v_x|_{u_0^*h}^2\,dx\,dy,
  \quad
  V_q(v)
  :=
  \frac12
  \int_{X_0\setminus Z(q)}
  |v_y|_{u_0^*h}^2\,dx\,dy.
\]
These quantities are globally well-defined because the transition maps
between \(q\)-natural coordinates are of the form
\(z\mapsto\pm z+c\), and \(Z(q)\) has measure zero. Set
\begin{equation}
  \mathscr V_q(Y)
  :=
  \inf_{v\in\mathscr H_{\mathrm{id}}}V_q(v).
  
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
  e^{-2t}E(t)
  \searrow
  \mathscr V_q(Y)
  \qquad
  \text{as }t\to\infty.
  
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}
  \lim_{t\to\infty}
  \frac{E(t)}{e^{2t}}
  =
  \mathscr V_q(Y),
  \qquad
  E(t)
  =
  \mathscr V_q(Y)e^{2t}+o(e^{2t}).
  
\end{equation}

Suppose, in addition, that \(q\) is Jenkins--Strebel and that its vertical
foliation is the contracting foliation of the ray. Write the complementary
components of its vertical critical graph as maximal flat cylinders
\(
  C_i
  \cong
  (0,h_i)\times
  \bigl(\mathbb R/c_i\mathbb Z\bigr),
\) \(
  i=1,\ldots,r,
\)
where \(q=dz^2\), \(z=x+iy\), the vertical trajectories
\(x=\mathrm{constant}\) are closed, \(c_i\) is their \(q\)-length, and
\(h_i\) is the transverse height of \(C_i\). Let \(\delta_i\) be the core
curve of \(C_i\), and put
\(
  M_i:=\operatorname{Mod}(C_i)=\frac{h_i}{c_i}.
\)
Then
\begin{equation}
  \mathscr V_q(Y)
  =
  \frac12
  \sum_{i=1}^r
  M_i\,\ell_Y(\delta_i)^2
  =
  \frac12
  \sum_{i=1}^r
  \frac{h_i}{c_i}\,
  \ell_Y(\delta_i)^2.
  
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
  \lim_{t\to\infty}
  \frac{E(t)}{e^{2t}}
  =
  \frac12
  \sum_{i=1}^r
  \operatorname{Mod}(C_i)\,
  \ell_Y(\delta_i)^2.
  
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["m is Lebesgue measure on R^n and L is its completion of the Borel sigma-algebra B","f is Lebesgue measurable with values in the extended reals","for part (i): Lebesgue measure is sigma-finite and outer regular, which is what supplies the Borel hull and kernel","for part (iii): (X, M-bar, mu-bar) is the completion of a measure space (X, M, mu)","the conclusion is equality off a null set, not everywhere"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.402310+00:00","domain":"measure theory, Borel versus Lebesgue measurability","id":"claim_56d067a642318476c9ea2c21c69cf1a4651cbf39b9d439c61824ee18654d3860","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let m denote Lebesgue measure on R^n, let B be the Borel sigma-algebra and let L be the Lebesgue sigma-algebra; recall that (R^n, L, m) is the completion of (R^n, B, m). (i) SETS: if E is in L then there are Borel sets B_1 contained in E contained in B_2 with m(B_2 minus B_1) = 0; consequently E = B_1 union N with N contained in a Borel set of measure zero, and every Lebesgue measurable set differs from a Borel set by a null set. (ii) FUNCTIONS: if f : R^n -> [-infinity, +infinity] is Lebesgue measurable, then there is a BOREL measurable g : R^n -> [-infinity, +infinity] and a Borel set N with m(N) = 0 such that g(x) = f(x) for every x outside N. One may take g with the same pointwise bounds as f (if a <= f <= b a.e. then a <= g <= b everywhere, and if f >= 0 then g >= 0). (iii) The same holds verbatim for the completion of any measure space: an M-bar-measurable function on the completion (X, M-bar, mu-bar) of (X, M, mu) agrees mu-almost everywhere with an M-measurable function. WHERE IT FAILS: (a) 'almost everywhere' cannot be strengthened to 'everywhere': let N be a non-Borel subset of the Cantor set (such subsets exist since the Cantor set has cardinality the continuum and carries continuum-many subsets, while there are only continuum-many Borel sets and all subsets of the Cantor set are Lebesgue null hence Lebesgue measurable); then the indicator of N is Lebesgue measurable but not Borel. (b) 'Borel' cannot be upgraded to 'continuous': Lusin's theorem only gives continuity of the restriction after deleting a set of arbitrarily small measure, not a continuous function agreeing almost everywhere (the indicator of [0,1] is a counterexample). (c) The distinction is not cosmetic in compositions: if h is continuous and f is Lebesgue measurable, f composed with h need not be Lebesgue measurable, whereas g composed with h is Borel measurable whenever g is Borel; this is the standard reason to replace f by its Borel representative before composing or before invoking a change of variables. (d) Statement (i) uses that Lebesgue measure is sigma-finite and Borel-regular; for a general non-regular measure there is no such inner and outer Borel approximation.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Countable underlying graph","Tail-trivial forest law","For the FUSF corollary use Lyons-Peres Theorem 10.18"],"created_at":"2026-10-10T08:08:30.940046+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_56d0ba3d36dbdba6d3c440c370af60307ea514a7e76d292c612048a660c35d55","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"For any random spanning forest on a countable graph with trivial edge-tail sigma-field, the event that it has infinitely many components has probability zero or one. p_i=\E\xi_i,
\qquad
W=\sum_{i\in I}\xi_i,
\qquad
\lambda=\E W,
\]
and let $N(i):=\{i\}\cup\{j:j\sim i\}$.
Define
\[
b_1
:=
\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in N(i)}p_ip_j,
\qquad
b_2
:=
\sum_{i\in I}
\sum_{\substack{j\in N(i)\\j\ne i}}
\E[\xi_i\xi_j].
\]
With the convention
\[
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mu,\nu)
:=
\sup_{A\subseteq\mathbb Z_{\ge0}}
|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|,
\]
one has
\[
d_{\mathrm{TV}}
\bigl(
\mathcal L(W),
\operatorname{Po}(\lambda)
\bigr)
\le
\frac{1-e^{-\lambda}}{\lambda}(b_1+b_2)
\le
(1\wedge\lambda^{-1})(b_1+b_2),
\]
where the factor is interpreted as \(1\) when \(\lambda=0\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["independence within each row (nothing assumed across rows)","mean zero and finite variances, with sum_i E[X_{n,i}^2] -> sigma^2 > 0","Lindeberg's condition for sufficiency; additionally uniform asymptotic negligibility for the converse"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.781577+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_56f2f3ba378c4a6f96900d8c87012af674a778ae0963a2aedce836ff95c4516e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For each n let X_{n,1}, ..., X_{n,k_n} be INDEPENDENT random variables within each row, with E[X_{n,i}] = 0 and sum_{i=1}^{k_n} E[X_{n,i}^2] -> sigma^2 in (0, infinity). Suppose the LINDEBERG CONDITION holds: for every eps > 0, sum_{i=1}^{k_n} E[ X_{n,i}^2 1{ |X_{n,i}| > eps } ] -> 0 as n -> infinity. Then S_n = sum_i X_{n,i} converges in distribution to N(0, sigma^2). FELLER'S CONVERSE: if in addition the row is UNIFORMLY ASYMPTOTICALLY NEGLIGIBLE, max_{i <= k_n} E[X_{n,i}^2] -> 0, and S_n converges in distribution to N(0, sigma^2), then the Lindeberg condition holds - so under negligibility the condition is necessary as well as sufficient. LYAPUNOV'S CONDITION, sum_i E|X_{n,i}|^{2 + delta} -> 0 for some delta > 0, IMPLIES Lindeberg and is usually easier to check. Two things the theorem does not require: identical distribution within a row, and any relation between rows. Two things it does require: independence WITHIN each row, and the variance sum converging to a strictly positive limit. Without negligibility the converse fails - a single summand can already be Gaussian and carry the whole limit while the others are wild. [Lindeberg (1922), Feller (1935); see Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorems 3.4.10 and 3.4.11]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f is entire and not identically zero","f has finite order ρ","zeros are listed with multiplicity, k = floor(ρ)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.483267+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_570f493d6254a84b12d4af388c5538960a086928a743a5eb5ffdc6321fa8dae8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f be an entire function, not identically zero, of finite order ρ = limsup_{r→∞} log log M(r)/log r, where M(r) = max_{|z|=r} |f(z)|. Let m ≥ 0 be the order of the zero of f at 0 and let (a_n) be the nonzero zeros of f listed with multiplicity. Put k = floor(ρ). Then Σ_n |a_n|^{-(k+1)} < ∞ and f(z) = z^m exp(Q(z)) Π_n E_k(z/a_n), where E_k is the Weierstrass elementary factor and Q is a polynomial of degree at most k (equivalently, of degree at most ρ). In particular an entire function of finite order with no zeros is exp(Q) with Q a polynomial of degree at most ρ, and an entire function of nonintegral order has infinitely many zeros.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A small parameter: bubble (SAW), triangle (percolation) or square (lattice trees) diagram small at criticality","Above the upper critical dimension: d > 4 (SAW), d > 6 (percolation), d > 8 (lattice trees)","Nearest-neighbour models need d >= 5 (SAW) or d >= 11 (percolation) with current methods"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T12:13:53+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_57375976b63bf663a8210d0e4c836fb9befaf15f16d6294ef02907a3056e8fcc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The lace expansion writes the two-point function of self-avoiding walk, Bernoulli percolation, oriented percolation or lattice trees as a renormalised random-walk Green function plus a correction series: for SAW, c_n(x) = sum_y D(y) c_{n-1}(x - y) + sum_{m=2}^{n} sum_y pi_m(y) c_{n-m}(x - y), with pi_m the alternating-sign lace coefficients obtained by inclusion-exclusion over self-intersections (for percolation the analogous expansion is in terms of pivotal bonds and sausages). The expansion is an exact identity; its use requires a bootstrap showing the coefficients are small in a norm controlled by a random-walk diagram: the bubble diagram for SAW (finite for d > 4), the triangle diagram for percolation (finite for d > 6) and the square diagram for lattice trees (d > 8). Proved regimes: nearest-neighbour SAW for d >= 5 (Hara-Slade), spread-out SAW for d > 4, nearest-neighbour percolation for d >= 11 (Fitzner-van der Hofstad) and spread-out percolation for d > 6 (Hara-Slade). Conclusions there: mean-field exponents (gamma = 1, eta = 0, beta = 1 and delta = 2 in bounded-ratio senses), Gaussian or super-Brownian scaling limits, and asymptotic expansions of critical points. It gives nothing at or below the upper critical dimension, and for nearest-neighbour percolation in 7 <= d <= 10 there is no small parameter, so the expansion holds only as an identity, not as a bound. Typical failure: Applying the expansion's mean-field conclusions (eta=0, Gaussian or super-Brownian scaling limit) to a model at or below its upper critical dimension without re-verifying the triangle or bubble condition; the coefficients pi_m are not shown small there, the bootstrap can fail to close, and the diagrammatic control silently assumed at the outset is exactly the open problem, which is why mean-field behaviour of nearest-neighbour percolation in dimensions 7 <= d <= 10 remains unproved although the spread-out (d > 6) and nearest-neighbour d >= 11 cases are resolved (below d = 6 mean-field behaviour is not expected, and at d = 6 logarithmic corrections are expected). Canonical reference: Hara and Slade, 1990, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Madras and Slade, The Self-Avoiding Walk, 1993, Birkhauser.","status":"unverified"}

We define two normalized derivative operators on $p$:

\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] The normalized standard derivative, denoted by $\partial_n$, is given by
    \[
        \partial_n p(z) := \frac{p'(z)}{n}.
    \]

    \item[(ii)] The normalized polar derivative (with respect to $0$), denoted by $D_n$, is given by
    \[
        D_n p(z) := \frac{z p'(z)}{n} - p(z).
    \]
\end{itemize}

More generally, for each integer $d$ with $0 \le d \le n$, the $d$th normalized standard derivative $\partial_n^d$ and the $d$th normalized polar derivative $D_n^d$ are defined recursively by
\[
    \partial_n^d := \partial_{n-d+1} \circ \partial_n^{d-1},
    \qquad
    D_n^d := D_{n-d+1} \circ D_n^{d-1},\qquad d\geq 1,
\]
    where $\partial_n^0$ and $D_n^0$ are the identity operators.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Eikonal equation |u'| = 1 on (-1,1) with zero boundary data","The correct symmetry is: u solves F = 0 in the viscosity sense iff -u solves -F(x,-r,-p) = 0; simply flipping the sign of F does not preserve the solution set","The sign convention pairs with vanishing viscosity: the viscosity solution of F = 0 is the limit of solutions of F(x,u_ε,Du_ε) - εΔu_ε = 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418207+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: viscosity solution theory","id":"claim_573bfbe8e5c9cedb4b4e443a344bb159372ae5341600e867e80decd2533c1068","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing convention: the definition of viscosity solution is tied to the SIGN with which the equation is written (with the convention that F is nonincreasing in the second-order term, i.e. that the vanishing-viscosity approximation is F(x,u,Du) - εΔu = 0). Multiplying the equation by -1 changes the solution. Concrete counterexample: on Ω = (-1,1) with boundary data u(-1) = u(1) = 0, consider |u'| = 1. Written as F(x,r,p) = |p| - 1 = 0, the viscosity solution is u(x) = 1 - |x| (the distance to ∂Ω): at x = 0 the function has a concave kink, no C^1 function touches it from below there, and the subsolution test at the kink only requires |p| - 1 ≤ 0 for p ∈ [-1,1]. Written as G(x,r,p) = 1 - |p| = 0 (the same equation pointwise!), the viscosity solution is u(x) = |x| - 1: at its convex kink at x = 0 the supersolution test requires 1 - |p| ≥ 0 for the touching slopes p ∈ [-1,1], which holds. Moreover 1 - |x| is NOT a viscosity solution of G = 0 (the subsolution test at the concave kink would demand 1 - |p| ≤ 0 for p = 0) and |x| - 1 is not a viscosity solution of F = 0. Both functions are Lipschitz with |u'| = 1 a.e. and the same boundary data.
