{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.164539+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_57969f10100f2bd46f36781f2fd50d579fc3fad2b1b29097213972227544a36f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 34 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall the definition of $z_\star$ from \eqref{e:fp.z.star}.
Recalling the expression for $V'(z)$ from \eqref{e:fp-V-pr}, define
    \beq
    \gamma(z)
    \equiv
    \alpha \sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j
    \bigg(
    \frac{ \hv_j}{\alpha - \hv_j m(z)}
    \bigg)^2\,.\eeq
Then, writing $\gamma_\star\equiv\gamma(z_\star)$, we have $\beta_\star(\gamma_\star) = z_\star$.

\begin{proof}
We divide the proof according to the cases from the definition
\eqref{e:fp.z.star} of $z_\star$:
\begin{itemize}
\item   First suppose $z_\star = z_{\min}$.
    Then, recalling \eqref{e:fp-V-pr}, we see that $z_\star$ solves the equation
    \[
    0 = V'(z_\star)
    = 1- m_2(z_\star) \gamma(z_\star)\,,
    \]
which rearranges to
$m_2(z_\star) = 1/\gamma_\star$.
This is precisely the characterization of $\beta_{\min}(\gamma_\star)$, so we conclude $ \beta_{\min}(\gamma_\star)=z_\star=z_{\min}$.
    Finally, since $z_\star = z_{\min}$, we have \[\hx \le
    \frac{\alpha}{m(z_{\min})}
    = \frac{\alpha}{m(\beta_{\min}(\gamma_\star))}
    \,,\] and therefore $\beta_\star(\gamma_\star) = \beta_{\min}(\gamma_\star) = z_\star$.
\item In the other case, we must have $\hx>0$, and
    \[
    z_\star = m^{-1}\bigg(\frac{\alpha}{\hx}\bigg) > z_{\min}\,.
    \]
Abbreviate $\beta_\star\equiv\beta_\star(\gamma_\star)$ and $\beta_{\min}\equiv\beta_{\min}(\gamma_\star)$.
We want to again conclude that $\beta_\star=z_\star$, so suppose for contradiction that this does not hold, in which case it follows from \eqref{e:fp-betast} combined with the above that
    \[
    \beta_\star
    =\beta_{\min}
    > m^{-1}\bigg(\frac{\alpha}{\hx}\bigg)
     = z_\star > z_{\min}\,.
    \]
Now we recall that $z_{\min}$ satisfies $V'(z_{\min})=0$, which by \eqref{e:fp-V-pr} rearranges to
    \beq
    1 = m_2(z_{\min})
    \gamma(z_{\min})
    =
    \frac{m_2(z_{\min})}{m(z_{\min})^2}
    \Big[
    m(z_{\min})^2\gamma(z_{\min})
    \Big]
    \,.\eeq
Meanwhile, $\beta_{\min}$ is characterized by the equation
    \beq
    1
    = m_2(\beta_{\min})
    \gamma(z_\star)
    = \frac{m_2(\beta_{\min})}
        {m(z_\star)^2}
    \Big[
    m(z_\star)^2\gamma(z_\star)
    \Big]
    \,.\eeq
We saw in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:freeprob.V.convex} that
the function $m_2(z)/m(z)^2$ is nonincreasing in $z$. Since $m_2$ is strictly decreasing in $z$, it follows that
\[
    \frac{m_2(\beta_{\min})}
    {m(z_\star)^2}
    <\frac{m_2(z_\star)}
    {m(z_\star)^2}
    \le \frac{m_2(z_{\min})}
    {m(z_{\min})^2}
    \]
We also saw in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:freeprob.V.convex} that
the function $m(z)^2\gamma(z)$ is strictly decreasing in $z$, which implies
$m(z_\star)^2\gamma(z_\star)<
    m(z_{\min})^2\gamma(z_{\min})$. This shows that the above equations \eqref{e:fp.char.of.zmin} and \eqref{e:fp.char.of.betamin} cannot hold simultaneously, a contradiction.
\end{itemize}
Thus we have shown in all cases that $\beta_\star(\gamma_\star)=z_\star$, as claimed.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:01:48.632953+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5796a36a7b9e2f7eb2be0d8f9765e704ef0a0810ac2d852309f07aa69fd29cfe","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma eq:rgg-pmf-lower-bound of arXiv:2607.02013, 'Resolution of the Detection Threshold Conjecture for Random Geometric Graphs in the $d>n$ '] For $d\ge (1+\epsilon)n$, we have $\mathbb{P}_{\operatorname{RGG}}(G\in \mathcal G)=1-n^{-\omega(1)}$. 

\begin{proof} Recall that 
    \[\mathcal{I} = 
    \mathcal{H} \cap \bigg\{
        \|W\|^2 \le \frac{2n^2}{d}
        \bigg\}\,,\]
and we already saw in Lemma~(l:W.is.subgaussian of the paper) that $\mathbb{P}_{0}(\mathcal{H}^c) \le n^{-\omega(1)}$. From Lemma~(l:prior.W.logconcave of the paper), the prior distribution $\mathbb{P}_{0}(\cdot|{\mathcal{H}})$ is $(c_0 d)$-strongly logconcave. The function $W\mapsto\|W\|$ is 1-Lipschitz, and 
\[(\mathbb{E}_0[\|W\|])^2 
\le \mathbb{E}_0[\|W\|^2] 
\le \frac{n^2}{d}\,,\] so it follows again from the Lipschitz concentration inequality for log-concave measures that 

    \[
    \mathbb{P}_{0}\bigg(\|W\| \ge \sqrt{\frac{2n^2}{d}}\bigg)
    \leq \mathbb{P}_{0}\bigg(\|W\| \ge \sqrt{\frac{2n^2}{d}}\bigg|{\mathcal{H}}\bigg) + \mathbb{P}_{0}({\mathcal{H}}^c)
    \le \frac{1}{n^{\omega(1)}}\,.
    \]
This proves $\mathbb{P}_{0}( W \in \mathcal I^c)=n^{-\omega(1)}$, and it then follows from Markov's inequality that
 \[\mathbb{P}_{\operatorname{RGG}}\Big(
 \mu_G( W \in \mathcal I^c)=n^{-\omega(1)}\Big)
 =1-n^{-\omega(1)}\,.\]
It remains to prove that
\[
\mathbb{P}_{\operatorname{RGG}}\bigg(\mathbb{P}_{\operatorname{RGG}}(G)\ge \mathop{\rm exp}(-10n^2h(p))\bigg)
\ge 1-n^{-\omega(1)}\,.
\]
For $p=n^{-\Omega(1)}$, this follows from a simple counting argument. First, we have \[\mathbb{P}_{\operatorname{RGG}}\bigg(|E(G)|\le \binom{n}{2} \cdot 2p\bigg)=1-n^{-\omega(1)}\,,\] for instance from the coupling between $\mathbb{P}_{\operatorname{RGG}}$ and $\mathbb{P}_{\operatorname{ER}}$ obtained by~[liu2022testing]. The total number of graphs satisfying this edge count constraint is upper-bounded by
    \[
    \mathop{\rm exp}\bigg\{
    \binom{n}{2} h(2p)
    \bigg\}
    \le \mathop{\rm exp}\{ 2 n^2 p \log n\}\,.
    \]
As a result, we can bound
    \[
    \mathbb{P}_{\operatorname{RGG}}\bigg(\mathbb{P}_{\operatorname{RGG}}(G)\le \mathop{\rm exp}(-10n^2h(p))\bigg)
    \le \frac{\mathop{\rm exp}\{ 2 n^2 p \log n\}}
        {\mathop{\rm exp}\{ 10 n^2 p \log n\}}
    \le \frac{1}{n^{\omega(1)}}\,,
    \]
which concludes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:53:10.158724+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_57a5ed266b86d692ae31d2b9801560d88160b52ada9213544625e391da1b1127","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop Vect-delta-RKE of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Evaluation at $1\in\textup{Glo}$ defines an equivalence
    \[

    \begin{proof}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:23:25.637910+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_57a6bd8f008cfec29baf37648128573105459be64b34a61d8cf857942ffd42ab","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn Standard path of arXiv:2609.01458, 'Confluence relations for $q$-analogues of multiple zeta values'] Let 
\[
u(z)\coloneqq\mathbb{L}_{k_{1},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1}(z),\dots,x_{d}(z))\in\mathcal{F}.
\]
For each $z$-dependent position $i$, there is a unique integer $r$
such that
\[
x_{i}(z)=zq^{r}\qquad\text{or}\qquad x_{i}(z)=z^{-1}q^{1-r}.
\]
We call $r$ the level of position $i$. The levels are determined
by the original word $u(z)$ and remain fixed throughout the following
procedure. Starting from $u(z)$, we replace all $z$-dependent entries
one at a time, in increasing order of their levels. Entries having
the same level are replaced from right to left. At each step, the
replacement is 
\[
x_{i}(z)\quad\longmapsto\quad x_{i}(zq).
\]
The resulting finite sequence consists of formal $q$MPLs ((thm:Fn_StandardPath of the paper))
and is denoted by 
\[
\operatorname{Std}(u)=(u_{0},u_{1},\dots,u_{l}),
\]
where $u_{0}=u(z)$ and $u_{l}=u(zq)$. We call it the standard path
from $u(z)$ to $u(zq)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.664354+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_57d0535860ab7c33d4b46986917981576af07ac69bb2319d5bb34fffec6f6a1a","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2607.25645, 'Estimates of the total variation distance between laws of Sobolev mappings on Gaussian spa'] Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $p>4k$, and let $b>0$.
Let
\[

\]

\[

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T01:16:46.697554+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_57e21f1b4fe13ff5e06612d77d832ec49837a804ac8c09b2dd8e1de3d81f232b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:barbour2019longterm of arXiv:2411.18563, 'Lower tails for triangles inside the critical window'] Let $P=(Y_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a Markov chain on $\Omega$ equipped with distance $\mathrm{dist}( \cdot,\cdot)$, and let $f : \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a $L$-Lipschitz function with respect to $\mathrm{dist}$. Suppose that $\Omega_{\text{typ}}\subseteq \Omega_{\text{con}} \subseteq \Omega$ are such that:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathrm{dist}(y,z) \leq 1$ for all $y,z\in\Omega$ such that  $P(y,z) > 0$, 
\item $\mathbb{P}(Py\neq y) \leq D$ for $y \in \Omega_{\text{typ}}$, 
\item $\Omega_{\text{typ}}^+  \subseteq \Omega_{\text{con}}$,
\item $P$ is $\rho$-contractive on $\Omega_{\text{con}}$. 
\end{enumerate}
Let $k$ be a positive integer and let
\[\mathcal{A}_k = \{Y_i \in \Omega_{\text{typ}}~\forall\,  i<k\}, \text{ and } e_k = \max_{y\in \Omega_{\text{typ}}^+}\mathbb{P}_y(Y_i\not \in \Omega_{\text{con}} \textup{ for some }i<k)\, .
\]

Then for all $y\in \Omega_{\text{typ}}$ and $m \geq 0$,
\[
\mathbb{P}_y(\{|f(Y_k) - \mathbb{E}_y[f(Y_k)]| > m\}\land \mathcal{A}_k) \leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{m^2}{4L^2(D\rho^{-1} + 12k^3e_k^2) + 4mL(1 + 6ke_k)}\right)\, .
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. observations with finite variance (Andrews states the result under moment conditions for the CLT)","the constraint is active at the true parameter (theta = 0); for theta > 0 the bootstrap is consistent"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T09:15:04.118127+00:00","domain":"resampling / constrained estimation","id":"claim_5803afc2cb107c5851acbdda8fe0e490d3b03266f3d6e659e596fdbcafb115fe","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $X_1, \\dots, X_n$ be i.i.d. with mean $\\theta \\ge 0$ and variance $\\sigma^2$, and let the estimator respect the constraint: $\\hat\\theta_n = \\max(0, \\bar X_n)$. When the true parameter is interior ($\\theta > 0$) the nonparametric bootstrap is consistent: the conditional law of $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n^* - \\hat\\theta_n)$ converges to $N(0, \\sigma^2)$, the law of $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n - \\theta)$. When the true parameter is on the boundary ($\\theta = 0$) it is not: $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n - \\theta) \\Rightarrow \\max(0, Z)$ with $Z \\sim N(0, \\sigma^2)$, a law with an atom of mass $1/2$ at zero, whereas the bootstrap law of $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n^* - \\hat\\theta_n)$ converges, conditionally on the data, to the law of $\\max(0, Z + \\zeta) - \\max(0, \\zeta)$ with $\\zeta \\sim N(0, \\sigma^2)$ a random shift that does not vanish - so the bootstrap distribution is random in the limit and does not equal the sampling distribution (Andrews 2000, Theorem 1). The same failure holds for maximum-likelihood and least-squares estimators under inequality constraints whenever the true parameter has an active constraint, in particular for nonnegatively constrained regression and portfolio weights with coordinates at zero: the bootstrap replicates flip the constrained coordinates between zero and positive values, and the spread of the replicates is not the spread of the estimator. Consistent alternatives: the $m$-out-of-$n$ bootstrap with $m \\to \\infty$, $m/n \\to 0$, and subsampling, both of which recover the limit law at the boundary.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:15:27.869621+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_581c9552f43e1f4cf92726d32a39b9a4720c921de8094cf33857ac37ef5fce39","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"FIRES WHEN a detection or coverage problem in a moving Boolean model has been reduced, correctly, to the volume of a union of swept regions, and you are about to call the problem solved. THE REDUCTION IS EXACT and motion-free: P(S_1 > s, S_2 > t) = exp(-lambda |A_1(s) union A_2(t)|) by the Poisson void probability, where A_i(t) is the set of grain initial conditions detecting K_i by time t. WHAT IS LEFT is the geometry, and the geometry is where the two models part. For BALLISTIC grains each A_i is a capsule with axis along -v, the axes are parallel, and the union volume is two capsule volumes minus an axial integral of the cross-sectional lens - a solid-angle computation, tractable. For BROWNIAN grains |A_1(s) union A_2(t)| is the joint volume swept by a single Brownian path around two given sets, i.e. a TWO-SET WIENER SAUSAGE volume, and that quantity has no closed form in any dimension. CONDITION OF FAILURE: Brownian, or any diffusive, grain motion. PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE, and it is why this is a scar and not a complaint: it says which case to attack first, and the inertial case was settled exactly because of it.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:18:27.580325+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_583a6a2d58ab2641021ba72d33552a23bcc7fcdd59ee5d70ec39e158a910086e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 17 (Stability of the subcritical domain; conditional on Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:red}) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] Let $\mathcal M_-=\{\theta:\rho(M(\theta))<1\}$ and $\mathcal M_+=\{\theta:\rho(M(\theta))>1\}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item ($\mathcal M_-$ is open.) $\rho(M(\cdot))$ is continuous (indeed real-analytic where $M$ is irreducible), so $\mathcal M_-$ is open and $\partial\mathcal M_-=\{\rho(M)=1\}$ is, where the gradient is nonzero, a smooth codimension-one submanifold (Proposition~\ref{prop:PF}(3) and the implicit function theorem).
\item (Convexity goes to $\mathcal M_+$, not $\mathcal M_-$.) In the scalar (Bethe) case $\rho=(d-1)p$, with $p$ log-concave, $\mathcal M_+=\{p>1/(d-1)\}$ is a superlevel set of a log-concave function, hence convex; $\mathcal M_-$ is its complement and is in general non-convex. Explicitly, if $p$ is jointly log-concave in $(\theta,\gamma)$ then $\mathcal M_-$ is the non-convex exterior of a convex region. Convexity of $\mathcal M_-$ cannot be deduced from log-concavity of $p$: the implication ``sublevel sets of a concave function are convex'' is false (it is superlevel sets that are convex).
\item ($\mathcal M_-$ is contractible.) $\mathcal M_-$ is star-shaped toward the zero-coupling locus $\{\gamma=0\}$: holding $(\theta,\alpha,\mu)$ fixed and sending $\gamma\downarrow0$ decreases every $p_{d,d'}$ (transmission increases in coupling), hence decreases $\rho(M)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:PF}(2)), keeping the path in $\mathcal M_-$. The straight-line homotopy $\gamma\mapsto(1-t)\gamma$ therefore retracts $\mathcal M_-$ to a point; $\mathcal M_-$ is contractible.
\item (Resolvent and gap.) On $\mathcal M_-$ the resolvent $R=(I-M)^{-1}=\sum_{k\ge0}M^k$ converges (finite matrix, $\rho(M)<1$) to a bounded nonnegative matrix; the halting probability is $\Prob(|S|<\infty)=1$; the expected cluster size is $\E|S|=\one^\top R\,\pi$, real-analytic in $\theta$; and the spectral gap $g(\theta)=1-\rho(M(\theta))>0$ gives quantitative stability: any $\Delta\theta$ with $\|\Delta\theta\|<g(\theta)/\|\nabla_\theta\rho\|$ keeps $\theta+\Delta\theta\in\mathcal M_-$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.475978+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_585c4383bc38881d1d843d168a1a7be60fb8adcc4e5d9ee4e9c0722dfcdb713c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] Let $f$ be a probability density on $G$ such that $\supp(f)$ is contained in some proper subgroup $H$ of $G$ with $\mu(H) > 0$ and Haar measure $\mu_H$ defined to be the Haar measure $\mu$ of $G$ restricted to $H$. 

Then if $g'$ is a symmetrizer for $\restr{f}{H}$ (the restriction of $f$ to $H$) in $H$, 
\[ g \coloneqq \begin{cases} g'(x) & x \in H \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \]
is a symmetrizer of $f$ in $G$. 

\begin{proof}
Since $g'$ is a symmetrizer for $\restr{f}{H}$, 
\begin{align*}
(g * f)(x) 
&= \int_{G} g(r)f(r^{-1}x) \,d\mu(r)\\ 
&= \int_{H} g(r)f(r^{-1}x) \,d\mu(r)
= (g' * \restr{f}{H})(x) 
= (g' * \restr{f}{H})(x^{-1}) 

= (g * f)(x^{-1}). \qedhere
\end{align*}
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:31:20.592800+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_586873d54cd9674eea96644a5305308f175f503006cc57be13f95a8b68a7482a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 of arXiv:2608.25221, 'Representing MAX functions using two-hidden-layer ReLU networks'] Fix any number $k\geq 1$. Define an {\em atom pattern of degree $k$} to be a list
\[
 P=[p_1,\ldots,p_k \mid q_1,\ldots,q_k],
\]
where $p_1, \ldots, p_k, q_1, \ldots, q_k \in \{1, \ldots, N\} \times \{1, \ldots, N\}$ be ordered pairs (with repetition allowed) of numbers in $\{1, \ldots, N\}$. 

Define the corresponding functions\[
 L_P(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}m_{p_i}(x),
 \qquad
 R_P(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}m_{q_i}(x),
\]
where $m_{(a,b)}(x)=\max\{x_a,x_b\}$. The {\em atom represented by $P$ is then defined as}
\[
 \A_P(x)=\max\{L_P(x),R_P(x)\}
\]
\medskip

For any permutation $\sigma\in \Sigma_N$ and any ordered pair $(a,b) \in \{1, \ldots, N\} \times \{1, \ldots, N\}$, define $\sigma((a,b))= (\sigma(a), \sigma(b))$. This defines a group action of the symmetric group $\Sigma_N$ on the set of all atom patterns of degree $k$ by defining $$\sigma P = [\sigma(p_1), \ldots, \sigma(p_k)\mid \sigma(q_1), \ldots, \sigma(q_k)].$$","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:19:06.752101+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_588edbd5c2828962ac8b82f8c458a6266b94be8cebd6837543533d7eb426c2dc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:finite-r-annular of arXiv:2606.08683, 'Exact Fourier dimensions of dyadic Mandelbrot cascades under minimal integrability'] Let \(0<s<1\), \(r>1\), and \(\delta>0\). Let \(U\ge0\) be a random variable with \(\mathbb{E} U=1\) and

\]
Let \(\nu_\circ=f_\#\widetilde\nu\) be the circle cascade generated by \(U\).  Then there exist constants \(C<\infty\), \(c>0\), and \(\eta>0\), depending only on \(s,r,\delta\) and on the law of \(U\), such that, for every \(n\ge1\),

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.820998+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_589202f03b99b9f1482c8a4024de03ebf8483baf5b41dc2e63ebbc1c538e4c68","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:compression-master of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Let $h\geq1$, $k\geq2$, and let
$A=(a_0<a_1<\cdots<a_{k-1})$ be an ordered real $k$-set.  If
$r=r_h(A)$, define its successive active-relation degrees by
\[
 p_i(A)=\min\{p\in\mathbb Z_{\geq1}:\dim L_p(A)\geq i\},
 \qquad 1\leq i\leq r.
\]
Put $d_A=k-1-r$.  Since $r\leq k-2$, one has $d_A\geq1$.
Then there is an integer set
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 A^*&=(0=a_0^*<a_1^*<\cdots<a_{k-1}^*),\\
 a_{k-1}^*
 &\leq d_Ah^{d_A-1}\prod_{i=1}^{r}p_i(A)
 \leq(k-1-r)h^{k-2},
 \end{aligned}
\]
where the empty product is one,
such that, simultaneously for every $1\leq j\leq h$ and every
$u,v\in\mathcal U_{j,k}$,
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{sgn}\bigl((u-v)\cdot A^*\bigr)
 =\operatorname{sgn}\bigl((u-v)\cdot A\bigr).
\end{equation}
Thus the ordered addition tables are identical in every degree $1\leq j\leq h$;
in particular, $|jA^*|=|jA|$ for $1\leq j\leq h$.

There is a complementary intrinsic statement.  Suppose $k\geq3$ and
\[
 B=(0=b_0<b_1<\cdots<b_{k-1}=d),
 \qquad \gcd(b_1,\ldots,b_{k-1})=1.
\]
For $1\leq i\leq k-2$, define the successive relation degrees
\[
 p_i(B)=\min\{p\in\mathbb Z_{\geq1}:\dim L_p(B)\geq i\}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{ndiam}(B)=d\leq\prod_{i=1}^{k-2}p_i(B).
\end{equation}
Consequently, for $h\geq2$,
\begin{equation}
 \max_{\substack{B\subset\mathbb Z,\ |B|=k\\r_h(B)=k-2}}
       \operatorname{ndiam}(B)=h^{k-2}.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:51:52.124612+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_589497cb22c0601f4233172e6504611e5354393949a454f1b5ce26fc69795f33","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma L:arc-tangent-angle of arXiv:2607.15966, 'Canonical Mandelbrot Cascades on Curves Are Rajchman'] There exists a \(C^1\) function

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.179777+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_58c2f90a212f274a241ad1ba9cc4d9d7695182d21fe0fbe058f607ce2eb09584","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 95 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix $L,\alpha>0$ and let $(\cA_N)^\circ$ be a sequence of $L$-Lipschitz algorithms in the sense of Definition~\ref{d:Lip}. Let $\cA_N$ be the perturbation of $(\cA_N)^\circ$ from Proposition~\ref{p:wlogable}. By passing to a subsequence $N_j\to\infty$, we assume that $\chi_{\cA_N}$ converges to a limiting function $\chi$, pointwise and in $L^1$. Denote $q_0\equiv \chi(0)\in[0,1]$. The function $p\equiv\chi^{-1}$ belongs to $\incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ and is concave, with
\[\frac1{L^2}
\le p'(q) \le L^2\] for all $q\in [q_0,1]$. Suppose $(\mu,\mu^\Ising)$ satisfies 
	\beq
	\bbW_2\big(\mu,\mu(\cA_N)\big)
	+\bbW_2\big(\mu^\Ising,
		\mu^\Ising(\cA_N)\big)
		\le \epsilon_\textup{apx}
		\,.
	\eeq
Then there exist $C(L) > 0$ and $q_*,b,\sigma,w,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising$ such that the following hold. Let $B(t)$ and $W(t)$ be standard Brownian motions and
\begin{align} 
        dX(t)
        &= p'(t)^{1/2} b_t\,dt
        + s(t) \sigma_t\,dB(t)\,,
        \\
        dX^{\Ising}(t)
        &= w_t\,dW(t) 
        \end{align}
on the time interval $q_* \le t \le 1$, with $X(q_*)\sim\zeta$ and $X^\Ising(q_*)\sim\zeta^\Ising$.  Then: 
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item 
$b_t=b(t,X(t))$,
$\sigma_t=\sigma(t,X(t))$,
and $w_t=w(t,Y(t))$ 
for functions $b:[q_*,1]\times \bbR\to[-C(L),C(L)]$ and $\sigma,w:[q_*,1]\times \bbR\to[0,C(L)]$, such that the functions $p'(t)^{1/2} b(t,x), s(t) \sigma(t,x), w(t,x)$, are $C(L)$-Lipschitz in $(t,x)$.
\item 
We have the diffusivity constraint
        \beq
            \max\bigg\{
            \Big|\bbE[w(t,X^\Ising(t))^2]-1
            	\Big|
	:q_* \le t\le 1
\bigg\} \leq  o(1)\,.
\eeq

\item 
    We have the approximate budget constraints
       \beq 
            \int_{q_*}^1
            \bigg\{
            \bbE\bigg[ b(t,X(t))^2+ \frac{(tp)'(t)}{p(t)}
            	(\sigma(t,X(t))-1)^2\bigg]
            -
            \frac{(\bbE w(t,X^\Ising(t)) )^2}{\alpha}
            \bigg\}_+
            \de t
            \leq o(1)\,.\eeq

 \item  The initial measures $\zeta,\zeta^\Ising$ satisfy $|\bE[X(q_*)^2]|\leq o(1)$ and  $|\bE[X^\Ising(q_*)^2] - q_*|\leq o(1)$.
\item  The initial time $q_*$ lies in $[q_0,q_0+ o(1)]$ and satisfies $p(q_*) \le o(1)$. 
\end{enumerate}
Lastly, we have
\beq
\begin{aligned}
	\bbW_2(\Law(X(1)),\mu)
	&\leq 
	O(\epsilon_\textup{apx}) 
	+ o(1)\,,\\ 
	\bbW_2(\Law(X^{\Ising}(1)),\mu^{\Ising})
	&\leq  O(\epsilon_\textup{apx})
	+ o(1)\,.
\end{aligned}
\eeq
In all the above assertions, the $o(1)$ denotes an error which can tend to zero as $L^{-\Theta(1)}$. Thus, the distributions $\mu,\mu^\Ising$ are well approximated by the distributions of the endpoints of the solution to the constrained SDE described above. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:41:33.836561+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_58c6c283671fb8da1e7792c6ed7d3a0caeda1eeeaf76b5fa52fe32f6231e4f69","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 3 (Random clock) of arXiv:2604.11434, 'Maxima of stationary systems of randomly time-changed L\'evy particles'] Given a L\'evy process $(L_t)_{t\ge 0}$ and a bounded function $\alpha:\RR \to (0,\infty)$, we define
\begin{align*}

  \ = \
  \int_0^t
  \alpha(L_r+x)
  \,\mathrm{d}r
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  T_x(t)
  \ = \
  \inf\{s\ge 0 \mid A_x(s)> t\}
  \,,\qquad
  t\ge 0 \,, x\in\RR\,.
\end{align*}
  We call $(T_x(t))_{t\ge 0}$ the random clock, $(A_x(t))_{t\ge 0}$ the inverse random clock, and $\alpha$ the mass function.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Invertible measurable P-preserving theta with measurable inverse","Measurable finite integer n(Z)"],"created_at":"2026-09-06T17:31:31.222891+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_58e1b5e4720fedc6b679f8a21fa4026f8e4610f74c61bbb03ccc4bff815529af","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Author-checked lemma; a parent-agent counter-check identified the mechanism, but the full proof has no independent review. Let theta be an invertible measurable measure-preserving transformation of (E,P), with measurable inverse, and n:E->Z measurable. The law of theta^(n(Z))Z for Z~P has density g(y)=sum over k in Z of 1_{n(theta^(-k)y)=k}. Consequently g is integer-valued and finite P-almost everywhere. An arbitrary noninteger target density requires additional randomness or a projection to a marginal.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A noisy weak-PRF family with uniform random input samples; polynomial parameter lengths and n>=lambda.","One shared independent seed,pad,permutation; fresh sample inputs,noise and filler per encoding.","At most polynomially many calls,with a fixed polynomial upper bound Q."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:49:17.343706+00:00","domain":"Pseudorandom codes and sampling couplings","id":"claim_58ed9e6ef15a9c4f1dc1d61d11f40b5735573a1dd8c9b15a2a5fec59e23069ac","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let lambda<=n(lambda)<=poly(lambda), and let m,N and the seed length be polynomially bounded positive integers with N>=(n+1)*m. Let F_s:{0,1}^n->{0,1} be an efficiently evaluable noisy weak-PRF family at a fixed q in[0,1/2), in the sample-oracle sense of Definitions3.1–3.2. Choose one uniform seed S, one independent uniform N-bit pad Z, and one independent uniform permutation Pi of N coordinates as the secret key. Each encoder call independently samples m uniform X_j in{0,1}^n, m independent Bernoulli(q) bits E_j, and a fresh uniform filler R of length N-(n+1)*m; it returns Pi applied to(C xor Z), where C concatenates the pairs(X_j,F_S(X_j) xor E_j) and R. For any probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher making at most Q polynomially many adaptive encoder calls, there is a polynomial-time weak-PRF sample-oracle distinguisher making at most M=Q*m calls whose advantage bounds the encoding-oracle advantage up to min(1,binom(M,2)/2^n). Here the reference encoding oracle returns a fresh independent uniform N-bit word at every call. Thus the encoder is undetectable under the noisy weak-PRF assumption. Locality of F_s and decoder robustness are not needed for this claim.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:29:21.917510+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_58ffc21014799f6ba9dde03765b16731732113257ed5337a11b7a7e9422e4c49","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 5 of arXiv:2608.01516, 'Nondegeneracy and regularity of polynomial pushforwards'] Let $a,b\in(0,+\infty)$, $\eta>0$, $k,d\in\mathbb N$, and $d\ge2$. There exists
a constant $C:=C(a,b,\eta,k,d)>0$ such that, for every
$X=(X_1,\ldots,X_k),Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_k)\in\mathcal P_{d,k}^{\rm lc}$
satisfying
\[
a\le \operatorname{Var}(X_j)\le b,
\quad
a\le \operatorname{Var}(Y_j)\le b
\quad
\forall j\in\{1,\ldots,k\},
\]
and
\[
\det \Sigma^d(X)\ge \eta,
\quad
\det \Sigma^d(Y)\ge \eta,
\]
one has
\[
d_{\rm TV}(X,Y)
\le
C d_{\rm KR}(X,Y)^{\frac{1}{k(d-1)+2}}.
\]

In particular, if a sequence
$X_n\in\mathcal P_{d,k}^{\rm lc}$ converges in distribution to an
$\mathbb R^k$-valued random vector $X_\infty$ whose distribution is absolutely
continuous, then the convergence holds in total variation and
\[
d_{\rm TV}(X_n,X_\infty)
\le
C d_{\rm KR}(X_n,X_\infty)^{\frac{1}{k(d-1)+2}}
\]
for some constant $C>0$ depending on the sequence and on the limiting
distribution. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:38:13.635990+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_592169432c2b95ccc1b27d69f321a5d51b40f31b5ac1c0310c55bc6264920664","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 14 (Second-order smooth consistency) of arXiv:2609.00673, '2609.00673'] Let \(\gamma\in C^6(I,\mathbb R^3)\) be a unit-speed space curve.
Assume that, on a compact subinterval \(J\Subset I\),
\[
\kappa(s)\ge \kappa_0>0,\qquad |\tau(s)|\ge\tau_0>0.
\]
Sample it uniformly by
\[
P_i=\gamma(s_i),\qquad s_i=s_0+ih.
\]
For the quotient indexed by $i$, call $C_i=[s_{i-1},s_{i+2}]$ its associated four-point cell. All quotient estimates below are uniform whenever $C_i\subset J$; estimates for the defect $D_i^h$, which involves two consecutive quotients, are uniform whenever $C_i\cup C_{i+1}=[s_{i-1},s_{i+3}]\subset J$.
Let \(\theta_i^h\) and \(\phi_i^h\) be the turning and signed torsion
angles of the chord polygon and set
\[
x_i^h=\tan\frac{\theta_i^h}{2}.
\]
There exists $h_0=h_0(\kappa_0,\tau_0,J)>0$ such that, for $0<h<h_0$ and all cells under consideration,
\[
0<\theta_i^h<\pi,\qquad \phi_i^h\notin\{0,\pi\}.
\]
Hence the sampled polygon lies in the generic Frenet branch and all quotients below are well defined.
With $m_i=s_i+h/2$, the midpoint convention compatible with the chord tangents gives the
asymptotic expansions
\[
x_i^h=\frac h2\kappa(s_i)+O(h^3),
\]
and
\[
\phi_i^h=h\tau\left(s_i+\frac h2\right)+O(h^3).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\frac{x_i^h+x_{i+1}^h\cos\phi_i^h}{\sin\phi_i^h}
=
\frac{\kappa}{\tau}\left(s_i+\frac h2\right)+O(h^2).
\]
If
\[
D_i^h:=
\frac{x_{i+1}^h+x_{i+2}^h\cos\phi_{i+1}^h}{\sin\phi_{i+1}^h}
-
\frac{x_i^h+x_{i+1}^h\cos\phi_i^h}{\sin\phi_i^h},
\]
then, uniformly on such cells,
\[
\boxed{
\frac{D_i^h}{h}
=
\left(\frac{\kappa}{\tau}\right)'(m_i)+O(h)
},
\qquad m_i=s_i+\frac h2.
\]
Thus the finite-step conservation law approaches $(\kappa/\tau)'=0$, equivalently \(\tau/\kappa=\mathrm{constant}\) on intervals where \(\kappa\tau\neq0\). The scalar quotient itself is second-order accurate, whereas its normalized finite difference is first-order accurate. If the underlying smooth curve is a general helix, then
\[
D_i^h=O(h^3).
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:52:47.241560+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_598e07ea2375a52e9d6b6e42cebfe08fec80ff91ff7170cea3f5881c896575e9","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 2 (Canonical solvability of the metric Hodge system) of arXiv:2609.01093, 'Ideal MHD below the classical well-posedness threshold'] Let $X:\Real_y^n\to\Real_x^n$ be an orientation-preserving global
bi-Lipschitz map with $d\mu=J dy$.  Fix $1<p<n$ and put
\[
 p^*:=\frac{np}{n-p}.
\]
For every $q\in L^p(\mu)$ there is a unique vector field $F=F^i\eframe_i$ along $X$, whose Cartesian components belong to
$L^{p^*}(\mu;\Rn)$, satisfying \eqref{eq:invdiv} in the conjugated
distributional sense: equivalently, $u:=F\circ X^{-1}$ satisfies
\[
 \partial_{x^i}u^j-\partial_{x^j}u^i=0,
 \qquad
 \partial_{x^i}u^i=q\circ X^{-1}
 \quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Real_x^n).
\]
The solution is
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal P_{\gmetric}q
 :=\mathcal C_X\nabla\Delta_x^{-1}\mathcal C_X^{-1}q, \qquad \mathcal{C}_Xf=f\circ X,
\end{equation}
and it satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \|\mathcal P_{\gmetric}q\|_{L^{p^*}(\mu)}
 \le C_{n,p}\|q\|_{L^p(\mu)}.
\end{equation}
In particular, for
\begin{equation}
    r_{\mathrm{HLS}}:=\frac{4n}{n+4},
\end{equation}
one has $1<r_{\mathrm{HLS}}<n$ for every $n\ge2$ and $r_{\mathrm{HLS}}^*=4$; hence
every $q\in L^{r_{\mathrm{HLS}}}(\mu)$ has a unique solution
$\mathcal P_{\gmetric}q\in L^4(\mu)$ which we refer to as the canonical Hodge vector field along $X$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.544044+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_59b71972a03cccd34a3b9f19358b0f2ad82bb2b26ccd049a537b06518a32a52b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a positive finite Borel measure mu on R, its STIELTJES TRANSFORM (also Cauchy transform) is m_mu(z) = integral (x - z)^{-1} mu(dx) for z in the open upper half plane C^+. It is analytic on C^+, maps C^+ into C^+ when mu is positive, and satisfies the a priori bound |m_mu(z)| <= mu(R)/Im(z). INVERSION: for a < b continuity points of mu, mu( (a,b) ) = (1/pi) lim_{eta decreasing to 0} integral_a^b Im m_mu(x + i eta) dx, so the transform determines the measure. CONTINUITY: a sequence of probability measures mu_n converges weakly to a probability measure mu if and only if m_{mu_n}(z) -> m_mu(z) for every z in C^+; convergence on any set with an accumulation point in C^+ suffices, by analyticity plus a tightness argument. In random matrix theory the transform of the empirical spectral distribution of a Hermitian matrix H is m_n(z) = (1/n) tr ( H - z I )^{-1}, the normalised trace of the RESOLVENT, which is why resolvent methods and Stieltjes-transform methods are the same method. Sign conventions differ across the literature: some authors define the transform with (z - x)^{-1}, which flips the sign of the whole calculus; the convention must be checked before importing a formula. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:02:34.835847+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_59e2ec10a29aad2ce21a11a16f2592e948f2f8a893c3141e52ad31c6bd0897e6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 13 (Posterior thresholds) of arXiv:2607.20373, 'Embedding martingale diffusions as binary posteriors in sequential inference'] Let $0<\alpha<p<\beta<1$ and $\tau_{\alpha,\beta}$ be the first exit time
    \(
        \tau_{\alpha,\beta}
        =\inf\{t\geq 0:P_t\notin(\alpha,\beta)\},
    \)
    where $P$ is the posterior for a binary experiment. Assume $P$ is an autonomous win-martingale with $P_0=p$. Then $\tau_{\alpha,\beta}<\infty$ a.s.~and
    \begin{equation}
        \widetilde{\mathbb P}(P_{\tau_{\alpha,\beta}}=\beta)
        =\frac{p-\alpha}{\beta-\alpha},
        \qquad
        \widetilde{\mathbb P}(P_{\tau_{\alpha,\beta}}=\alpha)
        =\frac{\beta-p}{\beta-\alpha}.
    \end{equation}
    If the decision is $1$ at $\beta$ and $0$ at $\alpha$, then
    \begin{align}
        \widetilde{\mathbb Q}^0(\textnormal{decide }1)
        &=\frac{1-\beta}{1-p}\frac{p-\alpha}{\beta-\alpha},
        \qquad
        \widetilde{\mathbb Q}^1(\textnormal{decide }0)
        =\frac{\alpha}{p}\frac{\beta-p}{\beta-\alpha}.
    
    \end{align}
    The expected decision time under the marginal law is
    \begin{align}
        \widetilde{\mathbb E}[\tau_{\alpha,\beta}]
        =2\bigg[&
        \frac{\beta-p}{\beta-\alpha}
        \int_\alpha^p\frac{y-\alpha}{\sigma^2(y)}\,dy
        +\frac{p-\alpha}{\beta-\alpha}
        \int_p^\beta\frac{\beta-y}{\sigma^2(y)}\,dy
        \bigg].
    
    \end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:26.250966+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5a149bb6e7718b3087427678a1beddfcaac907987a267282f2eb84406df0ced5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2605.23222, 'On global solutions to the semidiscrete stochastic heat equation'] If $\beta$ is sufficiently small, the following statements hold.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:14:46.355699+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5a1b5b99ef961db4070819ff0a8017bcad58fc5875e66260e258e72e200b1575","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given a differentiable function $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, we have:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The local minima and maxima of $f$ appear at the points where $f'(x)=0$.

\item Rolle theorem: if $f(a)=f(b)$, we must have $f'(c)=0$, for some $c\in(a,b)$. 

\item Mean value theorem: $\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}=f'(c)$, for some $c\in(a,b)$.

\item Main theorem: if $f'=0$ then $f$ must be constant.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

for some universal constant $c>0$, where $\|\bA\|_\Fnorm$ and $\|\bA\|_\op$ denote

    \begin{equation}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:54:18.238901+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5aae15f417c796ccacf0479a7b8204d192fab8a958a4bd33cb7cbe32a81bb366","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:prefix-free-ball-code-dimension of arXiv:2608.29561, 'Ball codes: A coding characterization of Hausdorff and packing dimensions'] Let \(\varphi\) be a prefix-free ball code.
For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(r\in\omega\), define
\[
K_\varphi(x;r)
=
\min
\left\{
|p|
:
p\in\dom(\varphi),
x\in \varphi(p),
\ \diam(\varphi(p))\le 2^{-r}
\right\},
\]
with the convention that \(K_\varphi(x;r)=\infty\) if no such \(p\) exists.
Define
\[
\dim_\varphi(x)
=
\liminf_{r\to\infty}
\frac{K_\varphi(x;r)}{r}.
\]
Finally, for nonempty \(E\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), define
\[
\dim_\varphi(E)
=
\sup_{x\in E}\dim_\varphi(x).
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["conjugate exponents with 1 <= p <= 2","convention e^{-2 pi i x . xi}, for which the constant 1 is available on R^d","on T the transform is the coefficient sequence, with the counting measure on Z"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.264720+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis, common errors","id":"claim_5aeb07b2cba38ad9cc3665ecb9550bf24a5d74fc445f8cf0332b5120f3c59861","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The inequality $\\|\\hat f\\|_{p'}\\le\\|f\\|_p$, $\\frac1p+\\frac1{p'}=1$, holds for $1\\le p\\le2$ (Riesz-Thorin interpolation between $\\|\\hat f\\|_\\infty\\le\\|f\\|_1$ and Plancherel) - and only there. The restriction $p\\le2$ is load-bearing: (i) On $\\mathbb T$, $L^p\\subset L^2$ for $p>2$, so the coefficients are automatically in $\\ell^2$, but no better exponent is available: Carleman's example provides a continuous (hence in every $L^p$) function $f$ on $\\mathbb T$ with $\\sum_n|\\hat f(n)|^q=\\infty$ for every $q<2$. So no bound $\\|\\hat f\\|_{\\ell^{p'}}\\le C\\|f\\|_{L^p}$ with $p'<2$ can hold for any $p>2$. (ii) On $\\mathbb R^d$ and $p>2$, the Fourier transform of an $L^p$ function exists only as a tempered distribution and need not be representable by a locally integrable function, so the left-hand side of the inequality is not even defined in general. (iii) The direction matters too: the dual statement '$\\hat f\\in L^{p'}$ implies $f\\in L^p$' is false in general; what is true is the companion inequality $\\|f\\|_{p'}\\le\\|\\hat f\\|_p$ for $1\\le p\\le2$. (iv) On $\\mathbb R^d$ the constant $1$ is not sharp: Babenko-Beckner give $\\|\\hat f\\|_{p'}\\le\\big(p^{1/p}/(p')^{1/p'}\\big)^{d/2}\\|f\\|_p$ for $1<p<2$, attained by Gaussians, whereas on $\\mathbb T$ and $\\mathbb Z$ the constant $1$ is sharp.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.433149+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5b2f1a3c50fbcde76c3148afa2540ddcf2e4fe34d40b000444da8a0b2f61fd46","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] \label[theorem]{thm:Bernoulli_calY_representation}
The set $\{\hat{f}_k^r \mid r \in [0,1] \text{ and } k \in I^r \}$ is a basis for ${\rm aff}(\Sym(f))$. 

That is, for $f \in \Sym$, denoting 

$ R_f = \{ r \in [0,1] \mid \supp(f) \cap S^r \ne \emptyset \}, $ we have
\[ f = \sum_{r \in R_f} \sum_{k \in I^r} \alpha_k^r \hat{f}_k^r , \qquad \text{and} \qquad \sum_{r \in R_f} \sum_{k \in I^r} \alpha_k^r = 1 . \]
\begin{proof}
The PMF $f$ is discrete, so its support is at most countable; therefore $R_f$ is at most countable. 
Write $f = \sum_{R_f} f\big\vert_{S^r}$ and for each $r \in R_f$ define $c_r = \sum_{z \in S^r} f(z)$. 
Then for each $r \in R_f$, $f_r = \frac{1}{c_r} f\big\vert_{S^r} \in \Sym$ by (lem:Sr_restriction_of_symmetrizers_produces_symmetrizers of the paper). 
Now apply the (lem:Bernoulli_calYr_representation of the paper) to each $f_r$ to find constants $\alpha_k^r[f_r]$; it is then obvious that $c_r \alpha_k^r[f_r] = \alpha_k^r[f]$ for all $k$ and $r$. 

Thus we compute 
\[ 
f = \sum_{r \in R_f} c_r f_r 
= \sum_{r \in R_f} \sum_{k \in I^r} c_r \alpha_k^r[f_r] \hat{f}_k^r 
= \sum_{r \in R_f} \sum_{k \in I^r} \alpha_k^r \hat{f}_k^r 
\]
as needed. 
Finally, 
\begin{align*} 
\sum_{r \in R_f} \sum_{k \in I^r} \alpha_k^r 
&= \sum_{r \in R_f} \sum_{k \in I^r} \alpha_k^r \bigg( \sum_{z \in \supp(f)} \hat{f}_k^r(z) \bigg) \\
&= \sum_{z \in \supp(f)} \bigg(\sum_{r \in R_f} \sum_{k \in I^r} \alpha_k^r \hat{f}_k^r(z)\bigg) 
= \sum_{z \in \supp(f)} f(z)
= 1 . \qedhere
\end{align*}
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.357189+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5b6f7b66106ac510bc178ea79662cbf40119d6a1b20f404e79fcc46b2807147f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 239 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix any $\alpha,L > 0$, $\fq \in [1,2]$, and $\mu \in \cP_2(\R)$. 
	Then, for any $L$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$,
	\begin{align}
		(\E \bbW_\fq(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu))^2
		&\ge \bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\mu)^2 - o_N(1)\,,\\
	
		(\E \bbW_2(\EmpDist(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\cP(\{\pm 1\})))^2
		&\ge \bbW_2(\mu^\Ising(\cA_N),\cP(\{\pm 1\}))^2 - o_N(1)\,.
	\end{align}
where $o_N(1)$ denotes a term tending to $0$ as $N\to\infty$, which may depend on $\alpha,L,\mu$.

\begin{proof}
	Abbreviate $X = \bbW_\fq(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu)$.
	By Jensen's inequality, we have
	\[
		\E[X^\fq]^{2/\fq} 
		\le \E[X^2] 
		= (\E X)^2 + \E[(X-\E X)^2] \stackrel{\eqref{e:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc.var}}{=} (\E X)^2 + o_N(1)\,.
	\]
By convexity of $\bbW_\fq(\cdot,\cdot)^\fq$, we have
	\[
		\E[X^\fq] = \E [\bbW_\fq(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu)^\fq] \ge \bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\mu)^\fq\,.
	\]
	Rearranging yields the first assertion \eqref{e:confinement.consequence.of.variance.bound}.
	The second assertion
	\eqref{e:confinement.consequence.of.variance.bound.ising} is proved in the same way, replacing $X$ with $J \equiv \bbW_2(\EmpDist(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\cP(\{\pm 1\}))$ in the above argument and using \eqref{e:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc.var.ising} from Lemma~\ref{l:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc} in place of \eqref{e:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc.var}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-07T10:34:20.210894+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis","id":"claim_5b782a41ff1e12f05a6fe36459437e9b75a21f04587cb4fc508fb13cb12016f9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A complex-valued function f: \\mathbb{R} \\to \\mathbb{C} is said to be positive definite (or positive semi-definite) if for every integer n \\ge 1, every choice of real points t_1, \\dots, t_n \\in \\mathbb{R}, and every choice of complex numbers c_1, \\dots, c_n \\in \\mathbb{C}, the inequality \\sum_{j=1}^n \\sum_{k=1}^n f(t_j - t_k) c_j \\overline{c_k} \\ge 0 holds.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:02:34.818458+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5b78a3ca829fe35633b76ff3be4a4770f0a5fd57eb0ac087cc26ad7c10671051","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 6 (Compact-time pathwise stability) of arXiv:2607.19752, 'Weak Equilibrium Measures and Capacity--Hitting Identities\\ for the Hypoelliptic Third-Or'] Fix $T<\infty$ and a compact set $K\subset\R^{3d}$.  Let $\calK$ be a compact
neighborhood of $K$, and let
\[
    \sigma_\delta:=\inf\left\{t\ge0:Z_t^\delta\notin\calK
    \text{ or } Z_t\notin\calK\right\}.
\]
If $Z_t^\delta$ and $Z_t$ start from the same point $z\in K$ and are coupled
by using the same Brownian motion $B$ in the $r$-coordinate, then, for every
$\eta>0$,
\[
    \sup_{z\in K}
    \Pbb_z\left(
        \sup_{0\le t\le T\wedge\sigma_\delta}\left|Z_t^\delta-Z_t\right|>\eta
    \right)
    \longrightarrow0
    \qquad\text{as }\delta\downarrow0.
\]
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
    \sup_{z\in K}
    \E_z\left[
        \sup_{0\le t\le T\wedge\sigma_\delta}
        \left|Z_t^\delta-Z_t\right|^2
    \right]
    \le C_{T,\calK}\delta .
\end{equation}
The same statement holds for the adjoint regularized processes.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.376193+00:00","domain":"general topology","id":"claim_5b83f139822195103c3c1ab119a904f870e3174a3d3e76e705114a8eea765198","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A metric space is a pair (X, d) where X is a set and d is a function from X x X to the real numbers satisfying, for all x, y, z in X: (i) d(x,y) >= 0, with d(x,y) = 0 if and only if x = y; (ii) symmetry, d(x,y) = d(y,x); (iii) the triangle inequality, d(x,z) <= d(x,y) + d(y,z). The open ball of center x and radius r > 0 is B(x,r) = {y in X : d(x,y) < r}. The metric topology on X is the topology generated by the open balls as a basis: a set U is open exactly when for every point x of U some open ball B(x,r) is contained in U. Convergence of a sequence x_n to x means d(x_n, x) tends to 0.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:09.061920+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5baf01bfb5abdc1615b4c9aa36d03e4af83f46bcc2735dfe6edefe53e5823e91","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 9 of arXiv:2606.27078, 'Semimartingale Optimal Transport with Jumps: A General Framework and Equivalent Formulatio'] Let $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{S}_+^d \times \mathcal{L}$ be measurable. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:53.193766+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5bb12fe1ad83e77252ac62dc01a007f8e25cd3f4eab3256370750d44415e2fdb","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 24 of arXiv:2606.31455, 'Discrete time-multidimensional renewal theory and applications'] Let $\lambda_1,\lambda_2>0$ and $0\le \rho<1$.
A random vector $(X_1,X_2)$ taking values in $\mathbb{R}_+^2$ is said to follow the
Moran--Downton bivariate exponential distribution if it has joint density
\begin{equation}
f_{X_1,X_2}(x_1,x_2)
=
\frac{\lambda_1\lambda_2}{1-\rho}
\exp\!\left(-\frac{\lambda_1 x_1+\lambda_2 x_2}{1-\rho}\right)\,
I_0\!\left(\frac{2\sqrt{\rho\,\lambda_1\lambda_2\,x_1x_2}}{1-\rho}\right),
\qquad x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}_+,
\end{equation}
where $I_0$ is the modified Bessel function of the first kind of order $0$,
\[
I_0(z)=\sum_{m=0}^\infty \frac{1}{(m!)^2}\left(\frac{z}{2}\right)^{2m}.
\]
Under the rate parametrization used in \eqref{eq:downton-pdf}, the marginals are exponential
with rates $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$, and $\rho=0$ yields independence.
(Alternative scale parametrizations appear in the literature; see, e.g.,
\cite{downton1970bivariate,hanandeh2013inference}.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Lebesgue measure on R^n (for a general Radon measure on a locally compact Hausdorff space, density of C_c in L^p, p < infinity, still holds)","1 <= p <= infinity as indicated"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.553780+00:00","domain":"real analysis, Lp spaces","id":"claim_5bc45a179230b3bc44038a44275348cd59550ba798a4169de50c05821e9e46a5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Standard approximation arguments in L^p silently use p < infinity. On R^n with Lebesgue measure: (1) DENSITY. Continuous compactly supported functions are dense in L^p for 1 <= p < infinity, but their closure in L^infinity is C_0(R^n) (continuous functions vanishing at infinity), a proper closed subspace; L^infinity(R^n) is not separable, while L^p(R^n) is for p < infinity. (Simple functions are dense in L^p for every p including infinity; simple functions with support of FINITE measure are dense only for p < infinity.) (2) MOLLIFICATION. If phi is an approximate identity then phi_eps * f -> f in L^p for 1 <= p < infinity, but not in L^infinity: for f = 1_{[0,infinity)} each phi_eps * f is continuous, and any continuous g satisfies ||g - f||_infinity >= 1/2, so the convergence fails; in L^infinity one only gets convergence at points of continuity (and weak-* convergence). (3) TRANSLATION. h -> f(. - h) is continuous from R^n to L^p for p < infinity; in L^infinity it is not: for f = 1_{[0,infinity)}, ||f(. - h) - f||_infinity = 1 for every h not equal to 0. Consequences for proofs: any argument that proves an estimate for nice functions and 'passes to the limit by density', or that uses continuity of translation (Riemann-Lebesgue, convolution identities, Lebesgue differentiation via density), must be carried out in L^p with p < infinity, or re-done by a separate weak-* / pointwise argument at p = infinity.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:57:51.766694+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5bd4c1726835221c5d5fda9b83b4589e84df194ca1e1f3f5d18a48455038de18","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 of arXiv:2608.30223, 'Fairness in Multi-class Multi-group Classification Problems via Contextual Coherent Risk M'] A lower semi-continuous functional $\varrho: \Lc_p(\Omega, \Fc, P;\Rb^M) \to \Rb\cup\{+\infty\}$ is a systemic coherent risk measure with preference to small outcomes if it satisfies the following properties:
        \begin{itemize}
            \item[A1.] \emph{Convexity:} For all $Z, Z' \in \Lc_p(\Omega, \Fc, P;\Rb^M)$ and $ \alpha \in (0,1)$, the following holds\\
                $ ~ \varrho[\alpha Z + (1-\alpha)Z'] \leq \alpha \varrho[Z] + (1 - \alpha)\varrho[Z']. $
            \item[A2.] \emph{Monotonicity:} For all $Z, Z' \in \Lc_p(\Omega, \Fc, P;\Rb^M)$, if $Z_i \geq Z'_i$ for all components $i = 1, \dots, M$, $P$-a.s., then $\varrho[Z] \geq \varrho[Z']$.
            \item[A3.] \emph{Positive homogeneity:} For all $Z \in \Lc_p(\Omega, \Fc, P;\Rb^M)$ and all constants $t > 0$, the relation $\varrho[tX] = t\varrho[X]$ holds.
            \item[A4.] \emph{Translation equivariance:} For all $Z \in \Lc_p(\Omega, \Fc, P;\Rb^M)$ and for all constants $a \in \Rb$, the following relation holds $\varrho[Z + a\one] = \varrho[Z] + a\varrho[\one].$
        \end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:43:45.387694+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5bd7c5acd4bda33e96d87cae15b1afc3e6d39b68c767eddc3b7dd8179ceda9b5","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 2 of arXiv:2609.04139, 'The conformally invariant metric on CLE$_4$ II:\\ existence of geodesics'] We define a \emph{geodesic CLE$_4$ metric coupling} to be a family of couplings
	\begin{equation*}
	 	D = \left\{\left( \Gamma_U, D_{\Gamma_U}^U \right)\right\}_U
	\end{equation*}
	where $U \subsetneq \BC$ ranges over all simply connected domains and $\Gamma_U$ is a non-nested CLE$_4$ in $U$, such that:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\Roman*), ref=\Roman*]
		\item {\bfseries (Geodesic metric)} $D_{\Gamma_U}^U$ is a.s.\ a metric on $\Gamma_U$ such that the following hold.
			\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), ref=\roman*]
				\item For each $\SCL_1, \SCL_2 \in \Gamma_U$, there exists an admissible path $P$ (which we refer to as a \emph{$D_{\Gamma_U}^U$-geodesic}) connecting $\SCL_1$ and $\SCL_2$ such that $D_{\Gamma_U}^U(\SCL_1, \SCL_2) = \len(P; D_{\Gamma_U}^U)$. The same is true with a deterministic connected arc (resp.\ two deterministic and disjoint connected arcs) of $\partial U$ in place of $\SCL_1$ (resp.\ $\SCL_1$ and $\SCL_2$).
				\item Let $\phi\colon U \to \BD$ be a conformal mapping. For every $\SCL \in \Gamma_U$, the process $(\phi(\SCB_t(\SCL; D^U_{\Gamma_U}){)})_{t\ge 0}$ is c\`adl\`ag for the Hausdorff distance, and the same is true with a deterministic connected arc of $\partial U$ in place of $\SCL$.
				\item For all $t, s\ge 0$, if $\SCB_t(\SCL_1; D^U_{\Gamma_U}) \cap \SCB_s(\SCL_2; D^U_{\Gamma_U}) \neq \emptyset$, then $D^U_{\Gamma_U} (\SCL_1, \SCL_2) \le t+s$. The same is true with a deterministic connected arc (resp.\ two deterministic and disjoint connected arcs) of $\partial U$ in place of $\SCL_1$ (resp.\ $\SCL_1$ and $\SCL_2$).
			\end{enumerate}
			Note that $\len(P; D_{\Gamma_U}^U) \ge D_{\Gamma_U}^U(\SCL_1,\SCL_2)$ for every admissible path $P$ connecting $\SCL_1$ and $\SCL_2$, by the triangle inequality along the chains in the definition of $\len$; a path attaining equality is thus 
			what the term geodesic refers to. 
		\item {\bfseries (Locality)} Let $V \subset U$ be a deterministic simply connected subdomain. Let $I \subset \partial U$ be a deterministic connected arc. Let $\{V_j\}_j$ be the connected components of $V^\star$. Then, conditionally on
				\begin{multline}
					\bigl\{\SCL \in \Gamma_U : \SCL \not\subset V\bigr\}, \quad \bigl\{\SCB_t(\SCL; D_{\Gamma_U}^U) : \SCL \in \Gamma_U, \ \SCL \not\subset V, \ t \in [0, D_{\Gamma_U}^U(\SCL, \partial V^\star)]\bigr\}, \\
					\text{and} \quad \bigl\{\SCB_t(I; D_{\Gamma_U}^U) : t \in [0, D_{\Gamma_U}^U(I, \partial V^\star)]\bigr\},
				\end{multline}
			the $(\Gamma_U|_{V_j}, D_{\Gamma_U}^U(\bullet, \bullet; V_j))$'s are independent and their conditional laws are those of $(\Gamma_{V_j}, D_{\Gamma_{V_j}}^{V_j})$, respectively. 
		\item {\bfseries (Conformal invariance)} Let $\phi \colon U \to \phi(U)$ be a deterministic conformal mapping. Then,
		\begin{equation*}
			\left(\phi(\Gamma_U), \left( D_{\Gamma_U}^U\left(\phi^{-1}(\SCL_1), \phi^{-1}(\SCL_2) \right) \right)_{\SCL_1, \SCL_2 \in \phi(\Gamma_U)} \right)
			 \overset{(\mathrm{d})}{=} \left( \Gamma_{\phi(U)}, \left(D_{\Gamma_{\phi(U)}}^{\phi(U)}(\SCL_1, \SCL_2) \right)_{\SCL_1, \SCL_2 \in \Gamma_{\phi(U)}} \right).
		\end{equation*}
		The equality in law is understood as in \Cref{def:weak_axioms}.
		
			
				
				
			
		
		
			
			
		\item {\bfseries (Uniform exploration)} The collection $\{(\SCL, D_{\Gamma_U}^U(\SCL, \partial U))\}_{\SCL \in \Gamma_U}$ has the law of a uniform exploration of $\Gamma_U$ (cf.~\cite{CoInCLEExpl}), in the sense of \Cref{def:weak_axioms}.
	\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:30:52.741400+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5be05496532c970f6df25c2f1fd093039de93cc8e38d2f05f156ccc94ee31d60","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 34 of arXiv:2506.10494, 'Geometric Jensen-Shannon Divergence Between Gaussian Measures On Hilbert Space'] [\textbf{Normalizing factor}]
	
	Assume the hypothesis of Theorem \ref{theorem:geometric-interpolation-equivalent-Gaussian-Hilbert-space}.
	Assume further that $S_i \in \SymTr(\Hcal)_{< I}$, $i=0,1$. Then the normalizing factor $Z_{\alpha}^G(p_0:p_1)$ is given by
	\begin{align}
		&Z_{\alpha}^G(p_0:p_1) \doteq \int_{\Hcal}p_0^{1-\alpha}(x)p_1^{\alpha}(x) \; d\mu_{*}(x)
		\nonumber
		\\
		& =  [\det(I-S_0)]^{-\frac{1-\alpha}{2}}[\det(I-S_1)]^{-\frac{\alpha}{2}}
		\nonumber
		\\
		& \quad \times \exp\left[-\frac{1-\alpha}{2}||(I-S_0)^{-1/2}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_0 - m_{*})||^2\right]
		\nonumber
		\\
		& \quad \times 
		\exp\left[-\frac{\alpha}{2}||(I-S_1)^{-1/2}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_1 - m_{*})||^2\right]
		\nonumber
		\\
		&\quad \times \det(I-S_{\alpha})^{1/2}\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}||(I-S_{\alpha})^{-1/2}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_{\alpha} - m_{*})||^2\right).
		
	\end{align}
Equivalently, with $I + A = (I-S_1)^{-1/2}(I-S_0)(I-S_1)^{-1/2} > 0$, with $A =(I-S_1)^{-1/2}(S_1-S_0)(I-S_1)^{-1/2}$, then $Z_{\alpha}^G(p_0:p_1)$ is given by
\begin{align}
	&Z_{\alpha}^G(p_0:p_1)
	\nonumber
	\\
	
	
	&= \det[(1-\alpha)(I+A)^{-\alpha} + \alpha (I+A)^{1-\alpha}]^{-1/2}
	\nonumber
	\\
	& \quad \times \exp\left[-\frac{1-\alpha}{2}||(I-S_0)^{-1/2}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_0 - m_{*})||^2\right]
	\nonumber
	\\
	& \quad \times 
	\exp\left[-\frac{\alpha}{2}||(I-S_1)^{-1/2}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_1 - m_{*})||^2\right]
	\nonumber
	\\
	& \quad \times \exp\left(\frac{1}{2}||(I-S_{\alpha})^{-1/2}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_{\alpha} - m_{*})||^2\right).
	
\end{align}
Furthermore, this expression is valid for $S_i \in  \SymHS(\Hcal)_{< I}$, $i=0,1$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the ambient space is R^d with Lebesgue outer measure defined by countable covers by boxes","L is the sigma-algebra of Caratheodory-measurable sets and lambda = lambda* restricted to L","R^d is sigma-compact, locally compact and second countable, and lambda is finite on bounded sets - this is what drives regularity","the axiom of choice is used only for the remark that non-measurable sets exist"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.815011+00:00","domain":"measure theory, real analysis","id":"claim_5be137db7963f504ae7ade7e44a43ba8c850915205425ffc83a5dcc77d7cfe50","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let lambda* denote Lebesgue outer measure on R^d, defined by lambda*(E) = inf of sum of volumes of countably many open boxes covering E, let L be the sigma-algebra of Caratheodory-measurable (Lebesgue measurable) sets, and let lambda = lambda* restricted to L. Then: (1) OUTER REGULARITY, valid for EVERY set E contained in R^d, measurable or not: lambda*(E) = inf { lambda(U) : U open, U contains E }. (2) MEASURABILITY CRITERION: E is in L if and only if for every eps > 0 there is an open U containing E with lambda*(U \\ E) < eps, if and only if there is a G_delta set G containing E with lambda(G \\ E) = 0, if and only if there is an F_sigma set F contained in E with lambda(E \\ F) = 0. (3) INNER REGULARITY by compact sets, valid for every E in L: lambda(E) = sup { lambda(K) : K compact, K contained in E } (both sides may be +infinity). Equivalently, for E in L with lambda(E) < infinity and eps > 0 there is a compact K contained in E with lambda(E \\ K) < eps. Thus lambda is a Radon measure: it is finite on compacta, outer regular and inner regular. (4) COMPLETENESS: if lambda*(N) = 0 then N is in L and lambda(N) = 0, and hence every subset of a null set is measurable with measure zero. Equivalently, (R^d, L, lambda) is the completion of (R^d, Borel, lambda|Borel): L = { B union Z : B Borel, Z a subset of a Borel null set }. SHARP EDGES. (a) The Borel sigma-algebra itself is NOT complete: the Cantor set is Borel and null, it has 2^continuum subsets, all of them Lebesgue null and hence Lebesgue measurable, while there are only continuum many Borel sets; so L is strictly larger than the Borel sigma-algebra, and 'measurable' must never be silently upgraded to 'Borel'. (b) Regularity statements about the MEASURE are for measurable sets. Outer regularity in the form (1) does hold for arbitrary sets because it is the definition of the outer measure, but inner regularity fails badly for non-measurable sets: a Vitali set has inner measure 0 and positive outer measure, so the two approximations do not meet. It is exactly the meeting of the two that measurability expresses. (c) Completeness is what makes 'a.e. defined' harmless: if f = g almost everywhere and f is measurable then g is measurable. That inference is FALSE in the Borel sigma-algebra, and is a frequent silent error. (d) Regularity is not automatic for general Borel measures: on a non-sigma-compact or non-locally-compact space a finite Borel measure need not be inner regular by compact sets. Lebesgue measure is regular because R^d is sigma-compact, locally compact and second countable, and because lambda is finite on boxes. (e) Not every set is measurable: the existence of a non-measurable set uses the axiom of choice, and translation invariance plus countable additivity forbid extending lambda to all subsets of R^d.","status":"unverified"}

For the Ising model, or more generally ferromagnetic spin systems with finite-range or summable interactions, let G(x,y) = <sigma_x sigma_y> be the two-point function. The Simon-Lieb inequality bounds G(x,y) across any finite set Lambda separating x from y (x in Lambda, y outside Lambda) by G(x,y) <= sum_{u in Lambda, v not in Lambda, u~v} G(x,u) J_{uv} G(v,y), a one-step recursive bound relating the two-point function across a separating surface to the two-point function up to the boundary of Lambda times the coupling crossing it. Iterating the inequality over a sequence of nested separating sets, such as concentric boxes, yields exponential decay of G(x,y) once the associated generating function drops below its self-consistency threshold, giving a classical route, predating and complementary to the Duminil-Copin-Tassion approach, to sharpness of the phase transition and analyticity of the free energy in the high-temperature regime. It does not determine the exact critical temperature directly, only characterizing it implicitly through the inequality's self-consistency condition, and it applies specifically to ferromagnetic spin systems with a workable notion of finite separating surfaces; it does not transfer automatically to percolation, which uses combinatorially different, though philosophically related, inequalities. Typical failure: Iterating the Simon-Lieb inequality across many nested separating surfaces while implicitly assuming a geometric decay rate that has not actually been verified to be summable; turning the one-step recursive bound into exponential decay requires checking that the relevant generating function, summing G times J over the boundary, lies strictly below its self-consistency threshold, and this check is exactly where the difficulty of locating beta_c resides, so skipping it silently assumes the conclusion. Canonical reference: Simon, 1980, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Lieb, 1980, Communications in Mathematical Physics.","status":"unverified"}

$$|\sigma|+\#\sigma=p$$

and the set of permutations $\sigma\in S_p$ which saturate the triangular inequality

where $\gamma\in S_p$ is a full cycle, is in bijection with the set $NC(p)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:57:30.970423+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5c4af63f01fa043c0fc1620209c3d84310c587020dc89813c7e27378b396d249","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 5 of arXiv:2608.12451, '2608.12451'] Fix $q\geq2$.  For each $n$, let
$\big(N_{n,i,j}:1\leq i\leq m_n,  1\leq j\leq q\big)$
be independent random variables with $N_{n,i,j} \sim \Pois(\alpha_{n,i,j})$.  
Put

\noi
\begin{align}
 \beta_{n,i}
 :=\prod_{j=1}^q\alpha_{n,i,j},
 \quad
 X_n

 \prod_{j=1}^qN_{n,i,j},

 \delta_n
 :=
 \max_{\substack{1\leq i\leq m_n\\1\leq j\leq q}}
 \alpha_{n,i,j}.

If
\noi
\begin{align}
 \delta_n\to0

 \sum_{i=1}^{m_n}\beta_{n,i}\to\lambda>0,

 such that

\begin{align}
 \dTV\bigl( X_n, P_\lambda\bigr)
 \leq C_{q,\lambda} 
 \left(
 \left|\sum_{i=1}^{m_n}\beta_{n,i}-\lambda\right|
 +\sqrt{\delta_n}\right)
 
\end{align}
for all
sufficiently large $n$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Sample an offset $U\sim\mathrm{Unif}\{0,1,\dots,B-1\}$.
  \item Work in the rotated coordinates $t'=\phi_{U}^{-1}(t)$ and partition
        $\{1,\dots,n\}$ into consecutive blocks of size $B$
        (except possibly the final block).
  \item On each block, independently sample a uniform random permutation.
        Let $\Pi$ denote the resulting blockwise permutation in the rotated
        coordinates.
  \item Define the final permutation on the original labels by
        \[
          \rho(t)
          \;:=\;
          \phi_{U}\bigl(\Pi(\phi_{U}^{-1}(t))\bigr),
          \qquad t=1,\dots,n.
        \]
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X, B, mu) is a probability space and T is measure-preserving","the partition is finite or countable and consists of measurable sets","for the two-sided join T must be invertible"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:23.250796+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, entropy","id":"claim_5c8ad06c4539071020c4a52ccb50fab1a5b23a0b5f4b9e11e00d40a599f8d3a6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \\mathcal{B}, \\mu, T)$ be a measure-preserving system on a probability space with $T$ invertible (a measure-preserving automorphism). A finite or countable measurable partition $\\xi = \\{A_1, A_2, \\dots\\}$ of $X$ is a (two-sided) generator if the smallest $\\sigma$-algebra containing all the sets $T^{-n} A_i$, $n \\in \\mathbb{Z}$, coincides with $\\mathcal{B}$ up to $\\mu$-null sets; in join notation, $\\bigvee_{n=-\\infty}^{\\infty} T^{-n}\\xi = \\mathcal{B}$ (mod $\\mu$). For a non-invertible $T$ one uses the one-sided join $\\bigvee_{n=0}^{\\infty} T^{-n}\\xi$ and speaks of a one-sided (strong) generator. Why it matters: by the Kolmogorov-Sinai theorem, if $\\xi$ is a generator with finite entropy $H_\\mu(\\xi) < \\infty$ then the measure-theoretic entropy of the system equals the entropy relative to $\\xi$, $h_\\mu(T) = h_\\mu(T, \\xi)$; no supremum over partitions is needed. Existence (Krieger): an ergodic automorphism of a Lebesgue probability space with $h_\\mu(T) < \\log k$ has a generator with $k$ atoms; a system with infinite entropy has no finite generator. Sharp edges: a partition may generate for one invariant measure and not another; the join over $n \\geq 0$ alone need not generate for an automorphism (e.g. the time-zero partition of a two-sided shift does not generate one-sidedly); and 'generates' is a statement mod null sets, not about separating every pair of points, although separating points does imply generating (see the Walters entry).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:48:17.118405+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5cb1147c8aa67ab196c57532cee91f3cc261ff327b72d78a1aa0e6562baadaf5","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 9 of arXiv:2605.27212, '2605.27212'] Let \(P\) be a coordinate-replacement kernel as in
\eqref{eq:abstract-fibre-decomposition} on \(\mathcal X=S^N\), with invariant
set \(\Omega\), product law \(\mu\), stationary law \(\pi=\mu(\cdot\mid\Omega)\),
and good set \(G\subseteq\Omega\).  Assume \(\pi(G)>0\).  Suppose that the
following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}, leftmargin=*]
    \item There is a constant \(A<\infty\) such that, for every nonnegative
    \(F:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) with \(\supp(F)\subseteq G\),
    \[
        \Ent_\mu(F^2)\le A\cE_P^\mu(F,F).
    \]
    \item There are \(t_*\ge0\), an integer \(L\ge1\), and \(\eta\ge0\) such
    that, uniformly in \(x\in\Omega\) and all integers \(s\ge t_*\),
    \[
        \Prob_x(\exists\,u\in\{0,1,\ldots,L\}:X_{s+u}\notin G)\le\eta.
    \]
\end{enumerate}
Set
\begin{equation}
    t_{\mathrm{conf}}=2A\log(e+\log|\Omega|),
\end{equation}
and define
\begin{equation}
    \zeta=\Prob(\operatorname{Poi}(t_{\mathrm{conf}})>L),
    \qquad
    R=e^{-t_{\mathrm{conf}}/A}\log|\Omega|+A\frac{\pi(G^c)}{\pi(G)}.
\end{equation}
Then, for every \(x\in\Omega\) and every integer \(s\ge t_*\),
\begin{equation}
    \left\|\delta_xP^s e^{t_{\mathrm{conf}}(P-I)}-\pi\right\|_{\TV}
    \le 2(\eta+\zeta)+\sqrt{R/2}+\pi(G^c).
\end{equation}
Consequently, if
\begin{equation}
    2(\eta+\zeta)+\sqrt{R/2}+\pi(G^c)
    +\Prob(\operatorname{Poi}(2t_*)<t_*)\le\frac14,
\end{equation}
then the continuous-time chain satisfies
\[
    t_{\mathrm{mix}}^{\mathrm{cont}}(1/4)\le 2t_*+t_{\mathrm{conf}}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_1, ..., X_n are independent","E[f(X)^2] < infinity"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T04:29:12.249334+00:00","domain":"square-integrable functions of independent random variables","id":"claim_5cdbdd16495fed6ca6991e9a0c532c6baef597f5b399e0356a72a6b856f9a5c3","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent random variables and Z = f(X_1, ..., X_n) with E[Z^2] < infinity. Then sum_i E[Var_i Z] = (1/2) sum_i E[(Z - Z^(i))^2], and sum_i E[Var_i Z] - Var Z = sum over S with |S| >= 2 of (|S| - 1) ||f_S||^2, where Z = sum over subsets S of {1, ..., n} of f_S is the Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:52:32.333344+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5cebffbb64d5b1bda122261e55afae0fd9ff228e7522de7b592b418e505d7af0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition eq:motivationnormaltrace of arXiv:2609.03980, 'Decay Rates and Domain Dependence of a Coupled Wave-Heat System with Spatially Dependant H'] Let $\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain with unit outer normal $\nu.$
    We denote by ${\operatorname{tr}}_N$ the normal trace operator
  \begin{align*}
      {\operatorname{tr}}_N&:H^{\operatorname{div}}(\Omega) \to H^{-1/2}(\partial \Omega) = (H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega))',
  \end{align*}    
    which extends the normal component trace operator 
    $$H^1(\Omega)\to H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega), f\mapsto {\operatorname{tr}} (f) \cdot \nu.$$
    The normal trace operator ${\operatorname{tr}}_N$ is well-defined, bounded and surjective, see e.g. Lemma 20.2 in [tartar2007introduction].
 For $f\in C^1(\Omega)^n, \psi \in H^1(\Omega)$,  we note the identity 
 \begin{align} 
    \int_{\partial \Omega}  {\operatorname{tr}}(\psi) f\cdot \nu \;\mathrm{d} \sigma &= \int_\Omega {\operatorname{div}}(f\psi)\;\mathrm{d} x 
    \\&= \int_\Omega f\cdot \nabla \psi + {\operatorname{div}}(f)\psi \;\mathrm{d} x,\nonumber
 \end{align} which extends by density to 
\begin{align}
      \duality{{\operatorname{tr}}_N(f)}{{\operatorname{tr}} (\psi)} &= \int_\Omega f\cdot \nabla \psi + {\operatorname{div}}(f) \psi \;\mathrm{d} x 
  \end{align} for $f\in H^{\operatorname{div}}( \Omega),\psi \in H^{1}( \Omega).$
      Here and in the following, we understand that if $\Omega$ is a one-dimensional domain and $f$ is some function defined on $\partial\Omega$, then $$\int_{\partial\Omega} f\cdot \nu\;\mathrm{d}\sigma = f\left(\sup_{x\in \Omega} x\right)-f\left(\inf_{x\in \Omega} x\right) ~\textnormal{ and }~\int_\Gamma f\cdot \nu \;\mathrm{d}\sigma = \int_{\partial\Omega} \mathds{1}_\Gamma f\cdot \nu \;\mathrm{d}\sigma. $$","status":"unverified"}
