 \le t_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon)
 \le(2+\beta)\log_{\theta+1}n+o(\log n).
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:43:55.659779+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_60ee9de8257d168e39392635ad5fc0fb7bb851ff59a37c588373302e702d8924","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def_Martingale_solution of arXiv:2604.07497, 'The Three-Dimensional Stochastic EMHD System: Local Well-Posedness and Maximal Pathwise So'] For $T > 0$, let $B_0 \in L^2(\Omega; H^s)$ be an ${\mathcal F}_0$-measurable $H^s$-valued random variable. \begin{enumerate}
\item $\widetilde{{\mathcal S}} = \bigl(\widetilde{\Omega}, \widetilde{{\mathcal F}}, \widetilde{{\mathbb F}}, \widetilde{{\mathbb P}} \bigr)$ is a stochastic basis such that $\widetilde{{\mathbb W}}$ is an $\widetilde{{\mathbb F}}$-adapted cylindrical Brownian motion with components $\{\widetilde{W}^k\}_{k \ge 1}$, \\

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:52:32.333436+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_60fcdebf44f7289647883a134f1d1e057e3090f40a3b289872a5566c397a7415","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:restrictedtraceoperators of arXiv:2609.03980, 'Decay Rates and Domain Dependence of a Coupled Wave-Heat System with Spatially Dependant H'] Let $\Gamma$ be a relatively open subset of the boundary $\partial \Omega$ of some bounded Lipschitz domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$.
 
 \begin{enumerate}
     \item  The restriction of ${\operatorname{tr}}(f)$ to $\Gamma$ for $f\in H^1(\Omega)$ induces the restricted trace operator 
    $${\operatorname{tr}}^{\Gamma}:H^1(\Omega)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma), f\mapsto {\operatorname{tr}}(f)|_{\Gamma},$$
    which is again bounded and surjective, see e.g.  Proposition 1.2.60 in [Meinlschmidt].
    \item We define the Lions-Magenes space $H^{1/2}_{0}(\Gamma)$ as the subspace of functions $f\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, for which the extension by zero $\Tilde{f}$ to $\partial\Omega$ is again an element of $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$. If $n=1$, one clearly has $H^{1/2}_{0}(\Gamma) = H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$. If $n\geq 2$, then $H^{1/2}_{0}(\Gamma)$ is an intrinsic, i.e., independent of $\partial\Omega$, Hilbert space when equipped with the norm
    \begin{align*}
        \|f\|_{H^{1/2}_{0}(\Gamma)}  \coloneq  \left(\|f\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)} +\int_\Gamma  \frac{|u(x)|^2}{\dist(x,\partial \Gamma)} \;\mathrm{d} x\right)^{1/2},
    \end{align*} see e.g.\ Chapter~33 in [tartar2007introduction].
    This norm is equivalent to the $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$-norm of the zero extension $\Tilde{f}$.
    Additionally, denote by $H^{-1/2}_{0}(\Gamma)$ the dual space of $H^{1/2}_{0}(\Gamma)$.
    \item We define the restricted normal trace operator
    $${\operatorname{tr}}^{\Gamma}_N:H^{\operatorname{div}}(\Omega)\to H^{-1/2}_{0}(\Gamma), f\mapsto \left( H^{1/2}_{0}(\Gamma)\to \mathbb{C}, g\mapsto
    \duality{{\operatorname{tr}}_N(f)}{\Tilde{g}}\right),$$ where 
    $\Tilde{g}$ denotes the extension by zero to $\partial\Omega$ of an element $g\in H^{1/2}_{0}(\Gamma)$.
    
    The restricted normal trace operator ${\operatorname{tr}}^{\Gamma}_N:H^{\operatorname{div}}(\Omega)\to H^{-1/2}_{0}(\Gamma)$ is well-defined, bounded and surjective, see Lemma~(lem:normaltracesurj of the paper).
    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:11:11.696523+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_60fd8a2a114e1494985da199b55e960f57466fdc983c5520b03f39cd28f13559","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:first-exit of arXiv:2609.00645, 'Global persistence of nearly radial concentrated vortices in a bounded domain'] Let $V\subset\mathbb R^m$ be bounded and open, and suppose that
$w\in C(\overline V)$ has a unique minimum point
$\mathbf p_*\in V$ on $\overline V$.  Let
$d:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous, and let $S$ be a set-valued
map from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R^m$ with nonempty compact values.  Fix
$\delta>0$.  Then there exist $\eta_*,r_*>0$, depending only on $V,w,\delta$,
with the following property.

Assume that $S$ is upper semicontinuous\footnote{As in
(lem:centers of the paper)(vi), this means that, for every $t_0\in\mathbb R$ and every open
set $O\subset\mathbb R^m$ with $S(t_0)\subset O$, there exists $\sigma>0$ such that
$S(t)\subset O$ whenever $|t-t_0|<\sigma$.} and that
\[
  \operatorname{diam}S(t)\leq r_*
  \quad\text{whenever }d(t)\leq\delta,
\]
and that
\begin{equation}
  d(t)+\sup_{\mathbf b\in S(t)}[w(\mathbf b)-w(\mathbf p_*)]
  \leq\eta_*
\end{equation}
whenever $S(t)\subset\overline V$ and $d(t)\leq\delta$.

{"assumptions":["h is a Gaussian free field with Dirichlet (or otherwise precisely specified) boundary conditions on domain D","U is a deterministic, or at least suitably measurable stopping-domain, subdomain of D","the Green's function and harmonic measure for D and U are well defined, requiring sufficient domain regularity","correct identification of phi_U as harmonic in U with boundary values equal to h on the boundary of U"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.988093+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_611d06babfa0bac3e6ad00051e94ec2a9160b2c2c47e76bdc0ac9037b7eb263d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Let h be a (discrete or continuum) Gaussian free field on a domain D with Dirichlet boundary conditions, and let U be a deterministic subdomain of D. The Gibbs-Markov (domain Markov) property states that h decomposes as h = h_U + phi_U, where h_U is a zero-boundary Gaussian free field on U, phi_U is the harmonic extension into U of the values of h on the boundary of U, h_U and phi_U are independent of each other, and phi_U is measurable with respect to the sigma-field generated by h restricted to the complement of U. This is the discrete and continuum analogue of the strong Markov property for Brownian motion and harmonic functions, and it is the fundamental tool enabling induction-on-scale arguments, the theory of local sets, and the construction of conformally invariant objects such as Liouville quantum gravity from the field. It does not hold for general non-Gibbsian or non-Gaussian log-correlated fields without separate verification, and it requires exact specification of the domain and boundary conditions, since the decomposition depends on the harmonic extension operator for the particular pair (D,U) being used. Typical failure: Applying the plain Gibbs-Markov decomposition with U chosen depending on the field h itself, such as a random subdomain determined by a level set or an exploration process, without checking that U is a valid stopping domain for the field's filtration; naively random domains destroy the independence between h_U and phi_U, and the correct fix requires the more delicate theory of local sets developed by Schramm and Sheffield, not the plain domain Markov property. {"assumptions":["All explicit definitions in proofs/BOUNDED_RELU_PAIRED.md","Even width; independent Gaussian hidden-weight pairs with equal hidden weights and opposite heads +/-nu, nu fixed in (0,1]; neurons are not iid","Unit-norm centered ReLU teacher with a nonzero interaction Walsh coefficient on the support","Noise standard deviation c_e=e^2/sqrt((1+e^2+e^4)(1+e^2)) tends to zero; n=4 stratified training and uniform test support","Risk averaged over sixteen independent label-noise sign patterns; GD step 1/2; width limit precedes feature-scale limit"],"created_at":"2026-10-22T00:34:14.190364+00:00","domain":"learning theory","id":"claim_6150b2543bd28a2853e880d5bd25f8624c1e1b6cb15383b4cea07167bb4daeae","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"# Unit-norm nonlinear ReLU teacher with paired initialization

T267 / Target 1 / C010 / proof draft (unaudited); novelty unestablished.

This removes the diverging teacher norm in C009, at the price of paired
initialization and noise that shrinks with the signal. It is a restricted
four-point, stratified-design, noise-averaged theorem. It does not establish
the generic iid Gaussian-input target or a fixed-positive-noise result.
The hardest remaining target step is sign-level population-risk control
for a genuinely sampled nonlinear model beyond this finite-support
infinite-width construction.

## Statement

Fix nu in (0,1]. For 0<e<1/4 let D=1+e^2+e^4 and use the same four inputs
x_(s,t)=(1,e s,e^2 t)/sqrt(D), s,t in {-1,1}. Training contains each once;
the test law is uniform on these four points. Let

u_e=(0,e,1)/sqrt(1+e^2),
c_e=e^2/[sqrt(D)*sqrt(1+e^2)], alpha_e=c_e/2,
g_e(x)=ReLU(u_e.x)-E_X ReLU(u_e.X).

The vector u_e has norm one. On this support u_e.x=c_e(s+t), so

g_e(x_(s,t))=alpha_e(s+t+st).

Thus the teacher is genuinely nonlinear even when restricted to the
support: no affine function of x has a nonzero st Walsh coefficient.
The centering constant is the population mean c_e/2. Labels are g_e(x_i)
plus independent equiprobable noise +/-c_e, so the noise standard deviation
is c_e, not a fixed positive constant as e decreases.

Take even width m=2N and initialize each independent pair by
w_(2j-1)=w_(2j)=W_j iid N(0,I_3),
a_(2j-1)=nu, a_(2j)=-nu.
Pairs are independent; the individual neurons are NOT iid. Initially f=0
exactly. Train both layers of every neuron by simultaneous GD at step 1/2,
loss ||f(X)-y||^2/(2n), n=4, with f=m^(-1/2) sum a ReLU(w.x) and gate
convention 1_{z>0}. No symmetry is imposed after initialization.

Let Q_(m,e)(k) be clean population squared risk, averaged over the sixteen
training-label-noise patterns, conditional on initialization. Let b_h be
C009's rates for the full initial tangent kernel h_nu=k+nu^2 g1, with mode
indices 0,1,2,12. Set

k0=ceil(e^(-1/2)), k1=floor(log(2)/b1),
k2=ceil(e^(-3/2)), k3=floor(log(2)/b2),
B=log[b1/(b2+b12)].

In the iterated limit m=2N->infinity first, then e->0, the probability of
failure of the strict witnesses

Q(k0)>Q(k1)<Q(k2)>Q(k3)

tends to zero. More precisely the four risks divided by alpha_e^2 converge
in probability, in that iterated sense, to 4,7/2,4,3.
For every fixed delta>0, every maximizer k_peak on the integer interval
I_e=[floor((B-1)/b1),ceil((B+1)/b1)] is interior and satisfies
|b1 k_peak-B|<delta with probability tending to one in the same iterated
sense. Consequently

k_peak ~ (4*pi/nu^2) e^(-1) log(1/e).

This localizes a central local peak, not a global maximum or all extrema.

## 1. Teacher identity and exact initialization

ReLU(s+t) takes values 2,0,0,0, whose mean is 1/2. Its centered version is
(s+t+st)/2. The unit norm and displayed teacher identity follow directly.
The nonzero interaction coefficient rules out an affine teacher on the
four inputs, even though two projections lie exactly at the teacher's
ReLU kink. No differentiability of the teacher is used in training.

Each pair has exactly cancelling outputs. Its two readout-Jacobian Gram
summands are identical. Its two hidden-Jacobian Gram summands are also
identical because their readout factors are squared. Dividing by m=2N
therefore gives the same expected full kernel as in C009:

C_(nu,e)(i,l)=[k(x_i.x_l)+nu^2 g1(x_i.x_l)]/4.

Strong laws apply to the N independent pairs. No independent-neuron
concentration or centered independent readout-sign argument is needed.

## 2. Transfer from the actual nonlinear GD

Here we specify why C009 Section 3 applies despite correlated pairs.
For e<1/4, c_e<e^2<1/16. The largest absolute teacher value is 3c_e/2;
the largest label magnitude is at most 5c_e/2<5/32. Thus ||y||<5/16<2.
The actual initial output is identically zero; use M=0 and R_0=2 in the
deterministic finite-horizon recurrences of C009 Section 3. Those bounds
are neuronwise and use no independence. They hold separately for both
members of every pair, even after their hidden weights separate.

The empirical mean of initial squared hidden norms converges almost surely
to 3 by the pairwise strong law. The weighted initial gate-band mass is
now exactly the mean over N independent W_j of
(1+||W_j||)^2 1{min_i|W_j.x_i| <= D_* (1+||W_j||)/sqrt(2N)}.
It tends to zero by the same rational-band strong-law and dominated-
convergence argument as C009. The initial kernel converges entrywise to
C by the pairwise strong law. These are the only probabilistic inputs to
the instantaneous-kernel and exact discrete-step remainder bounds in C009.
Their finite-horizon telescoping proof therefore gives

max_(k<=T) ||f_actual(k)-f_frozen(k)|| -> 0 in probability

for every fixed e,nu,T, uniformly over all sixteen noise patterns. The
frozen iteration starts at zero exactly. Here and below T may depend on e;
width tends to infinity separately for each fixed e. This does not claim a
uniform feature-scale rate or a feasible numerical width.

## 3. Risk margins

All three nonconstant teacher Walsh coefficients are alpha=alpha_e.
Independent +/-c_e label noise has Walsh variances c_e^2/4=alpha^2.
Parseval and the zero initial prediction give the exact frozen risk

Q_e^0(k)/alpha^2 = (1-q0^k)^2
                 + sum_(h=1,2,12) [q_h^(2k)+(1-q_h^k)^2],
q_h=exp(-b_h).

C009 Section 2 supplies b1~nu^2 e/(4pi), b2~nu^2 e^2/(8pi),
b12/b2->1, and b0 bounded away from zero. At k0 all nonconstant modes
remain unlearned, giving 1+1+1+1=4. At k1 the fast component has q1->1/2
and the two slow components remain at one, giving 1+1/2+1+1=7/2.
At k2 the fast component has q1->0 while slow components remain at one,
giving 4. At k3 both slow components have q->1/2, giving 1+1+1/2+1/2=3.
The three strict limiting margins are 1/2,1/2,1. For fixed e, alpha>0 and
the finite-horizon transfer changes risk by o_P(1), hence by o_P(alpha^2)
as width grows; division by a fixed positive alpha^2 is legitimate.
Then let e decrease. This proves the four strict actual-risk witnesses.

## 4. Central peak

Interpolate the frozen curve continuously and put z=(B+s)/b1 with
B=log[b1/(b2+b12)]. Uniformly for s in compact intervals,

(Q_e^0)'(z)/[2 alpha^2 (b2+b12)] -> exp(-s)-1,
(Q_e^0)''(z)/[2 alpha^2 b1 (b2+b12)] -> -exp(-s).

Indeed each nonconstant mode contributes 2 alpha^2 b_h q_h(1-2q_h).
The fast term contributes exp(-s); its quadratic correction is
O((b2+b12)/b1). The two slow terms contribute -b2/(b2+b12) and
-b12/(b2+b12), up to errors O(((b2+b12)/b1) B). The constant-mode
term and its derivatives vanish faster than any polynomial of e.
The same estimates after one further differentiation give the stated
second derivative. Thus the frozen central peak has scaled coordinate
s_e->0 and a strict value gap away from any fixed delta neighborhood,
of order alpha^2 (b2+b12)/b1, by integrating the derivative on [-1,1].
The grid spacing b1 tends to zero, so discrete maximizers obey the same
localization. When delta>=1, the conclusion follows from any smaller
positive delta, and interval endpoints are excluded as well.

For each fixed e the interval is finite and its positive peak gap is a
fixed positive number. Section 2 therefore transfers the maximizer
localization to the actual risk with probability tending to one as width
grows. No random initial-output perturbation occurs. Finally
b1/(b2+b12)~1/e and b1~nu^2 e/(4pi) give the peak asymptotic.

## Scope and dependencies

This proof depends on the unaudited deterministic bounds and Gaussian
kernel asymptotics in C009, not on an independent audit or a floating-point
fit. Pair cancellation is only an initial condition, not frozen weights.
The centering offset is part of the single-index link ReLU(z)-c_e/2.
The teacher has uniformly unit norm and is nonlinear on the support;
its variation and the label-noise standard deviation both vanish as e^2.
The design remains stratified, finite support, with every test input in
training, and risk averages over labels. No fixed-noise, iid-design,
macroscopic feature-learning, full-target or novelty claim is made.
Primary kernel source: Heckel--Yilmaz arXiv:2007.10099v2 Section 3 K1/K2.
The existence of two noise thresholds in Stephenson--Lee 2108.12006 is not
used to infer that this model has the same noise window.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.359970+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6164626031dbe84f0438c1f9ea9bb51a2b7ef90083e022c246bbf50fd4cd46c1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 250 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Suppose the random vector $\bX$ in $\R^N$ is \emph{subgaussian with variance proxy $\sigma^2$}, meaning that $(\theta,\bX)$ is subgaussian with variance proxy $\sigma^2$ for all $\theta$ in the unit ball $B_N\subset\R^N$. Then
    \[
    \P\bigg(\frac{\|\bX\|}{N^{1/2}} \ge t\bigg)
    \le \exp\bigg\{ -\frac{Nt^2}{16\sigma^2} \bigg\}
    \]
provided $t\ge 6\sigma$. It follows that
$\E(\|\bX\|^p) \le  C_p \sigma^p N^{p/2}$
where $C_p$ is a constant depending only on $p$.

\begin{proof}
To bound the norm of a random vector $\bX$ in $\R^N$, the standard argument is to let $N_{1/2}$ be a $1/2$-net of the unit ball $B\subset \R^N$, and note that
    \begin{align*}
    \|\bX\|
    &= \sup \Big\{
    (\theta,\bX) : \theta\in B\Big\}
    \le 
    \sup\bigg\{
    (\theta_1+\theta_2,\bX):
    \theta_1\in N_{1/2},
    \theta_2\in \frac12 B\bigg\} \\
    &\le
    \sup\Big\{(\theta,\bX) :\theta\in N_{1/2}\Big\}
    + \frac{\|\bX\|}{2}
    \equiv S + \frac{\|\bX\|}{2} \,.
    \end{align*}
Rearranging the above gives
    \[\|\bX\|
    \le 2\sup\Big\{(\theta,\bX) :\theta\in N_{1/2}\Big\}
    = 2S\,.
    \]
We can arrange for $|N_{1/2}| \le 6^N$. If $(\theta,\bX)$ is subgaussian with variance proxy $\sigma^2$ for all $\theta\in B_N$, then a union bound over the net $N_{1/2}$ gives
    \beq
    \P\bigg(\frac{\|\bX\|}{N^{1/2}} \ge 2t\bigg)
    \le \P(S \ge N^{1/2} t)
    \le 6^N 
    \exp\bigg\{ -\frac{Nt^2}{2\sigma^2}\bigg\}
    \le \exp\bigg\{ -\frac{Nt^2}{4\sigma^2}\bigg\}\,,
    \eeq
where the last bound holds provided
$t\ge 3\sigma$. Integrating (similarly to \eqref{e:subgaus.mmt}) gives the moment bound
    \beq
    \frac{\E[ \|\bX\|^p]}{N^{p/2}}
    \le
    \frac{2^p \E(S^p)}{N^{p/2}}
    \le (6\sigma)^p
    +2^p \int_{3\sigma}^\infty
    pt^{p-1}
    \exp\bigg\{ -\frac{Nt^2}{4\sigma^2}\bigg\}\, dt
    \le C_p \sigma^p
    \eeq
for a constant $C_p$ depending only on $p$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:25:44.985953+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_61767eec5c2be7bb17b7a16bcf686b6fb332e4d191a3c19f638bb079a04ab249","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 6 (Threshold Isolation Principle) of arXiv:2605.11783, 'Stability of Compensated Jump Integrals under Quadratic Variation Convergence'] Let $X$ and $\{X^n\}_{n\ge1}$ be c\`adl\`ag processes on $[0,t]$ such that
\[
[X^n-X]_t \to 0
\qquad \text{in probability}.
\]
Fix $r>0$, and for each $k\ge1$ define
\[
\delta(k,r):=\frac{r}{2^{k+2}},
\qquad
L(r,k):=r\Bigl(1-\frac{3}{2^{k+2}}\Bigr),
\]
and
\[
A_k(r)
:=
\Bigl\{
\omega:
\bigl||\Delta X_s(\omega)|-L(r,k)\bigr|>\delta(k,r)
\text{ for all } s\le t
\Bigr\}.
\]
Then
\[
\mathbb P\Bigl(\bigcup_{k\ge1}A_k(r)\Bigr)=1.
\]

Moreover, for each fixed $k\ge1$, if we define
\[
B_n(k,r)
:=
\Bigl\{
\sup_{s\le t}|\Delta(X^n-X)_s|<\delta(k,r)
\Bigr\},
\]
then
$
\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P\bigl(B_n(k,r)\bigr)=1.
$
On the event $A_k(r)\cap B_n(k,r)$, the classification of jumps relative to the threshold
$L(r,k)$ is preserved, i.e.
\[
|\Delta X_s|\le L(r,k)-\delta(k,r)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
|\Delta X^n_s|<L(r,k),
\]
and
\[
|\Delta X_s|\ge L(r,k)+\delta(k,r)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
|\Delta X^n_s|>L(r,k),
\]
for all $s\le t$.

In particular, on $A_k(r)\cap B_n(k,r)$,
\[
1_{\{|\Delta X^n_s|\le L(r,k)\}}
\le
1_{\{|\Delta X_s|\le L(r,k)\}}
\qquad \text{for all } s\le t,
\]
and therefore
\[
\sum_{s\le t} (\Delta X^n_s)^2 1_{\{|\Delta X^n_s|\le L(r,k)\}}
\le
2[X^n-X]_t
+
2\sum_{s\le t} (\Delta X_s)^2 1_{\{|\Delta X_s|\le L(r,k)\}}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:06:18.037218+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_61831ba8b0bd604dcf921075e9e7dc6365fec6a11310a3a8b5250c641ec5eede","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 20 (Exact form and zero set of $F_3$) of arXiv:2608.15805, 'Spectral duality structures and the Fisher--Rao geometry of reset distributions'] Assume the spectral scalars are square-integrable,
$f_\nu\in L^2(0,1)$. \textup{(}This is automatic in any resolvent
realisation, where they are bounded --- for the biased walk
$f_\nu(\gamma)=(1-\gamma)/(1-\lambda_\nu(1-\gamma))$ with
$|\lambda_\nu|<1$ --- but it does not follow from \textup{(S2)},
which gives analyticity only on the \emph{open} interval and so
does not by itself make $F_3$ finite.\textup{)}
Let $\pi^\ast\in\Sigma$ be the fixed reference distribution of
Section~\ref{subsec:orientation} --- reset-neutrality of $\pi^\ast$ is
what gives $\langle\pi^\ast,\mathbf n_\nu\rangle=0$, and without it the
zero set below is a translate of $\Sigma$ rather than $\Sigma$
itself. Let $a_\nu(\pi)=\langle\pi-\pi^\ast,\mathbf n_\nu\rangle$ and let
$G_{\nu\nu'}=\int_0^1 f_\nu(\gamma)f_{\nu'}(\gamma)\,d\gamma$ be
the Gram matrix of the spectral scalars. Then
\[
F_3(\pi)=\mathbf a(\pi)^{\!\top} G\,\mathbf a(\pi),
\]
a quadratic form in the affine coordinates $\mathbf a(\pi)$, with
$G$ positive definite by the linear independence of the $f_\nu$
\textup{(S2)}. Consequently
\[
F_3(\pi)\ge0,\qquad F_3(\pi)=0\iff\pi\in\Sigma:
\]
the functional detects the separatrix exactly.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:00:30.494454+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_618375d0d2f4d18935c1947d5e00865a7d8ff9303f56f13579b46fb59145e749","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 23 (Middle side of a double hive) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] \lab{prop:middle}
Let
\[
        \alpha=\spec(A),\qquad
        \beta=\spec(B),\qquad
        \eta=\spec(E),\qquad
        \phi=\spec(F)
\]
belong to \(\Spec_n^\circ\), and assume the trace compatibility condition
\[
        \sum_i\alpha_i+\sum_i\beta_i+\sum_i\eta_i - \sum_i\phi_i=0 .
\]
Let \(U_1,U_2,U_3,U_4\) be independent Haar-distributed unitary matrices and set
\[
        S=U_1AU_1^*+U_2BU_2^*,
        \qquad
        T=U_3EU_3^*-U_4FU_4^* .
\]
For \(\nu\in\Spec_n\), write
\[
        \nu^\vee=(-\nu_n,\ldots,-\nu_1),
\]
so that \(\nu^\vee=\spec(-X)\) whenever \(\nu=\spec(X)\).
Suppose that the double hive polytope
\[
        \mathcal D(\alpha,\beta,\eta,\phi^\vee)
        :=
        \bigcup_{\nu\in\Spec_n}
        H_n(\alpha,\beta;\nu)
        \times
        H_n(\eta,\phi^\vee;\nu^\vee)
\]
is full dimensional, where the two hives are glued along the common side with values
\(\nu\) on the first hive and \(\nu^\vee\) on the second. 
 If a double hive is
sampled from normalized Lebesgue measure on
\(\mathcal D(\alpha,\beta,\eta,\phi^\vee)\), then its middle side has the same
distribution as the regular conditional distribution of
\[
        \spec(S)
        =
        \spec(U_1AU_1^*+U_2BU_2^*)
\]
given the matrix equation
\[
        S+T=0 .
\]
Equivalently,
\[
        \spec(\text{middle side})
        \stackrel{d}{=}
        \spec(U_1AU_1^*+U_2BU_2^*)
        \,\big|\,
        U_1AU_1^*+U_2BU_2^*
        +U_3EU_3^*-U_4FU_4^*=0 .
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:43:00.033662+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_61a9cc3e1cd2b8c09bc3e114ec0504bfbbc73fdf2c8ee71141d9a466cd8265c7","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 1 of arXiv:2609.00739, '2609.00739'] Let $\mathcal S\subset\overline\Omega$ be countably $1$-rectifiable and let
$\lambda=\vartheta\,\cH^1\llcorner\mathcal S$.  A point
$p\in\mathcal S\cap\partial\Omega$ is a \emph{finite-type boundary junction
of $(\mathcal S,\lambda)$} if there are a neighborhood $U$ of $p$ and
finitely many regular embedded $C^1$ half-arcs
$\gamma_\ell:[0,r_\ell)\to\overline\Omega$ such that
$\gamma_\ell(0)=p$, the open arcs are pairwise disjoint, and
\[
 \mathcal S\cap U=\bigcup_\ell\gamma_\ell([0,r_\ell));
\]
thus no residual branch or weight is present in $U$.
The outgoing tangent is
$\tau_\ell:=\frac{\gamma_\ell'(0)}{\abs{\gamma_\ell'(0)}}$.  A
\emph{boundary-supported regular arc} is an open $C^1$ subarc of
$\mathcal S\cap\partial\Omega$ that has a neighborhood containing no other branch
of $\mathcal S$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Random walk in i.i.d. uniformly elliptic environment on Z^d, d >= 2","Regeneration structure of Sznitman-Zerner"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T15:09:50+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_61c8a9949e251c0a83a02320952cc97ce2592dcaeb1a540267753dd9e4a27639","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"PRIVATE REDUCTION, author-recorded. Under (UE) a trap of diameter r holds the walk at most exponentially long in r, so sub-ballistic behaviour needs polynomially rare traps of logarithmic size along the path, which i.i.d. environments do allow; the question is whether the tail P(tau_1 > n) can be as heavy as n^{-1+eps}. Let $\tau$ be any stopping time defined on the collection of variables $X_0,X_1,\ldots$ with $\EE\,\tau<\infty$, and let
\[
    \mathcal{A}_L=(\tau_j^L)_{j=1}^{\pi(1)-1},
    \qquad
    \mathcal{A}_R=(\tau_j^R)_{j=1}^{k-\pi(1)}
\]
be randomized online embedding algorithms for $L(\pi)$ and $R(\pi)$, respectively, with finite expected runtime. There is a randomized online embedding algorithm $\mathcal{A}=(\tau_j)_{j=1}^k$ for $\pi$ such that
\[
    \EE\tau_k
    =

    +

    \EE\,\Big(\frac{1}{1-X_\tau}\Big)\EE\,T_{\mathcal{A}_R}.
\]
If one of $L(\pi)$ and $R(\pi)$ is empty, the corresponding algorithm and term are omitted. In particular, for every subtree $S$ of $\mathcal{T}_\pi$, there is a recursive interval algorithm $\mathcal{A}_S^*$ with

\]

There exists a unique (up to a deterministic factor) collection of measurable functions $\Gamma^D \mapsto \rform{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^D}$ for each simply connected domain $D \subseteq \C$ where each $\rform{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^D} = ((\rformres{k}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^D}, \rfdomainres{\Upsilon_k}{\Gamma^D}))_{k \in \N}$ is a collection of resistance forms with the following properties. There is a further collection of resistance forms $((\rformres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^D}, \rfdomainres{V}{\Gamma^D}))_{V \in \metregions}$ such that the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[I.]
 \item For each $k \in \N$ we have that $(\rformres{k}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^D}, \rfdomainres{\Upsilon_k}{\Gamma^D})$ is a local, regular resistance form on $\Upsilon_k$. Its associated resistance metric $\rmetres{k}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^D}$ is topologically equivalent to $\dpathY[\Upsilon_k]$.
 \item Let $V_1,\ldots,V_n \in \metregions[k]$, $n \in \N$, such that $V_i \cap V_j = \emptyset$ for $i \neq j$ and $\bigcup_i \ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k = \Upsilon_k$. Then

  \text{and}\quad
  \rformres{k}{f}{f}{\Gamma^D} &= \sum_i \rformres{V_i}{f|_{\ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k}}{f|_{\ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k}}{\Gamma^D} .
 \end{align*}
\item If $V,V' \in \metregions[k]$, $V \subseteq V'$, and $f\colon \ol{V'} \cap \Upsilon_k \to \R$ is a continuous function that is constant on each $\dpathY$-connected component of $\ol{V'} \cap \Upsilon_k \setminus \ol{V}$, then

 & f \in \rfdomainres{V'}{\Gamma^D} \text{ if and only if } f|_{\ol{V} \cap \Upsilon_k} \in \rfdomainres{V}{\Gamma^D} \\
 \text{and}\quad & \rformres{V'}{f}{f}{\Gamma^D} = \rformres{V}{f}{f}{\Gamma^D} .
\end{align*}
 \item For each open set $U \subseteq \C$, the collection of forms $(\rformres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^D})_{V \in \metregions[U]}$ is a.s.\ a measurable function of $\Gamma^D|_U$ that does not depend on the choice of $D$.

\[ \rform{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^D} = \rform{T_{z}\cdot}{T_{z}\cdot}{\Gamma^D+z} \quad\text{a.s.,} \]
where $T_{z} f = f(\cdot -z)$ denotes translation by $z$.
\item There exists a constant $\resexp > 0$ so that the following holds. For each simply connected domain $D \subseteq \C$ and $\lambda > 0$, we have
\[ \rform{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^D} = \lambda^{\resexp}\rform{S_{\lambda}\cdot}{S_{\lambda}\cdot}{\lambda\Gamma^D} \quad\text{a.s.,} \]
where $S_{\lambda} f = f(\lambda^{-1}\cdot)$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:49:15.414168+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_61ee07d8214cde75f8b20dffa3e3e0d328e61dde1e1359faa0fca1a615574db8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2608.27904, 'Instantons, indefinite 4-manifolds, and Dehn surgery'] A \textit{stratified-smooth manifold} $(P,\Delta)$ (or simply $P$) of dimension $n$ is the following data: 
	\begin{itemize}
		\item a partially ordered set $\Delta$ equipped with a dimension function $d: \Delta \to \mathbb N$ with maximum value $n$, 
		\item a compact topological space $P$ equipped with a partition into locally-closed subsets $P_\sigma$ for $\sigma \in \Delta$, satisfying $\overline P_\sigma = \bigcup_{\tau \le \sigma} P_\tau$, 
		\item the structure on each stratum $P_\sigma$ of a smooth manifold of dimension $d(\sigma)$.
	\end{itemize}
	We demand that the following {\it locally standard} hypothesis holds: for each $p \in P_\sigma$, there exists an isomorphism of posets $\bar \phi: \Delta_{\ge \sigma} \cong \{0,1\}^k$ for some integer $k$. This isomorphism may be chosen so that for an appropriate neighborhood $p \in U \subset P$, there exists a homeomorphism $\phi: U \to [0,\infty)^k \times \mathbb R^{n-k}$ so that $\phi$ sends the stratum $P_\tau$ onto the stratum corresponding to $\bar \phi(\tau)$. Finally, we demand that $\phi$ is a diffeomorphism on each stratum.
	
	A \textit{stratified-smooth $SO(3)$-manifold} is a stratified-smooth manifold $P$ equipped with a continuous $SO(3)$-action, for which each $P_\sigma$ is $SO(3)$-invariant, and the action is smooth on each stratum.

	A \textit{diffeomorphism} of stratified-smooth manifolds $(\phi,\bar \phi): (P,\Delta)\to (P',\Delta')$  is the pair of an isomorphism of partially-ordered sets 
	$\bar \phi:\Delta \to \Delta'$ and a homeomorphism $\phi:P\to P'$ that restricts to a diffeomorphism from $P_\sigma$ to $P'_{\bar \phi(\sigma)}$ for each 
	$\sigma\in \Delta$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726454+00:00","domain":"hyperbolic systems of partial differential equations","id":"claim_61f88f542a4ccb5b73d71ec83ca39d41269940f02589236c6fbe2be28d174a87","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: in ∂_t u + Σ_j A_j ∂_j u = 0 the estimate ‖u(t)‖_{L²} ≤ e^{Kt}‖u(0)‖_{L²} comes from the Hermitian symmetry of the A_j (which makes u* A_j ∂_j u an exact divergence up to lower order). Real eigenvalues alone (weak hyperbolicity) are not enough. Concrete counterexample in n = 1, m = 2: take A = [[0,1],[0,0]], a Jordan block whose only eigenvalue is 0 (real, so the system is weakly hyperbolic) but which is not symmetrizable. The system ∂_t u1 + ∂_x u2 = 0, ∂_t u2 = 0 with data (f,g) has the solution u2(t,x) = g(x), u1(t,x) = f(x) − t g'(x). So ‖u(t)‖_{L²} ≥ t‖g'‖_{L²} − ‖f‖_{L²}, which is not bounded by any function of t times ‖(f,g)‖_{L²}: one derivative is lost per unit time, and the Cauchy problem is ill-posed in L² (and in every H^s). Consequences for auditing: (i) hyperbolicity claims must say symmetric, symmetrizable or strictly hyperbolic, never merely 'real eigenvalues'; (ii) the constant K in the energy estimate depends on sup|Σ_j ∂_j A_j| and sup|B|, so the argument needs the coefficients to be differentiable in x with bounded derivative — Lipschitz in x is enough (the derivative then exists a.e. and is bounded), but mere continuity is not, and for merely continuous, non-Lipschitz coefficients well-posedness can genuinely fail with a loss of derivatives; (iii) after an approximate symmetrization, the estimate holds with the symmetrizer's constants, not with 1.","status":"unverified"}

K^r), then mu_n converges in distribution to mu: the law of a random probability measure is determined by its moment measures under such a condition, and tightness is automatic on the compact scaling window. Integrated super-Brownian excursion satisfies the condition. {"assumptions":["N is a compact interval or the circle S^1 and f: N -> N is C^2 (not merely C^1)","Lambda is compact and forward invariant, f(Lambda) contained in Lambda","Lambda contains no critical point of f","every periodic point of f that lies in Lambda is hyperbolic repelling (no attracting or neutral periodic point in Lambda)","if N is the circle, f has at least one periodic point (excludes homeomorphisms of irrational rotation number, where the conclusion fails)"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:01:13.770157+00:00","domain":"one-dimensional real dynamics, hyperbolicity, interval and circle maps","id":"claim_626a47d09abfde2732f5b51624f4b49b88dc93b649aef5efde91c164e135a82b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Setting: $N$ is a compact interval or the circle $S^1$, and $f: N \to N$ is a $C^2$ map. Write $\mathrm{Crit}(f) = \{x : Df(x) = 0\}$ for the critical set. A periodic point $p$ of period $k$ is hyperbolic repelling if $|Df^k(p)| > 1$.

Theorem (Mañé, 1985). Let $\Lambda \subset N$ be a compact set which is forward invariant ($f(\Lambda) \subset \Lambda$) and such that
  (i) $\Lambda$ contains no critical point of $f$, and
  (ii) every periodic point of $f$ lying in $\Lambda$ is hyperbolic repelling (so $\Lambda$ contains no attracting and no neutral / indifferent periodic point);
  (iii) if $N = S^1$, assume in addition that $f$ has at least one periodic point in $N$. (This excludes in particular every circle homeomorphism of irrational rotation number, for which the conclusion is false; the literature states the caveat as 'f is not a homeomorphism without periodic points', and the hypothesis given here is the safe, slightly stronger form. Interval maps always have a fixed point, so (iii) is automatic on an interval.)
Then $\Lambda$ is uniformly expanding (a hyperbolic repelling set): there exist constants $C > 0$ and $\lambda > 1$, depending only on $f$ and $\Lambda$, such that
  $|Df^n(x)| \ge C \lambda^n$ for every $x \in \Lambda$ and every $n \ge 0$.

Standard corollary (the form usually quoted as the uniform expansion criterion). Suppose every periodic orbit of $f$ is hyperbolic repelling (and, on the circle, $f$ has a periodic point). Let $U$ be any open neighbourhood of $\mathrm{Crit}(f)$ and let $\Lambda(U) = \{x \in N : f^n(x) \notin U \text{ for all } n \ge 0\}$ be the set of points whose forward orbit never enters $U$. Then $\Lambda(U)$ is compact, forward invariant, disjoint from the critical set, and hence uniformly expanding: $|Df^n(x)| \ge C_U \lambda_U^n$ on $\Lambda(U)$. In words: 'all periodic orbits repelling' forces uniform expansion on any piece of the phase space that stays a fixed distance away from the critical points. Consequently every point either accumulates on the critical set or is uniformly expanded.

Where it FAILS if a hypothesis is dropped. (a) Without (i) the conclusion is false trivially: $Df = 0$ at a critical point. (b) Without (ii): an attracting or neutral periodic point in $\Lambda$ has $|Df^{nk}(p)| \le 1$. Attracting periodic orbits may exist elsewhere in $N$; the theorem only asks that none lies in $\Lambda$. (c) Without (iii): an irrational rotation, or any $C^2$ circle diffeomorphism with irrational rotation number, has $\Lambda = S^1$, no critical points and no periodic points at all (so (ii) holds vacuously), yet the derivatives $|Df^n|$ do not grow exponentially (each $f^n$ is a diffeomorphism of a circle of length 1, so $\min_x |Df^n(x)| \le 1$ for all $n$). (d) Smoothness: the proof uses $C^2$ (bounded distortion of iterates away from critical points); do not quote it for maps that are merely $C^1$. (e) Only one-dimensional: this is a theorem about interval and circle maps; there is no analogue for higher-dimensional maps or for holomorphic maps without further hypotheses. Note also that the theorem does NOT assume non-flat critical points and does NOT need to assume the absence of wandering intervals: both are handled inside the proof, and in particular no wandering interval can lie in a set $\Lambda$ satisfying (i)-(iii).","status":"unverified"}

$$f_{\kappa, \mathbf{M}}(x,y) \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}

Let $v(x,t)$ be a $C^1$ velocity field on an open set $U \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, $t \in (t_0, t_1)$, with flow $\varphi_t$ (so $\partial_t \varphi_t(y) = v(\varphi_t(y), t)$, $\varphi_{0} = \mathrm{id}$), and let $\Omega(t) = \varphi_t(\Omega_0)$ where $\Omega_0$ is a bounded open set with Lipschitz (e.g. piecewise $C^1$) boundary whose closure stays in $U$. Let $F(x,t)$ be $C^1$ on $U \times (t_0, t_1)$. Then
$$\frac{d}{dt} \int_{\Omega(t)} F\,dx = \int_{\Omega(t)} \partial_t F\,dx + \int_{\partial \Omega(t)} F\,(v \cdot \nu)\,dS = \int_{\Omega(t)} \big(\partial_t F + \nabla\cdot(F v)\big)\,dx,$$
where $\nu$ is the outward unit normal and $v \cdot \nu$ is the outward normal velocity of the boundary. Only the NORMAL component of the boundary velocity enters: two motions of the domain whose boundaries sweep the same sets (differing by a tangential reparametrisation) give the same derivative, so the formula can be stated with any $C^1$ boundary velocity having the correct normal component. The one-variable formula is the case $n = 1$, $\nu = \pm 1$ at $b$ and $a$.

WHERE IT FAILS OR NEEDS CARE. (1) $F$ must be continuous up to the moving boundary from inside; if $F$ jumps across $\partial\Omega(t)$ the boundary integrand is the one-sided limit from inside $\Omega(t)$. (2) $\partial_t F$ must be integrable over $\Omega(t)$ (continuity on a compact closure suffices); without domination, differentiation under the integral sign can fail. (3) The bounded-domain / Lipschitz-boundary hypothesis is what licenses the divergence theorem in the second equality; the first equality (Lagrangian form) needs only the change of variables. (4) If the domain is not transported by a $C^1$ flow but its boundary merely moves with a prescribed normal speed $w$, the same formula holds with $v \cdot \nu$ replaced by $w$, but the proof must build a flow with that normal speed.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:05:09.628303+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_62e797c4a89e268f072ee5853a7ca53df60e1eb04231b0e3b56cdfcb9f93478f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:augment_stable of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] Assume that $\bm{X}$ is an augmented $\alpha$-stable process and $\bm{Z}$ is an $\alpha$-stable process with $\alpha\in(0,2)\setminus\{1\}$ and fix any $q\in(0,1]\cap(0,\alpha)$ with $\mathds{E}[|\bm{X}_1|^q]<\infty$.
\begin{description}[leftmargin=0em, nosep]
\item[(a)]

Assume $|\mathcal{Q}(x,\bm{v})-c_\alpha| \leqslant K(1\wedge x)$ for  some $K>0$ and all $x>0$, $\bm{v}\in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. Then, for $\bm{X}^t\coloneqq(\bm{X}_{st}/t^{1/\alpha})_{s\in[0,1]}$,  
\begin{equation*}
c_1 t^{1-q/\alpha}
\leqslant\mathcal{W}_q\big(\bm{X}^t_1,\bm{Z}_1\big)
\leqslant\mathcal{W}_q\big(\bm{X}^t,\bm{Z}\big)\leqslant
c_2\big(t^{1-q/\alpha}\1_{\{\alpha<1\}} + t^{q(1-1/\alpha)}\1_{\{\alpha>1\}}\big),
\end{equation*}
for some $c_1,c_2>0$ and all sufficiently small $t>0$.

\item[(b)] Assume $\mathcal{Q}(x,\bm{v})\!=\! c_\alpha H(x)^\alpha$ for $x>0$, $\bm{v}\in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ and some monotone $H\in\mbox{SV}_0\cap C^1$. Set $\varrho(x)\!\coloneqq \!\int_x^\infty H(y)^\alpha y^{-\alpha-1}\mathrm{d} y$ and let $\varrho^{\leftarrow}$ be its right-continuous inverse. Suppose $G(x)\coloneqq H(\varrho^{\leftarrow}(1/x))$ satisfies Assumption~(\nameref{asm:S}) for some function $G_2\in\mbox{SV}_0$. Then, for $g(t)\coloneqq t^{1/\alpha}G(t)$, $a(t)\coloneqq G(2t)/G(t)$ and $\bm{X}^t\coloneqq(\bm{X}_{st}/g(t))_{s\in[0,1]}$, we have
\[
\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X}^t,\bm{Z})=\mathcal{O} ( G_2(t)^q),
\quad\text{as }t \downarrow 0,\quad\text{and}\quad
\max\big\{\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X}^t_1,\bm{Z}_1)
,\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X}^{2t}_1,\bm{Z}_1)\big\}
\geqslant |1-a(t)^q|\mathds{E}\big[|\bm{Z}_1|^q\big]/3,
\]
for sufficiently small $t >0$. The function $t\mapsto|1-a(t)^q|$ is not upper bounded by any non-decreasing function $\phi$ with $\int_0^1\phi(t)t^{-1}\mathrm{d} t<\infty$, $G$ is $C^1$ with $t\mapsto t|G'(t)|\in\mbox{SV}_0$ and there exists some $\phi\in\mbox{SV}_0\cap\mbox{SV}_\infty$ satisfying the inequality $\phi(x)\geqslant\sup_{t>0,y\in[x\wedge 1,x\vee1]}yG'(yt)/G'(t)$ for all $x>0$. Moreover, defining  $L(t)\coloneqq t|G'(t)|/G(t)$, there exist constants $c_1,c_2>0$ such that for all sufficiently small $t>0$, we have
\[
c_2L(t)
\leqslant\max\{\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X}^t_1,\bm{Z}_1)
,\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X}^{2t}_1,\bm{Z}_1)\}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X}^t,\bm{Z})
\leqslant c_1L(t)^q.
\]

\end{description}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:53:30.663230+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_62fde6d8025505de904b3d051e750004e097b6a1919a3d268f0aa3f653ab68ac","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm reg_existence of arXiv:2506.01746, '\bf Optimal Bregman quantization: existence and uniqueness of optimal quantizers revisited'] Let $r>0$ and let $\|\cdot\|$ denote any norm on  $\mathbb{R}^d$.  Assume $\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\|\xi\|^{r}\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{d}\xi)< + \infty$.

\smallskip
\noindent $(a)$ For every $n\ge 1$, there exists at least one $L^r$-optimal quantizer $\Gamma^{(r,n)}$ of size at most $n$, solution to the minimization problem
\[
\inf_{\Gamma: |\Gamma|\leq n}  e_r(\Gamma,P,\|.\|)
\]
i.e. such that 
\[
e_r(\Gamma^{(r,n)},P,\|.\|)=  e_{r,n}(P,\|.\|).  
\]

\smallskip
\noindent $(b)$ If ${\rm card}\big({\rm supp}(P)\big) \ge n$, then any $L^r$-optimal quantizer $ \Gamma^{(r,n)}$ has full size $n$ and for every $a\!\in  \Gamma^{(r,n)}$, $P(C_a( \Gamma^{(r,n)}))>0$. Moreover, 

\smallskip
 $(i)$ if the norm $\|\cdot\|$ is smooth~(\footnote{that $\|\cdot\|$ is differentiable on $\mathbb{R}^d\setminus\{0\}$, like Euclidean norms or $\ell^p$-norms, $1<p<+\infty$.}) and strictly convex then {\em the boundary of the Voronoi partition is $P$-negligible}: for every $a\!\in \Gamma^{(r,n)}$, $P\big(\partial C_a(\Gamma^{(r,n)})\big)=0$

\smallskip
  $(ii)$ if   $r\ge 2$ and the norm $\|\cdot\|=|\cdot|_e$ is Euclidean then these quantizers are {\em $L^r$-stationarity}: for every $a\!\in \Gamma^{(r,n)}$,
\[
a = \frac{\int_{C_a(\Gamma^{(r,n)})}\xi|\xi-a|^{r-2}P(\mathrm{d}\xi)}{\int_{C_a(\Gamma^{(r,n)})}|\xi-a|^{r-2}P(\mathrm{d}\xi)}.
\]
\
\noindent $(c)$ When $d=1$  and $P=U([0,1])$, then for every $r>0$, the $L^r$-optimal quantizer is unique and 
\[
\Gamma^{(r,n)} = \Big\{\frac{2k-1}{2n},\; k=0,\ldots,n\Big\}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.177765+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_63230d76d33c48f6c55846301fea421f5a025c648d7d40f1c3ba526c50649455","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 79 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] On the time interval $[q_0,\gamma(1)]$ let $\tilde{Y}$, $\tilde{W}$, $\tilde{w}$, $\tilde{\cF}_Y$ be as given by Lemma~\ref{l:time.change}.
It is possible to extend these to the full time interval $[q_0,1]$ such that
$|\tilde Y(1)| = 1$ almost surely, and the same conditions as before are satisfied: $\tilde{W}$ is a standard Brownian motion,
$\tilde{w}$ is progressively measurable with respect to
    \[
    \tilde \cF_Y(t) = \sigma\Big(
        (\tilde W_s)_{s\in [q_0,t]}, U', \tilde Y(q_0)
    \Big)
\]
with $\bbE[(\tilde w_t)^2] = 1$ for all $t$,
and
 \[
        \tilde Y(t) = \tilde Y(\gamma(1))
            + \int_{\gamma(1)}^t \tilde w_s\,d\tilde{W}(s)\,.
    \]

\begin{proof} Abbreviate $t_1=\gamma(1)$.
Let $Z$ be a standard Brownian motion on the time interval $[t_1,{{\infty)}}$ with initialization $Z(t_1)=\tilde{Y}(t_1)$. Let
    \[
    \bar{\tau}
    \equiv\inf\Big\{t\ge t_1 : |Z(t)|\ge1\Big\}\,,
    \]
and define the stopped martingale
    \[\bar{Z}(t)\equiv Z(t\wedge\bar{\tau})
    =\tilde{Y}(t_1)+ \int_{q_0}^t \ind\{t\le\bar{\tau}\} \,dZ(t)\,.
    \]
Then, similarly as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:time.change}, we define $\tilde{Y}$ to be the time change of $\bar{Z}$ satisfying the desired properties. Explicitly, let 
    \[
    \bar{\gamma}(t)
    = \E[\bar{Z}(t_1+t)^2] -\E[\bar{Z}(t_1)^2] 
    = \E \int_{t_1}^{t_1+t} \ind\{t\le\bar{\tau}\}\,dt\,,
    \]
and denote its generalized inverse $\bar{\lambda}$.
We then take $\tilde{Y}(t)=\bar{Z}(t_1+\bar{\lambda}(t-t_1))$, so that
$\E[\tilde{Y}(t)^2]=t$. As in Lemma~\ref{l:time.change}, we can express
    \[
    \tilde{Y}(t)
    = \tilde{Y}(t_1) + \int_{t_1}^t \tilde{w}_t\,d\tilde{W}(t)
    \]
where we can define explicitly    \begin{align*}
    \tilde{W}(t) 
    &=\int_{t_1}^{t_1+\bar{\lambda}(t-t_1)}
	\bar{\gamma}'(u-t_1)^{1/2}\,dZ(u)\,,\\
    \tilde{w}_t
    &= \frac{\ind\{t_1+\bar{\lambda}(t-t_1)\le\tau\}}
        {\bar{\gamma}'(\bar{\lambda}(t-t_1))^{1/2}}\,.
    \end{align*}
The claim follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542799+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_637545cab4581aec18b900458dddacc53f40eafaa957969735334b08e256a82f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be an event depending on the states of a finite set of edges, and let omega be a configuration. The edge e is PIVOTAL for A at omega if the occurrence of A is decided by the state of e alone, that is if omega with e forced open lies in A and omega with e forced closed does not, or the reverse. Pivotality is a function of the states of the OTHER edges only, so the event {e is pivotal for A} is independent of the state of e - a fact used constantly and easy to forget. The INFLUENCE of e on A under P_p is I_e(A) = P_p( e is pivotal for A ). Under the uniform measure on the discrete cube this coincides with the usual influence P( f(X) != f(X with coordinate e flipped) ) for the indicator f of A. The total influence sum_e I_e(A) is, by Russo's formula, exactly the derivative of p -> P_p(A) for increasing A, which is why influences govern the sharpness of the phase transition; and by the Kahn-Kalai-Linial theorem the maximum influence of a balanced Boolean function on n coordinates is at least of order log n / n, which is the quantitative input behind sharp-threshold results. [standard; e.g. Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Section 2.4, and O'Donnell, Analysis of Boolean Functions, Chapter 2]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["mu is a T-invariant probability measure","partitions are finite or have finite static entropy"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T12:13:53+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, entropy","id":"claim_637c65a50c50c4a412cd1517de9fbd833d8ddce462113a909e4ca6ed27e8e5e4","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \\mathcal{B}, \\mu, T)$ be a probability-preserving system. For a finite (or countable, with finite entropy) measurable partition $\\xi = \\{A_1, \\dots, A_k\\}$ put $H_\\mu(\\xi) = -\\sum_i \\mu(A_i) \\log \\mu(A_i)$ (with $0 \\log 0 = 0$), and $\\xi^n_0 = \\bigvee_{j=0}^{n-1} T^{-j}\\xi$, the partition into sets $A_{i_0} \\cap T^{-1}A_{i_1} \\cap \\dots \\cap T^{-(n-1)}A_{i_{n-1}}$ (the $n$-step itineraries). The entropy of $T$ relative to $\\xi$ is $h_\\mu(T, \\xi) = \\lim_{n\\to\\infty} \\frac1n H_\\mu(\\xi^n_0)$ (the limit exists because $n \\mapsto H_\\mu(\\xi^n_0)$ is subadditive; it also equals $\\inf_n \\frac1n H_\\mu(\\xi^n_0)$ and $\\lim_n H_\\mu(\\xi \\mid \\xi^n_1)$). The Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy is $h_\\mu(T) = \\sup_\\xi h_\\mu(T, \\xi)$ over finite partitions, in $[0, \\infty]$. Facts used constantly: $h_\\mu(T, \\xi) \\le H_\\mu(\\xi) \\le \\log k$; $h_\\mu(T, \\xi) \\le h_\\mu(T, \\eta) + H_\\mu(\\xi \\mid \\eta)$ for partitions $\\xi, \\eta$; $h_\\mu(T^m) = m\\, h_\\mu(T)$ for $m \\ge 1$; the Kolmogorov-Sinai generator theorem: if $\\xi$ is a generator ($\\bigvee_{j \\ge 0} T^{-j}\\xi$ generates $\\mathcal{B}$ mod $\\mu$, or $\\bigvee_{j\\in\\mathbb{Z}}$ for invertible $T$) then $h_\\mu(T) = h_\\mu(T, \\xi)$; and if $\\xi_m$ is an increasing sequence of partitions generating $\\mathcal{B}$ then $h_\\mu(T, \\xi_m) \\uparrow h_\\mu(T)$. On a compact metric space, finite Borel partitions $\\xi_m$ with $\\mathrm{diam}(\\xi_m) \\to 0$ also give $h_\\mu(T, \\xi_m) \\to h_\\mu(T)$ (for every finite partition $\\eta$, $H_\\mu(\\eta \\mid \\xi_m) \\to 0$), but not monotonically in general, since such partitions need not refine one another. The map $\\mu \\mapsto h_\\mu(T)$ on invariant measures is affine, but it is NOT in general continuous or even upper semicontinuous in the weak* topology; upper semicontinuity holds when $T$ is expansive (and for $C^\\infty$ maps of compact manifolds by Newhouse), which is what guarantees measures of maximal entropy exist in those cases.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:25:55.404162+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_639921dde429114996f15fa62cf047f0261b0a1e92299e184d41bb3bfcc87b42","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 7 (Concatenation of absorbed one-step weak solutions) of arXiv:2607.28078, '2607.28078'] Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open and $\overline{D}$ compact, let $0=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_N=T$, and put $\varphi(t):=s_i$ for $t\in[s_i,s_{i+1})$.  Let $b$ and $\sigma$ be jointly Borel measurable. For a continuous path $\xi$ on $[0,T]$, write
\[
\tau_D(\xi):=\inf\{t\in[0,T]:\xi(t)\notin D\},
\]
where the infimum of the empty set is $\infty$. Suppose that, for every $i\in\{0,\cdots,N-1\}$, $y\in\overline D$, and every $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$ supported by $\overline D$, there is a weak solution $(Y^i,B^i)$ on $[s_i,s_{i+1}]$ of the absorbed frozen-law equation
\begin{equation}
Y^i(t)=y+\int_{s_i}^t\mathbf 1_{\{r<\tau^i_D(Y^i)\}}b\bigl(r,Y^i(r),\mu\bigr)dr+\int_{s_i}^t\mathbf 1_{\{r<\tau^i_D(Y^i)\}}\sigma\bigl(r,Y^i(r),\mu\bigr)\,dB^i(r),
\,\,t\in[s_i,s_{i+1}].
\end{equation}
The solution is absorbed after $\tau^i_D(Y^i):=\inf\{t\in[s_i,s_{i+1}]:Y^i(t)\notin D\}$ and has a finite second moment.
Then the joint laws of these stopped solutions admit a universally measurable selection in $(y,\mu)$.  Consequently, every initial law $\nu_0\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$ supported by $\overline D$ admits a concatenation $(X,B)$ on a stochastic basis $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\{\mathcal{F}_t\},\mathbb{P})$ such that $B$ is a Brownian motion, $\mathcal L_{X(0)}=\nu_0$, and, with $\tau_D:=\inf\{t\in[0,T]:X(t)\notin D\}$, the process $X$ is absorbed after $\tau_D$ and satisfies
\begin{equation}
X(t)=X(0)+\int_0^t\mathbf1_{\{r<\tau_D\}}b\bigl(r,X(r),\mathcal L_{X(\varphi(r))}\bigr)dr+\int_0^t\mathbf1_{\{r<\tau_D\}}\sigma\bigl(r,X(r),\mathcal L_{X(\varphi(r))}\bigr)dB(r).
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["All explicit definitions and width/scale limit order in proofs/IID_FIXED_NOISE.md","Uniform four-atom input law, unit-norm centered-ReLU single-index teacher; n(e)~4sigma^2 e^-4","Label noise independent symmetric +/-sigma, sigma fixed in (0,1]; clean risk averages over labels conditional on input sample and initialization","Paired Gaussian hidden initialization and opposite nonzero heads +/-nu, nu fixed in (0,1]; step 1/2, both layers trained","Finite-horizon comparison through T_e=ceil(e^-5/2); population support remains finite and initialization is not iid across individual neurons"],"created_at":"2026-10-22T00:34:54.664213+00:00","domain":"learning theory","id":"claim_63eeb2ba518fa80ea62431166cebf7979ced645d133468563296bbc7eb2cb3ce","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"# Iid finite-support samples with fixed label noise and unit-norm ReLU teacher

T267 / Target 1 / C013 / proof draft (unaudited); novelty unestablished.
This removes stratification and vanishing label-noise amplitude from C010.
The remaining finite population support, paired initialization, tangent-
kernel limit and averaging over label noise are substantive restrictions.

## 1. Statement

Use C010's four unit inputs x_(s,t), uniform population distribution and
centered unit-norm ReLU teacher g_e=alpha_e(s+t+st). Fix nu in (0,1] and
label-noise amplitude sigma in (0,1], independently of feature scale e.
Take n(e)=ceil(sigma^2/alpha_e^2) independent population input samples,
and label each by g_e(x)+epsilon, with independent epsilon uniform +/-sigma.
Initialize an even-width two-layer ReLU net by independent Gaussian pairs
with equal hidden weights and opposite readouts +/-nu, as in C010.
Training inputs, label noises and initialization are mutually independent.
Train all parameters by simultaneous GD at step gamma=1/2 on empirical
squared loss divided by 2n(e). No post-initialization parameter tying.

Let Q_(m,e)(k) be clean population squared risk averaged over all training
label noises, conditional on input samples and network initialization.
Use C010's rates b_h and witness times k0,k1,k2,k3, and its central integer
interval I_e with B=log[b1/(b2+b12)]. Then in the iterated even-width-first,
feature-scale-second limit, with probability tending to one over iid
training inputs and initialization:

Q(k0)>Q(k1)<Q(k2)>Q(k3),
(Q(k0),Q(k1),Q(k2),Q(k3))/alpha_e^2 -> (4,7/2,4,3),

and every maximizer k_peak on I_e is interior and satisfies
b1 k_peak-B ->0. In particular

k_peak ~ (4pi/nu^2) e^(-1) log(1/e).

All convergence in probability uses the order lim_(e->0) limsup_(m->infinity)
of each failure probability. Sample size n(e) grows as 4sigma^2 e^(-4);
it is fixed during each width limit. The theorem does not assert high
probability over realized labels; risk itself averages over label noise.
No Gaussian-input or full Target1 solution is claimed.

## 2. Collapse repeated inputs exactly

Let N_i be the count of population point i, p_i=N_i/n, and
D=diag(4p_i). On the event all N_i>0 let bar y_i be the mean label in cell i.
The empirical loss equals

(1/2) sum_i p_i (f(x_i)-bar y_i)^2 + a parameter-independent constant.

Consequently every parameter update is exactly the update on these four
cell means with weights p_i. Conditional on counts, the cell-mean noise
has mean zero and diagonal covariance

V=diag(sigma^2/N_i)=(4sigma^2/n)D^(-1).

No Gaussian approximation or independence of Walsh coefficients is used.
The test law remains uniform on the population support, including when
the realized training counts are unequal.

## 3. Count concentration

Put delta=||D-I||. Each diagonal deviation has mean zero and variance 3/n,
because N_i is binomial(n,1/4). Chebyshev plus a union bound gives

P(delta>r)<=12/(n r^2).

Take r=e^(3/2). Since n is asymptotic to 4sigma^2 e^(-4), the failure
probability is O(e), for fixed sigma. For all small e, on the resulting
good event delta<=e^(3/2)<1/2, every cell is nonempty and
D lies between (1-delta)I and (1+delta)I. This is the only sample-count
event used. There is no fixed-count conditioning in the final theorem.

## 4. Weighted frozen-kernel stability without a slow-gap denominator

Let C be C009's deterministic full initial tangent matrix, with ||C||<=1,
and A=I-gamma C, gamma=1/2. Compare zero-start prediction iterations
using C and C D, both with the SAME cell-mean label vector bar y.
Write their residuals r_I(k),r_D(k) and prediction difference d(k).

The matrix I-gamma C D is similar, by D^(1/2), to the symmetric matrix
I-gamma D^(1/2) C D^(1/2). The latter has eigenvalues in [0,1] when
delta<=1/2, since gamma||D|| ||C||<=3/4. Thus

||r_D(k)|| <= kappa_delta ||bar y||,
kappa_delta=sqrt((1+delta)/(1-delta))<=sqrt(3)<2.

Subtracting the two iterations and using d(0)=0 gives

d(k)=-gamma sum_(j=0)^(k-1) A^(k-1-j) C(D-I)r_D(j).

For l>=0, spectral calculus yields
||gamma C A^l||<=1/(l+1): each eigenvalue is a(1-a)^l with a in [0,1/2],
whose maximum is bounded by 1/(l+1). Therefore

||d(k)||<=kappa_delta delta H_k ||bar y||,
H_k=sum_(j=1)^k 1/j <=1+log k, k>=1.

The crucial feature is logarithmic time growth rather than division by
the smallest eigenvalue of C. This argument does not assume that C and D
commute. For k=0 the difference is zero and H_0=0.

## 5. Uniform noise-averaged risk comparison

Let Q_D(k) denote the clean frozen risk using C D and the actual cell-
mean noise. Let Q_I,V(k) use C and the same noise covariance V. Since
||g||^2=12alpha^2 and tr V<=32alpha^2 on delta<=1/2 (n>=sigma^2/alpha^2),
E||bar y||^2<=44alpha^2<49alpha^2 and ||g||<4alpha.
The unweighted predictor has norm at most ||bar y||, and the weighted
predictor has norm at most (1+kappa_delta)||bar y||. Combining the risk
identity | ||a||^2-||b||^2 |<=||a-b||(||a||+||b||) with Section4 and
Cauchy--Schwarz, and dividing by four for the uniform population, gives

max_(k<=T)|Q_D(k)-Q_I,V(k)|/alpha^2 <=126 delta H_T.

For clarity this constant follows from kappa_delta<2,
(2+kappa_delta)E||bar y||^2+2||g||E||bar y|| <=252alpha^2;
the outside factor is kappa_delta delta H_T/4<delta H_T/2.

Now compare V with the balanced covariance V0=(4sigma^2/n)I.
The unweighted prediction noise map B_k=I-A^k has norm at most one.
Its risk covariance perturbation is at most

(1/4)||V-V0||_* <=4(sigma^2/n)delta/(1-delta)<=8alpha^2 delta.

Balanced covariance has Walsh variance sigma^2/n, while C010 uses alpha^2.
Let rho_round=sigma^2/(nalpha^2). Rounding n upward gives
0<=1-rho_round<=alpha^2/sigma^2. Each of four mode noise filters is at
most one, so the corresponding risk error is at most 4alpha^4/sigma^2.
Consequently, for C010's baseline zero-output curve Q_e^0,

max_(k<=T)|Q_D(k)-Q_e^0(k)|/alpha^2
 <=126 delta H_T+8delta+4alpha^2/sigma^2.

Choose T=ceil(e^(-5/2)). On the count-good event the right side is
O(e^(3/2)log(1/e))+O(e^4)=o(e). This is smaller than both C010's constant
normalized witness margins and its normalized central peak gap of order e.
All covariance arguments use exact second moments, not a central limit
approximation or a numerical experiment.

## 6. Actual nonlinear GD comparison under cell weights

We spell out the weighted extension of C010's finite-horizon argument.
On the count-good event ||D||<=3/2. For small e, each cell-mean label has
absolute value at most sigma+3alpha<2, hence ||bar y||<=4. The network
starts at zero. Use the deterministic neuronwise bounds of C009 with
R_0=4, S=14, L=2, n0=4, and replace its c_k by

gamma L (3/2)R_k/n0.

In its residual recurrence multiply the readout-kernel gradient term by
3/2 as well; the feature-motion term is already expressed through c_k.
This follows directly from replacing r by D r in both exact parameter
updates and bounding ||D r||<=3R/2. All resulting constants through a
fixed T are finite and uniform over D in [I/2,3I/2] and labels in [-2,2]^4.

Gaussian norm bounds, independent-pair strong laws, initial kernel
convergence and weighted initial gate-band mass are unchanged, since the
four possible input vectors are unchanged. Kernel drift and the exact
discrete-step gate remainder tend uniformly to zero. The frozen iteration
uses C D; its powers are bounded by sqrt(3) by Section4, so telescoping
still transfers predictions uniformly through T. Crucially the argument
is uniform over all bounded cell-mean label vectors; it does not take a
union over 2^n noise realizations or assume independent adaptive gates.
Uniform prediction control and the finite-horizon deterministic bounds
transfer noise-averaged risks as width tends to infinity for each fixed e.
Division by the fixed positive alpha^2 e is legitimate at this stage.

Thus max_(k<=T)|Q_actual(k)-Q_D(k)|/(alpha^2 e)->0 in probability over
initialization as width grows, on the count-good event, uniformly in its
counts. This claim does not give a uniform-in-e practical width threshold.

## 7. Witness and peak transfer, and remaining scope

The sample event fails with probability O(e). On it, Section5 gives
uniform surrogate-risk error o(alpha^2 e), and Section6 adds a vanishing
fixed-e width error. C010's positive risk witnesses and central peak
value gaps therefore transfer, first taking width to infinity and then
e to zero. Its entire integer peak interval and k3 lie below T for all
small e. The teacher identity and full tangent-kernel clocks are unchanged.
This proves the stated restricted theorem.

Fixed label noise, unit teacher norm and iid sampling are now explicit,
but n grows as e^(-4), the test population has only four atoms, readouts
are paired, risk averages over label noise and the proof is in a tangent-
kernel limit. It is not a generic Gaussian-design, macroscopic feature-
learning, realized-label high-probability, fixed-n, all-time, full-target
or novelty claim. C009/C010 and the uniform weighted nonlinear extension
await independent review. That extension is the least-trusted proof step.
No network training, dataset generation or large computation is needed.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:34:20.779119+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6408811a344d67630044300a300505dd43df6dce072e798ca3f873abedf2acf1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 6 (Triangular-array killed local limits) of arXiv:2609.02257, 'Aperiodic random walks: uniform estimates, local limits and invariance principles'] Let \(r_N\to\infty\), let \(t>0\), and suppose
\[
 L_N=\lfloor tr_N\rfloor,\qquad
 \frac{A_N}{\sigma_N\sqrt{r_N}}\longrightarrow h_0,\qquad
 \frac{B_N}{\sigma_N\sqrt{r_N}}\longrightarrow h_1 .
\]
Whenever \(h_0=0\), we assume \(A_N=0\), and whenever \(h_1=0\),
we assume \(B_N=0\).  
Whenever the endpoints are positive in the limit,
\begin{equation}
 \sqrt{r_N}\,q_{N,L_N}(A_N,B_N)
 \longrightarrow
 \frac1\sigma\mathbf F(t;h_1,h_0),
 \qquad h_0,h_1>0.                                  
\end{equation}
At a zero endpoint, let the constants \(a,b\) be the limits defined
in \eqref{eq:survival-constant-convergence}. Then
\begin{align}
 r_N q_{N,L_N}(0,B_N)

 && h_0>0,                                            \\
 r_N^{3/2} q_{N,L_N}(0,0)
 &\longrightarrow \sigma ab\,\mathbf F_{0,0}(t).
                                                           
\end{align}

\((0,\infty)\) and the positive limiting endpoints range over compact
subsets of \((0,\infty)\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:41:29.018055+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_641b62fc92d5c8898359a7adf2430065a5178c99d78656f8022d0e9bf63103fd","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 16 ({\citealp[Definition~9) of arXiv:2608.26288, 'Muon with Finite Newton--Schulz: The Smoothing Benefit in Nonsmooth Nonconvex Optimization'] {jiang26adaptive}}]

For $W\in\R^{m\times n}$ and $\rho>0$, let $\mathcal P(W;\rho)$ be the set of finitely supported probability distributions $p$ on $\R^{m\times n}$ such that $\E_{Y\sim p}[Y]=W$ and $\E_{Y\sim p} \lVert Y-W\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\rho$.
For $\epsilon\geq0$, a point $W$ is said to be a \emph{$(\rho,\epsilon)$-stationary point} if

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.199352+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_641ba78795f85f0feb35dc0641f55832e7cb0ba329000e2b4984465e67a536e9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 131 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $X^\frozen$ and $X^{\frozen,\Ising}$ be the unique solutions of the SDEs \eqref{e:actual.sde} 
such that   $X^\frozen(q_*)$ is equidistributed as $Y^\frozen(q_*)$, and 
$X^{\frozen,\Ising}(q_*)$ is equidistributed as $Y^{\frozen,\Ising}(q_*)$. The processes $X^\frozen$ and $Y^\frozen$ have marginals which are close in $L^2$-Wasserstein distance: for each fixed $t$, there exists a coupling of $X^\frozen(t)$ with $Y^\frozen(t)$ under which we have the bound
	\[
	\bE\bigg[\Big( X^\frozen(t)-Y^\frozen(t)\Big)^2\bigg]
	\le O(\sep)+
	C\bigg( \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	\bigg) \tep^{1/2}\,.
	\]
Likewise with the processes $Y^{\frozen,\Ising}$ and $X^{\frozen,\Ising}$.
 
\begin{proof}
First, $\vY^\frozen$ is close to 
$\hvY^\frozen(t)= \vY^\frozen(t-\sss)+\xxx$ because $\sss$ and $\xxx$ are both small: $\xxx$ is sampled from the spatial kernel $\sphi$ (Definition~\ref{d:sp.smooth}), so $\|\xxx\|_\infty \le\sep$. Meanwhile $\sss$ is sampled from the temporal kernel $\tphi$ (Definition~\ref{d:t.smooth}), so $|\sss| \le\tep$. We can apply  the bound \eqref{e:Y.I.Kolmogorov} from Proposition~\ref{p:Y.kolmogorov} for increments of $Y^{\frozen,\RomI}$, and the bound from Proposition~\ref{p:Y.notI.second.quenched}
for increments of $Y^{\frozen,\RomII}$, $Y^{\frozen,\RomIII}$, and $Y^{\frozen,\Ising}$. By Fatou's lemma, in the $N\to\infty$ limit we have the quenched second moment bound
	\[
	\bE\bigg[\Big\| \vY^\frozen(t)-\hvY^\frozen(t)\Big\|^2\bigg]
	\le O(\sep)+ L^{O(1)}
	 \tep\,.
	\]
Next recall that $Y^\frozen$ is the coordinate sum \eqref{e:Y.plus}, and 
recall that $\iY^\frozen$ is the coordinate sum  \eqref{e:iY.plus}.
Meanwhile, $\iX^\frozen$ solves the SDE \eqref{e:iX.sde}. By Proposition~\ref{p:fokker.planck},
$\iY^\frozen(t)$ and $\iX^\frozen(t)$ have the same marginal law for all $t$. We finally compare $\iX^\frozen$ to the solution $X^\frozen$ of the SDE \eqref{e:actual.sde}. By Corollary~\ref{c:reg.in.limit}\ref{c:reg.in.limit.a},  the coefficients are uniformly bounded by
$(\frac{\trK L}{\sep})^{O(1)}$. 
By Lemma~\ref{l:ideal.vs.actual.coeffs},
the coefficients of the two SDEs
are close:
	\[
	\sup\bigg\{
	\Big|\tF(t,y)-\iF(t,y)
	\Big|
	: y\in\R, t\in[q_*,1]\setminus\oJ
	\bigg\}
	\le
	\bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} \tep^{1/2}\,.
	\] 
Since for any $x,y\ge0$ we have $|x^{1/2}-y^{1/2}| \le |x-y|^{1/2}$, we immediately deduce a bound on $\tF^{1/2}-\iF^{1/2}$.
Lemma~\ref{l:gronwall} then implies the existence of a coupling under which
	\[
	\bE\bigg[ \Big( X^\frozen(t)-\iX^\frozen(t)\Big)^2\bigg]
	\le
	C\bigg( \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	\bigg) \tep^{1/2}
	\]
for all $q_*\le t\le 1$. Combining the above bounds gives the conclusion.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:25:49.897530+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_641bf4cba852ce182ce9c7bdfd685bda0b4a07d5ad63b1003a9676ef374f6422","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 60 of arXiv:2609.02065, '\textbf{From Bowditch's question to Goldman's conjecture for type-preserving representatio'] Let $\Sigma = \Sigma_{g,p}$ with $g\geqslant 2$ and $p\geqslant 1$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:20:07.912164+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_643b4a3904fa77c46a2feaf0b3c9178b870ec179be67eea4159f19210724d18c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn of arXiv:2608.29914, 'Fixed points in abstract provability structures'] Let $S = \langle L, \leq, \top, \bot, \Box, \boxtimes\rangle$ be an APS and let $x \in L$. 
    \begin{enumerate}

{"assumptions":["RSW crossing estimates and FKG at the critical point","Polychromatic arm events (or the monochromatic one-arm event)","Planarity and the separation-of-arms lemma"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.975245+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_644045ce021d905aa60b2d065f197a6a96352a41bb3aa633d62cefdb1144e0c6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For critical planar percolation on Z^2 or the triangular lattice, let alpha_k(r,R) be the probability of k disjoint arms of prescribed colours, at least one of each colour (polychromatic), crossing the annulus from radius r to radius R. Quasi-multiplicativity: there are constants 0 < c <= C < infinity depending only on k such that c alpha_k(r,r') alpha_k(r',R) <= alpha_k(r,R) <= C alpha_k(r,r') alpha_k(r',R) for all r <= r' <= R (Kesten 1987; Nolin 2008 for a complete account). It follows from RSW crossing estimates, FKG and the separation-of-arms lemma; it holds for polychromatic arm events of every k and, with a separate argument, for the monochromatic one-arm event; monochromatic k-arm events for k >= 2 need extra care. Consequence: alpha_k(1,R) is comparable to the product over dyadic scales of the one-scale factors alpha_k(2^j, 2^{j+1}), each bounded between constants. It does NOT give the existence of an exponent: that needs the one-scale factors to have a Cesaro-convergent logarithm, which on the triangular lattice comes from SLE(6) and on Z^2 is open (only the universal exponents, the 5-arm exponent 2 and the half-plane 2- and 3-arm exponents 1 and 2, are known there). Typical failure: Treating quasi-multiplicativity as exact multiplicativity, dropping the universal constants, when telescoping the estimate across many scales to compute an exponent; the accumulated multiplicative error, while bounded at each step, need not be negligible over a growing number of scales, and applying the estimate to arm counts or configurations outside the range covered by the underlying construction, without re-deriving the necessary cross-scale independence, is a further common overreach. Canonical reference: Kesten, 1987, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Nolin, 2008, Electronic Journal of Probability; Schramm and Steif, 2010, Annals of Mathematics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Ising model, or a model with an analogous current/high-temperature expansion, with ferromagnetic couplings J_xy>=0","finite volume, or a well-defined infinite-volume limit, so the current sums converge","correct bookkeeping of source sets and the associated parity constraints defining valid currents","the switching lemma's precise combinatorial hypotheses on which pairs of currents are being exchanged"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.988477+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_646353a0e9728355c63142b0d86b9eb47ec1664b2c790cc1273707fc13579553","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For the Ising model with ferromagnetic couplings J_xy >= 0, the random-current representation writes correlation functions as sums over integer-valued edge configurations n = (n_xy) weighted by prod_{xy} (beta J_xy)^{n_xy} / n_xy!, subject to a source condition specifying a subset A of vertices where the total current degree is odd (and even elsewhere); the two-point function <sigma_x sigma_y> is proportional to the sum of weights over currents with sources {x,y}, with higher correlations expressed via larger source sets. The switching lemma is the key combinatorial identity underlying this representation: summing over pairs of independent currents with sources A and B and comparing to pairs with sources determined by the symmetric difference of A and B allows swapping which edges are assigned to which current while preserving all parity constraints, reducing correlation inequalities such as the Griffiths and Lebowitz inequalities, and Aizenman's tree-graph inequality used in proving triviality of the phi^4 field theory scaling limit in dimension d>=4 (or d=4 with logarithmic corrections), to purely combinatorial statements about current configurations. The representation does not extend beyond the Ising model or closely related models admitting an analogous high-temperature expansion, and it requires ferromagnetic couplings for the current weights to be nonnegative and hence probabilistically interpretable. Typical failure: Attempting to apply the random-current representation and switching lemma to models with mixed-sign (non-ferromagnetic) couplings, where the current weights are no longer nonnegative and the entire probabilistic interpretation, along with any downstream FKG-type consequences, breaks down; a further common error is misidentifying the source-set parity condition when composing several currents, which silently produces an identity for a different correlation function than intended. Canonical reference: Griffiths, Hurst and Sherman, 1970, Journal of Mathematical Physics; Aizenman, 1982, Communications in Mathematical Physics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:06:42.725446+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_646f20599815ba4bc5b7ad9c0669124af4b1e54b98e500a6ab9a0d7906e69bb8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition propclass of arXiv:2411.04238, 'Holomorphic jump-diffusions'] Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^d$ be an open set.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item{\textbf{Cauchy integral formula}} 
 (Theorem 1.3.3 in [SC:05])

    
     Let $f:U\to \mathbb C$ be a holomorphic function and fix $z_0\in U$ and $R\in (0,\infty)^d$ such that   $\overline{P_R^d(z_0)}\subseteq U$. Then 
    \begin{align*}
     D^\alpha f(z_0)=\frac{\alpha!}{(2\pi i)^d}\int_{T^d_{R}(z_0)} \frac{f(w)} {(z_0-w)^{\alpha +1}}   dw,
    \end{align*}
    where $\alpha+1:=(\alpha_1+1,\ldots,\alpha_d+1)$, and 
    $$|D^\alpha f(z_0)|\leq \frac {\alpha!}{R^\alpha}\|f|_{T_R^d(z_0)}\|_\infty.$$

    
    \item{\textbf{Taylor expansion}} (Corollary 1.5.9 in [SC:05])
    
    Let $f:U\to \mathbb R$ be a holomorphic functions and fix $z_0\in U$ and $R\in (0,\infty]^d$ such that   $\overline{P_R^d(z_0)}\subseteq U$. Then 
\begin{equation}
        f(z)=\sum_{\alpha\in \mathbb{N}^d_0}\frac 1 {\alpha!}D^\alpha f(z_0)(z-z_0)^\alpha,
    \qquad \text{for all }z\in P_R^d(z_0).
\end{equation}
By~(class:it1 of the paper) and Example~1.5.7 in [SC:05], for $R\in (0,\infty)^d$  the reminder's term can be bounded as follows
\begin{align*}
\Big|\sum_{|\alpha|\geq k+1}\frac 1 {\alpha!}D^\alpha f(z_0)(z-z_0)^\alpha\Big|
\leq\|f|_{T_R^d(z_0)}\|_\infty\prod_{i=1}^d\frac 1 {1-\frac{|z_i-z_{0i}|}{R_i}}\sum_{|\alpha|= k+1}\frac{|z-z_0|^\alpha}{R^\alpha}.
        \end{align*}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:48:27.279100+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_64a78864a4e39c3ade7409427fe3cdc2fe9cb26801d23fc0ed124cb6b6cd84a9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 13 (\normalfont Hierarchical-star structure) of arXiv:2604.24684, 'Waning Immunity Fails to Restore a Positive Epidemic Threshold on Power--Law Networks'] We say that a graph $G=(V,E)$ \emph{contains a $( k_1 ,k_2)$--hierarchical-star} if there
exist distinct vertices
\[
v,\; u_1,\ldots,u_{\lceil k_1\rceil},\; w_{i,1},\ldots,w_{i,\lceil k_2\rceil}\qquad (i=1,\ldots,\lceil k_1\rceil)
\]
such that the following edges are present:
\begin{enumerate}[{\normalfont (a)}]
\item $v$ is adjacent to $u_i$ for every $i=1,\ldots,\lceil k_1\rceil$;
\item for each $i=1,\ldots,\lceil k_1\rceil$, the vertex $u_i$ is adjacent to $w_{i,1},\ldots,w_{i,\lceil k_2\rceil}$.
\end{enumerate}
The spanning subgraph on these vertices consisting \emph{only} of the edges
\[
\big\{\{v,u_i\}: i=1,\ldots,\lceil k_1\rceil\big\}\ \cup\ \big\{\{u_i,w_{i,j}\}: i=1,\ldots,\lceil k_1\rceil,\ j=1,\ldots,\lceil k_2\rceil\big\}
\]
is called a \emph{$(k_1,k_2)$--hierarchical-star}, with center $v$, first-layer vertices $\{u_i\}_{i\le \lceil k_1\rceil}$, and
second-layer vertices $\{w_{i,j}\}_{i\le \lceil k_1\rceil,\,j\le \lceil k_2\rceil}$.
We denote this designated subgraph by $\mathrm{HStar}(v;\{u_i\}_{i\le \lceil k_1\rceil};\{w_{i,j}\}_{i\le \lceil k_1\rceil,\,j\le \lceil k_2\rceil})$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a_{m+n} <= a_m + a_n for all m, n >= 1","nothing else; the limit may be -infinity"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542097+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_64ec21a222975d147ed73e8e88f795ade040338e0b25c8717e8284dec60c0d3e","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (a_n)_{n >= 1} be a sequence of reals with a_{m+n} <= a_m + a_n for all m, n >= 1. Then lim_{n -> infinity} a_n / n exists in [-infinity, +infinity) and equals inf_{n >= 1} a_n / n. In particular the limit is finite if and only if a_n / n is bounded below. The SUPERadditive version, a_{m+n} >= a_m + a_n, gives lim a_n/n = sup_n a_n/n in (-infinity, +infinity]. The lemma requires nothing beyond subadditivity - no monotonicity, no positivity, no continuity - and the limit can be minus infinity, as with a_n = -n^2. Fekete's lemma is the deterministic skeleton of Kingman's subadditive ergodic theorem: applying it to a_n = E[X_{0,n}] gives the existence of the constant that the ergodic theorem then identifies as the almost sure limit. [Fekete (1923); standard, e.g. Steele, Probability Theory and Combinatorial Optimization, Chapter 1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:04:39.211989+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_65196e174ef1dd43989c658788d80adb30aa4bf826047a93efdf298010d25fa6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2608.13687, 'Multiplicative chaos from random multiplicative functions'] Let $(b_n)_{n\in \N}\subset \R$ be a sequence  satisfying $b_n >0$ and $\sum_{n\in\N} b_n <\infty$. Consider a sequence of nonnegative random variables $U_n$ satisfying, for some $c,C>0$ and for all $u\geq 0$,
\[
  \P(U_n>u) \leq C b_n^{-2} e^{-cu^2/b_n^2}\,.
\]
Then $U\coloneqq \sup_{n\in\N} U_n$ satisfies $\E e^{\lambda U}<\infty$ for all $\lambda>0$.
\begin{proof}
We compute the tail of $U$ via union bound:
\[
  \P(U > u) \leq C \sum_{n\in\N} b_n^{-2} e^{-c u^2/b_n^2}\,.
\]
Observe that  $v^{3} e^{-cv^2/2} \leq C'$ for some constant $C'>0$ and all $v \geq 0$, and thus for all $u, n\geq 1$,
\[
  b_n^{-2} e^{-\frac{cu^2}{2b_n^2}}\leq C' u^{-3} b_n\,.
\]
Since $b_n \to 0$, we have $\eta \coloneqq \sup_{n\in\N} b_n <\infty$. It follows that, for $u\geq 1$,
\[
    \P(U>u) \ll u^{-3} e^{-\frac{cu^2}{2\eta^2}} \sum_{n\in \N} b_n \ll u^{-3} e^{-\frac{cu^2}{2\eta^2}} \,.
\]
This implies the exponential moment bound for any $\lambda >0$ via the layer-cake formula.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}
