{"assumptions":["a centered Gaussian process, almost surely bounded on the index set, for Borell-TIS","for Slepian/Sudakov-Fernique: two Gaussian processes on the same index set with pointwise increment-variance domination E[(X_s-X_t)^2]<=E[(Y_s-Y_t)^2]","for the classical Slepian tail comparison specifically: equal marginal variances or a nonnegative-correlation condition, beyond the plain increment domination Sudakov-Fernique needs","measurability and separability of the process so the supremum is well defined"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.986173+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_65504cb28ab92ac996647f611e0658cd9e04f5e99731dc3bc37859c9883f39af","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a centered, almost surely bounded Gaussian process (X_t)_{t in T}, let M = sup_t X_t and sigma^2 = sup_t Var(X_t). The Borell-TIS inequality states P(|M - E[M]| >= u) <= 2 exp(-u^2/(2 sigma^2)) for all u >= 0, giving Gaussian concentration of the supremum around its mean at the scale of the process's maximal pointwise variance, regardless of the cardinality or geometry of the index set. Separately, Slepian's inequality compares two centered Gaussian processes on the same index set with equal marginal variances: if E[(X_s-X_t)^2] <= E[(Y_s-Y_t)^2] for all s,t, then E[sup X] <= E[sup Y], and in its classical strong form also gives a tail comparison, typically under an additional nonnegative-correlation condition. The Sudakov-Fernique inequality removes the equal-variance requirement, needing only the pointwise increment domination, but concludes only the expectation comparison E[sup X] <= E[sup Y], not the stronger distributional comparison. Together these tools reduce bounding E[sup] of a complicated Gaussian field to bounding it for a simpler, dominating comparison field. Borell-TIS does not give the value of E[M] itself, which requires a separate chaining or Dudley-integral bound, and Sudakov-Fernique is strictly weaker in conclusion than the classical Slepian inequality even when both sets of hypotheses happen to hold. Typical failure: Invoking the classical Slepian inequality's tail or distributional comparison after only verifying the weaker Sudakov-Fernique hypotheses, namely increment domination without equal variances or a correlation-sign condition; Sudakov-Fernique licenses comparing E[sup X] to E[sup Y] only, and treating the two comparison theorems as interchangeable overstates what has actually been proven. Canonical reference: Borell, 1975, Inventiones Mathematicae; Tsirelson, Ibragimov and Sudakov, 1976, in Proceedings of the School-Seminar on Random Processes; Slepian, 1962, Bell System Technical Journal; Fernique, 1975, Ecole d'Ete de Probabilites de Saint-Flour, Springer Lecture Notes in Mathematics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:25:55.419507+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6585827fa57b1cba75cc4450775110bff75c4097e65160bca2568dc51d4f4b19","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 9 (Restricted Yamada--Watanabe theorem) of arXiv:2607.28078, '2607.28078'] Fix $\mu_0\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$ and define $\mathfrak K_{\mathcal V}\subset\mathcal P(\mathcal C_T)$ by

\nu\circ e_t^{-1}\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\text{ for every }t\in[0,T],\,\,
\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\mathcal V(t,\nu\circ e_t^{-1})<\infty\big\},
\]
where $e_t(w):=w(t)$ for $w\in\mathcal{C}_T$.
		
For any weak solution $(X,B)$ of \eqref{2.1} in the sense of Definition~$\rm\ref{de.2.1}$, defined on a filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\{\mathcal F_t\},\mathbb P)$, set
\[
Y:=\bigl(X(0),B|_{[0,T]}\bigr),\,\,Y_t:=\bigl(X(0),B|_{[0,t]}\bigr),\,\,t\in[0,T].
\]
Such a weak solution $(X,B)$ is called compatible if $X$ is continuous and adapted and, for every $t\in[0,T]$ and every bounded Borel function
\[
h:C([0,t];\mathbb R^d)\rightarrow\mathbb R,
\]
one has
\[
\mathbb E\left[
h\bigl(X|_{[0,t]}\bigr)|\sigma(Y)\right]
=
\mathbb E\left[h\bigl(X|_{[0,t]}\bigr)|\sigma(Y_t)\right]\,\,\text{a.s.}
\]
A compatible weak solution $(X,B)$ is called $\mathfrak K_{\mathcal V}$-admissible if $\mathcal L_X\in\mathfrak K_{\mathcal V}$. Assume that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[$\rm(1)$] There exists a compatible $\mathfrak K_{\mathcal V}$-admissible weak solution of \eqref{2.1}.
\item[$\rm(2)$] Pathwise uniqueness in the sense of Definition~$\rm\ref{de.2.1}$ holds within the class of $\mathfrak K_{\mathcal V}$-admissible strong solutions.

Then there exists a Borel measurable non-anticipative map

\]
such that, for every $t\in[0,T]$, there is a Borel map
\[
\Phi_t:\mathbb R^d\times C([0,t];\mathbb R^m)\rightarrow C([0,t];\mathbb R^d)
\]
satisfying
\[
\Phi(x,w)|_{[0,t]}=\Phi_t\bigl(x,w|_{[0,t]}\bigr).
\]
		
		Moreover, on every filtered probability space carrying an

{"assumptions":["Target depth q>=1 and frozen depth L>=q, equal square width D","Bounded input set and ReLU at every layer","All biases are trainable without size constraints","Assumption1: frozen weights and every stated partial low-rank correction are nonsingular","Rank threshold at least ceil(maximum block error rank /floor(L/q))","No claim about learnability or finite-sample excess risk"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:35:31.991783+00:00","domain":"Zeng Lee LoRA low-rank adaptation expressive power matrix products ReLU bounded input trainable biases","id":"claim_65ab79facc7e5634c486f22a7c53f79dafb40b4406cd3a7c8616bf7e22034ff9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let a target width-D ReLU FNN have depth q>=1, weights A_i and biases a_i, i=1,...,q. All weights are real D-by-D matrices; every layer, including the output layer, applies ReLU. Let X subset R^D be bounded, M=floor(L/q), and partition the frozen layers into consecutive blocks P_i={(i-1)M+1,...,iM} for i<q and P_q={(q-1)M+1,...,L}. For fixed integer 1<=R<=D, assume every W_l and every B_i+LR_j(E_i) for i=1,...,q and integers 0<=j<=R(M-1) are nonsingular, with fixed nested SVD truncations for each E_i. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:18:19.205719+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_65ac24b284fe06da02dd9db3fd83f33d440db54363f285fbabec083a0375e300","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 11 (Block RQ decomposition) of arXiv:2608.28991, 'Jigsaw-CRL: Recovering Global Latent Causal Order from Fragmented Multi-Client Interventio'] For client $k\in[K]$ with block ancestor structure $(\prec_k^\rblk,\cC_k)$, a block RQ decomposition of $\bH_k\in\bbR^{p_k\times n_k}$ is a factorization

{"assumptions":["n>=2, 0<a_i<b_i, b_i,kappa_i>0, h_i(s)=a_i+b_i tanh(kappa_i s), average logistic loss, continuous Euclidean gradient flow in (v,k,q). Complete leaf classification only for C!=0; open escaping basins in full space; no discrete full-space assertion."],"created_at":"2026-10-22T02:46:09.774847+00:00","domain":"optimization and attention dynamics","id":"claim_65ea29b518db264e147ffc601a13037ce84230f2e321f234075bb47770924c02","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"STATUS: proof (unaudited), own-work draft. For the coupled scalar two-token joint-head factored-attention logistic gradient flow, every nonzero-imbalance leaf k^2-q^2=C has a unique reduced saddle and two escaping basins. In full R^3 almost every initialization escapes with kq,v of matching infinite sign, factors O(sqrt(log |v|)), head-normalized limit +/-e_v and margin Gamma_+ or Gamma_-. The finite saddle-stable set plus balanced planes is null. Balanced k=-q, v>0 and max root<kq<0 instead collapse to uniform attention and margin min a_i, showing an actual third fate on a null surface.

# Target 1: almost-everywhere full-space factored gradient-flow classification

Version 1, proof unaudited. Own work; novelty unestablished.
This concerns continuous gradient flow, not arbitrary-step GD.

## Statement

For n>=2, b_i,kappa_i>0, 0<a_i<b_i, set
h_i(s)=a_i+b_i tanh(kappa_i s) and
L(v,k,q)=mean_i log(1+exp(-v h_i(kq))).
Let p_bar be the unique zero of mean_i h_i. For every initial point with
C=k^2-q^2!=0, the Euclidean gradient flow exists globally forward and has
exactly one of these outcomes:

1. convergence to a finite point on the stationary curve v=0,kq=p_bar;
2. v,kq->+infinity, loss->0, normalized direction (v,k,q)/norm ->(1,0,0);
3. v,kq->-infinity, loss->0, normalized direction ->(-1,0,0).

The set in outcome 1, together with the excluded balanced surfaces C=0,
has three-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. Hence almost every finite
initialization belongs to one of the two escaping basins. Both basins
are open in the FULL parameter space, are nonempty, and have respective
normalized minimum margins Gamma_+=min_i(a_i+b_i) and Gamma_-=min_i(b_i-a_i).
The second is strictly inferior, as in claim 010. The known imbalance
invariant is used for reduction, not claimed as a new result.

We do not classify trajectories on C=0 in this theorem. They really allow
another fate: on k=q=0, v solves v_dot=mean_i a_i/(1+exp(v a_i))>0,
so v->infinity and L->0 while attention stays uniform. In fact a relatively
open subset of the balanced plane has this fate: if k=-q!=0, v>0 and
R<kq<0, where R=max_i rho_i<0, then v increases, s increases toward zero,
and k,q tend to zero. To check this, all h_i(s)>=c>0, forcing v->infinity.
If s tended to a strictly negative limit, alpha=2|s| and all h_i' would
be bounded below there; ds/dv>=c_1 v would contradict bounded s. Thus
s->0 and both factors vanish. Its normalized margin is min_i a_i.
These null sets demonstrate why the almost-everywhere qualification
must not be omitted.

## Reduction and global existence

Put s=kq, F=mean_i g_i h_i(s), G=mean_i g_i h_i'(s)>0,
g_i=(1+exp(v h_i(s)))^-1. Flow equations are

 v_dot=F, k_dot=vqG, q_dot=vkG.

Differentiating gives d(k^2-q^2)/dt=0. Also
(k^2+q^2)^2=C^2+4s^2. Thus on a fixed nonzero-C leaf,

 v_dot=F(v,s), s_dot=alpha_C(s) vG(v,s),
 alpha_C(s)=sqrt(C^2+4s^2)>0.

If H=max_i(a_i+b_i), M=max_i b_i kappa_i, then |v_dot|<=H.
On any finite time interval v is bounded, and
|k_dot|+|q_dot|<=M|v|(|k|+|q|). Gronwall gives finite factors on that
interval. The smooth full flow therefore has no finite-time blow-up,
in either time direction. Nonzero-C leaf coordinates are global charts on
each sheet: for C>0 fix sign k, solve
k=sign(k)sqrt((alpha_C(s)+C)/2), q=s/k;
for C<0 instead fix sign q and use the symmetric formula.

## Leaf saddle and trapping

Let A=H^2/4 and F_0(s)=F(0,s)=mean_i h_i(s)/2. Then
-A<=F_v<=0, F_0 strictly increases with unique zero p_bar, and G>0.
The sole reduced equilibrium is (0,p_bar), corresponding to one point
on each sheet. With u=s-p_bar, the two good quadrants v,u>0 and v,u<0
are forward invariant: s_dot has sign v; on the boundary v=0 the vector
field F_0(s) points into the respective quadrant. More explicitly, in
the positive quadrant v_dot>=-A v, so a strictly positive v cannot hit zero
in finite time, and u increases. Reflection treats the negative quadrant.

In a bad quadrant v>0,u<0, F(v,s)<=F_0(s)<0 and s_dot>0.
Both coordinates move monotonically toward their axes until one axis is
crossed or the orbit stays forever. Crossing an axis enters a good quadrant;
uniqueness excludes hitting the equilibrium in finite time. If the orbit
stays in the bad quadrant, it has a finite limit. Continuity and monotonicity
force F=alpha_C vG=0 at that limit, hence it is the saddle.
The other bad quadrant is handled by the reflected links -h_i(-s).
Nonstationary points on an axis enter a good quadrant immediately.

## Escape from good quadrants

Consider the positive quadrant. Then s increases from s_0>p_bar.
Suppose s tends to finite P. If v is bounded, compactness and
alpha_C G>0 imply integral_0^infinity v(t)dt<infinity.
Since |v_dot|<=H, the nonnegative function v is uniformly continuous;
the elementary disjoint-triangle argument gives v->0. But then
v_dot->F_0(P)>0, contradiction.

If v is unbounded, put R=max_i rho_i, h_i(rho_i)=0. If P<=R,
an example j with root R has h_j(s(t))<=0, hence g_j>=1/2;
on the compact s interval its derivative is >=d>0. Consequently
s_dot>=|C| d v/(2n). A finite P again implies integral v<infinity
and, by the same bounded-derivative argument, v->0: contradiction.
If P>R, eventually all h_i>=c>0. Then v increases without bound and

 ds/dv=alpha_C(s) v (mean g_i h_i')/(mean g_i h_i)
       >=|C| d v/H,

contradicting finite P. Thus s->infinity. Eventually all h_i>=c>0;
v increases and cannot remain bounded, since bounded v keeps every g_i
bounded below. Therefore v->infinity. Reflection proves negative escape.

For the direction, let kappa_0=min_i kappa_i. On the positive tail,
alpha_C(s)<=|C|+2s and

 ds/dv<=(4M/c)(|C|+2s)v exp(-2kappa_0 s).

Thus d[exp(kappa_0 s)]/dv <=C_1 v, because
(|C|+2s)exp(-kappa_0 s) is bounded on the positive tail.
Integration gives s=O(log v). Since k^2+q^2=alpha_C(s), both
factors are O(sqrt(log v)) and are negligible relative to v.
The negative branch is identical after reflection. Endpoint margin and
zero-loss limits follow. By fixed C and |s|->infinity, both |k| and |q|
also tend to infinity (their squared difference is constant).

## Leaf-null implies full-space-null

At the reduced equilibrium the linearization is

 [[-A_s,B_s],[alpha_C(p_bar) B_s,0]],
 A_s=mean h_i(p_bar)^2/4, B_s=mean h_i'(p_bar)/2>0.

Its determinant is negative; it is a hyperbolic saddle. The local stable
manifold is one-dimensional. The global stable set on a leaf is contained
in its countably many backward integer-time flow images, so is planar null;
the flow is a smooth local diffeomorphism (indeed globally defined here).

The full stationary curve E={v=0,kq=p_bar} is closed. The set
S={initial points whose distance to E tends to zero} is Borel: express
the limiting condition using countable thresholds and integer times.
For C!=0 our classification shows S is exactly the convergent set;
the leaf coordinate formulas also show convergence of k,q when s->p_bar.
Use coordinates (v,s,C) on the four open regions C>0,sign k fixed and
C<0,sign q fixed. Each coordinate map is a smooth diffeomorphism.
Every fixed-C slice of S is planar null by the preceding argument.
Fubini gives a null set in these coordinates; local diffeomorphisms
preserve null sets under a countable cover. Finally C=0 is the union of
the two planes k=q and k=-q, also null. This proves the asserted full-space
almost-everywhere dichotomy, without assuming independence across examples.

The escaping basins are open even at balanced initial points: any escaping
orbit eventually enters a strict region v>0,s>max(R,0) or v<0,s<min rho_i.
Those regions are invariant and escape, also when C=0, by the same proof
with alpha=2|s| bounded below there. (Requiring s>0 on the positive branch
is essential; a balanced negative product can instead collapse to zero.)
The union of their finite-time preimages
is open. For arbitrary escaping points the converse follows from divergence
of s. They are nonempty by claim 010's sign regions. No assertion that every
balanced trajectory escapes is needed.

## Literature scope and remaining obstruction

The comparisons in proof 008 apply: 2308.16898 and 2403.08699 treat
fixed-head factored attention, while this is the stated scalar joint-head
logistic family. The balance reduction is standard and is not a novelty claim.
For simultaneous GD, C_+=(1-eta^2 v^2 G^2)C, so these invariant leaves
are unavailable. Extending this full-space result to GD remains open here;
claim 010 proves only its arbitrary-step open sign basins.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:43:04.688180+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_663938c108752f088bd0a3109d641860594767a03c711072c35d22e8326be053","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 27 of arXiv:2605.17296, 'Zero correlations and averaged fields of orthonormal Gaussian Functions'] For fixed $k \ge 1$, as $n \to \infty$, 
the short-range correlations between the zeros of
 $\spec_{h_{n}}\cW(z)$ and
 $\spec_{h_{n+k}}\cW(z)$ are 
\begin{equation*}
g_{n,n+k}(z,z) = 
\begin{cases}
\disp 1-\frac{5}{4n^{2}}+O\left( \frac{1}{n^{3}}\right) <1 & \text{if $k=1$}, \\[4mm]
\disp \frac{4}{3}+
\frac{1}{12n^2}+O\left( \frac{1}{n^3}\right) 
>1 &
 \text{if $k=2$}, 
\\[4mm]
\disp 1 & \text{if $k\geq 3$}.  
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}
Thus, the short-range correlations
between zeros of $\spec_{h_{n}}\cW(z)$ and zeros of 
$\spec_{h_{n+k}}\cW(z)$ display repulsion if $k=1$, 
attraction if $k=2$, and no short-range second-order correlation in the contact
 limit if $k\geq 3$. Moreover, $g_{n,n+1}(z,z)$ increases
 with $n$ and $g_{n,n+1}(z,z) \to 1$, and
$g_{n,n+2}(z,z)$ attains its maximum at $n=2$ and then
 decreases for $n\geq 2$,

{"assumptions":["all moments m_k of the measure are finite","the specific growth rate of the even moments m_{2k}, needed to check whether sum m_{2k}^{-1/(2k)} diverges","if a simpler sufficient condition is invoked instead, such as compact support or subgaussian tails, that condition must itself be independently verified","the moment-convergence method is being used to establish convergence in distribution to a specific candidate limit that is separately known to be moment-determinate"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.994936+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_66433380dc750c0be230a31fb21285dac83b7ea69a958dffd48040d2335c57a8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). A probability measure mu on R is moment-determinate if it is the unique probability measure sharing its full sequence of moments (m_k)_{k>=0}. The Carleman condition gives a simple sufficient criterion: if sum_{k=1}^infinity m_{2k}^{-1/(2k)} = infinity, then mu is moment-determinate. In practice this is most often invoked via a stronger, easier-to-check sub-condition, such as subgaussian or lighter tails, for instance P(|X|>t) <= C exp(-ct^2), which implies the even moments grow at most at Gaussian rate and hence satisfy Carleman's sum divergence; a common proof strategy in random matrix theory and random measure convergence is to show convergence of all moments to those of a known moment-determinate limit, such as the compactly supported semicircle law, and then invoke Carleman's condition, or compact support directly, to upgrade moment convergence to convergence in distribution. It does not hold automatically for every measure with finite moments of all orders: the classical log-normal distribution is the standard counterexample, having finite moments of every order yet failing to be moment-determinate, so other measures share its entire moment sequence, meaning that verifying Carleman's sum diverges, or invoking compact support, is a genuinely necessary step, not a formality. Typical failure: Assuming that finiteness of all moments, or even termwise convergence of a sequence's moments to a limit's moments, is sufficient to conclude convergence in distribution, without checking that the limit measure is itself moment-determinate; the log-normal-type failure of moment determinacy is the standard cautionary example, and in random matrix or random measure contexts, using the method of moments toward a limit whose determinacy has not been separately established, as happens for some heavy-tailed spectral limits, can produce a plausible-looking but invalid convergence claim. Canonical reference: Carleman, 1926, Les Fonctions Quasi Analytiques, Gauthier-Villars; Akhiezer, The Classical Moment Problem, 1965, Hafner Publishing; Anderson, Guionnet and Zeitouni, An Introduction to Random Matrices, 2010, Cambridge University Press.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Counterexample flux f(u) = u^4 - 5u^2 with states u_- = 2, u_+ = -2, shock speed σ = 0","Lax inequalities compare σ only with f'(u_-) and f'(u_+)","Oleinik's condition requires the graph of f between the two states to lie on the correct side of the chord at EVERY intermediate value","For nonconvex flux the Riemann solution is generally a composite of shocks and rarefactions given by the convex (or concave) hull construction"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418807+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: hyperbolic conservation laws","id":"claim_665fbc7218ee86a7f2a8fde5b2aa270eb45fa9903d84e1f03383d32859a141ad","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: the equivalence 'admissible shock ⇔ Lax inequalities f'(u_-) ≥ σ ≥ f'(u_+)' requires the flux to be convex (genuinely nonlinear) on the range of the data. For a nonconvex flux one must use Oleinik's full chord condition, which involves f at every intermediate state, not only the two endpoint derivatives. Counterexample: f(u) = u^4 - 5u^2 (so f'(u) = 4u^3 - 10u), left state u_- = 2, right state u_+ = -2. Since f(2) = f(-2) = -4, Rankine-Hugoniot gives the stationary shock σ = 0, and the Lax inequalities hold strictly: f'(2) = 12 > 0 > f'(-2) = -12. Yet the shock is NOT admissible: the chord joining (-2,-4) and (2,-4) is the constant -4, while f(0) = 0 lies ABOVE it, so Oleinik's condition fails; equivalently the Kruzhkov inequality with k = 0 requires σ(k - u_-) ≥ f(k) - f(u_-), i.e. 0 ≥ 4, which is false. The correct entropy solution of this Riemann problem is read off the least concave majorant of f on [-2,2] (the hull construction for a decreasing jump u_l > u_r): a shock from u_- = 2 down to u* = (√7 - 2)/3 ≈ 0.2153, the point at which the line through (2, f(2)) is tangent to the graph of f, then an attached rarefaction from u* down to -u*, then, by symmetry, a shock from -u* to u_+ = -2. The two shock speeds are -(16 + 14u*)/9 ≈ -2.113 and +(16 + 14u*)/9 ≈ +2.113, and the rarefaction sweeps the speeds between them. Auditor's check: whenever a proof calls a jump admissible using only characteristic speeds, verify convexity of the flux on the interval spanned by the two states; otherwise test the whole chord.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:07:17.249850+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_666b7060b785fe74fc5352b820b8d24171009509f3662e151db86ff156941cc7","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2603.12774, 'Synchronization by noise for stochastic differential equations driven by fractional Browni'] Let $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$ be a probability space. 
	The space of random Lipschitz functions denoted by \(\mathrm{BL}_{\Omega}(\mathbb{R}^d) \) consists of all functions \( g : \mathbb{R}^d \times \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) satisfying the following properties.
	\begin{itemize}
		\item For every \( \omega \in \Omega \), the function \( x \mapsto g(x,\omega) \) is continuous.
		\item For every \( x \in \mathbb{R}^d \), the function \( \omega \mapsto g(x,\omega) \) is measurable.
		\item There exists a constant \( M > 0 \) such that on a set of full measure in \( \Omega \) 
		\begin{align*}
			\| g(\cdot, \omega) \|_{\mathrm{BL}} < M,
		\end{align*}
		where
		\[
		\| g(\cdot, \omega) \|_{\mathrm{BL}} := \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}^d} |g(x,\omega)| + \sup_{\substack{x, y \in \mathbb{R}^d \\ x \neq y}} \frac{|g(x,\omega) - g(y,\omega)|}{|x - y|}.
		\]
	\end{itemize}
	Furthermore 
	\[
	\mathrm{Pr}_{\Omega}(\mathbb{R}^d) := \left\{ \nu \text{ is a probability measure on } \mathbb{R}^d \times \Omega \,\middle|\, \left( \Pi_{\Omega} \right)_{\ast} \nu = \mathbb{P} \right\},
	\]
	where $\Pi$ denotes the projection onto $\Omega$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:48:43.477475+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_669a46c315126270f9e734898a5539a740d6287194abc7f6cea0a4dd595a96db","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 6 (Universality for random polynomials) of arXiv:2608.06576, 'The Resultant Distribution Method: Universality for $p$-adic Random Matrices and Polynomia'] Let $K_1,\ldots,K_m$ be finite extensions of $\Q_p$, and let

$$

$$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:43:19.216147+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_66b87f22ee1c033d847f59481538289cacb7026929def84673dd9d49d1604edd","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 2605211341 of arXiv:2609.02626, 'Comparison principles and symmetry for subquadratic fractional $p$-Laplacian equations'] Let $N\ge 1$, $s\in (0, 1)$ and $p>1$. Suppose that $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ is a bounded open set, and $u\in \widetilde{W}^{s,p}(\Omega)$ is a weak solution of
\[
(-\Delta)_p^s u= g\quad \mbox{in } \Omega,
\]
for some $g\in L^1_{loc}(\Omega)\cap W_0^{s, p}(\Omega)'$. Let $v\in L^1_{loc}(\mathbb{R}^N)$  satisfy
\[
{\rm dist}({\rm supp}(v), \Omega)>0, \quad \int_{\Omega^c}\frac{|v(x)|^{p-1}}{(1+|x|)^{N+sp}} {\rm d}x<\infty.
\]
Define
\[
h(x)=2\int_{{\rm supp} (v)}\frac{J_{u+v}(x, y)-J_u(x, y)}{|x-y|^{N+sp}} {\rm d}y, \quad \mbox{for a.e. }x\in \Omega.
\]
Then $u+v\in \widetilde{W}^{s,p}(\Omega)$ and it solves weakly $(-\Delta)_p^s (u+v)= g+h$ in $\Omega$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:37:08.955232+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_66be1bf41a6e82448dfc48f38f1008a70134bd27f82cab6bf7cc104ad125256a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:explicit_current_1 of arXiv:2609.01581, 'Concentration of additive functionals of Stratonovich-type'] Let $(X_t)_{t\geq 0}$ be an ergodic diffusion with invariant measure $\mu$ whose
symmetric part $\mathcal{L}_S$ satisfies the Poincar\'e inequality~(equation eq:poincare of the paper)
with spectral gap $\lambda_\mathrm{gap}>0$ (Assumptions~(ass:dynamics of the paper)). 
Let $\overline{J}_t(U)$ denote the empirical current according to Definition~(def:empirical_current of the paper)
with ergodic mean $\E^\mu[\overline{J}_t(U)]=\E^\mu[v_{\textrm{s}}\cdot U]= \E^\mu[W]$,
and let $\nu\ll\mu$ with $\mathrm{d}\nu/\mathrm{d}\mu\in L^2(\mu)$.
Then for all $t > 0$ and $a > 0$,
\begin{align}
  \mathbb{P}^\nu\left(\overline{J}_t(U) - \E^\mu[\overline{J}_t] \geq a\right)
  \leq
  \left\|\frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}
  \exp\left[-t\frac{\tilde\sigma_{J,1}^2}{c_{J,1}^2}h\left(\frac{c_{J,1} a}{\tilde\sigma_{J,1}^2}\right)\right],
  
\end{align}
where $h(u) \equiv 1 + u - \sqrt{1+2u}$ and we define
\begin{align}
  \tilde\sigma_{J,1}^2 \equiv
  \frac{2\mathrm{Var}_\mu(W)}{\lambda_\mathrm{gap}} + 2\|Q\|_{L^\infty(\mu)},
  \qquad 
  c_{J,1} \equiv \frac{\|W-\E^\mu[W]\|_{L^\infty(\mu)}}{\lambda_\mathrm{gap}}.
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:09:34.479691+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_66c93fb63c7270b2380d77ed2a91e014ad71f870d0f8a4e5e3c55fd34dfb1499","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn local_multiple_radial_SLE_kappa of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] The locally commuting $n$-radial $\mathrm{SLE}(\kappa)$ is a compatible family of measures 
\[
\mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega; z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n, q\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n\right)}
\]
on $n$-tuples of continuous, non-self-crossing curves $\left(\gamma^{(1)}, \gamma^{(2)}, \ldots, \gamma^{(n)}\right)$ for all simply connected domains $\Omega$ with marked points $\left(z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n, q\right)$ and target sets $\left(U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n\right)$. These measures satisfy the following conditions:

\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] \textbf{Conformal invariance}: If $\varphi: \Omega \to \Omega^\prime$ is a conformal map, then the pullback measure satisfies
    \[
    \varphi^* \mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega^\prime; \varphi(z_1), \varphi(z_2), \ldots, \varphi(z_n), \varphi(q)\right)}^{\left(\varphi(U_1), \varphi(U_2), \ldots, \varphi(U_n)\right)} 
    = \mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega; z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n, u\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n\right)}.
    \]
    It suffices to describe the measure when $\left(\Omega; z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n, q\right) = \left(\mathbb{D}; z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n, 0\right)$. The definition for arbitrary $\Omega$ with a marked interior point $q$ can then be extended by pulling back via a conformal equivalence $\varphi: \Omega \to \mathbb{D}$ mapping $q$ to $0$.

    \item[(ii)] \textbf{Domain Markov property}: Let $\left(\gamma^{(1)}, \gamma^{(2)}, \ldots, \gamma^{(n)}\right) \sim \mathbb{P}_{\left(\mathbb{D}; z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n, q\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n\right)}$, and parametrize $\gamma^{(j)}$ by their own capacity in $\mathbb{D}$. For stopping times $\mathbf{t} = (t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_n)$, define
    \[
    \tilde{U}_j = U_j \setminus \gamma^{(j)}_{[0, t_j]}, \quad 
    \tilde{\gamma}^{(j)} = \gamma^{(j)} \setminus \gamma^{(j)}_{[0, t_j]}, \quad 
    \tilde{\Omega} = \mathbb{D} \setminus \bigcup_{j=1}^n \gamma^{(j)}_{[0, t_j]}.
    \]
    Then, conditionally on the initial segments $\bigcup_{j=1}^n \gamma^{(j)}_{[0, t_j]}$, we have
    \[
    \left(\tilde{\gamma}^{(1)}, \tilde{\gamma}^{(2)}, \ldots, \tilde{\gamma}^{(n)}\right) 
    \sim \mathbb{P}_{\left(\tilde{\Omega}; \gamma^{(1)}_{t_1}, \gamma^{(2)}_{t_2}, \ldots, \gamma^{(n)}_{t_n}, q\right)}^{\left(\tilde{U}_1, \tilde{U}_2, \ldots, \tilde{U}_n\right)}.
    \]

    \item[(iii)] \textbf{Absolute Continuity with respect to independent SLE($\kappa$)}: Let $\left(\gamma^{(1)}, \gamma^{(2)}, \ldots, \gamma^{(n)}\right) \sim \mathbb{P}_{\left(\mathbb{D}; z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n, 0\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n\right)}$. Let $z_j(t) = e^{i \theta_j(t)}$, the capacity-parametrized Loewner driving function $t \mapsto \theta_j(t)$ for $\gamma^{(j)}$ satisfies
    \[ 
    \begin{aligned}
    \mathrm{d} \theta_j(t) &= \sqrt{\kappa} \, \mathrm{d} B_j(t) + b_j\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}(t)\right) \, \mathrm{d} t, \\
    \mathrm{d} \theta_k(t) &= \cot\left(\frac{\theta_k(t) - \theta_j(t)}{2}\right) \, \mathrm{d} t, \quad k \neq j,
    \end{aligned}
    \]
    where $B_j(t)$ are independent standard Brownian motions, and $b_j(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ are $C^2$ functions on the chamber 
    \[
    \mathfrak{X}^n = \left\{(\theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots, \theta_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n \mid \theta_1 < \theta_2 < \cdots < \theta_n < \theta_1 + 2\pi \right\}.
    \]
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:00:46.818420+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_66dae1f263bfb73f200c971c2d1e6a91e3c0a4f3487b48b23f92b3734ce1557b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.12839, 'Spiking Neural Networks with Elephant Reinforcement'] Let \(N<\infty\). Consider the process
\[
Y_t=(V_t,S_t,K_t)
\in \mathbb N^N\times\mathbb Z^N\times\mathbb N^N.
\]
Assume that site \(i\) fires with rate
\[
\lambda_i(V,S,K)
=
\mathbf 1_{\{V_i>\alpha S_i^+\}},
\qquad
S_i^+=\max\{S_i,0\},
\]
and leaks with rate
\[
\gamma\mathbf 1_{\{V_i>0\}},
\qquad \gamma>0.
\]
When site \(i\) fires, \(V_i\) is reset to \(0\), its two neighbours receive
one unit of potential, and
\[
S_i\mapsto S_i+\xi_i,
\qquad
K_i\mapsto K_i+1.
\]
Then the process is non-explosive. More precisely, if \(N_t\) denotes the
number of events up to time \(t\), then
\[
\mathbb E[N_t]\leq (\gamma+1)Nt<\infty.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:47.660058+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_674525594e1400ab577a43864f32df8d210576f11d7338405146f3c32bb15242","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 22 (Two-parameter rough integral on rectangular domains) of arXiv:2605.08844, 'Signature Kernel and Schwinger-Dyson Kernel Equations as Two-Parameter Rough Differential '] Let 
\[
Z \in \mathcal{D}^{p, q}_{\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}}\big([a, b] \times [c,d], \mathrm{Hom}(V \boxtimes W, F)\big).
\] 
Then the limit
\[
\int_{[a,b] \times [c,d]} Z_{s, u} \, d(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y})  
   :=  \lim_{\left|\mathcal{P} \times \mathcal{D}\right| \to 0} 
   \sum_{\mathcal{P}\times \mathcal{D}} \Omega^Z
\]
exists and satisfies the estimate
\begin{align*}
\Bigg|
\int_{[a,b]\times[c,d]} Z_{s,u}\, d(\mathbf{X}_s,\mathbf{Y}_u)
- \Omega^Z\begin{pmatrix} a, b \\ c, d \end{pmatrix}
\Bigg|
&\le C_{p,q,T}\Big[
      A(\theta,T,\mathbf{R})\,
      \omega_{\mathbf{X}}(a,b)^{\theta}\,
      \omega_{\mathbf{Y}}(c,d)^{\theta} \\
&\qquad
      + B_X(c,d)\,\omega_{\mathbf{X}}(a,b)^{\theta}
      + B_Y(a,b)\,\omega_{\mathbf{Y}}(c,d)^{\theta}
\Big].
\end{align*}

where $\theta = \min(\frac{\floor{p} + 1}{p}, \frac{\floor{q} + 1}{q})$ and 
\begin{align*}
&A(p, q, \mathbf{R}) 
= \left( \sup_{j \in [0:\kappa)} \| \mathbf{X}^{(j+1)} \|_{p_j} \right)
  \left( \sup_{k \in  [0:\lambda)} \| \tilde{\mathbf{X}}^{(k+1)} \|_{\tilde{p}_k} \right)
  \left( \sup_{(j,k)\in [0:\kappa) \times [0:\lambda)} \| \mathbf{R}^{(j,k)} \|_{(q_j,\tilde{q}_k)} \right),\\
&B_{X}(c,d)
= 
\sup_{(j,k)\in [0:\kappa) \times [0:\lambda)}\left[ 
  \|\mathbf{X}^{(j+1)}\|_{\frac{p}{j+1}}\,
  \|\mathbf{Y}^{(k+1)}\|_{\frac{q}{k+1}}\,
  \big\| R^{1, (j,k)}
       \big\|_{\frac{p}{\kappa - j}}\,
  \omega_{\mathbf{Y}}(c,d)^{\frac{k+1}{q}}
\right],\\
&B_{Y}(a,b)
= \sup_{(j,k)\in [0:\kappa) \times [0:\lambda)}
\left[
   \|\mathbf{X}^{(j+1)}\|_{\frac{p}{j+1}}\,
  \|\mathbf{Y}^{(k+1)}\|_{\frac{q}{k+1}}\,
  \big\| R^{2,(j,k)}\!
       \big\|_{\frac{q}{\lambda - k}}\,
  \omega_{\mathbf{X}}(a,b)^{\frac{j+1}{p}}
\right].
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:48:27.285487+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_674b70b5dfcacb4443243655f9cf77d72cf2fe319fd2c5b29a9a9f5943515b20","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 13 of arXiv:2604.25470, 'A mathematical analysis of hierarchical Hopfield models'] Fix $\alpha$ and suppose that $\mathcal G_\alpha(\delta,\rho)$ holds.
	Then 
	\[
	\mathrm{score}^{\mathrm{pen}}_\alpha(x)
	\ge
	a(1-\delta)L_\alpha-bL_\alpha,
	\]
	and for every $\beta\neq\alpha$,
	\[
	\mathrm{score}^{\mathrm{pen}}_\beta(x)
	\le
	a\bigl(|S_\alpha\cap S_\beta|+\rho\bigr)-bL_\beta.
	\]
	
	Consequently,
	\[
	\mathrm{score}^{\mathrm{pen}}_\alpha(x)
	-
	\mathrm{score}^{\mathrm{pen}}_\beta(x)
	\ge
	a\bigl(
	(1-\delta)L_\alpha
	-
	|S_\alpha\cap S_\beta|
	-
	\rho	
	\bigr)
	-
	b(L_\alpha-L_\beta).
	\]
	
	In particular, if
	\[
	|S_\alpha\cap S_\beta|
	<
	(1-\delta)L_\alpha-\rho-\frac{b}{a}(L_\alpha-L_\beta),
	\]
	then
	\[
	\mathrm{score}^{\mathrm{pen}}_\alpha(x)
	>
	\mathrm{score}^{\mathrm{pen}}_\beta(x).
	\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:11:09.304561+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_675a8b029d9273fc136a6ef5d14c08043f9167b170d8ad1d220246b964fb881c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem RoughInt of arXiv:2411.06089, '{\Large \bf Averaging principle for semilinear slow-fast rough partial differential equati'] \emph{([GH19])}
For any $T>0$, let $\mathbf X=(X,X^2)\in \mathscr{C}^\gamma([0,T]; \mathbb R^d)$ for some $\gamma\in(1/3,1/2]$ and let
$(Y,Y^{\prime})\in\mathscr{D}_{S,\mathbf X}^{2\gamma}([0,T];\mathcal{H}_\alpha^d)$.
Then one has that the rough integral
$$\int_{s}^{t}S_{t-u}Y_{u}d \mathbf X_u:=\lim_{|\mathcal{P}|\to 0}\sum_{[u,v]\in\mathcal{P}}S_{t-u}(Y_u \delta X_{v,u}+Y_{u}^{\prime} X^2_{v,u})$$
exists in $\hat{C}^\gamma([0,T];\mathcal{H}_\alpha)$,
where the limit is taken along any partitions $\mathcal P$ of $[s,t]$ such that mesh $|\mathcal P| \rightarrow 0$.
Furthermore, for any $0\leq\beta<3\gamma$ one has the bound
\begin{align} 
& \Big \|\int_{s}^{t}S_{t-u}Y_{u}d \mathbf X_{u}-S_{t-s}Y_{s} \delta X_{t,s}-S_{t-s}Y_{s}^{\prime} X^2_{t,s} \Big\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\alpha+\beta}} \nonumber\\
 \lesssim &   \big(|R^{Y}|_{2\gamma,\alpha}|X|_{\gamma}+\|Y'\|_{\gamma,\alpha}|X^2|_{2\gamma}\big)|t-s|^{3\gamma-\beta},
\end{align}
and the map
$$(Y,Y')\rightarrow (U,U'):=\Big(\int_0^\cdot S_{\cdot-u}Y_u d \mathbf X_u,Y \Big)$$
is continuous from $\mathscr D_{S,\mathbf X}^{2\gamma} ([0,T]; \mathcal{H}_\alpha^d )$ to $\mathscr D_{S,\mathbf X}^{2\gamma} ([0,T]; \mathcal{H}_\alpha )$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:20:15.702053+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_675c989d65c4d53f6506a67febf1f7f850aa62de019999b575841303e75cda3e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:wall of arXiv:2609.00970, 'The unique predual problem for Lipschitz spaces, revisited'] A non-empty closed subset $W\subset M$ is a \emph{geodesic wall} in $M$ if there exist two sets $A,B\subset M$ such that
\begin{enumerate}[label={\upshape{(\alph*)}}]
\item $M$ equals the disjoint union $A\cup W\cup B$,
\item $W\subset\overline{A}\cap\overline{B}$,
\item $A,B$ are open and connected, and
\item for any $a\in A$, $b\in B$ there exists $w\in W$ such that $d(a,w)+d(w,b)=d(a,b)$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:00:46.820162+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6764c2c5345756f54b570979e587f66fce4f2efb3d452aa32b02a71a98d2b5da","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 4 of arXiv:2608.13208, 'Universality in dimension $1$ of kinetically constrained lattice gases'] KCLGs in one dimension divide in three universality
classes:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $c(-1,0,\bone_{(-\infty,-1]})\neq0$ and $c(-1,0,\bone_{[0,\infty]})\neq0$,
then $q_{c}=0$. In this case the model is \emph{noncooperative} (see
\cite{Shapira2024Noncooperative} and Section \ref{subsec:noncooperative}
below).
\item If $c(-1,0,\bone_{(-\infty,-1]})=0$ and $c(-1,0,\bone_{[0,\infty)})=0$,
then $q_{c}=1$. We say in this case that the model is \emph{blocked}.
\item If $c(-1,0,\bone_{(-\infty,-1]})\neq0$ and $c(-1,0,\bone_{[0,\infty)})=0$
or vice versa, then $q_{c}\in(0,1)$. We call such models \emph{one-sided}.
\end{enumerate}

mean the configuration filled in $(-\infty,-1]$ (respectively $[0,\infty)$)
and empty elsewhere. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:42:16.236948+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_67f17e10ee06ef353e9e48cc66153a614975698f804d78e94f0e600634ca3a55","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:conjugacy-poc-transfer of arXiv:2607.00149, '\bf Uniform-in-time Propagation-of-Chaos for\\ Stein Variational Gradient Descent'] Let $(\widetilde\pi,\widetilde K)$ be a finite-rank base pair with Stein
feature vector $\widetilde F$, and let $(\pi_H,K_H)$ be any conjugate pair
constructed from a diffeomorphism $H$ as in (equation eq:potential-transform of the paper)
and (equation eq:kernel-transform of the paper).  Denote its Stein feature vector by $F_H$.

Fix an initial law $\widetilde\mu_0$ for the base system, and define the conjugate initial law \( \mu_0^H := H_{\#}\widetilde\mu_0 . \) Let $(\widetilde\mu_t)_{t\ge0}$ be the base mean-field solution started from $\widetilde\mu_0$, and let $(\mu_t^H)_{t\ge0}$ be the transformed mean-field solution started from $\mu_0^H$. Let \( \widetilde X_1(0),\ldots,\widetilde X_N(0) \quad\text{be i.i.d. with law }\widetilde\mu_0, \) and define the transformed initial particles by \( X_i^H(0):=H(\widetilde X_i(0)), \, i=1,\ldots,N. \) Let $\widetilde\mu_t^N$ and $\mu_t^{H,N}$ denote the corresponding empirical particle solutions.

Then, for every $t\ge0$,
\begin{equation}
        d_{F_H}(\mu_t^{H,N},\mu_t^H)
        =
        d_{\widetilde F}(\widetilde\mu_t^N,\widetilde\mu_t).
\end{equation}
Consequently, any propagation-of-chaos estimate for the base pair in the
restricted feature metric transfers to every conjugate pair with the same rate
and the same constant.  In particular, if for some rate $\varepsilon_N\to0$,
\[   
        \mathbb E\left[\sup_{t\ge0}\, d_{\widetilde F}^2(\widetilde\mu_t^N,\widetilde\mu_t)\right]
        \le C\varepsilon_N,
\]
then
\begin{equation}
        \mathbb E\left[\sup_{t\ge0}\, d_{F_H}^2(\mu_t^{H,N},\mu_t^H)\right]
        \le C\varepsilon_N .
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H is a finite bipartite graph with specified parts L and R","the middle capacity is M = |L| + 1 and the terminal capacities are 1","a cut's capacity sums the arcs leaving its source side"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T02:29:07.665365+00:00","domain":"finite bipartite graphs and their flow networks","id":"claim_67f94dd459cead8c8c4fccb64843b16ef561d4bbb8b63c9f364ebef9ef5a0980","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H = (L, R, E) be a finite bipartite graph and take the network with a source s, a sink t, arcs s->u of capacity 1 for u in L, arcs u->v for each edge uv, and arcs v->t of capacity 1 for v in R, every middle arc u->v of capacity M = |L| + 1. For a minimum s-t cut with source side S, put X = S n L and Y = S n R; then Y = N(X) and the cut has capacity |L| - |X| + |N(X)|. Conversely, for every X in L of maximal deficiency |X| - |N(X)|, the set {s} u X u N(X) is a minimum cut. So the minimum cut value is |L| - max over X in L of (|X| - |N(X)|). The strict inequality M > |L| is needed: with one edge and M = |L| = 1, the cut {s, u} is minimum and crosses the middle edge.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:06:07.089445+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6806f8bbc9b1475131bfa1bc9c5de78225a3575a799773684086e264f0c471fc","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defi 13 of arXiv:2608.28148, 'Flows and homotopies of Banach Lie algebroids'] An \emph{almost Lie bracket} on an anchored bundle $\left(A,\pi, M,\rho\right)$ is a sheaf of antisymmetric bilinear maps
\[
\LB_{A_U} \colon \Gamma\left( A_{U}\right)  \times\Gamma\left(  A_{U}\right)
\to\Gamma\left(  A_U\right), U\subseteq M \text{open}
\]
which satisfies the following properties
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\textbf{AL \arabic*})]
\item  the Leibniz identity:
\[
\forall\left(   \mathfrak{u}_{1}, \mathfrak{u}_{2}\right)  \in \Gamma \left(A_{U} \right)  ^{2}, \forall f \in C^{\infty}(U)
,\ \LB[\mathfrak{u}_{1},f \mathfrak{u}_{2}]_{A_{U}}=f.\LB[\mathfrak{u}_{1}, \mathfrak{u}_{2}]_{A_{U}}+df(\rho( \mathfrak{u}_{1})). \mathfrak{u}_{2}.
\]
\item For any  open set $U\subseteq M$ and any $(\mathfrak{u}_1,\mathfrak{u}_2) \in \Gamma(A_{U})^2$, the maps
\[
\mathfrak{u}_1,\mapsto \LB[\mathfrak{u}_1,\mathfrak{u}_2]_{A_{U}} \textrm{ and } \mathfrak{u}_2,\mapsto \LB[\mathfrak{u}_1,\mathfrak{u}_2]_{A_{U}}
\]
only depend on the $1$-jets of $\mathfrak{u}_1$ and $\mathfrak{u}_2$, respectively.
\end{enumerate}
By abuse of notation, such a sheaf of almost Lie brackets will be denoted $\LB_A$. The quintuple $(A,\pi, M,\rho,\LB_A)$ is called an \emph{almost algebroid}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["realization space in vertex and facet-normal coordinates, facets normalised as a.x = 1 (the origin is interior)"],"created_at":"2026-09-23T00:45:57.099314+00:00","domain":"discrete geometry","id":"claim_68070e87930d46458de76cb25da42bcc","kind":"computation","schema_version":1,"statement":"At the regular 24-cell (vertices the 24 permutations of (+-1,+-1,0,0); facets a.x = 1 with a = +-e_i or a = (+-1/2,+-1/2,+-1/2,+-1/2)), the 144 vertex-facet incidence equations a_j.v_i = 1 in the 192 coordinates of the 24 vertices and 24 facet normals have rank 140: four of them are dependent at this point. The Zariski tangent space of the realization space therefore has dimension 52, against the expected dimension 48 (28 against 24 after quotienting by the 24-dimensional projective group), so a first-order count cannot certify the local dimension. This is why Brysiewicz and Sinn (arXiv:2609.02818) use a second-order (quadratic obstruction) test; the local dimension they certify is the expected one, 48, so the regular 24-cell is not locally projectively rigid.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:38:13.642083+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_682272fa91a23b289b7e5e88ab8e4bb955ba3f2d9df89f79fd487d00e64550d1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 6 of arXiv:2609.00702, 'On the Set-Valued Katugampola Fractional Integral: Properties and Regular Selections'] Let $F$ be a compact set-valued function such that $F:I\rightrightarrows \mathbb{R}$ and for each $u\in [a,b]$, $F(u)$ is compact. For any partition $\mathcal{T}=\{t_0,t_1,t_2,\ldots t_n\}\subset I= [a,b]$ and $n\in \mathbb{N},$ the total Jordan variation of $ F$ is
    \[ V_a^b(F)=\sup_{\mathcal{T}} \sum_{i=1}^nH_d(F(t_i),F(t_{i-1})), \]
    with the supremum over all partitions $\mathcal{T}$ of $I.$ If $V_a^b(F)< \infty,$ then we say that $F$ is of bounded variation on $I.$ 

 \begin{definition}
     A set valued map $F:I\to \mathbb{R}$ is said to be Lipschitz on $I$ with respect to $H_d$ if there exists a constant $C_F>0$ such that 
     \[ H_d(F(t_1),F(t_2)) \le C_F|t_1-t_2| \text{ for all } t_1,t_2 \in I \] 
     and such a constant $C_F$ is called the Lipschitz constant of $F.$","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:55:37.369054+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6823162ea13653b36b31490bbcb3749a3b9e007b626bcd33709ee80a5f10393f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 10 (Positive definiteness of the Mellin quotient) of arXiv:2606.18458, 'Stable size-biasing and the positive scale-mixture order of generalized Gaussian laws'] For $p,q>0$, the function
\[
\Phi_{p,q}(t)=\frac{2^{it/p}\Gamma((1+it)/p)\Gamma(1/q)}{2^{it/q}\Gamma((1+it)/q)\Gamma(1/p)}
\]
is a characteristic function if and only if $p\le q$. If $p<q$, then $\Phi_{p,q}$ is the characteristic function of
\[
\log V_{p,q}=\left(\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{q}\right)\log 2+\log W,
\qquad
W=\left(S_{p/q}^{-1/q}\right)^*,
\]
where the star denotes ordinary size-biasing of the positive random variable $S_{p/q}^{-1/q}$. If $p=q$, then $\Phi_{p,p}\equiv1$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:00:30.495476+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_683cc9a15b3f17360622ecb0d0fd601721ecf791773e2f3f7aa2085c62c4e651","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 35 (Double-hive KL bound using a shared large-gap side) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] \lab{lem:doubleKLhive}
Let \(w,w'>0\) and \(u,u'\geq 0\). Let \(G_n,\widetilde G_n,G'_n,\widetilde G'_n\) be independent GUE
matrices, and set
\[
D_n=\operatorname{diag}(\operatorname{spec}(\widetilde G_n)),
\qquad
D'_n=\operatorname{diag}(\operatorname{spec}(\widetilde G'_n)).
\]
Let
\[
X_n=\sqrt n\,(wG_n+uD_n),
\qquad
Y_n=\sqrt n\,(w'G'_n+u'D'_n),
\]
and put
\[
a^2=w^2+u^2,\qquad b^2=(w')^2+(u')^2.
\]
Assume
\[
\frac{u}{w^2}=\frac{u'}{(w')^2}.
\]
Let
\[
\lambda_n=\operatorname{spec}(X_n),
\qquad
\mu_n=\operatorname{spec}(Y_n).
\]
Let \(L_n\) be the corrected regularized large-gap side from
\eqref{eq:corrected-large-gap}, and set
\[
N_n=L_n+\operatorname{diag}(X_n),
\qquad
P_n=L_n - \operatorname{diag}(Y_n).
\]
Let
\[
h_n^{(1)}\in H_n(\lambda_n,L_n;N_n),
\qquad
h_n^{(2)}\in H_n(\mu_n,L_n;P_n)
\]
be the two hives obtained, via Proposition~\ref{gt-rem}(iv), from the
large-gap construction applied to the two deformed minor processes arising from
$X_n$ and $Y_n$ respectively.  Paste them along the common side \(L_n\), with
the exterior sides in clockwise cyclic order
\[
\lambda_n,\qquad \mu_n,\qquad P_n,\qquad N_n.
\]
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.9, every node/.style={font=\small}]
  \coordinate (L) at (0,0);
  \coordinate (T) at (2,2);
  \coordinate (R) at (4,0);
  \coordinate (B) at (2,-2);
  \draw[thick] (L) -- (T) -- (R) -- (B) -- cycle;
  \draw[thick] (L) -- (R);
  \node[below left] at (1,-1) {\(\lambda_n\)};
  \node[above left] at (1,1) {\(\mu_n\)};
  \node[above right] at (3,1) {\(P_n\)};
  \node[below right] at (3,-1) {\(N_n\)};
  \node[above] at (2,0) {\(L_n\)};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
Decorate these four exterior sides, with
independent uniform Gelfand--Tsetlin patterns.  Let \(q_n^{\mathrm{dbl}}\)
be the resulting density on the four-boundary double-hive cone \(\mathbb D^4\).

Let \(p_n^{\mathrm{dbl}}\) be the maximum-entropy density on \(\mathbb D^4\)
whose four exterior sides, in clockwise cyclic order, have the same expected
quadratic moments as
\[
\lambda_n,\qquad \mu_n,\qquad P_n,\qquad N_n .
\]
Then
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q_n^{\mathrm{dbl}}\Vert p_n^{\mathrm{dbl}}\right)
=O(n\log n).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Both semigroups strongly continuous with the SAME generator including the same domain - two operators that agree on a common core but have different domains can generate different semigroups, which is precisely the non-uniqueness phenomenon for symmetric operators with several self-adjoint extensions."],"created_at":"2026-09-12T14:06:45.871339+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, semigroup theory","id":"claim_684380ee4334e17df539211dc9360d736e96ca633045262ed3ef27d741f7e789","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be the infinitesimal generator of a strongly continuous (C_0) semigroup on a Banach space. {"assumptions":["Counterexample: sawtooth functions u_k = dist(·, (1/k)Z) for the eikonal equation |u'| = 1 on R","Viscosity stability requires locally uniform convergence of the solutions (convergence of the equations must also be locally uniform)","Half-relaxed limit techniques replace uniform convergence only when combined with semicontinuous envelopes, not with a.e. solutions"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418309+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: viscosity solution theory","id":"claim_686c4951f47d3257d9394437cec0033cb5f7dec3b6ad9bdad4ce29fab5a2d321","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis in the stability theorem: the approximating functions must be VISCOSITY sub/supersolutions and the convergence must be LOCALLY UNIFORM. Neither can be dropped. (1) Almost-everywhere solutions are not closed under uniform convergence: let u_k(x) := dist(x, (1/k)Z) on R. Then |u_k'| = 1 at every point of differentiability, 0 ≤ u_k ≤ 1/(2k), so u_k → 0 uniformly, yet the limit u ≡ 0 satisfies |u'| = 0 and solves the eikonal equation nowhere. The u_k are not viscosity solutions of |u'| - 1 = 0 (at each of their convex kinks, on (1/k)Z, the supersolution test with the touching slope p = 0 fails), which is exactly why the stability theorem does not apply. (2) The convergence hypothesis cannot be weakened to pointwise or weak-* convergence. What goes wrong in the a.e. setting is already visible in (1): Du_k = ±1 a.e. while Du_k ⇀ 0 weakly-*, and the nonlinear expression H(Du_k) does not pass to weak limits. For genuine viscosity sub/supersolutions the proof of the stability theorem uses LOCALLY UNIFORM convergence to move maximum points of u_k - φ to a maximum point of u - φ; for a family that is merely locally uniformly bounded the correct substitutes are the half-relaxed limits limsup* u_k and liminf* u_k (Barles-Perthame), which are respectively a subsolution and a supersolution but in general differ from a pointwise limit. (If the u_k are locally equi-Lipschitz, pointwise convergence already forces locally uniform convergence, so the gap between the two modes of convergence bites only in the absence of equicontinuity.) Auditor's check: any passage to the limit in a nonlinear first-order PDE that is justified only by 'u_k → u and each u_k solves the equation a.e.' is invalid.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T14:24:13.477138+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_68724c8134dfcc0ae4992f700876980e044d69d7ce8ec6254ca4f97fecc65d60","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (S, A) be a measurable space and mu a sigma-finite measure on it, the intensity measure. A Poisson point process with intensity mu is a random counting measure N on S (N(A) is a random element of {0, 1, 2, ...} union {infinity} for each A in A, and N is a measure for each outcome) such that (i) for every A with mu(A) < infinity, N(A) has the Poisson distribution with mean mu(A), and (ii) for pairwise disjoint A_1, ..., A_k the counts N(A_1), ..., N(A_k) are independent. Such a process exists for every sigma-finite mu (construct it on each piece of finite measure by throwing a Poisson(mu(A)) number of independent points with law mu restricted to A and normalised, then superpose the pieces). When mu has no atoms the points are almost surely distinct; when mu is a multiple of Lebesgue measure on R^d the process is homogeneous with rate equal to that multiple. Basic calculus: the mapping theorem (the image of a Poisson process under a measurable map is Poisson with the image intensity), superposition (independent Poisson processes add to a Poisson process with the summed intensity), thinning (keeping each point independently with probability p(x) gives a Poisson process with intensity p mu), and Campbell's formula E sum_{x in N} f(x) = integral f d mu.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["for the converse, the limit function is continuous at 0"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T17:07:35.475672+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_688616a08b5444c58184dbb29da4dd94","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Random variables X_n converge in distribution to X if and only if their characteristic functions converge pointwise, phi_{X_n}(t) -> phi_X(t) for every t. More usefully: if phi_{X_n}(t) -> psi(t) pointwise and psi is continuous at t = 0, then psi is the characteristic function of some random variable X and X_n -> X in distribution. This is the engine that turns the characteristic-function computation in the Central Limit Theorem into convergence in distribution.\n\nHere the random variables are real-valued and phi_X(t)=E[exp(i t X)]. In the forward direction X_n converging in distribution to X implies the stronger conclusion that, for every T<infinity, sup_{|t|<=T}|phi_{X_n}(t)-phi_X(t)| tends to zero. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.499359+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_68b8e8caeed23137397373bc1467fc091520c09bb87396b9d98dc79655f8f009","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Both hypotheses are used, and each failure has a clean counterexample on the unit disk D. (1) The set E where pointwise convergence is assumed must have an accumulation point in the open set U, not merely on its boundary. Take a_k = 1 - 1/k^2, so that the sum of (1 - a_k) converges, and let B be the Blaschke product with simple zeros exactly at the a_k; B is holomorphic on D with |B| < 1 and B is not identically zero (B(0) = product of the a_k, nonzero). The sequence f_n = (-1)^n B is uniformly bounded by 1 and converges (to 0) at every point of E = {a_k}, a set whose only accumulation point is the boundary point 1, yet f_n diverges at every point where B ≠ 0, for instance at 0. (2) Local uniform boundedness cannot be dropped: on U = D(0,2) the functions f_n(z) = z^n converge pointwise on E = D (a set with plenty of interior accumulation points) but diverge for |z| > 1; the family is not bounded on compact subsets of U. (3) Connectedness of U matters in the same way as for the identity theorem: if U has several components, the hypothesis must be met on each component separately, since the identity theorem step is applied there. When auditing an argument that upgrades pointwise convergence of holomorphic functions to locally uniform convergence, check exactly these three things, and check that the pointwise limits are finite complex numbers rather than ∞.","status":"unverified"}

A symmetric double divisor $(\boldsymbol{\sigma}^+, \boldsymbol{\sigma}^-)$ assigns a charge distribution on $e^{i\theta}$ and $\{u_1, \dots, u_k\}$, where
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma}^+ = a \cdot e^{i\theta} + \sum_{j=1}^{k} \sigma_j \cdot u_j,
\quad \text{and} \quad
\boldsymbol{\sigma}^- = \overline{\boldsymbol{\sigma}^+}|_{\mathbb{D}},
\]
and the total charge satisfies the neutrality condition $(\mathrm{NC}_b)$.

We define the rational $\mathrm{SLE}_\kappa[\boldsymbol{\sigma}]$ as a random normalized conformal map $g_t(z)$, with initial condition $g_0(z) = z$ and normalization $g_t'(0) = e^{-t}$. It evolves according to the radial Loewner equation:
\[
\partial_t g_t(z) = g_t(z) \frac{e^{i\theta(t)} + g_t(z)}{e^{i\theta(t)} - g_t(z)}, \quad g_0(z) = z.
\]

Let $h_t(z)$ be the covering map of $g_t(z)$, defined via
\[
e^{i h_t(z)} = g_t(e^{i z}),
\]
so that $h_0(z) = z$, and
\[
\partial_t h_t(z) = \cot\left( \frac{h_t(z) - \theta(t)}{2} \right).
\]

The driving function $\theta(t)$ evolves as
\[
d\theta(t) = \frac{\partial \log \mathcal{Z}(\theta)}{\partial \theta} \, dt + \sqrt{\kappa} \, dB_t,
\]
where the Coulomb gas partition function is
\begin{equation} 
\mathcal{Z}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \prod_{j < k} \sin\left( \frac{\theta_j - \theta_k}{2} \right)^{\sigma_j \sigma_k} 
\cdot \prod_j e^{\frac{i}{2} \sigma_j (\sigma_0 - \sigma_\infty)\theta_j}.
\end{equation}

The flow map $g_t$ is well-defined up to the first time $\tau$ when $\zeta(t) = g_t(w)$ for some $w$ in the support of $\boldsymbol{\sigma}$. For any $z \in \mathbb{D}$, the process $t \mapsto g_t(z)$ is defined up to time $\tau_z \wedge \tau$, where $\tau_z$ is the first time such that $g_t(z) = e^{i\theta(t)}$. Define the associated hull by
\[
K_t = \left\{ z \in \overline{\mathbb{D}} : \tau_z \le t \right\}.
\]

Furthermore, the law of the rational $\mathrm{SLE}_\kappa[\boldsymbol{\sigma}]$ Loewner chain is invariant under Möbius transformations $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{D})$, up to a time change, due to the conformal covariance of the Coulomb gas correlation functions. Thus, we define rational $\mathrm{SLE}_\kappa[\boldsymbol{\sigma}]$ in a general simply connected domain $\Omega$ via a conformal map $\phi: \Omega \to \mathbb{D}$ by pulling back the flow.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f, g in L^1(R^n) for the basic identity; the dual identity needs f, g in L^2 (or transforms in L^1)","normalisation exp(-2 pi i x . xi); with exp(-i x . xi) the identity acquires the factor (2 pi)^{n/2} or (2 pi)^n depending on the convention"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479276+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis","id":"claim_68ec73ffb62be77db080fa917d7d7adccc085f8817f70ee4d86c012bfa989123","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For f, g in L^1(R^n) the convolution (f * g)(x) = integral over R^n of f(x - y) g(y) dy is defined for almost every x, belongs to L^1(R^n) with ||f * g||_1 <= ||f||_1 ||g||_1, and its Fourier transform is the product of the transforms: (f * g)^(xi) = f^(xi) g^(xi) for every xi, with f^(xi) = integral f(x) exp(-2 pi i x . xi) dx (with another normalisation of the transform a constant factor appears). Dually, for f, g in L^2(R^n) (or in L^1 with transforms in L^1) the transform of the pointwise product is the convolution of the transforms: (f g)^ = f^ * g^. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:06:07.083959+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_68fde8dcff9a3d3bef409e9f880ad0bfd1e9d55ce6c16ac9b448f45124b27f58","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defini 12 of arXiv:2608.27934, 'An example of biquandle and an invariant of long virtual knots defined through it'] (Index of a crossing)\\
Let $G(D)$ be the pointed Gauss diagram of a long virtual knot diagram $D$. 
For each dashed arrow in $G(D)$, we assign symbols $+$ and $-$ to the endpoints of the dashed arrow so that the symbol assigned to the tail is the same as that of the dashed arrow and that the symbol assigned to the head is the opposite to that of the dashed arrow. 
For each classical crossing $c$ of $D$, corresponding dashed arrow in $G(D)$ cuts unique interval without the specified point $p$ from the circle. 
The signed sum of symbols on the interior of the interval is denoted by $\alpha(c)$ and called {\it the index of }$c$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:37:15.466711+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_692c7e9ce2ae00a9fd185647c2d04809523659c6743a0d78ba31b5d2d0cdf72f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 of arXiv:2607.12384, '2607.12384'] Let $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t\geq 0}, \mathbb{P})$ be a filtered probability space satisfying the usual conditions, and let $W(ds, dy)$ be a space-time white noise defined on this space.  An adapted and jointly measurable random field
	\[
	\{u(t,x):(t,x)\in[0,T]\times\mathbb R\}
	\]
	is called a mild solution to \eqref{eq:main equation} if
	\[
	\sup_{(t,x)\in[0,T]\times\mathbb R}
	\mathbb E|u(t,x)|^2<\infty,
	\]
	and, for every
	\((t,x)\in[0,T]\times\mathbb R\),
	\[
	\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R}
	G_{t-s}(x-y)^2
	\mathbb E\left[|\sigma(u(s,y))|^2\right]\,dy\,ds
	<\infty,
	\]
	so that the Walsh integral below is well defined in \(L^2(\Omega)\). Moreover,
	for every \((t,x)\in[0,T]\times\mathbb R\),
	\begin{equation}
		u(t,x)
		=
		1+
		\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R}
		G_{t-s}(x-y)\sigma(u(s,y))\,W(ds,dy)
	\end{equation}
	holds in \(L^2(\Omega)\).","status":"unverified"}

\[

 a_I^0=\abs{\partial_I\Psi_O(z_{-I},0)},\qquad

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:36:49.819483+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_69581bc07dcd3807aee9a6e3b21a27a717a81f11a0d3509c2c4f64f7c22eb21e","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:weighted-exp-conc of arXiv:2609.02829, 'Quantitative explosion and percolation of the divisible sandpile'] Let $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N$ be independent real-valued random variables, and let $F=F(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N)$ be real-valued and measurable. Let $\xi_i'$ be an independent copy of $\xi_i$, independent of all coordinates, and let $\xi^{(i)}$ be obtained from $\xi=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N)$ by replacing only $\xi_i$ with $\xi_i'$. Assume that, for deterministic numbers $\ell_i\geq0$, not all zero, for every $1\leq i\leq N$,
		\[
			|F(\xi)-F(\xi^{(i)})|\leq \ell_i|\xi_i-\xi_i'|\, .
		\]
		Write
		\[
			\|\ell\|_{\ell^2}\coloneqq\left(\sum_{i=1}^N\ell_i^2\right)^{1/2}\, ,
			\qquad
			\|\ell\|_{\ell^\infty}\coloneqq\max_{1\leq i\leq N}\ell_i\, .
		\]
		\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
			\item If $p\geq2$ and $\mathbb{E}|\xi_i|^p<\infty$ for every $i$, then there is
			$C=C(p)$ such that
			\[
				\bigl(\mathbb{E}|F-\mathbb{E} F|^p\bigr)^{1/p}
				\leq
				C
				\left[
				\left(\sum_{i=1}^N \ell_i^2\bigl(\mathbb{E}|\xi_i-\xi_i'|^p\bigr)^{2/p}\right)^{1/2}
				+
				\left(\sum_{i=1}^N \ell_i^p \mathbb{E}|\xi_i-\xi_i'|^p\right)^{1/p}
				\right]\, .
			\]

			\item If the $\xi_i$ are i.i.d.\ and
			$\mathbb{E} e^{\theta_0|\xi_1|}\leq K_0$, then there are $c>0$ and $C<\infty$, depending
			only on $\theta_0$ and $K_0$, such that, for all $r\geq0$,
			\[
				\mathbb{P}(|F-\mathbb{E} F|\geq r)
				\leq
				C\exp\left\{
				-c\min\left(
				\frac{r^2}{\|\ell\|_{\ell^2}^2}\, , 
					\frac{r}{\|\ell\|_{\ell^\infty}}
				\right)
				\right\}\, .
			\]

				\item If the $\xi_i$ are i.i.d.\ with $\mathbb{E}\xi_1=0$ and
				$\mathbb{E} e^{\theta_0|\xi_1|}\leq K_0$, then there are $c>0$ and
				$C<\infty$, depending only on $\theta_0$ and $K_0$, such that,
				for every $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ with
				$|\lambda|\,\|\ell\|_{\ell^\infty}\leq c$,
				\[
					\log\mathbb{E}\exp\Bigl\{\lambda\sum_{i=1}^N\ell_i\xi_i\Bigr\}
					\leq
					C\lambda^2\|\ell\|_{\ell^2}^2\, .
				\]

			\item Under the assumptions of part~\textup{(b)}, if
				$|\lambda|\|\ell\|_{\ell^\infty}<\theta_0$, then
				\[
					\mathbb{E} e^{\lambda(F-\mathbb{E} F)}
					\leq
					\exp\{C\lambda^2\|\ell\|_{\ell^2}^2\}\, ,
				\]
				where $C$ depends only on $\theta_0$, $K_0$, and
				$\theta_0-|\lambda|\|\ell\|_{\ell^\infty}$.
		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:31:49.914114+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_699de2d720ce703b5a31f147c03b08d7c8a592519e8e2bfb7341edc02aad6927","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:geometry of arXiv:2608.28330, 'Realising atomless laws as distance distributions on metric measure spaces'] Let $\Theta$ be an atomless Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R_+$ such
	that $0\in\operatorname{supp}\Theta$.  For every $L>1$, there is a realisation
	$(S,d,\mu)$ of $\Theta$ such that $\operatorname{supp}\mu=S$ and $d$ is
	$L$-bi-Lipschitz equivalent to an ultrametric $u$ on $S$.  In fact,
	\[
	u(x,y)\leq d(x,y)\leq Lu(x,y),
	\qquad x,y\in S.
	\]
	If $\Theta$ has bounded support, then $S$ may be chosen compact and
	homeomorphic to the Cantor space.  In this case,
	\[
	\{d(x,y):x,y\in S\}=\operatorname{supp}\Theta,
	\qquad
	\operatorname{diam} S=\max\operatorname{supp}\Theta.
	\]
	If $\Theta$ has unbounded support, then $S$ may be chosen proper and
	homeomorphic to a countable disjoint union of Cantor spaces.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:57:51.747753+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_69d9fc3e08309abe3aa101187617150dbe9f74efd797339ff4780d0660d3c2e3","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 11 (Compatibility conditions) of arXiv:2608.30138, 'High-frequency wave propagation for the viscoelastic wave equation with singular memory'] Fix $k\geq1$. Assume $ u_0\in H^{k+1}(\Omega)$, $v_0\in H^k(\Omega)$, 
and
\begin{equation}
\partial_t^\ell u_-
\in
C_{\mathrm b}\bigl((-\infty,0];
H^{k+1-\ell}(\Omega)\bigr),
\qquad 0\leq\ell\leq k.
\end{equation}
Assume also that
\begin{equation}
\partial_t^\ell f
\in
C\bigl([0,T];H^{k-\ell}(\Omega)\bigr),
\qquad 0\leq\ell\leq k.
\end{equation}
In particular, $\partial_t^k f\in C([0,T];L^2(\Omega))$. 

We say that $(u_0,v_0,u_-,f)$ satisfies the compatibility conditions of
order $k$ if the following two conditions hold.

(i) The forward jets agree with the corresponding prehistory jets:
\begin{equation}
\partial_t^j u_-(0-,\cdot)=U_j
\quad\text{in }H^{k+1-j}(\Omega),
\qquad 0\leq j\leq k.
\end{equation}

(ii) The forward jets satisfy the Dirichlet boundary condition:
\begin{equation}
U_j\in H^{k+1-j}(\Omega)\cap H_0^1(\Omega),
\qquad 0\leq j\leq k.
\end{equation}
 
For $0\leq j\leq k$, define the concrete differentiated initial history
by
\begin{equation}
\widehat\eta_j^{\,0}(s,\cdot)
:=
U_j-\partial_t^j u_-(-s,\cdot),
\qquad s\geq0.
\end{equation}
Then \eqref{eq:corner-compatibility} is equivalently
\[
\widehat\eta_j^{\,0}(0,\cdot)=0
\quad\text{in }H^{k+1-j}(\Omega),
\qquad 0\leq j\leq k.
\]
Here $\widehat\eta_j^{\,0}$ denotes the concrete history function. If

element, no pointwise value $\eta_j^0(0)$ is being asserted.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:38:25.214530+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6a257a9d22943842290a3846155fa791afed1689a64d30d1315bca773555e59a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2609.00233, 'A survey on mapping class groups of 3-manifolds'] Let $M$ be a closed hyperbolic $3$-manifold and let $\delta$ be a simple closed geodesic in $M$. Then $\delta$ lifts to a set of hyperbolic lines $\{\delta_i\}$ in $\mathbb H^3$. For each $i \ne j$, define the \textit{orthocurve} $s_{ij}$ to be the shortest hyperbolic line segment in $\mathbb H^3$ between $\delta_i$ and $\delta_j$. Define the \textit{midplane} $D_{ij}$ to be the hyperbolic plane in $\mathbb H^3$ which meets $s_{ij}$ orthogonally at its midpoint.

By considering the completion $\overline{\mathbb H^3}$ and corresponding boundary $\partial \mathbb H^3$ ($\cong S^2$), we have a curve $\lambda_{ij} = \partial D_{ij}$ which separates the pair of points $\partial \delta_i$ from the pair of points $\partial \delta_j$.
The set of simple closed curves $\{ \lambda_{ij} \mid i \ne j\}$ in $\partial \mathbb H^3$ is known as the \textit{Dirichlet insulator family} associated to the geodesic $\delta$.

We say that a Dirichlet insulator family $\{\lambda_{ij} \mid i \ne j\}$ is \textit{non-coalescable} if there does not exist $i, j_1,j_2,j_3$ such that $\lambda_{ij_1} \cup \lambda_{ij_2} \cup \lambda_{ij_3}$ separates the two points $\partial \delta_i$. See (fig:DIT of the paper) for an example where this condition fails.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A is self-adjoint","the perturbation is claimed to be small relative to A"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.772201+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, perturbation theory, Schrodinger operators","id":"claim_6a489f3aa69fc8c053255532a89d8dafa488b42e2454afe14d89e8625076239b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypotheses: (i) B is symmetric; (ii) D(A) ⊂ D(B); (iii) ‖Bx‖ ≤ a‖Ax‖ + b‖x‖ on D(A) with a strictly less than 1. What fails. Dropping symmetry: take A self-adjoint unbounded and B = icA with 0 < c < 1. Then D(A) = D(B) and ‖Bx‖ = c‖Ax‖, so the relative bound is c < 1, yet A + B = (1 + ic)A has spectrum (1 + ic)σ(A), which is not contained in ℝ, so A + B is not self-adjoint; it is not even symmetric. Losing the strict inequality: take B = −A (symmetric, relative bound exactly a = 1, b = 0). Then A + B = 0 on D(A), which is symmetric and essentially self-adjoint but not self-adjoint on D(A), since D(A) ≠ H when A is unbounded; the conclusion 'self-adjoint on D(A)' is false at a = 1, and only Wüst's weaker conclusion (essential self-adjointness) survives. Dropping relative boundedness entirely: A = −d²/dx² on H²(ℝ) and B = multiplication by −x⁴ (maximal domain) are both self-adjoint and C_c^∞(ℝ) is a common dense invariant-looking core, but −d²/dx² − x⁴ is not essentially self-adjoint on C_c^∞(ℝ) (it is in the limit circle case at both ±∞, with deficiency indices (2,2)); the sum of two self-adjoint operators is in general neither self-adjoint nor essentially self-adjoint on the intersection of their domains, and that intersection can even be {0}. Also note that the relative bound of the perturbation must be measured against A itself, not against A + B, and that the infimum defining the relative bound need not be attained, so 'a ≤ 1' in a cited inequality is not the same as 'relative bound a < 1'. Audit rule: check symmetry of B, the domain inclusion, and the strict inequality with the constants actually produced by the estimate.","status":"unverified"}

    half-plane. There are only finitely many nonreal zeros, counted with

$\mathcal Z_{n_\beta}$ consists of exactly $n_\beta$ simple zeros, and
\[
\begin{cases}
\text{all these zeros are nonreal}, & \text{if $n_\beta$ is even},\\
-3n_\beta-4\text{ is the unique real zero}, & \text{if $n_\beta$ is odd}.
\end{cases}
\]

\[
        \beta=n_\beta+\theta_\beta,
        \qquad 
        \text{with }

zeros, counted with multiplicity. If $n_\beta$ is odd, then

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:25:49.871039+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6a777788523b663ade5fbb08e22abdd98497026edb425c1f7ecee675e9993c72","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 4 (\textsf{Stationary Stein identity}) of arXiv:2609.02064, 'Coalescence and fluctuations of O'Connell--Yor polymers\\ via the free-energy correlation '] Fix $n\geq1$, $\be>0$, and $m\geq0$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:05:37.777397+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6a7e5e0626f734eea49b6bf89a01baa06d54732174bf37a83e5fc777001559ea","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm: percolation_reference of arXiv:2608.00399, 'The Heavy-tailed Frog Model'] Let $d\ge2$. For $m\ge1$ and $p\in(0,1)$, consider Bernoulli site percolation with parameter $p$ on $\mathbb{T}_m^d$, and let $\mathrm{GC}=\mathrm{GC}(m,p)$ denote its largest open cluster, with ties broken arbitrarily. 
    \begin{itemize} 
    \item[(i)] For every $p > p^{\mathrm{site}}_c(d)$, there exist constants $C=C(d,p)>0$ and $c=c(p)>0$ such that the following holds for all large $m$. Set
    \[
    n(m):=\left\lceil C(\log m)^{1/(d-1)}\right\rceil .
    \]
    Then, with probability at least $1-m^{-1}$, every box of side length $n(m)$ contains at least $c \, n(m)^d$ vertices of $\mathrm{GC}$. Moreover, we can choose $c(p)$ such that $c(p) \rightarrow 1$ as $p \rightarrow 1$.
    \item[(ii)] There exists $p_o(d) \in (0,1)$ such that, for every $p\in(p_o(d),1)$, there exists $\beta=\beta(d)>0$ such that, for every $m\ge1$ and every $U\subseteq\mathbb{T}_m^d$ 
    \[
    \mathbb P_p\bigl(U\cap\mathrm{GC}=\varnothing\bigr)
    \le
    \exp\left(-\beta |U|^{(d-1)/d}\right) + e^{-\beta m} \, .
    \]
    \item[(iii)] For every $p>p_c^{\mathrm{site}}(d)$ and every $\gamma>1$, there exists $C'=C'(d,p)>0$ such that, upon setting
    \[
    r(m):=\left\lceil(\log m)^\gamma\right\rceil ,
    \]
    we have
    \[
    \mathbb P_p\left(
    \mathrm{diam}(\mathrm{GC}\cap B)
    \le C'r(m)
    \ \text{for every box $B$ of side length $r(m)$}
    \right)
    \longrightarrow 1
    \]
    as $m\to\infty$. Here $\mathrm{diam}$ is measured in the intrinsic graph metric of $\mathrm{GC}$ on the full torus $\mathbb{T}_m^d$; thus, connecting paths may leave $B$.
    \end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:27:25.793471+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6a8747c1a0127e1e8eea47f6e07add2b122f247775eb05c61d8e770e8de18a85","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition E_rho of arXiv:2605.15066, 'The critical activation density in graph bootstrap percolation'] For a graph $H$, let 
${\mathcal A}(H)$ be the set of all 
pairs $(e,A)$ 
such that $A$ is a graph and $e$ is an edge in $\langle A\rangle_H\setminus A$. 
We define the {\it critical $H$-activation density}  as 
\begin{equation}
\rho(H)=\inf_{(e,\,A)\in{\mathcal A}(H)}\, 
\max_{e\subset F\subseteq A\cup e}\, 
\frac{e(F)-1}{v(F)-2}.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:38:25.215003+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6ad01b1f34e805dc6860e6d8483ed7c05faa65fd65eba0ea2ff8be713d9bb465","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def-standard fibred torus of arXiv:2609.00233, 'A survey on mapping class groups of 3-manifolds'] Let \(a\) and \(b\) coprime integers with $0 \leq b < a$. Define an automorphism \[f_{a,b} \colon D^2 \rightarrow D^2 ; \ z \mapsto e^{2\pi i b/a}z\] which is a rotation of the disc by an angle of \(2\pi b/a\).
Consider the mapping torus $f_{a,b}$.  For each $p\in D^2$ we take $\{p\}\times I$ and identify $\{p\}\times \{0\}$ with $\{f_{a,b}(p)\}\times \{1\}$.
Under this identification the union of intervals
\[
\cup_{k=0}^{a-1}\{(f_{a,b})^k(p)\}\times I
\]
is a simple closed curve in the mapping torus.
This collection of simple closed curves endows the mapping torus of $f_{a,b}$, which is diffeomorphic to $S^1\times D^2$, with a decomposition into disjoint copies of $S^1$.
A \emph{standard fibred torus} is the mapping torus of $f_{a,b}$, together with the induced decomposition into copies of $S^1$, for some \(a\) and \(b\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:49:05.487213+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6ae2035fcf1dab18f9b8b5bd02823eefe3b8f748d6c100841df329800fbf7b90","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Deff fractional-domains-deff of arXiv:2601.19145, 'Stochastic Persistence in Infinite Dimensions'] For $\vartheta > 0$, let $\mathcal{B}_{\vartheta,r} = \mathcal{D}((-A)^\vartheta) = \textrm{Range}((-A)^{-\vartheta})$

{"assumptions":["Symmetric PSD normalized training kernels; both discrete update operators are contractions","Training-kernel operator error eps and coupled population cross-row L2 error eps_cross; zero-start outputs","Both normalized initial residual norms <=Y, their difference <=delta; finite integer horizon T","All hypotheses, normalization and risk comparison stated in the card text"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T18:15:10.683091+00:00","domain":"two-layer ReLU learning; population neural tangent kernel limits","id":"claim_6ae56d81dd44d83317b1bd279b5af71051fba7c5019d752ae27102fe548ee1f6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own-work draft; proof (unaudited); independent mathematical review pending; novelty unestablished. This is a finite-horizon supporting method, not full Target1 closure.

## 1. Deterministic finite-horizon lemma
Use a coupling (Z,X) of two population laws, paired training samples z_i,x_i,
and the same n label noises. Write K_ij=H(z_i,z_j)/n and Ktilde_ij=H(x_i,x_j)/n.
Let b(Z)_i=H(Z,z_i)/sqrt(n), btilde(X)_i=H(X,x_i)/sqrt(n).
Assume K,Ktilde are symmetric positive semidefinite and their spectra lie in
[0,2/gamma]. Thus A=I-gamma K and Atilde=I-gamma Ktilde are contractions.
Assume ||Ktilde-K|| <= eps, ||b||_{L2(row Euclidean)} <= B,
||btilde-b||_{L2} <= eps_cross. Set v_0=-y/sqrt(n),
vtilde_0=-ytilde/sqrt(n), with both initial norms <= Y and
||vtilde_0-v_0|| <= delta. Define v_k=A^k v_0 and vtilde_k=Atilde^k vtilde_0.
Zero-start predictions are f_k=-gamma sum_{j<k} b v_j and the analogous ftilde_k.
These formulas are exactly kernel GD, not a continuous-time approximation.
Then, for every integer k <= T,

 ||ftilde_k-f_k||_L2 <= gamma k eps_cross Y + gamma B k delta
                         + gamma^2 B eps Y k(k-1)/2.                 (1)

Proof. The noncommuting telescoping identity is
 Atilde^j-A^j=sum_{l=0}^{j-1} Atilde^(j-1-l)(Atilde-A)A^l.
Consequently ||vtilde_j-v_j|| <= delta+gamma j eps Y.
Split btilde vtilde_j-b v_j=(btilde-b)vtilde_j+b(vtilde_j-v_j).
Cauchy-Schwarz on the coupled population and contraction give each summand
at most eps_cross Y+B(delta+gamma j eps Y). Sum j=0,...,k-1.
No commutation, eigengap, or training-only population inference is used.
If ||gtilde-g||_L2 <= delta_g and ||f_k-g||_L2 <= R, the clean risks differ by
at most 2 R E+E^2, where E is the right side of (1) plus delta_g.
The same statement holds in joint L2 over population and label noises if the
hypotheses hold uniformly over those noises. This follows by expanding
||(f_k-g)+(ftilde_k-f_k)-(gtilde-g)||^2 and Cauchy-Schwarz.","status":"unverified"}
