{"assumptions":["T is trace class (or positive) for the diagonal sum to be basis-independent","cyclicity tr(AB) = tr(BA) needs one factor trace class and the other bounded, or both Hilbert-Schmidt","Hilbert-Schmidt does not imply trace class"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.573399+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator ideals","id":"claim_6b062606a8899853447fad7c25599be3992c8f16f17ceb5224a67851c9805cf3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The expression sum_i <T e_i, e_i> is basis-independent and deserves the name 'trace' only when T is trace class (or T >= 0, where the sum is basis-independent in [0, infinity]). Two concrete failures. (1) Conditional convergence, basis-dependent value: on l^2 let T = diag((-1)^{n+1}/n) with respect to the standard basis. T is self-adjoint, compact and Hilbert-Schmidt, but not trace class since sum_n 1/n = infinity. In the standard basis sum_n <T e_n, e_n> converges conditionally to log 2, and permuting the orthonormal basis rearranges the series, so by the Riemann rearrangement theorem the 'trace' can be made any real number or made to diverge. (2) An absolutely convergent, even identically zero, diagonal without trace class: let T be the block-diagonal operator on l^2 whose n-th two-by-two block is [[0, 1/n], [1/n, 0]]. Every diagonal entry in the standard basis is 0, so the diagonal sum is 0, yet the singular values are 1/n twice each, so sum s_n = infinity and T is not trace class; the eigenvalues are plus and minus 1/n and no trace can be assigned consistently. Related traps: tr(AB) = tr(BA) requires a hypothesis such as A trace class and B bounded, or A and B both Hilbert-Schmidt. For merely bounded A, B the commutator identity fails: on l^2 with the unilateral shift S, the commutator [S*, S] = I - S S* is the rank-one projection onto the first coordinate, so it is trace class with trace 1, not 0, even though it is a commutator. Finally, 'T is Hilbert-Schmidt' does not imply 'T is trace class': sum s_n^2 < infinity is strictly weaker than sum s_n < infinity, as diag(1, 1/2, 1/3, ...) on l^2 shows.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:57:51.738203+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6b099a365ae0178fd9051ed1f2227e899312bd5e4a7e2cc9ca6ee2c2ede96ce0","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2608.30089, 'On the Coefficients of Hurwitz-Type Matrix Polynomials'] Let \(A_j\) be the coefficients of the matrix polynomial

 \begin{align}

    A_{2j+1}=&(-1)^{m+j+1} u_{2,m}^*(T_m^{m-j})^*\Sigma_{2,m}, \quad j=0,1,\ldots, m-1,m.

     In particular, the following equalities hold.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.815054+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6b0bff57f96de65d028bb9df7fb7ae1c171112ea22f8c1ba31d86264d91448b8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:maximal-rank-saturation of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix $k\geq4$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item \emph{Structured label saturation.}
There are constants \(0<\alpha_k<\beta_k\) such that, for every sufficiently
large $h$, there is a set
\[
 \mathcal L^{\mathrm{end}}_{h,k}\subseteq
 \Lambda^{\max}_{h,k}\cap[\alpha_kh^{k-1},\beta_kh^{k-1}]
\]
with
\begin{equation}
 |\mathcal L^{\mathrm{end}}_{h,k}|
 \geq h^{k-1}
 \exp\!\left(-O_k\!\left(\frac{\log h}{\log\log h}\right)\right).
\end{equation}
Each $n\in\mathcal L^{\mathrm{end}}_{h,k}$ has a primitive representative
$A$ satisfying
\[
 \begin{gathered}
  r_h(A)=k-2,\qquad
  p_i(A)\asymp_k h\quad(1\leq i\leq k-2),\\
  \operatorname{ndiam}(A)\asymp_k\prod_{i=1}^{k-2}p_i(A)\asymp_k h^{k-2}.
 \end{gathered}
\]
Its defining ideal is a prime toric almost complete intersection, while its
coordinate ring is arithmetically Cohen--Macaulay of type two, with total
Betti polynomial $(1+2\xi)(1+\xi)^{k-3}$ and graded Betti tower
(equation eq:endpoint-betti-tower of the paper).

\item \emph{One intrinsic rank layer.}
For every sufficiently large $h$ there are
\[
 r^\ast_{h,k}\in\{2,\ldots,k-2\}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \mathcal E_{h,k}\subseteq
 \mathcal L^{\mathrm{end}}_{h,k}\cap\mathcal R^{[r^\ast_{h,k}]}(h,k)
\]
such that every label in $\mathcal E_{h,k}$ retains a representative from
part~\textup{(i)} and
\begin{equation}
 |\mathcal E_{h,k}|\geq h^{k-1}
 \exp\!\left(-O_k\!\left(\frac{\log h}{\log\log h}\right)\right).
\end{equation}
For fixed $h$, the aggregate realization count
\[
 F^{(k)}_{h,\mathcal E}(q)
 =\#\{A\in\tbinom{[q]}k:|hA|\in\mathcal E_{h,k}\}
\]
is an exact quasipolynomial in $q-1$ of degree $k-r^\ast_{h,k}$.  If $A_q$
is uniform in $\binom{[q]}k$, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb P\bigl(|hA_q|\in\mathcal E_{h,k}\bigr)
 =\Theta_{h,k}(q^{-r^\ast_{h,k}})
 \qquad(q\to\infty),
\end{equation}
and, for every $n\in\mathcal E_{h,k}$, the normalized shape locus of $n$
has dimension $k-2-r^\ast_{h,k}$.
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{h\to\infty}
 \frac{\log\max_{2\leq r\leq k-2}|\mathcal R^{[r]}(h,k)|}{\log h}=k-1.
\end{equation}
When $k=4$, necessarily $r^\ast_{h,4}=2$ and

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:29:28.004217+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6b11b6a70a31e3952df211c69a320ccb096fa9ddc15b31e146ba62a6a04c8489","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 2 (Power-distance specialization) of arXiv:2608.24964, 'Common-Center Geometry and Certified Radial Reconstruction for Energy-Form Full Conformal '] For $\beta\ge1$, the abstract assumptions required for the deterministic geometry are satisfied with $q=0$.  The Fr\'echet objective
\[
F_\beta(t)=\sum_{i=1}^m\|t-y_i\|^\beta
\]
is coercive and therefore attains a global minimum, and each
\[
G_j(t)=\sum_{i\ne j}\|t-y_i\|^\beta
\]
is convex.  Thus
\[
I_j=\{t:G_j(t)\le d_j\},
\qquad
d_j=\sum_{i\ne j}\|y_j-y_i\|^\beta,
\]
all $I_j$ contain any chosen minimizer $c$ of $F_\beta$, and the conclusions of Theorem~\ref{thm:common-center} apply.

For $m=1$,
\[
I_1=\mathbb R^d,
\]
so finite-radius reconstruction is degenerate.  For $m\ge2$, each power-distance comparison set is bounded and has finite radial exits.

Under the conventional distributional energy-score interpretation, define
\[
\mathcal P_\beta
=
\left\{
P:\int\|x\|^\beta\,dP(x)<\infty
\right\}.
\]
On the appropriate finite-moment class, the conventional power-distance energy score is strictly proper for
\[
0<\beta<2.
\]
Hence the overlap between strict propriety and the deterministic star-shaped geometry is
\[
1\le\beta<2.
\]
At $\beta=2$, the score is proper but not strictly proper and its expected score depends only on the forecast mean.  For $\beta>2$, the Euclidean distance-power energy-form score is not proper.

For $d=1$ and $\beta=1$, the score is exactly the fixed-bin empirical-CRPS score used by \citet[Section~8.1]{toccaceli_2026_crps}.  Write the ordered observations as
\[
y_{(1)}\le\cdots\le y_{(m)}
\]
and define the full empirical median set
\[
\mathcal M
=
\arg\min_t F_1(t)
=
\left[
y_{(\lceil m/2\rceil)},
y_{(\lfloor m/2\rfloor+1)}
\right].
\]
Every point of $\mathcal M$ belongs to every comparison region.  In the nontrivial threshold regime $1\le k\le m$, every corresponding FullCP region is therefore a nonempty closed interval containing $\mathcal M$.  For $m\ge2$ this interval is compact, while for $m=1$ it is $\mathbb R$.  In particular, this proves the single-interval property reported for Toccaceli's fixed-bin empirical-CRPS construction and settles the motivating CRPS case of the connectedness question.  The scoring-rule facts and the CRPS/energy representation are classical \citep{gneiting_raftery_2007_scoring}; the interval conclusion follows from the deterministic comparison geometry above and does not by itself extend to proper distributional scoring rules in general.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(S, d) is a metric space with its Borel sigma-algebra","the members of the family are Borel probability measures"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:01:13.770398+00:00","domain":"probability, weak convergence of measures, tightness","id":"claim_6b379f9f39b8f899e353d04b96592d438754cd075fffcd3c5f233e7113013891","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(S, d)$ be a metric space. A family $\\Gamma$ of Borel probability measures on $S$ is tight (uniformly tight) if for every $\\varepsilon > 0$ there is a compact set $K_\\varepsilon \\subset S$ such that $\\mu(S \\setminus K_\\varepsilon) \\le \\varepsilon$ for EVERY $\\mu \\in \\Gamma$ - the same compact set works for all members of the family. A single measure $\\mu$ is tight if $\\{\\mu\\}$ is.\n\nFacts to keep straight. (1) On a Polish space (separable and complete metric space) every single Borel probability measure is tight (Ulam), and a finite family is then tight as well. (2) On a separable metric space that is not complete a single Borel probability measure can fail to be tight: for a set $S \\subset [0,1]$ with Lebesgue outer measure 1 and inner measure 0 (a Bernstein-type set) the trace of Lebesgue measure is a Borel probability measure on $S$ whose compact subsets are all null. (3) In a compact metric space every family is tight (take $K = S$). (4) On $\\mathbb{R}^k$ tightness of $\\Gamma$ means $\\sup_{\\mu \\in \\Gamma} \\mu(\\{|x| > R\\}) \\to 0$ as $R \\to \\infty$, i.e. no mass escapes to infinity uniformly in the family; in $C[0,1]$ tightness is characterised by the Arzelà-Ascoli type conditions (bounded initial values plus a uniform modulus-of-continuity control). (5) Tightness is the hypothesis of Prokhorov's theorem, which turns it into relative compactness in the weak topology.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. summands with zero mean, finite positive variance and finite third absolute moment","C absolute; no numerical value is asserted by this node"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T17:07:35.390398+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6b44f8f2cf7849479e4ac1266f5d003a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1,X_2,... be independent identically distributed real random variables with E[X_1]=0, E[X_1^2]=sigma^2 in (0,infinity), and rho=E|X_1|^3<infinity. For S_n=sum_{i=1}^n X_i and the standard normal distribution function Phi, the Berry-Esseen inequality is sup_{x in R}|P(S_n/(sigma sqrt(n))<=x)-Phi(x)| <= C rho/(sigma^3 sqrt(n)), where C is an absolute constant independent of n and the distribution. The explicit choice C=0.4748 is valid for every n>=1 (Shevtsova, 2011, Theorem 2 and Corollary 1, https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.6554); it is a proven historical upper bound, not an assertion of the exact or currently best constant. If C_opt denotes the infimum of all universally admissible iid constants, Esseen's lower bound gives C_opt >= (3+sqrt(10))/(6 sqrt(2 pi)) > 0.4097, while C_opt <= 0.4748. The order n^{-1/2} is optimal in general: symmetric two-point summands give lattice jumps of this order along a subsequence. For independent, not necessarily identically distributed, centered real summands with finite third absolute moments and V=sum_i E[X_i^2]>0, an absolute constant C_ind gives sup_x|P(sum_i X_i/sqrt(V)<=x)-Phi(x)| <= C_ind sum_i E|X_i|^3/V^{3/2}; no claim that the iid constant 0.4748 applies to this general version is made. The third absolute moment is an essential hypothesis for a bound of this form; finite variance alone gives the iid CLT but not this universal moment-based rate. [Berry (1941), Esseen (1942); Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 3.4.17.]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:31:47.860408+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_6b7236fbd383918903b04973e544cb8076d237ab81d7c669c598be85ba4f6727","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The Collatz conjecture is one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics. The conjecture asks whether repeating two simple arithmetic operations will eventually transform every positive integer into 1. It concerns sequences of integers in which each term is obtained from the previous term as follows: if a term is even, the next term is one half of it. If a term is odd, the next term is 3 times the previous term plus 1. The conjecture is that these sequences always reach 1, no matter which positive integer is chosen to start the sequence. The conjecture has been shown to hold for all positive integers up to 2.36×1021, but no general proof has been found.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Finite one-hot task identifiers with positive power-law task weights; independent uniform skill bits.","Fixed task parity functions; first N supplied as basis functions; noiseless target amplitude S>0."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:24:35.629108+00:00","domain":"Multitask sparse parity and skill emergence","id":"claim_6b8bb2f11abe9145368bad240c2dab04e24a2526e3b98efbfeac8938553e0ab6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Nam-Fonseca-Lee-Mingard-Louis fixed-basis multitask parity model. Fix integers n_s,n_b,m with 1<=m<=n_b, alpha>0 and S>0. The task I in {1,...,n_s} has probabilities p_k=A*k^(-alpha-1), A=(sum_{j=1}^{n_s} j^(-alpha-1))^(-1), and is represented by a one-hot n_s-bit control vector. Independently, X is uniform on {0,1}^{n_b}. For each task choose an m-element subset A_k of skill-bit coordinates and set g_k(i,x)=1_{i=k}*(-1)^(sum_{j in A_k} x_j). Distinct tasks have disjoint task support, so E[g_j(I,X)*g_k(I,X)]=p_k*1_{j=k}; these basis functions are not unit-normalized in the population measure. The noiseless target is f_star(i,x)=S*sum_{k=1}^{n_s} g_k(i,x). For 1<=N<=n_s the source multilinear model fixes the N most frequent skill functions in advance and trains only the 2N real scalars in f(i,x)=sum_{k=1}^N a_k*b_k*g_k(i,x). Its represented skill strengths are R_k=a_k*b_k. Define R_k=E_X[g_k(k,X)*f(k,X)] and conditional MSE L_k=(1/2)*E_X[(S*g_k(k,X)-f(k,X))^2]. For this model L_k=(1/2)*(S-R_k)^2 when k<=N, and L_k=S^2/2 when k>N. In contrast, for an arbitrary predictor f the definition gives L_k=(1/2)*(S^2+E_X[f(k,X)^2]-2*S*R_k), so skill strength alone need not determine skill loss. Population MSE is sum_k p_k*L_k. The skill functions in this exactly solvable model are supplied, rather than learned from examples.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:11:02.376193+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6b9d43713bc4bdf1eebb0779f4b9b5aed1f07112b43dafad1d1a9b10dfff6a6f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition of arXiv:2507.10294, 'Guessing Strategies for Shelf-Shuffling Machines'] We have $S_3\sim 2\Phi(1)-1\approx0.68$, where $\Phi$ is the cumulative distribution function of an $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ random variable.
    \begin{proof}
        Using symmetry and re-indexing, we may rewrite
            \[S_3=2\sum_{i=\frac{n}{2}-m}^{\frac{n}{2}}\frac{\binom{n-1}{i-1}}{2^{n-1}}=2\sum_{k=\frac{n}{2}-m-1}^{\frac{n}{2}-1}\frac{\binom{n-1}{k}}{2^{n-1}}\]
        We check that
        \[\frac{n}{2}-m-1=\frac{n-1}{2}-\left\lceil\frac{\sqrt{n-1}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\right\rceil-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{n-1}{2}+O(\sqrt{n})\]
        and this is clearly the farthest term from the central binomial coefficient. Lemma $(de Moivre-Laplace of the paper)$ implies that the central limit theorem holds. By a simple algebraic manipulation of the endpoints of the sum, we obtain
        \[S_3\sim 2\,\Phi\left(\frac{2m+1}{\sqrt{n-1}}\right)-2\,\Phi\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n-1}}\right)\]
        \[=2\,\Phi\left(\frac{\lceil\sqrt{n-1}\rceil}{\sqrt{n-1}}\right)-2\,\Phi\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n-1}}\right)\]
        \[\to 2\,\Phi(1)-1\]
        by the continuity of $\Phi$.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:10.192198+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6bc39b1eef2b3cf01f05c0f9b35e02f39ff04b8ceb31ec7f682cc14adac9634f","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 11 of arXiv:2605.03528, '\bf Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance and discrepancies {\em versus} Wasserstein distances'] Let $p>0$. Let $t>0$ be fixed and let $L: (0, +\infty)\to \R_+$ be defined by 

\[
L(u):=\sum_{\ell\ge 0} 2^{-p\ell} \min\big(u, 2^{d\ell}D^\infty(\mu,\nu)\big).
\]

The function $L$ satisfies the following upper-bounds depending on $p$ and the dimension $d$ where $C_{p,d}>0$ denotes    a positive constant only depending on $p$, $\b$, $d$ that may vary from line to line.
\begin{itemize}
\item If $p>d $, then 
\[
L(u) \le  C_{p,d}\min\Big(u,D^\infty(\mu,\nu)\Big).
\]

\item  If $p=d$ then,
	\[
	L(u) \le C_{p,d} (1+\left(\log(u/D^\infty(\mu,\nu))\right)_{{+}})D^\infty(\mu,\nu).
	
	\]

\item If $p < d $, then
$$
L(u) \le C_{p,d} \Big(u^{1-\frac pd}D^\infty(\mu,\nu)^{\frac pd}\mbox{\bf 1}_{\{u> D^\infty(\mu,\nu)\}}+ u\mbox{\bf 1}_{\{u\le D^\infty(\mu,\nu)\}}\Big).
$$
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a moment bound with a STRICTLY positive exponent to spare (beta > 0)","a complete metric target space","the conclusion is about a modification, not the original process"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.782051+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6bc3c6154eb242793c2a5c251a34ca7565adf2b8c40b69ee5551e9af7d6209b4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X_t)_{t in [0,T]} be a stochastic process with values in a complete metric space, and suppose there are constants alpha > 0, beta > 0 and C < infinity with E[ d(X_t, X_s)^alpha ] <= C |t - s|^{1 + beta} for all s, t in [0,T]. Then X admits a MODIFICATION Xtilde - a process with P(X_t = Xtilde_t) = 1 for every fixed t - whose sample paths are almost surely continuous, and indeed almost surely HOLDER continuous of every exponent gamma in (0, beta/alpha). The exponent beta/alpha is the boundary and is generally not attained. Applications: for Brownian motion E|B_t - B_s|^{2m} = c_m |t-s|^m, so taking alpha = 2m and beta = m - 1 gives Holder exponents up to (m-1)/(2m), which approaches 1/2 as m grows - matching the known fact that Brownian paths are Holder of every exponent below 1/2 and of no exponent at or above 1/2. The theorem produces a MODIFICATION, not the original process: the original may have wildly discontinuous paths, and the two agree at each fixed time but not, in general, simultaneously at all times. The strictly positive beta is essential: E|X_t - X_s|^alpha <= C|t-s| with no exponent to spare does not suffice, as the Poisson process shows, where E|N_t - N_s| = |t - s| exactly and the paths are genuinely discontinuous. The d-dimensional time-parameter version holds with 1 + beta replaced by d + beta. [Kolmogorov, published by Slutsky and by Chentsov; see Revuz and Yor, Continuous Martingales and Brownian Motion, 3rd ed., Theorem I.2.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:41:33.793866+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6bdd9a2a96582563d4ffe9687cbafed4ca08a387a9914df3dccb6ed35c4a0616","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 1 of arXiv:2604.10051, 'Ergodicity of the voter model with dynamic anti-voter bonds'] Let~$(\xi_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a Feller process defined on a metric space~$\mathcal C$ and~$(Z_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a Markov chain with a countable state space~$\mathcal S$ and~$Q
$-matrix~$\{q(x,y) : x,y \in \mathcal S\}$ that satisfy

where~$c(x) = -q(x,x)$. Assume that the processes are dual with respect to a function~$D:\mathcal C \times \mathcal S \to [0,\infty)$, that is,

Moreover, assume that

    \int D(\xi,z)\; \mu( \mathrm{d} \xi ) = \int D(\xi,z) \; \mu S_t( \mathrm{d} \xi ) \quad \text{for any } t \ge 0 \text{ and } z \in \mathcal S.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.649879+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6bf12581a2707be998f637d3709babc3528d8727bcb291609030049e5a8e5833","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 2 of arXiv:2607.24170, '\large\bf ON NON-MONOTONICITY OF LOGARITHMIC ENERGY\\ FOR RANDOM MATRICES'] Let
$\pentry\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}1/32$ and
$\qentry\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}31/32$.  Let $\mathsf{X}$ and
$\mathsf{G}$ be independent random variables such that
\begin{equation}
 \Prob\left(\mathsf{X}=-\frac1{\sqrt{31}}\right)=\qentry,
 \qquad \Prob(\mathsf{X}=\sqrt{31})=\pentry,
 \qquad
 \Prob(\mathsf{G}\in\mathrm{d}z)=\frac1\pi\mathrm{e}^{-|z|^2}\mathrm{d}^2z.

\begin{equation}
 \mathsf{Y}_\varepsilon\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}

 \E[\mu_{\mathbf{M}_{n,\varepsilon}/\sqrt n}].
\]
Then, $\mathsf{Y}_\varepsilon$ is centered, satisfies
$\E[|\mathsf{Y}_\varepsilon|^2]=1$, and has a strictly positive real-analytic
density, all moments, and sub-Gaussian tails.  Moreover,
\[
 \cE(\nu_{n,\varepsilon})\in\R,\qquad n\geq1,\quad\varepsilon>0,
\]
and there exists $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that
\[
 \cF_{\C}(\nu_{3,\varepsilon})>\cF_{\C}(\nu_{2,\varepsilon}),
 \qquad 0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:19:56.654736+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6bffcc9e21183b3bbb9035e35d2beba6468cc674195a4547bb86ffd94e304756","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 8 of arXiv:2608.30859, 'Conservation Laws with Discontinuous Flux:\\ A First Application to Traffic Flow'] A vector field $H : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ is said to have 
\emph{locally bounded directional variation} if, for every 
$(t_0,x_0) \in \mathbb{R}^2$, there exist $\delta>0$ and a constant $C>0$
such that
\[
\sum_{i=1}^N 
\bigl| H(t_i,x_i) - H(t_{i-1},x_{i-1}) \bigr|
\;\le\; C
\]
for every finite sequence $(t_i,x_i)$, $i=0,\ldots,N$, satisfying
\[
(t_0,x_0) \prec (t_1,x_1) \prec \cdots \prec (t_N,x_N),
\qquad t_N < t_0 + \delta .
\]
Here $\prec$ denotes the partial order on $\mathbb{R}^2$ induced by the cone
\begin{equation}
    \Gamma_M := \{ (t,x) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : |x| \le M t\}, 
\end{equation}
namely
\begin{align}
(t,x) \prec (t',x')
\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad
|x - x'| \le M (t - t') .
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:20:15.481467+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6c15a7de3fd5aad2a31f5ab8d1dfc9ffd682d2d712a82ff8c01cc7c24e64e2c1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 17 of arXiv:2509.01797, 'Relation between Wick powers and excursion clusters of the 2D GFF'] For every $D\subsetneq \C$ open simply connected domain,
for every $z,z',w,w'\in D$ such that
$\vert z' - z\vert \leq \frac{1}{2}d(z,\partial D)$,
$\vert w' - w\vert \leq \frac{1}{2}d(w,\partial D)$,
$\vert z' - z\vert\leq \frac{1}{4}\vert z-w\vert$,
and
$\vert w' - w\vert\leq \frac{1}{4}\vert z-w\vert$,
we have
\begin{eqnarray*}
\vert G_{D}(z',w') - G_{D}(z,w)\vert &\leq &
\dfrac{\log(2)}{\pi}\dfrac{\vert z' - z\vert +\vert w' - w\vert}{\vert z-w\vert}
\\  && +
16\dfrac{\vert z' - z\vert}{d(z,\partial D)}
\Big(G_{D}(z,w)+\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\log \dfrac{\vert z-w\vert}{d(w,\partial D)}\Big)
+ \dfrac{\log(2)}{\pi}\dfrac{\vert w' - w\vert}{d(w,\partial D)}.
\end{eqnarray*}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:17:17.061269+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6c496ee61efec6ccd94989fbfe47f2afc03dc2e64dbebc70d25a4225838caecc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 10 of arXiv:2608.19744, 'Conditioned Brownian motion and local equivalence of path ensembles'] Let $K$ be symmetric positive definite, let $\sigma>0$, and let
$Q:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous and nonconstant.  Define
\[
    A_T=\int_0^T \de s \, Q(X_s)
\]
for the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process
\[
    \de X_t=-KX_t\,\de t+\sigma\,\de B_t,
    \qquad X_0=x.
\]
Let $\lambda(\beta)$ and $\psi_\beta$ be the lowest eigenvalue and
normalized positive ground state of
\[
    K_\beta=-L_K+\beta Q
    \qquad\text{on }L^2(\mu_K).
\]
For $\theta\in\Theta_Q^{\mathrm{OU}}
       =\lambda'((0,\infty))$ and $\lambda'(\beta_\theta)=\theta$,
put $v_\theta=-\lambda''(\beta_\theta)>0$ as well as 
\[
    I_Q^{\mathrm{OU}}(\theta)
       =\lambda(\beta_\theta)-\beta_\theta\theta.
\]
Then, for every fixed $z\in\mathbb R$,
\[
    \bbP_x^{\mathrm{OU}}(A_T\leq\theta T+z)
    \sim
    \frac{
      \psi_{\beta_\theta}(x)
      \langle\psi_{\beta_\theta},\mathbf 1\rangle_{L^2(\mu_K)}
    }{
      \beta_\theta\sqrt{2\pi v_\theta T}
    }
    \exp\!\left(
       -I_Q^{\mathrm{OU}}(\theta)T+\beta_\theta z
    \right).
\]
The asymptotic is locally uniform in $(x,z)$.

Moreover, on every fixed time interval, the conditioned process converges
in total variation to the ground-state diffusion
\[
    \de Y_t
      =
      \left[
        -KY_t+\sigma^2\nabla\log
        \psi_{\beta_\theta}(Y_t)
      \right]\de t
      +\sigma\,\de B_t,
    \qquad Y_0=x.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628833+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6c8676d825f4a55fd3a14f69b1c08c5a1e3f9cf9297d3f4f48fbb82aef6f2234","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X >= 0 with 0 < E[X^2] < infinity. The second moment method is the chain of consequences of Paley-Zygmund and Chebyshev. FIRST FORM: P(X > 0) >= (E X)^2 / E[X^2]. This gives only a LOWER BOUND ON THE PROBABILITY, bounded away from 0 when the second moment is comparable to the square of the first; it does NOT give an event of probability tending to 1. SECOND FORM: if Var(X) / (E X)^2 -> 0 along a sequence of models, then X / E[X] -> 1 in probability by Chebyshev, so X > 0 with probability tending to 1 and moreover X is concentrated. Confusing the two is the standard error: E[X^2] <= C (E X)^2 with C > 1 fixed gives positive probability at least 1/C, and no amount of that alone upgrades to high probability. The repair when only the first form is available is usually a 0-1 law or a sprinkling or self-improvement argument that turns positive probability into probability one, not a better moment estimate. The typical use is a counting random variable X = number of structures of a given type: the first moment method (Markov: P(X >= 1) <= E X) gives the upper threshold, and the second moment method gives the lower one, and the two match only when the second moment is not inflated by correlated pairs. [standard; e.g. Alon and Spencer, The Probabilistic Method, Chapter 4]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:52:08.671459+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6c8d0c5a7b8827f610830e3444d9825c9b6c56f2484deb492840747c6ed23f8e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 31 (Iteration on a connected large-diameter interval) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Under the standing fixed-threshold application with cutoff \(c_0\), fix
\(\delta_0\geq c_0\), an integer \(N\geq2\), and \(\sigma\in(0,1)\).  There are constants \(\eta_0>0\) and
\(T_{\mathrm{p}}<\infty\) with the
following properties.  The constant \(\eta_0\) depends only on
\(K,\delta_0,N,\sigma\); the threshold \(T_{\mathrm{p}}\) may additionally
depend on the fixed Bamler tail data \(T_B(c_0)\) and
\(\eps_B^{c_0}\).  Neither depends
on the number \(D_1\) below.

Let \(I\) be a connected time interval on which
\begin{equation}
        \diam(M,g(t))\geq\delta_0\sqrt t.
\end{equation}
Suppose that \(S\in I\), \(S\geq T_{\mathrm{p}}\), and
\begin{equation}
        \diam(M,g(S))\leq D_1\sqrt S
\end{equation}
for some \(0<D_1<\infty\).  At time \(S\), choose the torus fibration from
case~\ref{item:bamler-large-slice} of
Proposition~\ref{input:bamler-fixed-threshold}, put
\[
        q_0(1)=S^{-1}g(S),\qquad r_0(1)=\overline{q_0(1)},
\]
where the average is taken in that fibration, and suppose that \(r_0(1)\) is
Riemannian and
\begin{equation}
 b_0=\|q_0(1)-r_0(1)\|_{C^{N,\sigma}(M,r_0(1))}<\eta_0.
\end{equation}

Set \(T_k=100^kS\).  Call the \(k\)th block \emph{controlled} if
\([T_k,T_{k+1}]\subset I\).  On every controlled block, the same retained
torus fibration supports stagewise families \(q_k(\tau)\), \(r_k(\tau)\),
\(1\leq\tau\leq100\), and the estimates
\begin{align}
 b_{k+1}&\leq\tfrac12b_k,                                      \\
 \|q_k-r_k\|_{X_{r_k}^N[1,100]}
        &\leq C_{\mathrm{st}}b_k,                              \\
 \|r_{k+1}(1)-100^{-1}r_k(100)\|_{C^{N,\sigma}}
        &\leq C_{\mathrm{st}}b_k.                              
\end{align}
Here and below the norm in the last line is taken relative to
\(100^{-1}r_k(100)\).  On the union of the controlled blocks these stages
assemble into a continuous piecewise smooth pullback
\(g'(t)=\Psi(t)^*g(t)\) and a right-continuous piecewise invariant family
\(h(t)\), as in Section~\ref{sec:deturck-iteration}.  There is a constant
\(C<\infty\), depending only on \(K,\delta_0,N,\sigma\) and \(D_1\), such that
\begin{equation}
        L(S^1,h_{yy}(t))\leq C\sqrt t
\end{equation}
on every controlled block, for either one-sided value at a switching time,
and
\begin{equation}
        \diam(M,g(t))\leq C\sqrt t
\end{equation}
for every \(t\in I\cap[S,\infty)\).  Thus the same theorem covers both an
unbounded persistent tail and a finite component with a terminal partial
block. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:51:11.463670+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6c975c36ce3e1381dd983237e5183500b4702a978fb483baac969df82a90241a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 24 ({\cite[Definition 7.13, 7.20, Corollary~7.24, and Theorem B) of arXiv:2609.02561, 'NON-NEF LOCI IN MIXED CHARACTERISTIC'] {BMP2}}]
Let $(V,\m)$ be a DVR of mixed characteristic $(0,p>0)$.
For every triple $(X,\Delta,\ideala^{t})$, where $X$ is a normal integral scheme of finite type and flat over $V$, $(X,\Delta)$ is a log $\Q$-Gorenstein pair, $\ideala$ is a coherent ideal of $\sO_{X}$, and $t\in\Q_{\geq 0}$,
there exists a coherent ideal $\tau(X,\Delta,\ideala^{t})\subset\sO_{X}$ satisfying the following:

\begin{enumerate}
\item For an open subset $U$ of $X$ flat over $V$,
$\tau(X,\Delta,\ideala^{t})|_{U}=\tau(U,\Delta|_{U},{(\ideala\sO_U)}^{t}).$
\item $\tau(X,\Delta,\ideala^{t})[1/p]=\J(X[1/p],\Delta|_{X[1/p]},(\ideala\sO_{X[1/p]})^{t})$.
\item For every point $x\in X_{\m}$,
\[ \tau(X,\Delta,\ideala^{t})\cdot \widehat{\sO_{X,x}}=
\taubcm(\widehat{\sO_{X,x}},\widehat{\Delta_x},(\ideala\cdot\widehat{\sO_{X,x}})^{t}). \]
\item (Uniform global generation)
Suppose that $X$ is projective over $V$. For a line bundle $M$ on $X$ such that $M- K_X -\Delta$ is big and nef,
$\tau(X,\Delta)\otimes\sO_{X}(nA+M)$ is globally generated for every $n\in\Z_{>0}$ with $n\geq\dim X_{\m}$.
\item The restriction formula, the summation formula, Skoda's theorem, and stability under small perturbations of divisors are satisfied.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["E[X] = 0","a <= X <= b almost surely, with a finite range"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627523+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6c9d93477a065d229939c4ab6740265c8239985eb02668e49f4af944926aeadb","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a random variable with E[X] = 0 and a <= X <= b almost surely. Then for every real lambda, E[exp(lambda X)] <= exp(lambda^2 (b-a)^2 / 8). Equivalently X is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy (b-a)^2/4. The constant 8 in the exponent is sharp for the two-point symmetric law on {-c, c}, where (b-a)^2/8 = c^2/2 and the bound is attained to second order. Only the RANGE enters, not the variance: for a Bernoulli variable with small p the bound is far from tight, and Bennett's and Bernstein's inequalities recover the variance. Summing the lemma over independent bounded summands and applying the Chernoff method gives Hoeffding's inequality P(sum (X_i - E X_i) >= t) <= exp(-2t^2 / sum (b_i - a_i)^2). [Hoeffding (1963); see Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Lemma 2.2]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:42:55.308651+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6ca1312c0d19b031f9efc63529d3f9edbde5086f46e1ded2921b035fdbb3d8fa","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 14 (Residual identity) of arXiv:2609.02389, 'The Class Edge-Reconstruction Number of a\\ Maximal Planar Graph Is One or Two'] Suppose the same card has completions \(G=C+e\) and \(H=C+e'\), and set
\[
                  Q=A_G(e)-A_H(e').
\]
If \(G-g\cong H-h\), then
\[
                  A_G(g)-A_H(h)=Q.                 \tag{C.1}
\]
Write \(Q=P-N\), where \(P,N\) have disjoint supports and nonnegative
integer entries.  Their common total mass \(r\) is zero, one, or two.  If
every edge card of \(G\) has a degree-sequence match among the edge cards of

For instance, on a finite set every infinite sequence must take some value infinitely often, by the pigeonhole principle. For subsets of Euclidean space, the analogous statement is sequential compactness: a set is compact if and only if every infinite sequence in the set has a subsequence that converges to a point of the set. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.346386+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6cc8b6971a2b56e38fec636072bd01de5d7f7b4519ba381b8103f7e3dbd1002b","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 144 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall $s$ and $s_\delta$ from 
\eqref{e:s.sqrt.fn} and \eqref{e:s.sqrt.fn.delta}.
  There exists $C=C(L)$ such that for all $t\in [q_0,1]$,
  \[
     \Big|s(t)
      -s_{\delta}(t)\Big|
  \le C\delta.
  \]

\begin{proof}
Since $p(q_0)\geq 1/L$ and $p$ is increasing, we have
\[
  s(t) + s_\delta(t) \ge s(t) \ge L^{-1/2}\,.
\]
By adjusting $C$ appropriately it suffices to show
  \[
     \Big|s(t)^2
      -s_{\delta}(t)^2\Big|
  \le C\delta.
  \]
Note that
$s_\delta(t)^2$ is the average value of $s(t)^2$ on the interval $[t_\delta,t_{\delta+}]$:
  \[
  s_\delta(t)^2
  = \frac{t_{\delta+} p(t_{\delta+})
    -
    t_{\delta} p(t_{\delta})
    }{\delta}
    = \frac{1}{\delta}\int_{t_\delta}^{t_{\delta_+}}
    (tp)'(t)\,dt
    = \frac{1}{\delta}\int_{t_\delta}^{t_{\delta_+}} s(t)^2\,dt\,.
  \]
By the mean-value theorem, it suffices to show that $s(t)^2=(tp)'(t)$ is Lipschitz, which is clear since assumption (\ref{i:IAMP-main-p}) of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main} gives that  $\|p\|_{C^2([0,1])}\leq L$.
    \end{proof}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:07:35.010868+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6cd551976b6872025b6d97b7a0081d1d3a7172b0b2e9c9bd93373f584d3860fe","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 21 of arXiv:2609.02850, 'Canonical-row Chern flow on Bott--Samelson towers:\\ realizable-volume models for Schubert'] For a vector bundle $E$, put

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:10.016626+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6ce7a521909fbddfb2bdd77d2558dc7a730a629f1b6639d3ad797514f4825995","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 55 (Optimality of the $\ell^1$ convolution bound) of arXiv:2602.14618, 'Finitary coding and Gaussian concentration\\ for random fields'] Let $b=(b_m)_{m\in\mathbb Z^d}$ be a nonnegative, absolutely summable kernel
on $\mathbb Z^d$, with
\[
\|b\|_1 := \sum_{m\in\mathbb Z^d} b_m < \infty.
\]
For any finitely supported vector $\delta=(\delta_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}$,
define the quadratic form
\[
Q(\delta) := \sum_{k,\ell\in\mathbb Z^d} \delta_k\,\delta_\ell\, b_{\ell-k}.
\]
Then
\[
\sup_{\delta\neq 0} \frac{Q(\delta)}{\|\delta\|_2^2} = \|b\|_1.
\]
Moreover, this supremum is asymptotically attained by block indicators:
if $\delta^{(L)}_k := \1_{\{k\in\Lambda_L\}}$ with
$\Lambda_L := [-L,L]^d\cap\mathbb Z^d$, then
\[
\lim_{L\to\infty}
\frac{Q(\delta^{(L)})}{\|\delta^{(L)}\|_2^2}
=
\|b\|_1.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:26.252970+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6cf5d29339a304b7d12ec6a58ff85fa079a9c58ccf5dbaa85a7f451e90c6aac8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theo 14 of arXiv:2605.23292, 'Second-order Poincaré inequalities and localization on the Poisson space'] (normal approximation of local U-statistics on metric measure spaces)
Let $(X,d,\nu)$ be a  metric measure space with $\sigma$-finite measure $\nu$ and metric $d$. 
Fix $\delta>0$ and a function $f_\delta:X^k \times \MM \rightarrow \R$ such that $f_\delta((x_1,m_{x_1}),\hdots,(x_k,m_{x_k}))=0$ whenever $\max(d(x_i,x_j): i,j \in \{1,\hdots,k\})\geq\delta$.  Let $W \subset X$ with $\nu(W)<\infty$.
We put
\[
c_\delta := \sup_{x \in X} \nu(B_{2\delta}(x)).
\]
and assume that $c_\delta < \infty$.
Let $(\MM,\QQ)$ be a space of marks and $\hat{\P}$ a Poisson measure of intensity $\nu \otimes \QQ$
on $X \times \MM$.
For $x\in W$ and $m_x \in \MM$, we define
\[
\xi((x,M_x), \tP) := 
\sum_{(x_1,...,x_{k-1}) \in (\P \setminus \{x\})^{k-1}_{\neq}} f_{\delta}((x, M_x),(x_1,M_{x_1}),\hdots,(x_{k-1}, M_{x_{k-1}})),
\]
where $(\P \setminus \{x\})^{k-1}_{\neq}$ denotes the set of $(k-1)$-tuples of distinct points in $\P\setminus \{x\}$.
We define the \textit{local U-statistic}
\[
H := \sum_{x \in \P \cap W} \xi((x,M_x),\hat{\P}),
\]
where $M_x$ is the independent mark associated to $x \in \P$. Then $H$ satisfies the bounds
\[
\mathbf{d}_K \left(\frac{H - \E H}{\smash{\sqrt{\Var H}}}, N \right) \leq c (M^\xi_{5})^{2/5} \max(1,c_\delta)^3 \frac{(\nu(W)+\nu(W_\delta))^{1/2}}{\Var H}
\]
and

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:01:48.617469+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6d0720427205cc9ce59fbb5a4e0d029ebb5316985550f8500169e6b8f38f5041","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma l:chi.square.lower.tail of arXiv:2607.02013, 'Resolution of the Detection Threshold Conjecture for Random Geometric Graphs in the $d>n$ '] If $X\sim\chi^2(d)$, then it holds for all $x\ge0$ that
    \[
    \mathbb{P}(X \le d-x) \le 
    \mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(-\frac{x^2}{4d}\bigg)\,.
    \]
\begin{proof}
From the moment-generating function of the chi-square distribution, for any $t<0$ we can bound
    \[
    \mathbb{P}(X \le d-x) 
    \le \frac{\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]}{\mathop{\rm exp}(t(d-x))}
    = \frac{(1-2t)^{-d/2}}{\mathop{\rm exp}(t(d-x))}
    \le \mathop{\rm exp}(tx + dt^2)\,.
    \]
Optimizing over $t<0$ gives the claimed bound.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:36:12.176868+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6d14089f819b519605f051b85d085649839f481c0020108ddc6f4386086b947b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 102 of arXiv:2609.03875, 'Measure theory without infinities'] Let $\mf A$ be a monoid, $K$ be a finite set, $f(k)\in \mf A$ for all $k\in K$, and $x = \finsum_{k\in K}f(k)$.
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item[(i)] Let $\tau\colon J\to K$ be a bijection. Then $x = \finsum_{j\in J}f(\tau(j))$.
  \item[(ii)] Let $g(k)\in \mf A$ for all $k\in K$. Then $\finsum_{k\in K}(f(k) + g(k)) = x + \finsum_{k\in K}g(k)$.
  \item[(iii)] Let $\mf B$ be a monoid and $\varphi\colon\mf A\to\mf B$ be a monoid homomorphism. Then $\finsum_{k\in K} \varphi(f(k)) = \varphi(x)$.  
  \item[(iv)] Let $K = I\cup J$, where $I\cap J = \varnothing$. Then $x = \finsum_{k\in I}f(k) + \finsum_{k\in J}f(k)$.
  \item[(v)] Let $f(k) = 0$ for all $k\in K$. Then $x = 0$.
  \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:30:07.957200+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6d1f5f3d04d8bc66bb3ac3bc4af67495e0356be027e2592d6a999659dc3db53c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:F-function of arXiv:2608.12415, 'Sharp Phase Transition for Ellipsoid Fitting'] Let \(\mu_{\mathrm{sc}}\) be the semicircle distribution on \([-2,2]\), with density
\(
    f_{\mathrm{sc}}(x)
    =
    \frac{\sqrt{4-x^2}}{2\pi}.
\)
Define

\[F(x)=\textup{max}(2x,0)=\begin{cases}
        2x, & x>0,\\
        0,  & x\leq 0.
    \end{cases}\]
Let
\(
    P_j(x):=U_j\left(\frac{x}{2}\right),
\)
where \(U_j\) is the \(j\)-th Chebyshev polynomial of the second kind. Then
\(\{P_j\}_{j\ge0}\) is an orthonormal basis for
\(L^2([-2,2],\mu_{\mathrm{sc}})\), with \(P_0=1\) and \(P_1=x\).

We write
\[
    F(x)
    =

\]

\(

    \mathbb E_{x\sim\mu_{\mathrm{sc}}}[F(x)P_1(x)]=1,
\)
and, for \(j\ge2\),
\(
    b_j\coloneqq
    \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mu_{\mathrm{sc}}}[F(x)P_j(x)].
\)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:48:17.126672+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6d31b63c516e8b1b61ff4becf648461b21a1798389fefbc279596d24e3549898","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 11 ({\cite[p.\ 1) of arXiv:2605.27974, 'Discrete approximation of semi-Dirichlet forms with non-symmetric perturbations of resista'] {oshima2013semi}}] 
$(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{F})$ is called a closed form on $\mathscr{H}$ if the following hold: 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[$\mathrm{(SD1)}$]
    There exists $\lambda \geq 0$ such that $\mathcal{A}_{\lambda}(u) \geq 0$ 
    for any $u \in  \mathcal{F}$.
    \item[$\mathrm{(SD2)}$]
    $\mathcal{A}_{\lambda+1}(\cdot)^{1/2}$ is a complete norm on $\mathcal{F}$.
    \item[$\mathrm{(SD3)}$]
    There exists $K \geq 1$ such that
    \begin{equation}
    \abs{\mathcal{A}(u,v)}
    \leq
    K\mathcal{A}_{\lambda}(u)^{1/2}\mathcal{A}_{\lambda}(v)^{1/2}, 
    \quad u,v \in  \mathcal{F}.
    \end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
When $\mathscr{H} = L^2(X,\mu)$ with a measure space $(X,\mu)$, 
a closed form $(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{F})$ on $L^2(X,\mu)$ is called a semi-Dirichlet form 
on $L^2(X,\mu)$ if the following holds in addition:
\begin{enumerate}[resume]
\item[$\mathrm{(SD4)}$]
For any $f \in \mathcal{F}$ and $a \geq 0$, we have $f \wedge a \in \mathcal{F}$ 
and $\mathcal{A}(f \wedge a,f-f \wedge a) \geq 0$.
\end{enumerate}
Condition $\mathrm{(SD4)}$ is called the Markov property. 

Also, a semi-Dirichlet form $(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{F})$ on $L^2(X,\mu)$ is called 
a Dirichlet form on $L^2(X,\mu)$ if $\mathcal{A}$ is symmetric and 
we can take $0$ as the constant $\lambda$ in $\mathrm{(SD1)}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H convex AND superlinear, g Lipschitz (or merely continuous with growth conditions, with care).","Without convexity of H the formula is not the viscosity solution;","uniqueness holds in the viscosity class, not among almost-everywhere solutions, of which there are many."],"created_at":"2026-09-12T14:06:45.870891+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations, Hamilton-Jacobi","id":"claim_6d4e57a39c0d79062ed31dca43b1f879c49b82a4677a743763d6bba4251da4c6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Consider the Hamilton-Jacobi initial value problem u_t + H(Du) = 0 in R^n times (0, infinity) with u = g at time 0, where H is convex and superlinear (H(p)/|p| tends to infinity) and g is Lipschitz. Then the function u(x,t) = min over y in R^n of ( t L( (x - y)/t ) + g(y) ), with L the Legendre transform of H, is Lipschitz, solves the equation almost everywhere, attains the initial data continuously, and is the unique viscosity solution. In particular, for H(p) = |p| the formula gives the distance-like representation u(x,t) = min over |x - y| <= t of g(y), and for g the indicator-style data of a set the solution is the signed distance function, which is why the Hopf-Lax representation is the control-theoretic tool for distance functions.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.166349+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6d55dae6ab493fc505e54915ea20ee6d6bd0c4d99f46a0949085288225688af9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2608.30848, '\huge \bf Limit Laws of the Iterated Logarithm Under Sub-linear Expectations'] \begin{itemize}
\item[(i)](Identical distribution) Let $\bm{X}_1$ and $\bm{X}_2$ be two $n$-dimensional random vectors defined on sub-linear expectation spaces $(\Omega_1,\mathscr{H}_1,\widehat{\mathbb E}_1)$ and $(\Omega_2,\mathscr{H}_2,\widehat{\mathbb E}_2)$, respectively. If for any $\varphi\in C_{b,Lip}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ we have
$$ \widehat{\mathbb E}_1[\varphi(\bm{X}_1)]=\widehat{\mathbb E}_2[\varphi(\bm{X}_2)], $$
then they are said to be identically distributed, denoted by $\bm{X}_1\overset{d}{=}\bm{X}_2$. If $X_i\overset{d}{=}X_1$ for each $i\geq 1$, then the sequence of random variables $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is said to be identically distributed.
 \item[(ii)](Independence) In a sub-linear expectation space $(\Omega,\mathscr{H},\widehat{\mathbb E})$, a random vector $\bm{Y}=(Y_1,\cdots,Y_n)$, $Y_i\in\mathscr{H}$ is said to be independent of another random vector $\bm{X}=(X_1,\cdots,X_m)$, $X_i\in\mathscr{H}$ under $\widehat{\mathbb E}$, if for every test function $\varphi\in C_{b,Lip}(\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n)$ we have
     $$\widehat{\mathbb E} [\varphi(\bm{X},\bm{Y})]=\widehat{\mathbb E} [\widehat{\mathbb E} [\varphi(\bm{x},\bm{Y})]\vert_{\bm{x}=\bm{X}}].$$

  If for each $i\geq 1$, $X_{i+1}$ is independent of $(X_1,\cdots,X_i)$, then the sequence of random variables $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is said to be independent.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:04:55.804494+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6d55deb143f41da8cfc7aafc0a30447967673b891e33bc7db1f30557dc65d16d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemm l:I-given-B of arXiv:2607.18194, 'Temperature chaos in directed polymers'] Fix any Borel set $B\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^2)$ and any square-integrable random variable $X\in L^2(\Xi,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$, and denote its chaos expansion by 
    $X = \sum_{n=0}^\infty I_n(f_n)$ (see (p:chaos-expansion of the paper)).
    Then we have
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb{E}[X|\mathcal{F}_B]
        = \sum_{n=0}^\infty I_n(f_n \1_{B}^{\otimes n})
        \qquad\text{in $L^2(\Xi,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$,}
    \end{align*}
    where for $n=0$, the $0\textsuperscript{th}$ tensor power of any function is identically $1$.
    Note that for $n\geqslant 1$, we have $\1_B^{\otimes n} = \1_{B^n}$, where $B^n\coloneqq B\times\cdots\times B$ is the $n$-fold Cartesian product.

    It follows by (equation e:parseval of the paper) that for any $X,Y\in L^2(\Xi,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$ with chaos expansions $X=\sum_{n=0}^\infty I_n(f_n)$ and $Y=\sum_{n=0}^\infty I_n(g_n)$, we have
    \begin{align}
        \mathbb{E}\Bigl[
            \mathbb{E}[X|\mathcal{F}_B]\cdot\mathbb{E}[Y|\mathcal{F}_B]
        \Bigr]
        &=
        \sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb{E}\left[
            I_n(f_n\1_B^{\otimes n})
            I_n(g_n\1_B^{\otimes n})
        \right].
    \end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:18:54.363836+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6d56022911857bff73d3a24153f6fe3c0c4b95a9e382194914f1917cda43e3c8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] We can talk about scalar products and lengths in $\mathbb C^N$,
$$<x,y>=\sum_ix_i\bar{y}_i\qquad,\qquad ||x||=\sqrt{\sum_i|x_i|^2}$$
which are related by the following conversion formulae,
$$||x||=\sqrt{<x,x>}\quad,\quad <x,y>
=\frac{||x+y||^2-||x-y||^2+i||x+iy||^2-i||x-iy||^2}{4}$$
and the following happen:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $<\lambda x,y>=<x,\bar{\lambda}y>=\lambda<x,y>$.

\item $<x+y,z>=<x,z>+<y,z>$.

\item $<x,y+z>=<x,z>+<y,z>$. 

\item $<x,y>=\overline{<y,x>}$.

\item $||\lambda x||=|\lambda|\cdot||x||$.

\item $|<x,y>|\leq||x||\cdot||y||$.

\item $||x+y||\leq||x||+||y||$.

\item $x\perp y\iff<x,y>=0$, by definition.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.350627+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6d5e2979f23b9667c548c3a48bbf9167e992933c6decbe5a89a6ac97fe2e42a7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 181 (annealed second moment bounds for $\bar{D}^{\Ising}$ and $\bar{D}^{\frozen,\Ising}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $\bar{D}^{\Ising}$ as in \eqref{e:drift.error.Ising}, we have

		{N}

for all $0\le d\le \dmax-1$, with $\BUCKETS$ as in 
\eqref{e:buckets.scB}. The same bound holds with $\bar{D}^{\frozen,\Ising}$ in place of $\bar{D}^\Ising$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:49:24.958848+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6d7f4c22813d13b5b77ab2af0f195a8c132c38ba2332bb4376eb564ac648c1e2","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:admissible of arXiv:2609.03264, 'Certified Spherical MUSIC for 3D Localization under Adversarial Subspace Perturbations'] Let $f\colon B_1(0)\to [0,\infty)$, let
		\[
		X=\{\bm{x}_1,\dots,\bm{x}_s\}\subset B_1(0),
		\]
		and let $\varepsilon,\rho,\tau_0,\tau_1$ satisfy
		\[
			0\leq\varepsilon<\rho,
			\qquad
			0\le \tau_0<\tau_1.
		\]
		We say that $f$ is a threshold-admissible optimization landscape for $X$,
		with parameters
		$(\varepsilon,\rho,\tau_0,\tau_1)$, if:
		\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
			\item for every $j=1,\dots,s$, the function $f$ has a 
			local minimum
			$\widetilde{\bm{x}}_j\in
			\overline{B_\varepsilon(\bm{x}_j)}$;
			\item the relevant minima are uniformly shallow and all points
			outside the certified neighborhoods are uniformly higher:
			\begin{eqnarray}
			\max_{1\le j\le s} f(\widetilde{\bm{x}}_j)&\le& \tau_0,\\
			f(\bm{z})&\ge &\tau_1, 
			\quad
			\forall
			\bm{z}\in B_1(0)\setminus
			\bigcup_{j=1}^s B_\rho(\bm{x}_j).
			\end{eqnarray}
		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:05:37.779036+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6d9b7e1ef52d934dc94f90127d61fd71337f5187524d9f0247be4e1d022a456a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:pseudo-bloch of arXiv:2608.01253, 'The pseudo-quantum representation of \\finite reversible Markov chains'] Let $N=2M$ and let $\{\Sigma_a\}_{a=1}^{d}$, with $d=\tfrac{N(N+1)}2-1$, be a
trace-orthonormal basis of the traceless complex-symmetric matrices, so that
$\operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma_a\Sigma_b)=\delta_{ab}$, $\operatorname{Tr}\Sigma_a=0$, and
$\Sigma_a^{T}=\Sigma_a$. Orthonormality here is meant for the bilinear trace form
$\operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma_a\Sigma_b)$, with no complex conjugation, and such a basis exists
because that form is nondegenerate on the complex-symmetric matrices, for instance
the symmetrised units $(E_{ij}+E_{ji})/\sqrt2$ for $i<j$ together with an
orthonormal set of $N-1$ real traceless diagonal matrices work. The
$\Sigma_a$ are complex symmetric, not Hermitian, so they are the bilinear analogue
of the Gell-Mann matrices rather than the matrices themselves. Write

\[
\rho_z=\frac{\operatorname{Tr}\rho_z}{N}\,\mathrm{I}+\sum_{a=1}^{d}r_a(z)\,\Sigma_a,\qquad
r_a(z)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_z\Sigma_a).
\]

Then the coordinate vector obeys the linear flow

\[
\dot r_a(z)=\sum_{b}\Omega_{ab}\,r_b(z),\qquad
\Omega_{ab}=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(\Sigma_a[K,\Sigma_b]\bigr),\qquad \Omega^{T}=-\Omega.
\]

Hence the flow lies in $\OO(d,\mathbb{C})$ and preserves the bilinear quantity

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:33:21.474298+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6dd82b3416d1cab599643a7a74c55c51f3145970063e0bb4624df8a741879e1f","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:finite-rank-lower-cluster of arXiv:2606.21006, 'Law of the Iterated Logarithm for Weighted Sums of Functionals of Long-Memory Gaussian Seq'] Let \(\mathfrak H\) be a real separable Hilbert space, and let \(W_n\), \(n\ge3\), be
isonormal Gaussian processes over \(\mathfrak H\). Let \(E\subset\mathfrak H\) be a
finite-dimensional subspace with orthonormal basis \(e_1,\ldots,e_N\).

Assume that for some \(\xi\in E\) with \(\|\xi\|_{\mathfrak H}\le1\), there exists a subsequence
\(n_k\to\infty\) such that
\[
    \frac{W_{n_k}(e_i)}{(2\log\log n_k)^{1/2}}
    \longrightarrow
    \langle e_i,\xi\rangle_{\mathfrak H},
    \qquad i=1,\ldots,N .
\]
Fix \(T<\infty\). Let \(Q_t\in E^{\odot m}\), \(0\le t\le T\), be a continuous finite-rank kernel family. Then
\[
    \frac{I_m(Q_t;W_{n_k})}{(2\log\log n_k)^{m/2}}
    \longrightarrow
    \langle Q_t,\xi^{\otimes m}\rangle_{\mathfrak H^{\otimes m}}
\]
uniformly in \(t\in[0,T]\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:30:14.147883+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6e07f2a2c69a84919c7855920dedbd38eba03f5ecbc58ca2adedcd2d746e572e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem th:poly of arXiv:2608.19358, 'An optimal Poincaré inequality\\for the complex Ginibre log-gas'] Assume that $n\geq2$, and consider the following:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Two symmetric functions, which are polynomials with respect to $z$ and $\bar{z}$:
    \begin{equation}
      S(z)=\sum_{j=1}^n z_j
      \quad\text{and}\quad
      R(z)=\sum_{1\leq j<k\leq n}|z_j-z_k|^2=n\sum_{j=1}^n\left|z_j-\frac{S(z)}n\right|^2.
    \end{equation}
  \item The normalized complex Hermite polynomial\footnote{The Rodrigues
      formula is
      $\mathrm H_{a,b}(s,\overline
      s)=\frac{(-1)^{a+b}}{\sqrt{a!b!}}\mathrm{e}^{|s|^2}\bar\partial_s^{a}\partial_s^{b}\mathrm{e}^{-|s|^2}$.}$\mathrm
    H_{a,b}$ of bidegree $(a,b)$ for $\gamma_1$.
  \item The classical generalized Laguerre polynomial\footnote{Defined by the
      Laguerre equation (equation eq:laguerre of the paper) and normalized by
      $L^{\alpha}_m(0)=\binom{m+\alpha}{m}$. These polynomials are orthogonal
      with respect to the probability distribution
      $\mathrm{Gamma}(\kappa,1)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\kappa)}x^{\kappa-1}\mathrm{e}^{-x}\mathbf{1}_{x\geq0}\mathrm{d}x$.
      However, they are not orthonormal.} $L_m^{(\kappa-1)}$ of degree $m$,
    with $\kappa=\frac{(n-1)(n+2)}{2}$.
  \end{itemize}
  Then for every $a,b,m\in\mathbb N$, the symmetric polynomial
  \begin{equation}
    P_{a,b,m}(z)
    =\mathrm H_{a,b}\bigl(S(z),\overline{S(z)}\bigr)
    L_m^{(\kappa-1)}\bigl(R(z)\bigr)
  \end{equation}
  is an eigenfunction of $A_n$ in the sense that
  \begin{equation}
    -A_nP_{a,b,m}  =\lambda_{a,b,m}P_{a,b,m}
    \quad\text{where}\quad
    \lambda_{a,b,m}=2\frac{\alpha_n}{n}(a+b+2m).
  \end{equation}
  Moreover, the family $\{P_{a,b,m}:a,b,m\in\mathbb{N}\}$ is a basis of the
  polynomial algebra $\mathbb C[S,\overline S,R]$. In particular, this algebra
  is invariant under $A_n$ in the sense that
  $A_n\bigl(\mathbb C[S,\overline S,R]\bigr)\subset\mathbb C[S,\overline
  S,R]$. Furthermore, the elements of the family are mutually orthogonal in
  $L^2(\mu_n)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["P is a product measure (independent coordinates)","A and B are increasing events (van den Berg-Kesten); Reimer's inequality removes this hypothesis","A box B is the disjoint-occurrence event, witnessed by disjoint coordinate sets, not the intersection"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.048828+00:00","domain":"percolation and correlation inequalities (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_6e1b259086d35f04b2f1c00edbbb017feb2ef912f0a7984e0cd00e9e6739eb28","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let P be a product measure on {0,1}^n and let A and B be increasing events. Write A box B for the disjoint occurrence of A and B: the set of configurations omega for which there are disjoint index sets I and J such that every configuration agreeing with omega on I lies in A and every configuration agreeing with omega on J lies in B. Then P(A box B) <= P(A) P(B) (van den Berg and Kesten 1985). This runs in the opposite direction to the Harris-FKG inequality for the plain intersection, P(A and B) >= P(A) P(B); the two are not in conflict because A box B is a subset of A and B. In percolation the standard use is P(two disjoint open paths) <= P(open path)^2.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:23:05.300717+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6e256730514d6bdd7558f3fa3d570bc1759c4d627d8820f64be9e366a63d3c5b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 18 (Projected total-covariance decomposition) of arXiv:2608.21709, 'Posterior Information Dynamics of Diffusion Models for Linear Inverse Problems'] Fix a measurement value $r$ and $t>0$, assume
$\E[\|X_0\|^2\mid R=r]<\infty$, and let $P$ be an orthogonal projector.  With
$m_t^r(X_t)=\E[X_0\mid X_t,R=r]$,
\begin{equation}

\begin{aligned}
\Tr\!\left(P\Cov(X_0\mid r)P\right)
&=
\E\!\left[
\Tr\!\left(P\Cov(X_0\mid X_t,r)P\right)
\,\middle|\,R=r
\right]\\
&\quad+
\Tr\Cov\!\left(Pm_t^r(X_t)\mid R=r\right).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The first term is conditional variance that remains after observing the noisy
state; the second is variation of the exact posterior mean across noisy states.
Under the Gaussian noising family, the second term tends to zero as
the channel SNR tends to zero and to
$\Tr(P\Cov(X_0\mid r)P)$ as the channel SNR tends to infinity.  Thus
across-state clean-estimate dispersion is the \emph{resolved} component of a
total-covariance decomposition, not the remaining posterior covariance. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:12:19.463164+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6e2879df1f45a2244b874b34b20210b465bf580b412d8b57f2e8c93ad21c2097","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 4 (A bounded Brownian perturbation in a mixed equation) of arXiv:2608.17540, 'Pathwise stability for one-dimensional SDEs driven by Brownian motion and a symmetric stab'] Let $\wt\eta\in(1/\alpha,1)$, let $0<\lambda<1$, let $\kappa\ne0$, and let $r\in L^2(0,T)$ be deterministic. Consider
\[
  b(t,x)=\wt b(t,x)\equiv0,
  \qquad
  a(t,x)\equiv\kappa,
  \qquad
  \wt a(t,x)=\kappa+r(t),
\]
and
\[
  \sigma(t,x)=\wt\sigma(t,x)=1+\lambda\bigl(|x|^{\wt\eta}\wedge1\bigr).
\]
Then the baseline equation contains both the Brownian and stable terms, the perturbed equation is driven by the same two noises, and the stable coefficient is bounded, bounded away from zero, and non-Lipschitz at the origin. For any coupled solution pair satisfying Assumption~\ref{ass:solutions}, the coefficient distances are
\[
  B=0,
  \qquad
  A^2=\int_0^T |r(t)|^2\dd t,
  \qquad
  S=0.
\]
Consequently, if $x_0=\wt x_0$ and $A=\|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}<1$, Theorem~\ref{thm:noncritical} gives
\[
  \sup_{0\le t\le T}\E|X_t-\wt X_t|^{\alpha-1}
  \le C\|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}^{\frac{2(\alpha\wt\eta-1)}{\alpha\wt\eta-\alpha+2}}.
\]
Thus, in this mixed Brownian--stable equation, the estimate reduces to the Brownian diffusion error, while the stable coefficient is H\"older and fails to be Lipschitz.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:33:21.477637+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6e4ba317c3c02f07a8a926ab6a28de23f447b28130f828e7ba3b6d6957e89135","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2606.21391, 'Extreme points and faces in the moment problem'] Let $(X,\mathcal{F})$ be a measurable space whose $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{F}$ contains all 
singletons in $X$. A \emph{measure} is a countably additive map $\mathcal{F}\to[0,\infty)$. 
A measure $\mu$ is \emph{concentrated} on $A\in\mathcal{F}$ if $\mu(X\setminus A)=0$.
A measure $\mu$ is a \emph{probability measure} if its total mass is $\mu(X)=1$. 
Let $P$ be the convex set of probability measures on $(X,\mathcal{F})$. The 
\emph{point measure} at $x\in X$, denoted $\delta_x$, is the measure with values 
$\delta_x(A):=1$ if $x\in A$ and $\delta_x(A):=0$ otherwise for every $A\in\mathcal{F}$. 
Let 
\[
P_1:=\{\delta_x: x\in X\}.
\]
A measure $\mu$ is \emph{$k$-atomic} [klerk-laurent19,lasserre10,nie23,schmuedgen17], 
$k\in\mathbb{N}_0$, if $\mu=\lambda_1\delta_{x_1}+\dots+\lambda_k\delta_{x_k}$ for mutually 
distinct points $x_1,\dots,x_k$ in $X$ and strictly positive real weights 
$\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k>0$. A measure is \emph{finitely atomic} if it is $k$-atomic 
for some $k\in\mathbb{N}_0$. Let
\[
P\!_\mathrm{fin}:=
\{\mu\in P : \text{$\mu$ is finitely atomic}\,\}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:37:08.955949+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6e55cf06ea9308239f2d44a5ad50b13b8949be43ffa5282bae83bf764ae0b06d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:ci of arXiv:2609.01581, 'Concentration of additive functionals of Stratonovich-type'] Under assumption~(ass:dynamics of the paper), let $\mathrm{d}\nu/\mathrm{d}\mu \in
L^2(\mu)$, and let $\tilde\sigma_A^2$ and $c_A$ be sub-gamma parameters for which
Eq.~(equation eq:uq_general of the paper) holds with $\overline{A}_t \in
\{\overline{\rho}_t(V), \overline{J}_t(U)\}$. 
Fix a confidence level $1-\alpha$, with $\alpha\in (0,1)$, and define
\begin{align}
  r_A(\alpha,t)
  =
  \sqrt{\frac{2\tilde\sigma_A^2}{t}\log\left(\frac{2N_\nu}{\alpha}\right)}
  +
  \frac{c_A}{t}\log\left(\frac{2N_\nu}{\alpha}\right),
  \quad
  N_\nu \equiv \left\|\frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\right\|_{L^2(\mu)},
  
\end{align}
where $N_\nu$ is a prefactor encoding the initial condition with $N_\mu=1$.
Then for every $t > 0$,
\begin{align}
  \mathbb{P}^\nu\left(-r_A(\alpha,t) \leq \overline{A}_t - \E^\mu[\overline{A}_t] \leq r_A(\alpha,t)\right)
  \geq 1-\alpha ,
  
\end{align}
that is, with probability of at least $1-\alpha$, under $\mathbb{P}^\nu$, the stationary mean lies in the confidence interval
\begin{align}
  \E^\mu[\overline{A}_t]
  \in
  \left[\overline{A}_t - r_A(\alpha,t),
  \overline{A}_t + r_A(\alpha,t)\right].
  
\end{align}
Moreover, the corresponding one-sided guarantees hold with a smaller radius $r_A^{(1)}(\alpha,t)$, 
obtained from Eq.~(equation eq:ci_radius of the paper) by replacing $2N_\nu$ with $N_\nu$, i.e., 
\begin{align}
  \mathbb{P}^\nu\left(\overline{A}_t - \E^\mu[\overline{A}_t]
  \leq r_A^{(1)}(\alpha,t)\right)
  \geq 1-\alpha,
  \qquad
  \mathbb{P}^\nu\left(\E^\mu[\overline{A}_t] -  \overline{A}_t
  \leq r_A^{(1)}(\alpha,t)\right)
  \geq 1-\alpha.
  
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

		g(r,X_{r-}^n,z)-g(r,X_{r_n-}^n,z)

		+
		u(r,X_{r-}^n+g(r,X_{r-}^n,z))
		-u(r,X_{r-}^n+g(r,X_{r_n-}^n,z))
		\bigg\}
		\widetilde N(dr,dz)
		\bigg|^{\bar p},
		\\
		W_t^9
		:=&\,
		\sup_{s\in[0,t]}
		\bigg|
		\int_0^s\int_{|z|<R}

\begin{equation} 
d_{\textnormal{TV}} \big( \mathcal{L}(V_{{\cal X }''} \mid V_{\partial {\cal X }'} = \v_{\partial {\cal X }'}),

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.684238+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6e7cd7e98724c20e6adffd7f500b07a914e7966db3811ced679e6a898a87bb70","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 3 of arXiv:2607.26254, 'A Simple Model of Sea Spray'] Suppose, $\mathcal{F}(dr)=\mathcal{F}(r) dr$ and $ \mathcal{F}(r)$ is strictly positive on a finite interval $[r_{min},r_{max}]$ and equal to zero otherwise. Suppose $r\to\zeta(r)$ is continuous on $[r_{min},r_{max}]$ and $(t,r)\to (r_t,z_t(r))$ is continuous on,  

$$
A=\{\,(t,r)\mid0\leq t\leq \zeta(r),\,\,  r_{min}\leq r\leq r_{max},\,\}.
$$

\mpar
Finally, suppose $m$ is a continuous function of $z.$ Then,
$$
z_{100}=\max_{(r,t)\in A} z_t(r).
$$
\begin{proof}
Let $z^{**}=\max_{(t,r)\in A} z_t(r).$ Note that  $z_{100}\leq z^{**}$ since no droplet ever exceeds this height. Suppose, on the other hand, that $w< z^{**}.$ Since $z$ is a continuous function and $A$ is a closed set, $z$ attains its maximum value, hence  $z_t(r)>w$  for all $(t,r)$ in an open subset of $A.$ In particular, there is an interval $[a,b]\subset [r_{min}, r_{max}]$ such that,
$$
\int_0^\infty r_t^31_{(0,w]}(z_t(r))dt  < \int_0^\infty r^3_t1_{(0,z_{100}]}(z_t(r))dt
$$
for all $r\in [a,b]$. Thus,
\begin{align*}
m(w) & = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi\rho   \int_0^\infty \negthickspace \int_0^\infty r^3_s\, 1_{(0,w]}(z_s(r))\mathcal{F}(dr) ds\\
& <\tfrac{4}{3}\pi\rho   \int_0^\infty \negthickspace \int_0^\infty r^3_s\, 1_{(0,z_{100}]}(z_s(r))\mathcal{F}(dr) ds\\
& = m(z_{100}),
\end{align*}
since $\mathcal{F}(r)$ is strictly positive on $[a,b].$ By continuity this implies,
$$
m(z^{**})=\lim_{z\to z^{**}}m(z)\leq m(z_{100}),
$$
and because $m$ is non-decreasing, we have $z^{**}\leq z_{100}$ which proves the result.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.345582+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6e9838daad033267a324612fda93794ababb91013b8c4bcf33990c572760ca95","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 138 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] If $\psi:\bbR^{d_1}\to\bbR^{d_2}$ is Lipschitz, then $\psi$ preserves $\bbW_2$ convergence.
If $d_1=2,d_2=1$ and $\psi(X,Y)=XY$, then $\psi$ preserves $\bbW_2$ convergence for sequences on which $X$ is uniformly bounded.

\begin{proof}
The first statement follows because $L$-Lipschitz maps increase $\bbW_2$ distances by at most a factor of $L$.
For the second statement, suppose 
$X_N\to X$ and $Y_N\to Y$ in $L^2$, with $|X_N|\leq C$ almost surely for all $N$. 
We will argue that this implies $X_NY_N\to XY$ in $L^2$, and the assertion then follows. First,
the uniform bound on $X_N$ gives
  \[
  \E\Big[(X_NY_N-X_NY)^2\Big]
  \le C^2 \E\Big[(Y_N-Y)^2\Big]
  = o_N(1)\,,
  \]
so $X_NY_N$ and $X_NY$ are close in $L^2$. For $T$ growing sufficiently slowly with $N$, we then bound
  \[
  \E\Big[ (X_NY-XY)^2\Big]
  \le T^2\E\Big[ (X_N-X)^2\Big]
  + 4C^2\E\Big[Y^2; |Y| \ge T\Big]
  \le T^2 o_N(1) + o_T(1)\,,
  \]
where the last term is because $Y^2\in L^1$. Therefore $X_NY$ converges to $XY$ in $L^2$, and the claim follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:53.191597+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6e9f4316f0743dedc3012c9ae8e1ca8090bea5746e3fba9bda64216912d113ae","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 2 of arXiv:2606.31455, 'Discrete time-multidimensional renewal theory and applications'] Let $\mathcal{R}:=\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}^d}$ be the set of all real-valued sequences on $\mathbb{N}^d$.
Equipped with pointwise addition $+$ and the convolution product $*$ in \eqref{eq:conv}, $(\mathcal{R},+,*)$ is a commutative ring
with unity. The identity element (unit) is the sequence $\ez$ defined by

\[
\ez(k)=
\begin{cases}
1, & k=0_d,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

If there exists $b:\mathbb{N}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $a*b=b*a=\ez$, then $a$ is \emph{convolutionally invertible} and $b$ is called
its \emph{convolutional inverse}, denoted by $a^{(-1)}$.

Moreover, the map $\Phi:\mathcal{R}\to \mathbb{R}[[x_1,\ldots,x_d]]$ defined by $\Phi(a)=P_a$ is a ring isomorphism. In particular,
for all $a,b\in\mathcal{R}$,
\[
P_{a+b}(x_{1:d})=P_a(x_{1:d})+P_b(x_{1:d}),\ \
P_{a*b}(x_{1:d})=P_a(x_{1:d})\,P_b(x_{1:d}),\ \
P_{\ez}(x_{1:d})=1.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726715+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis / Sobolev embedding","id":"claim_6eb2ea7b6a07326d6e5d6688779ae32153ce28e129f99091ad137afef25da73a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: H^s(R^n) embeds into L^∞(R^n) ∩ C^0 only for s > n/2, strictly; the borderline s = n/2 is excluded. Concrete counterexample, n = 2 (s = 1): u(x) = log log(1/|x|) for 0 < |x| < e^{−1}, extended by 0. Then ∫|∇u|² = 2π ∫_0^{e^{−1}} dr / ( r log²(1/r) ) = 2π < ∞ and ∫ u² < ∞, so u ∈ H¹(R²), yet u is unbounded at the origin. General n: choose f with f̂(ξ) = (1+|ξ|)^{−n} (log(2+|ξ|))^{−1} ≥ 0; then ∫ (1+|ξ|²)^{n/2}|f̂|² dξ < ∞ (radially, ∫ dρ/(ρ log²ρ) converges) so f ∈ H^{n/2}(R^n), while ∫ f̂ dξ = ∞ (∫ dρ/(ρ log ρ) diverges); since f̂ ≥ 0, an L^∞ bound on f would force ∫ f̂ < ∞ (test against a Gaussian approximate identity with positive Fourier transform and use monotone convergence), so f ∉ L^∞. Consequences: an energy-critical argument may not conclude a pointwise bound from the energy norm; ‖u‖_{L^q_t L^∞_x} estimates at the critical regularity generally require Besov spaces, since Ḃ^{n/2}_{2,1} embeds into L^∞ while H^{n/2} does not. The failure of the endpoints (q,r) = (2,∞) — Schrödinger in n = 2, wave in n = 3 — is a separate matter, proved by explicit counterexamples of Montgomery-Smith and of Klainerman–Machedon, not a corollary of this embedding failure.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0058-a-peeling-algorithm-exploring-site-percolation-on-boltzmann-maps","No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:26:45.042388+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6ee908b5f808cca14f04a9496a7df36b77c5fdd7c0ca2b7a7d3ee18a1cb155de","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Design the algorithm and check whether the exploration frontier remains Markov. Result: For bond percolation the peeling frontier is a two-colour boundary (free/blocked edges) and the algorithm peels the edge at the colour change, keeping the unexplored region a Boltzmann map with a boundary of the same type. For site percolation the colour lives on vertices and after peeling a face the newly exposed boundary vertices are uncoloured; the natural algorithm peels the edge whose left endpoint is black and right endpoint is uncoloured, colouring the new vertices as they appear. The unexplored region is then a Boltzmann map with a boundary condition that is a word in {black, white, uncoloured}, and the difficulty is that the length of the black segment is no longer a Markov chain by itself: the future depends on the positions of uncoloured vertices along the boundary. The frontier becomes Markov if one records the boundary word, which is an infinite-dimensional state. On triangulations the problem was solved (Angel-Curien) because degree-3 faces expose at most one new vertex per step, keeping the state finite; for general Boltzmann maps with large faces a peeled face exposes many uncoloured vertices at once. So a Markov site-percolation peeling exists exactly when faces expose boundedly many vertices, i.e. for bounded face degrees, and the general Boltzmann case requires a state space of boundary words; whether the threshold can still be computed from a word-valued Markov chain is the open part. Obstruction: Unbounded face degrees expose many uncoloured boundary vertices at once; the frontier state is a word, not an integer.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:01:48.617912+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f155acdc0830bd5aeb602e98085e3ef8a1c96bd1fe6b2fcecbea1503a83c8d7","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma l:W.is.subgaussian of arXiv:2607.02013, 'Resolution of the Detection Threshold Conjecture for Random Geometric Graphs in the $d>n$ '] Let
\begin{equation}
{\mathcal{H}} =  \{\|I_n+W\|_{\operatorname{op}}\le 4 \}.
    
\end{equation}
If $d \ge (1+\epsilon) n$ for some arbitrarily small constant $\epsilon>0$, then there exists a constant $c>0$ only depending on $\epsilon$ such that 
$\mathbb{P}_0(W \in {\mathcal{H}}^c) \leq \mathop{\rm exp}(-cn)$ 
and,
for any zero-diagonal symmetric matrix $U$,
\[
\mathbb{E}_{X\sim \mathbb{P}_{0}}[\mathop{\rm exp}( \langle U,W\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal H}\rangle)]\le \mathop{\rm exp}\left(\frac{2 \|U\|^2}{d}\right)+1\le 2\mathop{\rm exp}\left(\frac{2\|U\|^2}{d}\right).
\]

\begin{proof}

Recall that $W=XX^\top -I_n$, so 

${\mathcal{H}}$ is implied by the event
$\{\|X\|_{\rm op} \le 2\}$.
Let $Z$ be an $n\times d$ matrix with i.i.d.\ standard gaussian entries, and let $D$ be the $n\times n$ diagonal matrix with diagonal entries $\|z_1\|,\ldots,\|z_n\|$. Then $X$ is equidistributed as $D^{-1}Z$, so we can bound
    \[\|X\|_{\rm op} \le 
    \frac{\|Z\|_{\rm op}}
        {\min_i \|z_i\|}\,.\]
By the standard concentration inequality for Gaussian matrices~[vershynin2010introduction], we have
\[\|Z\|_{\rm op}
\le\sqrt{d} + \sqrt{n}
+t\]
with probability at least $1-2\mathop{\rm exp}(-t^2/2)$. By the standard concentration bound for chi-squared random variables (Lemma~(l:chi.square.lower.tail of the paper)), we have
    \[
    \min\Big\{ \|z_i\|
    : 1\le i\le n\Big\}
    \ge d-(2d)^{1/2} t
    \]
with probability at least $1-n\mathop{\rm exp}(-t^2/2)$.  Taking $t=cn^{1/2}$, we conclude that with probability at least $1-3n\mathop{\rm exp}(-c^2 n/2)$, we have
\[\|X\|_{\rm op} \le \frac{1+(1+c)/\sqrt{1+\epsilon}}{[1-\sqrt{2}c/\sqrt{1+\epsilon}]^{1/2}} \le 2\,,\]
where the last inequality holds by choosing $c$ to be a sufficiently small constant  depending on $\epsilon$. 

Next, let $W_m$ denote the principal submatrix of $W$ formed by the first $m$ rows and columns. We will truncate on the event
$\mathcal H_m= \{\| I_m+W_m\|_{\operatorname{op}}\le 4 \}$.
Note that ${\mathcal{H}}_{m+1} \subset {\mathcal{H}}_{m}$ for all $1 \le m \le n-1$ and $\mathcal{H} = \mathcal{H}_n$. Abbreviating $u_n$ for the last column of $U$, we can bound
\begin{align*}
     &\ \mathbb{E}_{X\sim \mathbb{P}_{0}}\Big[\mathop{\rm exp}( \langle U,W\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal H}\rangle)\Big]\\
   \le &\ \mathbb{E}_{x_1,\dots,x_n}
   \bigg[\mathop{\rm exp}\bigg( \sum_{i<j}u_{ij}\langle x_i,x_j\rangle\bigg)
   \mathbf{1}\{W_n \in \mathcal H_n\}\bigg]+1\\
   \le&\ \mathbb{E}_{x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}}\bigg[\mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(
   \sum_{i<j<n}u_{ij}\langle x_i,x_j\rangle\bigg)\mathbf{1}\{ W_{n-1} \in \mathcal H_{n-1}\} \mathbb{E}_{x_n}\bigg[\mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(
   \bigg\langle \sum_{i<n} u_{in}x_i,x_n
   \bigg\rangle
   \bigg)\bigg]\bigg]+1\\
    \le&\ \mathbb{E}_{x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}}\bigg[\mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(\sum_{i<j<n}u_{ij}\langle x_i,x_j\rangle\bigg)\mathbf{1}\{W_{n-1}\in \mathcal H_{n-1}\}\cdot \mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(\frac{ (u_n)^\top (I_{n-1}+ W_{n-1}) u_n}{2d}\bigg)\bigg]+1\\
    \le&\ \mathbb{E}_{x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}}\bigg[\mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(\sum_{i<j<n}u_{ij}\langle x_i,x_j\rangle\bigg)\mathbf{1}\{W_{n-1} \in \mathcal H_{n-1}\}\bigg]\cdot \mathop{\rm exp}\left(\frac{2 \|u_n\|^2
    }{d}\right)+1\,,
\end{align*}
where the second-to-last inequality is by Lemma~(lem:beta.mgf of the paper), and the
 last inequality holds because we have $\|I_{n-1}+W_{n-1}\|_{\operatorname{op} }
\le 4$ on the event ${\mathcal{H}}_{n-1}$.
Iterating the above gives the claimed bound.
\end{proof}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a well-defined Dirichlet form and reversible Markov chain with a reference measure mu","a valid Nash-type functional inequality with a specified effective dimension d","for two-sided estimates: matching volume-growth and effective-resistance-growth bounds on balls","typically also an elliptic Harnack inequality, or comparable regularity, to establish the matching lower heat-kernel bound"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.993577+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f33033cc6c015e74e17ecf03f84254fb9e59f13180becd49ac22b25d7db440b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). A Nash inequality on a graph with Dirichlet form E and reference measure mu has the form ||f||_2^{2+4/d} <= C E(f,f) ||f||_1^{4/d} for all f in the domain of the form, where d is an effective dimension parameter. Such an inequality is classically equivalent, by results of Nash and later Carlen-Kusuoka-Stroock, to an on-diagonal heat-kernel upper bound p_t(x,x) <= C' t^{-d/2} for the associated Markov semigroup, and combining it with matching volume-growth and effective-resistance-growth estimates, within the general framework relating resistance growth to heat-kernel decay used for fractal-like and random graphs, yields two-sided sub-Gaussian or Gaussian heat-kernel bounds. On graphs where effective resistance to the complement of a ball of radius n grows like n^zeta and volume grows like n^alpha, this gives sub-Gaussian heat-kernel estimates with off-diagonal decay governed by the exponent alpha+zeta, a technique central to analysis on fractals and on random graphs such as critical percolation clusters or random walk among random conductances. The technique does not give the resistance or volume exponents themselves, which are separate geometric inputs, and a full two-sided heat-kernel estimate typically requires both the Nash-type inequality, giving the upper bound, and a separate lower-bound argument, often via a chaining construction or an elliptic Harnack inequality. Typical failure: Assuming ordinary Euclidean Gaussian heat-kernel scaling, of the t^{-d/2} exp(-|x-y|^2/4t) form, transfers automatically to a random or fractal-like graph without re-deriving the resistance exponent zeta; on structures such as the incipient infinite cluster of critical percolation, or random conductance models with heavy-tailed conductances, the correct scaling is sub-Gaussian with zeta != 1, and using the Euclidean exponent silently mis-states both the walk dimension and the tail behavior of the heat kernel. Canonical reference: Nash, 1958, American Journal of Mathematics; Carlen, Kusuoka and Stroock, 1987, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincare; Barlow, 2004, Annals of Probability; Kumagai, Random Walks on Disordered Media and their Scaling Limits, 2014, Springer.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:09:41.190331+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_6f5cfee93cb76cd8d74924060da891f5b4881b2215fe5aa410d44ee0474d26de","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, the term homology, originally introduced in algebraic topology, has three primary, closely related usages. First, there is the homology of a chain complex, a sequence of abelian groups, called homology groups, which are regarded as fundamental invariants of the chain complex. Secondly, when one can associate a chain complex to a different mathematical object, one can also associate its homology to that object. Distinct procedures of associating chain complexes to a given object are grouped into homology theories. Finally, homology is important in the study of topological spaces. Under nice conditions in which distinct homology theories for a single topological space produce the same homology groups, one can define a single homology of a topological space. This last notion of homology is closely related to topological ideas frequently discussed in popular mathematics such as the holes of a surface or the cycles of a graph. There is also a related notion of the cohomology of a cochain complex, giving rise to various cohomology theories, in addition to the notion of the cohomology of a topological space.","status":"unverified"}
