{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.094911+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f628d213e948889bebd7b6cc96612958248be05cf576e45b6f16f5b6758c038","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:circuit-primitives of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] For an ordered finite set $S$ of oriented carrier labels, write
$\mathscr H_S=\bigotimes_{u\in S}H_u$, with every factor equipped with
the Euclidean Hilbert norm.  A \emph{normalized Brauer primitive} is a
signed carrier permutation, a wedge reversal, full transpose, a share
turn, a through string, the orthogonal antisymmetrizer, or a cup/cap
normalized so that its operator norm is one.  A share turn is the fixed
signed boundary permutation, possibly followed by full transpose,
induced when a principal pivot reverses one of the two ordered boundary
intervals.  The two coefficient primitives are
\[
 \widehat C_{uv}=\iota_{uv}C\pi_{uv}:H_u\otimes H_v\to H_u\otimes H_v,
\]
where $\pi_{uv}$ is the normalized orthogonal projection and
identification onto $\Lambda^2H$, and $\iota_{uv}=\pi_{uv}^*$; hence
$\widehat C_{uv}$ is zero on $\operatorname{Sym}^2H$ and has norm $K$.
The other coefficient primitive is the restriction/re-expression of
(eq:2.1.3 of the paper) as the Bianchi transfer
\[
 (\Phi_CY)_{ik}=\sum_{m,n}C_{in,mk}Y_{mn},
 \qquad Y\in\Lambda^2H.
\]
The first Bianchi identity identifies the latter with the physical action
of $C$.  A \emph{safe gate} is a typed composite of these primitives,
including the $AA$ words and correctly oriented $AB$ words used below.
Its degree is the number of coefficient primitives.  Thus a degree-$d$
safe gate $G:\mathscr H_S\to\mathscr H_T$ satisfies
$\|G\|_{\rm op}\le K^d$; untouched factors are ancillary identities.

A coefficient box has four darts
$L_{i,0},L_{i,1},R_{i,0},R_{i,1}$.  For a column pairing $q$, a
\emph{packet} is a connected component of the box-incidence graph whose
edges are the $q$-pairs joining different boxes.  A $q$-pair joining the
two darts of one wedge is forbidden and gives zero.  An allowed
\emph{smoothing} chooses at each box either
\[
 h_i^{\parallel}=\{L_{i,0}R_{i,0},L_{i,1}R_{i,1}\},\qquad
 h_i^{\times}=\{L_{i,0}R_{i,1},L_{i,1}R_{i,0}\}.
\]
The alternating circuits of $q\vee h$ are the \emph{smoothing
carriers}; adjoining one carrier means adjoining one identity factor
$I_H$.  The smoothing support $\operatorname{supp}_h(i)$ of a box is the
one- or two-element set of $q\vee h$ carriers containing its two
$h$-passages.  A \emph{ported pair comb} on two chosen carriers consists of all
boxes whose smoothing support is that pair, together with every singleton-support box
assigned to it exactly once; removing all other support groups leaves
their boundary darts as linearly ordered typed ports.  These definitions
fix the domains and codomains of every safe word, fold, comb, and
attachment below.

An \emph{ambient rooted ribbon record} $\Gamma$ consists of a common
finite dart set, its coefficient boxes and local wedge signs, a row
pairing $p$, a column pairing $q$, a rooted trace pairing $r$, and the
declared boundary/root data.  Thus $p\vee r$ is the disjoint union of the
original trace circuits in that record; its components, not temporary
proof cuts, receive the normalization bases below.  The more detailed
Weingarten data carried by $\Gamma$ are specified in
(def:ribbon-record of the paper).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:32:20.037306+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f7bba6049abfc5c9989de372a714c7cc8c00f70f6a858dbfc6c7896d99ab908","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 41 (The Metropolis--Hastings algorithm converges; Theorem \ref{thm:mhintro}) of arXiv:2608.03353, '\bfseries A Direct Route to Markov Chain Convergence\\[2mm] \Large via Asymptotic Equivale'] Let $(\XX,\XXA)$ be a measurable space, $\lambda$ a $\sigma$-finite measure on it,
and let the target be $\pi(A) = \int_{A} p \dd\lambda$ for a measurable map
$p : \XX \to (0,\infty)$ with $\int_{\XX} p \dd\lambda = 1$. Let the proposal be the
Markov kernel $Q(A \mid x) = \int_{A} q(y \mid x)\,\lambda(\dd y)$, given by an
$\XXA\otimes\XXA$-measurable map $q : \XX\times\XX \to [0,\infty)$ with
$\int_{\XX} q(y \mid x)\,\lambda(\dd y) = 1$ for every $x \in \XX$, define the
acceptance probability
\[
  a : \XX\times\XX \to [0,1], \qquad
  a(y \mid x) := \min\Bigl\{ 1,\ \frac{p(y)\,q(x \mid y)}{p(x)\,q(y \mid x)} \Bigr\}
  \quad\bigl(:= 1 \text{ when } q(y \mid x) = 0\bigr),
\]
and let $T$ be the Metropolis--Hastings kernel
\[
  T(A \mid x) := \int_{A} a(y \mid x)\,q(y \mid x)\,\lambda(\dd y) + r(x)\,\ind_{A}(x),
  \qquad
  r(x) := 1 - \int_{\XX} a(y \mid x)\,q(y \mid x)\,\lambda(\dd y) .
\]
Assume
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep,topsep=3pt]
  \item $q(y \mid x) > 0$ for $(\lambda\otimes\lambda)$-almost every $(x,y) \in \XX\times\XX$;
  \item for every $x \in \XX$ the set $\{ y \in \XX : q(y \mid x) > 0 \text{ and } q(x \mid y) > 0 \} \in \XXA$ has positive $\lambda$-measure.
\end{enumerate}
Then $\pi$ is the unique invariant probability measure of $T$, and
$\tv{T^{n}\circ\mu - \pi} \to 0$ for every initial distribution $\mu \in \Prob$.

Both hypotheses hold in either of the following two cases, which are the ones met in
practice and which give Theorem \ref{thm:mhintro}:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),nosep,topsep=3pt]
  \item $q(y \mid x) > 0$ for every $(x,y) \in \XX\times\XX$;
  \item $q$ is symmetric, $q(y \mid x) = q(x \mid y)$ for all $(x,y)$, and
        $q(y \mid x) > 0$ for $(\lambda\otimes\lambda)$-almost every $(x,y)$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.351977+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f97ed2f4a5f62c3336de36c19870ab905777e638f947f2f9b8aabcaf18277b6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 191 (annealed first moment bounds for 
$E^{\sigma,\tau}$ and $E^{\frozen,\sigma,\tau}$
with $\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let
$Q^{\sigma,\tau}=E^{\sigma,\tau}+\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}$ as in Definitions~\ref{d:Q} and \ref{d:tQ}. Then, for $N$ large enough, we have
	\[\bbE
	\Big|\Delta E^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d)\Big| 
	\le L^{O(1)}\bigg\{\eta\delta^{1/2} + \frac{\BUCKETS\delta}{N}
	\bigg\}
	\]
for all $\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$. The same bound holds with $E^\frozen$ in place of $E$.

By Lemmas~\ref{l:barD.II.second}--\ref{l:barD.Ising.second}, for all $\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$ we have

{"assumptions":["exactly quadratic loss with symmetric positive semidefinite Hessian","A=G^T H G>0","unbiased iid batch gradients with finite second moment","fixed current theta and one update only"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:45:33.839464+00:00","domain":"optimization.stochastic","id":"claim_6fb37bb81706cd7b2047938ebd218203941edcc87a60a57beca68c7bc19fa0f1","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let L be an exactly quadratic loss with symmetric positive semidefinite Hessian H. At theta let G=grad L(theta) satisfy A=G^T H G>0. Let g_B be the mean of B>=1 iid finite-second-moment gradients with mean G and per-example covariance Sigma. Write C=tr(H Sigma)>=0 and B_noise=C/A. For the update theta_next=theta-eta*g_B, E[L(theta_next)]=L(theta)-eta*||G||^2+(eta^2/2)*(A+C/B), exactly. The unique real minimizing step is eta_opt(B)=||G||^2/(A+C/B)=eta_max/(1+B_noise/B), where eta_max=||G||^2/A. The optimal expected loss decrease is Delta_opt(B)=Delta_max/(1+B_noise/B), where Delta_max=||G||^4/(2*A). If B_noise>0, batch B=B_noise in the continuous interpolation achieves half Delta_max. For a general smooth loss, the source obtains these expressions from a quadratic Taylor model; without a controlled remainder they are not exact guarantees, iteration-complexity bounds, or global convergence rates.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["alpha is irrational and satisfies ||q alpha|| >= C q^{-tau} for all integers q >= 1, with C > 0 and tau >= 1","||t|| denotes the distance from t to the nearest integer","in part (ii), f is C^infinity on the circle R/Z with mean zero, and the rotation is x -> x + alpha","solutions are sought up to an additive constant; L^2 and distributional solutions are compared by Fourier coefficients"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.732260+00:00","domain":"Diophantine approximation, small divisors, circle rotations","id":"claim_701f743bb2241950d3a8f90b87a8fd689c27198731a6afd43cc9166321190ecf","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a real number t write ||t|| for its distance to the nearest integer. Fix an irrational alpha and suppose alpha is DIOPHANTINE of type (C, tau): there are constants C > 0 and tau >= 1 with

  ||q alpha||  >=  C * q^{-tau}    for every integer q >= 1.

Then:

(i) (the small divisors are only polynomially small) for every nonzero integer q,
      | e^{2 pi i q alpha} - 1 |  =  2 | sin(pi q alpha) |  >=  4 ||q alpha||  >=  4 C |q|^{-tau}.
    The upper bound | e^{2 pi i q alpha} - 1 | <= 2 pi ||q alpha|| always holds, so the two sides are comparable to ||q alpha||.

(ii) (solving the cohomological equation) Let R_alpha(x) = x + alpha on the circle T = R/Z and let f be a C^infinity function on T with mean zero. Then the equation u(x + alpha) - u(x) = f(x) has a C^infinity solution u, unique up to an additive constant, given on Fourier coefficients by u-hat(q) = f-hat(q) / (e^{2 pi i q alpha} - 1) for q nonzero. Quantitatively |u-hat(q)| <= |q|^{tau} |f-hat(q)| / (4C), so one loses tau derivatives: in Sobolev scale ||u||_{H^{s - tau}} <= (4C)^{-1} ||f||_{H^s}, and the analogous statement holds in Holder scale with an epsilon loss.

(iii) (how common the hypothesis is) For every tau > 1, Lebesgue-almost every alpha is Diophantine of type (C, tau) for some C = C(alpha) > 0; for tau = 1 the alpha satisfying the condition are exactly the badly approximable ones (bounded partial quotients), a set of Lebesgue measure zero and full Hausdorff dimension; for tau < 1 no alpha satisfies it at all, by Dirichlet's theorem.

WHERE IT FAILS. If alpha is LIOUVILLE (no such C, tau exist), the conclusion of (ii) fails badly: choose q_1 < q_2 < ... with ||q_k alpha|| < q_k^{-k} and define f by f-hat(q_k) = f-hat(-q_k)-bar = ||q_k alpha||^{1/2} and all other coefficients zero. These coefficients decay faster than any power of q_k, so f is C^infinity with mean zero, yet |u-hat(q_k)| >= ||q_k alpha||^{1/2} / (2 pi ||q_k alpha||) = 1 / (2 pi ||q_k alpha||^{1/2}), which blows up faster than any polynomial in q_k. Hence no solution u exists in L^2, and not even a distributional solution exists. So the Diophantine condition is not a technical convenience: it is what separates solvability from non-solvability. Note also that (ii) gives no information at all about the SPEED of ergodic averages by itself, and that the estimates degrade as C -> 0, so any application that needs uniformity must track C and tau explicitly.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.167788+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7047fbc363730689224871ea7b3508059dbfb1af16c2c3095189e1af3a9864bc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 59 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] The set $\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha)$ from \eqref{e:sM.Lip} can be expressed as
    \[\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha) = \bigcup_{q_0 \in [0,1]}\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0)
    \]
for $\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0)$
as defined by \eqref{e:sM.Lip.q0}.
\begin{proof}
    For any $q_0 \in [0,1]$, the inclusion $\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0) \subseteq \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha)$ is trivial, so it suffices to prove
    \beq
        \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha) \subseteq \bigcup_{q_0 \in [0,1]} \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0)\,.
    \eeq
Consider any sequence $\epsilon_n\downarrow0$. Then, for $\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;L,\epsilon)$ defined in \eqref{e:cM.Lip}, we have
    \[ \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha) 
    =\adjustlimits
    \bigcap_n \bigcup_{L>0}
    \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;L,\epsilon_n)
    \,.
    \]
Consider any measure $\mu \in \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha)$. For any $n\ge 1$, there exists $L_n$ (depending on $\mu,\epsilon_n$) and a sequence of $L_n$-Lipschitz algorithms $(\cA^n_{N_j})_{j\ge 1}$ with 
    \beq
        
        \WERR(\cA^n_{N_j},\mu) =
           \max\bigg\{
            \bbW_2\Big(
            \mu(\cA^n_{N_j}),
            \mu\Big),
            \bbW_2\Big(
            \mu^{\Ising}(\cA^n_{N_j}), \cP(\{\pm 1\})\Big)
        \bigg\} \le \epsilon_n\,.
    \eeq
Abbreviate $\bsig_{n,j} 
\equiv \cA^n_{N_j}(\bG,\bg^\aux)$. 
By passing to a subsequence of the $N_j$, we can ensure that
    \beq
        
	q_0(n,j)
	\equiv \chi_{\cA^n_{N_j}}(0)
	= \frac{\|\bbE\bsig_{n,j}\|^2}{N_j}	
	\stackrel{j\to\infty}
	{\longrightarrow} 
	q_0(n)
    \eeq
    for some $q_0(n) \in [0,1]$.
    Let $q_0 \in [0,1]$ be any subsequential limit of the $q_0(n)$ as $n\to\infty$.
    We will show that $\mu \in \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0)$, from which the result follows.

    By passing to a subsequence of the $\epsilon_n$, we can assume that $q_0(n) \to q_0$ as $n\to\infty$.
    We will show that for $C_1(\alpha)$ as in Lemma~\ref{l:control.problems.approx}, 
    $\tilde L_n \equiv 2L_n$, and
    \[\tilde\epsilon_n 
    = \epsilon_n + 2\bigg(
    	C_1(\alpha) \Big[
	|q_0 - q_0^n| + \epsilon_n
	\Big]
	\bigg)^{1/2}\]
    there exists a sequence of $\tilde L_n$-Lipschitz $(\tilde\cA^n_{N_j})_{j\ge 1}$ with
    \beq
        
        \WERR(\tilde{\cA}^n_{N_j},\mu)=
        \max\bigg\{
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu(\tilde \cA^n_{N_j}), \mu\Big),
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu^{\Ising}(\tilde \cA^n_{N_j}), \cP(\{\pm 1\})
            \Big)
        \bigg\}
        \le \tilde\epsilon_n
    \eeq
as well as (with the abbreviation $\tilde{\bsig}_{n,j}
\equiv \tilde{\cA}^n_{N_j}(\bG,\bg^\aux)$) 
    \beq
        
     \tilde{q}_0(n,j)
     \equiv 
     \chi_{\tilde\cA^n_{N_j}}(0) 
    = \frac{\|\bbE\tilde{\bsig}_{n,j}\|^2}{N_j} 
     = q_0
    \eeq
for every $n,j$. This implies that
    \[
        \mu \in \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0;\tilde L_n,\tilde\epsilon_n)
        \subseteq \bigcup_{L>0} \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0;L,\tilde\epsilon_n)\,.
    \]
    Since this set is decreasing in $\tilde\epsilon_n$, and $\lim_{n\to\infty} \tilde\epsilon_n = 0$, we infer that
    \[
        \mu \in 
        \adjustlimits
        \bigcap_n \bigcup_{L>0} \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0;L,\tilde\epsilon_n)
        = \adjustlimits
        \bigcap_{\epsilon>0} \bigcup_{L>0} \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)
        = \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0)\,.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.692823+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_705cce3bc3c2f162b4275875c9b9a71f24d78fbec2f616fc38040dcbd9b51005","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 31 (Compatible prefix time) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed vector space with
$\dim V\geq2$, and let
$\gamma\colon[0,T]\to V$ be a continuous bounded-variation path. Set
\[
l=\log S(\gamma),
\qquad
v=\gamma_T-\gamma_0,
\]
and assume that
\[
R(l)=\infty,
\qquad
v\neq0.
\]
Fix $\ell\in V^*$ such that $\ell(v)=1$, put $W=\ker\ell$, and write
\[
\gamma_t-\gamma_0=x_t v+X_t,
\qquad
x_t=\ell(\gamma_t-\gamma_0),
\qquad
X_t\in W.
\]

Give $W$ an auxiliary Euclidean norm and let $W_{\C}$ be its
complexification. For every finite symmetric set
$\Lambda\subset2\pi\Q$, define the real Hilbert space
\[
E_\Lambda
=
\set{(z_\omega)_{\omega\in\Lambda}
\in\prod_{\omega\in\Lambda}W_{\C}:
 z_{-\omega}=\overline{z_\omega}}
\]
with the norm inherited from the Hilbert direct sum, the decorated
transverse path
\[
B_t^\Lambda(\gamma)
=
\left(
\int_0^t \e^{i\omega x_s}\dd X_s
\right)_{\omega\in\Lambda},
\qquad 0\leq t\leq T,
\]
and the orthogonal map
\[
T_\Lambda\colon E_\Lambda\to E_\Lambda,
\qquad
(T_\Lambda z)_\omega=\e^{i\omega}z_\omega.
\]
Denote by the same symbol the induced graded automorphism of tensor
series, and set
\[
r_t^\Lambda
=S\bigl(B^\Lambda(\gamma)|_{[0,t]}\bigr),
\qquad
h_\Lambda=r_T^\Lambda.
\]

Then there exists $t_*\in[0,T]$ such that, for every finite symmetric
$\Lambda\subset2\pi\Q$,
\begin{equation}
h_\Lambda
=a_\Lambda T_\Lambda(a_\Lambda)^{-1},
\qquad
a_\Lambda=r_{t_*}^\Lambda.
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
\[
r_{t_*}^\Lambda
=h_\Lambda T_\Lambda\bigl(r_{t_*}^\Lambda\bigr)
\]
for every such $\Lambda$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-13T03:42:25.818646+00:00","domain":"probability, Markov chains, random walks on graphs","id":"claim_70883747d2f8094e81f1250f92c005572a73779bc267e33d29fe488ce3c6f103","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign status: candidate_full_solution - author-checked, unrefereed] Aldous and Fill, Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, Open Problem 7.27 (Chapter 7, p. 259) asks whether, over arc-transitive graphs excluding the n-cycles, tau* = O(n log n), tau2 = O(n) and tau*/(2 tau0) = 1 + o(1). Our result (id P0208, 2026-09-08): all three claims are FALSE. The counterexample is the lexicographic product C_m[Kbar_2] for odd m >= 5 - the m-cycle with every vertex split into two non-adjacent twins - which is connected, 4-regular, arc-transitive and not a cycle, on n = 2m vertices. With g(j) = j(m-j) + m the mean hitting time at cycle-distance j and 2m the twin hitting time: tau* = 2*floor(m^2/4) + 2m ~ n^2/8 (quadratic, not O(n log n)); tau2 = 1/(1 - cos(2 pi/m)) ~ n^2/(8 pi^2), because A(C_m[Kbar_2]) = A(C_m) tensor J_2 so the relaxation time is the m-cycle's own; and tau*/(2 tau0) tends to 3/2, not 1 + o(1). Verification, as the source words it: exact hitting times by linear algebra at m = 5, 7, 9, 11, 15, 21 (all five formulas exact at every size); arc-transitivity checked mechanically at m = 5, 7, 9 (the group generated by the rotation, one reflection and one fibre swap has order 2^m * 2m and its orbit of one arc is all 8m arcs); and a Lean file P0208.lean with nine theorems, no sorry, axioms propext / Classical.choice / Quot.sound only. Not formalised: uniqueness of the solution of (I-P)h = 1 and the tensor eigenvalue computation, both standard and checked numerically. Prior art not cleared. odd m >= 5 simple random walk on the lexicographic product C_m[Kbar_2] (n = 2m vertices, 4-regular, arc-transitive, not a cycle)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:23:25.634591+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7089e0c06e1ce3f0d01d2a2851b0a77e3a83e3072340314f9dac3f0546320bdf","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm Inverse4 of arXiv:2609.01350, 'New classes of trace-form permutation polynomials and their compositional inverses'] Let $q=2^m$ with $m$ odd, and let
$f_2(x)=x+\gamma{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}\big(c_1x+c_2x^2+x^{2q-1}\big)$ with
$c_1,c_2\in\mathbb F_{q^2}$ and $\gamma\in\mathbb F_{q^2}\setminus\mathbb F_q$
satisfying
\[
  \gamma^{3(q-1)}=1,\qquad
  1+{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_1\gamma)=\gamma^{2q-1},\qquad
  {\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_2\gamma^q)=0,
\]
so that $f_2$ is a permutation polynomial of $\mathbb F_{q^2}$ by
Theorem~(Result2 of the paper)(3). Then
\begin{equation}
  f_2^{-1}(x)=
  \begin{cases}
    0
      & \text{if } x=0,\\[0.8em]
    x+\gamma^{q-1}\Big(h_2(x)+\dfrac{{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(x^3)}{x^{q+1}}\Big)
      & \text{if } x\neq0,\ r=0,\\[0.8em]
    x+\gamma^{q-1}\Big(h_2(x)+\dfrac{{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(x^3)}{x^{q+1}}
      +r^{1/3}+\dfrac{P}{r^{1/3}}\Big)
      & \text{if } x\neq0,\ r\neq0,
  \end{cases}
\end{equation}
where
\[
  P=h_2(x)^2+h_2(x)\,{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}\big(\gamma^{q-1}x^q\big)
    +\frac{{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(\gamma x)^3\,{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(x)^3}{\gamma^3\,x^{2q+2}},
  \qquad
  r=P\Big(h_2(x)+\frac{{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(x)^3}{x^{q+1}}\Big).
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:10.022418+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_70aaacc132bf006490a2efbd61e694a78c197fa1fcea406ad4ce694db2ff6bdd","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 3 of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] [Distinguishability With Respect to Fixed Sequences] 
Fix two sequences of distributions $\mu_{n}, \nu_{n}$ that take on values in the set $\mathcal{S}_{n}$, and let $f_{n}$ be a sequence of functions from $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}$.

We say the sequence $f_{n}$ \textit{weakly} distinguishes $\mu_{n}$ and $\nu_{n}$ if
\be 
\sqrt{\max(\Var_{\mu_{n}}(f_{n}),\Var_{\nu_{n}}(f_{n}))} = O(|\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{n}}[f_{n}] - \mathbb{E}_{\nu_{n}}[f_{n}] |),
\ee 
and \textit{strongly} distinguishes if the LHS is 
$o(|\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{n}}[f_{n}] - \mathbb{E}_{\nu_{n}}[f_{n}] |)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:49:05.363346+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_70f0fb268b1ece30100715ddcfee6caf52d2175e66905d7971576d0c2a24c440","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:orbit_kernel of arXiv:2601.07045, 'From Continuous to Discrete: \\ a No-U-Turn Sampler for Permutations'] Let $(m, b)$ specify a NURS orbit
\[
\mathcal{O} = (\sigma \circ \rho^i)_{i = a}^b,
\qquad a = b - 2^m + 1.
\]
Then the orbit selection kernel of NURS satisfies
\[
p_{\mathrm{orbit}}(m, b \mid \sigma, \rho)
=
\frac{1}{2^m}
\cdot
\mathbf{1}\Biggl(
\Phi(\mathcal{O})
\;\wedge\;
\bigwedge_{s = 1}^{m} \; \bigwedge_{t = 1}^{2^s}
\neg \textsc{Stop}\!\left(\mathcal{O}_{s,t}, \varepsilon, w\right)
\Biggr),
\]
where $\{\mathcal{O}_{s,t}\}$ are the dyadic sub-orbits of $\mathcal{O}$
(Definition~(def:dyadic-suborbit of the paper)), and where $\Phi(\mathcal{O})$ holds if and only if
\[
\textsc{Stop}(\mathcal{O}, \varepsilon, w)
\;\vee\;
\textsc{SubStop}(\mathcal{O}_+^{\mathrm{ext}}, \varepsilon, w)
\;\vee\;
\textsc{SubStop}(\mathcal{O}_-^{\mathrm{ext}}, \varepsilon, w)
\;\vee\;
|\mathcal{O}| = 2^M.
\]
The forward and backward extensions are defined by
\[
\mathcal{O}_+^{\mathrm{ext}} = (\sigma \circ \rho^i)_{i = b+1}^{b+2^m},
\qquad
\mathcal{O}_-^{\mathrm{ext}} = (\sigma \circ \rho^i)_{i = a - 2^m}^{a - 1}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f measurable and a.e. finite","|E| < infinity (or E sigma-finite, applied piecewise)","the measure is Borel regular, so that inner regularity by closed sets is available"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751562+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_70f1790178f49b91f5ee0ff4790936831774e34f8e840b54c67bc80f664a49ab","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f : R^d -> C be Lebesgue measurable and finite almost everywhere, let E be a measurable set of FINITE measure, and let eps > 0. Then there is a CLOSED set F contained in E with |E \\ F| < eps such that the RESTRICTION of f to F is continuous. Moreover one may take g in C_c(R^d) with g = f on F and sup |g| <= sup |f|. The theorem does not assert that f is continuous AT the points of F as a function on R^d: the indicator of the rationals is nowhere continuous on R, yet it agrees with the zero function off a set of measure zero, and Lusin's F can be taken to be any closed set of irrationals of nearly full measure. Finiteness of |E| may be relaxed to sigma-finiteness by exhausting E, at the price of stating the conclusion with |E \\ F| < eps for each piece. [standard; e.g. Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 2.24]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:28:49.121797+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_70f93b993bb6bb37c7bfcb078034702d78b2e5b7cd400a6962d5b950db4fff82","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:johnson-spectrum of arXiv:2608.18293, 'Critical tensor covariance at the Marchenko--Pastur threshold'] Assume $1\le q<n/2$. Let $A_q$ be the adjacency matrix of the Johnson graph
$J(n,q)$: two $q$-subsets are adjacent when their symmetric difference has size
two. For a $j$-subset $T$, define
\[
  f_T(I)=\1_{\{T\subseteq I\}},
  \qquad |I|=q,
\]
and let $U_j$ be the span of the functions $f_T$ with $|T|=j$. Then
\[
  U_0\subseteq U_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq U_q.
\]
Set $U_{-1}=\{0\}$. If $H_j=U_j\cap U_{j-1}^{\perp}$, then $A_q$ acts on $H_j$ by the scalar
\begin{equation}
  \alpha_j=(q-j)(n-q-j)-j,
  \qquad 0\le j\le q.
  
\end{equation}
In particular, when $q<n/2$, the largest eigenvalue of $A_q$ on the orthogonal complement of the constant vector is
\begin{equation}
  \alpha_1=q(n-q)-n.
  
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:09:34.497474+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_71012fbc4a10ccd6ccbbd74ad09769b158fb5d1f6cab2bb33003059607417a82","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm conformal_invariance_aut_D of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] Let \( \tau \in \mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{D}) \). The drift term \( b(\boldsymbol{\theta}, u) \) is a pre-Schwarzian form, satisfying:
\[
b_i = \tau' \widetilde{b}_i \circ \tau + \frac{6 - \kappa}{2} \left(\log \tau'\right)'.
\]
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] There exists a smooth function \( F(\tau, u): \widetilde{\mathrm{Aut}}(\mathbb{D}) \times \mathbb{D} \to \mathbb{R} \) such that:
    \[
    \log \psi - \log (\psi \circ \tau) + \frac{\kappa - 6}{2\kappa} \sum_i \log \tau'(\theta_i) = F(\tau, u),
    \]
    where \( F \) satisfies the functional equation:
    
    \begin{equation}
    
    F(\tau_1 \tau_2, u) = F(\tau_1, \tau_2(u)) + F(\tau_2, u).
    \end{equation}

    \item[(ii)] There exists a rotation constant \( \omega \) such that:
    \begin{equation}
    F(A_\theta, 0) = \omega \theta.
    \end{equation}

    If \( \omega = 0 \), \( \mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{D}) \) suffices to describe conformal invariance, and \( F \) reduces to a map \( \mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{D}) \times \mathbb{D} \to \mathbb{R} \).

    \item[(iii)] Suppose \( F_1(\tau, u) \) and \( F_2(\tau, u) \) correspond to partition functions \( \psi_1 \) and \( \psi_2 \). If their rotation constants \( \omega_1 = \omega_2 \), then there exists a function \( g(u) \) such that:
    \[
   \psi_2 = g(u) \cdot \psi_1.
    \]

    \item[(iv)] For \( \tau \in \widetilde{\mathrm{Aut}}(\mathbb{D}) \), let \( \tau(u) = v \). Decompose \( \tau = T_v \circ A_\theta \circ T^{-1}_u \), where \( u, v \in \mathbb{D} \) and \( \theta \in \mathbb{R} \). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:20:33.752427+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7124a5917977f2ae5f1f94d056ca5a53354973487bc04d551754f7e5081dc684","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 11 of arXiv:2609.03836, 'Koszul Orlik--Solomon Algebras from Non-supersolvable Arrangements'] Let $M$ be a matroid and $F, G \in \mathcal{L}(M)$.
    \begin{enumerate}

        \item If $F$ is modular in $M$, then $F \cap G$ is modular in $M|_G$.
        \item If $F, G$ are modular in $M$, then $F \cap G$ is modular in $M$.
        \item If $F$ is modular in $M$, then $(F \vee G)-G$ is modular in $M/G$.
        \item If $F$ is modular in $M$ and $S \subseteq E(M)$ contains $F$, then $F$ is modular in $M|_S$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:09:34.497957+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7136ddb39be635661b82383746e601fad68a079bdd47e3f5f06f6b57b54acc5c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn Monodromy of Coulomb Gas Correlation Differential of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] Let $\boldsymbol{\sigma} = \sum_{j=1}^n \sigma_j \cdot z_j$ be a divisor on $\mathbb{C}$ with associated Coulomb gas correlation differential
\[
C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}] = \prod_{j < k} (z_j - z_k)^{\sigma_j \sigma_k}.
\]
This function is multivalued due to the presence of non-integer exponents. Its multivaluedness is described by the \emph{monodromy representation} arising from analytic continuation around branch points.

To illustrate the basic mechanism, consider the case $n = 2$. Then
\[
C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}] = (z_1 - z_2)^{\sigma_1 \sigma_2},
\]
which is analytic in $z_1$ on $\mathbb{C} \setminus \{z_2\}$. If we analytically continue this function as $z_1$ travels once counterclockwise around $z_2$, the function picks up a multiplicative factor of $e^{2\pi i \sigma_1 \sigma_2}$. 

Thus, the monodromy representation
\[
\rho: \pi_1(\mathbb{C} \setminus \{z_2\}, z_1) \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}^*, \quad \rho(C_2) = e^{2\pi i \sigma_1 \sigma_2}
\]
captures how the function changes under analytic continuation around the singularity at $z_2$, where $C_2$ is the loop encircling $z_2$.

In general, for $\boldsymbol{\sigma} = \sum_{j=1}^n \sigma_j \cdot z_j$, the function $C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}]$ is analytic in $z_1$ on $\mathbb{C} \setminus \{z_2, \ldots, z_n\}$. The fundamental group $\pi_1(\mathbb{C} \setminus \{z_2, \ldots, z_n\}, z_1)$ is the free group generated by loops $C_j$ encircling each $z_j$ ($j = 2, \ldots, n$), and the monodromy representation
\[
\rho: \pi_1(\mathbb{C} \setminus \{z_2, \ldots, z_n\}) \to \mathbb{C}^*, \quad \rho(C_j) = e^{2\pi i \sigma_1 \sigma_j}
\]
describes the multiplicative factor acquired by $C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}]$ when $z_1$ loops around $z_j$ once in the counterclockwise direction.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["finite connected undirected allowed-support graph","n>=2","P real symmetric and entrywise nonnegative","P1=1","P supported on specified E"],"created_at":"2026-10-14T17:21:25.683145+00:00","domain":"probability, Markov chains and convex optimization","id":"claim_7178a86bd73804e416b4ec45d7b8498addc37421236e8ba87edb733406930e9b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let G be a finite connected undirected graph on n>=2 vertices, with a specified symmetric support E of allowed transitions including any permitted holding loops. Among real symmetric stochastic matrices P supported on E, the second-largest eigenvalue modulus is mu(P)=max_{i>=2}|lambda_i(P)|=||P-(1/n)11^T||_2, where one stationary eigenvalue 1 is excluded and repeated stationary eigenvalues, if any, remain in the maximum. Minimizing mu(P) is the convex semidefinite program: minimize real s subject to -sI <=_PSD P-(1/n)11^T <=_PSD sI, P_ij>=0 entrywise, P1=1, P=P^T, and P_ij=0 for (i,j) outside E. The feasible matrices have uniform stationary law. This optimizes continuous transition probabilities on fixed support, not a deterministic integral matching or actual total-variation mixing time. The formulation is originally due to Boyd-Diaconis-Xiao (2004) and restated in Boyd-Diaconis-Parrilo-Xiao, arXiv:0709.0955, Section 1.1, equations (1)-(2), PDF p.2.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:47.652013+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7186db882c863ea9073dea828e7af3f00cab1a8dfbe5aaa44a03333a136d9bd8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 13 ($\ell$-multigraph) of arXiv:2605.07050, 'Universality of the fluctuations of the free energy in generalized Sherrington--Kirkpatric'] We say that a multigraph $\gamma$ with nodes $1, 2, \dots, N$ is an $\ell$-multigraph if any pair of nodes can be connected by at most $\ell$ edges. The multiplicity $m^\gamma_{ij}$ between the nodes $i$ and $j$ is the number of separate edges connecting them, and we let $m^\gamma_{ij} = 0$ if the nodes $i$ and $j$ are not connected. (It is possible that $m_{kk}^{\gamma} > 0$, i.e., self-loops are allowed.) If $m^\gamma_{ij} = 1, 2, 3, 4$, we say that the edge between the nodes $i$ and $j$ is single, double, triple, quadruple, respectively.

The degree of the node $i$ is defined by
\[
	d^\gamma_i = m^\gamma_{ii} + \sum_{j=1}^N m^\gamma_{ij}.
\]
In particular, a single self-loop at the node $i$ increases the degree of the node $i$ by $2$. The size $m^\gamma$ and the length $n^\gamma$ of a multigraph $\gamma$ are defined by
\[
	m^\gamma = \sum_{i\leq j} m^\gamma_{ij} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^N d^\gamma_i, \quad n^\gamma = \sum_{i\leq j} \indi(m^\gamma_{ij} > 0),
\]
respectively. The number of the single (respectively, double, triple, quadruple) edges $n_1^\gamma$ (respectively, $n_2^\gamma, n_3^\gamma, n_4^\gamma$) is defined by
\[
	n_r^\gamma = \sum_{i\leq j} \indi(m^\gamma_{ij} = r), \quad r=1, 2, 3, 4.
\]
Similarly, the number of the single (respectively, double) self-loops $\tilde n_1^\gamma$ (respectively, $\tilde n_2^\gamma$) is defined by
\[ \tilde n_r^\gamma = \sum_{k=1}^{N}\indi(m^\gamma_{kk} = r), \quad r=1,2.\]

The set of all $\ell$-multigraphs with single and/or double self-loops is denoted by $\caG^\ell$. (The empty graph is a multigraph and included in $\caG^\ell$.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:48:24.296611+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_71e0d9ba818881c73222688b9d12a1a5628ea07bb86c0ba813ab26f2112a95b4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem optimaliq>1 of arXiv:2605.10452, 'A secretary for Messrs. Luce and Mallows'] Consider the secretary problem
with either  the  Mallows distribution
or the $P_n^{\mathcal{L}_\text{inv};\{q_n^i\}_{i=1}^n}$-type Luce distribution with  $q=q_n\in(0,\infty)-\{1\}$
in the case that the smallest number is  of highest rank.

\noindent i. Let $q_n=1-\frac cn$, where $c>0$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
\begin{equation}
M_n^*\sim n\Big(\frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)\Big),
\end{equation}
 and the corresponding  limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$

\noindent Also, $\lim_{c\to\infty} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)=0$ and $\lim_{c\to0} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)=\frac1e$.

\noindent ii.
Let $q_n=1-\frac c{n^\alpha}$, where $c>0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
M_n^*\sim\frac1c\left(1-\log(e-1)\right)n^\alpha\approx0.459\frac{n^\alpha}c,
$$
 and the corresponding limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$.

\noindent iii.
Let $q\in(0,1)$.  Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M^*)$, where
$$
M^*=\begin{cases}&\max\left\{M\ge1: \sum_{j=M}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}\ge\frac 1{1-q}\right\}, \ \text{if}\ \sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}\ge\frac1{1-q};\\
&0,\ \text{if}\ \sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}<\frac1{1-q}.\end{cases}
$$
(If  $\sum_{j=M^*}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}=\frac 1{1-q}$, then $M^*-1$ is also optimal.)

\noindent The corresponding limiting probability of success is given by
$$
\begin{cases}&(1-q)(1-q^{M^*})\sum_{j=M^*}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}\ge(1-q^{-M^*}),\ \text{if}\ M^*\ge1;\\
&1-q>\frac1e,\ \text{if}\ M^*=0.\end{cases}
$$
This limiting probability is always greater or equal to $\frac1e$ and is
strictly greater than $\frac1e$ for all but at most a countable number of $q$ with no accumulation points in $(0,\infty)$.

\noindent iv. Let $q_n=1+\frac cn$, where $c>0$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
\begin{equation}
M_n^*\sim n\Big(\frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)\Big),
\end{equation}
 and the corresponding  limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$.

\noindent Also, $\lim_{c\to\infty} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)=1$ and $\lim_{c\to0} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)=\frac1e$.

\noindent v.
Let $q_n=1+\frac c{n^\alpha}$, where $c>0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
n-M_n^*\sim\frac{n^\alpha}c,
$$
 and the corresponding limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$.

\noindent vi. Let $q>1$.  Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
M_n^*=n-L, \ \text{where}\ L \ \text{satisfies}\ \frac1{q-1}\le L<\frac q{q-1}.
$$
The corresponding limiting probability of success is given by
$$
\frac{q-1}{q^L}L>\frac1e.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:36:31.223822+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_71e98425fe4dbb8a7802a7e1bee535b588fa33d6d2fd777225f303dfc5d1e2f2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 17 (Unique Pinkall-modulus limit) of arXiv:2609.00501, 'Uniqueness of Finite-Time Varifold Limits for the M\"obius-Invariant Willmore Flow'] Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:anchored-profile}, orient the
profiles consistently with the reduced flow.  Let
\(\mathcal A_t\in\R/4\pi\mathbb Z\) be the oriented area class
enclosed by \(\gamma_t\), and let \(\mathcal A_T\) be the corresponding area class for
\(\gamma_T\).  Then
\begin{equation}
 
 \mathcal A_t\longrightarrow\mathcal A_T
 \qquad\text{in }\R/4\pi\mathbb Z .
\end{equation}
For \(t\) sufficiently close to \(T\), choose compatible real
representatives such that \(\mathcal A_t\to\mathcal A_T\).  Pinkall's
lattice is
\begin{equation}
 
 \Gamma_t=
 \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Z}
 \left\{(2\pi,0),
 \left(\frac{\mathcal A_t}{2},\frac{L(\gamma_t)}2\right)\right\},
\end{equation}
and the corresponding modulus is
\begin{equation}
 
 \tau_t=\frac{\mathcal A_t+iL(\gamma_t)}{4\pi}\in\mathbb H .
\end{equation}
It satisfies
\[
 \tau_t\longrightarrow
 \tau_T:=\frac{\mathcal A_T+iL_T}{4\pi}.
\]
Its imaginary part satisfies the quantitative bounds
\begin{equation}
 
 \frac14\leq\operatorname{Im}\tau_T\leq\frac2\pi.
\end{equation}
Consequently the conformal classes
\[
 [\tau_t]\longrightarrow[\tau_T]
 \qquad\text{in }\mathcal M_1=\mathbb H/\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb Z)
\]
have a unique finite-time limit, independent of the approaching time
sequence.  With the orientation induced by the fixed oriented profile
and the positively oriented Hopf fibres, the class \([\tau_T]\) is the
intrinsic oriented conformal class of the limiting \(C^1\) Hopf torus.
In particular, no conformal
degeneration occurs at the finite endpoint.","status":"unverified"}

	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]

		\item  The law of $\left(\textbf{O}^{(k)},\textbf{F}^{(k)}\right)$ is invariant under the permutation of the masses:
		For any permutation $r\in {\bf S}_k$ (the symmetric group on $\{0,\cdots,k-1\}$),
		\[{\cal L}\left (\left(\textbf{O}^{(k)},\textbf{F}^{(k)}\right)~|~ (m_0,\cdots,m_{k-1})\right)={\cal L}\left (\left(\textbf{O}^{(k)},\textbf{F}^{(k)}\right)~|~ (m_{r(0)},\cdots,m_{r(k-1)})\right)\]
		(where we have written, as a condition, the successive masses that are used).
		\item For $k\geq 1$, the number of free CC,  ${\bf N}_k$, has (almost) a binomial distribution:
		\begin{equation}
		 {\bf N}_k \sur{=}{(d)} 1+ B(m[k]), \textrm {~~where~~} B(m[k])\sim {\sf Binomial}(k-1,R_k) 
		\end{equation}
		where $R_k=1-W(m[k])$ is the final free space available after the deposition of the first $k$ masses.
		\item Take a uniform element $\theta$ in $\{0,\cdots,b-1\}$ (independently of everything). Conditional on ${\bf N}_k=b$, 
		\begin{equation}\left(\left|\textbf{F}^{(k)}_{i+\theta {~\sf mod~} b}\right|,0\leq i \leq b-1\right)\sur{=}{(d)} R_k\, ({\bf D}_0,\cdots,{\bf D}_{b-1})\end{equation}  where $({\bf D}_0,\cdots,{\bf D}_{b-1})\sim{\sf Dirichlet}(b;1,\cdots,1)$. 
		Hence, the sequence $\left(|\textbf{F}^{(k)}_{i}|,0\leq i \leq b-1\right)$ taken according to a uniform independent rotation, is unbiased. 
		\item 
		The process $({\bf N}_k,k\geq 0)$ is a Markov chain, and its transition matrix can be computed explicitly (see (sec:qefgrethry of the paper)). 
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:37:51.461737+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_723ad6b0fc4c418480ceff7855f9a1f82bb50dbef869d87ffa6e86fd1b67d24f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 3 (Long-time behavior in the scalar case) of arXiv:2604.04100, '\LARGE Learning Equilibrium Fluctuation Expansions from Overdamped Langevin Dynamics'] Assume $d=1$. Let $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and let $X_\varepsilon$,  $(\bar{X}_m)_{0\leq m\leq n}$,  $(a_m)_{0\leq m\leq n}$ be as in Proposition \ref{thm-weak-exp-intro}. If we further assume that Assumption \ref{A2} holds, then for every $F \in C^{n+1}(\mathbb{R})$ satisfying \eqref{assump-F}, the following assertions hold:\begin{enumerate}

\item[(i)] The limit
$$
b_0(F) := \lim_{t\to\infty} a_0(t,F)
$$
exists, and satisfies
\begin{equation}
b_0(F) = \mathbb{E}\Bigl[ \lim_{t\to\infty} F\bigl(\bar{X}_0(t)\bigr) \Bigr]
= F(1)\mathbb{P}(\xi_0>0) + F(-1)\mathbb{P}(\xi_0<0).
\end{equation}
\item[(ii)] For each $m \in \{1, \dots, n\}$ and $i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$, define
$$
S_{m,i}(t) := \sum_{(j_1,\dots,j_i)\in\mathcal{D}_i^m} \prod_{k=1}^{i}\bar{X}_{j_k}(t),\quad t\ge0.
$$
We adopt the convention that a sum over the empty set is equal to $0$, and hence
$$
S_{m,i}(t):=0
\quad\text{whenever }m<0,\ i<0,\ \text{or } i>m.
$$Then the conditional limits
$$
c_{m,i} := \lim_{t \to \infty}\mathbb{E}[S_{m,i}(t)\mid\xi_0>0],
\quad
\bar{c}_{m,i} := \lim_{t \to \infty}\mathbb{E}[S_{m,i}(t)\mid\xi_0<0]
$$
exist and are uniquely determined by the recursion formula
\begin{equation}
    c_{m,i} = \frac{i-1}{2}c_{m-2,i-2} - \frac{3}{2}c_{m,i+1} - \frac{1}{2}c_{m,i+2}, 
    \quad 
    \bar c_{m,i} = \frac{i-1}{2}\bar c_{m-2,i-2} + \frac{3}{2}\bar c_{m,i+1} - \frac{1}{2}\bar c_{m,i+2},
\end{equation}
with $c_{1,1}=\bar c_{1,1}=0$, $c_{2,2}=\bar c_{2,2}=\frac12$ and the convention that $c_{0,0}=\bar c_{0,0}=1$, and
		$$c_{k,j}=\bar c_{k,j}=0 \quad\text{whenever } (k,j)\notin \{(0,0)\}\cup\{(k,j): k\ge1,\ 1\le j\le k\}.$$ 
The recursion \eqref{eq-c-n-intro} is understood as a nested induction: one first increases the order $m$, and for each fixed $m$, computes $c_{m,i}$ backward in $i$ from $i=m$ to $1$. The same procedure applies to $\bar c_{m,i}$.

\item[(iii)] For each $m \in \{1, \dots, n\}$, the limit
\begin{equation}
b_m(F) := \lim_{t \to \infty} a_m(t,F)
\end{equation}
exists and is given by
\begin{equation}
    b_m(F) = \mathbb{P}(\xi_0>0)\sum_{i=1}^{m} \frac{c_{m,i}}{i!} F^{(i)}(1)
    + \mathbb{P}(\xi_0<0)\sum_{i=1}^{m} \frac{\bar{c}_{m,i}}{i!}F^{(i)}(-1).
\end{equation}
In particular, $b_m(F)=0$ for all odd $m$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:48:47.285596+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_724ba716dee584b88a079cd4cd275d735cec1cc38628e26a591a780eedd8b87f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Conjecture conj:quenched full of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] For $f\in D$, let $\theta$ be the optimizer in~(equation eq:quenched conj of the paper) and $\zeta$ the minimizer

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-05T06:00:09.358321+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning","id":"claim_725b1291163158659b5a95f154eb99cbd5bf0e3c3895a5a6a7c646f4cd804d39","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In a multi-output stacking problem scored by the mean per-sample relative error $\\frac{1}{n}\\sum_i \\|\\hat y_i - y_i\\|/\\|y_i\\|$, the per-output least-squares stack minimises the unweighted squared error, which is dominated by the cases with the largest $\\|y_i\\|$, while the score is dominated by the cases with the smallest. Interpolating the per-output weights toward one pooled simplex weight vector fitted on the relative error therefore improves the score even IN-SAMPLE on the very calibration rows on which least squares is optimal in squared error - the signature that distinguishes an objective mismatch from a generalisation (variance) effect, which can only appear out of sample. Measured on the EMIT lookup-table pool (seed 101, component Y2, 23 members, 932 calibration rows, 285 outputs): in-sample relative error 0.1105 for least squares against 0.1026 at interpolation weight 0.4 (-7.2 percent), the in-sample optimum at the same weight as the out-of-sample optimum (0.1292 to 0.1186), while the in-sample squared error is minimal at least squares (8.8e-5 against 1.2e-4); the out-of-sample gain is +15.9 percent in the smallest-norm quartile of targets and -9.6 percent in the largest, and 45 percent of the least-squares score comes from its worst decile of cases. Consequently no model of the sampling noise of the weight rows reproduces the cross-validated interpolation weight: the known-noise James-Stein amount is 0.00 and the heteroscedasticity-robust amount 0.03-0.05 where cross-validation chooses 0.10-0.40. Shrinking toward the pooled UNCONSTRAINED least-squares weights (entries up to 90 in magnitude) or toward the mean of the rows is much worse; the simplex constraint together with the relative objective carries the effect. The practical rule: when a stack is scored in a metric that weights cases differently from the fitting loss, the first question is the objective, not the estimator's variance.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["𝔄 is a unital Banach algebra (e.g. bounded operators on a Banach space, or square matrices)","A and B are elements of 𝔄 (bounded operators)","AB = BA"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.111181+00:00","domain":"operator theory, matrix analysis, one-parameter groups","id":"claim_72638ddfde3be7c71bd07c8d293de0f5da0036958c9131cd1b17e4853a1f9986","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let 𝔄 be a unital Banach algebra (for instance the algebra B(E) of bounded linear operators on a Banach space E, or the n×n complex matrices), and for A ∈ 𝔄 define exp(A) = e^A := Σ_{k=0}^∞ A^k / k!, a series that converges absolutely in norm for every A (‖A^k/k!‖ ≤ ‖A‖^k/k!), so that ‖e^A‖ ≤ e^{‖A‖}. If A, B ∈ 𝔄 COMMUTE, AB = BA, then e^{A+B} = e^A e^B = e^B e^A. Consequences: for every A and all scalars s, t, e^{(s+t)A} = e^{sA} e^{tA} (the one-parameter group law), e^A is invertible with (e^A)⁻¹ = e^{−A}, e^0 = 1, and t ↦ e^{tA} is norm-differentiable with derivative A e^{tA} = e^{tA} A. If P is invertible, e^{PAP⁻¹} = P e^A P⁻¹. Sharp edges. (1) Commutativity cannot be dropped: for the 2×2 matrices A = [[0,1],[0,0]] and B = [[0,0],[1,0]] one has e^A = I + A, e^B = I + B, so e^A e^B = [[2,1],[1,1]], whereas A + B = [[0,1],[1,0]] gives e^{A+B} = [[cosh 1, sinh 1],[sinh 1, cosh 1]] ≠ e^A e^B (and e^B e^A = [[1,1],[1,2]] ≠ e^A e^B, so the two products differ as well). For non-commuting A, B the product e^A e^B is instead described by the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff series e^{A+B+[A,B]/2+…} when it converges, and by the Lie–Trotter formula e^{A+B} = lim_{n→∞} (e^{A/n} e^{B/n})ⁿ. (2) The converse is false in general: e^A e^B = e^{A+B} does not imply AB = BA (there are non-commuting complex matrices with e^A = e^B = e^{A+B} = I); it does hold for Hermitian (self-adjoint) matrices A, B, because then e^{A+B} Hermitian forces e^A e^B = (e^A e^B)* = e^B e^A, so the positive definite matrices e^A and e^B commute, and hence so do their unique Hermitian logarithms A and B. (3) For UNBOUNDED operators (generators of semigroups) the series definition is unavailable and 'commuting' must be formulated with care (e.g. commuting resolvents / commuting semigroups); this statement is only about bounded operators and Banach algebras.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["α irrational (for the rational case the expansion terminates)","regular (simple) continued fraction with integer partial quotients a_k ≥ 1 for k ≥ 1","||t|| denotes the distance from t to the nearest integer"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:57.492004+00:00","domain":"Diophantine approximation, circle rotations, continued fractions","id":"claim_7271e0510379bbe55262f0b504298ebded2c36c4dd6bb321ac077750203941b8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let α be irrational with regular continued fraction [a_0; a_1, a_2, ...], convergents p_n/q_n (p_{-1} = 1, q_{-1} = 0, p_0 = a_0, q_0 = 1, p_{n+1} = a_{n+1}p_n + p_{n-1}, q_{n+1} = a_{n+1}q_n + q_{n-1}) and complete quotients α_{n+1} = [a_{n+1}; a_{n+2}, ...], so a_{n+1} < α_{n+1} < a_{n+1} + 1. Write ||t|| = dist(t, Z) and δ_n = |q_n α − p_n| (so δ_{-1} = 1).

(1) Exact size and alternating sign. For all n ≥ 0, q_n α − p_n = (−1)^n / (q_n α_{n+1} + q_{n-1}). Hence 1/(q_n + q_{n+1}) < δ_n < 1/q_{n+1}, the errors alternate in sign, δ_n is strictly decreasing, and δ_n = ||q_n α|| for every n ≥ 1 (because q_{n+1} ≥ 2 gives δ_n < 1/2); for n = 0 this holds when a_1 ≥ 2.

(2) The distances obey the same recursion as the denominators: δ_{n-1} = a_{n+1} δ_n + δ_{n+1} for all n ≥ 0. Equivalently δ_n = 1/(α_1 α_2 ··· α_{n+1}).

(3) Closest returns (Lagrange's theorem on best approximations of the second kind). For every n ≥ 0 and every integer q with 1 ≤ q < q_{n+1}: ||q α|| ≥ δ_n, with equality if and only if q = q_n. In dynamical words: for the rotation t ↦ t + α (mod 1), among all times 1 ≤ q < q_{n+1} the orbit of any point comes closest to its starting point exactly at time q_n; the record-breaking (closest-return) times of the orbit are precisely the denominators q_0 (when a_1 ≥ 2), q_1, q_2, ..., and successive closest returns land on alternate sides of the starting point, at distances δ_n.

(4) Growth. q_{n+1} ≥ q_n + q_{n-1}, hence q_n ≥ F_{n+1} (Fibonacci) and q_n ≥ 2^{(n−1)/2} for n ≥ 1; the golden ratio (all a_k = 1) is the slowest case.

Where it fails. For rational α the expansion terminates, the last δ is 0 and the recursion (2) stops. Statement (3) is about ||qα|| = min_p |qα − p| (best approximations of the SECOND kind). For the FIRST-kind problem of minimising |α − p/q| over q ≤ Q, intermediate fractions (p_{n-1} + k p_n)/(q_{n-1} + k q_n) with k > a_{n+1}/2 can also be best approximations, so the two notions must not be conflated. When a_1 = 1 one has q_0 = q_1 = 1, the n = 0 case of (3) is vacuous, and ||α|| equals δ_1, not δ_0.","status":"unverified"}

Every continuous real symmetric PSD kernel of rank <=p and diagonal <=R^2 on a nonempty compact X subset R^d admits an explicit raw-input normalized-ReLU-attention transformer for uniform noisy predictive forward KL <=eps, with positive noise s, labels bounded by B, and contexts <=n. The complete width/depth/MLP/head bound is given in C005 Section 1 in terms of the canonical kernel modulus Omega(r), a finite h-net cardinality J, and the solver constants. Complete theorem, constants and scope:
# Target 1 for continuous finite-rank kernels on compact raw domains

Claim T336-w727-C005 v2. Status: proof (unaudited), dependent on C002 v1 and the deterministic perturbation/encoder constructions in C004 v1. The entire result is not Lean-checked. No independent review or novelty certification is claimed.

The hardest step is removing the supplied-feature oracle without adding a hidden feature-computation cost. A finite Gram factorization fixes the encoder weights; a kernel modulus controls its error. The size explicitly includes the resulting encoder.

## 1. Statement and all parameters

Let X be a nonempty compact subset of R^d, d>=1. Let k:X times X -> R be a continuous real symmetric positive-semidefinite kernel of rank at most p, p>=1, with k(x,x)<=R^2 for R>=0. The prior is the zero-mean GP with kernel k. Observation noise is independent N(0,s), s>0. Labels are bounded by B>=0, contexts have length <=n with n>=0 an integer, and eps>0. The prediction concerns a new noisy observation.

Define the canonical kernel modulus in the ambient L1 metric by

    Omega(r)=sup_{x,y in X, ||x-y||_1<=r}
                sqrt(k(x,x)+k(y,y)-2k(x,y)).

The expression is nonnegative by positive semidefiniteness. Omega(r) tends to zero as r decreases to zero, as proved below.

Retain the following explicit constants from C004's deterministic perturbation bound:

    S=R+1, C_A=n(2R+1),
    C_m=nB[(R+S)/s+S C_A R/s^2],
    C_v=R+S+S^2 C_A/s>0,
    eta=min(1,sqrt(s eps)/(2(1+C_m)),s sqrt(eps)/(2C_v),s/(4C_v)),
    eps0=min(eps/4,1/16), e=eta/sqrt(p)>0.

Choose any **fixed admissible** r>0 with Omega(r)<=e/2. An explicit upper modulus for k can be used to choose r; continuity guarantees existence, not an algorithm for computing a modulus of an arbitrary black-box kernel. Put

    A_cone=(2R+e)/r>0, h=e/(2A_cone)>0.

Choose a finite h-net G contained in X, of cardinality J>=1. The size bound is explicit in J (or in a known upper bound for the covering number). For X=[0,1]^d one may take the regular grid with

    m=max(1,ceil(d A_cone/e)), J=(m+1)^d.

For the attention solver define

    kappa=1+max(1,n)S^2/s, M=nS^2B/s,
    delta0=min(1/2,s/(2S^2),sqrt(s eps0)/(1+M),s sqrt(eps0)/S^2),
    T=ceil(sqrt(kappa) log(2/delta0)/2).

There is a transformer, using normalized residual ReLU attention and tokenwise residual ReLU MLPs, with

    D=7p+6+d+Jd+pJ,
    H=2Jd+pJ+4p+1,
    L_total=T+5+ceil(log_2 J),
    at most five attention heads per layer,
    at most L_total(15D^2+2DH)+2D dense scalar parameters,

whose positive-variance Gaussian output has forward KL<=eps from the exact noisy GP predictive, uniformly over all admissible raw-input contexts and queries. Its input contains only raw coordinates, labels, fixed context/query flags, and constants. The encoder is counted. These are arbitrary-real-weight size bounds; no finite-bit, kernel-evaluation, offline factorization-time, SGD, or ERM-generalization bound is asserted.

## 2. Canonical finite-dimensional features and the kernel modulus

Form the vector space of finite formal combinations of symbols delta_x with bilinear form

    <sum_i a_i delta_{x_i},sum_j b_j delta_{y_j}>
       =sum_{i,j}a_i b_j k(x_i,y_j).

Positive semidefiniteness makes this a nonnegative quadratic form. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality follows by applying nonnegativity to u+t v for all real t; in particular a zero-norm vector is orthogonal to every vector. Quotient by the zero-norm subspace. For any finite list of symbols, the dimension of their quotient span is the rank of their Gram matrix. Every finite list of quotient vectors is contained in the span of finitely many symbols. Thus the dimension of the resulting inner-product space is the supremum of these Gram ranks, which is the kernel rank and is at most p. It is finite dimensional, so no completion issue remains.

Choose an orthonormal basis and pad with zeros in R^p. The coordinates z(x) of delta_x then satisfy

    k(x,y)=z(x)^T z(y), ||z(x)||<=R,
    ||z(x)-z(y)||^2=k(x,x)+k(y,y)-2k(x,y).

Thus z is continuous and ||z(x)-z(y)||<=Omega(r) whenever ||x-y||_1<=r. To justify Omega(r)->0 directly, suppose the contrary. There are sequences r_j->0 and x_j,y_j in X at distance <=r_j with feature distance bounded away from zero. Compactness supplies a subsequence x_j->x; then y_j->x as well. Continuity of k makes the squared feature distance tend to k(x,x)+k(x,x)-2k(x,x)=0, a contradiction. The supremum is finite because the kernel is continuous on the compact product. In particular every fixed positive e admits the required r.

The factorization at the finite net does not require evaluating any feature map on runtime inputs. Form the fixed J-by-J Gram matrix K_G=(k(a,b))_{a,b in G}. It is PSD of rank <=p, so a finite spectral factorization gives vectors v_a in R^p with v_a^T v_b=k(a,b). There is an isometry between the spans of z(a) and v_a: the map sum c_a z(a) -> sum c_a v_a is well defined and norm preserving because both squared norms equal c^T K_G c. Extend orthonormal bases of the two spans to R^p. The isometry extends to an orthogonal map on R^p. Applying it to all z(x) gives a representation, still called z, with z(a)=v_a for every a in G and with the same norm and modulus bounds.

Consequently **all feature values used as weights below can be obtained from the finite prior Gram matrix on G**. Computing this fixed factorization is preprocessing of the fixed prior, not an input-dependent inverse hidden in the predictive head. Its real entries are included in the encoder's parameter count.

## 3. Cone envelope for a general continuous feature map

Define, using the finite Gram feature values,

    ztilde_j(x)=min_{a in G}[v_{a,j}+A_cone ||x-a||_1].

This formula is valid even though z_j need not be Lipschitz. We claim |ztilde_j(x)-z_j(x)|<=e for every j,x.

For a with ||x-a||_1<=r, the modulus gives v_{a,j}>=z_j(x)-Omega(r)>=z_j(x)-e/2. Adding a nonnegative cone term preserves this lower bound. For a with ||x-a||_1>r, the coordinate bound |z_j|<=R gives

    v_{a,j}+A_cone ||x-a||_1
      >z_j(x)-2R+A_cone r=z_j(x)+e.

So every candidate is >=z_j(x)-e/2, and the finite minimum is too.

For the upper bound choose a net point with ||x-a||_1<=h. Since h=e r/(2(2R+e))<=r/2, the modulus bound applies. Therefore

    ztilde_j(x)<=z_j(x)+Omega(r)+A_cone h
                  <=z_j(x)+e/2+e/2=z_j(x)+e.

It follows that sup_x ||ztilde(x)-z(x)||<=sqrt(p)e=eta and ||ztilde(x)||<=R+eta<=S. All denominators above are positive, including R=0. For a cube grid, coordinate rounding gives L1 distance <=d/(2m)<=e/(2A_cone)=h, which verifies the displayed grid size.

## 4. Exact network realization and original-posterior KL

Use C004 Section 4's explicit register construction, with the J centers now the net points a and with the slope K in the cone layer replaced by A_cone. Layer 1 computes all Jd absolute differences with 2Jd ReLUs. Layer 2 forms the pJ affine cone values using these nonnegative absolute registers and the constant register. A balanced residual-min tournament takes ceil(log_2 J) layers, including zero layers when J=1. The last gating layer, using the binary context/query flags and |ztilde_j|<=S, writes the context/query feature registers exactly. For padding choose a fixed anchor point in X as its raw coordinates, rather than assuming the ambient origin belongs to X. Its flags are zero, so the computed features are gated to zero.

This uses E=3+ceil(log_2 J) encoder layers and precisely the width and hidden-width bounds in Section 1. This invokes the exact algebraic encoder construction, **not the Lipschitz-error assertion** of C004 Section 3. Section 3 above supplies the replacement uniform approximation guarantee.

C004 Section 2's perturbation proof uses only ||ztilde-z||<=eta<=1, not feature Lipschitzness. It therefore gives original-versus-encoded predictive errors

    |mu-mutilde|<=sqrt(s eps)/2,
    |v-vtilde|<=min(s/4,s sqrt(eps)/2).

Apply C002 v1 to the encoded features with bound S and accuracy eps0. The one-head query broadcast, T five-head Chebyshev layers, and four-head readout produce muhat,vhat with vhat>=s and errors

    |mutilde-muhat|<=sqrt(s eps)/2,
    |vtilde-vhat|<=min(s/4,s sqrt(eps)/2).

The original predictive variance is also >=s. Adding scalar errors gives |mu-muhat|<=sqrt(s eps) and |v-vhat|<=min(s/2,s sqrt(eps)). The Gaussian calculation in C002 Section 5 then yields forward KL<=eps from the **original kernel** predictive distribution to the transformer output. No triangle inequality for KL is used.

Combining the E encoder layers with the T+2 solver layers gives the depth. Count three D-by-D matrices for each of at most five heads, two MLP matrices of dimensions H-by-D and D-by-H per layer (even counting zeros), and a two-coordinate linear readout. This proves the displayed parameter bound.

## 5. Exact scope

C005 covers every continuous bounded finite-rank kernel on a nonempty compact Euclidean domain, with an explicit bound in terms of a kernel modulus and a finite covering number. It includes continuous kernels whose features are not Lipschitz. C004 gives the simpler closed grid formula when a coordinatewise Lipschitz feature bound is available. Define D_H=(I_H-FF*)^(1/2) and D_K=(I_K-F*F)^(1/2), the positive square roots. The Julia operator J=[[D_H,F],[-F*,D_K]] on H direct-sum K is unitary. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:25:35.795629+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_72ab84954d47f7ba9454aa464a4a285daf3fa8ca77bb4816fcfbb64e852b8950","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm.llt_stein of arXiv:2603.11043, 'An asymptotically optimal bound for the concentration function of a sum of independent int'] Let ${\bf Y}_i$, $1 \le i \le m$ be independent $\mathbb{Z}^d$-valued vectors with
    means $\mu_i$ and covariance matrices $\Sigma_i$. Let $\mu = \sum_{i=1}^m \mu_i$ and
    $\Sigma = \sum_{i=1}^m \Sigma_i$.
    Let $\gamma_i=\mathbb E \|{\bf Y}_i -\mu_i\|^3$.
    Define $u_i= \min_{1 \le j \le d} \{1-d_{TV}({\bf Y}_i, {\bf Y}_i+e^{(j)})\}$, where $e^{(j)} \in \mathbb{Z}^d$
    is the $j$th coordinate vector. 
    Let ${\bf S}_m = {\bf Y}_1 + \dots + {\bf Y}_m$, let ${\bf X} \sim N(\mu, \Sigma)$ and let $\left[ \bf X \right]$ be
    $\bf X$ rounded to the nearest integer vector, that is, for any $x \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, $\mathbb P(\left[ \bf X \right] = x) = \mathbb P({\bf X} \in x + [-\frac 1 2, \frac 1 2)^d)$.
    Then
    \[
        d_{TV}({\bf S}_m, \left[ \bf X \right]) \le C d^{\frac 7 2} \ln m (L + (\frac d m)^{\frac 1 2}) \sqrt{\frac m {\tilde{s}_m}}
    \]
    where 
    \[
        L = \frac {m^{- \frac 1 2} \chi} {{\rm Tr}(\frac 2 m \Sigma)^{\frac 3 2}},
    \]
    \[
        \chi = \mathbb E \|{\boldsymbol \xi}\|^3, \quad \quad \tilde{s}_m = \sum_{i=1}^m u_i - \max_{i \in \{1, \dots, m\}} u_i,
    \]
    ${\boldsymbol \xi} = {\bf Y}_K' - {\bf Y}_K$ for 
    ${\bf Y}_i'$ an independent copy of ${\bf Y}_i$ for $1 \le i \le m$, $K$ is a uniformly random element of $\{1, \dots, m\}$ such that ${\bf Y}_1, \dots, {\bf Y}_m, {\bf Y}_1', \dots, {\bf Y}_m', K$ are independent and we assume that $\tilde{s}_m > 0$. 
    Furthermore, $C$ depends only on $\lambda_{min}(m^{-1}\Sigma)$,  $\lambda_{max}(m^{-1}\Sigma)$ and  $d^{-1}{\rm Tr}(m^{-1}\Sigma)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:18:13.232634+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_72c467e008a478c48361d67caa0325c7229ae4c2ed22001b38458e4412b3be1b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:double-in-banach of arXiv:2506.17168, '{\bf Scaling limits for sample autocovariance operators of Hilbert space-valued linear pro'] Let $(\mathbb Y,\mu)$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure space, and let $\{W^{(r)}\}_{r \in \mathbb Y}$ be a family of Gaussian random measures on $(\mathbb R, \lambda)$ with covariances (equation eq:covWW of the paper). Consider a kernel $f: \mathbb Y^2 \times \mathbb R^2 \to \mathbb R$. We say that there exists an $L^2(\mathbb Y^2)$-valued double Wiener-It\^o integral of the kernel $f$, denoted $\mathcal{I}_2(f)$, if there exists a sequence $\{f_{(n)}: n \geq 1\}$ of $L^2(\mathbb Y^2)$-valued special kernels, defined on $\mathbb Y^2 \times \mathbb R^2$, such that
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item $\lim_{n \to \infty} \|f^{(r,s)} - f_{(n)}^{(r,s)}\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)} = 0$ $\mu^{\otimes 2}$-a.s.,
    
    \item the sequence $\{\mathcal{I}_2(f_{(n)}): n \geq 1\}$ is a Cauchy sequence in $L^1(\Omega:L^2(\mathbb Y^{2}))$.
    
\end{enumerate}
In that case, we define the double Wiener-It\^o integral by 
\[
\mathcal{I}_2(f) \doteq \lim_{n \to \infty} \mathcal{I}_2(f_{(n)}),
\]
where the limit is again understood in $L^1(\Omega:L^2(\mathbb Y^{2}))$. For an $\mathbb R^d-$valued kernel $f = (f_1,\dots,f_d)$ such that $\mathcal{I}_2(f_i)$ exists for all $i = 1,\dots,d$, we fix the notation $\mathcal{I}_2(f) \doteq (\mathcal{I}_2(f_1),\dots,\mathcal{I}_2(f_d))$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["for the unconditional statement: a_{ij} >= 0","for the signed statement: sum_{i,j} |a_{ij}| < infinity"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752086+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_72d3f867e705b3b93b077ab4f47183c52a31ef34fafaa00b3f9f2ffb66e77fac","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a doubly indexed family (a_{ij}) of NONNEGATIVE reals, sum_i sum_j a_{ij} = sum_j sum_i a_{ij} = sup over finite rectangles of the partial sums, all three being equal in [0, infinity] with no further hypothesis; this is Tonelli's theorem for two copies of counting measure, which is sigma-finite. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:01:48.633710+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_72f4b0d36bb96430ec80c8176f034705350ac15459ceb9958434cbf1c32581a0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lmm:m1m2 of arXiv:2607.02013, 'Resolution of the Detection Threshold Conjecture for Random Geometric Graphs in the $d>n$ '] With the above notations, we have
    \[
    m_2 = \frac{d-1}{d}am_1
    \]
and $1 \le a \le ( 2 \log (1/p))^{1/2}$.
Furthermore, assuming $a\le \sqrt d/2$, we have
\[ \zeta^2 \asymp pa^{2} \lesssim h(p)\,,
\]
where we recall that $\zeta$ is defined by ~((eq:zeta-def of the paper)).

\begin{proof}
In this proof, we fix $d$ and suppress it from the notation.  We abbreviate $\mathbb{P}=\nu$, and write $\mathbb{E}$ for expectation with respect to $\nu$.  We also abbreviate $c\equiv c_{d,1}$ and $f(t)\equiv f_d(t)$. Define
    \[ g(t)
    = c \bigg(1-\frac{t^2}{d}\bigg)^{(d-1)/2}\,,
    \]
and note that
    \begin{align*}
    \frac{d}{dt} g(t) &= -\frac{d-1}{d}  t f(t)\,,\\
    \frac{d}{dt} [tg(t)]
        &= -(t^2-1) f(t)\,.
    \end{align*}
It follows that
    \begin{align*}
    &m_1
    = \mathbb{E}[T;T\ge a]
    = \int_a^{d^{1/2} } t f(t)\,dt
    = \frac{d}{d-1} g(a)
    = \frac{cd}{d-1} \bigg(1-\frac{a^2}{d}
        \bigg)^{(d-1)/2}\,,\\
    &\mathbb E[T^2; T \ge a]-p
    =\int_a^{d^{1/2}} (t^2-1) f(t)\,dt
    =ag(a)
    = \frac{d-1}{d}am_1\,.
    \end{align*}
Rearranging the last expression gives
    \[
    m_2
    = \mathbb E[T^2 K(T)]
    = \mathbb E[T^2;T\ge a]-p
    = \frac{d-1}{d}am_1\,,
    \]
which proves the first claim. Next, recalling that $p=\mathbb{P}(T\ge a)$, to bound $a\ge1$ it suffices to prove that $\mathbb{P}(T\ge 1)> p$. In fact it is easy to argue that $\mathbb{P}(T\ge 1)$ is lower bounded by an absolute constant: $T$ is equidistributed as
    \[
    \frac{d^{1/2} Z}{(Z^2 + S)^{1/2}}
    \]
where $Z$ is a standard gaussian random variable, and $S$ is a chi-square random variable with $d-1$ degrees of freedom, independent of $Z$. If $Z \ge 2^{1/2}$ and $S \le 2(d-1)$ then the above ratio is $\ge1$, so we conclude
    \[
    \mathbb{P}(T\ge1)
    \ge \mathbb{P}(Z \ge 2^{1/2}) \mathbb{P}(S \le 2(d-1))
    \ge \frac{\mathbb{P}(Z \ge 2^{1/2})}{2}
    \ge 0.03\,.
    \]
This proves $a\ge1$, as claimed. On the other hand the upper bound on $a$ is equivalent to the bound 
\[p = \mathbb{P}(T\ge a) \le \mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(-\frac{a^2}{2}\bigg)\,,\] which follows from the fact that $T$ is $1$-subgaussian (Lemma~(lem:beta.mgf of the paper)). Next, recalling the definition ~((eq:zeta-def of the paper)) of $\zeta$, it is clear that $\zeta\gtrsim p^{1/2}a$. For the upper bound, we recall that the integration by parts above gives
    \[m_1 = \frac{d}{d-1} f_d(a) 
    \bigg(1-\frac{a^2}{d}\bigg)
    \leq 2 f_d(a)\,.
    \]
It is shown later in 
Lemma~(l:cap-tail-moment of the paper)
that under the assumption $1\le a\le \sqrt d/2$ we have
$p\geq c f_d(a)/a$ for some numerical constant $c$ (see display ~((eq:p-lb of the paper))). It  follows that
\[\zeta^2 = \frac{m_1^2}{p(1-p)}
\lesssim \frac{(ap)^2}{p} = pa^2
\lesssim h(p)\,,
\] as claimed.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.095116+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7309f0c264475260a89ace85ddc1e13394af8cf1389dfd37aca038a11e952075","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:port-interface of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Let $\Pi_{\rm core}$ be the finite set generated by the three
principal-pivot presentations $P_C,P_H,P_G$ listed explicitly in
(lem:pn1 of the paper) below, and by exchange and reversal
of the two carrier rails.  A \emph{circuit state} $\tau$ records, before
evaluation,
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item every original $p\vee r$ circuit, its ordered oriented interval
fragments, and one base fragment on that circuit;
\item the ten named physical gaps, every component, defect, and retained
root port, with their source and target tensor words; and
\item either one ordered pair of root fronts or one existing opaque
two-front token.
\end{enumerate}
The finite root states $\Pi_{\rm root}$ record the twenty ordered choices
of distinct core occurrences together with this data.

For later use we make the signed transport in this definition explicit.
Identify the five core vertices with $\mathbb F_5$ by
\[
 \kappa_5(0)=0,\qquad \kappa_5(1)=1,\qquad \kappa_5(2)=4,
 \qquad \kappa_5(3)=2,\qquad \kappa_5(4)=3.
\tag{2.2.6a}
\]
In these coordinates the oriented left and right rails are respectively
$x\mapsto x+1$ and $x\mapsto x+2$.  The transport group is
\[
 \mathscr O_{20}=\{g_{\alpha,\beta}:x\mapsto\alpha x+\beta:
       \alpha\in\mathbb F_5^\times,\ \beta\in\mathbb F_5\}.
\tag{2.2.6b}
\]
It acts on vertices through $\kappa_5^{-1}g_{\alpha,\beta}\kappa_5$.
Multiplication by $\alpha=1,4,2,3$ sends the ordered pair of oriented
rails $(L,R)$ to
\[
 (L^+,R^+),\qquad (L^-,R^-),\qquad
 (R^+,L^-),\qquad (R^-,L^+),
\tag{2.2.6c}
\]
respectively.  If $x_v^s$ is the gap leaving $v$ on the oriented rail
$s$ and $g$ sends $s$ to $t$ with orientation $\epsilon$, then
\[
 g(x_v^s)=
 \begin{cases}
 x_{g(v)}^t,&\epsilon=+1,\\
 (x_{\operatorname{pred}_t(g(v))}^t)^*,&\epsilon=-1.
 \end{cases}
\tag{2.2.6d}
\]
At a curvature gate the induced dart permutation carries the two physical
wedge pairs to the two physical wedge pairs.  Reversal within a wedge pair
contributes its skew sign, whereas exchange of the two wedge pairs is
signless.  Thus the product of the five local curvature signs is
\[
 \chi(g_{\alpha,\beta})=
 \begin{cases}+1,&\alpha\in\{1,4\},\\-1,&\alpha\in\{2,3\}.
 \end{cases}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:25:39.116307+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_733471e1b267fe76f9b33cbbbebb4e2ca1489cbfef0b2ecb9bc930e13e6da4f9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def: plus minus interface of arXiv:2606.13147, 'Scaling limits of the single-curve interface and outermost loops in the planar random fiel'] Let $$\mathtt{Dob}^+:=\partial\Lambda_N\cap \{z=(z^{(1)},z^{(2)})\in\mathbb Z^d, z^{(2)}\geq 0\},\quad \mathtt{Dob}^-:=\partial\Lambda_N\cap \{z=(z^{(1)},z^{(2)})\in\mathbb Z^d, z^{(2)}<0\}$$
    denote the upper and bottom half parts of the boundary of the box $\Lambda_N.$ Then the Dobrushin boundary condition (denoted $\pm$) is the boundary condition that being plus on $\mathtt{Dob}^+$ and minus on $\mathtt{Dob}^-.$ Now given any configuration $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^{\Lambda_N}$ satisfying Dobrushin boundary condition, we define the upmost plus--minus boundary interface $\gamma=\gamma(\sigma)$ as follows.

Let
$
\mathtt{Plus}(\sigma)=\{z\in\Lambda_N:\sigma_z=1\}
$
denote the set of plus spins. By definition, we have
$
\mathtt{Dob}^+\subset \mathtt{Plus}(\sigma).
$
Since $\mathtt{Dob}^+$ is connected in $\mathbb Z^2$, there exists a unique connected component of $\mathtt{Plus}(\sigma)$ containing $\mathtt{Dob}^+$, which we denote by $\mathtt{ConPlus}(\sigma)$.

Define
\[
\Lambda^+(\sigma)
=
\big\{
z\in\Lambda_N:
\text{every path from }z
\text{ to }\partial\Lambda_{N+1}
\text{ intersects }
\mathtt{ConPlus}(\sigma)
\big\},
\]
and let
$
\Lambda^-(\sigma)=\Lambda_N\setminus\Lambda^+(\sigma).
$
Intuitively, $\Lambda^+(\sigma)$ is obtained by filling in all holes of $\mathtt{ConPlus}(\sigma)$.

We then define
\[
\gamma^+(\sigma)
=
\{x\in\Lambda^+(\sigma):
\exists y\in\Lambda^-(\sigma)
\text{ with }
x\sim_* y
\}
\setminus \mathtt{Dob}^+,
\]
and
$\gamma^-(\sigma)=\partial_{\mathrm{ext}}\Lambda^+(\sigma)\setminus \mathtt{Dob}^-.$
Here $x\sim_* y$ means that $x$ and $y$ are $*$-neighbors. By planar duality, $\gamma^+$ forms a connected set of plus spins, while $\gamma^-$ forms a $*$-connected set of minus spins. Hence
$
\gamma=(\gamma^+,\gamma^-)
$
defines a plus--minus interface. Moreover, $\gamma$ is the upmost interface, since every $*$-connected minus path from $\mathtt{Dob}^-$ to $\mathtt{Dob}^-$ must intersect $\gamma^+$.

Finally, let $\Sigma_\gamma$ denote the collection of configurations satisfying $\gamma(\sigma)=\gamma$.
It is easy to see that 
$\Sigma_\gamma=\{\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^{\Lambda_N}: \sigma_{\mid \mathtt{Dob}^+\cup\gamma^+}=1, \sigma_{\mid \mathtt{Dob}^-\cup\gamma^-}=-1\}.$
For convenience, write
$
\mu^\pm_{\Lambda_N,\epsilon h}(\gamma)
=
\mu^\pm_{\Lambda_N,\epsilon h}(\Sigma_\gamma),
$
and similarly
$
\mu^\pm_{\Lambda_N,0}(\gamma)
=
\mu^\pm_{\Lambda_N,0}(\Sigma_\gamma),
$
where the superscript $\pm$ indicates Dobrushin boundary conditions.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:37:08.317781+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_733d5128b10f526ef8ef551d38a822d942fe8b13bd76d1e6063b6994468a5eec","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition {\cite[Definition 4.10 of arXiv:2608.30973, 'Pseudo-Anosov flow and dynamics on guts'] {Gabai1983_FoliationsAndTheTopologyOf3Manifolds_PUB},[AgolZhang2022_GutsInSuturedDecompositionsAndTheThurstonNorm_ARXv1]}]
Let \((N,\gamma)\) be a taut sutured manifold and let \(S\) be the maximal set of pairwise disjoint non-parallel product annuli and product disks in \(N\).
We define the \emph{sutured guts} \(\mathrm{Guts}(N)\) of \((N,\gamma)\) as the sutured manifold obtained from \((N,\gamma)\) by decomposing along \(S\) and discarding \emph{windows}, namely, product sutured manifold components.

The sutured guts is well-defined up to isotopy class of inclusion map by classical JSJ decomposition theory \autocite{Johannson1979_HomotopyEquivalencesOf3ManifoldsWithBoundaries_PUB} \autocite{JacoShalen1979_SeifertFiberedSpacesIn3Manifolds}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["tree family defined explicitly in this statement","fixed real beta","independent Bernoulli bonds"],"created_at":"2026-10-10T08:42:44.995044+00:00","domain":"Bernoulli bond percolation on trees","id":"claim_73940b8f752f653061271a4ad42a5effe1f5a5c763c770f5da1b4347ce73cb98","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT; INDEPENDENT MATHEMATICAL REVIEW PENDING. For a fixed real beta, let N=ceil(8(1+abs(beta))), B_n=floor(n/2+beta*log_2(1+n/N)), and let T_beta be the rooted tree with 2^(B_(n+1)-B_n) children at each vertex at depth n. T_beta has maximum degree at most 3 and p_c=1/sqrt(2). At criticality the root survival probability is positive exactly when beta>1. For beta<1, root connection probability to depth n is comparable to n^(beta-1); for beta=1 it is comparable to 1/log(n), for large n with beta-dependent constants. For beta>1, theta_o(p_c)>=(2-1/sqrt(2))/(1+N/(beta-1)); in particular theta_(T_2)(p_c)>=(2-1/sqrt(2))/25. When beta<=1 there is almost surely no infinite cluster anywhere. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:48:30.910023+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_739727807eea673d512f2edea09c5a7d7f69594351f1ad54d8f8f3f9c6b79d1d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 3 (Explicit Main Theorem for $n=2$ over Rational Numbers) of arXiv:2609.00974, 'On Algebraic Integrability\\ of Vector Fields \\ with Rational Function Coefficients\\ tha'] Let $f,g\in \mathbb{Q}(X)$ be nonzero rational functions.
    Let $D=f(x)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}+g(y)\frac{\partial}{\partial y}$ be a derivation on the field $\mathbb{Q}(x,y)$.

    Then the following are equivalent:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item There exists a non-constant $F\in \mathbb{Q}(x,y)$ such that $D(F)=0$.
        \item One of the following is true:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item All complex residues of $\frac{1}{f}$ and $\frac{1}{g}$ are zero.
        \item There exists irreducible polynomials $f_1,\ldots,f_n\in \mathbb{Q}[x],g_1,\ldots,g_m\in\mathbb{Q}[y]$ and rational numbers $c_1,\ldots,c_n, d_1,\ldots,d_m \in\mathbb{Q}$ such that
        \[
        \frac{1}{f}=\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{c_i f_i'}{f_i}, \hspace{1cm} \frac{1}{g}=\sum_{i=1}^m \frac{d_i g_i'}{g_i}.
        \]
        \item There exists a quadratic extension $L/\mathbb{Q}$, irreducible polynomials $f_1,\ldots,f_n\in \mathbb{Q}[x]$, $g_1,\ldots,g_m\in\mathbb{Q}[y]$ that split over $L$ into conjugate factors $f_i=f_{i1}f_{i2}$ and $g_j=g_{j1}g_{j2}$, and $c_1,\ldots,c_n\in L\setminus \mathbb{Q}$, $d_1,\ldots,d_m\in L\setminus \mathbb{Q}$ satisfying $c_i+\overline{c_i}=0,d_j+\overline{d_j}=0$ such that
        \[
        \frac{1}{f}=\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{c_i (f_{i1}'f_{i2}-f_{i2}'f_{i1})}{f_i}, 
        \hspace{1cm} 
        \frac{1}{g}=\sum_{i=1}^m \frac{d_i (g_{i1}'g_{i2}-g_{i2}'g_{i1})}{g_i}.
        \]
    \end{enumerate}  
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:18:54.364701+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_739a29ead985a79be2e73f66e0584169bb86bd5947560c259079b08afae76f6b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given a twice differentiable function $f:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R$, in order for $x\in\mathbb R^N$ to be a local extremum, we must have $f'(x)=0$, and:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $f''(x)\geq0$ is needed for $x$ to be a local minimum.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:07:35.009931+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_73bcb31239d41e9890cd7900fe624ca644493718e01d1a221369e09347e39dd3","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 7 of arXiv:2609.02850, 'Canonical-row Chern flow on Bott--Samelson towers:\\ realizable-volume models for Schubert'] For every field $\kk$, the class $\RV$ has the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item It is invariant under permutations of variables and nonnegative
rational linear substitutions, including coordinate restriction.
\item It is closed under products.
\item If $f\in\RV$, then every ordinary coordinate derivative
$\partial_x^\gamma f$ lies in $\RV$.
\item It is closed under coordinatewise lower and upper truncations in the
divided-power basis.
\item It is invariant under common divided-power translations:
\[
 \sum_\alpha c_\alpha x^{[\alpha]}\in\RV
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \sum_\alpha c_\alpha x^{[\alpha+\gamma]}\in\RV.
\]
\item If $f\in\RV$, then its factorial normalization $\Nrm(f)$ lies in
$\RV$.
\item If $F_1,F_2$ have realizable factorial normalizations, then
$\Nrm(F_1F_2)$ lies in $\RV$.
\item Full polarization preserves $\RV$.
\item Membership is invariant under arbitrary field extension; for
polynomials with rational coefficients, it depends only on
$\operatorname{char}(\kk)$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:52:08.667563+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_73d0c639faad0d6c7c76fd8740caf43e4cd9f3f12e44e8145caac13ef1aab777","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 17 (Fiber-equivalent torus fibrations) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let
\[
        \pi_i:M\to S^1_i,\qquad i=0,1,
\]
be torus fibrations.  The target circles are not part of the fixed data and may
be different.  Choose a basepoint \(x\in M\) and, for each \(i=0,1\), an identification
\(\pi_1(S_i^1,\pi_i(x))\cong\ZZ\), and let
\[
        \alpha_{\pi_i,x}:\pi_1(M,x)\longrightarrow\ZZ,
\]
be the surjective homomorphism induced by \(\pi_i\).  Changing the
identification changes \(\alpha_{\pi_i,x}\) by a sign.  Equivalently, \(\pi_i\)
determines a cohomology class \([\pi_i]\in H^1(M;\ZZ)\), well-defined up to
sign.  We say that \(\pi_0\) and \(\pi_1\) are \emph{fiber-equivalent}
if
\[
        [\pi_0]=\pm[\pi_1]\in H^1(M;\ZZ).
\]
