{"assumptions":["(X,B,mu) is a probability space and T preserves mu (invertibility is not needed)","P and Q are countable measurable partitions","H_mu(P) < infinity and H_mu(Q) < infinity","entropies are taken with a fixed logarithm base throughout"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090248+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, entropy","id":"claim_73e397e27849e65c29b0ad85dd4fc2d78bd89a46e9ea1748bcc9855a192424af","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let T be a measure-preserving transformation of a probability space (X, B, mu) and let P and Q be countable measurable partitions with H_mu(P) < infinity and H_mu(Q) < infinity. Write P_n for the join of T^{-i}P over 0 <= i <= n-1 and h_mu(T,P) = lim_n (1/n) H_mu(P_n) (the limit exists by subadditivity and equals the infimum over n). Then h_mu(T, Q) <= h_mu(T, P) + H_mu(Q | P). Two standard consequences: if P refines Q then H_mu(Q | P) = 0 and hence h_mu(T, Q) <= h_mu(T, P), so the partition entropy is monotone under refinement; and |h_mu(T,P) - h_mu(T,Q)| <= H_mu(P | Q) + H_mu(Q | P), i.e. the map P -> h_mu(T,P) is 1-Lipschitz for the Rokhlin metric. WHERE IT FAILS: finiteness of H_mu(P) and H_mu(Q) is used - with infinite-entropy partitions both sides can be infinite and the inequality carries no information. The inequality is one-sided: nothing bounds h_mu(T,P) from below in terms of h_mu(T,Q) unless the conditional entropy in the other direction is also controlled. It is an inequality between the entropies of PROCESSES, not of the partitions: H_mu(Q) <= H_mu(P) + H_mu(Q|P) is the (easier) static statement and must not be quoted in its place.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:19:42.577408+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7405fcfc60ba2e2b510f49b725ba23ec3d1ae5ec2bd38cd0f3790d4437a8427b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 1 of arXiv:2609.03512, ''] Let $G$ be a simple connected graph with vertex set $V(G)=\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}$, and let $m=(m_1,\ldots,m_n)$ be a vector of positive integers. The \emph{blow-up} $G\bigodot m$ is obtained from $G$ by replacing each vertex $v_i$ with an independent set
\[
V_i = \{v_i^1,\ldots,v_i^{m_i}\}
\]
of $m_i$ vertices, and joining $v_i^s$ to $v_j^t$ if and only if $v_iv_j\in E(G)$. We call $V_i$ the \emph{part of $G\bigodot m$ corresponding to $v_i$}, and say that $G\bigodot m$ is obtained from $G$ by \emph{multiplication of vertices} (Golumbic \cite{Graph-multiplication-Golumbic}, p.~53).

If $m_j=1$ for all $j\ne i$, we say $G\bigodot m$ is obtained from $G$ by \emph{multiplying the single vertex $v_i$}; if moreover $m_i=2$, this is called \emph{duplicating} $v_i$ (Henning and Southey \cite{Henning-Michael}). If $G$ has a vertex of degree $2$, \emph{degree-$2$ vertex duplication} denotes the operation of duplicating any such vertex.

For graphs $G_1,\ldots,G_k$, we write $\mathcal{M}(G_1,\ldots,G_k)$ for the family of all graphs obtainable from some $G_\ell$ by multiplication of vertices. Since $G\bigodot(1,\ldots,1)=G$, each $G_\ell$ itself belongs to $\mathcal{M}(G_1,\ldots,G_k)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.808109+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_743cf06b65abbce3837731c48aedf308156ff722d986e3dbe43f324ccbc4041f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm FirstPresentation of arXiv:2609.01501, 'Singularities of star cluster algebras'] Let $ \mathcal{Q} $ be an acyclic quiver with $ N $ vertices such that the vertices $ 1, \ldots, n $ are mutable 
	and $ n+1, \ldots, N $ are frozen.  
	Let $ K $ be a field
	and let $ \boldsymbol{x} = (x_1, \ldots, x_N ) $ be an $ N $-tuple of elements that are algebraically independent over $ K $.
	The cluster algebra $ \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{Q}) \subset K(\boldsymbol{x}) =  K(x_1, \ldots, x_n, \ldots, x_N) $ (defined over $ K $) corresponding to $ \mathcal{Q} $ is isomorphic to
	
	\begin{equation}
		 
		K[x_{n+1}^{\pm 1}, \ldots, x_{N}^{\pm 1}][x_1, \ldots, x_n, x_1', \ldots, x_n']
		/ \langle x_k x_k' - \prod_{i\rightarrow k} x_i^{b_{ik}} - \prod_{i \leftarrow k} x_i^{-b_{ik}} \mid k \in \{ 1, \ldots, n \} \rangle 
	\end{equation}
	where $ (x_1', \ldots, x_n') $ is another tuple of algebraically independent elements over $ K $, 
	the products range over those vertices $ i $ of $ \mathcal{Q} $ for which there is an arrow $ i \rightarrow k $ (resp.~$ i \leftarrow k $),
	and
	$ b_{ik} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} $ is the number of arrows $ i \rightarrow k $ which is negative if there are arrows $ i \leftarrow k $. 
	\\
	Moreover, 
	$ (x_k x_k' - \prod_{i\rightarrow k} x_i^{b_{ik}} - \prod_{i \leftarrow k} x_i^{-b_{ik}} \mid k \in \{ 1, \ldots, n \}) $ 
	is a Gr\"obner basis for the ideal which it generates with respect to any term order
	giving preference to $ x_1', \ldots, x_n' $ over $ \boldsymbol{x} $. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:01:01.827867+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_743d5d91ec5fa0d1bc263db5a121c45eb8eb88690abe3f623f6e6499dcabf8b6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:CGO-PhS_int-by-parts of arXiv:2609.00257, 'Stability estimates for the initial-to-final-state inverse problem'] [zbMATH07801151]\sl 
Consider $F \in L^2(\Sigma)$ such that 
there exists $c > 0$ so that $e^{c|\mathrm{x}|} F \in L^2(\Sigma)$.
Let $u \in C([0,T]; L^2(\mathbb{R}^n))$ satisfy the conditions

\[
\left\{

		\begin{aligned}
		& (i\partial_\mathrm{t} + \Delta) u = F & & \textnormal{in} \enspace \Sigma, \\
		& u(0, \centerdot) = u(T, \centerdot) = 0 &  & \textnormal{in} \enspace \mathbb{R}^n.
		\end{aligned}

	\right.
\]

For every $\nu \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ 0 \}$ with $|\nu| < c$,
consider a measurable function 
$v^\nu : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ such that

\[ \sup_{\alpha \in \mathbb{N}_0^2} \big[ 2^{-|\alpha|/2} \| e^{- \nu \cdot \mathrm{x}} v^\nu \|_{L^2(\Pi_\alpha^\nu)} \big] + \sum_{\alpha \in \mathbb{N}_0^2} 2^{|\alpha| \theta} \| e^{- \nu \cdot \mathrm{x}} (i\partial_\mathrm{t} + \Delta) v^\nu \|_{L^2(\Pi_\alpha^\nu)} < \infty, \]
for some $\theta \in (0, 1/2)$. Then,

\[\int_\Sigma (i\partial_\mathrm{t} + \Delta) u \overline{v^\nu} = \int_\Sigma u \overline{(i\partial_\mathrm{t} + \Delta)v^\nu} \, \]
for all $\nu \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ 0 \}$ with $|\nu| < c$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:35:05.847715+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_743d8ab82a44d95452e5859b4d8664f0515c640850c73fc24487dec1d16c4265","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:cheeger-M of arXiv:2606.27073, 'Retention Profiles and KL Contraction Bounds in Finite Markov Chains'] Let $A\subset S$ with $\pi(A)\le 1/2$ be a set achieving the Cheeger
constant~$h_P$, and assume $h_P \le 1 - \pi(A)$ (at equality the bound
below has zero numerator; see Remark~(rmk:cheeger-balanced of the paper)).
Then there exists $x^*\in A$ with $P(x^*,A)\ge 1-h_P$, and
\[
  M
  \;\ge\;
  r(x^*)
  \;\ge\;
  \frac{(1-h_P)\log\dfrac{1-h_P}{\pi(A)}
  +h_P\log\dfrac{h_P}{1-\pi(A)}}{\log\!\bigl(1/\pi(x^*)\bigr)}.
\]
The term involving $h_P$ is interpreted by continuity as $0$ when $h_P=0$.
In particular, for small $h_P$,
$M \gtrsim \log(1/\pi(A))/\log(1/\pi_{\min})$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:29:23.339073+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_745e5681f8b0886f342dc96352830c0936cd6c44a07fdad151e955aaaba841b8","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 16 of arXiv:2512.05687, '$L^p$-Boltzmann-Gibbs principle \\ via Littlewood-Paley-Stein inequality'] (Two-blocks estimate,
cf.\ Lemma 5.6 of \cite{BFS})
Let $p\ge 4$ and let $f$ be a local $L^{p'}(\mu_{u_0})$ function on
$\mathcal{X}_N$ for some $p'>p$ depending only on $\eta_{\La_{\ell_0}}$ 
such that $\tilde f(u_0)=0$ and $\tilde f'(u_0)=0$.  Then, there exists 
a constant $C = C(u_0,\ell_0)$ such that, for $\ell \geq  \ell_0$,  and 
a function $h$ on $[0,T]\times \T_N$, we have
\begin{align}  
&E_{\mu_{u_0}}\Big[\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\Big|\int_0^t\sum_{x\in{\T_N}} h(s,x)\\

\notag
\end{align}
On the other hand, when only $\tilde f(u_0)=0$ is known, we have
\begin{align}  
&E_{\mu_{u_0}}\Big[\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\Big|\int_0^t\sum_{x\in{\T_N}} h(s,x) \\
& \hskip 20mm \times \Big\{E_{\mu_{u_0}}[f(\tau_x\eta_s^N)|\eta_s^{N,(\ell_0)}(x)]-E_{\mu_{u_0}}[f(\tau_x\eta_s^N)|\eta_s^{N,(\ell)}(x)]\Big\} ds \Big|^p\Big]

&\hskip 10mm \leq CT^{(p-2)/2} N^{-p/2} \ell^p \|f\|^p_{L^{p'}(\mu_{u_0})}
\int_0^T \frac1N \sum_{x\in{\T_N}} |h(t,x)|^p dt.

\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:30.017980+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7463beeea5e6e439db51790c99eaf33807214ea361def5c7eb7baa2ed41e5398","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 31 of arXiv:2605.05864, 'Classification and Metrization of Classes of Smooth measures'] Let $\{\mu_n, \mu\} \subset {\cal D}$ and let $\{A^n, A\}$ be the corresponding PCAFs.
Assume that $d_{\cal D}(\mu_n, \mu) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. Then the following assertions hold:

$$
{\mathbb P}_x \left( \lim_{k \to \infty} \sup_{0 \le s \le t} \left| \int_0^s 1_K(X_u) \, dA^{n_k}_u - \int_0^s 1_K(X_u) \, dA_u \right| = 0 \text{ for all } t > 0 \right) = 1, \quad \text{q.e. } x \in E.

Then, there exists a further subsequence $\{n'_k\}$ such that $A^{n'_k}$ converges to $A$ locally uniformly in $t$ on $[0,\infty)$, ${\mathbb P}_x$-a.s. for quasi every $x \in E$:
$$
{\mathbb P}_x \left( \lim_{k \to \infty} \sup_{0 \le s \le t} |A^{n'_k}_s - A_s| = 0 \text{ for all } t > 0 \right) = 1, \quad \text{q.e. } x \in E,
$$

\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item For every $\omega\in\Omega_\varepsilon^{\mathbb D_T}$, the path
$t\mapsto X_t^{(m)}(\omega)$ is piecewise constant on the intervals $\big[k2^{-m}T,(k+1)2^{-m}T\big)$ for $k=0,1,\dots,2^m-1$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.432046+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_74ecfeb3596696dc875c4e1e12763ce9b3c90cb3eca1bd9b37058b930e3572e9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma Affine invariance of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] \label[lemma]{lem:affine_invariance}
Let $X \in_R \mathbb{R}^d$ be discrete, 
let $f_Y \in \Sym(X)$, 
let $A$ be a linear bijection on $\mathbb{R}^d$
and let $b \in \mathbb{R}^d$. 
Then $f_{AY - b} \in \Sym(AX + b)$. 

Moreover, for any fixed $c>0$, $H(AY-b) \ge cH(AX + b)$ iff $H(Y) \ge cH(X)$, 
and for $d=1$ and nonzero $a \in \mathbb{R}$, $\Var(aY-b) \ge c\Var(aX+b)$ iff $\Var(Y) \ge c\Var(X)$. 

\begin{proof}
For the first claim it is sufficient to check the symmetry equations, 
and indeed
\[ 
f_{AX+b + AY-b}(z)

= f_{X+Y}(A^{-1} z)
= f_{X+Y}(-A^{-1} z)

= f_{AX+b + AY-b}(-z). 
\]

Also, $H(AY-b) = H(Y)$ and $H(AX+b) = H(X)$. 
Finally, $\Var(aY-b)= a^2\Var(Y)$ and $\Var(aX+b) = a^2\Var(X)$. 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:31:57.880757+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_751309b82d7f82ca4bfb545cf6a1028a0c7b34cf49e805d99035691add0554ba","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition d:am-decbundle of arXiv:2510.13659, 'On the energy image density conjecture of Bouleau and Hirsch'] Let $\mu$   be a finite Borel measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then the \emph{decomposability bundle} is a Borel map $T^{AM}_\mu: \mathbb{R}^n \to \Gr(\mathbb{R}^n)$ such that the following
		statements hold:
		\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
			\item Every Lipschitz function $f \in \Lip(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is differentiable at $\mu$-a.e.~$x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with respect to the
			linear subspace $T_\mu^{AM}$, that is, there exists a linear function $df_x^{AM}: T^{AM}_\mu(x) \to \mathbb{R}$, such that
			\[ f(x+h) = f(x) + df_x^{AM}(h) + o(\lvert h\rvert)
			\quad \text{for } h \in T^{AM}_\mu(x). \]
			\item The previous statement is sharp:  there exists a Lipschitz function $f \in \Lip(\mathbb{R}^n)$
			such that for $\mu$-a.e.~$x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and every $v \not\in T^{AM}_\mu(x)$ the derivative of $f$ at $x$ in the
			direction $v$ does not exist. More precisely, for $\mu$-a.e.~$x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, we have
			\[
			\liminf_{t \to 0} \frac{f(x+tv)-f(x)}{t} < \limsup_{t \to 0}  \frac{f(x+tv)-f(x)}{t}, \quad \mbox{for all $v \not\in T^{AM}_\mu(x)$}
			\]
		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:11:09.330794+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7516ce6cea9b36bf80f52b4ce1efa40b8a6b6fb0e49dd8ae0cffae71ffffa512","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma exp of arXiv:2411.06827, 'The Exponential Lie Series and a Chen--Strichartz Formula for L{\'e}vy Processes'] The basis change formula expressing the elements of $({\mathbb A}^0)^\ast$ in terms of the elements of ${\mathbb A}^\ast$ in ${\mathbb R} {\langle}{\mathbb A}{\rangle}$ is obtained as

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:24:20.642499+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_751b254d8cf2a278ae251c1c875daa02e79c01b3c058605893d973b0f40bf5dd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Consider the Bessel and free Bessel laws, depending on parameters $s\in\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$ and $t>0$, which are the following compound Poisson/free Poisson laws,

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:41:29.035941+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_751c73dbc4a9b3c6f851dc22d88b5cb0ba550e33a9bce5e0b889e2df6e8082ec","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 16 of arXiv:2608.26565, 'A Horizon-Free Extrinsic Penrose Inequality'] Let $N\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a domain. 	\]

	$\Gamma=\Sigma_1\cap\Sigma_2$ is compact and smooth. Assume that the faces

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:01:54.385839+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_752838a63bc23468a49f15c95bdbab3c0855408b06abe9e00cb0871adccb0e8e","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lm:3.7.howard.newman of arXiv:2411.02046, 'Speed of Convergence and Moderate Deviations of FPP on Random Geometric Graphs'] For any~$d \ge 2$ and~$\uppsi \in (0,1/4)$, there exists~$c_\uppsi > 0$ such that the following holds.     \[

    \]
    second,

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:33.594397+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7595edbf1483c2774bb62f969143b9e22eac7713430eb484a56a692ec7c878ee","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Abstract of arXiv:2609.02590, 'Directional Optimal Sub-Gamma Scales for Infinitely Divisible Laws'] Fixing the quadratic proxy in a sub-gamma bound at the true variance leaves a scale to optimize, and a two-sided infinitely divisible law generally requires different scales in the two directions. The signed remainder obtained in this way gives exact variational formulas for the right and left scales. We prove that a directional scale vanishes exactly when the L\\'evy measure has no jumps in that direction, establish reflection, scaling, convolution, L\\'evy-time, and opposite-jump perturbation rules, and recover the L\\'evy triplet from the remainder law. The formulas give the two Gamma scales for bilateral Gamma laws and, for centered Skellam laws, the exact transition points $p_{\\pm}=(2\\pm\\sqrt{3})/4$ between local and interior control; when positive jumps are rare, the right scale is asymptotic to $1/\\log(1/p)$. The pair therefore records jump direction and the mechanism that controls the variance-exact sub-gamma pole.","status":"unverified"}

A cross-cut is an antichain C, containing neither 0 nor 1, that meets every maximal chain from 0 to 1. Call S inside C spanning when its join is 1 and its meet is 0, and let q_k be the number of spanning k-subsets. Then mu(0, 1) = sum_{k >= 2} (-1)^k q_k (G.-C. Rota, 1964). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.822200+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_75dd65ad3c90c552febfc6fcd0b31055cb83fad18c5584be8ed7ac94fb76baa8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:rank-frequency of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix $h\geq2$ and $k\geq3$.  For every $n\in\mathcal R(h,k)$, the function
\[
 F^{(k)}_{h,n}(q)=
 \#\left\{A\in\binom{[q]}k:|hA|=n\right\}
\]
is a quasipolynomial in $q-1$ (and hence in $q$).  Its degree is exactly
\[
 \deg F^{(k)}_{h,n}=k-r_{h,k}(n).
\]
In particular, there is an explicitly computable positive rational number
$c_{h,k,n}$ such that
\begin{equation}
 F^{(k)}_{h,n}(q)
 =c_{h,k,n}q^{k-r_{h,k}(n)}
  +O_{h,k}\!\left(q^{k-r_{h,k}(n)-1}\right).
\end{equation}
The possible frequency exponents therefore belong to
$\{2,3,\ldots,k\}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:57:44.942619+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_75f3feba910cc773f54b511a7f352aa50e21cd04aa787c111a17615bda234f11","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Perron 1 of arXiv:2606.24584, '2606.24584'] Let $A \in M_n$, $n \geq 2$, be irreducible with nonnegative entries. Then the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item There exists a  number $\mu > 0$, called the Perron--Frobenius eigenvalue of $A$, such that $\mu$ is a simple eigenvalue of $A$ and any other eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $A$ verifies $|\lambda| \leq \mu$. Thus $\rho(A)=\mu$.

\item The Perron–Frobenius eigenvalue of $A$ fulfils the row-sum inequalities
\begin{equation}
\min_{1\leq i \leq n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{ij} \leq \mu \leq  \max_{1\leq i \leq n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{ij}.
\end{equation}

\item The matrix $A$ is similar to $e^{2\pi i /h} A$ and the spectrum of $A$ is invariant under multiplication by $e^{2\pi i /h}$.

\item If $h>1$, there exists a permutation matrix $P$ such that
\begin{equation}
            P^{\intercal}AP =
            \begin{bmatrix}
        0&\!\!\!\smash{A_{{1,2}}}&\!\!\!0&\!\!\!\cdots&\!\!0 \\
        0&\!\!\!0&\!\!\!\smash{A_{{2,3}}}&\!\!\!\cdots&\!\!0 \\[-4pt]
        \vdots&\!\!\!\vdots&\!\!\!\vdots&\!\!\!\ddots&\!\!\vdots \\
        0&\!\!\!0&\!\!\!0&\!\!\!\cdots&\!\!\smash{A_{{h-1,h}}} \\
        \smash{A_{{h,1}}}&\!\!\!0&\!\!\!0&\!\!\!\cdots&\!\!0
\end{bmatrix},
\end{equation}
where the non-zero blocks are square matrices.

\item If $h=1$, then the limit $$\lim_{m \to \infty} \frac{A^m}{\mu^m}$$ exists. This limit is called the \emph{Perron projection} of $A$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:27:14.895558+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7630bcd8578b012b53c6ad45fac8a6b934b685cfad5321eaf6b48e5767bb2dbd","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 2 (Positive local maxima use one cluster) of arXiv:2608.24007, '2608.24007'] Consider the constrained maximization problem
\[
    \max_{b_1,\ldots,b_K,\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_K}
    F(b_1,\ldots,b_K,\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_K),
\]
where
\[
    F(b_1,\ldots,b_K,\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_K)
    :=
    -\frac{\zeta}{K\sqrt6}
    \sum_{c=1}^K
    b_c\varphi(b_c)\rho_c^3,
\]
subject to
\[
    \sum_{c=1}^K\frac{b_c^2}{R^2}
    +
    \sum_{c=1}^K\rho_c^2
    =
    1.
\]

Every constrained local maximum of $F$ with positive objective value has
exactly one nonzero predictive coordinate $\rho_c$. Moreover, if
$\rho_c=0$, then the corresponding routing coordinate $b_c$ also vanishes.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-10T02:20:17.000000+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_763385ef9e7316333ac3a58b77085518aa2854967b6182c2dc3d9f10ebd9af37","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In multivariable calculus, the implicit function theorem is a theorem that provides sufficient conditions under which a planar curve specified by an equation F(x, y) = 0 can also be specified as the graph of a function y = g(x), so that for each point (x, y) on part of the curve, one has y = g(x). An example is the unit circle, whose points satisfy x^2 + y^2 = 1, which can locally be solved by y = sqrt(1 - x^2), expressing the top semicircle as a graph. It is not always possible to solve the equation for y algebraically, and the implicit function theorem gives analytic conditions under which there exists a function g whose graph belongs to the given curve, and, in some formulations, also gives a way of constructing approximations to g.","status":"verified_replacement"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:48:25.219408+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7663636cd1e0dfa30578941f7c7e6f97c365af33ac796736a45470b15303a539","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:spectral-structure of arXiv:2607.05693, 'Free multiplicative convolution and Erlang moments in monitored quantum transport'] The limiting law $\mu_\tau$ has an atom at $1$ of mass
\[
  \mu_\tau(\{1\})=(1-\tau)_+.
\]
Consequently, the mass away from the atom at $1$ is $\min\{1,\tau\}$. Moreover,
the Stieltjes-transform equation has a real branch point at
\[
  x_*(\tau)=\tau \mathrm{e}^{1-\tau}.
\]
At $\tau=1$ this branch point reaches $1$, precisely where the atom at $1$
disappears.

\begin{remark}
Beenakker [Beenakker2501] computes the $\tau=1$ moments for the
\emph{orthogonal} version of the model, in which
$Q_N=\prod_{n=1}^N\bigl(I-u^{(n)}(u^{(n)})^\top\bigr)$ is a product of $N$
real rank-$(N-1)$ projectors, and obtains
\[
  \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\Tr(Q_NQ_N^\top)^p\bigr]
  =\frac{(p/\mathrm{e})^p}{p!}.
\]
This agrees exactly with the law identified here: setting $\tau=1$ in
(equation eq:moment-formula of the paper) and using $G_p(1)=p^{p-1}$ (a short induction,
or Cayley's formula for the number of labelled rooted trees on $p$
vertices) gives
\[
  m_p(1)=\mathrm{e}^{-p}\frac{p^{p-1}}{(p-1)!}
  =\mathrm{e}^{-p}\frac{p^p}{p!}
  =\frac{(p/\mathrm{e})^p}{p!}.
\]
Our rigorous results are stated for the complex (unitary) ensemble, whereas
Beenakker's computation is for the real (orthogonal) one; the two limiting
moment sequences coincide because the leading-order free limit does not
depend on the symmetry class, the difference appearing only in the $1/N$
corrections. Beenakker further notes, following a question of Bulatov, that
at $\tau=1$ the squared singular values are \emph{approximately} distributed
as $\mathrm{e}^{-\pi X^2}$ with $X$ standard normal, and asks for a direct
explanation. The measure $\mu_1$ identified here is the exact limiting law:
the approximate Gaussian form is its Stirling approximation, with the factor
$\pi$ originating from Stirling's constant in
$(p-1)!\sim\sqrt{2\pi p}\,(p/\mathrm{e})^{p-1}$.
\end{remark} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:56:49.285532+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7664c648bde9d0f4fa2006ba0b3ef2f6099ff7fe0ef540d61d4f68dcdbd042ca","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 11 (Majority rule) of arXiv:2606.22960, '2606.22960'] Let \((T_n,(B_v)_{v\in[n]})\) be the broadcast-coloured tree of size \(n\), where

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:32:35.566999+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_76a808fec1f29b8d01c2055814d3c6693c8a4a8eddd48767148cb64574d200a0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem.conditional-renewal-tau-k of arXiv:2605.26082, 'Quantitative Einstein relation for reversible diffusions in a random environment'] Let $k\ge 1$ and $R=R(\lambda)$. Define
		\[
			\mathsf L_k\coloneqq\{y\in\mathbb{R}^d:e_1\cdot y\le e_1\cdot X^\lambda(\tau_k)-4R\}\, ,
			\qquad
			\mathsf R_+\coloneqq\{y\in\mathbb{R}^d:e_1\cdot y\ge -2R\}\, .
		\]
		Let $\mathcal G_k$ denote the $\sigma$-algebra generated by:
		\begin{enumerate}
		\item[\rm(a)] the time $\tau_k$, the diffusion path $(X^\lambda(s))_{0\le s\le\tau_k-\lambda^{-2}}$, and the endpoint $X^\lambda(\tau_k)$;
		\item[\rm(b)] the auxiliary Bernoulli variables $(Y_n)_{0\le n<\lambda^2(\tau_k-\lambda^{-2})}$;
		\item[\rm(c)] the environment $(\mathbf{a},e^{-2V})|_{\mathsf L_k}$.
	\end{enumerate}
	Let the shifted future data be
		\[
			\mathcal Y_k\coloneqq\bigl(
				(X^\lambda(\tau_k+t)-X^\lambda(\tau_k))_{t\ge0},\
				(Y_{\lambda^2\tau_k+n})_{n\ge 0},\
				T_{X^\lambda(\tau_k)}(\mathbf{a},e^{-2V})\bigr|_{\mathsf R_+}
			\bigr)\, ,
		\]
		where $T_x(\mathbf{a},e^{-2V})(z)\coloneqq(\mathbf{a},e^{-2V})(x+z)$, and let $\mathcal Y_0$ be given by the same formula with $k=0$ and $\tau_0=0$. Then for every bounded measurable function $\Phi$ of such triples and every bounded $\mathcal G_k$-measurable random variable $H$,
		\begin{equation}
			\widehat{\mathbb E}_0^\lambda[\Phi(\mathcal Y_k) H]
			=\widehat{\mathbb E}_0^\lambda[\Phi(\mathcal Y_0)\mid D=\infty]\,\widehat{\mathbb E}_0^\lambda[H]\, .
		\end{equation}
		In particular, $\mathcal Y_k$ is independent of $\mathcal G_k$ under $\widehat{\mathbb P}_0^\lambda$, and the law of $\mathcal Y_k$ equals the law of $\mathcal Y_0$ under $\widehat{\mathbb P}_0^\lambda[\,\cdot\mid D=\infty]$.
		Moreover, writing $M_i\coloneqq(\Delta A_i^\lambda,\Delta\tau_i)$ for the clock-duration block:
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item[\rm(i)] for every integer $i$ with $1\le i\le k-2$, the block $M_i$ is $\mathcal G_k$-measurable;
			\item[\rm(ii)] there is a measurable map $\Psi$, defined on the common state space of the shifted future data, such that
			\[
				(M_k,M_{k+1},\ldots)=\Psi(\mathcal Y_k)
			\]
			holds $\widehat{\mathbb P}_0^\lambda$-almost surely.
		\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["finite reversible chain","continuous time"],"created_at":"2026-10-05T21:18:10.823960+00:00","domain":"probability/markov-chains/mixing","id":"claim_76b0d870245046ffaed4fd91ce5230e9","kind":"counterexample","schema_version":1,"statement":"Aldous-Fill Open Problem 4.48(a) is answered in the negative: tau_1 <= tau_0 fails. thus $\mathsf{x}_{\mathrm{alt}}$ is the asymptotically fastest initial condition on $G^{(n)}$. In particular, for Glauber dynamics for the Ising model on $\mathbb{Z}_n$ (the case $G^{(n)}=\mathbb{Z}_n$) at any inverse temperature $\beta>0$, the alternating initial condition $\mathsf{x}_{\mathrm{alt}}$ is the asymptotically fastest initial condition. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:58:24.517485+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7705c43eb63198ec74f754b5e6e5d52f598ef4d5d482adc600311aca8bca9f5c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem t:joint.sum.max.star of arXiv:2601.12677, 'Stable and Fréchet limit theorem for subgraph functionals in the hyperbolic random geometr'] $(i)$ If $\frac{1}{2} (k-1)<\alpha< k-1$, then as $n\to\infty$, 
\begin{align}
&\left( \frac{1}{a_{k,n}} \bigg( \sum_{i=1}^{[N_n\cdot\,]}\mathcal D_{k,n}(X_i) - [N_n\cdot\,]  \mathbb{E} [\mathcal D_{k,n}(X_1)] \bigg), \ \frac{1}{a_{k,n}}\bigvee_{i=1}^{[N_n \cdot \,]} \mathcal D_{k,n}(X_i)\right)  \Rightarrow (S_{2\alpha/(k-1)}(\cdot),\, Y_{2\alpha/(k-1)}(\cdot)),   
\end{align}
in the space $D\big([0,1], {\mathbb R} \times [0,\infty)\big)$ of right-continuous functions from $[0,1]$ to ${\mathbb R}\times [0,\infty)$ with left limits. The weak limit in (equation e:weak.conv.join.sum.max.star of the paper) is defined by the hybrid characteristic–distribution function
\begin{equation}  
\mathbb{E} \big[ e^{ivS_{2\alpha/(k-1)}(t)} {\mathbf 1} \{ Y_{2\alpha/(k-1)}(t) \le z \} \big] = t\int_0^z e^{ivy} g(v,y)^t e^{-ty^{-2\alpha/(k-1)}} \mathsf{m}_{2\alpha/(k-1)} (\dif y),  \  \ v\in {\mathbb R},\,  z\ge 0,  
\end{equation}
where
$$
g(v,y) := \exp \Big\{ \int_0^\infty \big( (e^{ivx}-1){\mathbf 1} \{ x<y \} -ivx \big) \mathsf{m}_{2\alpha/(k-1)} (\dif x)\Big\}, 
$$
and $\mathsf{m}_{2\alpha/(k-1)}$ is a Radon measure on $(0,\infty]$ satisfying $\mathsf{m}_{2\alpha/(k-1)}\big((y,\infty]\big)=y^{-2\alpha/(k-1)}$ for $y>0$. \\
Marginally, $S_{2\alpha/(k-1)}$ is a zero-mean $2\alpha/(k-1)$-stable L\'evy process whose characteristic function is given by (equation e:chf.first.comp.zero.mean.stable of the paper) below. Furthermore, $Y_{2\alpha/(k-1)}$ is an extremal $2\alpha/(k-1)$-Fr\'echet process; that is, for $0\equiv t_0<t_1<\cdots <t_m<\infty$ and $z_i\ge0$, $i=1,\dots,m$, 
$$
\mathbb{P}\big( Y_{2\alpha/(k-1)}(t_i)\le z_i, \, i=1,\dots,m \big)=\exp \Big\{ -\sum_{j=1}^m (t_j-t_{j-1}) (z_j \wedge \cdots \wedge z_m)^{-2\alpha/(k-1)} \Big\}. 
$$
$(ii)$ If $\frac{1}{2}<\alpha<\frac{1}{2} (k-1)$, then as $n\to\infty$, 
$$
\left( \frac{1}{a_{k,n}}  \sum_{i=1}^{[N_n \cdot\, ]}\mathcal D_{k,n}(X_i), \ \frac{1}{a_{k,n}} \bigvee_{i=1}^{[N_n \cdot \,]} \mathcal D_{k,n}(X_i) \right)  \Rightarrow (\widetilde{S}_{2\alpha/(k-1)}(\cdot), Y_{2\alpha/(k-1)}(\cdot)), \ \ \text{in } D\big( [0,1], [0,\infty)^2\big), 
$$
where the weak limit is defined by 
\begin{equation}  
\mathbb{E} \big[ e^{iv\widetilde{S}_{2\alpha/(k-1)}(t)} {\mathbf 1} \{ Y_{2\alpha/(k-1)}(t) \le z \} \big] = t\int_0^z e^{ivy} \, \widetilde{g}(v,y)^t e^{-ty^{-2\alpha/(k-1)}} \mathsf{m}_{2\alpha/(k-1)} (\dif y),  \ \ \ v\in {\mathbb R},\,  z\ge 0,  
\end{equation}
with 
$$
\widetilde{g}(v,y) := \exp \Big\{ \int_0^y (e^{ivx}-1) \mathsf{m}_{2\alpha/(k-1)} (\dif x)\Big\}. 
$$
Marginally, $\widetilde S_{2\alpha/(k-1)}$ is a $2\alpha/(k-1)$-stable subordinator (i.e., a stable L\'evy process with increasing paths) with its characteristic function given by (equation e:chf.first.comp.zero.stable.subordinator of the paper) below. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:45:27.977670+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7716321ff6de0969ba7144f6fe87b838b1edf749750c9f7f75a0a1fe3273e5ba","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:periodic-marked-winding-bridge-limit of arXiv:2607.04264, 'Macroscopic Feynman Cycles and Poisson--Kingman Universality in Bose Condensation'] Assume \(d>2\) and let \(N_L/V_L\to\rho>\rho_{\mathrm c}\).

(equation eq:periodic-limiting-eta of the paper).  More precisely, before conditioning on the
total macroscopic mass, the limiting tilted Poisson intensity is
$ du\,e^{-s x}dx/x\,\eta_x(dm)$,

  \bigl(X_i,U_i,R_i,Y_i,\zeta_i\bigr)_{1\le i\le m}.

$ (X_i)_{i\ge1}
  \sim

\[

  Y_i\sim N(0,2\beta X_iI_d),
  \qquad

\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:01:39.503084+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_77506cfe405be253e6695e7c8cc650b308b02010717284f043886beb76d4a19b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:graph_event_E_reg of arXiv:2607.22480, 'Distinguishability threshold for random geometric graphs'] Let $K^{\mathcal{E}}$ be a large constant. Define $\mathcal{E}$ to be the collection of graphs $H$ on the vertex set $[n]$ which satisfy the following inequalities (where $A$ denotes the adjacency matrix of $H$):
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item  For $k\in \{1, 2\}$ and any distinct $s_1, \dots, s_k\in [n]$ we have
    \[\sum_{1\leq i\leq n} |A_{s_1i}-p|\cdots |A_{s_ki}-p|\leq K^{\mathcal{E}}p^k n, \quad \text{ which implies}\quad
    \sum_{1\leq i\leq n} |\lambda_{s_1i}\cdots \lambda_{s_ki}| \leq O(K^{\mathcal{E}} z_p^k p^k n).\]

    \item  For $k\in \{1, 2\}$, any interval $I\subseteq [n]$ and any distinct $s_1, \dots, s_k\in [n]$ we have
    \[\Big|\!\sum_{i\in I} (A_{s_1i}-p)\cdots (A_{s_ki}-p)\Big|\!\leq\! K^{\mathcal{E}}\sqrt{p^k n\log n}, \text{ which implies } \Big|\!\sum_{i\in I} \!\!\lambda_{s_1i}\cdots \lambda_{s_ki}\Big|\!\leq \!O(K^{\mathcal{E}}z_p^k \sqrt{p^k n\log n}).\]

    \item  We have $\|A-pJ\|_{op}\leq K^{\mathcal{E}}\sqrt{np}$. If the $n\times n$ matrix $\Lambda$ is defined by $\Lambda_{ij}=\lambda_{ij}$, this also implies $\|\Lambda\|_{op}\leq O(K^{\mathcal{E}}z_p\sqrt{np})$.

    \item  For any $s\in [n]$ we have \[\sum_{s<i<j\leq n}\big|(A_{si}-p)(A_{sj}-p)(A_{ij}-p)\big|\leq K^{\mathcal{E}}p^3 n^2, \text{which implies} \sum_{s<i<j\leq n}\big|\lambda_{si}\lambda_{sj}\lambda_{ij}\big|\leq O(K^{\mathcal{E}}n^2p^3z_p^3).\]
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

For t >= E X it equals the Fenchel-Legendre dual (convex conjugate) sup over all real lambda of (lambda * t - psi_X(lambda)), which is Cramer's rate function; for t < E X the one-sided transform is 0, while the conjugate is in general positive (for a standard normal X the conjugate is t^2/2 for every t).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:48:27.284807+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7753f7bc0a38ebe95d83f1ecec140feee315d0ea53bf893c4ce4d58952365a43","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 8 (Overlap bound) of arXiv:2604.25470, 'A mathematical analysis of hierarchical Hopfield models'] Fix $\alpha$ and let $S_\alpha,S_\beta$ be independent uniform $L$-subsets of

	\[

	\le

	\]
	Consequently,
	\[
	\mathbb P\Bigl(\max_{\beta\neq\alpha}|S_\beta\cap S_\alpha|\ge t+1\Bigr)

	\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:27:25.791643+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7754caf2c164aae1fa5a545cc57e36008f3e9a844f3df67d5cc1aa5e1a256641","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem.mathcalY of arXiv:2605.11785, 'Regularization of a mean-field SDE by an additive common noise: the conditional expectatio'] For any $\mu_0\in \mathcal P_1(\mathbb{R}^d)$, there exists a unique Borel measurable map $\mathcal Y^{\mu_0}: [0,T]\times \mathbb{R}^d\times  {\mathcal C}\to \mathbb{R}^d$ such that, for any $(t,x,\bm{x})\in [0,T]\times \mathbb{R}^d\times {\mathcal C}$, 
$$
\mathcal Y^{\mu_0}(t,x, {\bm{x}}) = x-\overline \mu_0+\int_0^t  b(\mathcal Y^{\mu_0}(s,x, {\bm{x}})+{\bm{x}}_s, {\bm{x}}_s)ds - \int_0^t\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} b(\mathcal Y^{\mu_0}(s,y, {\bm{x}})+{\bm{x}}_s, {\bm{x}}_s)\mu_0(dy)ds. 
$$
In addition, $\mathcal Y^{\mu_0}$ is nonanticipating in the sense that 
$$
\mathcal Y^{\mu_0}(t,x, {\bm{x}}) = \mathcal Y^{\mu_0}(t,x, {\bm{x}}(\cdot \wedge t))
$$
and the map $(x,\mu_0)\to \mathcal Y^{\mu_0}(t,x,\bm{x})$ is Lipschitz continuous on $\mathbb{R}^d\times \mathcal P_1(\mathbb{R}^d)$, uniformly with respect to $t\in [0,T]$ and $\bm{x} \in {\mathcal C}$. Last, if $(y^1_t,\cdots,y^N_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$ solves 
\begin{equation}
   \forall t\in[0,T],\;y^i_t=x^i_0-\frac 1N\sum_{j=1}^Nx^j_0+\int_0^t  b(y^i_s+{\bm{x}}_s, {\bm{x}}_s)ds - \int_0^t\frac 1N\sum_{j=1}^Nb(y^j_s+{\bm{x}}_s, {\bm{x}}_s)ds,\;i\in\{1,\cdots,N\},
\end{equation}
then 
$$
(y^1_t,\cdots,y^N_t)_{t\in[0,T]}=(\mathcal Y^{m^N_{\vec{x}_0}}(t,x^1_0, {\bm{x}}),\cdots,\mathcal Y^{m^N_{\vec{x}_0}}(t,x^N_0, {\bm{x}}))_{t\in[0,T]},
$$ 
where we recall the notation $m^N_{\vec{x}_0}=\frac 1N\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{x^i_0}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:11:09.317987+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7769ad35ea798402e2d9dfb68648b26bba59b5f29562b4786a3e123a8f4beb65","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:vrjp-on-G-r-pos-rec of arXiv:2411.06195, 'Restrictions of some reinforced processes to subgraphs'] Let $G=(\Lambda,E)$ be a connected undirected graph without self-loops
  and take $l,r\in{\mathbb N}_0$ with $l\le r$.
  Let $(X,T)$ be vrjp in exchangeable time scale on the subdivided graph $G_r$ with
  starting point $\rho\in\Lambda$ and random weights $W_e>0$, $e\in E_r$, with
  respect to some probability measure with corresponding expectation ${\mathbb E}$. Its restriction
  $(X^{\Lambda_l\neq},T^{\Lambda_l\neq})$ to $\Lambda_l$
  with self-loops removed is again a mixture of vrjps on $G_l$ with random
  weights denoted by $W^{(l)}=(W_e^{(l)})_{e\in E_l}$. If the family $W=(W_e)_{e\in E_r}$ is
  independent or i.i.d., then so is the family $W^{(l)}$. Given $W$, the conditional
  law of $W^{(l)}$ can be described in terms of the restriction
  $\beta_{\Lambda_r\setminus\Lambda_l}$ of a $\nu_{\Lambda_r}^W$-distributed
  random field $\beta$. 
  For any finite subgraph $\tilde G$ of $G$ and the corresponding subdivision
  $\tilde G_l=(\tilde\Lambda_l,\tilde E_l)$, the restriction of $W^{(l)}$ to
  $\tilde E_l$ equals $W^{\tilde\Lambda_l}$ given in (equation def:W-J of the paper) with $J=\tilde\Lambda_l$
  and $I=\tilde\Lambda_r\setminus\tilde\Lambda_l$, and
  fulfills the recursion equations described in 
  Lemma (le:aux-W-l-1 of the paper), below. In particular, one has 
  \begin{align}
    
    &P_\rho^{W,\Lambda_r}((X^{\Lambda_l\neq},T^{\Lambda_l\neq})\in\cdot)=\int_{{\mathbb R}^{\Lambda_r}}
      P_\rho^{W^{(l)\neq}(\beta),\Lambda_l}((X,T)\in\cdot)\,
      \nu_{\Lambda_r}^W(d\beta).
  \end{align}
  Assume that the vertex degree of $G$ is bounded by $d$. Moreover, assume
  that the weights $W_e$, $e\in E_r$, are i.i.d.\ and satisfy
  ${\mathbb E}[W_e^\alpha]\le{c_1} 2^{\alpha(r-l)}$ for some $\alpha\in (0,\tfrac14]$
  with the 
  constant ${c_1}(d,\alpha)$ from Fact (fact:sabot-tarres-recurrence of the paper). 
  Then, the process $X^{\Lambda_l\neq}$ is a mixture of positive recurrent
  reversible Markov chains. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:55:37.821677+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_777c1f8dc11f0b211f115acdab510f10051796e40714785ffd737fbc7203d710","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defi defCBDI of arXiv:2605.06488, 'Continuous-state branching processes with L\'evy-Khintchine drift-interaction: Laplace dua'] \
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item  We call $\mathrm{CBDI}$ any $[0,\infty]$-valued càdlàg Markov process $\big(X, (\mathbb{P}_x)_{x\in [0,\infty]}\big)$, solution to the following martingale problem $\mathrm{MP}\big(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{C}^2_c((0,\infty))\big)$:
\[\forall x\in (0,\infty), \ f\in \mathrm{C}^2_c((0,\infty)), \quad \left(f(X_t)-\int_0^{t}\mathcal{X}f(X_s)\mathrm{d} s,\ t\geq 0 \right) \text{ is a } \mathbb{P}_x\text{ - martingale}.\]
\item  We call minimal and denote by $X^{\mathrm{m}}$, any $\mathrm{CBDI}$ process  whose boundaries $\{0,\infty\}$ are absorbing, namely: 
\[\forall x\in [0,\infty], \ \mathbb{P}_x-\text{a.s.}\  X^{\mathrm{m}}_t=\begin{cases} 0 &\text{ if } t\geq \sigma_0^{-} \text{ and }  \sigma_0^{-}<\sigma_\infty^{+}, \\
\infty  &\text{ if } t\geq \sigma_\infty^{+} \text{ and }  \sigma_\infty^{+}<\sigma_0^{-}.
\end{cases}
\]
\item  For $\Delta\in \{0,\infty\}$, we say that a process $\big(X^{\mathrm{e}\Delta},(\mathbb{P}_x)_{x\in [0,\infty]}\big)$ is a $\mathrm{CBDI}$ extended at $\Delta$, if it is a $[0,\infty]$-valued  Markov process, which once stopped at the boundary $\Delta$, has the same law as the minimal process: namely, if one sets  $\zeta^{\Delta}:=\inf\big\{t\geq 0: X_{t-} \text{ or } X_t =\Delta\big\}$, then one has
\[\forall x\in [0,\infty]\setminus \{\Delta\}, \ \  (X^{\mathrm{e}\Delta}_{t\wedge \zeta^{\Delta}},t\geq 0)\overset{\mathrm{law}}{=}(X^{\mathrm{m}}_t,t\geq 0)\ \text{ under } \mathbb{P}_x.\]
\begin{itemize}
\item[-]The process $X^{\mathrm{e}\Delta}$ is said furthermore to be a continuous extension if its boundary $\Delta$ is continuous in the sense of Definition~(def:boundary of the paper)-(def:continuous of the paper). 
\item[-] It is a Fellerian extension of $X^{\mathrm{m}}$ if  its semigroup $(P^{\mathrm{e}\Delta}_t)_{t\geq 0}$ satisfies for any $f\in \mathsf{C}([0,\infty])$,
    $P^{\mathrm{e}\Delta}_tf(x) \underset{t\rightarrow 0+}{\rightarrow} f(x),\ x\in [0,\infty]$ 	and $P^{\mathrm{e}\Delta}_tf \in \mathsf{C}([0,\infty])$.
\end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["U ⊂ C is open","all members of the family are holomorphic (respectively meromorphic) on the same open set U"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.483658+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_778fb0bb31baea70fbabe9efe4cbc496909f379fa127979c6c8cf41293005128","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let U ⊂ C be open and F a family of holomorphic functions on U. F is normal (in the finite sense) if every sequence in F has a subsequence converging uniformly on every compact subset of U; the limit is then automatically holomorphic, and it need not belong to F. F is normal in the extended sense if every sequence in F has a subsequence which, on each connected component of U, either converges uniformly on compact subsets to a holomorphic function or tends to ∞ uniformly on compact subsets (equivalently, the reciprocals tend to 0 uniformly on compact subsets). For families of meromorphic functions, normality means that every sequence has a subsequence converging uniformly on compact subsets with respect to the chordal metric of the Riemann sphere; restricted to holomorphic families this coincides with the extended sense, because a spherical limit of zero-free reciprocals is, by Hurwitz's theorem, either holomorphic or identically ∞ on each component. Normality is a local property: F is normal on U if and only if every point of U has a neighborhood on which F is normal. Normality asserts the existence of convergent subsequences only; it does not assert convergence of the family itself, and the limit function may leave the family (for instance the limit of injective functions may be constant).","status":"unverified"}

Method: Locate the rate bottleneck in the Hermitisation argument. Result: The Hermitisation proof controls the log-potential U_n(z) = (1/n) log|det(n^{-1/2}M_n - z)| through the singular-value distribution of the shifted matrix; the error has three parts: (a) the rate in the Marchenko-Pastur-type convergence of the singular-value distribution, of order n^{-1/2}-ish under four moments and degrading to n^{-c(eps)} under 2+eps moments through the truncation at level n^{1/(2+eps)}; (b) the smallest singular value lower bound, which contributes only a log-factor to the log-potential error; (c) the conversion from log-potential convergence to weak convergence of the ESD, which costs a power through the smoothing of the Laplacian. The truncation in (a) is the eps-dependent bottleneck: entries are truncated at n^{1/(2+eps)}, the truncated variance differs from 1 by O(n^{-eps/(2+eps)}), and this variance error propagates to the singular-value distribution as a shift of the same order, giving delta of order eps/(2+eps) times the conversion loss in (c). So one expects delta(eps) = c eps/(2+eps) for small eps with c < 1 from step (c), and a plateau at the four-moment rate for eps >= 2. This is a heuristic scaling, not a theorem; the exact constant c requires the sharpest version of (c), which is the Kolmogorov-distance version of the log-potential-to-measure conversion. Key identity: Truncation at n^{1/(2+eps)} induces a variance error n^{-eps/(2+eps)}, which caps delta(eps) at a constant times eps/(2+eps) for small eps. Obstruction: Sharp conversion constant from log-potential to Kolmogorov distance.","status":"unverified"}

 b_U=E[tau_U u], b_V=E[tau_V v],
 h_U=E eta_U, h_V=E eta_V,
 L_N=N-2+2*a_U^2+2*b_U^4.

Let independent Z have iid standard Gaussian entries, X=UV^T/sqrt(N),
Y=sqrt(s)X+Z, d=NP, alpha=P/N, beta=M/N, v_s=1+beta*s.
Set g=beta/v_s, m_N=E||X-E[X|Y]||^2/d and
B_N=log(v_s)/2-I(X;Y)/d, with natural logs.

## Explicit constants and result

Put A=beta^2*(N-1)*(P-1)/N^2 and

 E3=6*(N-1)*(P-1)*M*(t_U^2*t_V-1)/N^4,
 Ec=6*(N-1)/N^4 *
       [M*T_U^4*T_V^2*(v4+2*(P-1))+M*(M-1)*a_V^2],
 Eeta=2/N^3 * [M*P*e_U*T_V^2+M*(M-1)*h_U^2*b_V^2],
 Ezeta=2*N*M*z_V/N^3,
 E4=24*(N-1)*(P-1)/N^5 *
       [M*T_U^4*T_V^2*e_V*N+2*M*(M-1)*b_U^2*h_V^2],
 W=120*(N-1)*(P-1)*(P-2)/N^6 *
       [M*T_U^4*T_V^6*N*(N-1+u4)+M*(M-1)*L_N],
 F2=2*(Eeta+Ezeta), F3=2*(E3+Ec), F4=E4.            (2)

All constants are nonnegative. For all s>0,delta>0,

 g-m_N <= (1+delta)*s^3/v_s^2*(sqrt(A)+s*sqrt(W))^2
       +3*(1+1/delta)/v_s^2*(s^2*F2+s^3*F3+s^4*F4). (3)

For the exact R_N in038(10), define

 a=(N+u4-3)/N, b=(P+v4-3)/N,
 Q(s)=v_s^3+beta*(a+b)*v_s*s^2+beta*a*b*s^3,
 D(s)=v_s^2*Q(s), delta_N=1/floor(sqrt(N)),
 eps_N=delta_N*A+3*(1+1/delta_N)*(F2+F3+F4),
 K_N=A*(Q(1)-1)+(1+delta_N)*(A+2*W).

For 0<=s<=1 the requested estimate and its integral are

 0<=R_N(s)<=eps_N*s^2+K_N*s^4,                      (4)
 half integral_0^s R_N(t)dt<=eps_N*s^3/6+K_N*s^5/10. (5)

In particular the full finite-N two-sided information bound is

 -A*(D(1)-1)*s^5/10
 <= B_N(s)-A*s^4/8
 <= eps_N*s^3/6+K_N*s^5/10.                         (6)

For fixed priors with positive aspect ratios bounded above,
F2,F3,F4=O(1/N), W,A,Q(1) are uniformly bounded,
eps_N=O(N^(-1/2)), and K_N is uniformly bounded.
If alpha_N->alpha>0,beta_N->beta>0, every limiting information
envelope therefore satisfies

 B(s)=alpha*beta^2*s^4/8+O(s^5), 0<=s<=1,            (7)

with the explicit remainder constants in (6). Existence or uniqueness
of the information limit is not required. The finite-N error in (6)
is additive O(N^(-1/2)*s^3), not a pure uniform Taylor remainder
after dividing by s^4 arbitrarily close to zero.

Equivalently the normalized mutual information has the explicit
finite-N polynomial

 P4_N(s)=beta*s/2-beta^2*s^2/4+beta^3*s^3/6
                              -(beta^4+A)*s^4/8,

and

 -eps_N*s^3/6-K_N*s^5/10
 <= I(X;Y)/d-P4_N(s)
 <= [beta^5+A*(D(1)-1)]*s^5/10.                     (6a)

The elementary identity log(1+x)=x-x^2/2+x^3/3-x^4/4
+integral_0^x t^4/(1+t)dt, valid for all x>=0, pays the log remainder.
Thus the limiting quartic term in I/(NP) is
-(beta^4+alpha*beta^2)*s^4/8, and no prior fourth cumulant enters
at that order within this class. The channel parameter is s=1/Delta;
I(UV^T;Y)=I(X;Y) because deterministic nonzero rescaling of the
input is invertible.

## Non-Gaussian example and whole-family scope

Both priors may independently be uniform on [-sqrt(3),sqrt(3)].
For either law take tau(x)=(3-x^2)/2, eta(x)=x-x^3/3;
for the V law take zeta(x)=-eta(x)/2. Their endpoint values vanish,
and their negative derivatives are x, x^2-1, and tau(x)-1,
respectively. Ordinary one-dimensional integration by parts proves
(1), without a Gaussian prior or a boundary contribution.
Exact constants are T=3/2, fourth moment9/5, t=6/5,
e=8/35, z=2/35, a=3/5, b=h=0.
Gaussian priors also satisfy (1) with tau=1,eta=x,zeta=0.
The result applies to every fixed law satisfying the stated kernel
conditions, not just these examples. Discrete Rademacher priors do
not satisfy (1) for arbitrary smooth tests and are not covered.
Specifically choose a compact smooth cutoff of (3*x-x^3)/2 which
equals that polynomial near {-1,1}. At a Rademacher input, h(u)=u
and h'(u)=0, so E[u*h(u)]=1 while E[tau(u)*h'(u)]=0 for every
finite function tau on its support. This is an obstruction to
applying the present derivative-transfer route to that law, not a
counterexample to quartic universality for discrete priors.

More concretely, each of U and V may have any standardized beta
law, with its own arbitrary fixed positive shape parameters p,q.
Let k=p+q, C=1/k, B=(q-p)*sqrt(k+1)/(k*sqrt(p*q)), and
x=(t-p/k)/sqrt(p*q/[k^2*(k+1)]) for t~Beta(p,q). Then

 tau(x)=1+C+B*x-C*x^2,
 eta(x)=tau(x)*(x+B)/(1+C),
 zeta(x)=B*tau(x)-C*eta(x).

The beta density times tau vanishes at both endpoints, including
when the density itself is unbounded there, because p,q>0.
Direct integration of its derivative proves E[x h]=E[tau h'].
Writing Q=x^2-1, the identity tau-1=B*x-C*Q and applying this
first identity to x*h(x) give
(1+C)E[Q*h]=E[tau*(x+B)*h']; this proves the eta identity.
The zeta identity follows by the same linear relation tau-1.
All kernels are bounded on the compact standardized support, so
every hypothesis of (1) is paid. This covers two asymmetric beta
priors as well as the symmetric subfamily. For an asymmetric exact
check, Beta(2,3) standardized as x=5*t-2 has
tau=(6+x-x^2)/5, eta=tau*(1+5*x)/6, zeta=tau*(1-x)/6.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:15:36.157488+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_77fdca3bb28312596952beb32b6bebf13676562a75fe0943c5ce0317951c7fab","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 1 (Methodological scope and structural innovations) of arXiv:2609.01589, 'Uniform stability of expanding simple waves for Euler--Poisson--Boltzmann: a singular comp'] \normalfont
Write $\mathrm{N1}$--$\mathrm{N6}$ for the defining features of \cref{thm:main}:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(N\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item the warm-ion Euler--Poisson system with Maxwell--Boltzmann electrons,
  $p_i'(n)\ge p_*>0$;
\item the boundaryless cylinder $\R\times\T$ and a prescribed smooth
  expanding planar simple wave connecting two distinct neutral end states;
\item fully two-dimensional $H^s$ perturbations, completely removing any 
  irrotationality or zero-vorticity hypothesis;
\item stability under relative perturbations that are strictly independent of 
  $\eps$; $\eps$-preparedness is imposed only to capture the expansion rate;
\item for every finite $M$, the construction of an even Debye composite through 
  order $\eps^{2M}$ yielding a residual of $O(\eps^{2M+2})$;
\item a uniform lifespan on every fixed $[t_0,T]$, $t_0\ge0$, based on a novel 
  compensated topology that directly controls $\norm\psi_{H^s}+\eps\norm{\nabla\psi}_{H^s}$ 
  without $\eps^{-1}$ losses over the distinct end states.
\end{enumerate}
Contextualized against the existing literature, these contributions advance the 
state of the art in the following ways:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)},leftmargin=*]
\item Cordier--Grenier \cite{cordier2000quasineutral} laid the rigorous 1D foundation 
  for the ion--Boltzmann quasineutral limit. The present work substantially advances 
  this theory by capturing fully two-dimensional rotational dynamics \textup{(N3)} 
  and simultaneously managing the distinct distinct-end-state geometry \textup{(N2)} 
  over an arbitrary finite-order hierarchy \textup{(N4)}--\textup{(N5)}.

\item Wang \cite{wang2005quasineutral} provided multidimensional uniform-lifespan theories for 
  periodic problems yielding incompressible Euler and Navier--Stokes limits. Our 
  framework successfully addresses the distinct analytical challenges of a 
  compressible flow limit connecting heterogeneous far fields.

\item Peng--Wang--Yong \cite{peng2006quasi} rigorously justified finite-order 
  expansions for periodic non-isentropic flows. We pioneer this hierarchical expansion 
  for the compressible ion--Boltzmann limit \textup{(N1)}, introducing the relative 
  compensated topology \textup{(N6)} strictly required to handle the dispersing background.

\item G\'erard-Varet--Han-Kwan--Rousset \cite{gerard2013quasineutral,gerard2014quasineutral} 
  masterfully resolved the multidimensional half-space problem, where boundary data 
  generate Debye layers. We complement this by solving the Cauchy stability problem 
  for a boundaryless wave \textup{(N2)}, where the analytical stiffness stems entirely 
  from the internal singular electric transition.

\item Slemrod--Sternberg \cite{slemrod2001quasi} provided a comprehensive 
  center-to-wall asymptotic analysis for bounded plasmas. In contrast, our focus is 
  the Cauchy stability of the class \textup{(N2)}--\textup{(N4)} on an unbounded cylinder, 
  avoiding boundary layers to isolate the wave asymptotics.
\end{enumerate}
In summary, the present paper develops a novel compensated energy topology that 
rigorously isolates the stability of the smooth expanding wave from the singular 
Debye scaling. By establishing uniform nonlinear stability over a heterogeneous 
background, this framework provides a critical analytical stepping stone toward 
the full global geometric theory of multidimensional quasineutral rarefactions. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f(t, .) is mu-integrable for every t in the open interval I","t -> f(t, omega) is differentiable on I for mu-a.e. omega","a single g in L^1(mu) dominates |d_t f(t, omega)| for ALL t in I (or on a neighbourhood of each point of I)"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751130+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_7822c113585052dd029ffd5524924ae4013b85f7e3c8560bfcb2f576ac848d43","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (Omega, F, mu) be a measure space, I a nonempty open interval of R, and f : I x Omega -> R with: (i) for every t in I the function omega -> f(t, omega) is mu-integrable; (ii) for mu-almost every omega the map t -> f(t, omega) is differentiable on I, with derivative d_t f(t, omega); (iii) there exists g in L^1(mu) with |d_t f(t, omega)| <= g(omega) for all t in I and mu-almost every omega. Then F(t) = integral f(t, omega) dmu(omega) is differentiable on I and F'(t) = integral d_t f(t, omega) dmu(omega). It suffices to have (iii) LOCALLY: for each t_0 in I a neighbourhood J of t_0 and g_{t_0} in L^1 dominating |d_t f| on J x Omega, since differentiability is local. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:31:57.881531+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78322578f68fa80283707170c6e3d2fafa0ea032a9c87780340bca030a8bfd83","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2510.13659, 'On the energy image density conjecture of Bouleau and Hirsch'] Let  $(X,\mathcal{X},\mu,\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F})$ be a Dirichlet structure. The \emph{generator} $A:D(A) \to L^2(X,\mu)$ is the linear operator with domain
		\[
		D(A):= \{ f\in \mathcal{F} \vert \mbox{there exists $C>0$ such that $\abs{\mathcal{E}(f,g)} \le C \norm{g}_{L^2(\mu)}$ for all $g \in \mathcal{F}$}\}.
		\]
		For any $f \in D(A)$, the element $A(f) \in L^2(X,\mu)$ is defined by
		\[
		\mathcal{E}(f,g)= -\langle A(f), g \rangle_{L^2(\mu)}.
		\] 
		
		We define the \emph{energy measure} as $\Gamma(f,g)= \gamma(f,g)\cdot \mu$ for all $f,g \in \mathcal{F}$, where $\gamma: \mathcal{F} \times \mathcal{F} \to L^1(X,\mu)$ is the associated carr\'e du champ.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.377679+00:00","domain":"set theory","id":"claim_783ee34fc14e104fa620373620d7e9f6dc197a014b894eb8ac44b832183c96a2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Two sets A and B are equinumerous (have the same cardinality, written |A| = |B|) when there exists a bijection from A onto B. One writes |A| <= |B| when there is an injection from A into B. Equinumerosity is an equivalence relation, and <= is reflexive and transitive; by the Schroder-Bernstein theorem it is antisymmetric up to bijection (|A| <= |B| and |B| <= |A| imply |A| = |B|), all without the axiom of choice. With the axiom of choice any two sets are comparable (trichotomy), and every set is equinumerous with a unique initial ordinal, its cardinal number. A set is finite if it is equinumerous with {1, ..., n} for some natural number n; countably infinite if equinumerous with the set N of natural numbers; countable if finite or countably infinite; uncountable otherwise. Strict inequality |A| < |B| means |A| <= |B| and there is no bijection between A and B.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:53:11.417420+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78433c102bd8a631bb579606e6250487a8bf617b3d6c47b4642c64bef3a0d076","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 of arXiv:2606.08776, 'Approximation of certain stochastic integrals with anticipating integrands'] For $X$ as given in \eqref{equation:dX_t},
a Borel function $f:I^{\oM}\to \R$ with
$\E |f(X)|^2<\infty$, and a time-net
\[ \tau = \{0 = t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_N=1\} \]
we define the {\em $L_2$-approximation number of $f$ under the filtration $\G$} by
\begin{equation} 
      \pll a_{X}(f|\tau, \G)
      := \inf \noo f(X) - \Phi_{0}(L)
            - \sum_{n=1}^N g_{t_{n-1}} (X_{t_n}-X_{t_{n-1}}) \rrm_{L_2},

where the infimum is taken over all $g_{t_{n-1}}$ which are $\mathcal{G}_{t_{n-1}}$-measurable random variables such that

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:02:06.330894+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_784ec7e2ed65fb70a81235dc60632904164a652abe4233610a860a630d9bf272","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 4 (Cameron-Martin) of arXiv:2607.06745, 'Regularization and asymptotic behaviour of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck evolution operators in infin'] \textcolor{red}{ }Let $a\in X$ and $Q\in\mathcal{L}\left(X\right)$
be a non-negative, self-adjoint trace-class operator, and set $\gamma:=\mathcal{N}\left(a,Q\right)$.
Fix $h\in ImQ^{\frac{1}{2}}$.

Then the measure $\gamma\left(\cdot-h\right)$ is equivalent to $\gamma$,
and the density of $\gamma\left(\cdot-h\right)$ with respect to $\gamma$
has the form
\[
x\to\exp\left(\widehat{h}\left(x\right)-\frac{1}{2}\left|Q^{-\frac{1}{2}}h\right|_{X}^{2}\right)\quad\forall x\in X,
\]
where $\widehat{h}$ is a suitable function in $L^{2}\left(X,\gamma\right)$
satisfying:
\begin{align*}
i)\  & \int_{X}\hat{h}\left(x\right)\gamma\left(dx\right)=0,\\
ii)\  & \left\Vert \widehat{h}\right\Vert _{L^{2}\left(X,\gamma\right)}=\left|Q^{-\frac{1}{2}}h\right|_{X},\\
iii)\  & \gamma\circ\widehat{h}^{-1}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\left|Q^{-\frac{1}{2}}h\right|_{X}^{2}\right).
\end{align*}

Further, the map $h\mapsto\widehat{h}$ is linear. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-02T00:34:53.676945+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_786baef27484c882349030da986f5b5b3cf4e7af9fec029e5de101c7da79e5b0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, Itô's lemma or Itô's formula is an identity used in Itô calculus to find the differential of a time-dependent function of a stochastic process. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:43:55.659303+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78777a494d1ebb937c61f3d2519ec1a462cfff8698b75503205e420678fb79a0","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem LAN of arXiv:2604.07183, 'Stopping on the last success with unknown odds: asymptotic minimax optimality of the plug-'] Fix~$h>0$ and an integer~$k\ge2$, let
$$
p_n^\pm:=\frac1k\pm\frac{h\sigma_k}{\sqrt n},
\quad
\textrm{with }

\sigma_k:=
\sqrt{\frac1k\Big(1-\frac1k\Big)}
,

write~$N:=n-k$, and let~$\mathbb P^\pm_N$ denote the law of~$(X_1,\ldots,X_N)$ under~$\mathbb P_{p_n^\pm}$, with likelihood ratio~$L_N:=d\mathbb P^+_N/d\mathbb P^-_N$. Then, (i) one has

as~$n$ diverges to infinity (recall that~$\mathrm{TV}$ denotes the total variation distance).","status":"unverified"}

The model consists of discrete variables that represent magnetic dipole moments of atomic \"spins\" that can be in one of two states. The spins are arranged in a graph, usually a lattice, allowing each spin to interact with its neighbors. Neighboring spins that agree have a lower energy than those that disagree; the system tends to the lowest energy but heat disturbs this tendency, thus creating the possibility of different structural phases. The two-dimensional square-lattice Ising model is one of the simplest statistical models to show a phase transition. Though it is a highly simplified model of a magnetic material, the Ising model can still provide qualitative and sometimes quantitative results applicable to real physical systems, and in general, it can be seen as a specialization of Stanley's n-vector model for n = 1.","status":"unverified"}

Consider collections, for $i=1,\dots,m$, $\mathcal{C}_{X_i}$ of $\mu_{X_i}$-measurable subsets of $X_i$. Let $a,b\in \R\cup\{\pm\infty\}$ be such that for all non-empty $A_i\in \mathcal{C}_{X_i}$, $\sup_{\substack{x_i\in A_i \\ 1\leq i \leq m}} -c(x_1,\dots,x_m) \in [a,b]$ and consider a continuous, non-decreasing function $F \colon (a,b]\to [0,\infty)$ satisfying $F(a^+)=0$.

Then, the following are equivalent:\begin{enumerate}
    \item For every non-empty $A_1\in \mathcal{C}_{X_1},\dots,A_m\in\mathcal{C}_{X_m}$, one has
    \[
\prod_{i=1}^m\mu_{X_i}(A_i)^{\lambda_i} \leq F\left(\sup_{\substack{x_i\in A_i \\ 1\leq i \leq m}} -c(x_1,\dots,x_m) \right).
\]
\item For every $(m+1)$-tuple of measurable functions $f_1 \in \mathcal{F}(\mathcal{C}_{X_1}),\dots, f_m\in \mathcal{F}\left(\mathcal{C}_{X_m}\right)$ and $\Omega \colon (a,b]  \to [0,\infty)$, where $\Omega$ is non-increasing, that satisfy
\begin{align*}
\prod_{i=1}^mf_i(x_i)^{\lambda_i} &\leq \Omega(-c(x_1,\dots,x_m)) \text{ for all } 
\\
&(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in X_1\times\cdots\times  X_m, \text{ with } -c(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in (a,b],
\end{align*}
one has
\[
\prod_{i=1}^m\left(\int_{X_i} f_i(x) d\mu_{X_i}(x) \right)^{{\lambda_i}} \leq \int_{a}^b \Omega(r) dF(r).
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

	\Big|\breve{C}^N(t)
	-\bar{C}^N(t)
	\Big|
	\le \bigg(\frac{ \trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2
	\lambda^{1/2}
	\]
for all $t\in[q_*,1] \setminus J^N$.

\begin{proof}
We continue to use the abbreviations introduced above. The function $\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}$ is convex on the expanded domain $\{(b,v,u) : v \ge u^2-2\bar{\lambda}\}$. Recall $\tGam^N\equiv(\tbbb,\tvvv,\tuuu)^N$
and $\TGam^N\equiv(\Tbbb,\Tvvv,\Tuuu)^N$: we have from Lemma~\ref{l:t.smooth.domain} that
(with high probability)
 $\TGam^N(t,y)$ lies in the expanded domain for all $(t,y)\in[q_*,1]\times \R$, while
$\tGam^N(t,y)$ lies in the expanded domain for all $(t,y)\in ([q_*,1]\setminus J^N)\times \R$. Lemma~\ref{l:t.smooth.domain} implies, for $(t,y)\in ([q_*,1]\setminus J^N)\times \R$,
	\[
	\bigg|
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}
	\Big( \tGam^N(t,y)\Big)
	-\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}
	\Big( \TGam^N(t,y)\Big)
	\bigg|
	\le
	\bigg(\frac{ \trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2
	\lambda^{1/2}\,.
	\]
Integrating with respect to $\overline{\varrho_{\vY,N,t}*\sphi(y)}\,dy$ proves the second conclusion. For all $(t,y)\in[q_*,1]\times\R$, we can bound
	\begin{align*}
	& \Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}
	\Big(\TGam^N(t,y)\Big)
	=
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}\bigg( \tE \Big[\sGam(t-\sss,y)\Big]\bigg) \\
	&\qquad\le \tE\bigg[
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}\Big( \sGam(t-\sss,y)\Big)\bigg]
	= \int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}( \sGam(s,y) )\,ds\,.
	\end{align*}
Integrating with respect to $\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)\,dy$ gives
	\begin{align*}
	&\breve{C}^N(t)
	=
	\int_{\R} \Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}\Big(\TGam^N(t,y)\Big)
	\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)\,dy
	\le
	\int_{\R}
	\bigg[
	 \int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}( \sGam(s,y) )\,ds\bigg]
	\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)\,dy \\
	&\qquad=
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\bigg[\int_{\R}
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}( \sGam(s,y) )
	\overline{\varrho_s*\sphi(y)} \,dy\bigg]\,ds
	+O\bigg[ \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N
	\tep^{1/2}\bigg]\\
	&\qquad=
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\tilde{C}^N(s)\,ds
	+O\bigg[ \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N
	\tep^{1/2}\bigg]
	\,,
	\end{align*}
where the error estimate uses the bounds on $\sGam=(\sbbb,\svvv,\suuu)$ proved in Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.reg}, along with the regularity of the map $t\mapsto \overline{\varrho_s*\sphi}$ proved in Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.cty}. 
 Similarly, note that
	\[
	S_t(w)
	\equiv
	\bigg( \int_{\R} w(y)^{1/2} \varsigma_t*\sphi(y)\,dy\bigg)^2
	\]
is a concave function. It follows that
	\begin{align*}
	&\bar{W}^N(t)^2 
	=\bigg(\int_{\R} \twww(t,y)^{1/2} \varsigma_t*\sphi(y)\,dy\bigg)^2
	= S_t\bigg(\tE\Big[ \swww(t-\sss,\cdot)\Big]\bigg)
	\ge \tE\bigg[ S_t\Big( \swww(t-\sss,\cdot)\Big)\bigg]\\
	&\qquad= \int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\bigg( \int_{\R} \swww(s,y)^{1/2} 
		\varsigma_t*\sphi(y)\,dy\bigg)^2\,ds\\
	&\qquad=
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\bigg( \int_{\R} \swww(s,y)^{1/2} 
		\varsigma_s*\sphi(y)\,dy\bigg)^2
	\,ds
	+
	O\bigg[ \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N \tep^{1/2}\bigg]
	\\
	&\qquad=
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\tilde{W}^N(s)^2\,ds
	+
	O\bigg[ \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N \tep^{1/2}\bigg]
	\end{align*}
where the error estimate again follows from Lemmas \ref{l:sp.smooth.reg} and \ref{l:sp.smooth.cty}. The claim then follows by combining with
Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.budget}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:31:49.903450+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78b8151fd8a506bf10bc33657c81d9bd8f046318b73a8610cc25eb24ce0b1758","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma of arXiv:2608.25065, 'Detection of first homology via random geometric graphs in the thermodynamic regime'] \label[lemma]{induction}

    assume $L \ge (\Delta + 1)4Q\rho r|\log r| + 2r$,
    $r$ satisfies

    the event $A_{Q,\rho}(r)$ holds.
    To reduce clutter, 
    write $K = 4Q \rho r|\log r|$.

    Suppose we are given $\mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathcal{O}$,
    $z \in Z_1(\mathring{G}^n_M(r))$,
    and $\sigma \in C_2(M)$

            x_i \in U_i

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:49:05.487850+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78d7fcd70ba4df873666c92a5ed8a3bfe8077d4e2f6dec93806c45f83c40bee8","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem convolution-sup-bounds of arXiv:2601.19145, 'Stochastic Persistence in Infinite Dimensions'] Fix $2 \leq r < \infty$ and $\mathcal{B} \coloneqq L^r$. For all $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$, $\epsilon \in (0,1/2)$, $p > \epsilon^{-1}$, $T > 0$ the following hold:
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
        \item For $y \in L^p([0,T]; \mathcal{B}_{\alpha - 1 + \epsilon})$,
        $$[0,T] \ni t \mapsto (S*y)_t \in \mathcal{B}_\alpha$$
        is continuous and
        $$
        \sup_{t \leq T} \|(S * y)_t\|^p_\alpha \lesssim \int_0^T \|y_t\|^p_{\alpha - 1 + \epsilon} dt \,.$$
        \item For $Z \in L^p(\Omega \times [0,T];\gamma(\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{B}_{\alpha - 1/2 + \epsilon}))$,

    \end{enumerate}
    In the above, the constants in $\lesssim$'s do not depend on $x,y,Z$, and the dependence on $T$ is uniform over bounded subsets of $(0,\infty)$.","status":"unverified"}

Let G be a countable connected locally finite graph with p_c(G)>0 and sample iid Bernoulli bond percolation at p_c(G). Almost surely every infinite open component C, regarded as a fixed graph after conditioning on the sampled field, has quenched bond threshold p_c(C)=1. For rational r<1, independent r-thinning of the sampled open bonds is unconditionally iid bond percolation at p_c(G)r<p_c(G), so its probability of any infinite component is zero. Infinitude of C alone therefore supplies no robustness under thinning.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.451152+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78e7f9001e04ec0a27742070218a07fa32e55e4e094660e1750dd00ce2833cd7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem eq:abstract-pressure-bridge of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[theorem]{thm:conditional-transfer}
For all sufficiently large \(N\), suppose
\(\widehat Q_{N,L}\) and
\(\widehat P_{N,L}(\varepsilon,\eta)\) are finite for every
\(\varepsilon,\eta>0\).  Suppose also that there exist \(\Phi\in\mathbb R\) and a
function \(F\) on \((0,\infty)^2\) such that
\begin{equation}
 \widehat P_{N,L}(\varepsilon,\eta)\longrightarrow F(\varepsilon,\eta)
 \quad\text{for every fixed }\varepsilon,\eta>0,
 \qquad
 F(\varepsilon,\eta)\longrightarrow\Phi
 \quad\text{as }(\varepsilon,\eta)\to(0,0).
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{align}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\widehat Q_{N,L}
 &\le\Phi+\delta_{L,\mathrm{dr}}^{J,\mathrm{up}}(V),
 \\
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\widehat Q_{N,L}
 &\ge\Phi-\delta_{L,\mathrm{dr}}^{J,\mathrm{low}}(V).
 
\end{align}
Consequently,
\begin{align}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 &\le
 \max\{\Phi+\delta_{L,\mathrm{dr}}^{J,\mathrm{up}}(V),
            \overline\Lambda_L^J(V)\},\\
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 &\ge
 \max\{\Phi-\delta_{L,\mathrm{dr}}^{J,\mathrm{low}}(V),
            \underline\Lambda_L^J(V)\}.
 
\end{align}
If both de-regularization defects vanish, then
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N
 \log\widehat{\mathscr C}_{N,L}^J(V)=\Phi
\end{equation}
and the exact identities
\begin{align}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 &=\max\{\Phi,\overline\Lambda_L^J(V)\},
 \\
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 &=\max\{\Phi,\underline\Lambda_L^J(V)\}
 
\end{align}
hold.  In particular,
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)=\Phi
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \overline\Lambda_L^J(V)\le\Phi.
\end{equation}

A concrete sufficient condition for (equation eq:abstract-pressure-bridge of the paper)
is that, for any fixed \(L>0\), the disorder array and \(V\) satisfy the
hypotheses of (thm:bulk-universality of the paper) with \(m=2\).
Indeed, (equation eq:point-Haar-zero-cost of the paper) is automatic.  In this concrete
case,
\[
 \Phi=\Phi_p^{\rm bulk}(V)
 =\sup_{u\in\mathbb R}\{\theta_p(u)-V(u)\}.
\]
When the two de-regularization defects vanish,
(equation eq:exact-universality-iff-localized-defect of the paper) therefore gives a
criterion for the localized branch that is both necessary and sufficient. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:35:56.812556+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_791254e7e399998717c9474dc5f2a0192ed4c0f3ea1d23ff076ae18a74577e6b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition Separating_Surface_Prop of arXiv:2603.28520, 'The Supercritical Loop O(1) and Random Current Models: Uniqueness and Mixing'] Let $q\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2},$ $G=(V,E)$ be a graph and let $E_1,E_3\subseteq E$ be disjoint.     \item The induced graph $G(E_2)$ is connected.
    \item Any path $(\gamma_j)_{1\leq j\leq n}$ in $G$ with $\gamma_1\in G(E_1)$ and $\gamma_n\in G(E_3)$ must have a $1<j<n$ with $\gamma_j\in G(E_2).$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.188849+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7921c02af68dc652942368cd5bb06586646634155ca82d789995c416a9b6cf61","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 101 (coordinate sum) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any measure $\rho$ on $[0,1]\times\R^d$, let $\bar{\rho}$ be the measure on $[0,1]\times\R$ that satisfies
	\[
	\int_{t,y} f\bigg(t, \sum_{i=1}^d y^i\bigg)
	\,\rho(dt\,dy)
	= \int_{t,x} f(t,x)
	\,\bar{\rho}(dt\,dx)\,,
	\]
where $t\in[0,1]$, $y\in\R^d$, and $x\in\R$.
As above, let $\vY$ be an $\R^d$-valued semimartingale with drift $\vD$ and covariation $\vQ$. We now consider the one-dimensional projections
	\[
	Y = \sum_{i=1}^d Y^i\,,\quad
	\sum_{i=1}^d D^i\,,\quad
	\sum_{i,j=1}^d Q^{ij}\,.
	\]
Then $Y$ is a (one-dimensional) semimartingale with drift $D$ and covariation $Q$. We hereafter abbreviate $\rho\equiv\rho_{\vY}$ for the occupation measure of $\vY$ defined in Definition~\ref{d:intro.cts.occ}.
Then the occupation measure of $Y$ is $\bar{\rho}$. The occupation measures associated to the drift and covariation of $Y$ are
	\[
	\sum_{i=1}^d
	\bar{\rho}_{D^i}\,,\quad
	\sum_{i,j=1}^d
	\bar{\rho}_{Q^{ij}}\,.	
	\]
Let $\hvY$ be as defined by Lemma~\ref{l:ideal.smoothed.occ.msr},
and let $\iY$ be the one-dimensional projection, so $\iY(t)=Y(t-\sss)+\mathfrak{x}$ where $(\sss,\mathfrak{x})\sim\bar{\varphi}$ (the density $\varphi$ integrated over $x^1 + \ldots + x^d=\mathfrak{x}$). It follows that $\iY$ has occupation measure $\overline{\rho*\varphi}=\bar{\rho}*\bar{\varphi}$. Similarly, the occupation measures associated to the drift and covariation of $\iY$ have densities
	\[
	\sum_{i=1}^d
	\overline{\rho_{D^i}*\varphi}
	\,,\quad
	\sum_{i,j=1}^d
	\overline{\rho_{Q^{ij}}
		*\varphi}\,.	
	\]
Then, analogously to \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.drift} and \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.qv}, we define (with $x$ now a scalar)
	\begin{align}
	
	B(t,x) 
	&\equiv
	\sum_{i=1}^D \frac{
	\overline{\rho_{D^i}*\varphi}(t,x)
	}
		{\overline{\rho*\varphi}(t,x)}\,,\\
	A(t,x)
	&\equiv
	\sum_{i,j=1}^D \frac{
	\overline{\rho_{Q^{ij}}*\varphi}(t,x)
	}
	{\overline{\rho*\varphi}(t,x)}\,.
	
	\end{align}
Let $\iX$ be the solution to the (one-dimensional) SDE
	\[
	d\iX(t)
	= B(t,\iX)\,dt
	+A(t,\iX)^{1/2}\,dW(t)\,,
	\]
where $W$ is a one-dimensional standard Brownian motion.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:04:39.234443+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_792986087db3bc5424c0820217b456467a0df89076a5769424f84da4d611fe3c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 40 (The one-dimensional Stokes tree) of arXiv:2608.14475, '\vspace{-1.2cm}\textbf{Finite Gaussian Reconstruction of Polynomial Orbits:\\ From Correla'] Let \(F\) be a tame Morse polynomial of degree \(m\) in one variable and
fix an admissible direction.  Denote by
\[
 E_0,\ldots,E_{m-1}
\]
the \(m\) decay sectors at infinity.  There is a canonical boundary
isomorphism
\begin{equation}
 \partial:
 H_1^{\mathrm{rd}}(F;\mathbb Z)
 \xrightarrow{\ \simeq\ }
 \widetilde H_0(\{E_0,\ldots,E_{m-1}\};\mathbb Z).
 
\end{equation}
If \(\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_{m-1}\) is a distinguished integral thimble
basis, join two vertices whenever the corresponding thimble has its two
ends in those sectors.  The resulting oriented graph \(T\) is a spanning
tree.

Let \(\gamma\) be an admissible contour directed from \(E_p\) to \(E_q\).
Then
\begin{equation}
 [\gamma]
 =
 \sum_{e\in[p,q]_T}
 \epsilon_e(p,q)[\Gamma_e],
 \qquad
 \epsilon_e(p,q)\in\{-1,1\},
 
\end{equation}
where \([p,q]_T\) is the unique path from \(p\) to \(q\), and the sign is
positive precisely when the orientation of \(e\) agrees with that path.
Thus the physical Betti row is obtained by a finite path search and all

{"assumptions":["a sequence of (random) rooted graphs with controlled local neighborhoods, such as bounded degree, sufficient for tightness","existence of a limiting infinite, typically unimodular, random rooted graph as the local weak limit","the functional of interest is expressible as, or well approximated by, a sum or average of local, root-based quantities","for extensive functionals: an additional argument, such as subadditivity or concentration, to pass from the local limit to a law of large numbers for the global sum"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.994267+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_793f7dca888660c8d4669b9e22cd3be3e733262e6b2906c64e5ca49d47cf39e4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a sequence of finite, possibly random, rooted graphs G_n, local weak (Benjamini-Schramm) convergence means that for every finite radius r, the distribution of the isomorphism class of the r-ball around the (uniformly, or otherwise canonically) chosen root converges weakly to that of a limiting, typically infinite, random rooted graph (G*, o). The objective method, due to Aldous and Steele, is the broader program of analyzing this limiting infinite object directly, such as a Poisson weighted infinite tree or a unimodular Galton-Watson tree, to compute limiting constants for combinatorial optimization functionals on the finite graphs, such as the minimum spanning tree constant or the limiting value in the random assignment problem, by solving a recursive distributional (fixed-point) equation on the infinite limit rather than working with finite-n computations directly. It does not by itself establish that a given sequence converges locally weakly, which typically must be separately verified via a subsequential compactness argument together with uniqueness of subsequential limits, and it does not directly give convergence of global, extensive functionals without an additional concentration or summation argument beyond the purely local statement. Typical failure: Assuming that local weak convergence of the underlying random graph automatically implies convergence of a global extensive functional, such as the total weight of a minimum spanning tree, at the same per-vertex limiting rate; local convergence controls only typical local neighborhoods, and passing to a global average requires an additional uniform-integrability or concentration argument, often the genuinely hard part of an objective-method proof, which is easy to overlook once the local limit has been identified. Canonical reference: Benjamini and Schramm, 2001, Electronic Journal of Probability; Aldous and Steele, 2004, in Probability on Discrete Structures, Springer; Aldous and Lyons, 2007, Electronic Journal of Probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X, M) is a measurable space","mu and nu are positive measures on M (for signed or complex measures the definition is applied to their total variations)","the separating set E is required to belong to M"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.402012+00:00","domain":"measure theory, decomposition of measures","id":"claim_7949ee76619d07edbf68d03f6116561c0881f49a0a0bfc5d35c33818a908ff98","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let mu and nu be positive measures on M. One says that mu and nu are MUTUALLY SINGULAR, written mu perp nu, if there exists a set E in M with mu(E) = 0 and nu(X minus E) = 0; equivalently, X splits into two measurable pieces, one carrying all of nu and mu-null, the other carrying all of mu and nu-null. The relation is symmetric. For signed or complex measures the definition is applied to the total variations: mu perp nu means |mu| perp |nu|. Basic consequences: mu perp mu holds if and only if mu = 0; if nu is absolutely continuous with respect to mu (nu << mu) and nu perp mu, then nu = 0; if nu_1 perp mu and nu_2 perp mu then (nu_1 + nu_2) perp mu. CAUTIONS. (1) Mutual singularity is much stronger than 'nu is not absolutely continuous with respect to mu': a measure can fail to be absolutely continuous without being singular, and in general a measure splits into an absolutely continuous and a singular part (Lebesgue decomposition). (2) Singularity is a measure-theoretic, not a topological, smallness statement: the measure sum over n of 2^(-n) times the Dirac mass at the n-th rational is mutually singular with Lebesgue measure on R yet has full support, and the Cantor-Lebesgue measure is mutually singular with Lebesgue measure while being atomless. (3) The witness set E must be measurable; without that requirement the notion is vacuous or ill-posed. (4) Mutual singularity is not preserved by arbitrary uncountable sums of measures.","status":"unverified"}
