A rank-one bounded PSD kernel on [-1,1], k(x,xprime)=1{x>=0}1{xprime>=0}, with observation noise variance 1, prevents every continuous raw-input Gaussian predictor from achieving uniform forward KL below log(9/8)/4 > 1/36. An empty context, or one observation (-1,0), yields predictive variances 1 left of zero and 2 at zero. Status: proof (unaudited), T336-w727-C003 v1. Complete theorem, constants and scope:
# Raw-input obstruction for Target 1

Claim T336-w727-C003 v1. Status: proof (unaudited). This is a scope obstruction to the literal bounded-kernel raw-input statement; it does not contradict C002's supplied-feature theorem. No novelty or Lean certification is claimed.

## Statement

There is a rank-one bounded positive-semidefinite kernel on the compact raw-input domain [-1,1], observation-noise variance s=1, and bounded context labels, such that every predictor with continuous Gaussian output parameters (mu(x),v(x)), v(x)>0, has worst-case noisy predictive forward KL at least

    c0=(1/4) log(9/8)>1/36.

The conclusion applies in particular to every finite transformer whose raw-input encoding and subsequent operations are continuous and whose output is a Gaussian with positive continuous variance. It applies to normalized ReLU attention and softmax attention under these conditions. Therefore boundedness, compactness, finite rank, and positive observation noise alone cannot imply the raw-input version of Target 1 for arbitrarily small eps.

## Kernel and posterior

Define phi(x)=0 for x<0 and phi(x)=1 for x>=0. Set k(x,x')=phi(x)phi(x'). For any finite coefficients a_i,

    sum_{i,j} a_i a_j k(x_i,x_j)=(sum_i a_i phi(x_i))^2>=0.

Thus k is positive semidefinite, bounded by 1, and of rank exactly one (because k(0,0)=1). The GP can be represented as f(x)=Z phi(x), with Z~N(0,1). Observations add independent N(0,1) noise.

Use the empty context if allowed. Alternatively, for any n>=1 use one observation at x=-1 with label y=0, which satisfies every B>=0. This observation is pure noise independent of Z, so the posterior law of Z remains N(0,1). For either context, the new noisy predictive distribution is

    P_x=N(0,1) for x<0; P_x=N(0,2) for x>=0.

Hence the example does not rely on whether a context of length zero is included.

## Continuity forces two incompatible approximation requirements

Fix this context and any continuous output mu(x),v(x)>0. Let E=sup_x KL(P_x || N(mu(x),v(x))). If E is infinite the bound is immediate. Otherwise put mu0=mu(0),v0=v(0)>0. At x=0,

    D_2:=KL(N(0,2)||N(mu0,v0))<=E.

Take x_j=-1/j tending to zero from below. Since mu,v are continuous and v0>0, the explicit Gaussian KL formula is continuous along this sequence; all denominators remain positive near the limit. Therefore

    D_1:=KL(N(0,1)||N(mu0,v0))<=E.

No dominated convergence, probabilistic conditioning argument, or exchange of a supremum with a limit is used: every term in this deterministic convergent sequence is <=E.

For a>0 define

    D_a=(1/2)(log(v0/a)+(a+mu0^2)/v0-1).

Writing w=3/(2v0)>0 and combining logarithms gives the exact identity

    (D_1+D_2)/2
      = (1/4)log(9/8)+(1/2)(w-1-log w)+mu0^2/(2v0).

The inequality log w<=w-1 follows by integrating 1/t from 1 to w, separately for w>=1 and 0<w<=1, or by differentiating w-1-log w. Both additional terms are nonnegative. Consequently

    E >= (D_1+D_2)/2 >= (1/4)log(9/8).

Finally log(9/8)=integral_1^{9/8} dt/t > (1/8)(8/9)=1/9, since 1/t>8/9 except at the right endpoint. Thus c0>1/36. Every denominator and logarithm argument above is strictly positive.

## Interpretation for the dossier

C002 supplies phi as an input, so its input encoding itself is discontinuous as a function of raw x in this example; the continuity hypothesis here then fails. There is no contradiction. To close Target 1, the architecture must explicitly permit the fixed feature map in the input representation, or the theorem must add assumptions that make raw-input feature computation possible and account for its cost. Merely calling the kernel finite rank does not settle this issue.

The example is an obstruction to a named target interpretation, not a claimed solution of the entire T336 problem. The remaining feature-input theorem C002 and this obstruction both await independent review.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:49.564661+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7994b8eb14afe8df4ccbb96e64ddbced16fb44ee3fe5f57fd62aa626e183d505","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 17 (Inversion of the surrogate objectives) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] Regard both distortions as functionals of the transformed energy vector $v$ at
fixed $E=\sum_k v_k$, the shared-scale one on a \emph{uniform} grid.
\begin{itemize}
\item The \textbf{allocation-flexible} coding surrogate (\Cref{sec:classical})
$D_{\mathrm{vr}}(v)\propto(\prod_k v_k)^{1/d}$ is the geometric mean, the form the
variable-rate distortion takes while every coordinate draws positive rate
(\Cref{prop:schur}(i); once the water level of \Cref{prop:waterfill} rises above a
coordinate's energy the true distortion is floored by the un-coded coordinates' energy,
so the vanishing limit below is an idealization of the surrogate). It is strictly
Schur-\emph{concave} wherever all coordinates are positive and identically zero elsewhere; it decreases under majorization, so it is driven down by
\emph{concentration}, the direction in which the KLT moves the profile, reaching the
majorization-maximal \emph{reachable} one, the spectrum (\Cref{thm:klt}).
\item The \textbf{shared-scale AbsMax} surrogate (\Cref{sec:inv-flatness})
$D_{\mathrm{fr}}(v)=\sum_g\max_{k\in g}v_k$ obeys the max-vs-mean bound of
\Cref{prop:schur}(ii), so among all $v$ of fixed sum it is minimized at the
\emph{flat} $v$, the direction in which incoherence processing and the Hadamard move the
profile (\Cref{prop:rht}), and maximized under within-group concentration.
\end{itemize}
Over all $v$ of fixed total energy, then, the two surrogates are driven apart. The
geometric mean is strictly Schur-concave on the positive orthant, so every majorization
step toward concentration strictly lowers $D_{\mathrm{vr}}$ while every coordinate remains
positive, and it is maximized at the flat $v$;
while $E/G\le D_{\mathrm{fr}}\le E$, the lower bound attained exactly when every group
is internally uniform and the upper bound when each group's mass sits on a single
coordinate. Concentrating energy \emph{within} a group therefore strictly lowers the first whenever every coordinate remains positive, and never lowers the second, strictly raising it as soon as the group maximum rises; flattening within groups does the reverse. Along no \emph{within-group} step of the order do the two objectives move the same way.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space","T : X -> X is continuous and surjective","the definition quantifies over all nonempty OPEN subsets U"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090776+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics, mixing properties of non-invertible maps","id":"claim_79ea44cf7b3dcd7452df709c8e293198d63314337814289a89d9a84e9a0edffe","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a compact metric space and T : X -> X a continuous surjection. T is TOPOLOGICALLY EXACT, also called locally eventually onto, if for every nonempty open set U there is an integer n >= 1 with T^n(U) = X. Two consequences are what proofs actually use. (a) UNIFORMITY IN n: if T^n(U) = X then T^m(U) = X for every m >= n, because T is onto; hence for each nonempty open U there is N with T^n(U) = X for ALL n >= N. (b) DENSE BACKWARD ORBITS WITH ALL LARGE PERIODS: for every x in X and every nonempty open U there is N with U intersect T^{-n}(x) nonempty for every n >= N; in particular the full backward orbit of any point is dense. Property (b) is a genuine aperiodicity statement that topological transitivity does not give and that even topological mixing of an invertible system cannot give. Relations: topological exactness implies topological mixing, which implies topological transitivity; the converses are false. An invertible map is never topologically exact unless X is a single point, since T^n(U) = X forces U = X for a homeomorphism, so exactness is a hypothesis reserved for genuinely non-invertible maps: expanding maps of the circle or of a compact manifold, one-sided mixing subshifts of finite type, and Chebyshev-like interval maps are the standard examples.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:58:01.575452+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_79efc22e2efdf6b3517514085c1069b95d1e98df1cf7e1f83fb4c240025e816a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2608.27372, 'Universality and sharp thresholds for ellipsoid fitting'] Let $(x_i)_{1\leq i\leq n}\in \R^d$ be i.i.d. random vectors such that $x_1=(x_{1j})_{1\leq j\leq d}$ has indpenedent coordinates satisfying
	\begin{equation}
		\E[x_{1j}]=0,\qquad \E \left[x_{1j}^2\right]=1,\qquad
		\E \left[x_{1j}^4\right]=\kappa,\qquad \sup_{j\le d}\|x_{1j}\|_{\psitwo}\le K_x,
	\end{equation}
    where $\kappa>1$ and $K_x>0$ do not depend on $n,d$. Let
	$n,d\to\infty$ with $n/d^2\to\alpha\in(0,\infty)$.  There is an explicit
	threshold $\alpha_\star(\kappa)$, defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:alpha-star-def},
	which depends only on $\kappa$, such that the following holds.
	\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
		\item If $\alpha<\alpha_\star(\kappa)$, then with probability tending to one, there exists an ellipsoid fitting all $(x_i)_{1\leq i\leq n}$:
		\[
		\exists R\succ 0,\quad\textnormal{such that}\quad x_i^{\top}R x_i=1\quad \textnormal{for all}\quad 1\leq i\leq n.
		\]
		Moreover, such $R\in \R^{d\times d}$ can be chosen to be well-conditioned: $\lambda_{\max}(R)/\lambda_{\min}(R)=O(1)$. 
		\item If $\alpha>\alpha_\star(\kappa)$, then with probability tending to one
		there is no $R\succeq0$ such that $x_i^\top R x_i=1$ for all $1\leq i\leq n$. Moreover, the optimal squared fitting error converges in probability:
		\begin{equation}
			\Gamma_X:=\inf_{R\succeq0, \operatorname{Tr}R=d}\,\inf_{r\geq 0}\,
			\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{x_i^\top Rx_i}{\sqrt{d}}-r\right)^2
			\pto e_\star(\alpha,\kappa),
		\end{equation}
        where $e_\star(\alpha,\kappa)$ is defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:optimal-fitting-error-main}. For $\alpha>\alpha_\star(\kappa)$, $e_\star(\alpha,\kappa)>0$ holds, thus an approximate ellipsoid fitting is not possible with any $R\succeq 0$ with $\Tr R=d$.
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

(b) [minimal-time / control representation] d(x) = inf { T ≥ 0 : there is an absolutely continuous ξ: [0,T] → ℝⁿ with |ξ'(s)| ≤ 1 for a.e. s, ξ(0) = x, ξ(T) ∈ K } = inf { ∫_0^T |ξ'(s)| ds : ξ absolutely continuous, ξ(0) = x, ξ(T) ∈ K, T ≥ 0 } — the distance is the value function of the minimal-time problem for the control system ξ' = α, |α| ≤ 1, with target K, and the straight segment from x to a nearest point of K is an optimal trajectory. (c) [variational characterization] d is the largest 1-Lipschitz function that is ≤ 0 on K: if u: ℝⁿ → ℝ is 1-Lipschitz and u ≤ 0 on K then u ≤ d everywhere, and d itself is admissible; equivalently d(x) = max { u(x) : u 1-Lipschitz, u ≤ 0 on K }. (2) Uniqueness of viscosity solutions of |Du| = 1 in ℝⁿ \\ K vanishing on K FAILS without a sign or growth restriction: for K = {0}, the function u(x) = −|x| is a classical (hence viscosity) solution of |Du| − 1 = 0 in ℝⁿ \\ {0} with u(0) = 0, different from d(x) = |x|. The distance is singled out among solutions by (c), or by nonnegativity/boundedness-below conditions that this lemma does not assert. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:17:04.322958+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a112d984414996beb1871b3c4a78c359f37fdfc7dd3eb7542762ba4b443e657","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2606.01683, 'Singular-value gap of nonreversible Markov processes'] For a Banach couple $(E_0, E_1)$, denote by $\mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1)$ the class 
    of functions $F: \Bar{S} \to E_0 + E_1$ satisfying
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $F$ is continuous on $\Bar{S}$ and analytic on $S$
        \item $F(it) \in E_0$ and $F(1+it) \in E_1$ for all $t \in \mathds{R}$
        \item $\|F\|_{\mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1)} \coloneqq 
        \max \Big\{ \sup_{t \in \mathds{R}} \|F(it)\|_{E_0}, \sup_{t \in \mathds{R}} \|F(1+it)\|_{E_1}           \Big\} < \infty$ 
    \end{itemize}
    Then, for $0 \leq \theta \leq 1 $, the \textbf{complex interpolation space} $[E_0, E_1]_\theta$ is the 
    Banach space defined by
    \[
        [E_0, E_1]_\theta \coloneqq \{h \in E_0 + E_1: h = F(\theta) \ \ \text{for some} \ F \in \mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1)\}
    \]
    equipped with the norm
    \[
        \|h\|_{[E_0, E_1]_\theta} \coloneqq \inf_{\substack{F \in \mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1) \\
        F(\theta) = h}} \|F\|_{\mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1)}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:47.659910+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a37ce8165404fc566d24822af83b22605397f94fcfe11efc17e4145e45ac5d6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 20 of arXiv:2605.08844, 'Signature Kernel and Schwinger-Dyson Kernel Equations as Two-Parameter Rough Differential '] For every \(n\in [1:\kappa+\zeta]\), let \(\ell=\lceil n/2\rceil\). Then the homogeneous components of the Schwinger--Dyson kernel satisfy
\begin{equation}
K_0(s,t)=1 +  \int_s^t  K_{1}(s,u) d\mathbf{X}_u du,
\qquad
K_n(s,t)
=
-\int_s^t \sigma_n\bigl(K_{\ell-1}(s, \cdot),K_{n-\ell}(\cdot, t)\bigr)_u\,d\mathbf X_u .
\end{equation}
Here, for every word \(I=i_1\cdots i_n\) over the alphabet \(\{1,\dots,d\}\), we set
\(
\tilde I:=i_1\cdots i_{\ell-1},\,
\hat I:=i_{\ell+1}\cdots i_n,
\)
and,given a basis \(e_1,\dots,e_d\) of \(V\), define
\begin{align*}
&\sigma_n:
\mathrm{Hom}\bigl(V^{\otimes(\ell-1)},\mathbb R\bigr)\boxtimes
\mathrm{Hom}\bigl(V^{\otimes(n-\ell)},\mathbb R\bigr)
\to
\mathrm{Hom}\bigl(V,\mathrm{Hom}(V^{\otimes n},\mathbb R)\bigr),\\
&\sigma_n(\eta,\xi)[e_j](e_I)
=
\sigma_n(\eta,\xi)[e_j](e_{\tilde I}\otimes e_{i_\ell}\otimes e_{\hat I})
=
\eta(e_{\tilde I})\,\delta_{i_\ell j}\,\xi(e_{\hat I}),
\end{align*}
for every word \(I\) of length \(n\), and extend linearly on \(V^{\otimes n}\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.153335+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a4b687052c31d21a374350800babbe1e0bb54804bb21e625501c86003d4f73f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 of arXiv:2608.29406, 'Partially Totally Real Submanifolds of Sasakian Manifolds'] A submanifold $M$ of a Sasakian manifold, tangent to $\xi$, is called a \emph{partially totally real (PTR) submanifold} if there exists a nonzero constant-rank totally real distribution $\Dperp\subset TM\cap\ker\eta$, i.e.
\[
 \phi\Dperp\subset\Tperp.
\]
If $\Dtilde$ denotes the orthogonal complement of $\Dperp\oplus\langle\xi\rangle$ in $TM$, then
\begin{equation}
 TM=\Dperp\oplus\Dtilde\oplus\langle\xi\rangle.
\end{equation}
Following the K\"ahler PTR terminology, $\Dtilde$ is called the
\emph{ambiguous distribution}.  The PTR structure refers to this chosen
decomposition; maximality of \(\Dperp\), when needed, is imposed later
and is not part of the definition.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:31:49.841548+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a81ac31623a50a3f25ba9b1939e08c7b94160d7d3707fd83871d36816e029b1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Satz 6 of arXiv:2506.13661, 'Box-Covariances of Hyperuniform Point Processes'] Let $\eta$ be a stationary hyperuniform point process on $\mathbb{R}^2$ with truncated pair correlation measure $\beta.$ Suppose that $\beta$ is box-symmetric (with respect to reflection and swapping of the axes), that ${|\beta|(\mathbb{R}^2)<\infty}$, and that $F(x):=\beta(\Lambda_\infty(x))$ is non-positive (or, non-negative) for $\|x\|$ sufficiently large. 
	Assume further that both $H_\pm(y_1,y_2):= \int_0^{y_1}\int_0^{y_2}F(\pm x_1,x_2)\mathrm{d}x_1\mathrm{d}x_2$ are multivariate $(a_\pm,g_\pm)$-regularly varying, each with $a_\pm\in[0,1]$ and such that $g_-(x,y)=g_-(y,x)$. Moreover assume $K_+:=\lim_{n\to\infty}H_+(n,n)/H_-(n,n)$ exists and set $K_-=-1$.
	Then, $\mathrm{cov}(z)$ exists and can be expressed similar to \eqref{eq:Cov_non_int}. 
	
	
	More precisely, denoting $|z|:=(|z_1|,|z_2|)$ and $\tau(z)=\min(\mathrm{sign}(z_1),\mathrm{sign}(z_2))$ (i.e. $\tau(z)=-$ if and only if at least one of $z_1,z_2$ has negative sign), then for $z\in\Lambda_\infty(0)$, we have
	\begin{align*}
		\mathrm{cov}(z)= &  -K_+\|z\|^ag_+\left(\frac{z}{\|z\|}\right)+\sum_{\substack{e\in\mathbb{Z}^2\\ \|e\|=1}}\frac{K_{\tau(z+e)}}{2} \|z+e\|^ag_{\tau(z+e)}\left(\frac{|z+e|}{\|z+e\|}\right)\\
		&-\sum_{v\in\{-1,1\}^2}\frac{K_{\tau(z+v)}}{4}\|z+v\|^ag_{\tau(z+v)}\left(\frac{|z+v|}{\|z+v\|}\right)+ \ind_{\Lambda_1}(z)\frac{1}{2}\|z-\mathbf 1\|^ag_{\tau(z+v)}\left(\frac{|z-\mathbf 1|}{\|z-\mathbf 1\|}\right).
	\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:34:33.538462+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a97ad96f4b81f30399ab986caeac2453c3307cc069e9dec1196571c81a009e1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 5 of arXiv:2603.28702, 'Distribution of the magnetization of the critical Ising model on sparse random graphs'] \begin{itemize}
\item 
Let $G$ be a graph with vertex set $V$. The Ising model on this graph with inverse temperature $\beta$ is the probability measure $\mu$ on $\{-1,1\}^V$ satisfying
$$\mu_{\beta}(\sigma)=\dfrac{1}{Z_{\beta,G}}\exp\left(\beta\SL{u\sim v}\sigma_u\sigma_v\right).$$
\item
Fix a measure $\nu$ on $\{-1,1\}^V$. For a configuration $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^V$ and for some $v\in V$, let $\sigma^{\oplus v}$ be the configuration $\sigma$ in which the spin at vertex $v$ is flipped. For two configurations $\sigma,\tau\in\{-1,1\}^V$, we write $\sigma\sim\tau$ if $\tau=\sigma^{\oplus v}$ for some $v\in V$. The continuous time Glauber Dynamics on $G$ for $\nu$ at rate 1 is a Markov chain with transition rates, for $\sigma\neq\tau$, equal to
$$q(\sigma,\tau)=\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\nu(\tau)}{\nu(\sigma)+\nu(\tau)},\ \ \text{if}\ \ \sigma \sim \tau
\\ \\
0,\ \ \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}$$
Informally, every vertex gets updated at rate one, and the update happens conditionally on the configuration in the rest of the vertices.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:26.252202+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7aa3c8b1005683c1ef4fd5fc4e7f3fa59cc78590af426c95614b31f7da091b9f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theo 3 of arXiv:2605.23292, 'Second-order Poincaré inequalities and localization on the Poisson space'] (rates of normal convergence for sums of $BL$-space-time localizing scores on metric spaces) 
Let $\xi:(X \times \R \times \MM) \times \mathbf{N}_{X \times \R \times \MM} \rightarrow \R$ be a score function on the marked space domain $X \times \R \times \MM$ and $\P$ a Poisson process on $X \times \R$ with intensity $\nu \otimes \mu $ and $\hat{\P}$ its marked version. Define
\[
H:=H(\hat{\P}) = \sum_{(z,t_z) \in \P \cap (W \times \R)} \xi((z,t_z, M_z),\hat{\P}).
\]
Assume that $\xi$ satisfies  $BL\big(\tfrac{1}{240}, \tfrac{1}{120}\big)$ space-time localization according to Def.~\ref{def:space-time-loc}, with $M^\xi_{5,X}<\infty$.
For $\psi$ as in Def.~\ref{def:space-time-loc} and $q>0$, put 
\[
G_{q}:=\int_{X} \psi(d(x,W))^{q} \nu(dx) = 2^q \nu(W) + \int_{X\setminus W} \psi(d(x,W))^{q} \nu(dx).
\]
If $G_{1/120}<\infty$, then there is a 
$C_K<\infty$ given by
\[
C_K:= c\cdot  {\cal I}_{\psi,X}\big(\tfrac{1}{240}\big)^{3} \cdot {\cal I}_{\phi}\big(\tfrac{1}{120}\big)^{7/2},
\]
where $c<\infty$ is a universal scalar, such that
\begin{equation} 
    \mathbf{d}_K \left(  \frac{H - \E H} {\sqrt{\Var H}}, N \right) \leq C_K \cdot (M_{5,X}^\xi)^{2/5} \cdot \frac{G_{1/120}^{1/2}}{\Var H}
\end{equation}
and there is a $C_W <\infty$ given by
\[
C_W := c \cdot  {\cal I}_{\psi,X}(\tfrac{1}{50})^{3} \cdot {\cal I}_{\phi}(\tfrac{3}{200})^{4}
\]
such that
\begin{equation} 
    \mathbf{d}_W \left(  \frac{H - \E H} {\sqrt{\Var H}}, N \right) \leq C_K \cdot (M_{5,X}^\xi)^{2/5} \cdot \frac{G_{1/120}^{1/2}}{\Var H} + C_W  \cdot (M_{5,X}^\xi)^{3/5} \cdot\frac{G_{3/200}}{(\Var H)^{3/2}}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:02:17.985904+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7abd5943eeca0508bf674af20b2bef2fa66b54442080048fa79fc8c4ef9c274c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:standard-twostream of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix $\lambda \in (0,1)$
and a \emph{send sequence}  
$\overline{p}$ with $p_0=1$.
Let $Z=(Z^A,Z^B)$ be the two-stream process with birth rate~$\lambda$, send sequence~$\overline{p}$ and start time~$0$  
where for all $D\in \{A,B\}$ and all
positive integers~$k$,
$\mathbf{arr}_k^{Z^D}(\tau) = \emptyset$. 
Let $X$ be the backoff process with birth distribution~$\mathsf{Po}(\lambda)$, send sequence~$\overline{p}$, and cohort set $\mathcal{C}=\{A,B\}$ (Definition~(def:backoff-cohorts of the paper)).
The standard coupling of~$Z$ and~$X$ has the following invariants for every $i\geq 1$ and $t\geq 1$.
\begin{description}  
\item  [Inv-$b_i(t)$:] For each stream $D\in \{A,B\}$, $\mathbf{b}_i^{Z^D}(t-1) \subseteq \mathbf{b}_i^{X^D}(t-1)$.
\item  [Inv-$B_i(t)$:] For each stream $D\in \{A,B\}$, $\mathbf{B}_i^{Z^D}(t) \subseteq \mathbf{B}_i^{X^D}(t)$.
\item [Inv-$s_i(t)$:] 
For each stream $D\in \{A,B\}$, $\mathbf{s}_i^{Z^D}(t) \subseteq \mathbf{s}_i^{X^D}(t)$.
\end{description}
Initially, Inv-$b_i(1)$ holds for every $i\geq 1$ since all of these sets are empty.

For any $t$ assuming Inv-$b_i(t)$, the coupling at step~$t$ proceeds as follows.
For each $D\in \{A,B\}$, $\mathbf{n}^{Z^D}(t) = \mathbf{n}^{X^D}(t)$, so for all $i\geq 1$, 
Inv-$B_i(t)$ holds.
For every   
$D\in \{A,B\}$ and
$i\geq 1$, $\mathbf{S}^{X^D}_i(t)$ is formed by including each ball in 
$\mathbf{B}_i^{X^D}(t) \setminus \mathbf{B}_i^{Z^D}(t)$ 
independently with probability~$p_i$.
Then $\mathbf{s}^{X^D}_i(t) = \mathbf{S}^{X^D}_i(t) \cup \mathbf{s}^{Z^D}_i(t)$, establishing Inv-$s_i(t)$.

 
  

  
The assignments to $\mathbf{e}_i^{X^D}(t)$ follow deterministically, using  Definition~(def:backoffasgen of the paper)
and the assignments to $\mathbf{e}_i^{Z^D}(t)$  are chosen  following Definition~(def:two-stream of the paper).

Since $\mathbf{s}_i^{X^D}(t) \cap \mathbf{B}_i^{Z^D}(t) = \mathbf{s}_i^{Z^D}(t)$, Inv-$b_i(t+1)$  follows from  
$ \mathbf{s}_i^{Z^D}(t) \cap \mathbf{e}_i^{X^D}(t) \subseteq \mathbf{e}_i^{Z^D}(t)$, which holds:
If a ball~$\beta$ is in $ \mathbf{s}_i^{Z^D}(t) \cap \mathbf{e}_i^{X^D}(t) $ then
$\mathbf{s}^{X^A}(t) \cup \mathbf{s}^{X^B}(t)= \{\beta\}$ so
$\mathbf{s}^{Z^A}(t) \cup \mathbf{s}^{Z^B}(t) = \{\beta\}$ so 
$\mathbf{e}_i^{Z^D}(t) = \{\beta\}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:56:37.651622+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7ad26847ff861be199c6bd05ca3ce9408dd4e7aec539420e2a44e52a20c91d27","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:openpath of arXiv:2608.24830, 'Motion helps the contact process: survival below\\ the percolation threshold on Poisson Br'] Let $\lambda\in(0,\infty]$, $\mu\in(0,\infty]$ and $\mathfrak r\in\{\mathrm{u},\mathrm{i}\}$. path} from $(u_0,t_0)$ to $(u_n,t_{n+1})$ consists of particles $u_0,\dots,u_n$, such that
consecutive particles are distinct, and times $t_0<t_1<\dots<t_{n+1}$, such that
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item for $1\le j\le n$ there is an active transmission mark from $u_{j-1}$ to $u_j$ at time
  $t_j$; when $\lambda=\infty$ this says that $u_{j-1}$ and $u_j$ are in contact at $t_j$;
\item for $0\le j\le n$ there is no effective recovery mark of $u_j$ in $(t_j,t_{j+1}]$.

$t\in[t_n,t_{n+1}]$. Its jumps have size at most $2r$. The path is \emph{contained} in a

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:51:33.328314+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7b14ba8e7a519cb2c92fc84c492075b65cc6993ff31e0c70e5ca58cea8478ba7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma detect-pointed-presheaves of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let ${\mathcal{C}}$ be a cocomplete, pointed, and locally small $\infty$-category. Let ${\mathcal{I}}\subset{\mathcal{C}}$ be a small full subcategory containing the zero object and satisfying the following properties:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item For any $I\in{\mathcal{I}}$, the unique lift ${\mathcal{C}}\to\Spc_*$ of ${\textup{Hom}}(I,-)$ is cocontinuous.
        \item The functors ${\textup{Hom}}(I,-)\colon{\mathcal{C}}\to\Spc$ are jointly conservative.
    \end{enumerate}
    Then ${\mathcal{I}}\hookrightarrow{\mathcal{C}}$ extends to an equivalence $\PSh^0({\mathcal{I}})\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;}{\mathcal{C}}$.
    \begin{proof}
        As ${\mathcal{C}}$ is cocomplete and locally small, the inclusion extends to a functor $\Lambda\colon\PSh({\mathcal{I}})\to{\mathcal{C}}$ left adjoint to the restricted Yoneda embedding $\Upsilon$. By what it means to be a zero object, ${\textup{Hom}}(0,x)\simeq1$ for all $x\in{\mathcal{C}}$, i.e.\ $\Upsilon$ factors through $\PSh^0({\mathcal{I}})$, so we obtain a restricted adjunction $\PSh^0({\mathcal{I}})\rightleftarrows{\mathcal{C}}$. It remains to show that this is in fact an adjoint equivalence. As our second assumption guarantees that $\Upsilon$ is conservative, it will suffice for this that the unit $\eta\colon\textup{id}\to\Upsilon\Lambda$ is invertible. 

        Since ${\mathcal{I}}^{\textup{op}}$ has a zero object, postcomposing with the forgetful functor induces an equivalence ${\textup{Fun}}^0({\mathcal{I}}^{\textup{op}},\Spc_*)\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;}{\textup{Fun}}^0({\mathcal{I}}^{\textup{op}},\Spc)$. Moreover, the full subcategory ${\textup{Fun}}^0({\mathcal{I}}^{\textup{op}},\Spc_*)\subset{\textup{Fun}}({\mathcal{I}}^{\textup{op}},\Spc_*)$ is closed under colimits (as any colimit of initial objects is initial), so that colimits in ${\textup{Fun}}^0({\mathcal{I}}^{\textup{op}},\Spc_*)$ are computed pointwise. Thus, our first assumption guarantees that the right adjoint $\Upsilon$ is cocontinuous, so that the class of all pointed presheaves $X$ for which $\eta_X$ is invertible, is closed under colimits. It will therefore suffice to show that the unit $\eta_X$ is invertible whenever $X=\Upsilon(I)$ is representable. If we now let $Z\in{\mathcal{C}}$ arbitrary, then the composite
        \[
            {\textup{Hom}}(\Lambda(X),Z)\xrightarrow{\;\Upsilon\;}{\textup{Hom}}(\Upsilon\Lambda(X),\Upsilon(Z))\xrightarrow{\;{\textup{Hom}}(\eta,\Upsilon(Z))} {\textup{Hom}}(X,\Upsilon(Z))
        \]
        is invertible as it is just the adjunction equivalence. By assumption, $\Lambda(X)\simeq I\in{\mathcal{I}}$; if also $Z\in I$, then the first map is an equivalence by the Yoneda lemma, so that also the second map is an equivalence by $2$-out-of-$3$. We conclude that ${\textup{Hom}}(\eta_X,\Upsilon(Z))$ is an equivalence for every $Z\in I$. As $\eta_X\colon \Upsilon(I)=X\to \Upsilon\Lambda(X)\simeq\Upsilon(I)$ is a map in Yoneda image, this implies that $\eta_X$ is an equivalence.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:38:37.420239+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7b25ee3e400161990fdf7639b1ad6dc25de6b9392775d9e0c962056d2dbbf3b4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2605.16733, 'Concentration Inequalities for Sample Cross-Covariances'] Let \((X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^N\) be i.i.d. copies of a centered random vector
\((X,Y)\in\mathbb R^{d_X+d_Y}\). Assume that \(X\) and \(Y\) are
sub-Gaussian random vectors with covariance matrices \(\Sigma_X\) and
\(\Sigma_Y\), and sub-Gaussian constants \(K_X,K_Y\). Set
\[
r_{X}:=\frac{\tr(\Sigma_X)}{\|\Sigma_X\|},
\qquad
r_{Y}:=\frac{\tr(\Sigma_Y)}{\|\Sigma_Y\|}.
\]
For every \(u\ge 1\), it holds with probability at least \(1-\exp(-u)\) that
\[
\bigg\|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i Y_i^{\top}-\E X Y^{\top}\bigg\| \lesssim K_{X}K_{Y}(\|\Sigma_{X}\|\|\Sigma_Y\|)^{1/2} \bigg(\sqrt{\frac{r_{X}+r_{Y}+u}{N}}+ \frac{\sqrt{(r_{X}+u)(r_{Y}+u)}}{N}\bigg).
\]
As a corollary,
 \begin{align*}
\E \bigg\|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i Y^{\top}_i-\E X Y^{\top}\bigg\| \lesssim K_{X}K_{Y} (\|\Sigma_{X}\|\|\Sigma_Y\|)^{1/2} \bigg(\sqrt{\frac{r_{X}+r_{Y}}{N}}+ \frac{\sqrt{r_{X}r_{Y}}}{N}\bigg).
 \end{align*}
Moreover, if $(X,Y)$ is jointly Gaussian, then
\begin{align*}
\E \bigg\|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i Y^{\top}_i-\E XY^{\top}\bigg\| \asymp (\|\Sigma_{X}\|\|\Sigma_Y\|)^{1/2} \bigg(\sqrt{\frac{r_{X}+r_{Y}}{N}}+ \frac{\sqrt{r_{X}r_{Y}}}{N}\bigg).
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:18:54.363364+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7b262947ed144307f28c9e91556faeae15d903118928cde119af3ffc21efb8ba","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The following happen:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The rotation $R_t$ is not diagonalizable, unless at $t=0$ where it is the identity, $R_0=1$, and at $t=\pi$ where it is minus the identity, $R_\pi=-1$.

\item The symmetry $S_t$ is diagonalizable, with eigenvectors on the symmetry axis, and on its orthogonal, with respective eigenvalues $1,-1$.

\item The projection $P_t$ is diagonalizable, with the eigenvectors exactly as for the symmetry $S_t$, this time with respective eigenvalues $1,0$.

\item In fact, any projection is diagonalizable, with eigenvectors on it image, and on the orthogonal of its image, with respective eigenvalues $1,0$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

The event of never returning to 0 after the first step: the walk must never come back, which in the branching-process picture (right excursions counted by the number of down-crossings of each edge) means the branching process with migration started from the edge (0,1) never produces a down-crossing of (0,1) into 0... the escape probability equals the probability that the total number of down-crossings of the edge (0,1) is zero, which is P(the branching process with migration started at 1 individual at level 1 has zero descendants at level 0) - not directly a standard extinction probability but a hitting probability of the time-reversed process. For the source's example [Zer05, Th. 18] the closed form exists; for general bounded stacks the escape probability is the solution of a finite-dimensional fixed-point equation obtained by conditioning on the first cookie stack at sites 1, 2, ...: define q_k = P(never return to 0 | walk currently at k, all cookies at sites >= k intact, cookies at sites < k in their post-visit states); the states of the sites already visited matter only through the remaining cookie counts, which for M bounded is a finite vector, and the walk's returns to 0 require descending through all visited sites; the escape probability then equals the probability of survival of a Markov chain on finite cookie-count vectors, computable numerically for given (M, p) but with no closed form in general. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.529597+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7ba4a3df5386842b2c4221fb83a0783e036705f503467d2b1ca11633b8d4c27d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition eq:sparse-profile-net-bound of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[proposition]{prop:sharp-profile-energy}
Suppose that the random field satisfies \(({\rm PT})_p\).
Put
\[
 \pi_N(a):=
 \sup_{x\in\mathbb S^{N-1}(1)}
 \mathbb P\{\left\lverth_N^J(x)\right\rvert\ge a\}.
\]
Put
\[
 \mathcal S_{N,k}
 =\{x\in\mathbb S^{N-1}(1):
       \abs{\operatorname{supp}x}\le k\},
 \qquad
 \Lambda_p=\frac{p^{p+1}}{p!}.
\]
For \(1\le k\le N\), \(a>0\), and
\(0<\delta<\Lambda_p^{-1}\),
\begin{align}
 &\mathbb P\left\{
 \sup_{x\in\mathcal S_{N,k}}\left\lverth_N^J(x)\right\rvert\ge a
 \right\}\notag\\
 &\qquad\le
 \binom Nk\left(1+\frac2\delta\right)^k
 \pi_N\bigl((1-\Lambda_p\delta)a\bigr).
 
\end{align}
Consequently, if \(1\le k_N\le N\), \(k_N=o(N)\), and
\(a_N\to a>0\), then
\begin{equation}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log
 \mathbb P\left\{
 \sup_{x\in\mathcal S_{N,k_N}}\left\lverth_N^J(x)\right\rvert
 \ge a_N\right\}
 \le-\frac{a^2}{2}.
\end{equation}
The same conclusions hold for the standard symmetric-coordinate model
whenever its field satisfies \(({\rm PT})_p\); the profile MGF and

All finite stationary points, equivalently all GD fixed points, form the
curve E={v=0,kq=p_bar}. At such a point write S=k^2+q^2>=2|p_bar|.
The GD Jacobian has tangent multiplier 1 and normal multipliers

 mu_-=1-eta lambda_-, mu_+=1-eta lambda_+,
 lambda_+/-=(A +/- sqrt(A^2+4B^2 S))/2.

Here lambda_-<0<lambda_+, hence mu_->1 everywhere: no point of E is
linearly attracting in all normal directions. The other normal direction is

* strictly attracting in the linearization when eta lambda_+<2;
* neutral with multiplier -1 when eta lambda_+=2;
* strictly repelling with multiplier less than -1 when eta lambda_+>2.

Let
 J_eta=(4/eta^2-2A/eta)/B^2.

The first case is EXACTLY S<J_eta, the middle case exactly S=J_eta,
and the last exactly S>J_eta. Equivalently, with C=k^2-q^2,
S=sqrt(C^2+4p_bar^2): there is an attracting normal direction only if
J_eta>2|p_bar|, and then precisely at

 |C|<sqrt(J_eta^2-4p_bar^2).

Equality gives neutral normal points when J_eta>=2|p_bar|. If J_eta
is smaller than 2|p_bar|, every point is repelling in both normal directions.
In particular, for EVERY eta>0, sufficiently unbalanced factorizations on
E are normally repelling in both directions. There is no positive constant
step that preserves the flow's one attracting normal direction uniformly
along the entire stationary curve. This does NOT imply an open basin of
cycles or disprove a full-space almost-everywhere GD endpoint theorem.

## Proof

The fixed-point condition is gradient L=0, classified in proof 008.
Its loss Hessian at E is
 [[A,-Bq,-Bk],[-Bq,0,0],[-Bk,0,0]].
The tangent vector (0,k,-q) is in its kernel. In the orthonormal basis
e_v=(1,0,0), e_s=(0,q,k)/sqrt(S) of the normal plane, the Hessian is
 [[A,-B sqrt(S)],[-B sqrt(S),0]].
The quadratic characteristic polynomial is lambda^2-A lambda-B^2 S,
which yields lambda_+/- and their signs. The GD Jacobian is I-eta Hessian,
proving the multipliers and their linear classifications.

For equivalence with J_eta, consider the polynomial
f(z)=z^2-Az-B^2 S, whose positive zero is lambda_+ and negative zero
lambda_-. Since 2/eta>0, lambda_+<2/eta is equivalent to
f(2/eta)>0, or S<J_eta; equality and the reverse inequality follow likewise.
This avoids squaring a potentially negative expression 4/eta-A.
Finally S^2=C^2+4p_bar^2 by algebra, and S is unbounded along E by
taking k->infinity, q=p_bar/k. All asserted threshold statements follow.

## Scope of the obstruction

The obstruction is to a PARTICULAR transfer from flow to GD: retaining
one attracting normal direction uniformly on every imbalance leaf at fixed
step. It is not an obstruction to every possible discrete-time proof.
The imbalance leaves themselves are not invariant under GD:
C_+=(1-eta^2 v^2 G^2)C. Both facts must be accounted for in further work.
Normal multipliers on the unit circle require separate nonlinear analysis;
no attracting two-cycle is claimed. Scalar genuine self-attention embeddings
of this family are supplied in claim 008.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149322+00:00","domain":"elliptic regularity, Schauder and L^p theory","id":"claim_7bb2c58aa2918e859c731bf67503266f6c9b7d91791ab1a5552f2ca3db2a40ef","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: the Hoelder exponent satisfies 0 < alpha < 1 strictly, and the Lebesgue exponent satisfies 1 < p < infinity strictly. The reason is that the second derivatives of the Newtonian potential are given by a singular integral operator, which is bounded on C^{0,alpha} and on L^p only in the open ranges. Failure at alpha = 0 (continuous right-hand side does not give a C^2 solution): in the plane put u(x) = (x_1^2 - x_2^2) (log(1/r))^{1/2} for 0 < r = |x| < 1/2, u(0) = 0. A computation with u = p g, p = r^2 cos(2 theta) harmonic and g = (log(1/r))^{1/2}, using Laplacian(p g) = 4 p g'/r + p (g'' + g'/r), gives Laplacian u = -cos(2 theta) ( 2 (log(1/r))^{-1/2} + (1/4)(log(1/r))^{-3/2} ), which extends continuously by 0 at the origin, while D_{11}u = 2(log(1/r))^{1/2} + o(1) blows up. Since u is C^1 and C^infinity off the origin, it solves Laplacian u = f distributionally on the ball with f continuous; no C^2 solution of Laplacian v = f exists near 0, because v - u would be harmonic hence smooth. (Consistently, this f is continuous but not Dini continuous, and Dini continuity is the correct substitute hypothesis.) Failure at alpha = 1: with q = x_1^3 - 3 x_1 x_2^2 and g = log(1/r), the function u = q g has Laplacian u = -6 q/r^2 = -6 r cos(3 theta), which is Lipschitz, while D_{111}u = 6 log(1/r) + O(1) is unbounded, so u is not in C^{2,1}. Failure at p = infinity: u = (x_1^2 - x_2^2) log(1/r) has Laplacian u = -4 cos(2 theta) in L^infinity while D_{11}u = 2 log(1/r) + O(1) is not bounded, so Laplacian u in L^infinity does not give u in W^{2,infinity} = C^{1,1}; the correct endpoint statement is Laplacian u in L^infinity implies D^2 u in BMO. Failure at p = 1: let f_k = rho_{1/k} be standard mollifiers and u_k = Gamma convolved with f_k, so Laplacian u_k = f_k with ||f_k||_{L^1} = 1 and ||u_k||_{L^1(B_2)} bounded; on B_1 minus the origin D_{12}u_k converges pointwise to D_{12}Gamma, whose size is comparable to |x|^{-n} and hence not integrable near 0, so by Fatou ||D^2 u_k||_{L^1(B_1)} tends to infinity. No estimate of the form ||D^2u||_{L^1} <= C(||Laplacian u||_{L^1} + ||u||_{L^1}) can hold; the correct endpoint statements are weak-L^1 bounds and the Hardy space result Laplacian u in H^1 implies D^2u in L^1. Practical consequence: from f merely continuous (or bounded) one gets u in W^{2,p}_loc for every finite p and u in C^{1,alpha}_loc for every alpha < 1, but not, in general, u in C^2 - the first example above is exactly the obstruction (for particular right-hand sides, a smooth f say, the solution is of course C^2).","status":"unverified"}

If $f \\in L^m(\\Omega)$ with $m > N/2$ (so $f \\in H^{-1}$ and the weak solution $u \\in H_0^1(\\Omega)$ exists and is unique), then $u \\in L^\\infty(\\Omega)$ and $\\|u\\|_{L^\\infty} \\leq C\\,\\|f\\|_{L^m}$ with $C = C(N, \\lambda, m, |\\Omega|)$. (II) $L^1$ and measure data. If $f \\in L^1(\\Omega)$ (or more generally $f = \\mu$ is a bounded Radon measure on $\\Omega$), there exists a unique DUALITY solution: a function $u \\in L^1(\\Omega)$ with $\\int_\\Omega u\\,g\\,dx = \\int_\\Omega w_g\\,d\\mu$ for every $g \\in L^\\infty(\\Omega)$, where $w_g \\in H_0^1(\\Omega) \\cap L^\\infty(\\Omega)$ is the weak solution of the adjoint problem $-\\operatorname{div}(A^{T}\\nabla w_g) = g$ (bounded by part (I), which is all that is needed to pair with $f \\in L^1$); for MEASURE data one needs $w_g$ continuous on $\\overline\\Omega$ so that $\\int w_g\\,d\\mu$ makes sense - interior continuity is De Giorgi-Nash-Moser, continuity up to the boundary requires a mild regularity of $\\partial\\Omega$ (e.g. Lipschitz, or an exterior cone condition), which is then an extra hypothesis in the measure case. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:53:10.207646+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7bbcc3055ed966d80d6ae6e65031be16b5d3b953e5585a069d7d245f216acd91","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defi Def:W-cont-map of arXiv:2608.29013, 'Weighted Homology and Cohomology of Weighted Polyhedra'] Suppose $(X,\lambda)$ and $(X',\lambda')$ are
   weighted polyhedra of the same type. 
   A \emph{W-continuous map} from $(X,\lambda)$ to 
   $(X',\lambda')$ is a continuous map $f: X\rightarrow X'$   which satisfies: for all $x\in X$,
   $$ \begin{cases}
   \lambda'(f(x)) \mid \lambda(x),  &  \text{if  $(X,\lambda)$ and $(X',\lambda')$ are of ascending type}; \\
   \lambda(x) \mid \lambda'(f(x)),  &  \text{if  $(X,\lambda)$ and $(X',\lambda')$ are of descending type}.
 \end{cases}  
   $$  
    We also denote such a map by $f: (X,\lambda)\rightarrow (X',\lambda')$ to indicate its W-continuity
    since the definition of $f$ depends on the type of the weighted polyhedra involved.
   Moreover, $f$ is called \emph{weight-preserving} if 
$\lambda'(f(x))=\lambda(x)$ for all $x\in X$.\vskip 0.1cm

We say that $(X,\lambda)$ is \emph{isomorphic} to $(X',\lambda')$ if there exists a weight-preserving homeomorphism from $(X,\lambda)$ to $(X',\lambda')$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X a random element of {-1, 1}^n, n >= 1, under any law","given X_{-i}, X_i' is independent of X_i","u real-valued on {-1, 1}^n"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T09:29:33.705785+00:00","domain":"analysis of Boolean functions","id":"claim_7c3b9a530dbb12cbd24154e6e9dd868221769f4a6d4f8b6c34a52a93bff425e2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X take values in {-1, 1}^n, n >= 1, under any law, fix a coordinate i, and let X_i' be a replacement sign which, given X_{-i}, is independent of X_i; X^(i) is X with coordinate i replaced by X_i'. Hence (1/2) E[(u(X) - u(X^(i)))^2] = E[(D_i u(X))^2] for every u if and only if m m' = 0 almost surely: at each value of X_{-i} of positive probability, X_i or X_i' is conditionally fair, and the law of the other sign is then arbitrary (X_i' = 1 always is allowed when X_i is conditionally fair). If X_i' is a fresh draw from the conditional law of X_i (m' = m, the heat-bath step), the left side is E[Var(u(X) | X_{-i})] = E[(1 - m^2) (D_i u)^2]. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:48:30.907804+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7c467f19b4592dd8df546d3a11d4942b4dd70bc7734c79039ffe60cc5c816554","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 8 ({\cite[Corollary~5.6) of arXiv:2609.00936, 'Extended Abstract of Counting Divisorial Contractions with Centre a $cA_n$-Singularity'] {Pae24Counting}}] 
Let $U = \operatorname{Spec} (\mathbb C[x_1, \ldots, x_n] / I)$ be an affine variety properly containing the origin. Assign positive integer weights $w_1, \ldots, w_m$ to the variables $y_1, \ldots, y_m$ of $\mathbb C^m$ and assign the weights $1, \ldots, 1$ to $x_1, \ldots, x_n$. Let superscript ``an'' denote analytification. Let $\psi\colon (U^{\mathrm{an}}, \bm 0) \to (Z, \bm 0)$ be a biholomorphic map germ to a complex space subgerm $(Z, \bm 0)$ of $(\mathbb C^m, \bm 0)$. Define the variety $\hat U$ by
\[
\hat U := \operatorname{Spec} \frac{\mathbb C[x_1, \ldots, x_n, y_1, \ldots, y_m]}{I + (\psi_1^{<w_1} - y_1, \ldots, \psi_m^{<w_m} - y_m)},

where $\psi_j^{<w_j}$ denotes the truncation of the $j$-th coordinate power series of $\psi$ up to order $w_j - 1$. \item every proper birational morphism locally analytically equivalent to the weighted blowup of $Z$ is given by the weighted blowup of $\hat U$ for some local biholomorphism~$\psi\colon U \to Z$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.667208+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7c47931267c6498fbf94ff88cb702f4d48eb95ddccabb9e9f705872daa9099d2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 4 (Ambrosio/DiPerna-Lions) of arXiv:2607.25685, 'Mimicking diffusion processes with differential equations'] Let $v:\mathbb R^d\times(0,T)\to\mathbb R^d$ be a vector
field satisfying
\begin{align*}
\textnormal{(R1)}\quad&
v\in L^1\bigl((0,T);BV_{\mathrm{loc}}
(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)\bigr),\\
\textnormal{(R2)}\quad&
D\!\cdot v_t=(\nabla\!\cdot v_t)\mathcal L^d
\quad\text{for a.e. }s,
\qquad
[\nabla\!\cdot v]^-
\in L^1\bigl((0,T);L^\infty(\mathbb R^d)\bigr),\\
\textnormal{(R3)}\quad&
\frac{|v|}{1+|x|}
\in
L^1\bigl((0,T);L^1(\mathbb R^d)\bigr)
+
L^1\bigl((0,T);L^\infty(\mathbb R^d)\bigr).
\end{align*}
Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
For every $u_0\in L^1\cap L^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, the continuity
equation
\[
\partial_tu+\nabla\!\cdot(vu)=0,
\qquad
u(.,0)=u_0,
\]
has at most one bounded distributional solution 
$
u\in L^\infty\bigl((0,T);L^1\cap L^\infty(\mathbb R^d)\bigr).
$
\item
There exists a regular Lagrangian flow $Z$ associated with $v$,
unique up to $\mathcal L^d$-null sets, and
\[
Z(t,\cdot)_\#\mathcal L^d
\le
\exp\left(
\int_0^t
\bigl\|[\nabla\!\cdot v(\cdot,s)]^-\bigr\|_{L^\infty}\,ds
\right)\mathcal L^d.
\]
\item
For every nonnegative
$u_0\in L^1\cap L^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, the unique solution is
$
u_t\mathcal L^d
= Z(t,\cdot)_\#(u_0\mathcal L^d).$
\end{enumerate}
If, in addition,
\[
[\nabla\!\cdot v]^+
\in L^1\bigl((0,T);L^\infty(\mathbb R^d)\bigr),
\]
then the reverse flow is well posed and satisfies two-sided compression bounds;
in particular $Z(t,\cdot)$ is
essentially invertible. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

SCOPE/GAP: Independent audit pending. Uniform instability of the balanced Jacobian block for unequal head magnitudes remains open; 576 floating-point samples do not settle it.

# Balanced opposite-head two-cycles: complete implicit parametrization

T328-W698-017 v1, Target 1, proof (unaudited).

Consider L(v,k,q)=log(1+exp(-v h(kq))), h(s)=a+b*tanh(kappa*s),
0<a<b, kappa>0 and simultaneous Euclidean GD with fixed eta>0.
For this scalar signed link, every balanced period-two orbit whose heads have
opposite signs is covered by the following construction, up to interchanging
the two phases and simultaneously negating both factors. The construction
parametrizes cycles across the data/step parameters; for prescribed a,b,kappa,
eta these parameter equalities are necessary and sufficient, not a claim that
every prescribed model has such a cycle.

## Construction from four positive parameters

Choose 0<r<1 and T,y0,kappa>0. Define

    A=tanh T, B=tanh(r^2*T),
    D=cosh(T)^2/cosh(r^2*T)^2,
    sig(y)=1/(1+exp(-y)), f(y)=y*sig(y)^2.

There is a unique y1>0 solving

    f(y1)=f(y0)/(r*D).

Indeed f'(y)=sig(y)^2*[1+2y*(1-sig(y))]>0 on y>0,
and f increases continuously from 0 to infinity. Put

    g0=sig(y0), g1=sig(y1), c=g0/g1,
    t=y1/(y0*c),
    v0=sqrt((1-r)*(A-B)/((1+t)*(1+c)*kappa*sech(T)^2)),
    H0=y0/v0, H1=c*H0,
    b=H0*(1+c)/(A-B), a=b*A-H0,
    eta=v0*(1+t)/(g0*H0), w=sqrt(T/kappa).

All denominators are strictly positive. Also a/b=(c*A+B)/(1+c) lies
strictly between B and A, hence 0<a<b. These parameters give the exact
period-two orbit

    (v0,w,-w) <-> (-t*v0,r*w,-r*w).

The two signed margins are -y0 and -y1. In particular the logistic factors
are exactly g0 and g1, not factors obtained from a limiting approximation.

## Verification

h(-w^2)=-H0 and h(-r^2*w^2)=H1. Thus g0*H0=g1*H1 and
the two head increments are respectively -v0*(1+t) and v0*(1+t).
Let d0=b*kappa*sech(T)^2, d1=b*kappa*sech(r^2*T)^2=D*d0.
The first factor coefficient is

    delta0=eta*v0*g0*d0
          =v0^2*(1+t)*(1+c)*kappa*sech(T)^2/(A-B)=1-r.

For the second coefficient, the scalar equation gives

    t*(g1/g0)*D = y1*g1^2*D/(y0*g0^2)=1/r.

Consequently delta1=eta*(-t*v0)*g1*d1=-(1-r)/r=1-1/r.
On k=-q the factor multipliers 1-delta0=r and 1-delta1=1/r
return the factors exactly. The head changes sign, so the orbit is nonfixed.

## Completeness within the stated class

Balance means k^2=q^2. If k=q, the product is nonnegative, h(kq)>0,
and the head strictly increases at every finite point, so there is no finite
cycle. If k=q=0 the same argument applies. Thus a balanced cycle must lie
on k=-q with nonzero k. Interchange phases so v0>0>v1 and simultaneously
negate both factors so k0=w>0. Since delta_j=eta*v_j*g_j*h'_j,
delta0>0>delta1. The returning-factor equation is

    (1-delta0)*(1-delta1)=1.

The second factor is >1; therefore 0<1-delta0<1. Write this number r.
It follows that k1=r*w and delta1=1-1/r. In particular no factor sign flip
is possible for an opposite-head balanced two-cycle in this class.
The head update v1-v0<0 forces h0<0, and the reverse update forces h1>0.
Set H0=-h0, H1=h1, t=-v1/v0, T=kappa*w^2,
y0=v0*H0, y1=t*v0*H1. These are positive. The equal and opposite
head increments imply H1/H0=g0/g1=c, whence t=y1/(y0*c).
Dividing the two factor coefficients gives r*D*f(y1)=f(y0).
The identities h1-h0=b*(A-B), delta0=1-r and the head increment then
recover precisely the formulas for b,a,v0,eta above. This proves completeness.

## Full Jacobian test and its present limit

The normal two-step multiplier is exactly

    mu_U=(1+delta0)*(1+delta1)=(2-r)*(2-1/r)=5-2r-2/r.

It satisfies |mu_U|<1 precisely for (3-sqrt(5))/2<r<1,
equals -1 at the left endpoint, and is <-1 below it. It is zero at r=1/2.
The other two multipliers are exactly the eigenvalues of J1*J0, using
the general balanced Jacobian given in proofs/014_opposite_head_cycles.md.
This is an exact formula for the full spectrum, but no uniform inequality
for that balanced block has been proved for unequal head magnitudes.

The reproducible script scripts/asymmetric_cycles.py sampled 576 choices:
r in {.1,.2,.35,.4,.5,.65,.8,.9,.98}, T in {.1,.3,.6,.9,1.3,2,3,5},
y0 in {.01,.1,.4,1,2,4,8,16}, with kappa=1. It solved the monotone
equation by floating-point bisection and differentiated the full 3D loss.
It found zero attracting candidates; the smallest observed full spectral
radius was approximately 8.9666956. The largest relative cycle residual was
approximately 2.56e-13. These are numerical evidence, not rigorous bounds,
and cannot establish instability throughout the parametrization.

Claim 016 proves full instability and the complete second-multiplier phase
diagram on the equal-head-magnitude subfamily r=1/2,
cosh(T)^2=2cosh(T/4)^2. The SINGLE remaining hard step for upgrading
the wider numerical finding to a theorem is a rigorous spectral-radius
inequality for J1*J0 throughout (r,T,y0)>0 with 0<r<1. This proof
does not claim that step or almost-everywhere factored-GD convergence.","status":"unverified"}

Recurrence of M(1,1) would follow if the walk returns to the origin infinitely often; since the second coordinate performs a simple random walk on the column above the current first coordinate whenever the vertex was visited before, the walk behaves in each column like a 1D random walk (recurrent) until it hits an unvisited vertex, at which time the first coordinate steps. The number of new visits up to time n is the range R_n; the first coordinate after n steps is a simple random walk at time R_n, so |X^1_n| is of order sqrt(R_n), and R_n <= n, so |X^1_n| is typically at most of order sqrt n - not deterministically: n first-visit moves to the right, which have probability 2^-n, give X^1_n = n; a return to the origin requires both coordinates to vanish. (1D recurrence), and whether at those visits the second coordinate is 0 - not automatic. So recurrence of M(1,1) reduces to: at the (infinitely many) times the first coordinate is 0, the second coordinate, which then performs a 1D walk in the column of 0 with the visited interval of that column, returns to height 0 before finding a new vertex - which has probability bounded below by a constant each time if the visited interval around height 0 in column 0 has length bounded... the visited interval in column 0 grows, and the probability of returning to 0 from the boundary of an interval of length L before exiting is of order 1/L... summing over the visits to column 0 gives a divergent series only if the interval lengths grow slowly enough. This is the crux and I did not settle it; the reduction is recorded. Key identity: M(1,1) recurrent iff, at the infinitely many returns of the first coordinate to 0, the second coordinate returns to 0 in column 0 before finding a new vertex; the return probability is of order 1/(visited interval length). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:04:07.028572+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7ca31d3826e184062766df94b9df84d479b8435345ed91593519cc909daa6147","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:ising-cavity of arXiv:2607.29330, 'Large deviations for the maximum of\\ the generalized TAP free energy'] On the tree of Definition~(def:ising-rpc of the paper), let
		$B_s^i(\alpha)$, $1\le i\le N$, and $Y(s,\alpha)$ be centered
		continuous Gaussian martingales indexed by $s\in[0,1]$ and the
		leaves $\alpha$. The two families are independent of each other,
		of $H_N$, and of the Poisson point processes defining the
		cascade. Their covariances are
		\begin{align*}
			\mathbb{E} B_s^i(\alpha)B_t^j(\beta)
			&=
			\delta_{ij}\,
			\xi'\bigl(s\wedge t\wedge
			s_{\alpha\wedge\beta}\bigr),\\
			\mathbb{E} Y(s,\alpha)Y(t,\beta)
			&=
			N\vartheta\bigl(s\wedge t\wedge
			s_{\alpha\wedge\beta}\bigr).
		\end{align*}
		For $\mathbf{m}\in[-1,1]^N$, with
		\[
		q_\mathbf{m}:=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N m_i^2,
		\]
		define the multiscale cavity field by
		\[
		Z(\mathbf{m},\alpha)
		:=
		\sum_{i=1}^N m_i B_{q_\mathbf{m}}^i(\alpha).
		\]
		We call $Y(q,\alpha)$ the Onsager field at self-overlap $q$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:45:27.973962+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7ca5dc39c9e927b2ebeeddc6743e403d56054bb55ac8419111d8b3a924aa4e6a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:three-bc-unmarked-length-bridge of arXiv:2607.04264, 'Macroscopic Feynman Cycles and Poisson--Kingman Universality in Bose Condensation'] Let \(b \in \{\mathrm{per}, D, N\}\), and assume

\[

    \Longrightarrow
    \overline{\Xi}^{\, \rho - \rho_{\mathrm{c}}}
    \qquad
    \text{in }
    \mathcal{N}_\ell\bigl([0,1] \times (0,\infty)\bigr),
\]

\[

    \Longrightarrow
     (\rho - \rho_{\mathrm{c}})\, \bigl(P_1^{\downarrow}, P_2^{\downarrow}, \ldots\bigr),
\]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:30:08.198444+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7ca84d2e39642a45d6c97a354b7bbc5a7ab036ae56c67400b50142b3c153ec7e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary of arXiv:2608.13452, 'Wasserstein stability of the zero cell of a Poisson hyperplane tessellation under directio'] Let $\hat{f}^{(1)}_{\gamma, n}$ and $\hat{f}^{(2)}_{\gamma, n}$ be the estimators of a density $f$ as defined in Proposition (prop:density-robust of the paper).

    Further assume that $f$ is globally $L$-Lipschitz and $\operatorname{supp}(f) \subseteq [0,1]^d$, and that \(\phi_2\) satisfies (equation eq:phi_2_close_condition of the paper).
    Then there exist random probability densities
    $\hat{g}_{\gamma,n}^{(1)}$ and
    $\hat{g}_{\gamma,n}^{(2)}$, defined on a common probability space,
    such that, for every fixed $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$,
    \[
    \hat{g}_{\gamma,n}^{(i)}(x)
    \overset{(d)}{=}

    \begin{align*}
    &\mathbb{E} \left[\int_{[0,1]^d} \left|\hat{g}^{(1)}_{\gamma, n}(x) - \hat{g}^{(2)}_{\gamma, n}(x)\right| \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} x \right] \\
    & \leq \min\left\{\frac{\gamma^{d/2} \|f\|_{\infty}^{1/2} \left(\mathrm{vol}(\Pi_1)^{1/2} + \mathrm{vol}(\Pi_2)^{1/2}\right)}{n^{1/2}} + \frac{L \tilde{C}(\phi_1, d)}{\gamma}W_{\mathrm{geo}}(\phi_1,\phi_2)^{\frac{1}{d}}, C(\phi_1, d)W_{\mathrm{geo}}(\phi_1,\phi_2)^{\frac{1}{d}}\right\}.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:30:52.737095+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7cb88d363523b9a15633e50763e3f5ce3f4824173bbc065e9cddf6f19ac8a5e5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2506.10476, 'Construction of ergodic \textsc{idla} forests in $\mathbb{Z}^d$'] Let $d \geq 2$. The infinite-volume \textsc{idla} forests $\fdag{\infty}$ and $(\fdag{n})_{n\geq 0}$ satisfy the following properties: 
\begin{enumerate}
	\item Almost surely, the set of vertices of $\fdag{\infty}$ satisfies $V(\fdag{\infty}) = \mathbb{Z}^d$.
	\item The distributions of $\left(\fdag{n}\right)_{n \geq 0}$ and $\fdag{\infty}$ are invariant w.r.t. translations $T_k,\ k \in \mathcal{H}$.
	\item The distributions of $\left(\fdag{n}\right)_{n \geq 0}$ and $\fdag{\infty}$ are $\alpha$-mixing, that is for all $n\geq 0$, for all events $\mathcal{A},\ \mathcal{B}$, 
	\[
	\lim_{|k| \to \infty}\mathbb{P}\left( \fdag{n} \in \mathcal{A},\ T_k\fdag{n} \in \mathcal{B}\right) = \mathbb{P}\left( \fdag{n} \in \mathcal{A} \right) \mathbb{P}\left( \fdag{n} \in \mathcal{B} \right)
	\] 
	and
	\[
	\lim_{|k| \to \infty}\mathbb{P}\left( \fdag{\infty} \in \mathcal{A},\ T_k\fdag{\infty} \in \mathcal{B}\right) = \mathbb{P}\left( \fdag{\infty} \in \mathcal{A} \right) \mathbb{P}\left( \fdag{\infty} \in \mathcal{B} \right).
	\] 
	Consequently, the distributions of $\left(\fdag{n}\right)_{n \geq 0}$ and $\fdag{\infty}$ are ergodic, w.r.t. translations $T_k,\ k \in \mathcal{H}$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:04:39.224684+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7cbb3f38cc9008fe5190d9cf358dd75d03cff1d730d6ac392c830054f5a49e49","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 14 (Asymptotics via Taylor Expansion) of arXiv:2608.14143, 'Mod-$\phi$ convergence for random variables with cyclotomic generating functions'] Let $s_N \in \N$ be a sequence of natural numbers and, for each $N\in\N$, let $(a_{N,j})_{j=1}^N$ be a sequence of natural numbers. Let $h(w, z) := \log\bigl(\frac{1-e^{zw}}{-zw}\bigr)$ for $w \neq 0$ and $h(0, z):=0$. For each $N \in \N$, set $\delta_{N,j} := a_{N,j}/s_N$. Assume that $\max_{1\le j \le N} \delta_{N,j} \to 0$ as $N\to\infty$ and that the limit
\[
\Sigma := \lim_{N\to\infty} \sum_{j=1}^N \delta_{N,j}
\]
exists in $\R$. Then, for every compact set $K\subset\C$, the sum $S_N^a(z) = \sum_{j=1}^N h(a_{N,j}/s_N, z)$ admits the asymptotic expansion
\[
S_N^a(z) = \frac{z}{2}\,\Sigma + o(1),
\]
uniformly for $z\in K$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:11:09.318259+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7cbdacd25b676b140f82796e58a9af90780315b8f74861bc26e7e26ac78c989a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma le:bounds-W-l-one-step of arXiv:2411.06195, 'Restrictions of some reinforced processes to subgraphs'] \mbox{}\\
  Consider the setup of Theorem (thm:from-r-to-l of the paper). 
  For $l\in\{1,\ldots,r\}$, $\bar e\in E_{l-1}$, and $e'\in E_l$, 
  we have
  \begin{align}
    
    &{\mathbb E}[(W^{(l-1)}_{\bar e})^\alpha]\le 2^{-\alpha}{\mathbb E}[(W^{(l)}_{e'})^\alpha]
      \quad\text{for }\alpha\in[0,1],\\
    
&{\mathbb E}[(W^{(l-1)}_{\bar e})^\alpha]\le C_\alpha {\mathbb E}[(W^{(l)}_{e'})^\alpha]^2
      \quad\text{for }\alpha\in[0,\tfrac12),\\
    
    &{\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l-1)}_{\bar e}]\le\min\{{\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l)}_{e'}]-\log 2,2{\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l)}_{e'}]+{c_2}\}
  \end{align}
  with the constants $C_\alpha$ and ${c_2}$ from Theorem (thm:from-r-to-l of the paper).
  For $\alpha\in[0,\frac12)$,

  Similarly, the minimum in bound (equation eq:bound2-exp-w-l-log of the paper) equals
  ${\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l)}_{e'}]-\log 2$ if and only if
  ${\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l)}_{e'}]\ge -\log 2-{c_2}$.
  Note that the expectations do not depend on the choice of $\bar e$ and
  $e'$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:31:49.904487+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7ce7f56019b570410fee0b7305ff9a03ccecbc909d8a5812f77745baf1f6905e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor of arXiv:2608.25065, 'Detection of first homology via random geometric graphs in the thermodynamic regime'] Fix $\lambda \in (0, \infty)$
and let $r = (\lambda/n)^{1/d}$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item If $\lambda > \lambda_c$,
    then with high probability as $n \to \infty$, the natural map $H_1(\mathcal{C}) \to H_1(M)$ is surjective.
    If $\lambda < \lambda_c$,
    with high probability
    it is the zero map.
    \item If $\lambda > \lambda_c$,
    there exists $1 \le Q' < \infty$
    such that $H_1(M) \cong H_1(\mathcal{C})/H_1^{Q' r|\log r|}(\mathcal{C})$

    \item For fixed $\lambda < \infty$,

    In this case, the natural map
    $H_1(\mathcal{C}) \to H_1(M)$ 
    is also not an isomorphism.\footnote{This last result also follows from Bobrowski [Bobrowski22].}
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.179126+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7ceb1b95c0e64951a2d9f8f4b1393598463871053d23b3f68d1d750a84d515da","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 90 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recalling \eqref{e:sM.Lip.sym} and Definitions \ref{d:SDE.classification.sym}--\ref{d:measure.classes.sym}, we have
	\[\sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha) \subseteq \sM^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0)\,.\]

\begin{proof}
Consider any $\mu \in \sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha)$, as defined by \eqref{e:sM.Lip.sym}. 
    By Lemma~\ref{l:control.problems.Lip.to.Lip.sym}, we can find $\tilde\mu \in \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha)$ with $\sym(\tilde\mu) = \mu$.
It was shown in the \hyperlink{p:thm.control.problems.main}{proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:control.problems.main}} that $\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha) = \sM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,0)$, so $\tilde\mu \in \sM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,0)$.
Therefore, for any $\epsilon>0$ we can find $L>0$ and controls 
    \beq
        
        (q_*,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising) \in \Adm^{\IAMP}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)
    \eeq
such that (recalling that $\sym$ is a contraction) we have
    \[
        \bbW_2\Big(\mu, \mu^{\sym}(q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta)\Big)
        \le\bbW_2\Big(\tilde \mu, \mu(q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta)\Big)
         \le \epsilon\,.
    \]
We see from Definitions~\ref{d:SDE.classification} and \ref{d:SDE.classification.sym}
that the sets of controls $\Adm^{\IAMP}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)$ and $\Adm^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)$ are in fact identical, so the controls \eqref{e:Lip.general.in.IAMP.sym.controls} belong to $\Adm^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)$, and 
    \[
        \mu \in \cB_\epsilon\Big(\cM^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)\Big)\,.
    \]
    Since for all $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $L > 0$ so that this holds, we conclude $\mu \in \sM^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0)$.
    As this holds for all $\mu \in \sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha)$, the claim follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.396473+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7ced2486a96ae433761fd131678f1280ad28a899958e402f6b67d559d3c08f98","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 1. dfn: BTM of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [The Bouchaud trap model] 
  Fix an electrical network $G$.
  Let $\{\xi_{x}^{G}\}_{x \in V_{G}}$ be i.i.d.\ random variables with $\xi_{x}^{G} \stackrel{\mathrm{d}}{=} \xi$.
  Set $\nu_{G} \coloneqq \sum_{x \in V_{G}} \xi_{x}^{G} \delta_{x}$,
  which is a random measure on $V_{G}$.
  Conditional on $\nu_{G}$,

{"assumptions":["H is a Hilbert space","T is a bounded linear operator on H"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.571526+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator ideals","id":"claim_7d3da9c3c18db6a4a1b175a83b3a4853fd1bc3c0008d3153ce0be80e2db8b984","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H be a Hilbert space. A bounded operator T on H is trace class (nuclear) if it is compact and ||T||_1 := sum_n s_n(T) < infinity. Equivalently: sum_i <|T| e_i, e_i> < infinity for some (hence every) orthonormal basis (e_i), where |T| = (T*T)^{1/2}, and this sum then equals ||T||_1; equivalently, T = AB with A and B Hilbert-Schmidt operators. The trace of a trace-class T is tr T = sum_i <T e_i, e_i>; this series converges absolutely for every orthonormal basis and its sum does not depend on the basis. The trace-class operators S_1(H) form a two-sided ideal of B(H) and a Banach space under ||.||_1, with ||T|| <= ||T||_2 <= ||T||_1; finite-rank operators are ||.||_1-dense in S_1(H); under the pairing (T, B) -> tr(TB), S_1(H) is isometrically the dual of the compact operators K(H) and the predual of B(H). For a positive operator T >= 0 the sum sum_i <T e_i, e_i> in [0, infinity] is basis-independent and is finite exactly when T is trace class; for operators that are not positive, convergence (even absolute convergence) of sum_i <T e_i, e_i> in one basis does not imply trace class.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:09:23.970559+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7d866816abb2b2313aa7d616a31898808b56fba17a93a631553e530e89563a86","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 3 (Anti-diagonal equilibria and stability) of arXiv:2607.22438, 'A deterministic scalar reduction for the phase transition in two interacting urns'] Let \(\alpha>1\). The point \(\left(\frac12,\frac12\right)\) is an equilibrium for every
\(p\in[0,1]\). 
If $0\le p<\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}$,
then there is a unique \(u_{\alpha,p}\in[0,1/2)\) satisfying
\begin{equation}
 u=(1-p)h(u)+\frac p2 .
\end{equation}
The corresponding off-center anti-diagonal
equilibria are exactly
\[
 (u_{\alpha,p},1-u_{\alpha,p})\text{ and }
 (1-u_{\alpha,p},u_{\alpha,p}).
\]
If $ p\ge \frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}$,
there is no off-center equilibrium on the anti-diagonal.

Furthermore, there exists a unique number
\[
 p_{\mathrm{ad},*}=p_{\mathrm{ad},*}(\alpha)
 \in\left(0,\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}\right)
\]
such that, for \(0\le p<(\alpha-1)/\alpha\),
\[
 \lambda_+(u_{\alpha,p},1-u_{\alpha,p})
 \begin{cases}
 <0, & \text{if }0\le p<p_{\mathrm{ad},*},\\
 =0, & \text{if }p=p_{\mathrm{ad},*},\\
 >0, & \text{if }p_{\mathrm{ad},*}<p<\dfrac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Consequently, the off-center anti-diagonal equilibria are asymptotically stable for
\(0\le p<p_{\mathrm{ad},*}\) and unstable for
\(p_{\mathrm{ad},*}<p<(\alpha-1)/\alpha\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Counterexample: F(p,z,x) = p_1 (equation u_x = 0), Γ = {y=0}","Noncharacteristic condition: D_pF(p0,z0,x0)·ν(x0) ≠ 0","Compatibility (admissibility): F(p0,z0,x0) = 0 and p0 agrees with the tangential gradient of g on Γ","Even when the conditions hold, the conclusion is only local in a neighbourhood of the point"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418512+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: first-order equations, method of characteristics","id":"claim_7d8c544f22ddfa6bc426587ded0c72b9450163a966ed4890aa02b90253645958","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: local solvability of F(Du,u,x) = 0 with u = g on Γ requires D_pF(p0,z0,x0)·ν(x0) ≠ 0, i.e. the characteristic direction must be transversal to the data surface; and the initial triple must be admissible (the tangential derivatives of g must match p0). If the surface is characteristic, existence can fail outright and uniqueness can fail catastrophically. Counterexample: the equation u_x = 0 in R^2 (F(p,z,x) = p_1, so D_pF = (1,0)) with data on Γ = { y = 0 }, whose normal is ν = (0,1): D_pF·ν = 0, so Γ is characteristic — indeed the characteristics are the horizontal lines y = const, which lie IN Γ. Every C^1 solution satisfies u(x,y) = u(0,y), so u(·,0) must be constant: if g is not constant there is NO solution in any neighbourhood of a point of Γ; if g ≡ c there are infinitely many solutions u(x,y) = h(y) with h ∈ C^1 arbitrary and h(0) = c. The same pathology occurs for u_t + u_x = 0 with data prescribed on the characteristic line { x = t }. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:52:08.664699+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7d8db8fd4c67bde605a9b558b98bcad5b75ed77bb6f06554007dda7f09dc8a1c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (Main theorem) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let \(M\) be a closed connected three-manifold which admits a locally
homogeneous metric modeled on one of \(\RR^3\), \(\Nil\), or \(\Sol\), and let
\(g(t)\), \(0\leq t<\infty\), be any immortal Ricci flow on \(M\).  In all
three cases, for every basepoint \(\widetilde m\in\widetilde M\) in the
universal cover, the lifted blowdown flows
\((\widetilde M,\widetilde m,s^{-1}\widetilde g(s\tau))\), \(\tau>0\),
converge as \(s\to\infty\) in the pointed Cheeger--Hamilton sense to a
homogeneous expanding Ricci soliton solution.  The compact
and lifted limits are as follows.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If \(M\) has type \(\RR^3\), then, for every \(m\geq0\), \(g(t)\)
converges exponentially fast in the \(C^m\)-norm of any fixed smooth
background metric, as \(t\to\infty\), to a flat metric on \(M\).
The Gromov--Hausdorff limit of
\((M,t^{-1}g(t))\), as \(t\to\infty\), is a point.
The limit of the lifted blowdown flows is the flat expanding soliton solution
\[
        (\RR^3,0,g_{\mathrm{Euc}}(\tau)),
        \qquad
        g_{\mathrm{Euc}}(\tau)=dx^2+dy^2+dz^2,
        \quad \tau>0.
\]
\item If \(M\) has type \(\Nil\), then the Gromov--Hausdorff limit of
\((M,t^{-1}g(t))\), as \(t\to\infty\), is a point.  The limit of the lifted blowdown flows is the Nil
expanding soliton solution
\[
        \left(\RR^3,0,
        \frac{1}{3\tau^{1/3}}
        \left(dx+\frac12 y\,dz-\frac12 z\,dy\right)^2
        +\tau^{1/3}(dy^2+dz^2)
        \right).
\]
\item If \(M\) has type \(\Sol\), then the Gromov--Hausdorff limit of
\((M,t^{-1}g(t))\), as \(t\to\infty\), is a metric circle or a compact
interval of positive length.  The limit of the lifted blowdown flows is the Sol expanding soliton solution
\[
        \left(\RR^3,0,e^{-2z}dx^2+e^{2z}dy^2+4\tau\,dz^2\right).
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.424632+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7d922fc74e165300d4137e2753b638ed7631e6a80e9f43ecedeb9ceeee2e31a4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem eq:bounded-block-max of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[theorem]{thm:bounded-block-counterexample}
Fix \(p\ge3\) and an integer \(r\ge2\).  There is a symmetric,
compactly supported probability law \(\mu\) with a \(C^\infty\) density
such that
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2em]
\item \(\mu\) matches the standard Gaussian moments through order \(r\)
(hence is centered and has variance one);
\item for i.i.d.\ ordered-tensor entries with common law \(\mu\), there
is a compact interval \(B\subset(0,\infty)\) for which
\begin{align}
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log
 \mathbb E_\mu\operatorname{Crt}_{N,\max}^J(B)
 &>\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Crt}_{N,\max}^G(B),\\
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log
 \mathbb E_\mu\operatorname{Crt}_N^J(B)
 &>\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Crt}_N^G(B).
\end{align}
The reflected local-minimum inequality holds on \(-B\).
\end{enumerate}
In particular, for every fixed \(\varepsilon\in[0,1/2)\),
\begin{equation}
 \max_{I\in[N]^p}|J_I|\le N^{1/2-\varepsilon}
 \qquad\text{almost surely for all sufficiently large \(N\)}.
\end{equation}
Thus an \(N^{1/2-\varepsilon}\) entrywise cutoff, or even an
 \(N\)-independent entry bound, does not restore universality of the
 unregularized annealed count.  The obstruction in this theorem is a
 coherent block involving on the order of \(N^{1/p}\) coordinates,
 rather than a single quadratic-scale entry. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:56:17.352496+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7dc8d5560e962181bc027758d37b6bf2ab9eb94d14f988ed537bf73a53b9c014","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:TASEPcp of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] For each $\alpha>0$ and $d\in \mathbb{N}$, we defined the \textbf{$d$-coupling} of half-space TASEPs with boundary parameter $\alpha$, as follows.

        Take the Poisson process $\Pi$, and view this as a collection of Poisson clocks on $\Lambda_d$. These clocks generate half-space TASEPs as follows.
        Let $\pi:\{(x,a)\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\times \mathbb{Z}, x+a\in 2\mathbb{Z}\} \to \Lambda_d$ be the projection map.
        Recall that we can define half-space TASEP as a Markov process $(h_t: t\ge 0)$ on the state space $\SRW_+$ (from (equation eq:defSRW+ of the paper)). 
        We flip $h_t(i) \mapsto h_t(i) + 2$ according to the Poisson clock at the vertex $\pi(i, h_t(i))$. In words, there is a flip $h_{t}(i)= h_{t-}(i)+2$ if and only if the Poisson clock at $\pi(i, h_t(i))$ rings at times $t$, and $h_t(j)=h_{t-}(i)+1$ for $j\in \{i-1, i+1\}\cap \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$.

        By using the same set of Poisson clocks, we get a coupling of half-space TASEPs with boundary parameter $\alpha$, started from all initial configurations and all times.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:31:20.880849+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7dcb93c91b72dbbc704681fcb49b1f1be63d1effc3db4273f0d92be16d174472","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 17 of arXiv:2506.11707, 'Fluctuations of two-dimensional determinantal processes associated with Berezin--Toeplitz '] Let $\delta>0$ and, for $j\in\{1,2\}$, let $\chi_j : \C \to[0,1]$ be smooth functions such that 
\[
\1\{V\le \mu-\delta\} \le \chi_2 \le \1\{V\le \mu-\tfrac12\delta\}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\1\{|V- \mu| \le 2\delta\}\le  \chi_1 \le \1\{|V- \mu| \le 3\delta\}.
\]
Let $f : \C \to \R$ be a smooth bounded function, and let ${\rm f}_j:= f \chi_j$ for $j\in\{1,2,3\}$ where \[\chi_3 :=(\chi_1+\chi_2-1)\1\{V<\mu\}.\] 
Then, for every $\alpha>0$,
\[\begin{aligned}
\Upsilon(f;\Pi_N) = \Upsilon({\rm f}_1;\Pi_N)+ \Upsilon({\rm f}_2;\Pi_N) - \Upsilon({\rm f}_3;\Pi_N) + \O(e^{-\alpha \sqrt{N}}). 
\end{aligned}\]
By construction, ${\rm f}_1 ,{\rm f}_3$ are smooth, supported in the bulk $\{V\le \mu-\tfrac12\delta\} $, and ${\rm f}_2$ is smooth, supported in a neighborhood of the boundary $\{|V- \mu| \le 3\delta\}$.","status":"unverified"}

Let $\vX\equiv \vX^N$ be the process defined by \eqref{e:X.decomp}

	\[
	\E'\Big[\|\vX(1)-\vX^\trstar(1)\|^2\Big]
	\le O(\epsilon) + o_{\trK}(1)\,,
	\]
uniformly in $N$.

\begin{proof} 
For $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$ we have $X^{\trstar,\sigma}(1,a)=X^\sigma(\tau(a),a)$, with $\tau$ the stopping time defined by \eqref{e:trstar.stopping.time}. It follows that, for $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$, we have
	\[
	\E'\Big[( X^\sigma(1)-X^{\trstar,\sigma}(1))^2\Big]
	\le O(1)
	\E'\bigg[
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	X^\sigma(q_d)^2;\tau<1\bigg] 
	\le O(\epsilon) +o_{\trK}(1)\,,
	\]
where the last bound is by Proposition~\ref{p:max.X.process.on.trstar.stopped.event}. Similarly,
	\[
	\E'\Big[( X^\Ising(1)-X^{\trstar,\Ising}(1))^2\Big]
	\le O(1)
	\E'\bigg[
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	X^\Ising(q_d)^2;\tau^\Ising<1\bigg] 
	\le o_{\trK}(1)\,,
	\]
again by Proposition~\ref{p:max.X.process.on.trstar.stopped.event}. The conclusion follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:49:05.348709+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7def1206eddf00c91658d97780b1ffab0fee35eaf0bb4911c71e3ea1841c7d20","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition defn:no-underrun of arXiv:2601.07045, 'From Continuous to Discrete: \\ a No-U-Turn Sampler for Permutations'] Let $\mathcal{O} = (\sigma \circ \rho^k)_{k = a}^{b}$ be an orbit indexed by
consecutive integers from $a$ to $b$, and let $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$.
We say that $\mathcal{O}$ satisfies the \emph{no--underrun condition},
denoted $\textsc{Stop}(\mathcal{O},\varepsilon,w)$, if
\[
\max \!\left\{ w(\sigma \circ \rho^{a}),\, w(\sigma \circ \rho^{b}) \right\}
\;\le\;
\varepsilon \sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{O}} w(\tau).
\]
Equivalently, the combined weight at the two boundary points of the orbit
accounts for at most an $\varepsilon$ fraction of the total weight accumulated
along $\mathcal{O}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:18:54.372086+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7e0786242cae037154dde86085a7965ebe039fcbada5c7994298c08bdcafb103","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The orthogonal polynomials for $L^2[-1,1]$, with measure

$$(1-x^2)P_k''(x)+(b-a-(a+b+2)x)P_k'(x)+k(k+a+b+1)P_k(x)=0$$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:07:17.249588+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7e083884be832f46cce336a829a5c3bbb9a3bd4adca8daaa024694c1282c7fdc","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:backoff of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix a send sequence
$\newsym{p}{send sequence, Def~(def:backoff of the paper)}{\overline{p} = (p_0,p_1,p_2,\ldots)}$  and a birth rate 
$\newsym{lambda}{birth rate, Def~(def:backoff of the paper)}{\lambda}>0$. Each~$p_k$   is  a real number in~$(0,1]$.   $W_k$   denotes~$1/p_k$.
The \emph{backoff process} $X$
with send sequence~$\overline{p}$ and birth rate~$\lambda$ is defined as follows.
For each $i\geq 0$ and $t\geq 1$, 
$\mathbf{b}^X_i(t)$~is the set of balls that  collide exactly $i$ times during steps $1,\ldots,t$. 
The process starts from the empty state, so  
for each~$i\geq 0$, 
$\mathbf{b}^X_i(0) = \emptyset$.
For each $t\geq 1$, $\mathbf{n}^X(t)$ is the set of balls that are born at time~$t$. Its size is given by $n^X(t)$,  which 
is a Poisson random variable with mean~$\lambda$.
After the births, but just
before the sends at step~$t$, the bin populations are defined as follows.
$\mathbf{B}^X_0(t) = \mathbf{n}^X(t) \cup \mathbf{b}^X_0(t-1)$. For every $i\geq 1$, $\mathbf{B}^X_i(t) = \mathbf{b}^X_i(t-1)$.  
For every $i\geq 0$, the set of balls that send from bin~$i$ at time~$t$,  {$\mathbf{s}^X_i(t)$}, is
formed by including each ball from $\mathbf{B}^X_i(t)$ independently with probability~$p_i$.  The
set of balls that escape from bin~$i$ at time~$t$,  $\mathbf{e}^X_i(t)$, is equal to $\mathbf{s}^X_i(t)$ if 
$|\mathbf{s}_i^X(t)| = |\cup_{k\geq 0} \mathbf{s}_k^X(t)| = 1$. Otherwise,
$\mathbf{e}^X_i(t) =  \emptyset$.
Finally, $\mathbf{b}_0^X(t) = \mathbf{B}_0^X(t) \setminus \mathbf{s}_0^X(t)$ and for all  $i\geq 1$,
$\mathbf{b}_i^X(t) = (\mathbf{B}_i^X(t) \setminus \mathbf{s}_i^X(t)) \cup (\mathbf{s}^X_{i-1}(t) \setminus \mathbf{e}^X_{i-1}(t))$.
For every variable $\mathbf{b}^X_i(t)$, $\mathbf{B}^X_i(t)$, $\mathbf{s}^X_i(t)$, and $\mathbf{e}^X_i(t)$, the roman (non-bold-face) version represents its size, so, for example, $b^X_i(t) = |\mathbf{b}^X_i(t)|$.","status":"unverified"}
